10990-selected-speeches-on-british-forei:
Edgar R. Jones, MP, edited this 1914 anthology of British foreign policy speeches, spanning 1738 to 1914. Chatham opens with a 1738 speech on the convention with Spain, followed by Sheridan on the partition of Poland, Pitt on peace overtures to France, and Canning on Spain. Peel, Russell, Palmerston, and Brougham carry the story through Belgium, Cracow, and Italy.

Later speakers include Bright on principles of foreign policy, Gladstone on Belgian neutrality and Russian expansion, and Disraeli on Denmark and Germany. Each speech is dated and placed in Commons or Lords. The collection lets readers hear two centuries of debate on war, empire, and Europe, in the orators' own words, and it serves as a compact history of British diplomacy.
11219-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The August 8, 1829 Mirror opens at Ferney, Voltaire's château six miles from Geneva. where the philosopher lived for twenty years before leaving in his eighty-fourth year for a short triumph and death in Paris in 1778. The article describes the house as travelers found it around 1800, with Voltaire's bedroom shown as he left it, and recalls earlier Mirror descriptions of the place. Shorter items include the marriage of Lady Jane Grey and the death of Murat.

Ferney serves as the issue's anchor, a place where literary fame and domestic routine meet. The surrounding miscellany, from portraits to natural history, keeps the weekly's pace brisk. Readers get a sense of how Voltaire's reputation was kept alive for English readers a half century after his death.
11222-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This October 24, 1829 Mirror leads with the original Royal Exchange, tracing London merchants from their benches in Lombard Street among the Lombard bankers to Sir Thomas Gresham's covered Exchange of 1566. Richard Gresham's failed 1534 proposal under Henry VIII, inspired by the Antwerp Bourse, sets up his son's success under Elizabeth. The article explains how covered walks let merchants trade in all weather.

Shorter pieces on sonnets, Jersey, and St. Sepulchre's bell fill the rest of the sheet. The Exchange history is the issue's substance, connecting a familiar City building to Tudor trade policy. For readers of London history, it offers a compact, contemporary account of a landmark's origins.
11233-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, July 4, 1829, this weekly number opens a new volume of the Mirror with a proud note about its fresh type and an engraved view of Milan Cathedral. The cathedral piece praises the building's white marble, clustered pillars, and forest of statues, ranking it beside St. Peter's and St. Paul's. Shorter pieces follow on rustic amusements, poetry, and curious facts.

As a whole the issue shows how a cheap twopenny weekly fed curious readers in 1829: pictures, travel notes, verse, and snippets of history in a few pages. Nothing here is deep, and that is the point. The number preserves the browsing habits of ordinary readers, moving briskly from architecture to anecdote.
11234-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated November 7, 1829, this Mirror number opens with Burleigh House in Northamptonshire, seat of the Cecil family and property of the Marquess of Exeter. The article traces the mansion to William Cecil, Baron Burleigh, noting the 1577 inscription. additions of 1585 and 1587, and a park, lake, great hall, and collection of art that made it a show-house. Later possessors' alterations are also recorded.

The rest of the sheet follows the weekly's pattern of pictures, anecdotes, and short essays for twopence. Burleigh anchors the number because it joins architecture with Elizabethan politics, letting readers tour a great house through print. For local historians, the description preserves the house as early nineteenth-century visitors saw it.
11235-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplementary number of the Mirror, numbered 399, offers a survey of the illustrated gift annuals for 1830, the small decorated volumes readers bought as presents. It opens with an engraving of Verona after Bonington, praising the city's towers, the Maffei Palace, and the Adige winding past vineyards and cypress groves. Other annuals are sampled in turn, with pictures and short sketches.

The issue captures a particular Regency fashion: literature as a pretty object, meant to be given at New Year. Its tone is light and admiring, and its value now is documentary. Readers see which pictures and verses publishers thought would sell, and how a weekly magazine marketed the year's prettiest books.
11245-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The October 10, 1829 number of the Mirror leads with Glammis Castle in Strathmore, a castellated palace tied to Malcolm II, Macbeth legend, and the Strathmore family. The article weighs rival claims about where Duncan was murdered, citing Scott, Boethius, and Fordun, and describes walls fifteen feet thick and a spiral stair of 143 steps. Shorter items on London localities, sleep, and Peruvian pastoral life follow.

This number shows the Mirror at its most characteristic: a famous place, a historical dispute handled lightly, and miscellany to fill the sheet. Readers interested in how Scots history reached English breakfast tables will find it instructive. The castle engraving, now lost in plain text, once anchored the whole issue.
11246-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The October 17, 1829 Mirror leads with Lord Grosvenor's gallery in Park Lane, the western wing of his town mansion. designed by Cundy with a Corinthian colonnade, statues, and swags of fruit and flowers. The article praises Earl Grosvenor's patronage of the fine arts, recalling Eaton Hall, while quoting critic Mr. Elmes on stopped-up windows and an overpowering balustrade that keep the building from ranking first in the metropolis.

The gallery was built to house the Grosvenor collection, one of Britain's great private holdings. Shorter items fill the rest of the number. The piece shows the Mirror doing cultural reporting for readers who would never enter Park Lane, describing art architecture in plain, opinionated prose.
11258-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated December 24, 1829, this closing number of the Mirror's fourteenth volume opens with the volume title page, listing its contents. Original essays, historical narratives, biographical memoirs, sketches of society, topographical descriptions, novels and tales, poetry, and useful domestic hints, printed by J. Limbird at 143 Strand. The main piece is a memoir of Thomas Campbell, with his portrait engraved on steel.

Campbell is praised as the Tyrtaeus of modern English poetry, a chaste and tender writer whose war odes matched few in English for energy and fire. The memoir follows him from Glasgow studies and Argyleshire wanderings to fame, and prints his Dirge of Wallace. An index to the whole volume and a list of engravings close the number, making it a useful key to the volume.
11332-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The July 18, 1829 Mirror leads with Apsley House, the Duke of Wellington's mansion at Hyde Park Corner, newly encased in a fine stone front by Benjamin Wyatt in the Palladian style. The article first laments London noblemen's plain brick houses, then praises Apsley: a rusticated basement. a pediment on four Corinthian columns, a bold cornice, Corinthian pilasters, and a bronzed palisade on Piccadilly, with Grecian honeysuckle throughout. Door and window cases seem rather too small.

The renovation marks architecture's move from public buildings to private mansions. Shorter items follow. For Wellington enthusiasts, the number preserves Apsley as contemporaries saw it, fresh from Wyatt's improvements and already a London landmark.
11411-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The September 19, 1829 Mirror leads with Clifton, called the Montpellier of England, a mile west of Bristol on cliffs above the winding Avon. The article praises Clifton's airy rocks, picturesque Somerset shore, cottage comforts, and splendid crescents and terraces reared on the brow, with. Dundry Hill's tower serving as a weather prophet, misty before rain and clear before fine weather. Wealthy visitors, drawn by salubrity, have nearly turned the village into an elegant city.

Downs covered with verdure and aromatic turf complete the health-resort picture. Shorter items follow. For Bristol historians, the number preserves Clifton at its fashionable peak, before the suspension bridge changed its skyline.
11433-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The November 14, 1829 Mirror turns from castles and cathedrals to curiosities of nature, with engravings of the praying mantis, or walking leaf, and a branched starfish. The mantis, a species of cricket in the Hemiptera order, is described from Blumenbach's four varieties: gigantic from Amboyna, gonglyodes from Guinea, religious mantis, and a Cape variety sacred to Hottentots. It walks on four legs, holding two shorter ones up, and resembles a dry willow leaf.

The article argues nature's economy surpasses art's sumptuous productions. Shorter items follow. For natural-history readers, the number shows popular science in 1829, curious, systematic, and fond of strange resemblances.
11442-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The December 19, 1829 Mirror leads with new buildings at the Inner Temple, part of an immense range from Fleet Street to the Thames and Lombard Street to Essex Street. The Temple takes its name from the Knights Templars' principal English establishment, where Henry III, the Pope's nuncio, and ambassadors were entertained, and the king's treasure kept in the Middle Temple. After suppression, common lawyers bought the buildings, converting them into Inns of Court, Inner and Middle Temple.

The hall and chapel, repaired in 1819, form the nucleus, with unsightly brick buildings along a terrace to the south. Shorter items follow. For legal historians, the number gives the Temple's topography and history in a compact weekly form.
11446-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The November 21, 1829 Mirror leads with the Limoeiro, Lisbon's common jail, described lightly in outline since nothing is more disagreeable than filling in its horrors. Mr. W. Young, an Englishman married in Leiria, supplies the account: arrested in May 1828 on suspicion of disaffection to Don Miguel, suffering in Leiria and Lisbon jails. discharged the following September on condition of leaving Portugal, he published Portugal in 1828 with his narrative as a state prisoner.

Locks, bolts, and bars head the piece, with Don Miguel's shadow over it. Shorter items follow. For Portuguese historians, the number preserves an English victim's testimony during Miguel's repression, reported while events were fresh.
11447-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The November 28, 1829 Mirror leads with the Siamese Twins, an accurate sketch of an extraordinary lusus naturae already exciting curiosity among scientific and sight-loving ranks. The earliest account, by Dr. I. C. Warren of Boston in Silliman's Journal, tells how Captain Coffin and Mr. Hunter received the boys from their mother in a Siamese village, where Hunter saw them fishing. Their father dead, they lived with their mother in poverty, confined by government order, supporting themselves by fishing.

The article insists their appearance raises no unpleasant emotion, fitting the Mirror's pages. Their exhibition to the world was suggested to their guardians. Shorter items follow. For historians of medicine and spectacle, the number records Chang and Eng's arrival in Western print.
11455-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The August 15, 1829 Mirror leads with Hampton Court, from a bird's-eye view copied from Kipp's Views in Great Britain in Queen Anne's time, showing the palace in olden splendour. Built magnificently by Cardinal Wolsey on the Thames two miles west of Kingston, the palace excited envy. In 1526 Wolsey gave it to Henry VIII, receiving license to lie at Richmond instead. In 1527 French ambassadors were entertained there with surpassing splendour, Cavendish detailing carpenters, joiners, and masons at work.

The article follows Stow and Cavendish for its history. Shorter items follow. For Tudor historians, the number offers Hampton Court as Wolsey built it, before later alterations, seen through an early engraving.
11456-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The October 3, 1829 Mirror leads with the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Gardens, built in 1671 about a century after theatres were regularly established in England. in what the article calls the brazen age of drama, when Puritan prosecutions had ceased and legitimacy and licentiousness danced hand in hand. Restoration players under Davenant at the Red Bull and Rhodes's Cockpit company, with Betterton and Kynaston as stars. united as the Duke's Company, moving to Wren's Dorset Gardens theatre on November 9, 1671.

Shorter pieces include four sonnets on the seasons, exercise, air, and sleep, an incident at Fondi, and pieces on liberty. The theatre history anchors the number. For Restoration scholars, it gives a compact account of companies, patents, and playhouses.
11457-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplementary Mirror number for 1829 reviews the Landscape Annual, London and Paris, 1830. subtitled The Tourist in Italy and Switzerland, with twenty-five plates from drawings by Prout and descriptions by Thomas Roscoe. Subjects run from Geneva, Lausanne, Chillon, and the Bridge of St. Maurice through Milan Cathedral, Lake Como, Verona, Padua, Petrarch's house at Arqua, the Rialto and Ducal Palace at Venice, to Bologna, Rome, and Constantine's Arch. A Bologna plate is selected for reproduction.

The article quotes Parisian exclamations, magnifique and superbe, for plates shown in the Galerie Vivienne and Cheapside alike. Bologna, mother of studies, celebrated in arts and letters, anchors the sample. For print collectors, the number surveys a fashionable annual at the height of its appeal.
11458-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The December 5, 1829 Mirror leads with the Fall of the Staubbach in Lauterbrun valley. Switzerland's most picturesque district, described from Simond's ascent beside the Lutschine torrent among rock fragments and beautiful trees. The article argues poets, philosophers, and lovers of the sublime feel ecstatic admiration and awe before such a scene, while the mere man of the world. clogged with commonplaces, is overwhelmed as by the torrent itself, recovering soon, unlike nature's lover who reads infinite wisdom in falls.

Shorter pieces on psalmody, a thief, Shakespeare, an infant, and a wreck on a coral reef follow, with a sketch-book column. The Staubbach piece is pure romantic nature writing. For Alpine readers, it preserves the fall as early tourists saw it, before railways eased the valley.
11459-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The October 31, 1829 Mirror leads with Blarney Castle, four miles northwest of Cork, described from T. Crofton Croker's Researches in the South of Ireland. Croker recalls a thriving manufacturing village in 1815, neat cottages around a green shaded by fine old trees, now roofless cottages, felled trees, and barley ripening in the square by 1821. The castle grounds, though timber has been cut, remain beautiful, rock and water defying neglect.

The massive square castle anchors the piece, its blarney associations acknowledged with a wink. Shorter items follow. For Irish readers, the number preserves Blarney at a moment of decay, before tourism restored its fortunes.
11460-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 26 December 1829, priced at twopence, begins at Virgil's tomb on Posilipo hill near Naples. The small square building has a flat roof and stands on a platform at a cliff edge. An old ilex spreads from the rock above and covers the roof with evergreen leaves. Shrubs and ivy clothe the walls and hang in festoons over the precipice below.

The writer follows Eustace up a winding street and through a vineyard to reach the tomb. Short pieces follow in the same weekly pattern throughout the number. They cover books, pastimes, printing, and curious facts for a general reader. A reader could take in the whole sheet in one sitting, and learn a little about many subjects at once.
11462-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 25 July 1829, priced at twopence, sends its reader out of town in search of the picturesque to Hagley Park. Lyttleton, Pope, Shenstone, and Thomson are called to mind there, and Thomson's Spring is quoted at length. Woods overhang the dale, mossy rocks line the way, and gushing waters play along the valley.

Other short items turn to building and craft in the same number. Roman stone roofs made with pumice and cement are one subject, with Bonomi quoted on fires in large buildings. The mix is typical of the weekly magazine. A scenic walk comes first, then useful notes, odd facts, and short essays for a reader at leisure.
11463-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The December 12, 1829 Mirror leads with the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, timely in almanack season as the spot whence English astronomers make calculations. Built by Charles II in 1675, possibly to imitate Louis XIV's Paris observatory, it was placed under Flamsteed. appointed astronomer-royal in 1676, who worked with instruments largely at his own expense and patron James Moore's. The Quarterly Review notes Britain has only one observatory, Greenwich, scarcely government-supported.

Flamsteed's hill still bears his name. The article treats parsimony as hereditary in English government. Shorter items follow. For astronomy historians, the number gives Greenwich's early struggles in a popular weekly's plain prose.
11516-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 11 July 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Mercers' Hall in Cheapside, an engraving of seventeenth-century London. Mercers once gathered in West Cheap, called the Mercery, and Lydgate's London Lyckpenny lists velvet, silk, and lawn offered there.

Pennant's history of the spot follows, with the Hospital of St. Thomas of Acon on the north side of Cheapside, founded by Thomas Fitz-Theobald and his wife Agnes, sister of Thomas Becket. A later tale of a youth reaching London with nine shillings and seven pence keeps the number's mix of place and story.
11518-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 29 August 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Constantinople, called the queen of the morning and sultana of the East. The engraving runs from Seraglio Point to the Janissaries' Tower, taking in the domes of Santa Sophia and Sultan Achmet among towers, palaces, and minarets.

The writer notes the city's seat-of-war interest and its claim to fit dominion over the whole world. A later story in the same number turns to a butcher's daughter scorned by her sisters-in-law, showing the weekly blend of a grand view with social comedy.
11519-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The August 1, 1829 Mirror leads with Tunbridge Wells in 1748, from a drawing once owned by Samuel Richardson and found among his papers at his death in 1761. The engraving's characters include Dr. Johnson, Bishop Gilbert, Lord Harcourt, Colley Cibber, Garrick, Mrs. Frasi, Beau Nash, Miss Chudleigh, Pitt, Speaker Onslow, Lord Powis, Lyttleton, a German gamester, and Richardson himself. Tunbridge, second only to Bath in its best days, was a gay, anecdotal resort, unlike today's fashionable haunts.

The article contrasts the Wells with Brighton, once a fishified village called Brighthelmstone. Shorter pieces on Humphry Davy, soda water, and sisters of charity follow. For spa historians, the number revives Tunbridge's eighteenth-century sociability in a single crowded print.
12063-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Number 388 of The Mirror, dated Saturday, September 5, 1829, opens with St. Dunstan's, Fleet Street, illustrated from the church in the West. The editor notes that no church in London is perhaps better known, and that its celebrity owes little to external elegance.

Fame came instead from the two wooden figures placed on a pediment, the clockwork giants that struck the hours and drew crowds in Fleet Street. The article's blend of topography, illustration, and London lore typifies the twopenny magazine: a famous sight explained briefly, for readers who might pass it the next day.
12214-admiral-peters-odd-craft-part-14:
George Burton, a naval pensioner dozing at his seaside lodgings, meets an old shipmate he barely knows in Admiral Peters, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. Joe Stiles, shaven and handsome, claims rank and glory Burton remembers differently.

Stiles courts a widow with tales of standing alone under fire at the bombardment of Alexandria, while Burton, who says he stood just behind him, is ordered to hold his tongue. The joke turns on stolen valor: a man who borrows another record for love and pension. Jacobs lets the widow, the pensioner, and the pretender play out a small war of memory. The story is a gentle fraud tale, where the past itself becomes disputed property.
12294-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch for January 7, 1914, volume one hundred forty-six, opens the new year with a cartoon. The monarch of the glen appears redone as a Landseer, beside a verse of New Year repentance. The speaker confesses sloth and procrastination as the clock ticks.

Inside, a paper chase piece follows a frosty afternoon walk home before tea, and political cartoons cast Lloyd George as Malvolio, notoriously abused. The number looks back at 1913 and forward to an election year, with jokes on ministers, manners, and money. It captures Punch on the eve of war: still witty, still political, unaware that the year would break its world. For historians, the ordinary jokes are the point.
12465-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
This 21 January 1914 number of Punch, the London comic weekly, mixes jokes, cartoons and short satire on the news of the week. Its Charivaria column pokes fun at an American general's plea for guns, at Ulster politics and at the Zabern affair in Alsace. It also runs a golf joke: even earthquakes can improve the links.

Cartoons, verses and mock letters fill out the issue in Punch's familiar style, teasing public men and manners without sparing any party. The number captures Britain on the eve of war, confident, amused and quarrelsome in print. As a weekly record it is best read for tone: what London laughed at, and what it took seriously enough to mock.
12536-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch's 14 January 1914 number opens with Charivaria, short jokes on the week's news. The Chancellor, in North Africa, studies camels to learn the last straw that breaks their backs. Lloyd George, it is denied, has dropped precautions against Suffragettes to prove his faith in disarmament.

Turkey's purchase of the dreadnought Rio de Janeiro for over two million pounds prompts a joke: surely the Turks will not risk so costly a ship in war. Cartoons, verses and mock letters follow in Punch's usual mix. The issue captures pre-war London humour, topical, confident and fond of puncturing ministers.
13359-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction for September 26, 1829, mixes invention, books, and stage history in a cheap weekly number. Its lead piece shows Gurney's improved steam carriage, whose boiler was split into forty welded iron pipes to divide the danger of high pressure steam.

Other pages review new books with a note that half a volume of good reading beats a whole volume of padding. They explain Roman theatre fronts, where bow-like projections let separate parties share a stage without seeing each other. At two pence, the Mirror gave ordinary readers pictures, science, and polite learning in a single Saturday sheet.
14011-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A September 1829 number of the same two-penny weekly opens on the Thames at Sion House, praising its white towers and river front. From London scenery it wanders to Paris, where a writer collects tales of pickpockets and their tricks. One thief steals a purse under a portico and coolly asks for a theatre ticket with the victim's own coin.

Theatre gossip closes the run. A manager apologizes to a restless crowd for a missing star, only to spot the actor himself in a stage box. Short, chatty, and fond of odd facts, the issue suits readers who wanted a little of everything. A great house, a foreign city, and a night at the play all fit inside a few pages.
14101-dew-drops-vol-37-no-10-march-8-191:
Francie Fisher's fish leads the March 8, 1914, Dew Drops. On a Primary Room wall hangs a river picture, and each of fourteen fish stands for a new scholar someone brought to class. Francie, a Fisher boy, longs to catch one fish himself and earn a red tag from Miss Florence. A new family moving in gives him hope.

Betty's kindness and a Lapland winter fill the rest. Betty promises to call for Robbie each morning, then must choose between a cousin's sleepover and her pledge. Farther north, Lapp parents drive reindeer sleighs ten or fifteen miles to church, then bed their babies in snow outside while they worship. Twenty or thirty infants may lie buried in snow around a church, warm in skins and safe. Gentle morals and far places share the weekly page.
14111-dew-drops-vol-37-no-15-april-12-19:
Dated April 12, 1914, this weekly children's paper from Elgin, Illinois, offers Easter stories, verses, and short moral tales. Julia H. Johnson's opening story finds Myra crying because her mother cannot finish a white Easter dress. Neighbors, small gifts, and kind words soften the loss, and the lesson lands gently rather than by scolding.

Playful pieces balance the sober ones. A runaway umbrella, blown by a mischievous south wind, chases a four-year-old girl through town. A jasmine plant becomes a lesson in cheering a sick mother, and a watchdog named Berry guards an electric plant by night. Short, clean, and meant for Sunday reading, the number shows what editors offered children a century ago: faith, fun, and good temper in small doses.
14116-dew-drops-vol-37-no-07-february-15:
February 15, 1914, brought a Dew Drops number full of valentines. May G. Mooar's Arthur, given paints at Christmas, decides to paint his own valentines instead of buying them. He nearly spills yellow paint on a Japanese lady's pink dress in his excitement, then tells his mother his plan. Handmade flowers may fall short of Aunt Frances's, he admits, but they will mean more.

Mothers, ponies, and sweethearts fill the rest. Mrs. Forbes sends valentines every February 14 and teaches Davie that love day belongs to more than sweethearts. Harold's Shetland pony, decked in roses for a parade, wins prize money that Harold spends on a screen window for the pony's stall, to keep flies away. Flo wonders where to send her valentine to her dearest friend. Kindness, craft, and small gifts make the weekly theme.
14138-dew-drops-vol-37-no-18-may-3-1914:
Elizabeth Noyes's Singing Heart leads the May 3, 1914, Dew Drops. Francis pouts at rain that spoils his outdoor games, while his mother sews at her machine. He hums along with the machine, louder and louder, until a robin's song joins the household music. A warm May afternoon, flowers stretching for rain, and a lonely boy's invention make the story.

Guilt, kindness, and natural history fill the rest. Minnie lies awake while her clock ticks I know, I know, and a parrot cries Polly did, exposing a secret she would hide. Kitty's anger melts when Miss Maggie offers a rose and sweet words, and Emma finds a happy sister at home. A Knowledge Box note names the Australian duckbill Tambreet, Tohunbuck, and Malingong. Small morals, told gently, make the weekly whole.
14147-dew-drops-vol-37-no-34-august-23-1:
Helen Hawley's Billikens' Surprise leads the August 23, 1914, Dew Drops. Gilbert, a little boy, travels to Branton with father and mother for his first suit of clothes not made at home. An event indeed, the story agrees, and fitting-out becomes a small adventure in growing up. City shops, careful parents, and a proud boy fill the opening pages.

Wishes, fears, and a baby's name follow. Helen I. Castella's verses weigh duck, hen, guinea, squirrel, and rabbit lives, then settle on a goose, since fretting wastes time. Jean names a new baby Daisy, ready and waiting. Chalmers invents Biters, horned and growling fears, until a real animal show camps behind his father's orchard and leaves a wagon behind. Made-up terrors fade beside real tents, lions, and wagons, and childhood courage grows.
14148-dew-drops-vol-37-no-08-february-22:
February 22, 1914, brought another weekly Dew Drops, edited by George E. Cook in Elgin, Illinois. Julia H. Johnston's opening piece, Doing and Being, answers little girls who think they cannot help anyone. A teacher shows Grace Mayne and her class that small kindnesses count, and the lesson unfolds in gentle dialogue rather than lecture.

Stories and verses fill the rest. Poor Harry, shabby but courteous, gives up a streetcar seat and picks up a woman's gloves, earning the name of gentleman. Ralph, Emma, and little Paul sit among toys that please nobody until play turns kind. Leslie acts out Little Red Riding Hood with Granny Graham, trading oranges for kisses. Sweet, plain, and Sunday-safe, the number teaches children that manners and mercy begin at home.
14180-dew-drops-vol-37-no-17-april-26-19:
Margaret E. Hays's Among the Rocks leads the April 26, 1914, Dew Drops. Toby and his twin Nancy, red curls under a sunbonnet, paddle at low tide toward dark rocks in still water. Ships must have wrecked there, Nancy guesses, and treasure may wait. They hurry on until water rises above their knees and Toby lays a hand on rock, finding no wrecks but plenty of adventure.

Grandmothers and rabbits fill the rest. Eloise, dressed in her best with a small valise, boards a train to visit a grandmother Marjorie never knew she had, to Marjorie's dismay. Pauline Randall builds rabbits a big dry-goods box house with a wire yard, shaming John into clearing weeds, rubbish, and tin cans for his own pets. Friendship grows from shared work, and April, the verses add, opens doors for toads, grasshoppers, and bumblebees alike.
14283-dew-drops-vol-37-no-16-april-19-19:
April 19, 1914, brought a Dew Drops number led by Mary Gilbert's Syrup-Can Mother. Dorothy Deane and little Laurence watch for papa, race to the corner, and guess at his dinner pail: candy, oranges, and more, until mamma takes her turn. A nickel rewards the right guess, and family fun fills the opening pages with chubby legs and eager questions.

Fairies, washday, and a shocked kitten follow. Maisie finds a boy who lost his father's pocketbook after driving ten sheep to market. She teaches him a fairy rhyme, and the pocketbook appears within six inches of his hand, money all there. A washday fantasy calls spider webs fairy baby clothes drying in sun. A black Persian kitten with white mittens, boots, nose, and shirt front meets a shock in Miss Mary's rooms. Gentle wonder and household cheer make the weekly whole.
15494-dew-drops-vol-37-no-09-march-1-191:
David C. Cook published this weekly children's paper, Dew Drops, in Elgin, Illinois, edited by George E. Cook. This number, volume thirty-seven, number nine, is dated March 1, 1914. Its opening story, by Julia H. Johnston, is How Lilian Helped Her Brother, a short moral tale for young readers.

Lilian and her brother Earl beg to attend a children's lawn party, but their mother fears for Earl, weak after illness and forbidden ice-cold food and drink. Lilian pledges herself as surety for her brother, promising he will keep his word amid ice cream, berries, cake, and lemonade. The tale teaches keeping promises under temptation, in the gentle, direct manner of Sunday-school papers of the day.
16107-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for January 14, 1920, volume one hundred fifty-eight, opens its Charivaria column with the prime minister's new white terrier puppy from Colwyn Bay. Malice, the joke adds, claims Lloyd George himself taught it to chase its own tail. A tenant of an experimental wooden house advertises for the man who held up a London post office, and a London carman earns a quip of his own.

The rest of the weekly would mix cartoons, verses, and satire on postwar Britain, from housing to politics. Punch's humor is brisk, topical, and fond of puncturing the great. Readers can enjoy this number as a funny, compact record of London life in the first weeks of 1920.
18004-told-in-a-french-garden-august-191:
Mildred Aldrich wrote Told in a French Garden in 1916, printed in Boston by Small, Maynard. Aldrich, author of A Hilltop on the Marne, gathered a circle in a French garden in August 1914, just as war broke over Europe.

Each guest told a tale. A youngster tells of a bride's new home at midnight. A nurse tells of a foundling son. A critic tells of an actress in Indian summer. A doctor tells of a youth's dream. The garden talk is warm, witty, and sad by turns, a portrait of friends who told tales while the guns drew near.
18333-the-illustrated-war-news-number-15:
Number fifteen of The Illustrated War News, dated November 18, 1914, is a British illustrated weekly from the first months of the First World War. Each number stood complete in itself, sold for sixpence in London, and mixed photographs, drawings, and short captions with news comment. Advertisements for razors and other goods for soldiers at home and abroad fill its early pages.

This number reports the Australian cruiser Sydney's destruction of the German cruiser Emden, and the trapping of the Konigsberg in the Rufiji River by the Chatham. It also marks the death of Field Marshal Earl Roberts at French headquarters, shows a French trench shower bath, and debates British casualties. Readers get the war as Britons first saw it in pictures: proud, partisan, and close to the front.
18334-the-illustrated-war-news-number-21:
Number twenty-one of The Illustrated War News, dated December 30, 1914, is a British illustrated weekly from the first winter of the First World War. Each number stood complete in itself, sold for sixpence in London, and was published on Wednesday mornings. The issue carries a leaflet notice for posting and advertisements aimed at readers sending comforts to the troops.

Its pages repeat the simple request heard from all quarters: send us tobacco and cigarettes. Thousands of regulars and territorials still waited in Great Britain for orders, and gifts sent now were sure to reach their man. Readers get the home front in picture form: a war now settling into winter, with shops, parcels, and illustrated news binding soldiers to the families behind them.
18468-the-fife-and-forfar-yeomanry-and-1:
Major D. D. Ogilvie wrote this regimental history of the Fife and Forfar Yeomanry and the 14th Fife and Forfar Yeomanry Battalion, Royal Highlanders, covering 1914 to 1919. A frontispiece shows officers at Fakenham in 1915, named row by row, with the King, Brigadier-General Lord Lovat, and Major-General Bruce Hamilton in later plates. The history is a record by and for the regiment.

Chapters run from home in 1914 to 1915, abroad in 1915, Egypt in 1916, Egypt and Palestine in 1917, Palestine in 1918, and France in 1918. Lists of officers, honors and awards, and casualties close the volume, with an index. August 4, 1914, the author says, ended peace training and began thirteen months of strenuous war training for thirty-seven months abroad. Readers get a yeomanry regiment's war, told in order, with names, places, and losses.
18622-captain-sam-the-boy-scouts-of-1814:
George Cary Eggleston published this boys' tale at New York in 1876. Its hero, Sam Hardwicke, is not yet eighteen when the story opens, yet he drills a company of boys as if they were real soldiers. Set in 1814, the book follows their camp life, disputes, and marches with a firm, good-humored tone. Eggleston dedicates it to a boy friend, Montague Douglas, in memory of walks they took together.

Sam leads by cool nerve rather than bluster, a point the opening mutiny scene makes at once. The tale mixes fun, pluck, and lessons in command for young readers. It is an early example of the boy-soldier stories that filled late-1800s shelves.
19115-roman-britain-in-1914:
Francis Haverfield wrote this 1915 survey for the British Academy of Roman finds made in Britain during 1914. It lists digs from Raedykes and Traprain Law in the north to Holt, Cardiff, and Richborough in the south. Plans, pottery stamps, and small finds fill the report.

A full section describes the fort at Borrans near Ambleside, with granaries, headquarters, gates, and ditches laid out in a clear plan. Wood barracks, corn stores, and kilns show daily fort life. Readers get a concise, scholarly snapshot of Roman Britain as diggers found it on the eve of war.
20250-the-fifth-battalion-highland-light:
The Fifth Battalion, Highland Light Infantry, kept a record of its war from 1914. The battalion moves fast over the span from mobilization to active service. Those early events now seem of small interest, the writers admit. Later readers, they felt, would want the front itself above all.

Glasgow men filled the ranks of this city battalion in wartime. Its path ran through training camps to trenches in France and beyond. Battalion histories name actions and losses that grand histories blur. This record lets families trace one unit's hard road through the war.
2114-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
This volume covers August 1742 to July 1744, when Frederick, his own peace made and Silesia his, hoped the wider European war would end. Book Fourteen finds him back at peaceful pursuits while the continent kept fighting. The peace of 1742 gave Frederick Silesia, but it left Austria and France still at war.

Voltaire praises the young king in letters until Frederick politely asks him to stop, and the hope of a general peace fades. Carlyle uses the pause to show a king who wanted settlement, caught in a war that would not close. Voltaire's praise embarrassed Frederick, since a king who loves flattery seldom keeps a clear head.
22563-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 146, dated January 28, 1914, finds comedy in diplomacy. The American Ambassador, readers were told last week, has a cold. He is confined to his room at the Embassy by it.

Colds, Punch observes, are nasty catching things among people. The staff, it jokes, show cowardice in their chief's confinement. They have apparently locked their chief in his room against infection. Such a squib shows the weekly's habit of deflating dignitaries gently. This issue appeared months before the First World War began. Its lightness reads poignantly against what followed for its laughing readers. Punch kept London smiling on the edge of catastrophe.
22573-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 146, dated February 11, 1914, turns to boxing politics. Kid Lewis's victory last week over Paul Til prompts its joke. Many Germans, Punch claims, hold a strong opinion about that result.

The French Government, they supposedly believe, protected the Entente at all costs. France was determined that the alliance should not be imperilled then. So France sent over a French boxer an Englishman could defeat. The joke ties sport to the alliances arming Europe for war. Within months, those alliances would pull nations into real fighting. Readers today feel the chill under the weekly's light tone. Punch still makes the item funny, which is its own historical interest.
22576-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 146, dated February 18, 1914, invents books for a chancellor. An enterprising publisher has supposedly persuaded Lloyd George to write. Several works of creative fancy are promised at an early date.

Essays on Lamb (shorn) heads the imaginary list of titles. The Fortunes of Montrose follows as another promised fancy work. Punch's joke turns a busy politician into a hack author overnight. Readers were meant to laugh at titles twisted from real books. Such squibs filled the weekly between longer, sharper cartoons and verses. This issue sits in the last calm spring before war. Its trifling gives historians a taste of ordinary Edwardian laughter.
22940-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Darkness falls on Tooting in Punch's issue of April 15, 1914, from volume 146. Punch picks up a Mail report of failed electric lighting across parts of Tooting and Mitcham one evening. One host in Garden Avenue had invited a dozen friends to a card party. He secured candles, and the party played on in their dim light.

That small mishap gets the full Punch treatment, turned into a paragraph of dry delight. The rest of the number mixes cartoons, verses, and jokes from the last spring of peace before the Great War. Nobody in its pages knows what August will bring. Reading it now carries that shadow. As a slice of Edwardian humor, the issue is complete and characteristic.
22989-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Lancastrians dine in London in Punch's issue of April 1, 1914, from volume 146. London's Lancastrians gathered for their yearly dinner the week before, Punch notes in passing. It would have been a kindly act, Punch suggests, to offer a seat to Mr. Masterman, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, now back in town.

That gentle prod at a minister sets the number's peacetime tone. Jokes turn on dinners, clubs, counties, and the small vanities of public men, all before the war rearranged every subject. Cartoons and verse fill out the week's entertainment. Read today, the issue's calm is its most striking feature. It catches London laughing in the last spring when its favorite targets were as mild as a missed invitation.
23032-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
An elephant goes collecting in Punch's issue of April 8, 1914, from volume 146. Kensington's Reservists need a headquarters, so Camp Week hires a full-sized elephant to tour the main streets collecting coins. Punch proposes training the beast to tread, purely by accident, on refusers' toes.

The joke catches the number's world, suburban reservists, charity weeks, and a London still treating soldiering as a part-time hobby. Four months later that world ended. The rest of the issue keeps the same light step, cartoons and paragraphs unaware. Its innocence, preserved whole, is what makes it moving now.
23087-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Hall Caine takes a ribbing in Punch's issue of March 18, 1914, from volume 146. Caine prefaced his serial with a note called Why I Wrote the Story. Punch summarizes the note's purpose as shifting blame, or at least sharing it around. One day, it seems, Mr. Caine heard the story on which the novel rests.

Punch loved puncturing bestsellers, and Caine's solemn self-importance made a broad target. The rest of the number keeps the peacetime mix, cartoons, verse, and theatre jokes for a London amusing itself. Spring 1914 issues like this one read now with an ache their makers never felt. The laughter is genuine, the targets small, and the abyss four months away and wholly invisible.
23658-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Dated July 15, 1914, this issue of Punch captures the famous London humor magazine in the last weeks before the First World War. Its Charivaria column trades jokes about bomb plots in Paris and a town giving up gas for electricity. It also jokes about a postcard ten years in the post, and suffrage campaigners drafting lists of ladies deserving royal honors.

Beyond the jokes, the issue carries the magazine's cartoons, verses, and satirical notes on theatre, politics, and daily life, all in the confident voice of Edwardian London. Read today, it is both funny and sobering: a light-hearted weekly that had no idea how soon its world would change.
23726-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for March 11, 1914, opens its Charivaria column with jokes on the news of the week. A contemporary calls one of the deported Nine the Brain of the party, a distinction that just eluded Mr. Bain. The Admiralty plans a surprise mobilisation, announced five months in advance to ensure its success.

Other jokes touch the Bishop of London's advice that every man be his own Columbus and find the continent of truth. A Russian writer expelled from Germany gets a joke too, as do millionaire amateur jockeys at Sandown Park. Futurist frocks at the Chelsea Arts Club ball get a nod as well. The issue shows Punch at its Edwardian height, confident, topical, and quick with a pun.
23760-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for February 25, 1914, opens Charivaria with the news that the German Crown Prince has the mumps, without consulting his Imperial Father first. Further domestic differences are anticipated. The joke sets the tone for an issue confident in its satire.

Other items report that the King of Cambodia raised a white elephant to the rank of princess, to the jealousy of the London Zoo. A Prussian general also banned the tooth-brush moustache as unsuited to the German character. A note on Sir Edward Grey's French adds a final twist: on one occasion, a little bird says, he was speaking Greek.
23815-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for April 22, 1914, opens Charivaria with a Times lament that Britain shows too little interest in sending a minister to Durazzo. Here, Punch suggests, is a post for poor Mr. Masterman. The Kerry News, preferring pigs to Englishmen, earns a note on Home Rule manners.

Oil discovered in Somaliland prompts a rumor that the Government will at last move against the Mullah. Futurism, spreading even to animals, appears in an advertisement for a fancy color dyer for ostrich. A dispute over who invented revues, and villagers of Bugsworth dissatisfied with their village name, complete a brisk, topical issue.
24157-punch-or-the-london-charivari-may-:
This weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 146, is dated May 27, 1914. It opens with Charivaria, the paper's column of brief, sharp news jokes. Readers learn that President Huerta's troops cheered the defeat of Travers, Evans, and Ouimet in the Amateur Golf Championship. Two million pounds sunk in the German liner Vaterland left the ship, happily, still afloat.

Other quips cover a blaze at the Press Club off Fleet Street, six glum faces atop an omnibus under a false advertisement, and the Anglo-American Exposition's mild version of New York. Punch mixed such paragraphs with cartoons and mock reports. The issue gives a lively taste of British humor weeks before the First World War.
24207-punch-or-the-london-charivari-may-:
This weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 146, is dated May 6, 1914. It opens with Charivaria, the paper's column of brief, sharp news jokes. Readers learn that the late Dowager-Empress of Japan composed thirty thousand poems, never published, and died universally respected. A hoax told Dublin Castle that Ulster loyalists had bought a Dreadnought disguised as an outrigger.

Other quips cover General Villa's wish that Americans bottle up Vera Cruz tight. King Ferdinand of Bulgaria buys four elephants as pets. Sir Ernest Shackleton's expedition dogs come to London for a good time. Punch mixed such paragraphs with cartoons and mock reports. The issue gives a lively taste of British humor in the spring of 1914.
24265-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 146, is dated February 4, 1914. It opens with Charivaria, the paper's column of brief, sharp news jokes. Readers learn that the report of 245 policemen injured in the Dublin strike riots has done much to allay discontent among the belabouring classes. A headline, Coaling the Stores, should after the strike be followed by Storing the Coals.

Other quips cover a Russian officer who shot a gipsy choir leader in a St. Petersburg restaurant over his daughter, a Navy standard of sixteen Dreadnoughts to ten, a New York Parents' League that worries children into a Hands-off-our-jam party, and Mrs. Carlyle's cat as a selfish, immoral, improper beast. Readers get Punch at its sharpest, weeks into 1914.
24318-punch-or-the-london-charivari-may-:
This weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 146, is dated May 13, 1914. It opens with Charivaria, the paper's column of brief, sharp news jokes. Readers learn that Stock Exchange men, pinched by continued depression, walked all the way to Brighton for their holiday on May 1. The canvas drawing most feminine attention is the Honorable John Collier's Clytemnestra, with its guess at tomorrow's fashion.

Other quips ask what a Picturegoer is, and note that suffragettes go for pictures. They propose that a statue of Peter the Great wear its linen collar inside out, marked Peter the Great, Winter Palace. In a duel, Caillaux fired at the sky and missed, while d'Allieres fired at the ground and hit it. Readers get Punch's cool, amused view of May 1914.
24357-punch-or-the-london-charivari-july:
This weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 147, is dated July 1, 1914. It opens with a poem called Progress, built on evidence before a Select Committee of the House of Commons. Miss C. E. Collet of the Home Office told the committee that big laundries were killing the small hand laundry.

The poem laments little crafts dying, cottage doors where no shuttle clicks, and hand-looms ousted by large firms. Pistons throb, great chimneys rise on the Thames, and the same change reaches Sheffield and Oldham. The housewife makes no more rare preserves, since the factory fakes raspberry jam with chips of wood. Engines supplant the Amazons the poet loved in youth. Readers get Punch on machines taking over the wash.
24358-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 146, edited by Owen Seaman, is dated March 25, 1914. It opens with Charivaria, the paper's column of brief, sharp news jokes. Readers learn that the American Ambassador has been warned of the danger of after-dinner speaking, since many a true word is said in digestion and truth hurts sensitive nations.

Other quips cover art circles seething over the National Gallery outrage, where only a Velasquez was injured, though next time it might be a Bomberg or a Wyndham Lewis. Sir Hiram Maxim writes Mrs. Pankhurst asking questions before joining her party, and Liverpool suffragettes form a Women's Church with frequent fasts. A Wellesley girl fire brigade draws a protest for unwomanly conduct. Readers get Punch's amused view of March 1914.
24414-punch-or-the-london-charivari-june:
This weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 146, is dated June 10, 1914, and opens with Charivaria, its column of brief news jokes. Readers learn that Mr. Redmond opposed sending British troops to Durazzo, lest home defences be weakened, and that ladies on the Holyhead links so disturbed Mr. Lloyd George that he foozled a shot. The government, it is reported, contemplates serious steps against the suffragettes.

Other quips note Lord Strathcona's seat for sale, and draw Mr. Masterman's attention to it, and Francis Joseph's recovery has ended his doctor's calls, though a long motor-bicycle ride is declared an exaggeration. Corsica claims Columbus was born there, not Genoa, with much evidence, though Genoa may yield if repaid for its heavy statue. A strike leaves Ascot short of patent-leather boots, so visitors must spend the day in comfort. Readers get Punch's June 1914 jokes.
24453-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Dated 17 June 1914, this weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, gathers a week of British satire, jokes, and cartoons. Punch was the country's long-running comic paper. The issue opens with Charivaria, a column of brief, sharp news jokes. It includes a mock announcement of a Pocket Asquith, and a gold-rush sparked by particles found in a duck's gizzard.

Inside, readers find quips on land valuation, politics, and daily life. Longer comic pieces and drawings poke fun at public figures and fashions. Published just weeks before the First World War began, the issue captures Britain in the last summer of peace, laughing at itself in short paragraphs and pictures.
24538-1914:
Field-Marshal Viscount French of Ypres wrote this account of 1914, published at London in 1919 with maps. He dedicated it to David Lloyd George, to whose foresight, energy, and tenacity, he says, the army and the empire owed much. French had commanded the British Expeditionary Force in France in the war's first months.

His book covers the retreat from Mons, the Marne, the Aisne, and the race to the sea, as seen by the commander himself. It is frank, defensive, and full of argument about decisions taken under fire. Readers of First World War history will find it an essential, if partisan, record of the opening campaign.
24720-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Dated 20 May 1914, this weekly number of Punch, or the London Charivari, gathers a week of British satire, jokes, and cartoons. It opens with Charivaria, noting with comfort that even the worst politician may hold one good quality. The Express, it reports, tells us that Winston Churchill reads The Express.

Inside, readers find quips on politics, society, and daily life, with drawings that poke fun at public figures. Stage directions in the issue's plays are marked with equal signs, as the transcriber notes. Published weeks before the First World War, the issue captures Britain laughing at itself in the last spring of peace.
24992-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
The July 22, 1914 number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 147, opens with Charivaria, the magazine's column of sharp topical jokes. Lloyd George's supposed ruin of landowners prompts a Bazaar advertisement priced in German marks, a joke about entrapping an ignorant foreigner. The Socialist ideal gets its turn when the Abergavenny Board of Guardians accepts Lord Abergavenny's offer to buy the local workhouse for three thousand pounds.

New peers provide more material: Edgar Vincent becomes Baron d'Abernon, Brocklehurst becomes Baron Ranksborough, and Edward Lyell becomes Baron Lyell, which Punch calls rather lazy. A lioness escapes at Bourg-en-Bresse and a gendarme is shot in the leg, presumably by his own party, since the lioness was not armed. Suffragettes, bearded professors' predictions about bald women, and boxing fill out an issue on the edge of war.
25010-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
The April 29, 1914 number of Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 146, opens with Charivaria's jokes on the edge of war. Captain Fort, a French army airman from Châlons, flies over the German frontier by mistake, lands in Lorraine, and flies back before the German police arrive. Punch wishes he had prolonged the discourtesy. The Great Eastern Railway's new American manager, H. W. Thornton, says his ideal is to satisfy the public, disposing of the rumour that he serves shareholders.

The pugilist Jack Johnson is about to become a naturalized French subject, which Punch blames on America. A garbled newspaper paragraph about the Blake and Borrell fight supplies comedy. Stafford House, home of the London Museum, becomes Lancaster House, and a verse protest against Lloyd George's taxes ends with Phoebus asked to defend the poet's nib. The issue is Edwardian satire at stretch.
25560-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for 24 June 1914 opens with Charivaria, its weekly round of short jokes on public life. Cambridge Boat Club plans to spend eight thousand pounds improving the Cam, with talk of making it into a river. A writer warns against living in a houseboat during a flood.

Noah, Punch replies, always said he owed his life to doing just that. French politics supplies further jokes, as Ribot's cabinet objects to the label One-Day Ministry, having lasted some hours longer. The issue captures London humour on the eve of war, sharp and topical.
25676-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for 3 June 1914 opens its Charivaria with a royal visit joke. One item notes the King and Queen's Nottinghamshire visit, hosted at Welbeck by the Duke and Duchess of Portland. There, three colliery owners and four working miners are to be presented at Forest Town.

Punch calls that a most embarrassing gift, one that cannot without hurting feelings be passed on to the Zoological Society. French tact supplies the next joke, as Minister Maginol, an inch taller than Christian of Denmark, the tall king, is introduced at Paris. A Bow County Court woman litigant follows, in Punch's topical weekly patter.
25860-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
The July 29, 1914 number of Punch catches London wit on the edge of war. Charivaria jokes run first. An inventor of F rays is said to have eloped with an admiral's daughter. General Huerta flees with securities worth one million two hundred thousand pounds, and Berlin cafes are ordered shut at two in the morning. A water plane that will not rise earns a quip about a change of name.

Deeper pieces turn to the crisis over Ulster, with the premier rising in a still, packed House to speak on peace or war. Cartoons add their sting, from a maid judged by the shape of her tongue to verses on the uses of ocean and the progress of man. The number is a sharp, funny record of a week when jokes and dread shared the page.
26012-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
The August 5, 1914 number of Punch, edited by Owen Seaman, meets the war's first week with jokes, cartoons, and debate notes. Hints to millionaires advise engaging all the bathing boxes to keep the sea to oneself uncontaminated. Charivaria notes a church burned by suffragettes, militants wanting a woman architect for its rebuilding, and two suffragettes at Bow Street refusing their ages.

A water board report says Thames water is purified at least one thousand times before delivery, prompting a quip that it may explain complaints of flavorlessness. Parliament notes record debate carried with marvelous repression of party passion, though Lord Bob suggests ministers be hanged, or suspended, as he puts it. The number catches a nation turning from jokes to war.
26119-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
A single issue of Punch, the London comic weekly, dated August 12, 1914, days after Britain went to war. Its opening Charivaria column jokes about a suspect arrested near the Tyne shipyards. It also jokes about French cooks leaving the House of Commons and the fate of Olympic funds meant for Berlin. Other items note boxer Georges Carpentier joining up as a volunteer.

The rest of the issue mixes short jokes, verses, and longer comic pieces, all aimed at wartime news as Londoners first met it. For a modern reader it captures the mood of that first war week. That mood was nervous and patriotic, yet still ready to laugh. The South Pole and the suffrage movement are drawn into the jokes as well.
26693-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 147, dated August 26, 1914, is a wartime number, published three weeks after Britain entered the Great War. Its Charivaria jokes that an eclipse was the sun's attempt to stop Germans finding a place in it. It jokes that the Kaiser was vexed at South Africa fighting under the British flag. It jokes that he was vexed at English people resuming seaside holidays.

Expeditionary soldiers arrive in France singing It's a Long Way to Tipperary. The lie about the cutting-up of the Black Watch is scotched. A newsvendor shouts European War, Result. Other items cover the Goeben's inglorious scuttle full of Turkey's coal and the Duc d'Orléans returning his Golden Fleece collar. Cambridge public houses close at nine. Mock advertisements offer frozen whales, mock turtles to amuse children, and sheep-folds to fit a tennis court.
26969-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for August 19, 1914, catches Britain's famous humor weekly two weeks into the First World War. Cartoons, verses, and short comic pieces poke at the new wartime world, from a quick change of front on the cover to jokes about gold, banks, and debts.

One sketch turns on children puzzling over a moratorium, a word they take for a ship, a tomb, or anything but a freeze on debt payments. The issue reads as a snapshot of a country still joking in peacetime style while war news filled the papers around it.
27055-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for September 2, 1914, shows the London humor weekly turning its wit on the first month of war. Its Charivaria column jokes that Germany raged when Britain joined the war, as if being asked to let friends be robbed and murdered were a small request.

Other squibs mock German appeals over Kiao-chau leases. A Tokio version of the Kaiser's Yellow Peril cartoon shows the Kaiser himself as the peril, and a bear dressed to represent the King of the Belgians gets denied in Germany. A rumour adds that Wilhelm II has despatched his British uniforms. The issue captures wartime satire at full sting.
27360-punch-or-the-london-charivari-sept:
Punch, or the London Charivari, volume 147, dated 9 September 1914, catches Britain's famous comic weekly five weeks into the First World War. Its Charivaria column trades in short, sharp jokes on the news of the week, and the war fills nearly every paragraph.

Readers meet the Deutsche Tageszeitung vowing a war not to be stopped by notice, and German fines on towns recast as temporary loans. They also meet the Kaiser recalled as the Tin Soldier of his English relatives, and a threat to make Gurken-salad of the Goorkhas. Louvain, the Louvre pictures, and President Wilson all get a joke. The issue is a vivid snapshot of wartime humor at its most confident.
27440-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Volume 147 of Punch, or the London Charivari, dated 16 September 1914, comes a week after the 9 September number, and the war still rules its Charivaria column. The jokes bite at German claims, at the Kaiser, and at the flood of rumor that filled the first weeks of fighting.

The Kaiser once boasted that Germany's future lay upon the water, and a German soldier, when the Belgians flood the Antwerp dykes, remarks that the present lies in it. German victories turn out to be scraps of paper, and the new Pope's plea for peace is called a capital idea by Austria-Hungary. The issue shows Punch settling into its wartime voice.
27893-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for September 23, 1914, volume one hundred and forty-seven, shows the famous comic weekly turning its wit on the first months of the Great War. The issue opens with a cartoon of the Alien, its chorus jeering at one who kissed the Kaiser's hand.

Charivaria jokes that the Kaiser travels with an asbestos hut, that German troops retreat to a bottle-neck exit, and that the only goods Germany makes better than Britain are lies. The number captures Punch's wartime blend of satire, patriotism, and topical jokes, with news and cartoons for a nation at war.
27967-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for September 30, 1914, continues the comic weekly's wartime commentary in volume one hundred and forty-seven. Charivaria notes that German troops who set out for a pleasure trip to Paris are now taking their pleasures sadly, under British influence.

Other jokes cover the destruction of Rheims Cathedral, a Scotsman glad the French are getting their Aisne back, and a German soldier captured in a mail-bag in Lorraine. The issue shows Punch finding humor in grim news, with the confidence of a paper sure its readers shared its jokes and its cause.
3564-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This fourteenth volume of Bourrienne's memoirs continues the story of 1815 into its later months. After Waterloo and the second abdication, Napoleon leaves France for good, and the Bourbons return to a changed country. Bourrienne writes as a former secretary watching old colleagues choose between loyalty to a fallen emperor and service to a restored king.

The volume covers arrests, exiles, and the settling of accounts, as well as Napoleon's voyage toward St Helena. Its tone is that of aftermath: letters burned, careers broken, and memories guarded. Readers who have followed the series through victory and defeat will find here the quiet, often sad close of the Napoleonic age in France.
3594-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This fourteenth volume opens Book Three of Montaigne's Essays, with chapters one through four. They treat profit and honesty, repentance, three commerces, and diversion. Montaigne opens by noting that no man is free from speaking foolish things. The worst case is a man who labors to play the fool, quoting Terence on saying a mighty trifle with great effort.

The essays ask whether a man can profit without dishonesty, whether repentance can remake a life, and what company suits different ages. Diversion, Montaigne argues, can heal a mind fixed on grief. The volume suits readers starting Book Three, where Montaigne writes more freely about his later life and his own conduct.
5288-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels continue in this fourteenth volume, in English verse translation. Its contents are The Countryman Who Sought His Calf, Hans Carvel's Ring, The Hermit, and The Convent Gardener of Lamporechio, each tale mixing rustic cunning with marital and monastic comedy.

The opening tale follows a countryman who loses his calf, crosses a forest, and climbs the tallest tree for a better view, only to find a lady and her lover below. Readers get four tales in La Fontaine's light, ironic manner, where country folk, hermits, and gardeners outwit their betters.
5916-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
A long inn and road sequence fills chapters forty-one through fifty-two in this Don Quixote portion. Chapter forty-one continues the captive's adventures, as a renegade buys an excellent vessel for more than thirty persons and plans a voyage to lend the transaction colour. Chapters forty-two through forty-six return to the inn, its muleteer, helmet debate, and Holy Brotherhood officers, while chapters forty-seven through forty-nine carry Quixote off enchanted and debate books of chivalry.

Chapters fifty through fifty-two close with the canon controversy, a goatherd's tale, and Quixote's quarrel with the goatherd. Readers get volume one's great gathering, as stories, captives, and officers converge at the inn before the road resumes. The part suits readers who want the first volume's climax in one sweep, from captive's escape to caged knight.
7599-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part fourteen of The Caxtons joins high theology to a practical moral for its hero. Its homelier lesson comes from watching Fortune at work: she offers each person one chance in a lifetime, and she returns if he seizes it and uses it well. That rule turns luck into a test of conduct.

The theology behind it comes from Dante on Fortune, in a passage the narrator thinks deserves more attention. The stern Florentine defends Fortune against popular blame, presenting her as a heavenly power set by God to guide human greatness. She obeys God's will, blessed and deaf to blasphemy. She stays calm and high among the other angelic powers as she turns her course. Popular Fortune, blamed for every turn, looks small beside her.
9602-history-of-the-french-revolution-fr:
F. A. M. Mignet wrote his History of the French Revolution in 1824, covering the years 1789 to 1814. Mignet, a French historian of high repute, traces the Revolution from its first hopes to Napoleon's fall. Chapters move through the Constituent Assembly, the Legislative Assembly, and the National Convention. The Directory and the Consulate close the arc.

Mignet writes with clear, brisk prose, judging men and parties by their deeds, not their slogans. His history, long a standard work, shaped how Europe read the Revolution. A reader gets a classic, compact account of a world-shaking age, from Bastille to empire, told by a historian close to its sources.
a-midsummer-night-s-dream-pg1514:
William Shakespeare's comedy is presented here with a full cast list and a scene-by-scene contents table, moving between Athens and a wood nearby. Theseus, Duke of Athens, will marry Hippolyta, while four young lovers tangle: Hermia loves Lysander, Demetrius wants Hermia, and Helena wants Demetrius. The cast also lists the fairy court and a crew of Athenian workmen.

Oberon, Titania, and Puck stir the night with quarrels and love juice, while Bottom the weaver and his friends rehearse their play. The five acts end with weddings, a comically sad performance of Pyramus and Thisbe, and fairy blessings. This edition's clear layout suits readers new to the play.
abrams-human-energy-1914:
Albert Abrams, a San Francisco doctor, set out his healing theory in Human Energy in 1914. The book is the founding statement of radionics, the fringe practice he built his name on. Abrams claimed the body gives off fine electronic signals that a trained hand can read.

He argues that each disease sends out its own rate of vibration, which can be picked up from a drop of blood. From that rate, he says, a doctor can name the illness and judge its strength. His 'electronic reactions' later filled clinics with his black boxes, and drew sharp fire from medical science.
arxiv-2509-00214:
A. Ederoclite leads a team of forty authors who present the first data release of the J-VAR survey in 2025. Variability studies watch how sky sources change over time, which reveals astrophysical events as they happen. J-VAR uses the JAST80 telescope at the Javalambre site in Spain, with a wide two-degree field of view.

Its edge is a set of narrow-band filters placed on key stellar spectral features, such as calcium and hydrogen lines. Wide field plus narrow filters is a new pairing for a variability survey. The release describes the survey design and its first data. Time-domain data in many narrow bands can sharpen studies of stars and transient events alike.
arxiv-2509-00414:
Juraj Vladika and Florian Matthes present MedSEBA in 2025, an interactive system that synthesizes evidence-based answers to medical questions from evolving literature. People seek medical advice online, where reliable sources are hard to tell from misleading ones. Millions of studies appear each year, and they can reach differing conclusions that search tools fail to reflect.

MedSEBA uses a large language model to draft coherent answers, grounded in studies retrieved live from PubMed, the medical research database. Answers consist of key points and arguments that users can inspect and trace to sources. Grounding in current studies aims to keep pace as findings change. The system targets both lay readers and researchers tracking a fast field.
arxiv-2509-00614:
Shikun Liu leads six authors in total, with Deyu Zou, Nima Shoghi, Victor Fung, Kai Liu, and Pan Li, in benchmarking robust fine-tuning for molecular graph foundation models. Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model to a new task, but these molecular models face small pre-training data and severe label scarcity downstream.

Liu and his co-authors sort eight fine-tuning methods into weight-based, representation-based, and partial groups, then test them on regression and classification tasks across pre-trained models and labeling settings. Their new method, ROFT-MOL, blends simple post-hoc weight interpolation, averaging weights after training, with weight ensemble fine-tuning. It improves performance on both task types while keeping the ease of the post-hoc approach.
arxiv-2509-00914:
Hainan Wang, with two co-authors, presents TinyMusician for on-device music generation. Transformer models set new marks for music generation quality. But their many parameters demand huge compute and time. That makes them infeasible on edge devices like phones and wearables. TinyMusician is a lightweight model distilled from MusicGen.

Distillation trains a small student to mimic a larger teacher. The model adds two key innovations. One is a stage-mixed form of KL-divergence training. The other is adaptive mixed-precision quantization, which stores numbers at varied precision. Tests show TinyMusician keeps most of MusicGen-Small's performance. It does so with fifty-five percent less model size. It is the first mobile music model with no cloud dependency.
arxiv-2509-01314:
Large language models can summarize text in many fields, but adapting them to a new, low-resource domain is costly and labeled data may not exist. Anum Afzal, Mehul Kumawat, and Florian Matthes test whether training on rich domains can help unseen poor ones. They use parameter-efficient fine-tuning, methods that adjust only a small part of the model.

The team benchmarked six such methods on a Llama model across fourteen training data sets from science, medicine, law, and news. They asked whether shared language traits between fields can carry skill across domains. For low-resource targets, adapters trained within a related domain beat few-shot prompting and other baselines in their tests. The findings suggest smaller, cheaply tuned models can do better than expected when domain links are used well.
arxiv-2509-01514:
Retrieval systems that feed language models usually take the top few matches of a simple semantic search, which lets irrelevant or repeated material crowd the context. Andreas Ottem presents MeVe, a modular system for memory verification and effective context control. The design rethinks that pipeline as five distinct phases, each open to audit and tuning on its own.

The phases are initial retrieval, relevance verification, fallback retrieval, context prioritization, and token budgeting. Together they give fine-grained control over what knowledge reaches the model, with filtering that adapts to the task. Ottem releases a reference implementation as a proof of concept and tests it on knowledge-heavy questions over a subset of English Wikipedia. Results show that actively verifying retrieved information before use improves the quality of the context the model receives.
arxiv-2509-02014:
Daniel Bissinger proves new results on uniform Steiner bundles over projective space. A Steiner bundle is a vector bundle with a lean presentation tied to a simple module pattern. Uniform means the bundle splits the same way on every line in the space. Homogeneous bundles are the most symmetric subclass, and uniform ones need not be homogeneous.

For each type level from four upward, he builds uniform but non-homogeneous examples with disconnected splitting type. Almost uniform bundles, a near miss class, are investigated as well. His route reads Steiner bundles as relative projective representations of a Kronecker quiver. Functors from restriction, inflation, and reflection then move results between settings. The work widens the known landscape of bundle behavior on projective spaces.
arxiv-2509-02314:
Stanisław Kiedrzyński, Emilia Witkowska, and Miłosz Panfil wrote a 2025 mathematical physics paper on quantum hard rods, a one-dimensional model where particles cannot overlap. They study how density patterns in the model change over time and in space.

The authors derive compact formulas for density form factors, the building blocks used to compute correlation measures. Their semi-analytic method cuts the cost of computing dynamic and static structure factors, which describe how fluctuations spread. They also find when the factors vanish and confirm behaviour expected for a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, a standard theory of gapless one-dimensional fluids. The results give simulators exact benchmarks for testing strongly interacting quantum systems.
arxiv-2509-02414:
Marina S. Cagliari, Zucheng Gao, and Azadeh Moradinezhad Dizgah wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on cleaning line-intensity maps, which record total glow from many faint galaxies at once. A target emission line gets mixed with background continuum light and with lines from other distances.

The team trains a neural network to pull the three parts apart, working with the angular power spectrum, a summary of pattern strength by scale. Test maps mimic the SPHEREx mission, with varied interloper brightness and optional noise scatter. Cross-channel links proved essential when scatter was present. Without continuum light, the target spectrum came back within a few percent. With continuum included, target and continuum were recovered well, while the fainter interloper lines resisted recovery.
arxiv-2509-02614:
Xinbo Zhang and four co-authors present a 2025 insurance analytics paper predicting near-miss driving events from vehicle telematics and driver-assistance warnings. Near misses give a timely risk signal for usage-based insurance, but weekly counts are mostly zero and drivers differ widely.

The authors show standard models underfit such sparse, uneven data. Their zero-inflated Poisson frameworks learn hidden behaviour groups and fit count models by expectation-maximization, an iterative fitting routine. Data came from a commercial fleet followed for a year, covering millions of kilometres. The grouped models beat baselines and earlier telematics models on fit and on out-of-sample calibration. Sensitivity checks on group count kept the gains. The authors pitch weekly, context-aware pricing that treats driving styles fairly.
arxiv-2509-02714:
Derek Sikorski and twenty-one co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy paper asking how early a dense environment shapes galaxy growth, using the Hyperion proto-supercluster. Counting galaxies by mass, through the stellar mass function, records that growth history at high redshift.

The team built a three-dimensional density map from survey photometry plus new Hubble grism spectroscopy, assigning galaxies to density peaks, outskirts, or the field. Repeated Monte Carlo runs carry redshift and mass uncertainty through the analysis. Peaks show a clear surplus of massive galaxies, about ten times the field density at the heavy end, versus a modest boost for light galaxies. Outskirts mirror the field. Environmental influence on mass growth thus appears long before cluster quenching, the shutdown of star formation in mature clusters.
arxiv-2509-02814:
Mehmet Erbay, Birgit Jacob, and Timo Reis wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on equations that mix change over time with fixed algebraic constraints. Such systems are called differential-algebraic equations. The authors work in spaces with infinitely many dimensions, a setting used for large or continuous systems.

Their main move is to carry a tool called integrated semigroups over from a simpler classic problem. A semigroup describes how a system evolves step by step. The extended version lets them study forms of these equations that include outside forcing terms. It also helps pin down what counts as a solution. Readers in applied analysis gain a cleaner framework for hard, constrained systems.
arxiv-2509-02914:
Cristóbal Méndez and 3 co-authors presented a 2025 theory paper on protecting superconducting surfaces with noble metals. Superconductors carry current without resistance, and thin oxide layers on their surfaces spoil that performance. The problem hits radio-frequency cavities and quantum circuits alike, where surface chemistry matters at tiny scales.

Their framework joins two tools: calculations of interface energies and a strong-coupling theory of superconductivity.
