Screening candidates this way points to gold and gold-based alloys as good protective caps. The model also predicts that adding a thin wetting layer beneath the cap makes it stick far better. Stronger sticking would allow thinner caps, easing a long-standing practical headache.
arxiv-2509-03114:
Miao Xu and 5 co-authors worked in 2025 on making computer-generated hand-object contact look and behave realistically. Systems that reconstruct hands holding objects often let fingers sink into surfaces or hover above them. Real hands also deform on contact, a detail earlier methods largely ignored.

Their method, GravityDB, treats contact as attraction: a gravity-like field pulls a flexible hand surface toward rigid objects until they meet properly. Text descriptions feed semantic guidance into that field, steering contact toward sensible regions. The diffusion bridge part of the model shapes the process step by step. Tests on several datasets showed grasps without penetration, with stable holds and believable hand deformation. The work targets animation, robotics, and virtual reality.
arxiv-2509-03314:
Michaël Maex gave a 2025 synthetic proof of a generalized Pythagorean theorem for curved surfaces. On a sphere or on a hyperbolic surface, the classic rule linking a right triangle's sides changes form. One elegant version, found for the hyperbolic case by Calapso and extended to spheres by Maraner, uses areas of disks whose radii are the triangle's sides.

All earlier proofs were analytic, relying on calculation, and Maraner asked whether a purely geometric proof exists. Maex first restates the theorem in language a wide audience can follow. He then proves it with elementary geometry, using the ordinary sphere sitting in Euclidean space for the spherical case. For the hyperbolic case he uses the hyperboloid model inside Minkowski space, the geometry behind relativity.
arxiv-2509-03714:
Maxim Kurkov builds an action principle for a noncommutative gauge theory from Lie-Poisson electrodynamics in a 2025 physics paper. Noncommutative theories treat spacetime coordinates as quantities that do not fully commute, changing the rules of electrodynamics. Lie-Poisson electrodynamics is a semiclassical stand-in for such theories when the noncommutativity has a Lie-algebra form.

Kurkov obtains a local classical action that respects gauge invariance, and whose commutative limit correctly returns ordinary electrodynamics. Its Euler-Lagrange equations, the standard output of an action, are deformed Maxwell equations. For the four-dimensional kappa-Minkowski spacetime, a leading example of this geometry, the action reproduces the deformed Maxwell equations found earlier on separate grounds. The same action yields those laws for every noncommutativity of Lie-algebra type, not just that one case. The result gives a relatively simple Lagrangian formulation for a problem that had resisted one for years.
arxiv-2509-03814:
Electric flux tubes in the SU(3) gauge theory behind the strong nuclear force are examined in a 2025 theoretical physics paper by Jude Pereira and one co-author. A flux tube is a narrow channel of electric field stretched between charges, like the string thought to bind quarks together. Their setup adds scalar fields, here in the fundamental representation, alongside the gauge fields.

Such tubes may come in two classes, tied to SU(3)'s two maximally commuting generators, labelled 3 and 8. They build the 3-type case with two scalar fields. It resists decay via Schwinger pair production, where a strong field tears particle pairs from the vacuum and would normally break the tube. The 8-type case, however, resisted construction despite their attempts. Both outcomes are reported plainly, marking a partial but concrete advance for flux tubes in the full theory, not just simpler toy versions.
arxiv-2509-04214:
Tyler Shumaker and three co-authors build an automated pipeline that measures how much private data an AI model might leak in a 2025 research paper. Model inversion attacks work backward from a trained model to reconstruct pieces of its training data. Judging that privacy loss has been slow, subjective work, since reconstructions are hard for people to read. Military users face extra pressure, with many model types needing checks before deployment.

Vision-language models help grade the reconstructions automatically, by captioning images and classifying them without prior examples. Four risk dimensions score the privacy loss. Tests across several attack methods and image classifiers typical of military tasks show the pipeline scales. Security teams gain a repeatable yardstick for model privacy.
arxiv-2509-04414:
Toni Ikonen, writing alone, proves a rigidity result for conformal curves that stretch forever in a 2025 mathematics paper. A conformal curve bends space while preserving angles locally, and an entire one is defined on the whole real line or space. Ikonen shows only two outcomes are possible. Either the curve is affine, meaning it follows a straight linear pattern, or its average energy inside growing balls keeps rising and eventually explodes without bound.

The proof blows the curve down to large scales and leans on generalized Cauchy-Riemann equations plus a sharp inequality for surfaces. One application says every nicely tame entire conformal curve must be affine, echoing a classic complex analysis fact. Related results describe curves factoring through calibrated submanifolds.
arxiv-2509-04714:
A thumbnail that promises what a video never delivers damages trust on YouTube. Wajiha Naveed, lead author with two co-authors, build a detector for such misleading thumbnails in a 2025 paper. Their dataset spans thousands of videos from eight countries, including many misleading examples with billions of combined views.

Their pipeline combines video-to-text descriptions, thumbnail images, and subtitle transcripts for a full view of each video. They test several leading large language models with extensive prompt design. One model reaches strong accuracy, precision, and recall in their scenarios. The authors discuss moderation, user experience, and ethics of deployment at scale.
arxiv-2509-04814:
Relaxation after a disturbance can stretch or compress in time, and one crystal can switch between the two. Tyler Carbin, lead author with eight co-authors, observe that crossover in a 2025 condensed matter paper. They photoexcite a single crystal across a structural phase transition and track how it relaxes.

A simple lattice model explains the switch. Spatial inhomogeneity and local, strain-mediated interactions work together. They produce stretched behaviour in one regime and compressed behaviour in another. The authors present photoexcited solids as clean platforms for studying anomalous relaxation, a hallmark of disordered systems whose origins have remained unclear despite its wide occurrence.
arxiv-2509-05514:
The coldest brown dwarfs, failed stars barely warmer than a household oven, get a colour census from S. K. Leggett, Mark W. Phillips, and Pascal Tremblin in a 2025 astronomy paper. New space telescope spectra give the first near-infrared views of many faint T and Y dwarfs.

The authors combine those data with published sources to synthesise brightness measures on three telescope filter systems for dozens of dwarfs. One mid-infrared brightness turns out to track temperature well, and they fit a formula linking the two for the coolest range. Comparing five very cold dwarfs with model atmospheres links bluer colours to lower gravity or richer metal content. Colour diagrams scatter widely, with temperature, gravity, and composition entangled.
arxiv-2509-06014:
Two recent frameworks for perfect spin hydrodynamics agree more deeply than expected, shows Zbigniew Drogosz in a 2025 paper. Spin hydrodynamics describes fluids whose particles carry spin polarization, modeled here for spin one-half particles. One framework grows from classical kinetic theory, the other from the Wigner function, a quantum phase-space tool, and both expand in powers of the polarization.

Drogosz compares the conserved currents order by order in that expansion. At every order the two approaches give currents of exactly the same form. The only difference is a multiplicative factor, equal to one at the lowest nontrivial order and growing monotonically as the order rises. The match ties the classical and quantum routes to spin fluids tightly together.
arxiv-2509-06214:
Clustering a graph without leaking who is connected to whom is the goal of a 2025 paper by Haochen You and Baojing Liu. Differential privacy protects individuals, but private clustering usually suffers heavy noise, low speed, and opaque answers. Their approach starts from a metric embedding initialization: an SDP optimization extracts a key set, and a tree-based scheme seeds a well-initialized configuration.

A k-median strategy then produces the clusters, and explanations are offered by comparing query points with cluster centers. Experiments on public datasets beat existing methods across clustering metrics while keeping strict privacy guarantees. The authors present interpretability as a first-class requirement for private graph analysis, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2509-06314:
Wasted dimensions inside a neural network's hidden representation can now be measured directly, propose Mehmet Can Yavuz and Berrin Yanikoglu in a 2025 paper. Latent spaces often carry redundant coordinates that encode overlapping information, shrinking effective capacity. Accuracy and reconstruction loss only hint at that failure indirectly.

Their redundancy index reads coupling matrices built from latent codes and compares off-diagonal statistics against a normal distribution by energy distance, giving a compact, plain score. Across image benchmarks from MNIST variants to CIFAR-100, low redundancy predicts strong accuracy or low reconstruction error, while high scores accompany collapse. The index can steer network design search, and the authors note that a popular tuning method already drifts toward low-redundancy regions on its own.
arxiv-2509-06514:
Private database lookups that run inside memory chips are proposed by Mpoki Mwaisela and three co-authors in a 2025 computer systems paper. Private information retrieval lets a client query servers without revealing what was asked for. Strong as that promise is, current systems are slow because they must scan gigabytes of data through limited memory bandwidth.

Processing-in-memory hardware adds computing power right where data sits, easing that bottleneck. The authors design the first multi-server private retrieval system for such hardware and build it on UPMEM, the first openly sold processing-in-memory platform. They explain why the method's operations suit this hardware: wide parallelism and fast memory access. In tests, query throughput rises more than threefold compared with a standard processor-based system, a meaningful step toward practical private search.
arxiv-2509-06614:
Cheating by the middlemen of fast blockchain rollups is targeted by Margarita Capretto and four co-authors in a 2025 security paper. Rollups do most work off the main chain and post compressed batches to it. A sequencer orders incoming transactions, and a data availability committee translates stored hashes back into full batches when needed.

Dishonest sequencers or committees could distort the rollup's history, so the authors design fraud proofs judged by contracts on the main chain. Crucially, these proofs check the fixed algorithms that define correct committee behavior, which makes them cheaper and easier to verify than general execution proofs. The games are modeled as two-player contests, with honest winning strategies proven. A formal version in the LEAN4 proof assistant is provided, covering both the honest strategies and ways to expose false claims.
arxiv-2509-06714:
Teaching a robot its controller on the real hardware, despite slow thinking, is addressed by Zakariae El Asri and four co-authors in a 2025 robotics paper. Learning directly on a robot demands extreme sample efficiency, since each trial is real. Model-based reinforcement learning is the most frugal approach, but its inference can be too slow for fast control loops.

The authors first define a general framework for inference delays, where a slow controller hands the robot a sequence of actions so motion never stalls waiting for the next command. Several learning algorithms are compared under that lens. Their own method, RT-HCP, offers a strong trade-off among performance, sample efficiency, and inference time. It was validated by learning a controller directly on a fast Furuta pendulum, a swinging-arm platform that punishes slow control.
arxiv-2509-06814:
Oxygen atoms, usually erased from simple theories of high-temperature superconductivity, are restored to the center by Tom G. Saunderson and two co-authors in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Cuprate superconductors have resisted explanation for decades, and influential theories reduce them to one band centered on copper. Altermagnetism, a newer magnetic concept, produces a d-wave-like texture from rotated cages around atoms.

In the parent compound of a famous cuprate, alternating pairing strength on the two copper sublattices already yields a d-wave-like gap. Tilts of the structure, however, are not the driver and even hurt related nickelates. The authors show the in-plane oxygen sublattice itself realizes the needed symmetry. Imposing oxygen-centered staggered pairing gives a d-wave gap with perfect fourfold symmetry, confirmed self-consistently in a nickelate from first principles. Possible origins of the order are outlined.
arxiv-2509-07014:
Charles D. Coleman and Thomas Bryan propose loss functions for spotting outliers in panel data, in a 2025 paper. Finding outliers matters because data quality depends on it. A strange value might signal that something went wrong when the data were produced. It might also be an honest, if rare, fact about the world.

The authors build their tools without assuming any distribution for the data. Part one deals with nonnegative values. They derive an unsigned loss function from stated axioms, then a signed version that treats high and low outliers apart. For nominal time they obtain an exact form, and a version that does not change with time lets values from different periods be compared fairly. Worked examples include one where another variable sorts the outliers. Part two repeats the development for data of mixed sign.
arxiv-2509-07314:
Tanvi Bajpai and 1 co-author ask how Reddit moderators actually work through their moderation queue in a 2025 study. The modqueue is the review list where reported posts and comments wait for a decision. Reddit leans on volunteer moderators to keep communities healthy, yet little was known about how this central tool fits their daily work. One moderator quoted in the title compares the queue to firefighting.

The authors surveyed 110 moderators who together oversee more than 400 subreddits. Habits vary widely: some treat the queue as a daily checklist, others scan it for community-wide patterns, and many find it lacking for real decisions. Coordination gaps, unclear interface signals, and reliance on outside tools recur in the answers. The authors argue for more modular and customizable tools that fit the many ways moderators actually work.
arxiv-2509-07514:
Jaemin Kim and 3 co-authors present a carrier-assisted method in 2025 for purifying noisy entanglement. Entanglement purification, also called distillation, upgrades weak shared quantum links into strong ones and is a building block of quantum networks. Standard schemes need quantum memory holding many copies plus coherent operations across them, both hard in practice.

The new protocol needs memory for only a single shared entangled pair, plus single qubits that travel between the parties as carriers. With noiseless carriers, the protocol provably purifies the shared state. With noisy carriers, success depends on the noise channel, and the authors characterize which Pauli channels allow purification. Adding more carriers pushes the achievable fidelity toward unity for any Pauli channel that does not break entanglement outright. The design lowers the hardware bar for quantum network links.
arxiv-2509-07714:
V. L. Katkov and 1 co-author calculate how phonons limit electron mobility in specially coated carbon nanotubes in a 2025 paper. The tubes are zig-zag nanotubes fully coated with hydrogen or fluorine, leaving one-dimensional chains of carbon atoms with pi-bonds to carry current. Mobility measures how easily electrons move, and scattering off phonons, the vibrations of the lattice, is the limiting factor studied here.

Mobility depends periodically on tube diameter through the chirality index, because tubes with an even number of conducting chains escape scattering on one phonon type thanks to mirror symmetry. Overall, the computed phonon-limited mobility values are small. The authors conclude such tubes suit gas sensors better than electronic device elements. Calculations use a self-energy relaxation time approximation inside a non-orthogonal tight-binding model.
arxiv-2509-07814:
Neutrino interactions on water and hydrocarbon are measured in a 2025 particle physics paper led by K. Abe and colleagues from the T2K experiment in Japan. The team uses the WAGASCI-BabyMIND detector, placed off the main beam axis in the T2K near detector hall since 2018. They study charged current reactions that produce no charged pions.

Counts of these events give a total cross section, a measure of how likely the interaction is, for each target material. The detector sits at a different angle from the beam than the other near detector, so it samples a more energetic neutrino stream. Precise cross sections help future experiments turn raw event counts into reliable statements about how neutrinos behave and change type.
arxiv-2509-07914:
Nicholas Di and 2 co-authors widen the reach of a Monte Carlo trick for hard optimisation problems in a 2025 mathematics paper. Many first-order optimisation methods split a problem into pieces handled by proximal operators, mathematical steps that pull a point toward good values. Closed formulas for those steps exist only for limited function classes.

A recent method called HJ-Prox approximates the proximal step by random sampling, drawing on partial differential equation theory, with no formula needed. The authors prove it can be dropped into standard splitting schemes while keeping convergence guarantees. Nonsmooth problems, where the target has sharp corners, appear throughout imaging and machine learning, so a sampling-based step broadens where these trusted algorithms can be applied.
arxiv-2509-08114:
Soft materials under shear can now be watched structurally while their flow is measured, thanks to an instrument paper by Chiara Marraffa and 1 co-author from 2025. Their two-axes shear cell squeezes samples between parallel plates, each driven by a precision linear stage with voice coil motors and feedback control from contactless encoders.

Both strain-controlled and stress-controlled tests are possible, and driving the plates together allows parallel and orthogonal superposition measurements. The cell couples to an optical microscope and a photon correlation imaging setup, so rheology, meaning flow response, and microscopic dynamics are recorded at once. Watching structure and flow together helps explain why gels, pastes, and other soft matter stiffen, yield, or heal under load.
arxiv-2509-08414:
Faint absorption bands in starlight, called diffuse interstellar bands, may carry the fingerprint of buckminsterfullerene ions floating in space. Daniel Majaess and 5 co-authors re-examine one contested band in a 2025 research paper. The band in question sits at a wavelength tied to ionized carbon-60. Its attribution has been debated for thirty years.

The team compared band strengths along eleven sightlines toward stars. The contested band's strength tracked a band already linked to the fullerene ion very closely. Contamination from a neighboring line was removed with careful fitting. Combined with a separate study linking two other bands, three interrelated bands now match laboratory results for the ion. The authors say two weaker candidate bands still need work. Confirming carbon-60 ions in space would anchor a rare case of a known molecule explaining interstellar features.
arxiv-2509-08714:
Ahmed Sadaqa and 1 co-author propose hybrid pruning to compress CNN models for small devices in a 2025 paper. Convolutional networks are accurate but often too large for edge hardware. Pruning removes parts of a network to cut size and delay.

Their framework prunes both channels and layers together. It is inspired by EfficientNet scaling, applied in reverse to shrink a network. Experiments show a notable drop in complexity with only a small loss in accuracy. The pruned models also run with lower latency on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 embedded device. The approach helps deploy vision models where power and memory are tight.
arxiv-2509-09014:
Urdu has more than a quarter-billion speakers and almost no large image-caption datasets, a gap that skews multilingual AI. Umair Hassan closes it in a 2025 research paper written alone. COCO-Urdu derives from the standard MS COCO image collection. It holds tens of thousands of images with several hundred thousand Urdu captions, drawn to keep the original distribution intact.

Captions were machine-translated with a modern multilingual system. A hybrid quality framework then scored each caption for translation quality, visual grounding, and semantic consistency. Weak captions were refined iteratively with open-source language models. Benchmark scores on standard captioning metrics came out consistently strong. Hassan releases both the dataset and the quality pipeline. The release gives Urdu-language vision research its first large public foundation, and a template other low-resource languages can copy.
arxiv-2509-09314:
Thuy Ngoc Nguyen and 2 co-authors measure hidden spatial coordination in teams in a 2025 paper. Fire, military, and rescue teams must align their moves in space with few words and no sight of each other. Past work dealt mostly with sports teams or desk based knowledge work.

Three traits are tracked: how widely members spread their search, how much each sticks to a zone, and how gaps between members adapt. Data come from thirty-four four person teams in an online search and rescue task with limited chat. Zone focus predicts team score well. Gap adaptation shows a mild inverted U, so a middle level is best. Time patterns split top and low teams.
arxiv-2509-09414:
Fifteen years ago a Netflix researcher warned that recommender research was doing it all wrong. Three veterans now argue the field mostly kept doing it. Alan Said, Maria Soledad Pera, and Michael D. Ekstrand revisit that diagnosis in a 2025 position paper. The original critique targeted statistical misreading and methodological shortcuts. The authors find those failures persisting in subtler, more systemic forms beneath new layers of sophistication.

Drawing on recent work about reproducibility, evaluation, environmental cost, and participatory design, they show complexity outrunning introspection. Community initiatives, workshops, and new evaluation frameworks are trying to shift the paradigm. The authors insist metrics and tooling alone will not suffice. The field must reframe what its research is for, whom it serves, and how its knowledge gets validated. Their call is for epistemic humility and human impact to sit at the center of recommender research.
arxiv-2509-10114:
MohammadAli Hamidi and 3 co-authors present a light method for judging face image quality in a 2025 paper. Face recognition systems fail more often on poor photos, so a fast quality check helps filter bad inputs. General image quality tools miss face-specific flaws, while the strongest face-specific models are heavy to run.

Their method joins two compact neural networks, MobileNetV3-Small and ShuffleNetV2, and averages their predictions. Training used a loss that combines plain error with a term rewarding correlation with human judgments. On the VQualA benchmark the method reached correlation scores near the top of the field. It stayed inside strict efficiency limits. That suits phones, cameras, and other devices with little computing power.
arxiv-2509-10214:
Yannik Kopyciok and 2 co-authors hunt for spies inside the Monero network in this 2025 paper. Monero is a privacy-focused cryptocurrency, and its peer-to-peer network carries transactions and blocks between nodes. Some nodes appear to pose as normal peers while quietly watching others, which would weaken the privacy the currency promises.

The team recorded more than 240 hours of network traffic from five vantage points around the world. They built a formal scheme for defining odd peer behavior, then classified what they saw. Roughly one peer in seven behaved in non-standard ways, in patterns that hint at several monitoring efforts running at once. They released their detection pipeline so node operators can spot and block suspicious peers.
arxiv-2509-10514:
Continuous attractors are stable patterns that neural networks settle into. Shaoxin Tian and seven co-authors give them a geometric treatment in this 2025 study. Brains use such patterns for navigation and memory. Artificial networks use them, too. Yet no single framework described them across architectures.

The authors view the network's state space as a smooth manifold. They link attractor behavior to the eigenvalues of the local Jacobian. That matrix shows how small changes grow or fade. They check the framework against earlier results. They also find a pattern that looks universal. Singular values stratify in the same way across common models and datasets. The hint is that such attractors may be nearly everywhere in neural networks. The framework offers a basis for a general theory.
arxiv-2509-10914:
Somayeh Kianpisheh and 3 co-authors defend federated learning systems with a moving-target strategy in this 2025 paper. In federated learning, edge devices train a shared model, and a poisoned participant can corrupt it. Simple outlier checks on models can fail when devices differ or attacks get clever. The authors instead judge participants by their network traffic, watched over time by recurrent networks.

A defense layer then keeps changing which devices take part in training, so attackers cannot count on staying inside. Deep reinforcement learning tunes that reshuffling against each device's suspected status and channel quality, inside a 6G network model. In tests built around botnet-driven denial-of-service detection, malicious models were excluded more reliably and detection got faster.
arxiv-2509-11114:
Yuqiu Liu, Jialin Song, Manolis Savva, and Wuyang Chen present WildSmoke in this 2025 computer vision paper. Their goal is a reusable smoke asset. One ordinary video of smoke, shot outside a lab, becomes a moving three-dimensional asset. Artists can then reuse and edit it.

Earlier methods need clean, controlled footage. Wild video brings three problems. The smoke must be cut away from its background. Starting particles and camera positions must be set up. Plausible extra viewpoints must be invented. The team tackles all three. The finished asset can also feed a simulator. Users can then restyle how the smoke moves. On test videos, the method beat earlier approaches on reconstruction quality. It also supports realistic editing of the smoke's behavior.
arxiv-2509-11214:
Francesco Preti and five co-authors review the toolkit for reading answers off quantum computers in this 2025 quantum computing paper. Estimating observables is a central chore on near-term hardware. Gradients matter too, since algorithms need tuning. Noisy sampling makes both harder than they look.

The paper surveys standard estimation methods first. Some use quantum amplitude estimation. Others do not. Cost functions and gradients both get covered. The survey tracks how variance grows through circuits. Circuits built from linear combinations of unitaries are included. The team then develops a general gradient framework. It covers gates on any number of qubits. It covers time-dependent control problems too. Detailed circuit layouts serve near-term and fault-tolerant machines.
arxiv-2509-11414:
Abraham Toluwase Owodunni and Sachin Kumar tackle a sore point with multilingual language models. This 2025 paper asks how to teach such a model a new language. Retraining from scratch costs too much. Plain fine-tuning erases old skills. The first training data are rarely on hand for replay.

Their method is Layer-Selective LoRA. Most of the model stays frozen. Small low-rank adapters go only in the first and last layers. Those layers seem to read the input language in and translate back out. An English-like middle does the reasoning. The team added Galician, Swahili, and Urdu in mixes. The method gave the best balance of new gains and old retention. Model arithmetic later added instruction following with no such data in the new tongues.
arxiv-2509-11514:
Zhengxiang Wang and four co-authors test whether vision-language models can follow human conversational shorthand. This 2025 artificial intelligence paper looks at referring expressions. People working together coin new phrases for objects. They reuse those phrases in later chats. An embodied agent would need the same skill.

Seven leading models sat as overhearers. Human pairs played a joint object-matching game on tape. The game ran for several rounds. Every model found the task hard. None improved steadily as it heard more rounds from the same speakers. The humans' phrases grew more settled over those rounds. The team releases its corpus and code. Others can probe the gap between passive watching and true conversational grasp.
arxiv-2509-11614:
Erick Eduardo Ramirez-Torres and eight co-authors turn undersea cables into listening posts. This 2025 sensing paper starts from a risk. Submarine cables carry the world's connectivity. They face accidents and sabotage. Recent Baltic Sea incidents made the risk plain. Radar and satellites cannot watch them at all times.

Distributed acoustic sensing reads vibrations along the fiber itself. A telecom cable becomes a vast sensor array. It works with no ship cooperation. Light and weather do not matter. The authors give a method to detect vessels and gauge their distance. Machine learning sharpens the readings. Ten straight days of varied traffic were studied. Detection scored above ninety percent. Distance error averaged about one hundred forty meters.
arxiv-2509-11714:
Hafza Eman and 3 co-authors build a computer-aided diagnosis system for lung nodules in chest CT scans in a 2025 paper called EMeRALDS. Lung cancer kills largely because diagnosis comes late, so early, exact nodule detection and sorting matter greatly.

The pipeline pairs a detection module with a diagnosis module. Detection adapts a general segmentation model, swapping its visual prompt for a text prompt encoded by a vision-language model. Diagnosis scores how alike segmented nodules and radiomic features are; those features are measurable image traits. Fake medical records made from expert radiologists' assessments add clinical context for the final call. On a public dataset of over a thousand scans, segmentation was strong and malignancy sorting beat fully supervised methods on specificity.
arxiv-2509-11814:
Sigurd Nese reports an ALICE measurement probing gluons inside lead nuclei in a 2025 paper. In ultra-peripheral collisions, two nuclei pass close without hitting head-on. A photon from one can strike a gluon in the other. That hit makes a pair of charm quarks, while the target nucleus breaks apart.

Those charm quarks become charm hadrons or vector mesons that detectors can see. Past work with protons has tightly bounded the proton's gluon spread at low momentum fractions. Nuclear gluon spreads remain much less known. ALICE measured the transverse momentum spread of a specific charm meson at midrapidity. The measure reaches down to zero momentum for the first time. Nese compares the results with model calculations, offering fresh bounds on how gluons fill heavy nuclei.
arxiv-2509-12014:
Entanglement cannot grow without limit, and Donghoon Kim with eight co-authors sharpen that speed limit in 2025 into a statement about the entanglement spectrum itself. The classic small-incremental-entangling theorem bounds the overall rate, but says little about the fine structure of Schmidt coefficients.

Their spectral version bounds Rényi entanglement growth at every order from one half upward and uncovers a decay threshold in the spectrum, beyond which growth is unbounded. The edge case proves both qualitatively and quantitatively optimal. With that control, truncation errors in simulations become rigorously manageable, and a generalized area law follows under an adiabatic-path condition. The payoff: one-dimensional long-range systems admit polynomial bond-dimension approximations for ground, evolved, and thermal states, closing a long-standing quasi-polynomial gap, with an error guarantee for a standard simulation algorithm.
arxiv-2509-12414:
Noemi Fabri, Gino Isidori, and Davide Racco ask whether gravitational waves could reveal a theory of flavor in a 2025 paper. Flavor deconstruction is an extension of the Standard Model that tries to explain why particle families differ. Its link fields form a rich scalar sector with sizable couplings at energies near the TeV scale.

Those conditions can produce strong first-order phase transitions in the early universe, changes akin to boiling that release energy as gravitational waves. The authors identify which parameters control the wave spectrum and its detectability. Signals typically peak at higher frequencies than the millihertz band of the planned LISA observatory, so a LISA detection is possible but not guaranteed. Mid-band proposals match the expected range better.
arxiv-2509-13014:
Xinghu Jin and Xiaolong Zhang prove best rates in 2025 for steady laws of ergodic equations driven by heavy-tail stable noise. Noise is multiplicative and spin-invariant, with tail index in a mid range. Steady laws shift as the index shifts, and the shift rate was open.

In Wasserstein distance the shift is linear in index gap on closed bands. Near the Gaussian end the rate gains a size factor. Both rates are proved sharp via a classic linear system. Past work covered only the end case with added noise. New methods handle the full multiplicative span.
arxiv-2509-13314:
Anosh Joseph and Arpith Kumar test in 2025 a configurational temperature gauge for complex Langevin dynamics in the 3D XY model. Complex Langevin tackles sign problems at finite chemical load, but wrong convergence can hide. A physics-driven check was needed.

The new gauge checks thermodynamic consistency via configurational estimates. It is run beside the drift-decay test across couplings and loads. Dynamics proves sound in the ordered phase, yet fails in the disordered phase. Failure shows up even in runs where sign trouble stays light. The gauge flags bad convergence clearly. Lattice work with complex actions gains a practical guard.
arxiv-2509-13414:
Nikhil Keetha, Norman Muller and 15 co-authors introduce MapAnything in 2025, a single feed-forward transformer for metric 3D reconstruction from one or more images. Optional inputs span camera traits, poses, depth, or partial builds. Output gives metric scene geometry plus cameras in one pass.

A factored form holds depth maps, local ray maps, poses, and one metric scale. That scale lifts local builds into one global metric frame. Shared training across diverse sets plus flexible input mixing covers many tasks: structure from motion, stereo, mono depth, localization, and completion. Tests match or beat specialist feed-forward models with leaner joint training.
arxiv-2509-13714:
Benoit Pit-Claudel, Muriel Médard, and Manya Ghobadi present LINC in a 2025 networking paper. Hybrid backbones mix fiber, satellite, and microwave links. They serve latency-critical users such as financial traders. But weather and blocked sight lines cause bursts of packet loss. Standard protocols misread that loss as congestion, triggering needless slowdowns.

Network coding can repair losses. Yet older schemes need control of both end hosts. LINC instead codes inside the network, link by link. It uses systematic block coding with no host cooperation. The authors model the trade-off between retransmissions and redundant packets. They optimize the coding settings and simulate real backbone topologies. Latency fell by up to about eighteen percent, because wasted retransmissions disappeared.
arxiv-2509-13814:
Kartik Shinde and four co-authors report the findings of the third AutoMin challenge in a 2025 paper, a shared task on turning meeting transcripts into structured minutes automatically. The 2025 edition kept the main minuting task and added question answering over meeting transcripts.

Minuting covered English and Czech across project meetings and European Parliament sessions. The question answering task used project meetings only, in English and in a cross-lingual setting where Czech questions targeted English meetings. Turnout was smaller than in earlier years, with one team entering minuting and two entering question answering. The organizers therefore added several baseline systems of their own, giving a broad evaluation of what current large language models achieve on both tasks.
arxiv-2509-14014:
Francesco Antonio Denisi, Nikolaos Tsakanikas, and Zhixin Xie develop deformation theory for Enriques varieties in a 2025 geometry paper. These varieties arise as quotients of primitive symplectic varieties. The group actions involved do not respect the symplectic form. Only mild singular points are allowed. Deformation theory asks how such spaces can vary in families, and what stays fixed.

The authors establish a local Torelli theorem for these spaces. The local deformation space is captured by period data from their cohomology. That is a landmark structural result. As uses, they describe how certain of these varieties behave under locally trivial deformations. Those changes do not alter the space's local analytic structure. The picture clarifies which features are rigid and which can move.
arxiv-2509-14414:
Rafael S. do Carmo and four co-authors extend a quantum method in 2025 for the travelling salesman problem, finding a short tour through many stops. Variational quantum methods promise gains on hard routing problems, but encodings often demand too many qubits.

Pauli correlation encoding cuts qubit needs sharply and avoids flat training zones. Their warm start version adds a classical bias from the Goemans-Williamson rounding method into the training loss. That bias guides the quantum search toward better tours. Tests recast the salesman problem as a MaxCut problem and run several circuit layers. Warm starting is a pragmatic bridge: classical insight seeds a quantum search instead of leaving it to wander from a blank start.
arxiv-2509-14514:
Jade Kandel, Sriya Kasumarthi and Danielle Szafir study physical therapy for older adults in 2025 and where mixed reality could help. Therapy manages chronic conditions and weakening muscles, yet fatigue, memory loss and travel strain the experience. Remote tools exist but clinics rarely use them.

Interviews with three clinicians and six older patients map the real challenges of therapy care. Mixed reality promises immersive, context aware sessions at home that once needed a clinic visit. The authors compare that promise with practical barriers patients described. Findings point to design needs around guidance, safety and memory support. Technology for ageing users must fit daily limits first, or even powerful systems will sit unused.
arxiv-2509-14614:
Jennifer Brown and Ricardo Suárez study the countable condensation on linear orders in 2025, an equivalence that lumps points together when only countably many points lie between them. Orders that collapse to a single class under this lumping are the focus. Which orders do so needed a clean characterisation.

The authors build a linear order that is universal for all collapsing order types. They also define a multiplication on order types using lexicographic products followed by condensation. Right identities for that multiplication turn out to be exactly the uncountable suborders of the universal order. Order theory gains both a universal example and an algebra for how condensation interacts with products.
arxiv-2509-15314:
Ramón Miranda-Quintana and four co-authors limit coupled cluster sums by seniority in a 2025 chemistry paper. Coupled cluster methods set the bar for electron link gauges, but their cost climbs fast. Seniority counts the unpaired electrons in a wavefunction. Past pair methods stayed in the zero-seniority part alone.

The new seniority-restricted family lets the excitation steps reach picked seniority parts, not all of them and not just one. That picked access scans link effects part by part. Cost and accuracy can then be traded in a tuned way. Strongly linked systems, where many parts matter at once, stand to gain most. The frame turns a knob that past methods had fixed at one setting into a dial users can set.
arxiv-2509-15414:
Yiyang Wu leads a team of eight that forecasts stock price moves. Market data is jumpy, shifts over time, and bends in complex ways, so forecasts are hard. Their model, SPH-Net, is a deep learning system built for time based market data. It first reads time patterns with a vision style model, then refines them with a shared focus step that weighs global and local links.

They test the model on eight stock data sets, from tech firms to energy firms. Each set uses six standard market measures, such as open, close, and volume. The model beats rival systems on all scores they track. The team credit its joint focus step, which catches both broad trends and short swings in the data.
arxiv-2509-15514:
Junbiao Pang, Tianyang Cai, and Baochang Zhang shrink neural networks to very few bits without losing much skill. Training a network while it is shrunk is called quantization aware training. At extremely low bit counts, the shrinking warps what the network learns. The team argue this bias is why shrunk models lag full ones.

Their method, MEC-Quant, sets a training goal based on entropy, a measure of how much a code can say. They make that goal trainable by using the shortest code length as a stand in. A mixture of experts form speeds the math and handles skewed value ranges. Tests on vision tasks show the method beats rivals. It pushes low bit training to new limits.
arxiv-2509-15614:
Sajib Biswas leads a team that sums up online news stories by picking key sentences. News volume is huge, so short sums help readers and site managers alike. Their method keeps the story's own sentences and meaning. They build it on a large set of over a million story and summary pairs.

Text is first turned into number codes by a language model called BERT. The task is then cast as a yes or no choice for each sentence. They try several models, from a simple regression to memory networks that track order. The memory network wins, beating a lead sentences base line and simpler models on two score types. The work supports auto sums for news sites.
arxiv-2509-15714:
Jonas Mayer Martins leads a team that teaches a small language model through feedback on its stories. Children learn language by interacting, not by listening alone. Big models, by contrast, learn by guessing the next word over huge text piles. The team ask whether high level feedback can shrink the data a model needs.

A student model writes stories, and a teacher model grades them on ease of reading, flow, and inventiveness. The team vary how much plain pre-training comes before the feedback loop. With just one million words in the loop, story skill grows as much as with hundreds of millions of words of plain training. Feedback, they find, is highly data efficient.
arxiv-2509-16314:
When a massive star explodes, the radioactive nickel it forges shapes the light we see for months. David Vartanyan and six co-authors run the first three-dimensional study of how that nickel spreads in a family of exploding red giant stars. Their codes follow the blast from core bounce through breakout and into free expansion.

The nickel's main tilt, set in the first seconds, survives all the way out. Nickel punches through the oxygen shell and mixes deep into the outer envelope in many models. The leftover neutron star tends to kick the opposite way. These patterns link early blast physics to what telescopes later see.
arxiv-2509-16414:
The highest-energy neutrinos in nature can be caught by listening for radio pulses from their crashes in polar ice. Marco Stein Muzio reports the status of the first array-wide search with the Askaryan Radio Array, five stations of antennas buried deep in South Pole ice. The search draws on about twenty-eight station-years of data, the most the array has gathered.

Above a set energy, the search should be the most sensitive of any neutrino detector, enough to probe a flux hinted by another observatory. The effort also proves that array-wide searches work, a need for the much larger radio arrays now planned.
arxiv-2509-16614:
Bojan Derajić, Sebastian Bernhard, and Wolfgang Hönig work on keeping robots safe in a 2025 control paper. A barrier function acts like an invisible fence that a robot must not cross. Designing such fences by hand is hard. Learned fences help, but they must adapt to what the robot sees around it.

Their method learns a fence that adjusts to sensor input. A second network shapes that adjustment on the fly. Tests ran in simulation and on real hardware. A ground robot and a drone both took part. Success rates rose, and the method held up in new places. Safer fences could widen where robots can work alone.
arxiv-2509-16714:
Shuli Chen and co-authors study how glass relaxes in a 2025 math and physics paper. When glass settles, its stiffness fades in a stretched pattern over time. A series formula is often used to mimic that pattern for ease of computing. The team give that shortcut a firm proof.

They link the pattern to clusters of eigenvalues, which are key numbers of a matrix. Their theory matches numerical checks. They also solve a reverse problem: reading the clusters to infer traits of the glass. Such work helps engineers model glass in screens, fibers, and lenses with more trust in the math behind the shortcut.
arxiv-2509-16814:
Mattea Reid and co-authors build a phone app for eye scans at home in a 2025 paper. Photos of the retina can flag diseases like glaucoma. Machine models can read those photos, but clinics still need human checks. The team aim for a home tool that tracks change over time, not one that replaces doctors.

The app folds in a glaucoma detection model. It also measures how twisted the eye's vessels are. Users upload photos on a regular basis. The app then shows trends in eye measures tied to age-related disease. Home tracking could catch change early and prompt a clinic visit sooner.
arxiv-2509-17514:
Tianyi Chen, Pengxiao Lin, Zhiwei Wang, and Zhi-Qin John Xu probe a blind spot in the Mamba architecture. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that state space models such as Mamba rival attention-based designs and scale linearly with sequence length. What Mamba cannot do, compared with transformers, has stayed fuzzy, so the team built synthetic tasks to expose the gap.

The tasks reveal an asymmetry bias from Mamba's nonlinear convolution. On composite function and reversed sequence matching, Mamba strongly favors compositional answers over symmetrical ones. It struggles to match a sequence against its own reverse. Careful tests trace the flaw not to the state space core but to the convolution before it, which fuses tokens in an uneven direction. The findings name a concrete weakness, the authors' Achilles heel, and point to design fixes for future sequence models.
arxiv-2509-17614:
N. Diepstraten, L. M. T. Somers, and J. A. van Oijen built a shortcut model for gas injectors in engines. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves simulations of gas-fueled combustion engines, where modeling the flow inside an injector is costly. Their Global Conservation Model instead computes the nozzle exit state from reservoir conditions plus two measured coefficients, one for discharge and one for momentum.

Those coefficients come from standard flow bench tests or a trusted simulation, and the model can use real gas thermodynamics, as engines often require. Validation covers three common injector types, pressures up to a high ceiling, and both subsonic and choked flow, at bench and engine conditions. With real gas physics, the model's exit values land within a small margin of full simulations. That margin sits inside the spread of lab momentum measurements, so the shortcut can safely spare the costly inner-flow runs.
arxiv-2509-17714:
Feihu Liu, Sihao Tao, and Guoce Xin tackle a sign puzzle in a branch of shape counting. Their 2025 paper looks at Ehrhart counts for a product shape built from a pyramid and a cube. The core ask is which signs the terms of these counts can take.

For shapes in four or more dims, they find shapes where many low terms are below zero and high terms stay above zero. They also prove five ways to lift a sign pattern from a small shape to a larger one. Those tools settle the full ask for dims seven, eight, and nine.
arxiv-2509-17814:
Marcin Tombinski sorts maps that keep shortest paths intact. His 2025 maths paper works in complex domains, where a Kobayashi metric sets the length of curves. A map keeps geodesics if the image of each such curve lies inside one such curve in the target.

Tombinski aims to list all maps with that trait for key cases. Those cases use curves through a point in the unit disc or the unit ball. He also gives some results for the full complex plane and for higher complex dims. The list form makes the rare trait easy to check.
arxiv-2509-18014:
Joshua Ward and 3 co-authors build a test kit to audit if fake data still leaks who was in the real set. Their 2025 tool, Synth-MIA, deals with tabular data, such as rows of patient or client facts. Fake sets are said to guard privacy, but plain likeness scores miss the real risk.

Attack tests that guess if a person was in the source set give a sharper read. Many such attacks exist, each in its own form, and none wins all the time. The kit runs a pack of attacks through one simple interface. It reports the worst leak found, so risk is not understated.
arxiv-2509-18314:
Training language models to reason is held back by one hard problem. When a long answer earns a single score at the end, which steps deserve the credit? Hieu Tran, Zonghai Yao, and Hong Yu study this credit problem in their 2025 paper. They focus on tasks where the final answer can be checked, like math and medical questions.

Their method first groups sampled answers into a tree that shares common opening steps. From that tree they compute a value for each shared opening, with no extra trained model. Their algorithm, TEMPO, adds tree-based fixes to the group scoring method GRPO at branch points only. On two sizes of the Qwen3 model, TEMPO beat PPO and GRPO on test sets in and out of its training area. It also reached higher accuracy in about the same training time.
arxiv-2509-18614:
Monte Carlo methods estimate hard quantities by random sampling, and quantum computers may speed some of them up. Jose Blanchet, Mark S. Squillante, Mario Szegedy, and Guanyang Wang wrote this 2025 tutorial to connect the two fields. It is aimed at readers who know classic simulation and want the quantum view. Finance supplies the running examples.

The tutorial starts with Grover's search algorithm to build intuition for quantum speed-ups. It then steps slowly to amplitude estimation, the quantum tool behind faster counting and integration. A hands-on Python and Qiskit example applies the ideas to a finance problem. The closing part weighs open hurdles in scaling quantum simulation. The authors keep the pace slow and the math tied to code. It serves as a bridge for simulation experts eyeing quantum methods.
arxiv-2509-19214:
Finding the largest tight-knit group in a network is a classic hard problem, and the k-plex relaxes it: each member may miss links to at most k others. Xiaofan Li and two co-authors attack that maximum k-plex problem with quantum computing. The relaxed model fits real networks better, since real data are noisy and perfect cliques are rare. Uses range from community detection to spotting covert networks. Classic algorithms have steadily cut the running time, but the problem stays hard.

The team designs two gate-based quantum algorithms that improve the time scaling further, and a third that recasts the problem for quantum annealers, using qubits more sparingly. They test proof-of-principle versions on IBM's quantum simulator and a D-Wave machine. The approach should extend to other clique relaxations, like n-clans and n-clubs, widening its reach in network analysis.
arxiv-2509-19414:
Last passage percolation is a growth model where a path collects random weights and the best path wins. Pantelis Tassopoulos and Sourav Sarkar study a version driven by Brownian motion with uneven starting heights. They ask how the law of the path's steps compares with plain Brownian motion. Their answer uses a density ratio, and they show that ratio stays well behaved in a strong sense.

For flat starting heights, they pin down the exact growth rate of that ratio's size as the number of paths grows. The flat case links to a classic model of repelling random paths. As a use case, they show the same good behavior for toy models of the KPZ growth class. These results firm up the math base under a widely used model of random growth.
arxiv-2509-19514:
Weak lensing maps how dark matter bends light, but hot gas pushed around by stars and black holes clouds the signal. Calvin Leung and six co-authors propose a way to cancel that clouding with fast radio bursts. These brief radio flashes carry a measure of the gas they passed through. By pairing lensing maps with burst data, the gas effect can be subtracted with no gas model at all.

The team tested the trick on the FLAMINGO computer simulations of the universe. At the scales that matter most, the method cut sensitivity to gas effects by about ten times. New radio surveys and lensing surveys are coming online in the same years. Their overlap could give cleaner dark matter maps than either could alone.
arxiv-2509-19714:
Operator theory on the unit disc gains new room when weights bend the rules of size. Ashish Kujur and Md. Ramiz Reza study higher-order weighted Dirichlet-type spaces whose weights come from a poly-superharmonic family. They prove a higher-order version of the Littlewood-Paley formula, a tool that converts energy integrals into countable sums. That formula links repeated Laplacians of the weight to defect operators of the shift.

From those links they define Dirichlet-type operators of finite order. The class covers several known families, including m-isometries and their expansive cousins. Every cyclic operator in the class is then modeled as the shift on a matching weighted space. One model theory thus unifies cases once treated apart. Such unification helps operator theorists transfer results between families.
arxiv-2509-19914:
A thief packing a knapsack online faces items one by one, never knowing what comes next. Matthias Gehnen, Kübra Güven, and Moritz Stocker add two twists: items may be packed repeatedly, and packed items may be removed for free. Value must be maximized under a fixed weight cap. Online problems usually deny deterministic algorithms any good guarantee.

This variant is a rare exception. The authors give a deterministic algorithm with a competitive ratio near one point seven, matched by a lower bound. When value equals weight, the ratio improves to exactly three halves. Removability is the liberating twist: regret can be undone. The problem is playful in dress but speaks to real allocation under uncertainty, from bandwidth to cargo.
arxiv-2509-20014:
Atom-thin semiconductors could shrink transistors further, but the gate insulator touching them can make or break performance. Theresia Knobloch leads a large author team in setting criteria for choosing that dielectric. Reports of promising candidates abound, yet each study grades a few traits in isolation. Capacitive control, leakage, reliability, and fabrication ease all matter at once.

The perspective paper formulates general standards for a good gate stack. The interface with the channel shapes nearly every device metric, the authors stress. Two-dimensional channels have no bulk to hide interface flaws. A shared checklist lets labs compare claims honestly. Foundries weighing these materials for future chips need exactly that discipline. The work is guidance for a field rich in demos and poor in consensus.
arxiv-2509-20514:
Students who build their own processor learn computing from the inside out. Ian McDougall and three co-authors assemble a teaching-ready RISC-V ecosystem in a 2025 arXiv paper. The RISC-V instruction set is free and open, unlike commercial rivals. Many open implementations exist, yet few suit the classroom well.

The authors first propose criteria for judging a processor ecosystem by teaching value. They then score existing open-source implementations against those criteria. Gaps found in that audit shape their own comprehensive solution, released openly for other instructors. The framework is composable, so each course can take only the components it needs. A limited study of student feedback rounds out the report. The work targets teachers and hobbyists who want real hardware logic without license barriers.
arxiv-2509-20714:
A hidden trigger inside a neural network can be a weapon or a shield. Anh Tu Ngo, Anupam Chattopadhyay, and Subhamoy Maitra examine both faces of cryptographic backdoors in a 2025 paper. They build on ideas from earlier theoretical work on such backdoors.

On the attack side, a carefully planted backdoor lets someone fool the network in a way that stays invisible. On the defense side, the same machinery supports three tools. These are a robust watermarking scheme for models, a protocol for user authentication, and a protocol for tracking unauthorized sharing of a model. The authors argue that all three practical protocols are provably robust, giving the backdoor concept a constructive use.
arxiv-2509-20814:
Error bounds tell how far a point is from the solution set of a system of inequalities. Zhou Wei, Michel Thera, and Jen-Chih Yao study how hard those bounds are to compute in a 2025 mathematics paper. The topic goes back to a classic 1952 result by Hoffman.

The authors recast the problem as a finite family of min-max optimization problems on the unit sphere, one for each subset of rows of the matrix. They then prove the problem lies outside P, the class of problems solvable in polynomial time. Seventy years after Hoffman's bound, the work shows the intrinsic complexity of computing such bounds is genuinely high.
arxiv-2509-20914:
Faint stars at the edge of a small galaxy can reveal whether it is being torn apart. Kyosuke Sato and nine co-authors report such a finding for the Ursa Minor dwarf spheroidal galaxy in a 2025 paper accepted by the Astrophysical Journal Letters. Deep Subaru telescope images made the work possible.

The team mapped main-sequence stars along the galaxy's major and minor axes. Beyond the nominal tidal radius, they found a clear excess of stars along the minor axis. Number density profiles in seven directions, fitted with a two-part function, show shallower falloff toward that axis. The symmetry of the extended component remains uncertain. Still, the discovery suggests Ursa Minor's outskirts are more spread out than its tidy inner shape implies.
arxiv-2509-21014:
Neural networks steer robots and vehicles, but they can misbehave on odd inputs and their software stacks are hard to secure. Federico Nesti and six co-authors apply the simplex architecture to that problem in a 2025 paper on safe autonomous systems. The design keeps a trusted fallback beside the smart controller.

The architecture runs two isolated execution environments. A high-performance channel hosts the deep learning controller, with its speed and unpredictability. A safety channel runs simpler, verified logic on a more predictable stack. A decision module switches control when the smart channel looks unsafe. Isolation also shrinks the attack surface for cyber threats. The authors present the software design as a route to deploying learning-based autonomy with safety, security, and timing guarantees.
arxiv-2509-21314:
Very high energy gamma rays from the galaxy M87 vary between quiet periods and flares. It comes from Nibedita Mondal and 2 co-authors. M87 has a jet that emits light across many energies. New data from the LHAASO observatory extend the range of very high energy gamma ray work. The data also allow study of how the source varies over time. The authors model both quiet and flare states.

Their model uses two zones in the jet. In the quiet state, gamma rays come from both the inner sub parsec jet and the large kilo parsec jet. In the flare state, the inner jet dominates. Spectral and timing traits of the TeV gamma rays match this two zone picture. The inner jet contribution rises sharply during flares.
arxiv-2509-21514:
Knowledge tracing models predict what a student knows, but they rarely know when to stay silent. Joshua Mitton and 3 co-authors add selective prediction to tracing in a 2025 paper. Uncertain predictions are deferred to a human teacher. Monte Carlo dropout, which samples from a network with random units dropped, quantifies that uncertainty. No retraining of the base model is required.

Three architectures were tested on the Eedi mathematics data set. Abstaining on the most uncertain fifth of predictions lifted accuracy by a few points. Gains also appeared in AUC and F1 scores. The deferred set held far higher error rates than the kept set, showing sharp targeting. The pattern held across question difficulty levels and stayed fair across student ability levels.
arxiv-2509-21614:
Smart gradient methods dominate training, yet their small learning rate behaviour lacked a unified random picture. Luca Callisti and 2 co-authors analyse smart random gradient descent in a 2025 paper. Random modified equations supply the system, following earlier work by Li and co-authors. Working non stop random dynamics are derived for popular smart methods. Sampling noise plays a surprising role in the limit.

In the limiting dynamics, sampling induced noise appears as independent Brownian motions. Those motions drive both setting evolution and gradient second momentum evolution separately. Scaling rules between learning rate and key hyperparameters are also investigated, extending Malladi and co-authors. All nontrivial limiting dynamics are described. The analysis clarifies how smart methods behave when learning rates shrink.
arxiv-2509-21914:
Pawel Weichbroth and Tomasz Szot study how mobile apps can avoid usability problems before they are built. Phones limit screen size and power, and user groups differ widely in their needs. Their 2025 paper notes that usability stands out among app quality concerns, yet few studies list concrete steps developers can take to prevent problems rather than fix them later.

The authors surveyed twenty practitioners who design and build mobile software. They coded the answers in the experts' own words to keep the original meanings intact. From that material they built the MUG-10 framework: ten guidelines and three activities that apply broadly. Working closely with users, testing with them, and gathering their feedback came up again and again at every stage. The authors suggest future work should test how well the framework works in live projects and across different groups.
arxiv-2509-22114:
Decompiling turns a program's machine code back into readable source, and language models have become a promising tool for it. Hanzhuo Tan and six co-authors present SK2Decompile in this 2025 paper. Existing model-based decompilers still lose the original structure of a program and invent poor names for its parts. The authors split the job into two phases, which they call skeleton and skin.

First, a structure recovery model translates the binary into an intermediate form that keeps the control flow and data structures, with all names replaced by placeholders. Reinforcement learning rewards it for structures that obey compiler rules. Second, an identifier naming model fills in meaningful names, trained with its own reward for closeness to the reference code's meaning. Because the phases are separate, structure and naming can improve independently. In evaluations, the system beat leading baselines on re-executability and on name quality across two benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-22214:
Leonardo Iurada, Simone Bombari, Tatiana Tommasi, and Marco Mondelli show that a trained model can leak its entire training set under the right conditions. Memorization in deep learning is usually discussed as fitting labels. Their 2025 paper, accepted at ICLR 2026, reframes it as reconstruction: can the individual training samples be recovered from the model's parameters? In the random features model, they prove recovery is possible once the parameter count exceeds the sample count multiplied by the data's dimension.

The argument is geometric: above that threshold, the span of the training samples in feature space pins down each sample in input space. The authors test it beyond the tidy model, on two-layer networks and on deep residual networks, where it performs well. The result sharpens a privacy-relevant question for large models: past a certain size, the training data is, in principle, inside the weights.
arxiv-2509-22514:
Emanuele Caputo, Francesco Nobili, and Tommaso Rossi carry classic shape comparisons to rough spaces. On smooth spaces, Ricci curvature bounds yield comparisons for volume, diameter, and eigenvalues. The team works on metric measure spaces with a synthetic, variable Ricci lower bound. They allow the bound to dip below a constant, as long as the total deficit is integrable, meaning small in aggregate.

Their method localizes the problem to one-dimensional weighted intervals, where comparison estimates are tractable. From there they recover three classics in the rough setting: the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, the Myers diameter bound, and the Cheng eigenvalue comparison. The results widen comparison geometry beyond smooth manifolds.
arxiv-2509-22914:
Teaching robots by guiding their arms or by remote control is slow and needs costly gear. Rohan Walia and 5 co-authors present ARMimic, which learns from passive human demos in augmented reality. A user wears a consumer headset while a fixed camera watches the work space. The system tracks hands, shows a virtual robot overlay, and senses depth in real time.

Those parts keep demos safe and within what a real robot arm can do. One learning pipeline treats human and virtual robot paths as the same kind of data. On two tasks, demos took half the time of remote control. Trained robots also beat a strong baseline on task success.
arxiv-2509-23014:
Yihao Sun and 3 co-authors plan robot actions with unified multimodal models that both take in and produce images and text. Most prior planners reason in words alone, which limits what they can foresee. Their framework, Uni-Plan, lets one model play three roles at once. It acts as the policy, the world dynamics model, and the value judge.

Imagined futures can contain fake dynamics, so they add a guard. The same model grades its own imagined steps and filters out invalid ones. On embodied tasks, Uni-Plan raised success rates well past vision-language baselines. It needed no expert demos and scaled well with more training data.
arxiv-2509-23314:
Transformers that loop their latent steps can spend more compute before speaking, and those loops have a shape. Francesco Pappone, Donato Crisostomi, and Emanuele Rodolà map that geometry. Inside one looped block, updates act as small refinements. Across blocks, the state drifts on a larger scale. Over training, loop steps shrink and turn more orthogonal.

That pattern suggests finer local modeling, not just pushing one way. It also motivates a new early-exit rule. The rule reads the second-order change in step size. It beat KL-based and first-order exits on performance, stability, and time cost.
arxiv-2509-23514:
A classic rule tells where a quantum particle's energy levels sit in a smooth well. Abdelwaheb Ifa, the sole author, gives a fresh form of the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rule at second order for a Schrödinger operator. His setting is the algebraic and microlocal framework of Helffer and Sjöstrand. The rule holds exactly when a Gram matrix, built from inner products of WKB solutions under a flux norm, cannot be inverted.

The condition comes from a microlocal Wronskian, not from the usual matching of solutions. Action-angle variables simplify it further. Ifa notes the route may extend to matrix-valued Hamiltonians, such as the Bogoliubov-de Gennes type used for superconductors.
arxiv-2509-23914:
Colloids drifting in a cellular flow do not quite follow the fluid when salt gradients push them sideways. Florence Raynal and 2 co-authors study that diffusiophoresis experimentally in a two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard cell. The colloids gain a small extra velocity along the log gradient of salt concentration. Theory from Volk and co-workers in 2022 predicted either enhanced transport or blockage, depending on a blockage coefficient.

Using high-dynamic-range light-induced fluorescence, the team tracks the colloid concentration field at large Peclet number. Agreement with theory is good even though the experiment is spatially uneven and transient. Injecting salt and colloids at both ends sped transport; injecting them together blocked it when the phoretic push was strong.
arxiv-2509-24014:
Diffusion language models are slow partly because their attention cannot borrow the sparse tricks of left-to-right models. Zeqing Wang and 4 co-authors first map how sparsity actually behaves in these models: patterns differ per head, stay similar across denoising steps, and the early steps matter most. Their method, SparseD, precomputes head-specific sparse patterns once and reuses them at every step.

Full attention guards the early steps, then sparse attention takes over. The result is acceleration the authors call lossless: at very long contexts with many denoising steps, SparseD ran up to one and a half times faster than FlashAttention in their tests.
arxiv-2509-24114:
Angelos Karakonstantakis and 2 co-authors simulate how heavy particles scatter near black holes and naked singularities. Both sit in the Reissner-Nordström geometry, where charge shapes the space. The team sent in a stream of particles with fixed spin of motion and a range of energies, then solved for their paths.

Particles bounced off a black hole stayed in a tight, stream-like family with a narrow spread of bend angles. Near a naked singularity, particles scattered in all directions in their plane. The team traces the split to a barrier near the unstable circular orbit, plus a horizon that swallows particles in one case and a repulsive core in the other. Such contrasts could show up in tidal disruption events.
arxiv-2509-24314:
A shaky first read of evidence can send medical reasoning down a wrong branch that ends in a confident error. Hongjun Liu and 6 co-authors built MedMMV, a multi-agent framework meant to keep clinical reasoning stable and checkable. Short, varied rollouts diversify the first steps instead of locking onto one path.

Intermediate steps are grounded in a structured evidence graph watched by a hallucination detector. A combined uncertainty scorer then merges candidate paths. Across six medical benchmarks, accuracy rose by up to about an eighth. Blind physician reviews found the reasoning more truthful without loss of content. The design offers a robust route for high-stakes clinical support.
arxiv-2509-24414:
Anomaly hunting in sensor streams is hard because space and time effects tangle together in multivariate data. Tao Yin and 7 co-authors noticed that samples scatter in high-dimensional space, and anomalous ones scatter much more. They formalize that spread as scattering, measured by the mean pairwise distance between representations, and use it as a signal.

Their system, ScatterAD, pairs a topological encoder for graph-shaped scattering with a temporal encoder that reins in excess spread across time steps. A contrastive fusion keeps the two views complementary. Theory links their objective to sharper, more consistent representations. On public benchmarks, ScatterAD set the top scores for multivariate anomaly detection.
arxiv-2510-00014:
Luo and colleagues group stocks by how they move together. Sector labels can mislead here. Apple and Microsoft share a tech label. Yet the two stocks reacted differently during recent market shocks. The team looks for groups whose prices rise and fall in sync at some times. At other times those stocks drift apart.

Their tool is called FTSCommDetector. It reads price records for many stocks at once. A two-scale design tracks both fast shifts and slow trends. A fixed link map with shifting weights shows which stocks move together. Tests used four market lists. They were the S and P 100, 500, and 1000 lists and the Nikkei 225 index. Scores beat the best tools by 3.5 to 11.1 percent. Results barely changed when the time window grew from 60 to 120 days. The method needs no tuning for each new data set.
arxiv-2510-00114:
Srimoyee Sen and Varun Vaidya wrote this 2025 theory paper on hot, dense matter with a chiral imbalance. Such matter may occur in supernovae and in merging neutron stars. An imbalance between left- and right-handed electrons can, in principle, grow strong magnetic fields. Earlier work said the effect dies unless the imbalance is very large.

Sen and Vaidya rechecked that claim over a wider range of conditions. At higher temperatures the old verdict flips, and fields can grow from a much smaller imbalance. They also find a new effect in which density ripples drive a current that heats the matter fast. Even a modest imbalance could dump huge energy within seconds this way. The authors suggest this heating may shape the dynamics of supernovae and neutron star mergers.
arxiv-2510-00314:
Xiaotang Zhang and three colleagues published this 2025 graphics paper on animating two characters who interact closely. Motion in-betweening fills the movement between poses an animator sets by hand. For single characters the problem is well studied, but partners who box or dance must match each other precisely. Their method, Cross-Space In-Betweening, models each character's motion across several representation spaces at once.

Dense interaction constraints shrink the space of valid motions, so quality decays over long takes. One fix learns the repeating patterns inside an interaction to sustain it. Another fix refines the drifting latent state to stop pose errors from piling up. The system produced long, controllable boxing and dancing sequences across many key poses. Quantitative tests and user studies both favored it over existing methods. The authors note that poses demanding unseen interactions can still defeat the model.
arxiv-2510-00414:
Matthew Yue and five colleagues published this 2025 paper presenting RELATE-Sim, a simulator for long-term romantic relationships. Dating apps optimize the first meeting, not the years that follow, the authors note. Their simulator instead stages the turning points where couples thrive or falter. Two language model agents, one per partner, act out each scripted scene.

A central Scene Master frames each turning point, such as exclusivity talks or conflict and repair. After each scene it infers how states like clarity and commitment have shifted. The team validated the approach on 71 real couples followed for two years. Simulation-aware forecasts beat a baseline that used partner personas alone. The runs also surface readable markers, like whether repair attempts get acknowledged, that explain diverging paths. The platform aims to shift relationship research from matchmaking toward maintenance.
arxiv-2510-00514:
Samuel Pfisterer and three colleagues published this 2025 paper building a speech corpus from Europe's parliamentary recordings. Speech recognizers need mountains of transcribed audio, and most languages starve. Existing multilingual sets spread thin, leaving most languages with scraps. The team's pipeline harvests debates from twenty-two parliaments and aligns text to audio automatically.

A two-stage aligner copes with loose, non-verbatim transcripts and very long recordings. The haul exceeded sixty-one thousand hours of aligned speech segments. Nineteen languages cleared one thousand hours each, and all twenty-two cleared five hundred. Fine-tuning an existing recognizer on the corpus cut word error rates sharply. The average reduction across low-resource test languages was about forty-two percent. The authors release both dataset and pipeline, so any audio with a rough transcript can become training data elsewhere.
arxiv-2510-00614:
Chen Lu and four colleagues published this 2025 physics paper showing a textbook route to ferromagnetism can fail. The Stoner rule says interactions should tip a metal toward aligned spins when spin response peaks at zero momentum and diverges. The rival order shares that same instability channel, the authors note. In a two-orbital model near special band fillings, the rival order wins instead.

Orbital-resolved spin fluctuations, amplified by strong hopping between orbitals, stabilize the rival magnetic order. A quantum phase transition then separates it from ferromagnetism at a critical Hund coupling. The tiebreaker is which response diverges faster as interactions approach the critical strength. The authors propose directional spin current patterns as an experimental fingerprint of the switch. Nonlocal spin transport measurements could catch the uneven response in real materials. The work makes the rival order a central player in correlated electron systems.
arxiv-2510-00914:
Azzouz, Vuissoz, and Laprie, working with CNRS, Inria, and Inserm teams in Nancy, invert speech acoustics into vocal tract shapes in this 2025 arXiv paper on speech science. Acoustic-to-articulatory inversion recovers how the throat and mouth were configured from the sound. Work relied on electromagnetic articulography, whose glued sensors reach only the front articulators. This study trains on a real-time MRI database holding more than three hours of speech, with segmented articulator contours.

Bidirectional LSTM models learned to predict the tract contour, from glottis through tongue and velum to lips. The authors tested inverting each articulator separately against inverting all of them simultaneously. Average test error came to 1.65 millimetres, essentially at the 1.62 millimetre pixel size of the images. They describe the result as the first complete inversion of the vocal tract.
