Such maps could serve speech therapy, phonetics, and silent-speech interfaces.
arxiv-2510-01114:
Levine and five co-authors present PRISM-Consult in this 2025 arXiv paper on clinical decision support. Emergency department care arrives as a stream of events, from complaints and vital signs to lab orders and diagnoses. Predicting the likely diagnosis early can guide time-critical choices, but the first signals are sparse and noisy. PRISM-Consult turns each episode into tokens and routes it, from just its first few tokens, to a specialist model.

Specialists cover cardiac-vascular, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and psychogenic domains, all sharing one small transformer backbone. On real emergency department cohorts, the specialists trained smoothly with low perplexity in every domain. The router scored high on routing quality and saved large amounts of compute versus consulting every specialist. The authors outline the validation steps still needed before prospective clinical deployment.
arxiv-2510-01414:
Li and Sonthalia map exactly when overfitting turns benign, stays tempered, or goes catastrophic in a spiked regression world. Modern models interpolate training data yet generalize, a puzzle with sharp edges. Their analysis uses data with one dominant direction, the spike, and varies its strength and alignment with the target.

An exact risk formula sorts behavior into the three regimes cleanly. Stronger spikes can, surprisingly, trigger catastrophe before benignity in well-aligned problems. Alignment with the spike sometimes harms rather than helps, against intuition. The counterintuitive alignment effect persisted when checked in nonlinear models. Minimum-norm interpolation is the solution concept under the microscope. Risk decomposes into interpretable parts inside the formula. Aspect ratio, the overparameterization dial, steers the regime boundaries. Double descent is the famous backdrop for the classification. Intuition about alignment fails in carefully mapped territory.
arxiv-2510-01514:
Curtis, Kasiviswanathan, and Eisty investigate why open-source maintainers stamp issues as wontfix, mining over three thousand popular GitHub repositories. The label closes issues permanently, yet its prevalence and motives were never systematically mapped. Their mixed-method study counts usage quantitatively and reads reasoning qualitatively.

About thirty percent of projects apply the label to at least some issues. User-submitted bug reports and feature requests attract it most often. Open coding distilled eight recurring themes, spanning user-side causes and maintainer decisions. The map helps communities reject work more transparently and consistently. Datasets are published openly for replication attempts. Multiple coders resolved disagreements by consensus to discipline subjectivity. Popular active repositories bound the study's external validity honestly. Private repositories may play by different rejection norms. Thirty percent adoption makes wontfix a major governance tool. Rejection is a decision communities should understand.
arxiv-2510-01614:
Lee and co-authors build a follow-up method that listens to one slice of a gravitational-wave burst at a time. Dying massive stars should broadcast waves shaped by the instabilities that drive their explosions. Low tones point to a sloshing shock instability or bubbling convection, so isolating frequencies tests explosion theory.

The dedicated-frequency approach reruns burst analysis inside chosen bands with minimal assumptions. Waveforms from five explosion models, with different low-frequency strengths, supplied the trials. Low-band follow-ups helped read the mechanism behind candidate events. One loud real event gained significance when only its high tones were examined. Focused listening extracts physics that broad scans blur. BayesWave supplies the follow-up machinery inside the framework. A 2019 supernova served as the demonstration case. Silence in the low band also teaches, since models predict different strengths there. Focused bands keep noise from diluting the signal.
arxiv-2510-02114:
Shen proposes federated segmentation training for clients that hold no labeled data in this 2025 paper. Federated learning promises privacy, but domain shift between hospitals or cities degrades segmentation models. Most methods quietly assume clients can label their data, which real deployments rarely allow. The proposed task starts from a labeled server dataset, then trains across unlabeled clients without touching the source again.

The framework, FRIEREN, borrows knowledge from a vision foundation model. A vision-language decoder guided by CLIP text embeddings sharpens semantic distinctions. Weak-to-strong consistency learning trains local models on their own pseudo-labels robustly. Benchmarks covered synthetic-to-real transfer and clear-to-adverse-weather shifts. The framework handled both settings effectively. Language guidance substitutes for the missing annotations by naming what regions mean. The work defines a harder, more honest federated task and a first working solution for it.
arxiv-2510-02214:
Baldwin and Sivek prove that a knot has only finitely many fibered predecessors in this 2025 topology paper. Ribbon concordance orders knots by the existence of a special cobordism without local maxima. Gordon introduced the relation and conjectured it is a genuine partial order. Fibered knots, whose complements sweep around a surface, are central examples.

Given any knot, the authors show only finitely many hyperbolic fibered knots sit below it in this order. Hence every fibered knot has finitely many hyperbolic predecessors at all. The proof mixes Floer homology maps from ribbon cobordisms with the monodromy's fixed points for fibered knots. A second result bounds volumes across the relation for hyperbolic fibered knots. Those inequalities use work of Cornish and Kojima-McShane on surface automorphisms. Finiteness tames a relation that might have sprawled infinitely. Knot theorists gain new control over how fibered knots can precede one another.
arxiv-2510-02314:
Ke and co-authors attack 3D scene models by planting objects that only some viewpoints can see. Their 2025 security paper targets 3D Gaussian Splatting, a popular scene format. Such scenes are built from many training photos. Poisoned photos can smuggle fake content into the scene. The team hides illusory objects in sparse regions of the scene. A density estimate finds those thin spots. The fake object shows clearly from poisoned angles. Innocent angles stay almost unchanged. Adaptive noise further breaks the agreement between views.

Experiments beat earlier poisoning methods on their benchmarks. The illusions looked convincing while side damage stayed low. The authors also propose a density based scoring protocol. Future attacks and defenses can share that yardstick. Widely shared 3D scenes need this kind of audit. A scene file can lie to some viewers only.
arxiv-2510-02514:
Ohayon and co-authors define a distance between signals from how well they can be cleaned. Their 2025 paper introduces the Information-Estimation Metric. The idea links probability with optimal denoising error. A signal that is easy to clean sits in a dense region. Comparing denoising error vectors across noise levels gives a distance. Geometrically, the test compares score fields around each signal. The authors prove the construction is a true global metric. A closed form local version yields a curved Riemannian geometry. For Gaussian data, the metric reduces to the classic Mahalanobis distance.

Complex data bends the metric to local structure automatically. A learned denoiser, much like a diffusion model, computes it in practice. Distances then respect the shape of the data cloud. Tasks from retrieval to anomaly spotting use distances daily. A geometry aware ruler can sharpen all of them. Estimation theory and information theory meet in one object.
arxiv-2510-02914:
Kasthuri Arachchige, Boeva, and Abghari add fairness to federated learning. In that setup, many devices train one shared model. Data never leaves the device, which guards privacy. Real data, though, differs sharply across clients. Some clients lag, and the shared model can favor the strong. Their framework, FeDABoost, attacks both problems at once. It borrows its weighting idea from the classic AdaBoost method.

Servers give more weight to clients with low local error. That makes the merged model lean on reliable work. Weak clients get a boost during their own training. A focal loss setting shifts focus to their hard examples. Tests used MNIST, FEMNIST, and CIFAR-10 data. FeDABoost beat FedAvg and Ditto on fairness in most runs. Overall accuracy stayed competitive with both rivals. Gains were largest when client data diverged most. Cross-silo settings, like hospital groups, look like a natural fit.
arxiv-2510-03014:
Flinckman and Hassan check a multi-metric gravity theory for a fatal flaw. Theories with several interacting spin-2 fields often breed ghost modes. A ghost carries the wrong sign of energy and wrecks stability. The flaw is named after Boulware and Deser. The authors study a multivielbein theory with many frame fields. They run a full Hamiltonian constraint analysis on it. Constraints are the equations that fence off the bad modes.

The secondary constraints take exactly the needed form. They bind the dynamical variables as required to block the ghosts. Under mild limits on the solution space, tertiary constraints appear too. Those remove the momenta tied to the ghost modes. The counting of healthy modes then comes out right. One massless field plus the rest massive gives the total. No Boulware-Deser instability survives at the nonlinear level. Ghost-free multi-gravity thus stands on firmer ground.
arxiv-2510-03414:
Khairi, Lian, and Shumlak present a 2025 arXiv paper measuring how a graphite electrode wears away inside a fusion test device. The device, ZaP-HD, runs a sheared flow stabilized Z-pinch, where the electrode touches the core plasma. Heat and particle loads eat at that surface and limit device life. The team measured the erosion without touching the plasma, by watching ultraviolet light from carbon ions near the electrode and converting glow into atom flow.

Measured carbon flows came out vastly larger than forecasts for sputtering, where ions knock atoms loose. The values instead matched forecasts for sublimation, where the surface boils atoms away. After correcting for plasma expansion near the electrode, the flows stayed far above the sputtering level. That finding changes how engineers should model electrode wear and redeposition in this device family. It also warns high energy versions to design for heat driven loss first.
arxiv-2510-03614:
Solinas and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper introducing Neural Bayesian Filtering, a learned way to track beliefs about hidden states in partly observable systems. A belief is a probability distribution over possible states, and keeping it updated is costly when it has many modes. Their method compresses each belief into a fixed length embedding vector, learned from sample sets of example beliefs. A generative model turns embeddings back into state samples. Incoming observations then drive particle style updates inside the embedding space.

Tests in three partly observable environments show the filter tracking fast shifting, multimodal beliefs faithfully. It matched the robustness of particle filtering while using fewer particles. Classical filters either assume bell shaped beliefs or drown in particles as dimensions grow. Learned embeddings promise a middle path: compact, expressive belief tracking for robots and game playing agents. The update handles changing dynamics and control inputs, which deployments require.
arxiv-2510-03714:
Udugampola and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper designing routing for LoRa mesh networks that must work underground, where internet gateways cannot reach. LoRa radios are cheap and range but slow, and flooding messages wastes their bandwidth. The team's strategy starts with a position learning phase, letting repeaters learn where they sit. Routing then adapts to conditions, wakes standby repeaters to rescue packets lost in collisions, and shifts routes to spread battery drain across the network.

In simulations of an underground network, the design lifted maximum throughput by about one hundred eighty five percent over a flooding baseline. Energy use fell by about seventy five percent. Latency dropped by about half, and packet delivery rose from about eighty nine percent to about ninety seven percent. Mines and tunnels need communication that survives harsh conditions without mains power. Routing that respects position and battery state extends how long such networks can run.
arxiv-2510-03814:
Eisenmann and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on the hidden dynamics inside recurrent neural networks. These networks forecast time series and rebuild the behavior of real systems, including brain activity. What a network can do depends on its state space shape and the surfaces that split it into regions. The authors focus on networks built from ReLU units, whose math is piecewise linear.

The team introduces an algorithm that finds the stable and unstable manifolds attached to repeating network states. Tracing these surfaces reveals borders between basins of attraction, which shows when a network is multistable. The algorithm also finds where the surfaces cross, and those crossings prove chaotic behavior exists in such networks. As a real test, they applied the method to recordings from a single cortical neuron. Such tools help scientists explain why a trained network behaves as it does.
arxiv-2510-03914:
Chen and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on whether language models can clean up code like expert humans. Refactoring improves code structure without changing behavior, but developers often skip it because it pays off slowly. The authors turned Martin Fowler's famous refactoring guidelines into instruction strategies for language models. Those guidelines cover sixty-one named refactoring types, with motives and steps for each.

They tested the strategies on benchmark examples and on real code taken from GitHub projects. With Fowler-based instructions, the models performed every benchmark refactoring type. The refactored code preserved program behavior in real-world samples, a basic requirement for safe refactoring. Rule-based instructions often beat the friendlier descriptive ones, despite being harder for humans to read. Letting a model aim at the overall goal, rather than one named transformation, sometimes improved code quality most. DeepSeek's model completed more refactorings than the smaller OpenAI model.
arxiv-2510-04314:
Dukhovny presents this 2025 arXiv paper extending entropy-style reasoning from probability distributions to grading functions on partially ordered sets. The maximum entropy principle picks the least presumptuous distribution consistent with known constraints. Dukhovny's relative divergence generalizes the Kullback-Leibler notion to order-preserving grading functions on posets. Maximizing that divergence under prior information formalizes an insufficient reason principle for ordered structures.

The paper develops the definition across standard posets, including power sets and products of chains, using additivity and infimum principles. Classical formulas for conditional probability and independent events reappear as solutions of these maximum divergence problems on specially conjoined posets. Two applications receive detailed treatment. In population group testing, the method updates a group cost function from a null assumption as observations arrive. In a queueing model, servers form service batches from several waiting lines, and the product poset supports least-presuming cost estimates.
arxiv-2510-04614:
Huaian Diao, Xieling Fan, and Hongyu Liu wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a borderline kind of blowup in wave equations. Classic blowup makes a solution infinite at a point, while smooth solutions stay tame. The team studies hyperbolic wave equations in dimensions two and three, both linear and nonlinear. They prove some inputs push the wave field past any smoothness bound in finite time. Yet the field never quite forms a singularity.

The set of points where the near blowup happens shrinks to measure zero as the bound grows. Smooth coefficients and smooth inputs do not prevent the effect. The roughness grows from the structure of the wave equation itself, fed by input shapes. The authors call this state a quasi singularity. Their tools include Herglotz approximation and fixed point arguments for the nonlinear case. The result warns modelers that smoothness of ingredients is no promise of calm solutions.
arxiv-2510-04714:
KunHo Heo, GiHyun Kim, SuYeon Kim, and MyeongAh Cho wrote this 2025 paper on teaching machines the layout of three dimensional scenes. A scene graph lists objects in a room and the relations between them, such as chair beside table. Robots and augmented reality systems use graphs to reason about space. Prior systems leaned on graph neural networks while feeding them object features. The authors show that object feature quality drives the accuracy of the graph.

They built an object encoder and pretrained it with contrastive learning on objects. That training is separate from scene graph prediction, so features learn to tell objects apart. Plugging the encoder into existing frameworks lifted metrics they tracked. They fused geometric and semantic cues for predicting relations between objects. On the 3DSSG benchmark, the approach beat state of the art methods. The lesson travels: in structured prediction, representation quality matters more than fancier message passing.
arxiv-2510-04814:
Isabelle Krauss, Victor Lopez, and Matthias Müller wrote this 2025 paper on estimating the state of a system without constant radio contact. Moving horizon estimation infers a system state by fitting recent measurements over a window. It handles nonlinear systems well, but it needs data sent often. Event triggered designs send a measurement only when a rule says the news is worth it. Between events, the estimate coasts on model predictions alone.

The authors pair that scheme with a new triggering rule. Under a detectability condition, they prove the estimator is robustly stable. Errors shrink exponentially and stay bounded when noise and disturbances hit. Letting the horizon length vary tightens the error bound further in their analysis. Two worked examples confirm the scheme behaves as the theory promises. Sensors on batteries are the natural users of such methods. Sending less data saves energy and bandwidth while the guarantee holds.
arxiv-2510-04914:
Maximilian Delto, Alexander Penin, and Lorenzo Tancredi work on a hard corner of particle physics in this 2025 arXiv paper. When particles collide at very high energy, some effects shrink as the energy grows. Physicists call these power-suppressed contributions. Predicting how they change with energy has resisted standard methods.

The authors derive a new class of evolution equations for these smaller terms. Their trick is a multidimensional cutoff that separates the energy scales in play. The equations act like a renormalization group flow tied to that cutoff. They test the approach on electron-positron annihilation and on Higgs boson production through light quarks. The method should extend to massive and wide-angle scattering as well.
arxiv-2510-05014:
Xuanming Cui and twelve co-authors, mostly at Meta, improve how AI systems search across text and images in this 2025 arXiv paper. Embedding models turn content into vectors so similar items sit close together. Good search must also follow the user's instruction, not just match content. That mix demands real reasoning about the request.

Their framework, Think-Then-Embed, adds a reasoning step before the embedding is computed. A large model first thinks through the instruction in words. A compact reasoner is then distilled from those traces for speed. On the MMEB benchmarks, the method beat a range of recent baselines by clear margins. On one standard photo search test, it beat a recent rival by almost twenty points of precision.
arxiv-2510-05214:
Jiayi Sun and eleven co-authors map the insides of thousands of nearby galaxies in this 2025 arXiv paper. Knowing how much molecular gas a galaxy holds requires converting carbon monoxide light into hydrogen mass. That conversion factor varies from place to place. The team predicts it across more than 5,000 local galaxies.

They built radial profiles from GALEX ultraviolet and WISE infrared images. Those profiles yield stellar mass and star formation rate at each radius. Modern prescriptions then predict the conversion factor ring by ring. Validation against observations worked best when the model included CO-dark gas. That correction matters most in low-mass galaxies. Emissivity and excitation effects dominate instead in massive, actively star-forming systems.
arxiv-2510-05314:
Thomas A. Trainor re-examines what particle collisions at the LHC really say about quark-gluon plasma in this 2025 arXiv paper. He analyzes identified-hadron spectra from lead-lead and proton-proton collisions at 2.76 TeV. A two-component model splits each spectrum into soft and hard contributions. The hard part carries the jet signal that plasma should suppress.

Trainor questions the standard geometry estimates behind plasma claims. Mean transverse momentum data suggest central lead-lead collisions involve about a third of the participants that Glauber models assume. He also rejects factorizing the jet contribution against a proton-proton reference. Exclusivity and time dilation of participant partons explain the patterns instead, he argues. Under this reading, jet suppression tied to quark-gluon plasma formation is not evident.
arxiv-2510-05414:
Ziheng Geng and five co-authors automate structural frame analysis with a team of AI agents in this 2025 arXiv paper. Finite element modeling of two-dimensional frames demands geometry, domain knowledge, and careful reasoning. The authors split the job among specialized agents. Each agent is powered by the lightweight Llama-3.3 70B model rather than a frontier giant.

A Problem Analysis Agent extracts geometry, boundary, and material parameters from user input. A Geometry Agent derives node coordinates and element connectivity using expert rules. Translation and Validation Agents convert the structure into checked OpenSeesPy code, and a Load Agent applies the loads. Across 20 benchmark problems, the system topped 80 percent accuracy in most cases. It beat both Gemini-2.5 Pro and ChatGPT-4o overall.
arxiv-2510-06214:
Zhu and four co-authors fix a credit assignment flaw in training language model search agents in a 2025 machine learning paper. Search agents solve multi-step problems by calling tools, trained by reinforcement learning from rewards. Their trajectories differ structurally in how many searches they make and with what outcomes. A single global baseline then compares unlike runs, an apples-to-oranges error they name cross-stratum bias.

Stratified GRPO partitions trajectories into homogeneous strata by structural properties. Its core, Stratified Advantage Normalization, computes advantages locally, so every run is judged against true peers. They prove this removes cross-stratum bias while keeping unbiased unit-variance estimates per stratum. For finite-sample stability, they blend the stratified estimator with the global one. On single-hop and multi-hop question answering, Stratified GRPO beat plain GRPO by up to about eleven points. Training rewards rose, training stabilized, and search policies improved.
arxiv-2510-06414:
Qureshi and four co-authors translate classic process models into database queries in a 2025 business process management paper. Process management has turned data-driven, yet execution data sits in relational databases. Imperative models, usually Petri nets, do not apply directly to such data. Many existing models therefore go unused.

The approach converts imperative models into relaxed process data queries. The output is plain SQL running on databases holding execution records. Analysts can then check conformance with ordinary database tools. Relaxation is key: exact model behavior rarely survives real data intact. The translation preserves each model's control-flow intent while tolerating deviations in recorded executions. Results confirm imperative models still matter for data-driven process management. They highlight behavioral footprints and declarative ideas as bridges between the two worlds. The paper recovers decades of built models as usable assets, not shelf ornaments.
arxiv-2510-06814:
Lee, whose initials are M. D. K., leads a team measuring clock transitions in lutetium ions with extreme precision. Their 2025 paper supports a microwave clock based on the isotope lutetium-176. Atomic clocks need their transition frequencies pinned down without outside disturbances. The team measured two hyperfine transitions in the ion's D state.

Their fractional uncertainty reached four parts in a hundred trillion. Both frequencies are now known to about ten digits of precision. At that level, subtle effects mediated by the hyperfine structure became visible. Comparing the two transitions revealed a small leftover quadrupole moment in the ion. Its value matched an earlier, less direct assessment of the same quantity. With the undisturbed frequencies known, clock builders can compute a pesky frequency shift exactly. That shift comes from electric field gradients in the trap. The work tightens the error budget for a lutetium microwave clock standard.
arxiv-2510-07414:
Li and a large team argue that long-context language tests must engineer their haystacks, not just lengthen them. Their 2025 paper introduces HaystackCraft, a needle-in-a-haystack benchmark built on the full English Wikipedia link network. Classic tests hide one fact in clean filler text. Real deployments face messier noise: biased retrievers inject tempting distractors, and agent workflows compound their own errors. HaystackCraft varies how sparse, dense, hybrid, and graph retrievers compose the context, then asks multi-hop questions. A dynamic mode goes further, letting the model refine queries and decide when to stop searching.

Fifteen long-context models were tested. Stronger dense retrievers sometimes planted harder distractors, while graph-based reranking both improved retrieval and removed the most harmful ones. In the dynamic mode, even flagship models suffered cascading failures from their own earlier missteps. They proved poor at noticing and correcting self-made distractions.
arxiv-2510-07614:
Barrak opens the black box of multi-agent language model pipelines and asks who broke what. The 2025 paper studies a sequential Planner, Executor, Critic pipeline for software tasks. Such chains automate complex work, but errors pass silently between stages, making failures hard to trust or debug. Barrak evaluates eight configurations built from three state-of-the-art models across three benchmarks, tracking where errors originate, how they propagate, and whether later stages repair or amplify them.

Structured, accountable handoffs markedly improve accuracy and prevent the failure cascades that plague simple chains, in one benchmark by more than thirty-six points. Models also show role-specific profiles: planner quality dominates outcomes, and repair rates differ measurably between executor and critic roles. Accuracy, cost, and latency trade-offs prove task-dependent, with mixed-model pipelines often most efficient.
arxiv-2510-07914:
Zhang and Wei wrote this 2025 general relativity paper on spinning particles orbiting a magnetized rotating black hole. The Kerr solution describes spinning black holes without external magnetic fields. Real black holes sit in magnetized plasma, so a newer Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson solution adds that field. The authors follow test particles that spin as they orbit this black hole. They use the equations for spinning bodies in curved spacetime.

They map precessing orbits, circular orbits, and the innermost stable circular orbits. The magnetic field's grip grows strongest at large radial distances, which surprised simpler expectations. A stronger field demands more orbital angular momentum to hold a particle in the same orbit. Both the field and the particle's spin can keep trajectories safely timelike in reasonable ranges. The results help model how spinning bodies, from stars to compact objects, move near magnetized black holes.
arxiv-2510-08014:
Chang and four coauthors wrote this 2025 theoretical study of black phosphorene, an atom-thin semiconductor for nonlinear optics. Its response depends on layer count. The team asked how a gate voltage reshapes its second-harmonic generation, the doubling of light frequency in the material. They modeled electrons with a tight-binding description. Semiconductor Bloch equations then tracked the dynamics.

The monolayer response peaks along the armchair direction and resonates when incoming photon energy nears half the bandgap. Raising the gate voltage widens the monolayer gap and shifts the resonance toward blue. The bilayer behaves very differently. Strong fields drive it from semiconductor to semimetal, closing the gap and forming Dirac cones. The nonlinear signal then switches from interband peaks to intraband motion of Dirac fermions near zero photon energy. Gate-tunable doubling points toward compact devices with electrically switched frequency conversion.
arxiv-2510-08314:
Andrea Pugnana and co-authors offer a richer way for AI systems to use human experts, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Decision support tools help people classify cases, from medical scans to loan files. A known approach, Learning to Defer, lets a model pass hard cases to a human expert. But that treats human and model as rivals, and the expert only gives a final label.

Their framework, Learning to Ask, lets the model request expert feedback as extra input. One model works alone, while an enriched model also sees the expert's added information. A formally optimal rule decides when paying for that input is worth it. They give two implementations, one training the models in stages and one jointly. Tests with synthetic and real expert data showed stronger, more flexible collaboration than defer-only designs.
arxiv-2510-08514:
Mu-Chun Chen and Yan Cao ask whether a dark field can help supermassive black hole pairs merge faster in a 2025 arXiv paper. Two orbiting supermassive black holes stall at about a parsec apart, the famous final-parsec problem. Stars and gas may not push them to merger within the universe's age. A dark scalar or vector field sourced by the binary could drain extra energy through dipole radiation.

The authors derive radiation fluxes for eccentric charged Keplerian binaries from general formulas for periodic sources. Dipole radiation alone cannot fully solve the final-parsec problem, they find. It does extend the mass range that merges within a Hubble time, however. It also alters the background hum of gravitational waves from such inspirals at low frequencies. A simplified spectral model, tested by Bayesian analysis against current pulsar timing array data, explores the effect.
arxiv-2510-09114:
Yang and co-authors ask whether privacy protection itself is handed out fairly, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Differentially private training limits how much any one person's data can leak from a model. But the protection may be uneven: some groups' records might remain easier to expose than others'. Earlier audits measured only average risk, which can hide the worst cases, and the truest worst-case audit was too slow to use.

The team designs a membership inference game, a guessing contest about who was in the training data, that estimates near-worst-case risk efficiently. Their audits measured group privacy risk more stringently and exposed real disparities. They then upgrade the standard private training algorithm with clipping limits that adapt to each group, an idea borrowed from canary tests used in privacy auditing. In experiments, the change shrank the gap in group privacy risk while keeping the model private overall.
arxiv-2510-09214:
García-Ardila, Marcellán, and Marriaga analyze a family of orthogonal polynomials defined by a sharply decaying weight cut off at the origin, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The weight falls like the exponential of the fourth power, the signature of Freud weights, but integration runs only over positive values. Orthogonal polynomials are sequences where each member is perpendicular, under the weight, to all lower-degree ones. They underpin approximation theory, and this truncated family had not been worked out.

Because the weight is semiclassical, the recurrence coefficients obey nonlinear difference equations called Laguerre-Freud equations. The authors derive them, plus the coefficients' long-run behavior. Ladder operators, which raise and lower the degree, yield a second-order differential equation for the family. From it they read an electrostatic picture of the zeros, and test the smallest and largest zeros numerically.
arxiv-2510-09614:
Mo Javed and Amit Maji settle when a class of operators can be inverted, in a 2025 arXiv paper in complex analysis. Toeplitz operators act on the Bergman space, a space of analytic functions on the unit disc weighted by area. Whether such an operator has an inverse matters for solving the equations built from it, and simple tests have been lacking.

The authors study symbols of a special form, built from a constant blend of a bounded analytic function and its conjugate. For these symbols they prove a clean criterion. The Toeplitz operator is invertible exactly when the symbol's Berezin transform, a smoothed average of the symbol, stays bounded away from zero across the disc. They show this condition matches the symbol itself staying away from zero. The result gives a necessary and sufficient test where previously only partial answers were available for this symbol class.
arxiv-2510-09714:
Shiyuan Guo, Henry Sleight, and Fabien Roger test whether language models can hide their reasoning in ciphers in a 2025 arXiv paper. Safety teams monitor chains of thought to catch harmful actions and misalignment. A model that reasoned in encrypted, translated, or compressed text could evade that monitoring, so the authors measure how capable current models are at ciphered reasoning.

For each of twenty-eight ciphers, they fine-tune and prompt up to ten models to reason in that cipher, scoring accuracy on maths problems as a proxy for reasoning. A sharp asymmetry appears: accuracy drops in ciphered text, even though the same models translate such text into English accurately. Frontier models handle famous ciphers such as rot13 well but struggle with obscure ones. Ability tracks how common each cipher is in pretraining data and improves slowly with more fine-tuning. The authors conclude ciphered evasion looks ineffective for current models.
arxiv-2510-09814:
Martinez, with Felipe Garrido-Lucero and Umberto Grandi, examines stability in online assignment games in this 2025 arXiv paper in game theory. The assignment game models a housing market. Buyers and sellers are matched, and prices are set so that no pair wants to break away. In online markets, though, agents arrive one by one, so the matching is often less than the best possible.

The authors introduce two complementary measures of instability for allocations built on such sub-optimal matchings. They link both measures to the optimality ratio of the matching, which compares its value with the best achievable value. Using that framework, they study how well randomized algorithms perform on stability in online assignment games.
arxiv-2510-10914:
Jiajie Qiu, Dakota Thompson, Kamal Youcef-Toumi, and Amro M Farid build one model that runs traffic and the power grid together, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Transport burns more than a quarter of national energy, and electrifying it ties vehicles tightly to the grid. Their framework jointly optimizes five decisions: vehicle dispatch, route choice, charging station queuing, coordinated charging, and vehicle to grid stabilization. Unlike static traffic models, theirs tracks individual electric vehicles and their battery charge over time.

The model spans five charging modes, from home charging to inductive public chargers and discharging back to the grid. On the power side, a formulation with global optimality guarantees handles the electrical subproblems. Comparing coordinated operation against today's siloed management, where roads and grids are run separately, the analysis shows substantial value in coordination.
arxiv-2510-11014:
Subhransu S Bhattacharjee, Hao Lu, Dylan Campbell, and Rahul Shome let robots imagine the room beyond the doorway, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A robot peering through a door sees only part of a room, yet safe navigation and goal directed action need the hidden geometry and where target objects likely are. The team asks whether pretrained generative vision models can supply this missing structure as zero shot priors, with no task specific training. Their pipeline combines language model guided outpainting, monocular depth estimation, and semantic segmentation.

The output is a set of semantically labeled 3D point cloud hypotheses for the hidden room, which support queries about object likelihood and occupancy in unseen regions. They built MatterDoor, a benchmark of doorway occluded indoor scenes derived from Matterport3D. Evaluation used generative metrics plus simulated tasks where a Stretch robot reaches for objects.
arxiv-2510-11114:
Gromov hyperbolic spaces are curved spaces that behave roughly like trees, and warping their distances by conformal deformations can turn them into uniform spaces. Vasudevarao Allu and Alan P Jose study when that uniformity survives a change of space in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Recent work showed that deformations built from Busemann functions are uniform for small deformation parameters.

Allu and Jose prove that if two proper, roughly starlike Gromov hyperbolic spaces are roughly isometric, then uniformity of their conformal deformations is a shared property. Roughly isometric means their large-scale geometry matches up to bounded error. Either both deformed spaces are uniform, or neither one is. The result is a counterpart to earlier work by Lindquist and Shanmugalingam on the bounded case. It ties the uniformization of a space to the rough geometry of the whole class in this unbounded setting.
arxiv-2510-11214:
Wireless receivers need fresh knowledge of the channel they are receiving through, but measuring it costs pilot signals and the channel ages quickly anyway. Mehdi Sattari and co-authors propose forecasting that knowledge with generative models in this 2025 arXiv signal processing paper. Earlier predictors learn one fixed mapping, which cannot express the random behavior of real channels.

Their framework splits prediction into a temporal encoder that pulls channel dynamics from past data and a diffusion model that generates the future channel state. They test autoregressive and sequence-to-sequence inference schemes and several diffusion backbones, including U-Net and Transformer designs. A variant drops the explicit temporal encoder and uses DDIM scheduling to cut complexity. In simulations the predictors clearly beat the best baselines for channel state information prediction.
arxiv-2510-11314:
Readers with intellectual disabilities often need pictures alongside simplified text, yet image generators usually aim for beauty rather than clarity. Belkiss Souayed, Sarah Ebling, and Yingqiang Gao study how to prompt vision-language models for accessible images in this 2025 arXiv paper. They designed five prompt templates with different spatial arrangements, all obeying access constraints such as limits on object count and separation between objects.

Using 400 short sentences from four established datasets, the team first scored the templates by computer, then had four access experts annotate the generated images across ten visual styles. The Basic Object Focus template achieved the highest semantic alignment, showing that minimalism improves language access. Experts rated the Retro style as the most accessible and the Wikipedia material as the best source. Agreement between annotators was strong on text simplicity but weaker on image quality, which proved more subjective.
arxiv-2510-11414:
Autonomous AI agents inside a company will propose tasks nobody wrote a policy for, and a static access-control list cannot judge whether a novel request is safe. Charles Fleming, Ashish Kundu, and Ramana Kompella propose letting a language model judge them in this 2025 arXiv security paper. Their framework extends task-based access control so the model weighs the agent's intent, the risk of the target resource, and its own uncertainty.

When an agent proposes a new task, the judge synthesizes a just-in-time policy and computes a composite risk score plus an estimate of its own reasoning uncertainty. High-risk or high-uncertainty requests trigger stricter controls, such as requiring human approval. Low-risk, confident decisions can pass automatically, preserving the agents' speed. By combining external risk with internal confidence, the model enforces an adaptive version of the principle of least privilege, aiming at safer autonomous systems.
arxiv-2510-11514:
Monitoring a patient's breathing and heartbeat without touching them, while keeping the data private and the wireless link efficient, is a three-way engineering challenge. Yinchao Yang and co-authors propose an integrated framework for it in this 2025 arXiv signal processing paper. In their design a service robot uses radar to locate patients and track vital signs contactlessly, then reports semantically extracted health features, not raw data, to medical devices.

Sending features instead of raw data improves throughput and protects privacy, since sensitive signals never leave the robot. The robot tracks patient motion with an interacting multiple model filter and steers its beams accordingly. The authors jointly optimize the beamforming matrices and the semantic extraction ratio under computing and power constraints, aiming to maximize both the semantic secrecy rate and sensing accuracy. Simulations showed it beating conventional joint sensing-and-communication methods on all three goals.
arxiv-2510-11814:
Georgios Papas pursues deep questions about special function values in this 2025 arXiv paper, the second in a series. G-functions are power series that arise from families of geometric objects. Papas studies a one-parameter family of elliptic curves, which are a central class of curves in number theory. He focuses on points where the curve gains extra symmetry, the so-called CM case.

Papas constructs relations among the G-function values at such points. Using André's method built on these functions, the relations yield bounds on the height of the points. The payoff reaches toward a famous gap in number theory: Siegel proved that class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields grow, but his proof gives no usable rate. Effective versions of that lower bound, tied to the Brauer-Siegel theorem, remain a major goal. Height bounds like Papas's are one route toward them.
arxiv-2510-11914:
Liliana Apolinário, Chiara Le Roux, and Korinna Zapp ask whether jets can change character without losing energy. In nuclear collisions, fast partons plowing through hot matter normally shed energy, a suppression called jet quenching. The team's paper, published in Physics Letters B and posted on arXiv in 2025, studies a subtler scenario. A hard parton suffers one soft re-scattering that leaves its motion untouched but swaps its color charge.

That color exchange breaks the coherence between the parton and its future fragments. The authors show this coherence loss is observable. The formation time of the first splitting, reconstructed from real jets by a formation-time clustering algorithm, responds to lost coherence. Crucially, the same observable ignores small energy losses, whose formation time patterns stay unchanged. The measure can therefore tell the two scenarios apart. This matters for hunting the onset of collective behavior in small collision systems.
arxiv-2510-12014:
Eric He and six colleagues teach fast image search to understand gifts, not just pictures. Embedding systems like CLIP retrieve products by vector similarity, which scales beautifully. But they train on literal captions and stumble over persona-driven requests, like a present for a mother who loves gardening. Big vision-language models grasp such nuance, yet their small context windows cannot scan a whole catalog. Their 2025 arXiv paper bridges the two.

The framework distills a powerful vision-language model's preference rankings into an embedding system. The student learns the teacher's taste while keeping the cheap, scalable search of vector retrieval. On persona-driven product recommendation tasks, the distilled system significantly outperformed existing embedding baselines. Shoppers' abstract intents, the authors argue, need not be sacrificed for catalog scale. A teacher that occasionally ranks a shortlist can permanently upgrade a retriever that must rank millions of items in milliseconds.
arxiv-2510-12114:
Wenjie Li and four colleagues restore faces in damaged old photographs using a diffusion model that teaches itself. Scratches, fading, and blur gang up on the same cheeks. Pre-trained diffusion methods lean on explicit damage priors or global statistics and stumble on localized breakage and color. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes SSDiff, self-supervised and selective.

The trick is pseudo-reference faces: the diffusion model, weakly guided, first imagines what the portrait plausibly looked like, and those imaginings supervise the real restoration. Guidance is staged to match diffusion's coarse-to-fine rhythm, structure enforced throughout and color refined late. Face parsing maps and scratch masks target repairs at broken regions, avoiding identity swaps elsewhere. The team also built VintageFace, a benchmark of three hundred real old photos at varying damage levels. On it, SSDiff beats GAN-based and diffusion-based rivals in perceptual quality, fidelity, and regional control.
arxiv-2510-12514:
Long and Gao analyze how a droplet crawls across a surface with two wettabilities, in a 2025 arXiv paper published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics. A chemical step is a sharp border between a water loving and a less wettable region. Droplets crossing such borders reshape in ways that matter for printing, coating, and microfluidics.

Within lubrication theory, which describes thin fluid layers, the authors handle the contact line singularity with a Navier slip condition. For two and three dimensional droplets they identify two stages. First comes migration across both regions. Then asymmetric spreading follows on the hydrophilic side, while the rear contact line stays pinned at the border. In two dimensions a matched asymptotic analysis agrees with numerical solutions. The droplet can travel at constant speed. Three dimensional simulations show the same outline, modified by lateral flow. Length and width vary non monotonically before the droplet detaches and settles.
arxiv-2510-12814:
Sarkar and Shukla study cyber slavery in this 2025 arXiv paper, a form of trafficking where victims are forced to commit online crimes. In Southeast Asia, criminal networks lure and confine people, then coerce them into running fraud and phishing operations. The practice merges human trafficking with digital exploitation and strains systems built to separate victims from offenders.

The authors combined a systematic narrative review with case metadata from real incidents gathered with Indian law enforcement. They propose a five-tier framework tracing victims from financial deception through physical exploitation to prosecution caused by trace-based misattribution, where digital trails wrongly point at the victim. They also warn that some victims later continue voluntarily for money and anonymity, and they argue that binary legal categories block victim-centered investigation and raise misclassification risks.
arxiv-2510-13014:
Myers and colleagues measure neutron capture element abundances in distant open clusters in this 2025 arXiv paper, part of the OCCAM survey effort. Open clusters calibrate stellar ages and chemical clocks, methods that infer a star's age from its composition. Neutron capture elements, built when atomic nuclei absorb neutrons, trace how heavier elements were seeded through the galaxy over time.

The team gathered new high-resolution optical spectra with the Keck telescope's HIRES instrument for member stars in seven distant outer Galaxy clusters, using survey data to confirm membership. From those spectra they derived neutron capture abundances cluster by cluster. Such measurements extend abundance work beyond the infrared data the parent survey relied on, strengthening the calibration of age-chemistry relationships for field stars across the Milky Way.
arxiv-2510-13414:
Fan, Kellison, and Pollard mechanize Olver's error arithmetic, a model for rounding errors in computer arithmetic. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in a proof assistant, software that checks each logical step. Computers store numbers with limited precision, so results drift from exact values. Tracking that drift with proof is key for high-stakes software. Mechanize means encoding the definitions and proofs in machine-checked form.

The model rests on relative precision, a measure proposed as a replacement for relative error. Unlike relative error, relative precision forms a true metric, a consistent notion of distance. The team formalizes this property inside the proof assistant. They also prove rules for converting between relative precision and relative error. Their model slightly overstates the standard rounding model, which keeps its bounds safe. A worked inner product example shows the model yields certified error bounds in practice.
arxiv-2510-13614:
Tan and co-authors present MemoTime, a framework that sharpens how language models reason about time. Their 2025 arXiv paper grounds models in temporal knowledge graphs, structured stores of dated facts. Models stumble when questions span several entities, compound operators, and evolving events. Existing graph-based methods still lose temporal faithfulness across multi-step chains.

MemoTime breaks a hard temporal question into a hierarchical Tree of Time. The tree enforces rising timestamps and binds several entities under shared time limits. A retrieval layer adapts its strategy to each temporal operator in the question. A self-evolving memory stores verified reasoning traces for reuse on later questions. On several temporal question-answering benchmarks, MemoTime set new overall records. It beat the strongest baseline by up to twenty-four percent on their headline comparison. It also let a small four-billion-parameter model rival GPT-4-Turbo at temporal reasoning.
arxiv-2510-13814:
Rahman, Mishra, and Hu turn tools built to explain AI models around to study human experts instead. Their 2025 arXiv paper looks at operators tuning a particle accelerator, a hard real-world control task. Those who study minds watch human thinking from outside, while XAI tools dissect how models think. Using the second toolkit on the first job is the paper's move.

The authors build graphs of staff subtasks from stored control-room data. Group-finding and layered grouping methods then expose how staff chunk the problem. The patterns show experts breaking the accelerator task into simpler linked parts. Those ways of working visibly shift as staff gain skill over time. The findings reveal how humans craft smart strategies where no single best answer exists. The authors argue XAI tools can shed light on human thinking far beyond this one machine.
arxiv-2510-14314:
Shivangi Yadav and Arun Ross build a synthetic image generator to defend iris recognition systems against presentation attacks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The fakes include printed eye photos or cosmetic contact lenses shown to the scanner. Attack detectors need training data, but real attack samples are scarce because they are difficult to construct and image.

Their framework, MID-StyleGAN, combines diffusion models with generative adversarial networks in a multi-domain architecture that translates between genuine eye images and several attack domains, including printed eyes and cosmetic lenses. An adaptive loss function tailored to ocular data maintains domain match while the generator produces diverse eyes. In experiments, MID-StyleGAN outperformed methods at making high-quality ocular images. Training attack detectors on its output improved their performance. It offers a scalable way to harden iris biometrics without collecting real attack artifacts.
arxiv-2510-14514:
Daniel Owusu Adu and Yongxin Chen extend flow matching, a modeling technique for moving between distributions, to ensembles of linear systems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Averaging over system parameters introduces memory into the problem: in the stochastic setting the path becomes non-Markovian, so the control now depends on the history, not the state.

The authors characterize the control law achieving distributional controllability, steering the ensemble's distribution to the target. It is a conditional expectation of a Volterra-type control. They derive forms for distributions plus a numerical procedure. A by-product is a split between regimes. For stochastic systems, history dependence matters, and they implement it with a recurrent network. For deterministic systems the flow is memoryless, and a feedforward network learns a time-varying gain. A deterministic pairing between source and target samples is fixed, by optimal transport.
arxiv-2510-14614:
Kim and co-authors, in a 2025 arXiv paper, redesign the transformer architecture to cut the cost of training very large language models. Training is usually spread over many graphics processors. One standard scheme, tensor parallelism, forces an expensive all-reduce communication step in every block. The authors found that the link between each block's attention part and its feed-forward part can be bypassed.

Their architecture, FAL, sends the first layer's attention output directly to the feed-forward inputs of later layers. That removes the per-block communication and lets attention and feed-forward work run in parallel on one processor. A variant, FAL+, also adds a normalized copy of that first attention signal to later layers to protect quality. In evaluations, FAL cut multi-processor training time by up to forty-four percent. Both versions reached better perplexity, a standard quality score, than the baseline model.
arxiv-2510-14814:
Zhao, Liu, and Prakash tackle, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a quiet failure mode of forecasting models: the world changes after training. They separate two kinds of change in time-series data. Temporal shift alters the timing structure of the series. Concept drift changes the underlying relationship the forecaster relies on. Most research fights temporal shift, while concept drift in forecasting has drawn little attention.

Their framework, ShifTS, is method-agnostic, so it can wrap around existing forecasters. It repairs temporal shift first, then addresses concept drift, in one unified approach. For the drift stage, a soft attention mechanism hunts for patterns that stay invariant, drawing them from both the lookback window and the forecast horizon. Across several datasets, ShifTS consistently improved the accuracy of the models it wrapped, beating baselines aimed at each shift type alone or both.
arxiv-2510-15114:
Marios-Nektarios Stamatopoulos and four colleagues demonstrate flying robots that build a brick wall together, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their system pairs two specialized drones: one carries and places bricks using a ball-joint gripper, while the other applies adhesive through a servo-controlled nozzle. A reactive planner coordinates the pair so construction can adjust on the fly.

The planner juggles a dependency graph of the wall layout against a conflict graph, so the drones never compete for the same space or step. Smooth minimum-jerk flight paths guide pickup and placement, and the carrier drone reads marker tags on bricks to estimate their positions in real time. In filmed experiments the pair completed the masonry sequence without human control. The authors describe the trial as the first fully autonomous aerial masonry build using two different kinds of drones.
arxiv-2510-15314:
Arthémise Altman and seven colleagues pin down exact frequencies for radio lines of water molecules that astronomers rely on. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns lines of common water listed as protected for radio astronomy by global and U.S. bodies. Protecting a line means other users must avoid it, so its true frequency needs to be known very precisely.

The precision comes from a spectroscopic network: a web of measured transitions that reinforce each other. The network combines hundreds of near-infrared lines recorded with a frequency-comb spectrometer and a few very precise rotational readings. The team remeasured fifty-five target lines at high accuracy for this study. As a result, every protected water line between 750 and 3,000 gigahertz now has a sharper frequency than direct radio measurements had given. Forty-three of them gained accuracy from the new infrared measurements reported here.
arxiv-2510-15414:
Huining Yuan and thirteen colleagues teach language models to reason as a team by letting them play strategy games against themselves. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces MARS, a reinforcement learning framework for multi-agent reasoning. Single-agent training is well understood, but multi-turn games raise hard questions about which move deserves credit for a win.

MARS scores credit at the level of each turn, aligning the learning signal with the interaction that caused it. It also normalizes advantages separately for each agent, which steadies training when several models learn at once. Trained from Qwen3-4B through self-play, the agent improved on held-out games by up to about twenty-nine percent. The skill also transferred beyond games. Plugged into leading systems, it raised AIME math scores by ten points and a graduate-level science score by twelve and a half.
arxiv-2510-15514:
Boyin Liu and ten colleagues stabilize a popular training method in which one AI grades another's answers. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that using a language model as judge avoids slow human annotation, but judges contradict themselves. The sharpest problem is preference cycles, where the judge ranks A above B, B above C, and then C above A, feeding the learner incoherent rewards.

Their framework detects and repairs those conflicts inside the training loop. A new metric, the conflict detection rate, counts how often judgments clash. A second component rebuilds the reward signal by turning raw judgments into a preference graph, then pruning it into cycle-free form. The cleaned signal works with any standard policy optimizer. Experiments showed steadier training and better final performance than strong baselines. The authors argue logical consistency is a dimension of AI feedback the field must manage.
arxiv-2510-15614:
Science questions often allow several different explanations for the same observations. Tingting Chen and seven colleagues ask whether language models can propose sets of such explanations well. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces HypoSpace, a test suite that treats models as samplers of hypothesis sets. It scores validity, uniqueness, and recovery, meaning precision, non-redundancy, and coverage of all allowed answers. The suite covers causal graphs, voxel reconstruction in 3D, and Boolean genetic interactions with exact answer lists.

Across tuned and reasoning-focused models, validity often stays high while uniqueness and recovery fall. As the space of valid answers grows, models collapse onto a few repeated guesses. The authors offer HypoSpace as a probe for such methods, not a leaderboard.
arxiv-2510-15714:
Second-order optimization uses curvature to converge faster, but computing Hessians is very expensive. El Mahdi Chayti and Martin Jaggi split that work across clients in this 2025 arXiv paper. In their framework, one client computes gradients while another handles curvature, asynchronously. This matches real delays and stale curvature updates without the hand-tuning lazy Hessian methods need. They focus on cubic regularization, a standard way to use curvature safely.

The split approach keeps strong convergence guarantees from the synchronous theory. It also achieves a provable wall-clock speed-up tied to how costly Hessians are. Experiments on synthetic and real data confirm asynchronous curvature beats the baselines tested.
arxiv-2510-16014:
Hanyin Cheng leads seven co-authors with an adapter that teaches time series foundation models to respect machine states. Anomaly detection on industrial streams matters for safety and uptime. Real series mix smooth signals such as temperature and flow with discrete state variables. A valve being open is one such variable. The day of the week is another. Foundation models treat both kinds alike, which wastes state facts and can hurt detection.

Their plug-in module, STAR, works at fine-tuning time in three parts. An identity-guided encoder with a learnable state memory captures what each category means. A bottleneck adapter builds its low-rank updates from the current state. A matching module hunts anomalies inside the state variables themselves. On real data sets, STAR lifts the detection scores of current foundation models, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-16214:
Sarah Chehade, Andrea Delgado, and Elaine Wong find ways to play quantum games with fewer qubits than the standard recipe demands. The games are non-local games, where split players must answer in sync without talking, and shared entanglement helps them win. Playing many games at once normally stacks their costs, one full setup per game.

Their trick is to embed the games' rule algebras, their math of allowed moves, into one shared frame where the rules commute. When a referee picks one game at random, a single entangled state sized for the biggest game serves for all. Under set conditions, several games can also run in parallel on fewer qubits than the stacked cost. They give a recipe for building such embeddings using tools from Lie theory. The payoff is leaner quantum setups for shared, resource-tight tasks.
arxiv-2510-16314:
Moshe Kamensky and Rahim Moosa prove a result in pure maths in their 2025 paper. They study difference equations, where a rule shifts a value step by step. Their question asks when solutions to such a rule link up in a neat number pattern. A shift moves each value to its next form under the rule.

They show that if linked solutions exist at all, then three solutions already show such a link. A weaker form holds when the shift also moves the base field. On the way, they prove more facts about simple shift systems. The proof uses model theory, the study of what maths claims mean. The bound keeps hard searches small.
arxiv-2510-16614:
Xuan Zhang leads nine co-authors in a 2025 study on why reward design shapes reasoning in AI. Models trained by reward learn to favour acts that pay off. Sparse final rewards leave them stuck in dull loops of thought. Their method, MERCI, adds a built-in bonus for fresh lines of thought. A light coin-flip net gauges how new each path of thought is.

That net turns counts of past paths into a sense of doubt. Fresh paths earn a bonus, while task rewards still rule the training. MERCI plugs into known reward training frames with ease. Tests on hard reasoning sets show richer chains of thought. Scores beat strong rivals, and models escape stale loops more often.
arxiv-2510-16814:
Simon Jaxy and five co-authors teach a computer to guess where undiscovered archaeological sites hide. Confirmed sites are rare, and most land is simply unlabeled rather than empty, which makes standard training fail. Their method, asymmetric dual pseudolabeling, learns straight from multi-band geospatial imagery without hand-built features or guesses about where sites are absent.

On the Sagalassos data set, checked against a separate field survey, the method beat the LAMAP baseline clearly on F1 score and recall, though LAMAP ranked probabilities better. On the Cyprus data set, it kept telling sites apart where plain supervised learning flipped its rankings. Standard baselines failed badly when negatives were uncertain, and the team reports those failures as useful bounds.
arxiv-2510-17114:
Hodaka Kawachi and six co-authors hide marks in room light in this 2025 paper. Their marks must stay unseen by people yet clear to phone cameras. Normal light talk uses fast blinks, which need fast cameras. The team instead shifts the color mix of white light in fine steps.

The light still looks white to the eye under a standard daylight mix. Camera sensors, though, read the shifts as a clear code. The method works at normal video rates of thirty to sixty frames per second. It can store one hundred twenty-eight bits in a ten-second clip. That is enough for basic facts that guard privacy and prove a clip is real.
arxiv-2510-17214:
Chenyan Fei, Dalin Zhang, and Chen Melinda Dang check fuel cell health with a neural net in this 2025 paper. A key health sign is high-rate impedance, the drag on fast current shifts. Live tests of that sign are hard and dear on real stacks. The team wants a cheap stand-in that reads health from plain data.

Their deep sparse auto-encoder net learns to guess and sort that sign. It scores above ninety-two percent right on the health sort task. The net then runs on a field chip for fast on-site use. On the chip it still scores near ninety percent right. The work points to low-cost health checks built into fuel cell gear.
arxiv-2510-17314:
Scoring the answers of large language models often relies on reward models that act as opaque black boxes. Lipeng Xie and eleven co-authors propose replacing hidden number weights with plain written rules, called rubrics, that anyone can read. Their framework learns such rules without training a new scoring network from scratch.

The method draws candidate rules from a small set of judged examples, checks them, and then squeezes them into a compact core set arranged by broad checks and detailed tests. With only seventy preference pairs, judges guided by these rubrics beat fully trained reward models on standard tests. Xie and his co-authors argue that human preference signals can be packed into far less material than assumed.
arxiv-2510-17614:
Clinicians choosing among possible orders for a patient need ranked lists that are fast, and reasons they can check. Praphul Singh and five co-authors present OG-Rank, a ranking system built on a single decoder model that scores every candidate in one pass. A pooled score from the first generated token does the fast ranking, and a separate explanation step wakes up only when the list is genuinely ambiguous, which keeps the delay predictable.

Training follows a curriculum that spends more effort on hard cases and less on easy ones. Singh and his co-authors report that activating the explanation gate lifted top choice recall clearly on encounter based order selection, while simpler encoder models trailed on both accuracy and flexibility. The pattern, rank fast by default and explain when it helps, is offered as a recipe for other decision tasks.
arxiv-2510-17714:
Atticus McWhorter and Daryl DeFord introduce a new sampling walk for redistricting maps in a 2025 arXiv paper. Analysts model district plans as partitions of a graph built from map units. Random sampling methods generate large ensembles of plans for comparison. Popular methods lean heavily toward plans favored by a spanning tree count, which can bias the ensemble. A spanning tree is a skeleton linking all units without loops.

Their Marked Edge Walk moves across spanning trees that carry marked edges. Its transition chances can be computed exactly, which suits the Metropolis-Hastings sampling method. Tests on real map graphs for New Hampshire and Texas showed broad convergence. Target goals like competitiveness and compactness could be aimed at directly. The spanning tree bias shrank compared with older methods.
arxiv-2510-18114:
Dario Shariatian and three co-authors strengthen discrete diffusion models by giving them a hidden helper channel. These models promise fast text generation, but simple reverse steps ignore how tokens depend on each other, which hurts short runs. Their LADD design diffuses over words and learned latent variables together, so joint structure has somewhere to live.

Two versions use continuous and discrete latents, and two schedules either denoise both together or settle latents first. Training goals and design trade-offs are worked out in detail. Language model researchers get a route to few-step generation that respects word links.
arxiv-2510-18414: Hideaki Noda, writing alone, offers a short note on powers of two. He studies a function built from their decimal digits. He asks how fast that function can grow. The note states an open problem on the best upper bound for this growth. It also gives a matrix form for the function. That form acts like a finite-state transfer tool. It is meant to help attack the open problem. Deeper study of the dynamics is left for later work.
arxiv-2510-18514:
Thorsten Groh, with Felix Affeld and Simon Stellmer, measures how the color of light absorbed by mercury atoms shifts slightly between isotopes, versions of the element with different nuclear masses. Working with laser-cooled atoms held in a magnetic-optical trap, they studied several transitions in the five naturally occurring even isotopes, including a rare one. Their precision reached down to twenty kilohertz, resolving the shifts to a tiny fraction of their size.

Comparing transitions in a King plot, a graph that should give a straight line, revealed a clear bend with significance close to five standard deviations. The team analyzed whether the bend comes from higher-order effects of the nucleus's size and deformation. Beyond testing nuclear structure models, the measurements set benchmarks for theory and support using mercury to hunt for hypothetical new forces between electrons and neutrons.
arxiv-2510-18614:
René Coignard and Anton Rygin present a scheme called Qatsi. It generates passwords and secrets, yet stores nothing. A vault file can be stolen, so Qatsi re-derives each secret on demand. The inputs are one strong master secret plus context layers. The derivation is memory-hard, which makes brute-force attacks costly. Outputs come from a rejection method the authors prove gives perfectly uniform results. It works over long word lists or character sets.

Their analysis times a single graphics card on the strongest settings. Cracking an eighty-bit master secret would take an astronomically long time. The Rust code wipes memory on its own and checks its word list at compile time. Tests on a 2021 laptop timed each derivation. Times ran from about half a second to just over two seconds. That is a fair price for air-gapped use.
arxiv-2510-18714:
Changkun Liu and his eight co-authors rebuild indoor rooms in three dimensions from just two unposed photographs, using flat planes as the building blocks. Indoor spaces are full of planar surfaces, walls, floors, and tabletops, so describing a scene as a set of planes is both compact and natural. Their system, PLANA3R, needs no camera positions in advance and outputs real-world metric scale, not just relative shape.

Vision transformers extract a sparse set of planar pieces and estimate how the two cameras were positioned relative to each other. Learning is supervised by rendering the planes back into depth and surface-direction maps and comparing them with annotations, avoiding any need for labeled planes during training. Across indoor data sets the method reconstructed surfaces, estimated depth, and recovered camera motion well, generalized to new environments, and could segment the planes it found.
arxiv-2510-18814:
Mengqi Li and her four co-authors ask a bold question. Can a language model train itself to reason better? It would learn from its own imperfect answers. No rewards would guide it. No teacher solutions would be given. Their method is Self-evolving Post-Training. It alternates two steps. The model first generates fresh responses at set randomness. It then trains on those responses by next-token likelihood. One response per prompt is the default. No filtering for correctness is applied.

Six mathematics benchmarks tested the method. It beat a strong no-training baseline by about eleven points on a math model. The gain was about seven points on a general model. Responses from a trained model taught a fresh student well. Their opening steps helped an unchanged model finish solutions. The gains live in the model's token rankings. No decoding tweak could reproduce them.
arxiv-2510-18914:
Afrozah Nadeem, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem propose a fairer way to steer language models at the moment of use, rather than by retraining. Models carry unwanted behaviors in their internal representations: bias, drift, and harmful patterns that grow over long conversations. Training-time fixes are expensive and permanent, while existing pruning methods, which silence the neurons behind a behavior, are static and cannot adapt when context changes.

Their framework prunes dynamically and reversibly. It watches for context-aware neuron activations during generation and applies adaptive masks that dial those neurons' influence up or down as the conversation evolves, keeping a memory of past context. The authors report more coherent, knowledge-preserving behavior across multilingual single-turn and multi-turn dialogues. The pitch is practical: fairness control that can respond in real time, in deployed systems, without rebuilding the model.
arxiv-2510-19114:
Martin Minchev and Mladen Savov survey two decades of progress on exponential functionals of Lévy processes, random quantities built by integrating an exponential of a wandering random process over time. Since an earlier landmark survey, the structure of these variables has become much clearer, and uses for them have spread across applied probability.

The authors first explain the special functions that drove recent progress, then group the main results by theme. They also fill in several results and place them in a wider frame. The survey serves readers who need these functionals for finance, queues, or other random models.
arxiv-2510-19314:
Jinwu Hu and seven co-authors propose Continual Knowledge Adaptation, a reinforcement learning method for agents whose tasks keep changing. Real environments are not stationary, and agents that learn task after task tend to forget old skills or fail to reuse what earlier tasks taught them.

Their strategy keeps a pool of task-specific knowledge vectors and draws on past knowledge dynamically as new tasks arrive, rather than starting fresh or overwriting blindly. Accumulating and reusing experience this way should help agents adapt to shifting conditions in robotics and other long-running applications where retraining from zero is wasteful.
arxiv-2510-19714:
Joseph Aziz and Richard Howl challenge a key premise behind a proposed test of whether gravity is quantum. The test, first suggested by Feynman, puts a mass in a superposition of two places. Gravity then lets it interact with a second mass. If the two become entangled, that is usually read as proof that gravity must be quantum. The logic rests on theorems that treat classical gravity as able to pass only classical information.

Aziz and Howl argue that a classical gravitational interaction can, through purely local steps, pass quantum information and so create entanglement. They also find the effect scales unlike the expected quantum gravity signal. Their analysis, if right, changes what the test would need to look like to settle the question.
arxiv-2510-19914:
Alfred Li, Ankit Mahajan, and Sandeep Sharma derive the Fokker-Planck equation that governs the walker population in auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo. That method is a workhorse for quantum many-body problems. The algorithm is normally told as a random walk through an overcomplete space of Slater determinants, driven by a Langevin equation. But the equation for the spread of walkers itself had never been written down.

With it in hand, plus a new scheme to solve it, the sampled wavefunction becomes visible directly. Surprisingly, even when the exact ground state guides a constrained-path run, the wave actually sampled is not exact. That contradicts a common assumption. The authors outline how this framing can guide step-by-step gains in the method's accuracy.
arxiv-2510-20014:
Carlos A. Bertulani studies low-energy nuclear reactions that could be explored at the future Electron-Ion Collider at Brookhaven National Laboratory. He compares those reactions with similar measurements made in ultraperipheral collisions at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN. The focus is nuclear fragmentation, meaning how a heavy nucleus breaks apart after a collision.

Bertulani estimates that fragmentation rates at the new collider are roughly one thousand times smaller than at the Large Hadron Collider. At the larger machine, uranium breakup shows a double-peaked mass pattern linked to fission. At the Electron-Ion Collider, the breakup is instead marked by neutron loss and far fewer fission pieces, about ten thousand times fewer events.
arxiv-2510-20214:
Talha Ilyas and fifteen co-authors work toward objective detection of fetal movement from ultrasound video, a signal of prenatal health. Abnormal movement can point to problems such as placental dysfunction or fetal distress, yet standard checks rely on maternal perception or cardiotocography, both limited in accuracy. Their framework, called CURL, learns from long ultrasound recordings without manual labels.

CURL uses a dual contrastive loss with both spatial and temporal terms to learn strong motion representations, plus a sampling strategy that keeps movement and non-movement segments apart during training. A probabilistic fine-tuning step allows flexible use on recordings of any length. On ninety-two subjects with thirty-minute sessions, the method reaches solid sensitivity and discrimination scores.
arxiv-2510-20414:
Sishun Liu and four co-authors tackle mark imbalance in neural marked temporal point processes, which model streams of events and predict the type and arrival time of the next event. In many real applications a few marks are frequent while others are rare, and that imbalance hurts prediction most for the rare events. Existing models also predict the mark directly from its raw probability, which favors the frequent marks.

Their thresholding method instead tunes the mark probability by the mark prior probability using learned thresholds, and the model predicts the mark first and the time second.
