A new neural model supports efficient time sampling and mark probability estimation without expensive numerical integration. Experiments on real-world datasets beat various baselines on both tasks.
arxiv-2510-20514:
Lea Salome Brugger, Xavier Denis, and Peter Müller ask why deductive checks stay rare in real work, though they can prove a system acts as meant. Their study runs on talks with 30 workers from firms and schools who use such checks. The talks are semi-structured, and the team sorts the text by theme in a set way.

Known blocks show up, such as the high skill proof work needs. Fresh blocks show up too: proof upkeep, weak grip on rote steps, and poor ease of use. The team draws out helps and blocks from the data. They then give firm tips for users, tool makers, and scholars, with rules for ease, rote steps, and fit with work flows.
arxiv-2510-20614:
David Landa-Marbán and four co-authors test an open-source, image-based history matching workflow on a benchmark dataset of carbon dioxide storage in a meter-scale, geologically complex reservoir. The FluidFlower dataset gives dense spatial and temporal images of fluid displacement, a rare chance to validate calibration methods for geological carbon storage. The team adjusts uncertain model parameters to reduce the mismatch between simulation and the observed phase distributions.

Simulations run in the open-source OPM Flow simulator while the Everest tool conducts the history matching itself. After calibration, results agree well with the experimental storage data, suggesting standard flow equations and conventional property models describe the system effectively. The Wasserstein distance proves a particularly effective metric for comparing simulated and observed images in this setting.
arxiv-2510-21114:
Yanguang Sun leads three co-authors on Controllable-LPMoE, a fine tuning method that adapts large foundation models to hard object segmentation using dynamic local priors from a mixture of experts. Full fine tuning updates enormous parameter counts and creates a training efficiency bottleneck.

Prompt based tuning of frozen models is cheaper but prompts lack built in semantic priors, limiting adaptability. Their paradigm supplies dynamic local priors while keeping trainable parameters few. Challenging segmentation targets, where boundaries are subtle and classes shift, stand to gain most from priors that adjust to each image region.
arxiv-2510-21414:
Hoang Ly, Emina Soljanin, and Michael Schleppy speed up maximum-likelihood decoding, the best but famously costly way to recover a message from a noisy channel. For a general block code, the textbook search checks every codeword, and no method had beaten that worst-case cost when measured in multiplications.

Their insight recasts the score of each codeword as a dot product between two built vectors, one from the received signal and one from the codeword itself. Scoring the whole codebook then becomes a single vector-matrix multiplication, and picking the winner is trivial. A fast multiplication algorithm trims the total work by a factor equal to the code length, for linear and nonlinear codes alike, under hard or soft decisions. The saving costs a large precomputed table, and the idea extends to list decoding and interference channels.
arxiv-2510-21814:
Zhuoming Li and seven co-authors build Gestura, a system for understanding free-form hand gestures in real time. The co-authors are Aitong Liu, Mengxi Jia, Yubi Lu, Tengxiang Zhang, Changzhi Sun, Dell Zhang, and Xuelong Li. Fixed gesture menus are limiting. The one earlier open-ended system was slow and often inaccurate.

Gestura leans on a large vision-language model. It connects varied hand movements with their meanings. A dedicated module feeds in anatomical hand landmarks. That sharpens the model's sense of fine motion. A step-by-step reasoning strategy helps with unclear gestures. The team also released the first open dataset for this task. It holds more than three hundred thousand annotated question-and-answer pairs about gesture intent.
arxiv-2510-21914:
Tal Shpigel and five co-authors, Dylan Folsom, Mariangela Lisanti, Lina Necib, Mark Vogelsberger, and Lars Hernquist, build a recipe for measuring how fast dark matter particles move near the Sun. Underground detectors count on that speed pattern, yet it has mostly been borrowed from simulated galaxies that only resemble our own.

Working with ninety-eight Milky Way look-alikes from the TNG50 simulation, the team tests whether nearby stars can stand in for the invisible matter. Dark matter from old mergers and quiet accretion follows a simple bell-shaped speed pattern. Matter from recent large mergers can be traced through the star debris those mergers left behind. Star speeds run slightly low compared with their dark matter twins, but a simple correction lines the two up well.
arxiv-2510-22014:
Sarah Ball and six co-authors, Niki Hasrati, Alexander Robey, Avi Schwarzschild, Frauke Kreuter, Zico Kolter, and Andrej Risteski, investigate why jailbreak suffixes travel. Short strings of nonsense text, tuned to make one language model produce forbidden content, often work on prompts and models they were never tuned for. Nobody had a rigorous account of when that transfer happens.

Three measurable properties turned out to track transfer success closely. How strongly a bare prompt already activates the model's internal refusal signal, how hard a suffix pushes against that signal, and how much movement happens in unrelated directions. How similar two prompts are in meaning, by contrast, barely mattered. Experiments that intervened on those properties confirmed the story, giving defenders a sharper picture of what makes an attack portable.
arxiv-2510-22314:
Christian Imenkamp and five co-authors borrow a trick from ecology for streaming process mining. Analysts watch live event streams from business or software processes. They cut the stream into windows for study. The window size quietly decides what the analysis can see. Fix it, and process drift makes the snapshot biased.

Their method lets the window adapt instead. Sizing uses estimators developed for species estimation in biodiversity research. Those estimators judge how representative a sample is of the whole. On real-world datasets, adaptive windows beat static ones in accuracy. They also stayed robust when the process drifted. The co-authors are Martin Kabierski, Hendrik Reiter, Matthias Weidlich, Wilhelm Hasselbring, and Agnes Koschmider. The transfer works because an event stream, like a forest, hides types a small sample has not revealed.
arxiv-2510-22414:
Mertcan Sevgi leads twenty eight co-authors in testing whether an AI system can help eye doctors reason through real clinical cases. They study AMIE, a medical conversational system with web search and self critique, on case stories a general ophthalmologist should manage. Two studies check both joint work with doctors and the quality of the system alone.

After reading the system output, doctors ranked the correct diagnosis higher, agreed more with each other, and enriched their test and treatment plans. Gains appeared even when the system top choice was wrong, which suggests structured support helps doctors rethink rather than just copy.
arxiv-2510-22814:
Could advanced AI make humanity obsolete or even extinct? Mohamed El Louadi and Emna Ben Romdhane examine that risk in a 2025 article. They trace a path from current AI to ultraintelligence. Their sources include Irving J Good and Nick Bostrom. Recent scenario works are also discussed.

The article covers AGI and superintelligence. AGI means general machine intellect at human level. Superintelligence would far exceed human minds. The authors stress how alien such a mind could be. Extinction might come without malice. It could come from unchecked, indifferent superiority. Ethical and existential stakes run through the analysis.
arxiv-2510-22914:
Gamma ray burst prompt emission has three rival origin models. None explains all data collected so far. Yang-Dong-Jun Ou leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they use missing neutrinos to weigh the models. Neutrinos are nearly invisible particles. No diffuse neutrino glow from bursts has been detected.

They compute expected diffuse flux two ways. One sums individual burst contributions. The other uses assumed luminosity functions. Both point the same way. Most bursts should come from the ICMART model. ICMART involves magnetic reconnection and turbulence. Photosphere and internal shock shares are tightly bounded. Those bounds are near zero in their results.
arxiv-2510-23214:
Robin Schmocker, Alexander Dockhorn, and Bodo Rosenhahn introduce AUPO, a drop-in change to Monte Carlo Tree Search that abstracts actions until proven otherwise. The method builds its abstraction only from reward distribution statistics gathered during search. It needs no transition probabilities and no acyclic search graph, unlike rival abstraction methods.

Because of that freedom, AUPO can detect symmetric actions that state-of-the-art frameworks miss. On a range of IPPC benchmark problems, the authors report that AUPO clearly outperforms plain tree search. A cheap, general abstraction could speed planning in games and robotics alike.
arxiv-2510-23414:
Ivan Sipiran and six co-authors present Symmetria, a synthetic data set for learning on point clouds. Point cloud methods lack the huge data sets that image and text learning enjoy. Symmetria is formula-driven, so it can be generated at any scale with precise ground truth guaranteed by construction.

The design promotes data-efficient experiments needing fewer samples, broad generalization across geometric settings, and easy extension to new tasks and modalities. Synthetic symmetry-rich data could let researchers prototype three-dimensional learning ideas quickly, then validate on scarce real scans with more confidence. Full details of the setup, tests, and limits appear in the paper.
arxiv-2510-23514:
Md Habibur Rahman, Maitreyo Biswas, and Arun Mannodi-Kanakkithodi built a tool for studying defects in cadmium telluride solar cells. Tiny flaws and added impurities inside the absorber layer shape how well these cells turn light into power. Testing every possible defect mix with full quantum calculations is far too slow, because the combinations and charge states multiply quickly.

Their framework, DeFecT-FF, trains machine learning force fields on a growing library of high-quality density functional calculations. The models predict energies and atomic forces for bulk and alloyed crystals, with or without defects, across many charge states. Screening with the models turned up many new low-energy defect shapes, later confirmed with precise follow-up calculations. The tool is free online through nanoHUB, so users can upload a crystal file and get defect energies without running costly calculations themselves.
arxiv-2510-23614:
Erika Bérczi-Kovács and András Frank revisit a cornerstone of discrete optimization: the Nash-Williams and Tutte theorem on spanning trees in graphs. The theorem gives conditions for a graph to contain several edge-disjoint spanning trees, and a matching result covers packing all edges into a few forests. These elegant statements launched decades of research with reach far beyond their original setting.

The authors' first aim is exposition: to walk non-experts through some of the developments these theorems triggered, including far-reaching generalizations. They also trace applications in areas that seem distant from graph theory at first glance. At the same time, they promise specialists some novelty in how the story is told. The piece works as both an invitation for newcomers and a fresh arrangement of a well-loved theory for experts.
arxiv-2510-23714:
Saiyad Ashanujjaman and four co-authors hunt for a heavy Higgs pair signal that dedicated searches have partly missed. In two-Higgs-doublet models, a heavy neutral Higgs A often decays to a Z boson plus a lighter heavy Higgs H, which then decays to top quarks. ATLAS and CMS searches required both tops to be on-shell, leaving the lower-mass region, where one top is off-shell, uncovered.

The authors recast Standard Model measurements of top pairs plus a Z boson from both experiments to fill the gap. Their limits on the rate land between 0.12 and 0.62 picobarns across the mass range. Curiously, the data prefer a real signal, up to two and a half sigma. The hint is strongest near an A mass of 450 GeV and an H mass of 290 GeV. A top-loving version of the model can fit that hint with an extra coupling.
arxiv-2510-23814:
Tong Bao and seven co-authors classify the faint soft X-ray sources that the eROSITA all-sky survey found toward the inner Galactic disk. That slice of sky is rich but poorly understood at the faint end, because surveys lacked sensitivity. The team followed up 189 eROSITA sources with deeper XMM-Newton observations and combined X-ray spectral fits with Gaia positions and photometry.

The catalog turns out to be dominated by coronal sources — active stars and binaries — at about seventy-four percent. Roughly eight percent are wind-powered massive stars, and eighteen percent are accreting compact objects, the prized minority. A hardness-ratio cut separates the non-coronal sources. Stacking the sources, the authors estimate that about six percent of the Galactic Ridge's soft X-ray glow resolves into point sources above the survey limit. The hard-band glow, by contrast, comes mainly from X-ray binaries.
arxiv-2510-23914:
Arsenii Mustafin and two co-authors revisit value iteration, the foundational algorithm of reinforcement learning, and close a gap between its theory and its observed speed. Classic theory promises geometric convergence in the discounted-reward case, while recent work on average rewards suggested only slow, sublinear convergence. In practice the algorithm often races ahead of both stories.

Through one geometric analysis covering both reward settings, the authors prove convergence is geometric in each, assuming a unique optimal policy that keeps the system in one communicating class. They also show the rate is faster than earlier analyses claimed. The unified lens explains why practice looked better than the textbooks said: the pessimistic average-reward bound was an artifact of the proof technique, not the algorithm. For practitioners, the result firms up the theory behind a tool used everywhere from control systems to game-playing agents.
arxiv-2510-24214:
Jinhong Deng and three co-authors propose SCOPE, a method to prune visual tokens in multimodal large language models for lower cost. These models process many image tokens, much of them redundant, which drives up computing cost. Prior pruning keeps only the most salient tokens by attention score, but that can drop parts of the scene and leave the meaning incomplete.

SCOPE selects tokens by both saliency and coverage together. It defines a coverage measure for a chosen token set based on how well the set spans the image's content. By keeping tokens that jointly cover the scene, the method preserves fuller meaning while still cutting the token count and speeding up the model.
arxiv-2510-24314:
Sahil Islam and two co-authors use a cell based model to link cell motion to how a young tissue bends and flows. The tissue is part of the early embryo. It shifts shape over wide scales and sheds stress as cells swap places. A clear link from cell scale drive to whole tissue response was missing. In their model, each cell is a polygon that can push and pull.

They first checked the model against lab data on how this tissue relaxes after stress. They then pulled out key time scales from stress decay and shaking tests. The model shows how cell drive shifts the tissue from spring like to flow like response. It also shows fast stress decay next to stress that lasts. With force pulsed in set zones, the tissue acts like a system whose shape can be steered.
arxiv-2510-24514:
Huanyu Zhang and eleven co-authors introduce Latent Sketchpad, a framework that lets multimodal language models sketch visual thoughts while reasoning. These models understand images well but struggle with tasks needing visual planning and imagination. Humans sketch to develop and share ideas, and the authors give models an internal visual scratchpad for the same purpose.

The method repurposes the model's internal visual representations, normally used only for perception, to support generative visual thought without weakening reasoning. Visual generation is integrated directly into the model's native autoregressive process, so it can draw intermediate images as it thinks. The goal is stronger multimodal reasoning on complex visual problems.
arxiv-2510-24814:
Phi-Hung Hoang, Nam-Thuan Trinh, Van-Manh Tran, and Thi-Thu-Hong Phan gauge fish freshness from shots with a mix of deep and classic tools. Hand checks of fish are slow and rest on taste and feel, which shift from judge to judge. Deep tools can sort shots, but their traits can be hard to trace.

Their frame first tunes five known vision nets to set a base. Traits from those nets then feed seven classic sort tools. Last, three pick rules shrink the trait set to a small, rich core. Tests on a known fish shot set checked how well the mix holds. The aim is a grade that plants and shops can trust.
arxiv-2510-24914:
Laurent Massoulie, the sole author, sets hard limits on when two linked graphs can be lined up by a fast tool. The task is to guess the hid match of points from two graphs whose edges shift in sync. He views it as a high size stat task, with a sparse chance graph as one key case.

For that case, he finds a sharp line for the edge link strength: above it, a local note pass tool can line the graphs up. Below it, no local tool can. The line turns on a linked model of chance trees. He then maps a like line for a fast ghost tool on noise based grids, with a noise scale for when match reads fail.
arxiv-2510-25514:
Maik Overmars, Jasper Goseling, and Richard Boucherie study time difference learning. Their 2025 paper analyzes off-policy TD(0) convergence. Linear function approximation is used for value values. The goal is expected discounted reward in Markov chains. Off-policy learning with approximation can diverge in general. Current results modify methods to restore convergence guarantees.

Their method analyzes the standard method unchanged instead. Reversibility is a mild structural setting in many uses. They show convergence under that reversibility setting. A discount factor bound governs the guarantee explicitly. It depends on on-policy and off-policy process differences. Projected Bellman error reaches zero. They adapt a stochastic approximation approach. Examples include random walks on weighted graphs.
arxiv-2510-25614:
Niklas Jost, Adolfo Escobedo, and Alice Kirchheim ask why districting becomes hard. Their 2025 paper studies edge-based districting computational intractability. Districting divides regions into districts for elections or services. Objective functions and several constraint groups form it.

Districting is known NP-hard in general cases. They study relaxing or removing certain constraint groups. Precise edges emerge between tractable and intractable subproblems. Some relaxed versions lie in polynomial class P. Others remain NP-hard despite removing constraints. Implications for node-based analogs are also discussed. Alternative notions of certain criteria enter their study. Understanding hardness sources helps design useful districting methods. Tractability maps guide method choice for planners.
arxiv-2510-25714:
Dan Barry led four co-authors presenting Binaspect. Davoud Shariat Panah, Alessandro Ragano, and Jan Skoglund helped. Andrew Hines closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper releases a Python library for binaural audio. Interpretable azimuth maps are generated by the library.

Time-frequency bins cluster into stable time-azimuth histograms. Multiple active sources appear as distinct azimuthal clusters. Binaspect operates blindly on audio without head models. No prior knowledge of head geometry is required. Codec and renderer design choices cause such degradation. VBAP source positioning is also showed clearly. Features export as structured features for learning. Machine learning models can train on those features. Quality prediction and spatial classification are uses.
arxiv-2510-25914:
Ngoc Phuoc An Vo, Manish Kesarwani, Ruchi Mahindru, and Chandrasekhar Narayanaswami build an AI agent to help firms control cloud spending. FinOps, short for finance plus operations, is the practice of making engineering, finance, and business teams share responsibility for cloud value. The hard part is that billing data arrive in mixed formats and measures from many providers, yet choices must be made fast.

Vo and the team simulate a full industry process, from pulling data and merging it to analysis and cost saving advice. They define scores to judge the agent and test several open and closed language models. The agent understood, planned, and carried out tasks at a level matching a human FinOps practitioner in their setup.
arxiv-2510-26214:
Yu. D. Fomin, working alone, examines the melting line of silicon computed with a machine learning potential called SNAP. Silicon is a key semiconductor, and its phase diagram, the map of which solid or liquid form wins at each pressure and temperature, matters for both industry and planetary science. The SNAP potential is trained to mimic accurate quantum calculations at far lower cost.

Fomin finds that the melting line of the diamond phase is a linear function of pressure, in good agreement with experimental data for its shape. At the same time, the model strongly underestimates the melting temperature itself. The potential also fails to predict the high pressure phases of silicon, which limits its use for deep pressure studies.
arxiv-2510-26314:
Stein Andreas Bethuelsen and Christian Monch prove a strict shift result for percolation models. Percolation studies whether random links create one giant linked part. The critical point is the threshold where that part appears. Their models are long range and independent. They live on graphs that are finite in each local view and the same at each point.

The authors use coupling ideas. Two models are built on the same chance, so they can be compared at once. This improves on the classic essential enhancement method. Their proof needs only two mild inputs. The model must be the same under shifts, and the link rule must have a finite sum. The result covers both two way and directed bond cases.
arxiv-2510-26414:
Edoardo Suerra, with nine co-authors, reports a light source that makes squeezed states, a quantum form of light with noise pushed below the usual level in one aspect. Their device is a synchronously pumped optical parametric oscillator, a cavity fed by pulses in step with its round trips. It runs at ninety-three megahertz and emits light at a wavelength of 1035 nanometres.

Suerra and the team use a counter-running beam from the same cavity to steady it and to serve as the reference for detection, which gives a clean overlap between the beams. Two light modulators shape the pump and reference in colour and phase. Measures matched a detailed model well. Squeezing reached minus three point three decibels in the lab, or minus five point seven at the device output, in their stated units.
arxiv-2510-26514:
Katsuhiko Matsuzaki and Fei Tao work in complex analysis, on curves with special smoothness traits. A chord-arc curve is one whose arc length stays close to the straight distance between its points. The pair ask whether a curve that is asymptotically conformal, meaning it flattens out in a stated sense at small scales, must also be asymptotically smooth.

Matsuzaki and Tao answer no, by building an explicit curve that meets the first trait and fails the second. That single example has knock-on effects: a function in two named spaces need not lie in a third, and a map with two symmetry traits need not have a stronger one. They also give a full test for when such curves are asymptotically smooth, in terms of flatness plus uniform approximability, the ability to be approached evenly by nicer curves.
arxiv-2510-26614:
Christoffer Koo Øhrstrøm, Ronja Güldenring, and Lazaros Nalpantidis rethink how to feed data from event cameras to AI systems. An event camera reports only changes, as a sparse stream of timed events, rather than full frames. Common stand-ins, frames and voxels, force that stream into a regular grid and lose its sparse, asynchronous nature.

The three authors propose Spiking Patches, a tokenizer that cuts the event stream into tokens while keeping those traits. They test it with three kinds of networks on gesture recognition and object detection. Inference ran up to about three times faster than voxel tokens and about ten times faster than frames. Accuracy matched the older routes and sometimes beat them, with gains of up to about four points on gestures. The team frames tokenization as a fresh direction for event-based vision.
arxiv-2510-26714:
Jamie Lanyon, Axel Finke, Petros Andreou, and Georgina Cosma warn that machine unlearning results can hinge on a hidden choice. Unlearning aims to remove certain data's influence from a trained model without full retraining. Most methods are approximate, so their quality is judged by experiment.

Lanyon and his three co-authors note that common practice runs the unlearning step many times from one trained model, varying only the unlearning seed. In image classification tests, results swung with the training seed, so single-seed studies can mislead. The issue is sharpest for deterministic methods, which repeat exactly from the same start. Further tests on federated learning-to-rank and large language models show the problem is wider, and more unlearning seeds cannot generally make up for missing training seeds. The paper gives guidance on choosing both counts.
arxiv-2510-26914:
Sam Allen, Enrico Pescara, and Johanna Ziegel present a new forecast method in 2025. A forecast here is a full distribution, a curve that gives odds for each outcome. Good forecasts must be calibrated, meaning their stated odds match real rates over time.

Their residual method builds forecast curves from left-over errors of a fitted model. A residual is the gap between a real value and a model guess. In the split case, it nests a common form of conformal prediction. Conformal prediction scores how well a new outcome fits past data. In the full case, it avoids strict demands on that score. It can pair with any regressor, a model that guesses numbers from inputs. Tests on made-up data show it matches the older method in skill. The authors note room to try it with many other regressors.
arxiv-2510-27014:
Sean Patten, Pin-Yu Chen, Christina Schweikert, and D. Frank Hsu combine several models to judge whether movie reviews sound positive or negative. Their method, combinatorial fusion analysis, scores how differently the models rank items and then blends their predictions by that diversity. The idea favors cognitive diversity, meaning genuinely different viewpoints, over simply building one larger model.

The blend joins a RoBERTa transformer model with random forest, support vector machine, and XGBoost models. On the IMDB review dataset it reaches accuracy the authors report as state of the art, near ninety-seven percent. It also beats standard ensemble methods while using computing resources more efficiently. The work shows careful fusion can rival scale as a path to better classification.
arxiv-2510-27214:
Callum Dewsnap, Pauline Barmby, and Sarah Gallagher test how reliably active galactic nuclei can be separated from their host galaxies in Webb telescope images. Splitting the bright central engine light from the fainter galaxy depends heavily on image sharpness and depth. With JWST delivering unmatched quality, the team checks whether standard tools still measure galaxy shapes faithfully.

They fit two-component models to dozens of X-ray selected active galaxies from a deep survey. One point-spread function builder consistently fails to match real point sources. Two fitting codes then settle in different parameter regions, giving consistently different host properties despite accurate total magnitudes. Host shape measures prove poorly determined and strongly linked, warning that the standard profile may not uniquely represent these hosts.
arxiv-2510-27414:
Tommaso Del Carro, Gerson Portilla, and two other co-authors design a fuel-saving way to dock spacecraft in this 2025 paper. In a rendezvous, one craft creeps up on another in orbit. Thruster firings steer the approach but burn fuel and wear hardware. Their control law fires only at chosen moments, not on a fixed clock.

The law reads the craft's state, its place and speed, and switches thrust on when set conditions are met. It rests on the Hill-Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, which describe motion near a circular orbit. Stability is proven with Lyapunov analysis, a check that errors shrink over time, cast in matrix inequality form. In a worked case, the closed-loop system stayed stable with the fewest firings they could manage. A standard predictive control scheme served as the yardstick.
arxiv-2511-00214:
Finding hidden groups inside a network gets harder when links carry weights, such as strengths or counts. Filippo Radicchi and four co-authors ask when a standard spectral method can still recover the true split. They use a planted-partition model, a test network built with two equal groups, and derive a formula for the most mixing the method can tolerate.

The threshold turns on how node degree and link weight vary. Weights that spread out more make groups harder to spot. When weights carry no clue about group membership, adding them hurts rather than helps. Five weight patterns are compared, from fixed weights to weights drawn from spread-out distributions.
arxiv-2511-00314:
Rohit Kishan Ray reframes a basic question in quantum physics: instead of asking whether a state breaks Bell-type limits, ask directly whether the state is local, meaning explainable by classical means. Checking Bell violations is a global task that needs full correlation data. Ray introduces local perception operators, tools that compress global measurements into statistics a local observer can actually access.

From those operators he derives two witnesses, tests that flag nonlocal behavior: one usable by a single party with classical side information, and one that needs both sides. The criteria use only first moments and standard measurements, and they depend on local data and measurement geometry. They can certify classical explanations in cases where standard Bell tests stay inconclusive.
arxiv-2511-00614:
Zora Tung prepares astronomy for a flood: the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will record light curves for ten billion sources and flag millions of transient candidates each night. Classifiers must be fast, accurate, and frugal with labels. Using the ELAsTiCC simulation challenge as a proving ground, Tung presents ATCAT, a causal transformer for astronomical time series with refined light curve encoding.

ATCAT sets new state-of-the-art scores on the challenge, both for light curves alone and combined with metadata, and it leads at every early time cutoff, which helps prioritize follow-up observations. Stripping away ninety percent of training labels barely dented performance, thanks to regularization, bootstrap ensembling, and unsupervised pretraining. A calibration fix and a fast GPU implementation, nine times quicker than rivals, complete the package.
arxiv-2511-00714:
Sarah Gibson and eight co-authors sharpen a polarization trick for locating solar eruptions in three dimensions. Sunlight scattered by electrons is polarized, and the ratio of radial to tangential polarization reveals where compact structures sit along the line of sight. The PUNCH mission was designed around exactly this diagnostic for coronal mass ejections and the background solar wind.

The same ratio, the authors note, doubles as a local measure of how steeply density falls off in the quiet wind, which creates ambiguity. Judging whether a structure is compact enough for 3D positioning becomes essential. Building from single sight lines to full three-dimensional ejection models, they measure how accurately polarization properties of both eruptions and quiet wind can be diagnosed. The challenges and opportunities of PUNCH data are mapped together.
arxiv-2511-00814:
Stella Kombo, Masih Haseli, Skylar Wei, and Joel Burdick ask whether a robot can learn, in real time, how a nearby moving object will behave next. Forecasts must come from partial and noisy sensor data, and they must arrive fast enough to guide motion planning.

Their method builds a Hankel matrix from recent measurements, trims it to a clean low rank form, and derives a local linear predictor that changes over time. The leftover errors also yield running estimates of noise level, useful for risk aware planning. Tests cover simulations with both mild and heavy tailed noise, plus a real crane testbed, and show stable cleaning of the signal with reliable short range forecasts.
arxiv-2511-00914:
M. Klazar and R. Horsky generalize a famous result of Polya about random walks. Polya's theorem describes the limiting chances that a walk on a grid, starting at the origin, ever visits a given point. Their version replaces the grid with the complete directed graph on the natural numbers, where every vertex connects to every other.

Edges carry complex number weights, and coefficients in generating functions may themselves be infinite series, extending the symbolic method of enumerative combinatorics. The authors obtain sixteen generalizations of Polya's theorem, and the approach also covers Markov chains on the natural numbers starting at one. An appendix proves key values of an auxiliary function used in the argument.
arxiv-2511-01114:
John Graf constructs Hall-Littlewood functions, a family of symmetric functions that extend the classical Schur functions, by deforming a well known operator. The Bernstein operator builds Schur functions by adding a part to the index. Its pieces give their vertex operator representation.

Graf defines a t-version of that operator, with the parameter t woven in. He shows it yields a construction of Jing's vertex operator for Hall-Littlewood functions. The classical involution on symmetric functions turns out to be central to the construction, showing extra combinatorial structure. As one use, the operator proves stability of certain structure coefficients, including the Hall polynomials, which count extensions in finite abelian group theory.
arxiv-2511-01214:
Weifeng Xu and colleagues forecast the El Nino Southern Oscillation, the Pacific climate pattern that shapes weather and disaster risk worldwide, with a conditional diffusion model. Long range ENSO forecasts are limited by incomplete understanding of its physics, and both numerical and deep learning methods struggle to balance accuracy with physical sense.

Their model builds a probabilistic map from past to future states using a higher order Markov chain, so uncertainty is quantified directly. It extends the lead times of leading methods, catches early signals of the spring predictability barrier, and reproduces the evolution of past extreme events. Strikingly, the reverse diffusion process turns out to encode the classical recharge discharge mechanism of ENSO, matching the governing principles of the van der Pol oscillator.
arxiv-2511-01414:
Angelos Gkekas, Nikos Mitsiou, Ioannis Souldatos, and George Karagiannidis ask a question at the border of information theory and computability. Can a program actually find the best possible error-correcting codes for a noisy channel? Or does theory only promise that such codes exist?

Their answer is that a Turing machine can do it. Given a channel, a target rate below capacity, and an error tolerance, the machine searches through codes of growing block length until one meets the targets. The construction leans on Shannon's channel coding theorem and is written formally as a recursive function. The authors also argue that their assumptions about computable numbers cannot be weakened any further.
arxiv-2511-01814:
Michael Turner reviews the state of Lambda-CDM, the standard model of cosmology, and where it should go next. The paradigm earns its standing from an expansive account of the universe's history, deep connections to particle physics, and the large body of data supporting it. Yet supporters and critics agree it is not the final theory, and both camps are eager for a successor.

Turner surveys some of the most impactful recent events in cosmology since the last Le Workshop gathering. Then he focuses on a possible lever for change. It is the recent evidence that dark energy evolves over time, rather than remaining constant. If that evidence holds, it may be the thread that leads cosmology to a better theory, and the review maps the role it could play in the path forward.
arxiv-2511-02014:
Tuan Truong, Guillermo Jimenez Perez, Pedro Osorio, and Matthias Lenga benchmark large multimodal models. The models act as detectors of protected health information burned into medical images. These are the names and identifiers printed directly onto scans. They must be scrubbed before sharing. Traditional pipelines chain optical character recognition with named entity recognition; the question is whether modern multimodal models do the whole job better.

Three models, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Qwen 2.5 7B, were tested in two configurations, text analysis alone and OCR plus semantic analysis. The multimodal models read text far more accurately than EasyOCR, with word error rates of only a few percent. Yet better reading did not reliably mean better privacy detection overall; the strongest gains appeared on cases with complex imprint patterns, while clean, high-contrast text made the pipelines equivalent. The authors close with empirically grounded selection advice for different operational constraints.
arxiv-2511-02614:
Mohammed Al-Jaff and seven co-authors fix a family of generative models that kept collapsing. Idempotent networks are trained to act as the identity on real data and to project anything else back onto the data manifold. One network both generates samples and repairs corrupted inputs. In practice their training borrowed adversarial ingredients, and with them came the familiar diseases of such training: mode collapse, dropped modes, and instability.

The replacement, NAIGN, removes the adversarial part entirely. Its loss combines plain repair with the non-adversarial objective of implicit maximum likelihood estimation. The new models restored corrupted data better and produced samples matching the data distribution more closely than the original design. As a bonus, the trained networks turn out to encode the distance to the data manifold, and with it an energy-based model of the data.
arxiv-2511-03114:
Qi Zhang, Yifei Wang, and Yisen Wang explain why contrastive learning works, through a new theory of augmentation overlap. Contrastive methods train on paired views of one sample and learn to cluster similar items, but the mechanism was murky. Earlier theory assumed conditional independence between views. Their 2025 paper first tightens the bounds under that assumption, then drops it for a more practical one.

Under strong augmentation, the supports of views from the same class overlap more, and simply pulling paired views together then drags whole classes into clusters. From that picture they derive nearly closed bounds on downstream performance. They also build an unsupervised score for learned representations that tracks downstream results closely, without extra modules, giving practitioners a cheap quality gauge.
arxiv-2511-03314:
Tetsuya Takaishi looks closely at how sample size bends a measure of roughness in Bitcoin price swings. Realized volatility tracks how much prices jump over short spans. A statistic called the Hurst exponent hints at whether swings look smooth or jagged, yet the span chosen for sampling can shift its value.

With Bitcoin data, the exponent falls as the sampling span grows, and a simple finite-sample curve fits that fall well. Pushing the span toward zero gives values under one half, a sign of rough volatility. The common five-minute choice carries only about one percent of relative error. A wider check also finds layered scaling in swing patterns, though weaker than in price returns themselves.
arxiv-2511-03414:
Mao-Jing Liu, Ying Li, and Zhi-Tian Zou give a joint account of several B meson decays that test lepton flavor rules. Their method blends perturbative calculations at low momentum transfer with lattice results stretched across the full range by a model-free expansion. That hybrid yields precise shape factors for the decays.

Predicted flavor ratios for the semileptonic decays land near the latest measured averages, easing earlier hints of tension. The team then studies a related decay with a pion, splitting its amplitude into factorizable and harder parts. A correlated treatment keeps shared uncertainties honest across all channels. Joint fits like this sharpen the hunt for physics beyond the standard model in flavor data.
arxiv-2511-03614:
Han Wang and colleagues separate internal tides from slower balanced flows in ocean surface data with deep learning. The two motions overlap in satellite views, yet they carry different energy and mixing roles. Classic harmonic fitting fails when tides lose coherence or sampling runs thin, as with global satellites.

Wide-swath satellites give two-dimensional snapshots, recasting the split as an image translation task. A simpler, cheaper network matches their earlier heavy model once its learning rate is annealed during training. Adding surface temperature and other fields beside height is tested for gains. Cleaner tidal maps from space would sharpen estimates of ocean mixing, a key input to climate models.
arxiv-2511-03714:
Bao-Jun Cai, Bao-An Li, and Yu-Gang Ma ask whether a key stiffness measure inside neutron stars bottoms out at the very center. The measure compares pressure with energy density and tracks how stiff matter has been on average from the surface inward. Its behavior in the core bears on what superdense matter really is.

From the structure of the stellar balance equations alone, that average stiffness falls steadily outward, whatever detailed model is fed in. Evidence for a peak in sound speed inside the star sharpens the question further. A model-free monotonic fact is precious in a field forced to guess the core recipe. The authors argue the center value anchors the whole profile and deserves direct observational hunting.
arxiv-2511-04114:
Paul Badu Yakubu, Lesther Santana, Mohamed Rahouti, Yufeng Xin, Abdellah Chehri, and Mohammed Aledhari build an automated, clear system for detecting distributed denial-of-service attacks in networks guarded by AI intrusion detection. Older detectors struggle to scale and to explain themselves, slowing response and hiding attack structure.

Automated pipeline tuning selects and tunes the learning model and features, cutting manual trials. Shapley notes then show how each feature pushes a detection call. Two packet features, mean backward packet length and minimum forward packet header length, proved critical in experiments. Automation plus clear notes, the team argue, gives a detection route that is both scalable and open to audit.
arxiv-2511-04314:
Tomasz Kania, writing alone, proves that no separable Banach algebra can serve as a universal host for all separable Banach algebras under homomorphic embedding, whether embeddings must be contractive or merely bounded. The same negative answer holds inside the commutative category, and the proof is advertised as short and direct.

For each closed subspace of the sequence space c-zero, a separable commutative algebra is built whose multiplication records the pairing between the subspace and its dual. Any injective homomorphism from that algebra forces the identity on the dual to factor through the host. A universal algebra would then be complementably universal for those duals, contradicting a theorem of Johnson and Szankowski.
arxiv-2511-04714:
Ljudmila Kamenova and her co-author study when complex shapes can be covered by flat complex space. A shape with such a covering map is called dominable. Smooth rational shapes have this trait, as do abelian varieties and Kummer surfaces.

Elliptic K3 surfaces were already known to admit holomorphic covering maps. The pair extends those results to some hyperkähler shapes, which generalize K3 surfaces. They give examples and tests for both meromorphic and holomorphic maps. The work also links dominability to the vanishing of the Kobayashi metric, a sign that a shape is far from hyperbolic.
arxiv-2511-04814:
Sebastian Ojeda leads ten authors setting a shared test for computer tools that sort antimicrobial peptides. These small proteins are promising weapons against drug-resistant microbes. Split datasets and clashing labels have slowed the search for new ones.

Their ESCAPE set merges over eighty thousand peptides from twenty-seven checked sources. Each peptide carries labels for up to four kinds of action. It can kill bacteria, fungi, viruses, or parasites, and some do more than one. A transformer model is built and tested on the set. One shared, multilabel test should let research groups compare new tools fairly.
arxiv-2511-04914:
Hardik B. Sailor leads twenty-nine authors with MERaLiON-SER, a speech emotion model for English and Southeast Asian languages. Emotion systems must name feelings and grade their strength at once. Their training mixes two losses to cover both sides of that job.

A weighted class loss handles discrete labels like happy or angry. A concordance loss tracks arousal, valence, and dominance as continuous scores. Tests span Singapore's English, Chinese, Malay, and Tamil speech plus public benchmarks. Strong results across that mix matter for call centers, health tools, and assistants serving multilingual regions where emotion cues vary by language.
arxiv-2511-05114:
Álvaro Guglielmin Becker and co-authors test how well three large language models can code board games and invent new variants of them. Writing a board game program by hand takes long, careful work, so fast code help would be welcome if it proves sound.

The team set Claude, DeepSeek, and ChatGPT the same game tasks, from plain rules to fresh twists on known games. Their method checks what each model builds and where it fails. The study gives a clear gauge of how far chat models can go on rule-bound code with clear win states.
arxiv-2511-05214:
Filipe Thewes and co-authors propose one field model that unites phase separation with non-local interactions. Phase separation drives mixtures to split, and plain theory says split zones grow without bound, yet many real systems freeze into patterns of a fixed size.

Their model shows that long-range links tend to halt that growth. Systems with non-local short-range links also show a smooth phase shift into patterned states, which only that second kind allows. The frame sorts a zoo of pattern cases into two clear classes, which helps read past data and plan new tests.
arxiv-2511-05314:
B. Liagre and co-authors extend seismic diagnostics for quadrupolar mixed modes in evolved sun-like stars. Mixed modes mix core and surface waves, and the dipolar kind showed a surprise: core and envelope spin at near the same rate.

Quadrupolar modes could add proof, but they are faint and hard to sort, since split parts can sit close or overlap. The authors build an asymptotic account that keeps those near-degeneracy effects in view, then fit it to data. The work opens a second window on how old stars spin deep inside.
arxiv-2511-05414:
Suprokash Hazra introduces special domains in higher complex dimensions and studies the envelope of truncated tube domains, regions built over a cut-off base in complex space. Envelopes mark the largest region to which all holomorphic functions on a domain must extend.

Hazra shows every pseudoconvex truncated tube domain is special. He then proves an envelope theorem for special domains that widens a recent result by Jarnicki and Pflug. A schlichtness result in two dimensions closes the paper, with two higher-dimensional extensions. Such theorems chart where complex analysis is forced to live.
arxiv-2511-05514:
Tristan Barkman proves an operator-level necessity result for the Chapman-Enskog expansion, the bridge from kinetic theory to fluid laws. In closed, unforced kinetic systems, he asks when first-order deviatoric stress, the part of stress that shapes flow, must appear.

His answer is an if and only if: that stress arises at first order exactly when the first Chapman-Enskog correction is non-zero. Past work assumed or derived the stress in a formal way. Under set terms on the collision operator, such as coercivity and Fredholm solvability, Barkman makes the link exact, which closes a gap in kinetic theory texts.
arxiv-2511-05714:
Nicholas Generous, Brian Cook, and Jason Pruet argue that powerful AI breaks the assumptions under today's United States defense plans. The current program of record was designed before capable machine intelligence arrived. On its own, they say, it cannot preserve national security against fast-growing AI-enabled threats.

Shoring up old systems is not enough, in their view. Wholly new parts must be added to the defense setup. The authors outline prompt steps to adapt the national labs run by the nuclear security agency. The goal is speed and strength in an era of strong AI. Their paper is a policy case made to defense planners.
arxiv-2511-06514:
Vamsi Addanki and colleagues give a leaner proof that the Harmonic policy for network buffer sharing is nearly optimal. A switch with many output ports stores arriving packets in one shared buffer and must accept or reject each instantly to maximize throughput. The Harmonic policy was known to achieve the best proven guarantee, but its original proof was long and intricate.

The note first shows the policy needs only a constant number of threshold checks per packet, matching the widely deployed Dynamic Threshold policy in practical cost. A direct new proof then splits packets into three groups to establish the competitive ratio of two plus the natural log of the port count. Simplicity serves both theory and deployment.
arxiv-2511-06614:
Ruyin Wan, George Em Karniadakis, and Panos Stinis swap the neuron inside spiking networks used for scientific computing. Spiking networks compute with brief pulses like real brains, but they are rarely used for continuous regression in science. The standard leaky integrate-and-fire neuron fires in jumps, which roughens training and leaves jagged response surfaces.

Quadratic integrate-and-fire neurons spike smoothly and differentiably, so ordinary gradient training works cleanly. The team tested them in direct training and in networks converted from standard models, across multilayer perceptrons, operator networks, and physics-informed solvers. Quadratic neurons gave smoother, more accurate, and more stable predictions on function fitting, operator learning, and equation solving benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-06714:
Emad Abukhousa and colleagues stress-test machine learning guards that must tell cyber-attacks apart from physical faults in power systems, fast. Their evaluation runs electromagnetic transient simulations with a digital substation emulation streaming data at high rate, built for decisions inside a single cycle. Twelve models, ensembles and a multilayer perceptron among them, trained on labeled time-domain measurements.

Offline, several models scored near perfect accuracy. In the live stream, only the neural network held coverage near ninety-nine percent, while ensembles kept flawless precision on the anomalies they flagged but abstained so often that coverage fell sharply. The gap warns that bench accuracy alone cannot certify field readiness for grid protection.
arxiv-2511-06914:
Kawshik Kumar Paul, Mahdi Hasnat Siyam, and Khandokar Md Rahat Hossain built a low-cost device that manages patient queues in small private medical offices. A single ATmega32 microcontroller runs two stations: a self-service corner where patients enter their details and measure temperature and pulse. A doctor's corner that displays the current patient and advances the queue.

The design uses a temperature sensor, a pulse sensor, matrix keypads, and two small LCD screens for guidance. Unlike internet-based systems, it works fully offline with predictable local behavior, suiting clinics with limited resources. Tests showed temperature readings within one degree Celsius, resting pulse within three beats per minute, and screen responses in under 1.2 seconds, confirming reliable real-time operation on modest hardware.
arxiv-2511-07214:
Elias Döhrer and Nicolas Freches prove that gradient flows of certain energies on knotted curves settle down fully. The energies are arc-length restricted tangent-point energies. They penalize a curve for nearly touching itself, and so keep knots from passing through themselves during evolution. Full convergence to a critical point is stronger than the usual statement that a subsequence converges, and it is proved through a Łojasiewicz-Simon gradient inequality for these energies.

Reaching that inequality requires showing the tangent-point energies are analytic on the manifold of immersed embeddings. It also requires their Hessian to be a Fredholm operator of index zero on arc-length parametrized curves. As a by-product, the metric on the manifold of embedded immersed curves defined by the first author is also shown to be analytic, strengthening the geometric base.
arxiv-2511-07714:
Suyeon Son, Minjin Kim, and Luis Ho investigate why two hydrogen lines from active black holes change their ratio. The Balmer decrement compares red and blue hydrogen emission from gas near a feeding black hole. Dust, density, and radiation can all move that ratio, and its true driver was unsettled.

Multi-epoch Sloan spectra of nearby active nuclei track both lines over time. Average ratios ignore luminosity but fall as feeding rate rises. Within single objects, ratio swings anti-correlate with luminosity even more strongly. Brightness changes themselves therefore drive much of the behavior. The finding cleans a diagnostic used across black hole studies.
arxiv-2511-07814:
Fangu Chen extends a theorem about special prime reductions of abelian surfaces. Superspecial primes matter in arithmetic geometry, and Elkies proved infinitely many supersingular primes for elliptic curves. Baba and Granath carried that result to abelian surfaces with quaternionic multiplication of discriminant six over the rationals, under conditions at two and three.

Chen allows the field of moduli to be any number field with a real embedding and weakens the small-prime conditions. Intersection theory of Heegner divisors on Shimura curves drives the proof. Broader infinitude results strengthen the toolkit for studying reductions of Shimura varieties and their cryptographic echoes.
arxiv-2511-08114:
Manasa and colleagues introduce a data set for detecting face presentation attacks that use nylon face masks. Face recognition guards phones, buildings, and borders, yet attackers can present fake faces to fool it. Nylon masks are elastic and photorealistic, and when worn they copy a victim face shape closely, making a worrying three dimensional spoof.

Collected with an iPhone, the data set holds samples from one hundred subjects and tens of thousands of mask attacks across four scenarios with people and mannequins. Five leading detection methods vary widely in performance on the unseen attacks. The gap shows why defenses must generalize to new spoofing tools.
arxiv-2511-08214:
Yi Huang and colleagues propose perception guided self supervision to reduce causal confusion in end to end self driving systems. Imitation learning copies expert drivers well in open loop tests, yet performance drops in closed loop driving. Expert trajectories carry noise that cannot be credited to any cause, so models learn spurious links between surroundings and actions.

Their framework supervises the driving module mainly with perception outputs, such as lane centre lines and predicted motions of nearby agents. Positive and negative self supervision on the ego trajectory aligns decisions with those perceived facts. On the Bench2Drive closed loop benchmark, the method posts a strong driving score and success rate.
arxiv-2511-09014:
Xue Jiang, Yuanhe Li, and Zhe Li extend a recursive algorithm for a classical fitting problem. Birkhoff interpolation asks for a polynomial that matches not just function values but derivative values at chosen points. It is a broader and trickier task than the Hermite version, where derivatives come in unbroken runs.

Building on the Schur complement and the Sylvester identity, the new recursive algorithms handle any setup formed by joining a scoring functional with a differential polynomial. A built-in judgment step checks that the problem is well-posed before computing. The loop yields a Newton-type basis of lower degree, which is also a strongly proper basis, together with the fitting polynomial itself. Worked examples and complexity checks against Gaussian elimination show savings in both time and storage.
arxiv-2511-09114:
Tim Dudman and Martyn Bull build a cyber defence agent that can guard networks it has never seen, without retraining. Deep reinforcement learning agents have learned to defend simulated networks, but most memorize one topology and fail when the network's size or shape changes, as real networks constantly do.

Their extension, TERLA, wraps a standard PPO agent in two generalizing layers. Heterogeneous graph neural networks compress any observed network state into a fixed-size embedding, and the action space is cut down to a fixed, interpretable set of meaningful moves. Training happens in the CAGE Challenge 4 environment, which mimics real operations with intrusion detection events and multiple defended segments. A single TERLA agent redeploys across segments of different topology and size, keeps the defensive performance of specialized agents, and acts more efficiently.
arxiv-2511-09314:
Tomáš Bezděk and four co-authors benchmark the classical optimizers in depth that steer variational quantum algorithms. Their test case is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm applied to generalized mean-variance problems, under realistic noise. They compare dual annealing, a linear-approximation method, and the Powell method across noiseless, sampling-noise, and thermal-noise settings.

Landscape analysis revealed that one family of circuit angles barely mattered in the noise-free case. Filtering the search to active parameters cut the work sharply for the fastest optimizer. In noise-free tests the count fell from 21 to 12. Sturdiness improved as well. The lesson is practical: using the landscape's structure is an effective, structure-aware way to blunt noise in near-term quantum optimization.
arxiv-2511-09614:
Peter W. Graham, Harikrishnan Ramani, Olivier Simon, and Erwin H. Tanin use cosmology to set the strongest limits yet on long-range forces between dark matter particles. Their model couples fermionic dark matter to a light scalar, creating Yukawa forces stronger than gravity in regimes experiments had not excluded. The dynamics turns out richer than a static potential suggests.

An attractor in the background evolution funnels many initial conditions onto one track per parameter choice. Across a large parameter region, the dark sector departs drastically from cold dark matter during observable epochs. Existing constraints on its equation of state and small-scale perturbations rule that region out. The limits cover self-interactions at scales below one hundred kiloparsecs, with repulsive forces constrained even more strictly.
arxiv-2511-10214:
Federica Ferrarese, writing alone, surveys control plans for steering magnetized plasma toward desired configurations with an external magnetic field. The modeling focus is the Vlasov equation in a two-dimensional bounded domain, including a self-induced electric field and a strong applied field. The whole overview is cast in polar coordinates, a natural fit for toroidal fusion devices such as tokamaks and stellarators.

A shared feature of the plans is feedback based on an instantaneous prediction of the discretized system, letting the controller react to where the plasma is heading. Numerical tests in the two-dimensional polar setting show that the approaches work as intended. The paper serves as an approach review, organizing plasma control methods around one coordinate choice.
arxiv-2511-10914:
Zihan Gu, Ruoyu Chen, and their colleagues present PhaseWin, a faster way to show which parts of a picture led a vision model to its answer. Good checks of this kind pick small sets of regions, but the standard greedy pick is slow and costs too much for real use. PhaseWin searches in phases, from coarse to fine.

The method prunes weak regions early, then picks with care inside small windows under live checks. In tests it kept over ninety-five percent of the greedy method's faithfulness while using only a fifth of the work. It also beat other methods on detection and grounding tasks with two large models.
arxiv-2511-11014:
Sumin Yu and Taesup Moon present SP-Guard, a safety method for models that turn text prompts into pictures. Such models can easily be asked to make harmful images, so guardrails are needed at the time of use. Older guards apply the same push to every prompt and to the whole image, which can spoil safe parts.

SP-Guard first judges how harmful a prompt looks, then masks the push so it acts only on unsafe regions. Strength follows the judged risk, so mild prompts are left mostly alone. Tests show safer images than prior methods with less unwanted change, which points to clearer and more controlled generation.
arxiv-2511-11214:
Jooyoung Lee and Jader Martins Camboim de Sá build a semantic classification for adverbs to fill a gap in WordNet, the widely used word database. WordNet gives rich meaning classes for nouns and verbs, but adverbs lack any systematic scheme. Without one, software tools that rely on WordNet handle adverbs in a patchy way.

Their typology sorts adverbs by roles such as manner, time, frequency, degree, domain, and speaker or subject stance. A pilot hand-labeling study shows the classes cover adverbs in natural text well and that labelers can assign them reliably. Adding the scheme extends WordNet and supports tasks from sense choice to sentiment analysis.
arxiv-2511-11614:
Arturo Urías Jiménez argues that field-programmable gate arrays deserve a strategic place in artificial intelligence hardware, beyond the graphics processors that dominate today. GPUs are fixed machines; an FPGA can be rewired in the field so its circuits match one specific model exactly.

Parallel pipelines for convolutions, attention, and post-processing can run with predictable timing and lower power, and chips can sit next to sensors so raw data never travels far. The trade-offs of cost and design effort are weighed against gains in latency and efficiency. For workloads needing steady, customized performance, the case made here is that reconfigurable hardware is an option planners should not ignore.
arxiv-2511-11714:
Daniel M. Jimenez-Gutierrez and four co-authors test federated learning for pneumonia in children's chest X-rays. Hospitals cannot share patient data. Privacy law blocks pooling, and hospitals differ in how they image. Yet models need diverse data to work well in new places.

Hospitals train one shared classifier together. The images never leave their home sites. A federated platform coordinates the joint training. Uneven data, differing protocols, and image transfer costs are treated as core obstacles. Early, accurate pneumonia detection speeds care and isolation. A privacy-safe route to multi-hospital models has direct value for child health.
arxiv-2511-12014:
Truong Vo and Sanmi Koyejo build CURE, a benchmark suite for whether language models understand culture thickly, in lived situations, rather than thinly, as trivia about norms. Deployed models serve culturally diverse users, but most evaluations probe decontextualized statements or force choices that real cultural competence never faces.

Benchmarks present realistic situational contexts demanding culturally grounded reasoning. Beyond exact match scoring, four new metrics, coverage, specificity, connotation, and coherence, grade different facets of response quality. Frontier models are analyzed under this richer lens. Alignment claims about culture need instruments sensitive to context, and CURE is an attempt to build one.
arxiv-2511-12114:
Chengyi Liu and four co-authors propose CDRec, a recommender system that learns user tastes by diffusion over past interactions. Recommenders fight information overload, and diffusion models can uncover broad interests by adding noise to interaction data and then reversing the process. Most prior versions work in continuous space, which can lose detail and cost more.

CDRec instead diffuses in discrete space while time stays continuous. It uses operations such as masking, guided by transition rules that carry domain knowledge, so the paths it builds stay meaningful. The continuous-time form also allows flexible sampling steps. The design aims at a sharper picture of how user behavior changes.
arxiv-2511-12414:
Yuting Tan, Yi Huang and Zhuo Li uncover a stealthy backdoor in fine-tuned language models that needs no harmful training data at all. In their attack, a small share of prompts in a mostly benign dataset get a one-word trigger added, and are paired only with the harmless reply Sure. No unsafe output appears anywhere in training.

Despite that, the fine-tuned model generalizes the pattern: unseen unsafe prompts carrying the trigger draw harmful continuations, while more strongly aligned models emit only the compliance word. A sharp threshold appears after just tens of poisoned examples, largely independent of dataset or model size. The effect acts as a behavioral gate rather than a memorized answer.
arxiv-2511-12614:
Artem Moroz and six co-authors present OPFormer, a system that estimates the full six-degree-of-freedom pose of an object in an image, joining detection and pose estimation in one end-to-end pipeline. A versatile onboarding stage builds the object representation first, either from a standard three-dimensional CAD model or, when none exists, from a neural reconstruction made quickly from several views.

At test time a detector localizes the target objects. For each one, OPFormer uses a transformer built on a foundation model for robust features, and encodes many template views together with explicit three-dimensional geometric priors in a normalized coordinate space. A decoder then matches image points to three-dimensional points to fix the pose. Standard benchmarks show a strong balance of accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2511-12714:
George Z. Li, Jason Li, Satish Rao, and Junkai Zhang improve the running time for shortest paths in directed graphs whose edges can have negative weights. Negative edges rule out the fastest classic methods, and dense graphs have resisted speedups. Building on work by Fineman and by Huang, Jin. Quanrud, the authors cut the time bound for graphs with many edges, a step forward on a long-studied problem in theoretical computer science.

Their main device is a shortcutting procedure. It rewrites the graph step by step so that shortest paths use a smaller share of negative edges each round. Shrinking the hard part of the problem by a constant factor at a time. The paper is purely theoretical, with no experiments. Its contribution is the faster guarantee and a technique that other algorithm designers may reuse on related path problems.
arxiv-2511-12814:
Yuejun Shen and six co-authors make the first experimental measurement of dissipation during a many-body phase transition, and then shrink it. When a system is driven through a transition in finite time, defects form and extra energy is lost, because the system cannot follow the control smoothly near the critical point. The Kibble-Zurek mechanism predicts defect counts, but dissipation had never been measured in a many-body system, nor had protocols been optimized to cut it, and its link to defects was open.

Using a voltage-driven liquid crystal transition, the team measured dissipation with extreme sensitivity. They observed the predicted scaling of dissipation and where it breaks down, matching theory. An automated in-situ search then found driving protocols that cut dissipation threefold versus a simple linear ramp.
arxiv-2511-12914:
Xiaoyan Xu and Xuding Zhu prove a coloring theorem for planar graphs with no cycles of length four or five. Steinberg conjectured in 1976 that all such graphs are three-colorable; the claim drew decades of work before being refuted in 2017. Interest then shifted to stronger notions, such as multiple colorings and list colorings, where each vertex must receive several colors from its own allowed list. Earlier results gave progressively better ratios for this family of graphs, while other work showed limits on plain choosability.

Xu and Zhu prove that for every positive integer m, these graphs are DP-colorable in the ratio seven m to two m, which settles the list coloring statement. DP-coloring generalizes list coloring, so the theorem is correspondingly strong. The paper closes one line of the post-Steinberg program.
arxiv-2511-13014:
Solon P. Pissis finds every maximal palindrome in a huge string, in parallel, with a simpler algorithm than the problem previously had. A palindrome reads the same backward and forward. The longest palindromic substring problem asks for the longest one hidden in a string, a task with uses from text processing to genome analysis. In the massively parallel computation model, where many machines each hold a slice of memory, an earlier team solved it in a constant number of rounds with near-linear total memory.

Pissis matches those bounds with linear total time and memory, and the same procedure also returns all maximal palindromes at no extra cost. His insights also remove a restriction on per-machine memory in the adaptive variant of the model. The algorithms are randomized and succeed with high probability. Simplicity matters here: a cleaner parallel algorithm is easier to implement correctly on real clusters.
arxiv-2511-13214:
Guillaume Infantes and 3 co-authors tackle project scheduling when task times are not known in advance. Their method, called Wheatley, pairs graph neural networks with deep reinforcement learning. The goal is a single baseline schedule that still works well across many possible timing outcomes.

Wheatley learns a priority rule for ordering tasks and combines it with a standard scheme that builds the full schedule step by step. Tests on standard benchmark problems show stronger results than earlier approaches and good transfer to new cases. The team released Wheatley in public so other groups can check and extend the work.
arxiv-2511-13614:
Jerick Shi and Burton Hollifield test how communication design affects teams of language model agents that generate trading strategies. Multi-strategy funds must decide whether analysts should talk, and in what style. The study runs five-agent systems through hundreds of experiments over twenty-one months, comparing lone work with joint and rival talk styles.

Communication helped overall, but the best style depended on the market. Competitive talk won in volatile technology stocks, joint talk won in stable general stocks, and finance stocks resisted every style. All groups still converged to similar strategy mixes, so differences came from behavior, not lost diversity. Strikingly, talk quality scores showed no link to returns at all.
arxiv-2511-13714:
Junwei Yu, Trevor Darrell, and XuDong Wang present UnSAMv2, a self-supervised upgrade that lets the Segment Anything family cut images at any granularity without human labels. Users of SAM often need finer or coarser masks than one prompt gives, and labeling every scale by hand is far too costly. Ambiguous prompts make the gap worse.

UnSAMv2 discovers many mask and granularity pairs on its own and adds a small control embedding that tunes segmentation scale continuously. With only a few thousand unlabeled images and a tiny parameter addition, it sharply improved SAM-2 across interactive, whole-image, and video tasks. A language-guided variant that predicts granularity from text also beat prior best results.
arxiv-2511-13814:
Marc Geiller, Pujian Mao, and Antoine Vincenti extend a classic framework for describing gravity far from a source. The Bondi formalism covers spacetimes that flatten out at large distances, but it assumed the outgoing light rays do not twist. The authors remove that assumption and work out how the Einstein equations are solved when twist is present.

They derive the twisted versions of the solution space, the flux-balance laws, and the symmetry rules at infinity. The twist turns out to act like a connection in a Carrollian picture and adds new boost symmetries. Their setup also gives a clean finite form for known solutions such as Kerr-Taub-NUT and for shifted Schwarzschild black holes.
arxiv-2511-14314:
Gabdolla Akishev studies a Lipschitz space whose smoothness is measured with a mixed logarithmic refinement. The functions are periodic in several variables, and the mixed smoothness tracks regularity direction by direction rather than in one lumped index. Spaces of this kind sit close to Besov spaces in the classical scale of function spaces used in approximation theory and partial differential equations.

Akishev obtains equivalent descriptions of the space's norm, giving researchers several interchangeable ways to measure the same regularity. He then proves embedding theorems that say precisely when this Lipschitz space sits inside a Besov space or the reverse. Such embeddings let results proved in one scale transfer to the other.
arxiv-2511-14414:
Yu Mei, Xutong Wang, Ziyao Zhang, and eight co-authors build an AI assistant that coaches parents, not children, through emotion education. Children aged three to six learn about feelings mainly through their parents, yet most technology talks to the child directly. Co-design sessions with five kindergarten teachers and five parents surfaced the challenges parents face and where AI could help.

The resulting system, PACEE, gives real-time conversational guidance to the parent, trackable feedback for later reflection, and modeling of the child's emotional state. Sixteen families evaluated it, reporting stronger engagement, deeper emotional communication, and better parental skill. The study extends emotion coaching into the generative AI era.
arxiv-2511-14714:
Connor Fitchett, Ayon Mukherjee, Sofía S. Villar, and David S. Robertson improve a popular design for phase II clinical trials. The Bayesian Optimal Phase II framework can adapt a trial as results come in, but it splits patients evenly and spaces interim checks evenly. The authors ask whether smarter choices would do better.

They add response-adaptive randomization, which sends more patients to the treatment doing best, and they optimize when interim checks occur. Simulations show better allocation and smaller expected sample sizes with little loss of statistical power. The paper gives practical advice and free code, so trial teams can apply the changes with confidence.
arxiv-2511-15114:
Yin-Fa Shen and Alfredo Gurrola develop a gauge invariant resummation method for broad new particles at colliders. Wide peaks break the usual Monte Carlo treatment that inserts a simple width. That shortcut can create unphysical gauge artifacts. Their approach pairs a resummed propagator with resummed vertices needed by gauge identities.

The method is implemented for a standard event generator tool. In a seesaw model, heavy neutrinos naturally have width comparable to mass. Lineshapes, angular patterns, and channel motion then depart strongly from simple approximations. Standard schemes can badly misestimate rates and distributions. The authors argue existing limits on broad peaks should be revisited under full resummation.
arxiv-2511-15214:
Giuseppe Matera shows that the stories told on corporate earnings calls move analyst beliefs beyond what the numbers alone explain. Executives frame results in narratives, and those frames shape how listeners read the same figures. Matera extracts narrative themes from call transcripts and shows they improve forecasts of both realized earnings and analyst expectations.

To isolate the effect, a text-morphing method uses language models to rewrite transcripts, changing the emphasis of the story while holding every number fixed. Analysts turn out to over-react to upbeat sentiment and under-react to talk of risk and uncertainty. The method gives researchers a clean way to price the persuasive layer of corporate communication.
arxiv-2511-15414:
Mingyang Feng, Shaoyuan Li, and Xiang Yin improve how robots plan a safe path through cluttered, changing spaces. Classic sampling methods grow a tree of random trial points toward a goal and then pick the best route. Those methods often ignore what the scene looks like and what earlier trials already learned.

Their method, RRT*former, pairs that tree search with a transformer network, a model that weighs which details matter most. The network reads the scene and past samples, then guides where to sample next. In wide tests it found better paths and sampled more wisely than RRT*, Neural RRT*, and similar methods, and the authors share their code openly.
arxiv-2511-15514:
Jakob Kresse, Alexander Sikorski, and Marcus Weber present an approach that reveals atomistic ways behind rare events in molecular motion. Rare conformational changes matter, yet their pathways are hard to interpret. Their method learns a neural membership function for the dominant slow process without prior knowledge of variables or endpoints. Shift paths are rebuilt as minimum energy paths aligned with that function.

Gradient based sensitivity analysis quantifies each atom's contribution to the process. Iterative enhanced sampling enriches shift regions and raises reach. Tests recover known ways and chemically interpretable rearrangements at atomic resolution. The Müller potential case is among the demonstrations. Interpretable reaction coordinates could guide study of folding, binding, and catalysis.
arxiv-2511-15614:
Sai Puppala, Ismail Hossain, Jahangir Alam, and Sajedul Talukder introduce Optimus-Q, a robot designed to monitor air inside nuclear power plants. Such plants need constant checks for contamination and hazardous gases in a high-stakes setting. The robot carries infrared sensors and streams live environmental data to predict releases of gases such as carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane.

Learning is federated, meaning the robot improves its predictions by collaborating with systems at other plants without sharing private raw data. Quantum key distribution, a method that uses quantum signals to share secret keys, protects the transmitted data.
