Their single-layer tensor network combines a nested network method with automatic differentiation, the technique that lets computers take derivatives of code. The pairing cuts computing cost by about a thousandfold in the network's bond dimension.

Tests covered the square-lattice Heisenberg model and the frustrated Shastry-Sutherland model. Even without graphics processors or symmetry tricks, the method reached a bond dimension of nine with energies matching earlier studies. It also confirmed an intermediate plaquette pattern, called an empty-plaquette valence bond solid, in the Shastry-Sutherland ground state.
arxiv-2512-14814:
Marcus Högås and three coauthors test whether a hidden fifth force of nature could explain a puzzle in cosmic measures. The puzzle is the Hubble tension: nearby measures of how fast the universe expands give a higher rate than early universe data suggest. A fifth force, if screened in dense places, might shift the nearby measures.

The team rebuilds the local distance ladder, the chain of measures based on Cepheid stars and supernovae, with the fifth force built in. Across their models, the force is tightly limited and its size stays near zero. The rate they find, 73.1 plus or minus 1.0 kilometers per second per megaparsec, keeps the tension strong. Adding red giant data limits the force further, so this idea does not ease the puzzle.
arxiv-2512-14914:
Federico Achini and four coauthors rethink a small but vital step in fast image computing. The Fast Fourier Transform needs data on a neat grid, so real tools first grid messy samples, using a kernel to spread each sample onto the grid. The classic kernel, the first prolate spheroidal wave function, was long taken as the best possible.

The authors redefine what best means using vector optimization, which weighs several error goals at once. In their frame, top kernels are Pareto efficient solutions of an error shape operator, and they show how to build kernels aimed at a chosen error profile. In tests, their kernels beat both the classic choice and a leading toolkit in chosen regions, cutting mean absolute errors by orders of magnitude. The idea could serve MRI, CT, and radio astronomy tools that rely on gridding.
arxiv-2512-15314:
Feiyi Liao and two coauthors design a finite element method for Maxwell eigenvalue problems, the math behind resonant cavities and waveguides. Standard methods struggle because the solution space for curl based problems mixes two kinds of fields. Their regular decomposition technique splits that space into a vector potential part and the gradient of a scalar part, both smoother than the whole.

On that new high order decomposition they build a method from standard high order Lagrange finite elements, the workhorse elements every code already has. They prove full convergence orders for the computed eigenpairs, eigenvalues and eigenfunctions alike. Numerical examples then validate the scheme and confirm the theory. The result gives engineers a reliable route to Maxwell resonances without exotic element types.
arxiv-2512-15914:
Saliha Kivanc shows that certain Whitehead doubles of the trefoil are Legendrian non simple in a 2025 knot theory paper. Legendrian simple knots are fully classified by two classic invariants, and finding families that escape that classification is a live topic in contact geometry. Twist knots that are Whitehead doubles of the unknot were earlier shown non simple by Oszvath and Stipsicz.

Kivanc extends that result to some Whitehead doubles of the trefoil knot. The proof uses properties of knot Floer homology together with the distinguished surgery triangle. The conclusion is that this family is Legendrian non simple in the standard contact 3-sphere, so the classical invariants do not determine its Legendrian representatives.
arxiv-2512-16014:
Amir Eskandari-asl and Adolfo Avella build a theory tool in their 2025 arXiv paper on ultrafast optics. The magneto-optical Kerr effect lets researchers watch magnetism change by shining laser pulses on a material and measuring how the reflected light rotates. Modeling that signal for materials hit by a strong pump pulse is hard.

The authors develop a general framework that computes the time-resolved Kerr signal from a single-particle density matrix. Their method is cheaper to run than earlier approaches and can include damping, the gradual loss of the excited state. They test it on a simple two-band model and on germanium, a real material with a complex band structure. The framework reproduces both the fast response during the pulse and the slower dynamics after it.
arxiv-2512-16114:
Yanhao Sun and four co-authors study a quantum key distribution setup in a paper published on arXiv in 2025. In measurement-device-independent QKD, an untrusted third party performs the key measurements, which removes detector-side attacks. Real high-speed systems, though, spread the light across many temporal modes, so the measurement mode may not match the sender's mode.

Using temporal mode analysis, the team shows a mismatch on Bob's side hurts far more than one on Alice's side. With the receiver near Bob and just a 5 percent mode mismatch, the secure distance collapses from 87.96 kilometers to 18.50 kilometers. The same mismatch for Alice only trims it to 86.83 kilometers. At 15 kilometers, mismatch cuts the secret key rate by 83 percent, so careful mode calibration is essential.
arxiv-2512-16514:
Diodato Ferraioli and three co-authors study blockchain incentives in their 2025 paper on arXiv. A blockchain must reward strong participants for performance while keeping stake spread out enough to stay decentralized. The authors analyze algorithmic reward policies where participant capability types are public and token stakes evolve over time.

Under full participation, fixed virtual-stake rules, which blend type and stake to pick winners, show strong path dependence: early luck locks in. Time-varying weights push outcomes toward purely stake-based or purely type-based selection. In a repeated game where agents may sit out and token value depends on decentralization, winner-take-most policies can collapse the system to minimum decentralization under short-sighted play. Policies that spread eligibility across top types, simulate lookahead, or share rewards broadly each rescue participation at some cost to performance priority.
arxiv-2512-16614:
Giulia Boato and four co-authors argue for agent-based media forensics in a paper released on arXiv in 2025. Faked and manipulated media keep improving, and single detectors each catch only part of the problem. The authors propose AI forensic agents: orchestrators that select and combine forensic detectors for each case at hand.

A good agent would also establish provenance and context, where an image or clip came from and what it claims to show, and report assessments with calibrated uncertainty instead of flat verdicts. The title carries the motto: do not guess, escalate. The paper highlights pitfalls in current solutions, such as overconfident single-tool pipelines, and introduces a unified framework meant to make authenticity verification more reliable and explainable. It is a position and framework paper aimed at reshaping how forensic tools are assembled.
arxiv-2512-16814:
William English and coauthors present GraFT, a method that turns plain English into temporal logic for robots and self-governing systems. The job splits into lifting, naming the basic facts in a sentence, and translation into formal rules, and past tools stumbled on both.

GraFT cuts the search space hard. At each step the language model may pick only a handful of valid tokens, not its whole vocabulary, using traits of each sub-task. The team proves why that cut speeds learning. On the CW, GLTL, and Navi benchmarks, GraFT lifted end-to-end accuracy by 5.49 percent on average, and out-of-domain accuracy by 14.06 percent.
arxiv-2512-16914:
Nikhil Prakash and coauthors present Constructive Circuit Amplification, a way to boost math reasoning in language models by editing only the inner circuits that do the work. Past studies found sparse subnetworks, called circuits, behind set tasks, and noted that fine-tuning often just strengthens them.

The method finds key tokens in model reasoning traces and the parts tied to the target task, then updates only those parts. On math reasoning, accuracy rose by up to 11.4 percent across models, while as little as 1.59 percent of model parts changed. Side skills barely moved, as checks on MMLU, TriviaQA, and TruthfulQA showed, proof that narrow edits can lift one skill cleanly.
arxiv-2512-17114:
Jofre Costa, Eric Luu, David R Wood, and Jung Hon Yip work on Hadwiger's conjecture, a famous open problem about graph coloring. The claim says any graph that needs k colors must contain a fully linked set of k points hidden inside it as a minor. They focus on graphs where no three points are all unlinked, the case written alpha of G equals 2.

Rather than settle the whole case, the team builds tools for attacking it and gathers older results into a wider form. With those tools they prove the claim for several named families, among them the Clebsch, Mesner, and Gewirtz graphs. They also flag families where the answer is still unknown. Note the conjecture itself stays open; these are claimed proofs for special classes only.
arxiv-2512-17514:
Sairam VCR and coauthors work on object detection that must adapt to new settings without any labeled examples from the original training data, a setup called source free object detection. When the scene changes, detectors often light up background clutter as if it were an object, which poisons the labels they teach themselves. Their 2025 system is named FALCON-SFOD.

One part, SPAR, borrows masks from a vision foundation model to push the detector's attention toward real object regions. The other part, IRPL, makes the self teaching process fairer and more tolerant of noise when background pixels far outnumber object pixels. Theory in the paper ties these choices to tighter error bounds for locating and naming objects. Tests across standard benchmarks reached competitive scores with leading methods.
arxiv-2512-17614:
Hugo Candan, Karim Noui, and David Langlois set black holes spinning, slowly, inside a family of gravity theories that extend Einstein's. DHOST theories add a scalar field to gravity while dodging mathematical diseases that plague other extensions. A spinning solution is far harder to find than a still one, so the team expands around stillness with the classic Hartle-Thorne approach.

One clean result anchors the paper: the equation for frame dragging, the swirl spacetime picks up from the spin, can be solved outright in any DHOST theory. Letting the swirl vary with angle turns out to be forbidden by smoothness at the horizon and far away. As a test case, they spin up a black hole carrying primary hair and track how spin shifts the innermost stable orbit and light rings.
arxiv-2512-17714:
Charles-Edouard Bréhier and three co-authors speed up the long-run simulation of noisy heat-like equations. Such random partial differential equations settle, over time, into a steady statistical pattern called the invariant distribution. Sampling that pattern accurately is slow: the standard method creeps with error shrinking like the square root of the step count.

Their preconditioning reshapes the equation first, smoothing its time behavior while leaving the steady pattern untouched. On that smoother stage, postprocessed integrators can take far larger, higher-order steps. For the one-dimensional heat equation with white noise, they build samplers of order 1 and 2, up from one half. The extra cost stays minor, and simulations confirm the theory. Faster sampling feeds weather, materials, and finance models alike.
arxiv-2512-18014:
Shubham Kumar Nigam leads a nine author team testing whether reinforcement learning can train legal AI for India. Their system, ReGal, first tunes a model on many legal tasks, then refines it with feedback from another AI, guided by a method called PPO. Two jobs test the system: guessing court outcomes with reasons, and summing up long legal papers.

On standard scores, ReGal trails both supervised models and top commercial tools. The authors share the shortfall openly and trace it to reward design, dense legal language, and the jump to a new field. Their maps of what went wrong give later teams a firmer base for learning based legal tools.
arxiv-2512-18114:
Robert Calef, Arthur Liang, Manolis Kellis, and Marinka Zitnik argue that protein AI should learn the parts, not just the whole. Proteins are built from reused blocks, like binding sites and domains, where much of the action sits. Most models still read a protein as one long letter chain or squeeze it into one summary vector.

Their open Magneton kit lists 530,601 proteins tagged with over 1.7 million such blocks of 13,075 types, plus tools to teach them and 13 grading tasks. A fine tuning method that adds block knowledge lifted function forecasts across top models. Models even handled block types they had never been taught, which hints the lesson runs deep.
arxiv-2512-18314:
Philipp Langsteiner, Jan-Niklas Dihlmann, and Hendrik P. A. Lensch spray material knowledge from flat images onto 3D scenes. Rebuilt scenes often look right until the light changes, because their surfaces lack true traits like roughness and metal content. Image diffusion models are good at guessing those traits in 2D, but moving the guesses onto 3D shapes is the hard part.

MatSpray rebuilds the scene as soft 3D blobs, paints trait maps from the photos, then either tunes the blobs to match or projects the traits on with ray tracing. A small neural touch up step sharpens fine detail across views. The results beat past methods on scores and on looks, easing film and game asset work.
arxiv-2512-18614:
Ruiqi Chen, Kaitong Cai, Yijia Fan, and Keze Wang at Sun Yat-sen University build PTTA, which generates animation from text alone. Video models such as Sora and Kling excel at natural footage but struggle with animation styles. Earlier attempts fine tuned image to video models needing a starting image. Text to video animation, with no visual input, remained largely unexplored before this study.

First they construct a small, high quality dataset pairing animation clips with text. They fine tune the pretrained text to video model HunyuanVideo to adopt the animation style. Visual evaluations across multiple dimensions show it outperforming comparable approaches. Pure text control lowers the barrier to animation production, which demands complex pipelines and heavy manual labor. Independent creators could draft scenes from a sentence, then refine them by hand. The work shows that modest, curated datasets can steer a huge video model into a new style.
arxiv-2512-19614:
Grid operators must choose which power plants to switch on before they know demand or wind and solar output. That puzzle is called the two-stage stochastic unit commitment problem. Yannick Werner and four co-authors review scenario reduction. The method swaps a huge set of possible futures for a small set. The small set should still lead to near the same first choices.

The team first sums up the classic theory. It rests on distances between chance distributions and on optimal mass transport. They then compare the cost rules that past work has used. With a forward selection method, they prove one cost rule picks the best scenario on the first draw. Tests on a changed IEEE 24-bus system back this up. About two percent of 200 scenarios can match the full solution well.
arxiv-2512-19714:
Johannes Fiedler and Drew Parsons refine a classic model of how molecules feel a surface through a liquid. A force called the Casimir-Polder force pulls a small molecule toward nearby matter. In a liquid, the molecule sits in a cavity, as Onsager's real-cavity picture says. The authors extend that picture to solid surfaces. They work out the shape of the cavity mouth in exact form.

They then derive closed-form curves for the force at each distance. The sums use measured data for water, propanol, and PTFE. They also use known values for oxygen and nitrogen molecules. The results show how screening, cavity shape, and material response set the force together. They also show the switch between open-cavity and closed-cavity regimes. The frame splits the force into clear parts that can be read at a glance.
arxiv-2512-20114:
Kashinath Chavan, Ihsan Boustani, and Alok Shukla compute the properties of boron shaped into hollow cages. Using density functional theory with an extended basis set, they studied cage-like clusters of twenty to one hundred twenty-two boron atoms systematically. Vibrational frequency analysis checked each cage's dynamic stability, and binding energies per atom ranked their thermodynamic stability.

The thirty-two-atom and ninety-two-atom cages emerged as the most stable of the small and large structures respectively. Time-dependent density functional calculations then produced optical absorption spectra for the cages. Those spectra suggest applications in optoelectronic devices operating in the visible range, a concrete motivation for the otherwise fundamental question of which boron cages nature prefers.
arxiv-2512-20214:
Philipp Schröer, Darion Haase, and Joost-Pieter Katoen improve the error messages of tools that verify probabilistic programs. Their method is slicing: cutting a proof down to the parts that matter. They define slicing formally inside HeyVL, a quantitative verification language, so the ideas carry over to many probabilistic programming languages.

Slices serve three purposes here: pinpointing why a proof failed, simplifying proofs, and preserving parts that already verified. The team implemented the diagnostics in a tool called Brutus, built on the Caesar verifier. Brutus searches for small, informative slices using binary search and solver-based methods. Tests on existing and new benchmarks show the slices stay small enough to genuinely help users debug proofs.
arxiv-2512-20514:
Matthias Hertel and co-authors make Transformer forecasts explain themselves, fast. Shapley-based explanations are trusted but slow, and sampling what-if cases usually assumes features act on their own. Their model, SHAPformer, bakes explanation into the forecast design itself through attention manipulation.

Because the model predicts from chosen feature subsets by construction, exact Shapley-style scores come out without any sampling. Answers arrive in under a second, orders of magnitude faster than the standard explainer. On synthetic data with known ground truth, they match reality. On real power load data, predictions stay competitive while they expose sensible behaviour, such as leaning on past load and treating the Christmas period specially.
arxiv-2512-20614:
Debashish Dutta and Sayan Choudhury chart a ladder where bands go flat and eigenvalues go complex. Their system is a non-Hermitian Creutz ladder with one-way hopping, which maps onto two decoupled SSH chains of the same kind. Boundary conditions reshape the whole story.

With periodic edges, a fine-tuned line in setting space keeps every value real, and leaving it triggers a real-to-complex transition without passing exceptional points. Open edges instead give exact solutions: broad regions of purely real or purely imaginary spectra, separated by exceptional lines whose intersections form triple-junction points. Flat bands appear both as ordinary degeneracies and as such points with stricter dynamics. The phase diagram is a tidy laboratory for band engineering of this kind.
arxiv-2512-20714:
Iman Reihanian, Yunfei Hou, and Qingquan Sun review what tailored help from generative AI is really doing to computer science students. From two hundred fifty-nine records, they picked thirty-two studies from 2023 to 2025 in higher education. Five areas organize the field: smart tutoring, tailored materials, feedback on drafts, AI-aided grading, and code review.

Designs that explain first, hold back full solutions, build hints in steps, and anchor in the student's own code support learning better than open chat tools. Winning setups share four traits: help tied to student work, hint ladders that demand thought, pairing with autograders and rubrics, and human checks on quality. Risks around honesty, privacy, bias, and over-reliance recur. The authors urge a pilot-first path: test small, measure well, keep defaults that protect learning, and scale only on proof.
arxiv-2512-21014:
Dhwani Gangal and K. K. Venkataratnam ask how a black hole radiates when the quantum field around it is in a distinctly non-thermal state. Earlier work used thermally modified squeezed states. They instead analyze two fully nonclassical configurations: the squeezed number state and the coherent squeezed number state. The setting is semiclassical gravity in an expanding, spatially flat universe. State-resolved formulas follow for the Hawking temperature, the entropy change, and the mass the hole loses.

Both control knobs, the squeezing parameter and the number-state parameter, push the temperature upward monotonically, and the entropy variations grow strongly and nonlinearly once squeezing is moderate or large. Hawking emission, in other words, is sensitive to the exact quantum configuration, not just to temperature. The framework gives cosmologists a finer tool for studying gravitational particle creation.
arxiv-2512-21114:
Palak Gupta, Sapana Yadav, and Ritu Garg predict particles that no experiment has seen yet. Their targets are radially excited F-wave mesons containing a bottom quark, with and without a strange partner. Their orbital and radial excitation makes these states rare and hard to produce. Working within heavy quark effective theory, they transfer what is known from the observed charm-meson cousins through flavor-symmetry parameters to forecast the bottom states' masses.

Strong decay widths follow from two hadronic coupling constants, and with current estimates of those couplings the authors quote upper bounds on the widths. The numbers are deliberately framed as benchmarks. When the next generation of heavy-flavor experiments reports new resonances, these predictions say where to look and how broad the peaks should be. Any mismatch will discipline the theory in return.
arxiv-2512-21214:
Nadine Aburumman, Cigdem Sengul, and two co-authors ran a computing programme built like a miniature world summit. Microtopia aims to widen participation in computer science among ethnic minority girls by marrying coding to design thinking, with artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and robotics as the headline technologies. Pupils formed 'nations' and tackled sector projects in healthcare, transport, fashion, tourism, food, and architecture, framed by the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the Chinese Five Elements philosophy.

Pre- and post-programme questionnaires let the team ask two questions: how do background and culture shape girls' preconceptions of computing, and does the programme move them? Statistical analysis finds significant gains in confidence, enjoyment, and motivation, strongest when computing was presented as a tool for sustainability and global challenges. Outreach designers gain evidence that relevance, framed through community-scale problems, recruits students whom abstract pitches leave cold.
arxiv-2512-21414:
Christina Liu, Ehsan Adeli, and their co-authors propose a new way for vision-language models to read medical images. Recent systems let a model call specialized tools and then combine their answers through text. In medicine, though, the key evidence is often a localized pattern in the image, which text combines poorly.

Their Tool Bottleneck Framework first uses a medical vision-language model to choose tools that extract clinically relevant features from an image. A learned bottleneck model then fuses the outputs with a neural network instead of text to produce the final prediction. The design works with whatever tools the first model happens to select. On histopathology and dermatology tasks, the framework matches or beats standard classifiers and other tool-use systems, with the largest gains when training data is scarce. Its predictions stay tied to recognizable clinical features, which makes them easier to interpret.
arxiv-2512-21714:
Jintao Chen, Shanghang Zhang, Mu Xu, and their co-authors propose AstraNav-World, a world model for robot navigation that predicts the future and plans inside a system. Navigating changing environments requires foresight: the robot must imagine how scenes will evolve and how its actions will unfold.

The model couples a diffusion-based video generator with a vision-language policy in one system. Predicted scenes and planned actions are rolled out together, each updating the other. Training optimizes two directions at once: generating multi-step predictions conditioned on actions, and deriving trajectories conditioned on the predicted visuals. This two-way constraint keeps predictions executable and decisions grounded, reducing the error build-up of pipelines that first imagine and then plan. Across navigation benchmarks, trajectory accuracy and success rates improved. Removing either branch hurt both prediction and control, and in tests the system adapted zero-shot to unseen settings.
arxiv-2512-21814:
Tianjiao Wang, Xiang Xu, and Yue Zhao study an inverse scattering problem where the unknown potential in a Schrödinger equation is random. Instead of one fixed potential, the medium is a generalized Gaussian random function, described by its covariance operator. The goal is to recover that covariance from waves scattered by a single realization of the randomness.

For the direct problem, the authors establish well-posedness by studying the resolvent's meromorphic continuation, and derive a Born series expansion. For the inverse problem, they prove a probabilistic stability estimate for the main symbol of the covariance operator. The estimate bounds the probability that the symbol can be recovered from multi-frequency backscattered far-field data from one draw. The proof draws on ergodic theory and analytic continuation. Such results tell readers how much to trust reconstructions from random data.
arxiv-2512-22114:
Leron Borsten and Hyungrok Kim address a failed shortcut in gauge theory. A theory in one extra dimension can be mimicked by truncating its tower of modes. One might expect Maxwell theory to arise the same way, from a finite-valued version as the number of values grows. That limit instead gives a flat theory with no local degrees of freedom, losing what makes electromagnetism work.

The authors build a family of replacement theories whose large-value limit does recover Maxwell theory when no magnetic monopoles are present, though Wilson loops may remain. Each theory can be read as Maxwell theory with a nonlocal operator inserted. That operator projects out the bundle sectors that cannot arise from the finite-valued theory, including monopole sectors.
arxiv-2512-22814:
Scott Martin, Noah Brenowitz, Dale Durran, and Michael Pritchard tackle long-range weather prediction, where AI models usually advance step by step and errors pile up over weeks. Models that jump straight to long lead times avoid that pileup, but forty years of reanalysis data is too little to train them without overfitting. Their answer is long-range distillation: a stepwise teacher model simulates more than ten thousand years of climate, and a long-jump student learns from that synthetic record.

In perfect-model tests the students beat climatology and nearly match the teacher while replacing hundreds of steps with one. In the real world, students pretrained on the synthetic data and finished on real reanalysis reached subseasonal forecast skill competitive with a leading operational ensemble. The work is presented as the first case of real forecast skill gained from AI-generated training data at this scale.
arxiv-2512-23214:
Saif Al Mazrouei introduces Anka, a programming language designed so that large language models can write it reliably. His hypothesis blames the errors models make on multi-step code on the host language: general-purpose languages allow many valid approaches and demand implicit state management, inviting sequencing and variable mistakes. Anka is a domain-specific language for data transformation pipelines with explicit, constrained syntax that removes the ambiguity.

The striking test is that models had never seen Anka in training. Working from in-context examples alone, one model reached near-perfect parse success and about ninety-six percent task accuracy on one hundred benchmark problems. On multi-step tasks Anka beat Python by forty percentage points, and a second model family confirmed the advantage. The author releases the implementation, benchmark suite, and evaluation framework, arguing that languages designed for model generation can outperform the languages models know best.
arxiv-2512-23414:
Zheng Li works on Gaussian quantum Markov semigroups, mathematical models of open quantum systems that lose information to their surroundings over time. A central question is whether such a system returns to its steady state at a guaranteed rate, a property called a spectral gap. Earlier work settled that question for one version of the gap, tied to the system's steady state.

Li proves the matching criterion for the KMS spectral gap, a version adapted to systems at different temperatures. After grouping the system's modes by temperature, the gap is positive exactly when a shared kernel built from the noise coefficients is trivial inside every temperature group. The condition is weaker than the older global one, since full rank is needed only within each group.
arxiv-2512-23614:
Lázaro Rodríguez Díaz rewrites the history of the Jacobian conjecture, a famous open problem in algebraic geometry about when a polynomial map can be inverted. Standard histories credit Ott-Heinrich Keller with proposing it in 1939. Rodríguez Díaz reports finding the conjecture's statement much earlier, as the main result of an 1884 paper by L. Kraus.

Kraus's proof, he argues, fails only at its final step, and the ideas Kraus introduced anticipated approaches that resurfaced more than a century later. The flaw is also instructive: the root of Kraus's error, controlling ramification at infinity, remains the principal obstacle for algebro-geometric attacks on the problem today. The paper is a work of mathematical history with a technical moral for researchers still chasing the conjecture.
arxiv-2512-23814:
Filip Bělík, Yanlai Chen, and Akil Narayan compress big dynamical models into small ones. Their setting is tunable linear time-invariant systems, engineering models whose behavior depends on adjustable settings. In the frequency domain, model reduction becomes a clean fitting problem: find a low-order rational function that mimics a high-order one across frequencies and parameters.

They build that approximant with a reduced basis method run as a greedy algorithm, adding the most informative pieces one at a time. The greedy choices are driven by an error estimator that exploits the linearity of the frequency-domain representation, so judging candidate additions stays cheap. Math results on how well rational functions can fit the target motivate the whole construction. The payoff is a principled route to rational compression and to fast surrogate models of parametric systems. Small models that act big are the prize here.
arxiv-2512-23914:
Bin Xu, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep Gupta survey the hardware that runs neural networks, a workload that now dominates both cloud and edge computing. The bottleneck has shifted: raw arithmetic is cheap, while moving data, communicating between chips, and handling irregular operators consume the budget. The survey organizes a sprawling landscape spanning graphics processors, tensor cores, and domain-specific accelerators such as TPUs and NPUs.

Further families include FPGA designs, dedicated inference ASICs, language-model serving chips, in-memory and near-memory computing, and neuromorphic or analog approaches. The taxonomy crosses workloads, from convolutional and recurrent networks to transformers, with execution settings and optimization levers such as reduced precision, sparsity, operator fusion, and memory design. Open challenges close the survey, including long-context inference with its key-value cache burden, dynamic and sparse workloads, energy and security, and fair benchmarking.
arxiv-2512-24014:
Sijia Chen and Di Niu let language models plan silently, in vectors rather than words. Explicit written plans help models reason step by step, but generating a good plan in text is itself error-prone and varies wildly by task. The inspiration is human implicit cognition: the subconscious use of compact patterns distilled from experience, guiding decisions without verbalization.

Their framework, iCLP, first extracts explicit plans from existing reasoning traces, then compresses them into discrete latent codes with a vector-quantized autoencoder. Fine-tuning pairs the latent plans with their reasoning steps, teaching the model to plan in latent space while it reasons in ordinary language. On mathematics and code generation tasks the method improved both accuracy and efficiency, and it generalized across domains while keeping chain-of-thought output interpretable, a combination explicit planning struggles to deliver.
arxiv-2512-24214:
Sina Jahromi, Farshid Hajati, Alireza Rezaee, and Javaher Nourian classify medical images under skewed data. In disease datasets, one class often dwarfs the others. Pandemic data makes the imbalance worse. Fast, accurate detection of COVID-19 drew many machine learning efforts. Balanced data stayed scarce throughout.

Their remedy generates synthetic images with a progressive GAN. Synthetic data supplement the real images. A weighted scheme mixes the two before classification. The classifier is a ResNet network. A multi-objective meta-heuristic tunes its settings. The test bed is a large, imbalanced chest X-ray dataset. Reported accuracy beat existing methods in cross-validation. Two-class accuracy reached the high ninety percent range. Four-class accuracy also led the comparisons. The authors present the pipeline as a template for imbalanced medical imaging during pandemics.
arxiv-2512-24514:
Oleg Vassiliev and Radhe Mohan challenge a belief in radiation therapy physics. Monte Carlo simulation is often called the most accurate dose calculation method. The authors call that a case of misattributed credit. Leading Monte Carlo codes perform well because their physics is accurate. Random numbers only simplify their algorithms. They also contaminate solutions with noise, the authors argue.

Fast Monte Carlo keeps the noise while trimming the physics, they say. Their strategy reverses the trade. They build a deterministic Boltzmann solver for proton beams. The physics matches the most advanced Monte Carlo systems. Random noise disappears by construction. The method also extends to heavier ions like helium and carbon. Treatment planning could then gain speed without losing accuracy. The paper lays the foundation for that goal rather than claiming a finished clinical tool.
arxiv-2512-24814:
Wanyun Chen, Chih-Ting Lu, and Hanxin Shen search for signs of a dark sector at the Large Hadron Collider through exotic Higgs boson decays. A QCD-like dark sector could produce dark hadrons, and a light pseudoscalar mediator links it to ordinary matter through the Higgs portal. The lightest unstable dark meson, near three gigaelectronvolts, mainly decays to gluons and lives long enough to travel.

Various Higgs production channels are considered for producing gluon-rich dark jets from those decays. Readers in collider phenomenology get a target that earlier searches largely missed. Long-lived dark mesons decaying to gluons would leave unusual jet patterns worth dedicated analysis.
arxiv-2512-24914:
Vinoth Punniyamoorthy, Akash Kumar Agarwal, and Bikesh Kumar present an AI-driven approach for tuning cloud assets across multiple clusters. Multi-cluster rollouts aid scale, strength, and regional spread, yet control tools stay reactive and cluster-focused, wasting assets and adapting slowly. Predictive learning is built-in into their adaptive tuning approach.

System-wide pattern under dynamic workloads is the target, rather than local fixes per cluster. Cloud engineering readers get a design for expecting demand across a fleet and shifting assets before pressure hits. The promised gains are better use, faster change, and lower working extra cost in distributed places.
arxiv-2512-25014:
Haozhe Jiang, Nika Haghtalab, and Lijie Chen prove diffusion language models are provably optimal parallel samplers. Diffusion models create tokens in parallel, hopeful faster inference than autoregressive models that go one by one. Formalizing parallel sampling, they show such models with polynomial-length chain-of-thought can mimic any parallel sampling method using an optimal number of stepwise steps.

Whenever a target distribution needs few stepwise steps, a diffusion model can match that optimum. Machine learning theory readers get a strict foundation for the speed edge, not just benchmarks. Parallel generation is shown to lose nothing in stepwise efficiency, under the stated model.
arxiv-2601-00514:
Liv d'Aliberti and Manoel Horta Ribeiro ask whether reasoning models really have sudden moments of insight. Reports about models such as DeepSeek-R1-Zero describe mid-answer realizations, marked by phrases like a sudden turn, that seem to fix the reasoning and produce correct answers. The authors set out to measure those shifts directly.

They instrumented training runs and examined more than a million reasoning traces across hundreds of checkpoints, three reasoning domains, and several settings. Mid-reasoning shifts turned out to be rare, did not grow more common with training, and seldom improved accuracy, so they look more like symptoms of unstable reasoning than genuine insight. However, deliberately triggering a shift when the model is highly uncertain did reliably help, a finding with practical uses.
arxiv-2601-00914:
Richard Yun is the sole author of a 2026 working paper on why homelessness sticks even when rents fall. He builds a fresh panel of counts for United States metro areas, from federal housing data. Rent rises predict large rises in homelessness rates. Rent falls, by contrast, predict almost no drop at all.

That one-way response is the paper's core fact, and it holds under a second check with a different maths frame. Yun builds a model of the low-end rental market that can explain the one-way pattern. He lays out a plan to pin cause more firmly, using predicted job growth and local housing supply traits. His reading is that homelessness is at root a housing problem. But since falls in rent do not undo past rises, rent policy alone will not be enough. Help must also clear the bars that keep people on the street.
arxiv-2601-01014:
Haoran Su and Chenyu You argue, in 2026, that deep transformer models fail for a geometric reason. Transformers are the models behind AI language tools. Stacked too deep, their inner codes grow alike, lose rank, and collapse. The authors say the flaw is in how each layer adds its update. Plain addition assumes more is always better, and never erases stale parts.

Their fix has two parts that work at right angles. One clips each update to the valid local directions of the code's curved surface. The other lets updates subtract as well as add, so stale parts can be wiped. Together they split the choice of direction from the choice of sign. The result is a design they call the Manifold-Geometric Transformer. They lay out a test plan for models past one hundred layers. If their claim holds, geometry, not depth, caps how deep such models can grow.
arxiv-2601-01514:
Matej Kucera and three co-authors compare two ways of requesting code review at Mozilla Firefox. One asks a named person; the other asks a whole group, letting any member pick it up. Review speed is a prized metric, but assignment style might trade speed against quality in ways nobody had measured.

The team modeled about sixty-six thousand Firefox revisions statistically and ran a focus group with practitioners. Group requests were linked to better quality, seen in fewer regressions after the code landed, while their link to review speed was negligible. Developers also credited group requests with fairer workload sharing and training chances for new reviewers, echoing how shared task queues behave in other industries. The study gives engineering managers rare evidence on a daily decision: the shared queue seems to cost nothing in speed and buys quality and resilience.
arxiv-2601-02014:
Linking a gravity-wave signal to its source relies on multipole expansions. Both the radiation and the source are expanded. Cutting those series short can break consistency. Forbidden logarithmic terms creep into the far-away waveform. Ghanashyam Date and Harsh revisit the problem in de Sitter spacetime. That is the expanding background that cosmology needs.

Earlier work flagged the clash and proposed a particular four-pole cut. A later claim blamed the gauge choice. That claim was wrong, they argue. The authors sum the gauge conditions over conformal time. They also work through the source conservation equations. From that work they derive a general procedure for a consistent cut. It is verified in general harmonic gauge. It is also verified in Bondi gauge. The result keeps truncated waveform models honest about conservation laws.
arxiv-2601-02314:
Sourena Khanzadeh asks whether the step by step reasoning that language model agents show is the real cause of their answers, or a story written afterward. That difference matters as agents take on high stakes decisions. His framework, Project Ariadne, tests faithfulness with the tools of causal modeling rather than by comparing texts on the surface.

The audit intervenes directly on single reasoning steps, flipping a piece of logic, negating a premise, or reversing a factual claim, and then measures how much the final answer moves. That movement is a causal sensitivity score. Across leading models the tests reveal a persistent faithfulness gap, with a common failure mode the author names and defines, where answers stay fixed even when their stated reasons are broken.
arxiv-2601-02514:
Ahmad Terra and four co authors build a framework that explains a reinforcement learning policy in plain text, and then checks whether the explanation is actually right. A textual explanation is easy to read, but a fluent story can still misdescribe what an autonomous agent will do. Expert knowledge can be fed into their framework, and a predicate generator extracts the meaning of a state automatically.

A large language model drafts explanations from conditions found by clustering states the agent visits often. Those conditions are converted into transparent rules, whose fidelity and performance can be measured in the live environment. Two refinement methods then improve the explanations. The point is a full loop, generate, formalize, test, and repair, so explanations of agent behavior can be trusted rather than merely plausible.
arxiv-2601-02714:
Zhi Liu and Guangzhi Wang argue that what modern AI agents most lack is time scaling, the ability to spend sequential reasoning time well. Early AI split cognition apart, neural networks for perception, reinforcement learning for decisions, and symbolic systems for knowledge. But transformer based large models and world models are merging those strands into agents that perceive, decide, and act in a loop. Humans, with limited resources, solve hard problems by reasoning step by step in time.

Prompting methods that externalize intermediate steps, chain of thought and tree of thought, lengthened the reasoning path and helped, and recent models trained with explicit reasoning traces went further. The authors find those methods still limited in how completely and efficiently they search. Their position is that scaling the time dimension of reasoning, deliberately and structurally, is the next lever for agent capability.
arxiv-2601-03314:
Marcial Sanchis-Agudo and Ricardo Vinuesa extend their stochastic theory of turbulence into a two-field framework. In earlier work they argued that viscous dissipation is the large-scale imprint of small-scale path uncertainty. They showed that a kernel variance field can yield both the Kolmogorov scales and the logarithmic wall law from one principle. Here that field is promoted to a full dynamical variable, with units of kinematic viscosity.

Velocity and the new intermittency field now evolve together. The effective viscosity is the molecular value plus the field. The stress tensor gains a nonlinear closure, driven by the commutator of strain and rotation. This makes the stress depend on direction. The field's own evolution mixes a Wasserstein gradient flow for its shape with a local flow driven by a coupling term. Near walls, the framework recovers the expected limiting behavior.
arxiv-2601-03414:
Dan Levy compares the prime power factors of factorials. For each prime p, look at the largest power of p that divides n factorial, as n grows. Then ask which prime's power ends up biggest. Levy proves that, for any fixed prime p, there is a threshold. Past it, every larger prime's maximal power dividing the factorial is strictly smaller than p's. In other words, smaller primes eventually dominate the prime power landscape of factorials, permanently.

For twin primes, where the larger prime is exactly two more than the smaller, he pins the threshold down precisely. The minimal starting point is given by a simple formula: half of p squared plus p. The result is a clean statement about the arithmetic anatomy of factorials, with an exact answer in the twin prime case.
arxiv-2601-03614:
Feng-Xiao Liu, Xian-Hui Zhong, and Qiang Zhao analyze hypothetical particles made entirely of strange quarks: fully-strange tetraquarks. A tetraquark combines four quarks, and this family would have no lighter quarks at all. The team studies how such states would fall apart into ordinary particles, computing patterns for several wave families of these states.

Most of the states turn out to have fairly narrow decay widths, on the order of ten MeV, which makes them easier to spot in experiments. A new BESIII state called X(2300) may match one predicted low-lying state, and the earlier X(2500) may match another. The authors name the strongest decay channels to search, giving experimentalists a concrete shopping list for collider data.
arxiv-2601-03914:
Hugh Mee Wong, Rick Nouwen, and Albert Gatt examine how language models answer multiple-choice questions, a format that hides a subtle second task. The model must both solve the problem and emit the symbol, such as a letter, that stands for its chosen answer. Reasoning errors and symbol-binding failures get tangled in the final score. The team used representational analyses and causal interventions to watch the process unfold inside the model.

States at option boundaries carried strong signals about each option's correctness. The winning option's identity in content space became decodable right after the last option was read, while the output symbol appeared later, near the answer position. Permuting symbols and content supported a two-stage picture: first pick the winner, then bind it to its symbol. That separation helps explain odd multiple-choice failures.
arxiv-2601-04014:
Koustav Banerjee returns with Kathrin Bringmann and William J. Keith to settle more cases of a conjecture by Andrews and Bachraoui. The conjecture concerns a generating function tied to certain two-colour partitions. It claims that for one parameter choice, all coefficients are non-negative.

Andrews and Bachraoui had shown the claim for the first four values of the other parameter. Banerjee and his two co-authors prove it for the next six values, from five through ten. They also show that as that parameter grows without bound, the function links to a third-order mock theta function of Ramanujan and to ratios of q-binomial coefficients. The note thus extends a finite check and reveals a limiting shape.
arxiv-2601-04114:
Ran J. Tessler and Yizhen Zhao build the genus-one part of open r-spin theory, a counting theory on spaces of cylinders. Open intersection theories in higher genus are rare. Only one earlier all-genus construction existed, and its genus-one case matches the r equals two case here.

To build the theory, Tessler and Zhao had to handle dimension jump loci, a problem that closed theories solve with virtual classes not yet available in the open setting. They rely instead on a point insertion technique from related work, which makes the construction involved. After a change of coordinates, the genus-one potential equals the genus-one part of the Gelfand-Dikii wave function, as conjectured. Their intersection numbers also satisfy the expected genus-one recursion.
arxiv-2601-04414:
Ayush Bidlan, Paulo Moniz, and Oem Trivedi chart the possible violent ends of the universe inside one dark energy model, in a 2026 arXiv paper. In fractional holographic dark energy, the cosmos may finish in a rip. A big rip that tears everything at a finite time. A little rip that pulls structures apart ever faster without a final moment, or a pseudo-rip that coasts toward a fixed expansion rate.

Starting with the Granda-Oliveros cutoff, they map which values of the fractional Lévy index allow each fate, finding big rips across the allowed range and ruling the pseudo-rip out there entirely. The little rip needs a contrived cutoff shape in that setting. they rebuild the analysis with a simple Hubble cutoff and an ansatz method, plotting the equation of state and sound speed over time for linear and nonlinear interaction between the dark sectors.
arxiv-2601-04714:
Chang Zhao and six co-authors teach a small driving model to think out loud before it steers, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Language models are entering autonomous driving, but existing systems reason in unstructured ways, generalize poorly, and drift from human driving intent. Chain-of-thought explanations could fix the opacity, except supervised fine-tuning underuses them and plain reinforcement learning is unstable and shallow.

ThinkDrive stages the training. Supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought explanations comes first; then a progressive reinforcement learning phase runs a difficulty-aware optimizer that adjusts learning intensity to each sample's complexity. On a public driving benchmark the method edges out strong RL baselines on exam and accuracy scores by roughly one to two points. a two-billion-parameter model trained this way beats the far larger GPT-4o on the exam metric by over three points, suggesting reasoning quality can trump scale.
arxiv-2601-04814:
Kobe Wullaert and Niels van der Weide study a tool from category theory in a 2026 paper. They work in a branch of math where proofs can be checked by a computer. In that branch, a good category has the nice trait that sameness of objects and sameness up to a strong match mean the same thing. But many useful ways of building a category do not give that trait at the start.

The tool they use, the Rezk completion, turns such a category into one that does have the trait. The pair extend the tool to elementary topoi, a type of category that acts much like a world of sets. Their work helps folks who write proofs with computer help, since their builds must move cleanly from one form to a matched form.
arxiv-2601-05014:
Robust robot perception across streets, air, and indoor spaces is the goal of the RoboSense Challenge, described by Lingdong Kong and colleagues in a 2026 paper. Autonomous systems increasingly work in open, dynamic environments where sensor noise, weather variation, and platform shifts degrade even strong perception models. The RoboSense 2025 Challenge was designed to advance robustness and adaptability under exactly those pressures.

The challenge joins five research tracks that complement each other. They span language-grounded decision making, socially aware navigation, and more. Teams must sense anything, navigate anywhere, and adapt across platforms rather than excelling on one clean dataset. Shared hard benchmarks push the field toward robots that keep working when conditions stop matching the training set.
arxiv-2601-05314:
Andrea Afruni and 4 co-authors model the wind blowing out of the Milky Way's centre in a 2026 paper. Observations from radio to X-rays reveal multiphase high-velocity gas near the Galactic centre, likely tied to powerful outflows. The region is a unique laboratory for studying feedback, the process by which a galaxy's centre pushes back on its surroundings, and the physics of winds that mix hot and cold gas.

Their physically motivated semi-analytical models pair a very hot gas phase with much colder embedded clouds. The models include the Milky Way's gravitational potential and the drag the hot phase exerts on the clouds. Matching how clouds accelerate tests whether supernova-driven winds can explain the observed gas without invoking the central black hole.
arxiv-2601-05414:
Minda Zhao and 2 co-authors test, in a 2026 audit, whether large language models can produce truly random numbers on request. Random sampling matters when models are used inside systems that need fair draws from a stated probability distribution. The team benchmarked eleven frontier models across fifteen distributions.

Two protocols were compared: asking for a large batch in one reply, and making many separate stateless calls. Batch replies passed statistical checks only rarely. Separate calls performed far worse, with most models passing none of the distributions. Performance also fell as distributions grew more complex. Downstream tests showed biased quiz answer positions and missed demographic targets, arguing for external sampling tools.
arxiv-2601-05514:
Marco A Jimenez-Valencia and Charles A Stafford examine, in a 2026 physics paper, how the second law of thermodynamics emerges in an exactly solvable quantum wire. The second law says entropy, a measure of disorder, must be produced in real processes. Joule heating, warming from electric current, is their test case.

In the exact unitary model, entropy production does not appear on its own. It emerges when many floating probes along the wire measure the system locally. Those measurements inject entropy and cause decoherence, an effect like the inelastic scattering in real wires. The study shows measurement-like disturbance is essential, not incidental, to heating in this microscopic picture.
arxiv-2601-05814:
Md Sultanul Islam Ovi and 3 co-authors present in 2026 a dual-pipeline machine learning approach for screening sleep disorders such as insomnia and sleep apnea. Clinical sleep studies are accurate but expensive and hard to scale for population screening. Their system works from a sleep health and lifestyle dataset instead.

One pipeline targets linear patterns using mutual information and discriminant analysis. The other selects aspects with the Boruta method and learns nonlinear representations with an autoencoder. A hybrid resampling plan corrects class imbalance between disorder categories. Extra Trees and nearest-neighbor classifiers reportedly reached the best accuracy, beating recent baselines on the same data, with statistical tests backing the gain and fast inference suitable for screening use.
arxiv-2601-06014:
What goes wrong when the chosen embedding dimension is off? Roddy Taing and 1 co-author study that question in a 2026 paper on low-rank network models. Network nodes are mapped to points in a low-dimensional space, so similar nodes land near each other. Those points are meant to estimate hidden positions that drive connections.

Working with the random dot product graph, a broad family that includes the stochastic blockmodel, the authors give theory for both errors. Picking too few dimensions brings lower bounds on estimation error. Picking too many still works, but convergence is slower than with the correct choice. Synthetic experiments back the theory, and a side result shows noise eigenvectors spread out rather than concentrate.
arxiv-2601-06214:
Predicting how mutations change protein interactions is vital for drug design, yet mutant structures are hard to obtain. Fang Wu and 1 co-author present Refine-PPI in a 2026 paper on protein-protein interaction modeling. Interactions also unfold dynamically, a feature most deep learning models ignore.

A structure refinement module learns from known natural structures through a masked mutation task, then hallucinates the missing mutant structures. A second component, a probability density cloud network, captures three-dimensional dynamic variation and atomic uncertainty. On the SKEMPI benchmark, which records energy changes from mutations, Refine-PPI beat all existing tools at predicting free energy change. The results support generating missing structures instead of waiting to measure them.
arxiv-2601-06414:
A beam that bends with heat and time keeps a trace of its past shape. Linfang Liu and 2 co-authors study how such a beam acts in the long run in a 2026 math paper. Their beam rule folds in the whole past, back to no start date at all. Loss of motion at the edge is of a broad, spread kind.

The team recasts the beam as a self-run system and proves a strong claim: all paths of the weak form drift to one tight set that draws them in. In a mild case, that set has a fixed count of ways to vary and a smooth skin. When the pull on the beam is of the spring type, a wider home holds a like set that draws paths in at a fast rate. The work maps the fate of the beam for all time.
arxiv-2601-07014: Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar, Girish, and Muskaan Singh present DIVINE in a 2026 arXiv paper. DIVINE is a tool that reads both the voice and the face to spot signs of nerve and face disorders. The team holds that shared cues and cues found in just one stream should be kept apart. Each stream comes from a large pre-trained model. Kept apart, the cues may help the tool work well on new cases. They may also help doctors see why the tool flags a case.
arxiv-2601-07314: Research by Sebastian Nehrdich and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with mitrasaṃgraha. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. While machine translation is regarded as a "solved problem" for many high-resource languages. Close analysis quickly reveals that this is not the case for content that shows challenges such as poetical language. Philosophical concepts, multi-layered metaphorical expressions, and more. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07414:
E. Poultourtzidis and a large team wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on three new planets. Each planet crosses the face of its star, a pass called a transit. Two of the planets are sub-Neptunes, worlds a bit smaller than Neptune. The third is a rocky world like Earth in kind. All three stars are M dwarfs, small cool stars.

The planets first showed up in data from TESS, a space telescope that hunts for transits. The team then checked each world from the ground. They took light reads to firm up the transits. They took radial velocity reads with CARMENES, a tool that tracks how a star wobbles as a planet tugs it. The three hosts are called TOI-1243, TOI-4529, and TOI-5388. Each planet has a short year. The years run 4.65 days, 5.88 days, and 2.59 days. The checks let the team confirm all three worlds as real.
arxiv-2601-07514:
Matteo Garbelli links machine learning forecasts to routing decisions for utility repair crews. His 2026 preprint studies a stochastic vehicle routing problem with time windows and capacity limits. The setting is gas meter maintenance, where each job's duration is uncertain. Better duration forecasts should lead to better routes and schedules.

He trains XGBoost, a tree-based gradient boosting method, on eight years of maintenance data. It produces both point predictions and uncertainty estimates for job durations. Those outputs then drive a search routine with more than one goal, bred and tested over many rounds. The study shows how forecasting and optimization can feed each other, rather than sit in separate boxes. Utility workforce managers are the natural readers. The crews fix and check gas lines and meters at homes and firms each day.
arxiv-2601-07714:
Igor Uljarević writes a short note on loops in contact geometry with a positivity twist. Contactomorphisms are the symmetry maps of contact manifolds, spaces that model odd-dimensional geometry. He considers contractible loops of such maps that are positive over some nonempty closed subset. Such subsets are called immaterial. His 2026 note argues a geometric point about their complements.

Specifically, the complement of a Reeb-invariant immaterial subset can be seen as big in contact geometric terms. Big here means large in the sense that matters to contact rigidity results. Short notes like this often supply one clean idea that later work builds on. The paper is aimed at symplectic and contact geometers. It sharpens how positive loops constrain the space around them.
arxiv-2601-08314:
Tian-Liang Feng and four co-authors study CP violation in rare baryon decays. Their 2026 arXiv paper follows a recent LHCb report of the first CP violation seen in baryon decays. That observation carried significance above five sigma, a strong discovery threshold.

The result motivates checks in more baryon decay processes. The authors examine decays of Lambda-b and Xi-b baryons into a Lambda(1520) plus a meson. CP violation measures how matter and antimatter behave differently. Finding it in baryons, not just mesons, tests the Standard Model account of the matter-filled universe. Each new channel adds a place where that account could fail.
arxiv-2601-08814:
Gianluigi Del Magno, Joao Lopes Dias, and Jose Pedro Gaivao study chance driven maps that keep area fixed. Think of a ball that jumps by a rule picked at random at each step. Such maps model gas flow and other spread out motion. A key ask is when the motion stays tame, with no fast split of near paths.

The team proves a firm rule for this class. If all growth rates of path splits are zero, then a fixed spread law must live on a linked bundle of lines. That law is a sign of tame, near clock like motion. A reader in dynamics gets a test that ties flat growth to deep order. It helps split tame random motion from wild random motion.
arxiv-2601-09014:
Agata Barsotti and three co-authors study how noise in a drive tone can harm a qubit. A qubit is the base unit of quantum work. It is steered by tones with a set phase, like a clock hand. If that phase jitters, each steer step errs a bit. As lab qubits live long and read tools get sharp, tone noise grows as a cap on score.

The team sums how phase noise builds through long chains of steer steps. Small phase slips can add, not cancel, in a chain. Their sums tell lab staff how pure a tone must be for a set task. A reader who builds quantum gear gets a firm noise cap to design to.
arxiv-2601-09114:
Yufan Xia and three co-authors use learn tools to set thread counts for a core math task. The task is matrix times matrix, the work horse of science code. On one thread, the best tune is well known. On many threads that share RAM, the best count of threads is hard to call. Too few wastes cores. Too many clogs the RAM path.

The team trains a model to call the best thread count for each new task shape. It learns from past runs on like tasks. At run time it sets the count in a flash, with no trial runs. A reader who runs science code gets a way to cut wait time on a task that eats much of world compute.
arxiv-2601-09214:
Jiri Cerny and Flavio Dalessi study the far edge of a branching walk in a chance land. Walkers branch and step on a line of whole points. The land shifts at random from site to site, yet stays fixed once set. The far edge is the most far point a walker has reached. Past work found how that edge tends to sit in a plain land.

In a chance land, they prove the edge law stays tight round its mid point. Tight here means the edge does not spread out with out bound as time grows. That holds for near all lands, not just on mean. A reader in chance work gets a firm tale for a walk where the land itself is a throw of dice.
arxiv-2601-09314:
Gerold Alsmeyer and Anita Behme study the tail of a class of chance flows that pull back to a mean. Such flows model rates, winds, and counts that jump, then drift back. Here the drift rules are set by a hid chain that flips state. Each state has its own pull and jump form. The tail asks how oft a vast value can still show.

They read the tail through a chain of random affine maps. Each map scales and shifts the last value. Tails of such chains have known power forms, with rates set by the maps. A reader in chance work gets a tail law for a flow that can flip its own rules as it runs.
arxiv-2601-09514:
Sagardeep Talukdar, R. Ramakrishnan, Sudipta Nandy, and M. Lakshmanan follow bright pulses as they travel down a flawed fiber. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies soliton dynamics through the variable-coefficient Fokas-Lenells equation. The fiber is inhomogeneous: its dispersion, nonlinearity, and gain or loss change with time.

The authors set up the model for ultrashort pulses in such fibers. They then examine how bright solitons interact, along with conservation laws, modulation instability, and soliton tunneling. Solitons that survive a changing fiber are prized for fast optical links. Knowing when they pass through barriers, or break up, guides fiber design.
arxiv-2601-09614:
Xiang-Xiang Sun and six co-authors compute the electric shape of two light nuclei from first principles. Their 2026 arXiv paper predicts charge form factors and radii for lithium-6 and beryllium-8. The method is the Jacobi-coordinate no-core shell model.

The forces come from chiral two- and three-nucleon interactions, with matching one- and two-nucleon charge operators. Two-body charge terms are the paper's focus: do they matter at this precision? Form factors tell how charge is spread inside a nucleus, and radii give its size. Clean predictions give experiments a theory benchmark with no fitted knobs at all.
arxiv-2601-09914:
Nathaniel Grimes, Christopher Costello, and Andrew Plantinga study fishers and a new form of cover. Fish stocks face shocks from storms and shifts in the sea. These shocks hit both the stock and the pay of those who fish. Index cover pays out when a set index drops, not when one boat has a bad trip.

Such cover could shield fishers from risk. But it may also change how they fish. If cover makes risk feel low, effort may rise. That could add strain to stocks that are prone to over use. The paper weighs this trade off. It urges care in how such plans are set up and rolled out.
arxiv-2601-10314:
Eske Pedersen and co authors pull a faint bias from galaxy shapes in survey data. Galaxies tend to point in ways set by their birth place. That lean can fake the weak lens signal that maps dark mass. The lean is named intrinsic alignment.

The team add a self tune step to a known lens pipe. The pipe is the LSST DESC 3x2pt chain. They run it on year one data from the Dark Energy Survey. The step uses the data itself to split lean from lens. It shows the pipe can do both jobs at once. That bodes well for the vast LSST runs to come.
arxiv-2601-10514:
Madeline Lucey and co authors report the first five carbon rich metal poor stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Such stars hold far more carbon than iron for their age. In our own galaxy, they are a large share of old halo stars. They code facts about the first stars and their bursts.

No such stars were known in that dwarf galaxy till now. The team found five. Each is a clue to how the first bursts seeded that galaxy. The mix in a dwarf may part from our own in key ways. The finds give a first base for that match.
arxiv-2601-10614:
Yair Hayut and Alejandro Poveda study the Rudin-Keisler order, a way of ranking ultrafilters on measurable cardinals. Set theorists use such rankings to compare very large infinite sets. The paper asks how directed this order is: can two ultrafilters always be bounded by a third? Their main theorem gives a precise answer in terms of consistency.

For regular cardinals in the stated range, two theories turn out to be equiconsistent with ZFC, the standard axioms of set theory. That means each can be true if the other can. Results like this map the possible shapes of the ultrafilter order. They guide set theorists who probe what large cardinals force and what they leave free.
arxiv-2601-10914:
Francis N. Nji and Jianwu Wang present a factorized-attention ConvLSTM for climate data. Learning useful patterns from high-resolution Earth data is hard. Local weather shifts fast, distant regions sway each other, and the whole system drifts over time. ConvLSTM2D is a common baseline, but its dense gating costs much compute. Its local view also misses long-range structure.

The authors add factorized attention to widen the model's reach while cutting cost. The design aims at physically meaningful space-time patterns across many variables. Climate data are a natural test: teleconnections link oceans and continents. A leaner, wider model could sharpen forecasts and help scientists pull apart tangled climate dynamics.
arxiv-2601-11214:
Hanchen Xia, Baoyou Chen, Yutang Ge, Guojiang Zhao, and Siyu Zhu train diffusion language models. Their 2026 preprint names its method T-star, built on TraceRL. Masked diffusion models write text by filling blanks in blocks. Block size sets a trade-off between speed and quality of the text.

The team's plan grows the block size in steps during training. It starts from a small-block model first trained in the standard way. Then it moves to larger blocks in a smooth path. Larger blocks let the model decode more text in parallel. Tests on math reasoning tasks show small loss of quality. The gain is faster decoding with far more done at once.
arxiv-2601-11314:
Jiatong Yi and Yanyang Li test membership attacks on language models in the wild. Their 2026 preprint deals with large language models as found in use. A membership attack asks if one text trained the model. That test audits what opaque training sets truly held.

Most past tests lean on things users cannot see. Logits and other internals are hid by real services. In a strict black-box case, only the output text shows. Tests also tend to fail when the domain shifts. The team's work targets that real-world black-box case. It aims at an audit tool that needs no inside access. Such a tool helps check privacy and copyright claims.
arxiv-2601-11514:
Yawar Siddiqui and seven coauthors rebuild 3D shapes from casual captures. Their 2026 preprint presents ShapeR, a conditional generation method. Recent 3D generation methods post strong results on clean inputs. Clean means unoccluded and well segmented from the start.

Real captures rarely meet those tidy conditions at all. Phones grab cluttered scenes with parts hidden from view. ShapeR takes casually captured sequences as its input. It generates the object's full 3D shape from them. The conditioning comes from the messy footage itself. Robust shape tools serve scanning, retail, and robot work. The method aims to close the lab-to-life gap.
arxiv-2601-12014:
Elio Masciari, Vincenzo Moscato, Enea Vincenzo Napolitano, and their co-authors test language models on a new structured output format called TOON. Models in pipelines must now give outputs that code can read at once. Good prose is not enough if the form is wrong.

Their test weighs two goals: strict form skill and lasting cost. A format may be cheap yet hard for models to keep valid. Or it may be safe yet waste tokens. The trade map helps teams pick formats for machine-to-machine work with eyes open.  The test also tracks cost per task for each format.
arxiv-2601-12114:
Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi, and Yamir Moreno model vaccine choice under peer pressure in groups of three. Vaccine games in higher-order settings are still little studied. Yet group pressure shapes views and joint choices in real life.

Their model has two layers. One layer spreads disease by the SIR process on a grid. The other is a hypergraph of triad links where views are pressed. The pair shows how group pressure can lift or sink uptake. Such models can guide fair, peer-led health drives.  Group size in the model is fixed at three peers.
arxiv-2601-12214:
Ahhyun Jeong, Aditya N. Singh, Josh Portner, and a large team align atoms in superlattices of lead sulfide nanocrystals. Nanocrystals are building blocks for new materials, and their self-assembly can yield traits no bulk solid has. The team use compact inorganic ligands on the crystal surfaces.

They reach atomic alignment via reversible oriented attachment, where crystals join and can still adjust. Aligned lattices can carry charge and light in new ways. The work shows a route to ordered films with atomic registry. Such films suit sensors and solar tools.  Atomic registry is the main gain over past films.
arxiv-2601-12314:
Yiwen Zhang, Hui Zhang, and Fanqin Meng link musical structure to military strategy via a similarity network. Music perception is a multi-sense act tied to synesthesia, and it is a core part of music aesthetic education. Grasping music structure aids both perception and teaching.

In music, many strands of information join to form a melody. In strategy, many acts join to form a plan. Their network maps likeness between the two kinds of structure. That odd link may give new tools for music teaching.  The link is drawn for use in aesthetic education.
arxiv-2601-12414:
Nawaf Mohammed compares two classic ways to measure spread in a set of risks. One is the standard deviation, taught in every basic stats course. The other is the Gini mean difference, less known but widely used in economics. A natural question is which of the two tends to be larger, and when.

Mohammed drives the whole analysis with one structural object. That object is the mean excess function of the gap between two draws of the same risk. The tail of that gap turns out to govern the order of the two measures. Work of this kind helps users know what each spread measure is really picking up. It also warns when the two can rank the same risks in opposite ways.
arxiv-2601-12514:
Graph total colorings get extended to cell complexes in work that links coloring with domination. A total coloring paints both the vertices and the edges of a graph. It is called efficient when each color class forms an efficient dominating set on the vertices. Efficient domination is a strict form of coverage with no overlap or waste.

The focus falls on two cell complexes whose one dimensional skeletons are toroidal graphs. Toroidal graphs live on a doughnut shaped surface, which gives them a rich, regular structure. Extending coloring ideas from graphs to complexes tests how far the concepts stretch. Results here sit in combinatorics and topology at once. The author line in the record is blank, so no creator is named here.
arxiv-2601-12614:
Neural surrogates for global space plasma simulations are built in work with no author named in the record. The target simulations use a hybrid Vlasov method that resolves ion kinetic effects. They model how the solar wind interacts with the magnetosphere of Earth. Even reduced five dimensional runs of this kind are very expensive to compute.

The team train graph based machine learning emulators on four such runs. All four runs use identical steady solar wind conditions. The emulators learn how fields and ion moments evolve in near Earth space. Both deterministic and probabilistic surrogates are built and compared. A fast surrogate could let researchers scan many scenarios that full runs cannot afford.
arxiv-2601-13114:
Abdelrahman Soliman, Ahmed Refaey, Aiman Erbad, and Amr Mohamed build a smart agent for next gen mobile nets. Such nets aim to run by intent. An operator states what the net should do, in plain high level terms, and tools make it so.

Their agent is called IntAgent. It is built on a large language model. It draws on NWDAF, the net data analytics role in 5G cores, plus a set of tools. With that mix it can read net state and act to meet an intent. For net teams, the work shows how language agents may cut hand work in day to day net care.
arxiv-2601-13514:
Ronan Perry, Snigdha Panigrahi, and Daniela Witten do post pick inference for penalized M estimators by score thinning. An M estimator fits a model by a loss sum. A sparsity penalty picks which parts stay. Inference past that pick is hard, since the pick used the same data.

Old routes need a bespoke proof for each penalty. Their route is more plain. They add and take a crafted noise from a Gaussian count. That split yields two free Gaussian counts. One can drive the pick. The next can drive a plain trust span past the pick. A shared trick for many penalties beats a new proof per task.
arxiv-2601-13614:
Bo Peng, Sirui Chen, Lei Xu, and Chaochao Lu study how machines can find cause and effect in data in 2026. Pure data methods can stall, since two causes may look the same in the numbers. Newer methods ask large language models for help with cause hunts. But some ignore the data proof, and others trust model guesses that no one has checked.

Their system, CauScientist, aims to make models respect the data first. Model ideas must face the stats proof found in the data itself. The goal is cause claims that stay tied to what was seen. Sound cause work backs both science and hard choices in real life.
arxiv-2601-13914:
Lars Georg, Robert Harlander, and Robert Mason compute a coupling in quantum electrodynamics with a new scheme in 2026. The gradient-flow scheme defines the QED coupling in a smooth, flow-based way. They evaluate it in three and four space-time dimensions. Their general result applies to any theory with a U(1) gauge field.

Other fields and arbitrary interactions are allowed in the result. As an example, they treat QED with a set number of flavors. They evaluate the beta functions, which show how the coupling runs with energy. Such results test field theory methods across dimensions.
arxiv-2601-14114:
Liam Chung and Tobias Kappé extend a logic for reasoning about programs in 2026. Kleene algebra is a tool for proving general program equivalences. Its equational theory is decidable and complete. Yet it cannot always prove equivalences between specific programs.

For those cases, users add hypotheses that encode program-specific knowledge. Linear hypotheses are the focus of this work. The team studies partial reductions for Kleene algebra with such hypotheses. Better tools here help verify compilers and program transformations with proof. The cuts keep proofs short while the added facts stay in view. Tool builders can add these cuts to their own provers.
arxiv-2601-14214:
Julia Venturini and co-authors build a global formation model for planets in binaries in 2026. Binary stars are as common as single stars in the galaxy. The number of detected planets orbiting binaries is rapidly increasing. Transit surveys, Gaia, and high-resolution direct imaging campaigns drive that synergy.
