Global planet formation models around binary stars are still underdeveloped. That gap limits theoretical understanding of planets in binary systems. Their PAIRS project aims to close the gap with a global model. Observers need such models to interpret the growing census of two-sun worlds.
arxiv-2601-14614:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches leads a large team on AI in cybersecurity in this 2026 paper. They define cybersecurity superintelligence as artificial intelligence exceeding the best human capability in both speed and strategic reasoning. They call it the next frontier in security. The paper documents the emergence of such capability through three major contributions that pioneered AI Security.

The first contribution they name is PentestGPT from 2023. It established LLM-guided penetration testing. The paper's title traces a shift: from AI-guided humans to human-guided AI. The tone is bold. The team claims a new age is here, and they lay out the proof step by step. Readers get a field history and a claim about where the balance of initiative between analyst and machine now sits.
arxiv-2601-15014:
Michelle Ching, Ioana Popescu, and co-authors study how transformers learn a task from the prompt itself. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with in-context learning for nonparametric regression. The unknown curve is only assumed to be smooth, in the Hölder sense, with no fixed formula.

In-context learning means the model adapts from examples shown to it, with no new training. The authors ask how well a transformer can fit such curves this way. Their results are of the efficient and minimax-optimal kind. That means no method can do much better in the worst case.
arxiv-2601-15114:
Valerio La Gatta, Gian Marco Orlando, and co-authors give simulated social media users more lifelike habits. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with generative agent-based models. Large language models drive agents that mimic people on social platforms.

Such models can show how posts spread and how influence flows. But most agents are defined by demographics, personality traits, and interests alone. They lack behavioral traits, the leanings that shape how a person acts on a platform. So all agents engage in much the same way. The authors add those missing behavior traits to the agents.
arxiv-2601-15214:
Yoshiki Nakamura completes a logic for a common tool in computing. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with regular expressions with lookahead, a pattern language used to match text. Reasoning about when two such patterns match the same text needs firm rules.

Nakamura gives an axiomatic account of that reasoning. He covers both plain language equivalence and the largest substitution-closed equivalence that stays sound. His route uses a variant of propositional dynamic logic on finite linear orders. Two extra operators restrict a stated relation to the identity or else to its complement.
arxiv-2601-15514:
Shome Chakraborty asks whether broad economic signals can help forecast public health capacity in a 2026 arXiv paper. Economic conditions shape the setting in which health systems work. Yet no one had checked in a systematic way whether they act as leading signals. That gap is what the study takes up. The question is practical: can today's economic data hint at tomorrow's strain?

Chakraborty tests a set of macroeconomic indicators for useful signal. The targets are all tied to capacity. They include jobs in the health and social assistance workforce. They include new business applications in that sector. They also include spending on health care construction. If such links hold, planners gain an early-warning tool. Forecasts could draw on data that already arrives fast and often.
arxiv-2601-15714:
Ryoma Sato proposes a strict yardstick for language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. He calls it the Zero-Error Horizon. It is the maximum range over which a model solves tasks with no errors at all. Averages can hide rare slips. The horizon exposes them: one slip ends the run. Sato argues that this simple measure yields rich insight. He tests it on state-of-the-art models.

His example is pointed. Even GPT-5.2, he reports, fails at counting to five under his test. The title uses that failure as a warning. Trustworthy use needs error-free stretches, not just high average scores. A surgeon-grade tool must be right every time in its working range. The horizon frames exactly how far that range extends for each model.
arxiv-2601-15814:
Ryosuke Yamano and Tetsuo Shibuya improve an algorithm for genome-style string problems in a 2026 arXiv paper. The shortest common superstring problem asks for one short string. It must contain each given string as a substring. A variant adds reverse complements. For each input, either the string or its reverse complement must appear. That variant arises naturally in bioinformatics, where DNA strands come in both orientations.

The authors improve approximation ratios for this variant. An approximation ratio bounds how far a fast method can stray from optimal. Better ratios mean shorter superstrings, found with guarantees. Genome assembly leans on such problems. Reads must be merged into longer sequences with little waste. Sharper guarantees help assemblers promise more about their output.
arxiv-2601-16014:
Eder Baron-Prada, Adolfo Anta and Florian Dörfler study how to test if a power grid stays stable. Their 2026 preprint looks at grids where much of the power now comes through grid tied converters. Old checks can be slow and hard to use. The team uses Scaled Relative Graphs, a graph tool, to split the grid part and the converter part apart.

By split, the authors mean each part can be checked on its own. The checks then join to show if the whole loop stays stable. The method works for both linear loads and loads that do not act in a straight line way. That breadth helps grid teams who must plan for real loads. It gives them a fast and clear way to judge new converter setups.
arxiv-2601-16114:
Alex Plyukhin asks if a known noise form is in fact not needed. His 2026 preprint deals with the broad Langevin maths for systems with drag. Tests of that maths oft use a set noise form. They check if long time ends match true rest states. The noise in his study is heat noise from in the system. Its form is not the bell curve form.

Plyukhin shows the maths can hold true with this noise form. Yet he argues the extra form adds no new use. The same ends can be reached with the plain form. That claim trims need less parts from the theory. The work is a close read of what the maths needs.
arxiv-2601-16414:
John Wu and coauthors set out PyHealth 2.0, a tool kit for ward deep learning. Their 2026 preprint deals with blocks that slow ward AI work. Blocks span hard base lines, high compute cost and need for deep ward facts. The kit aims to cut all three blocks at once. It claims a full model can be built in just a few lines.

Few line builds let more teams test ward task ideas fast. Shared base lines make scores fair to weigh side by side. Low cost paths open ward AI to small teams and schools. The kit is free and open for all to use. It builds on the first PyHealth set of tools.
arxiv-2601-17114:
Heng-Yu Chen, Nick Dorey, Sanefumi Moriyama, Rishi Mouland, and Canberk Şanlı tie two brane tales in one claim. M2 and M5 branes are vast sheets in M-theory. Each hosts its own field tale on its face. Their 2026 preprint claims a tight link twixt two such tales. One tale is the ABJM tale in three dims. It rules stacks of M2 branes in flat space-time.

Count marks, called indices, are the link's test. A giant graviton growth gives one side of the tie. If the tie holds, counts in one tale fix the next. Such dual ties are gold in string work.
arxiv-2601-17514:
Nitin Jha and Abhishek Parakh survey if quantum voting can work in practice. Quantum voting aims for ballot secrecy with public proof of the tally. Its shield rests on physics, not just hard math. Superposition, no-cloning, and entanglement are the core tools. The authors weigh those promises against real-world needs.

Elections demand scale, ease of use, and trust by non-experts. A scheme can be sound in theory and fail at the polls. The survey maps that gap in plain terms. It helps officials judge claims from quantum vendors. It also shows researchers which flaws to fix first. Ballot trust is too key to rest on lab demos.
arxiv-2601-17614:
Yimeng Liu, Misha Sra, and Chang Xiao present AlignUI for interface design with language models. Good interfaces match user taste, but finding that match takes long cycles. Teams prototype, test, and refine again and again. LLM-based UI generation speeds the build phase. AlignUI aims to steer that speed toward user preference.

A fast tool that misses taste saves little time. Alignment methods close the gap between first draft and fit. Designers can explore more options in the same span. Users gain screens shaped to their habits. The work joins generation with feedback in one loop. It serves product teams under real deadlines.
arxiv-2601-17914:
Casper Vedder, Thomas Bakx, Nora Elisa Chisari, Henk Hoekstra, and Matthieu Schaller measure a subtle effect in how galaxies line up. Their 2026 preprint uses the FLAMINGO simulations, a large set of virtual universes. Galaxies and their dark matter halos tend to align with the web around them. These intrinsic alignments can mimic the lensing signal that cosmologists use to weigh the universe, so they must be modeled with care.

The team goes past pairs and measures three-point statistics. They compute a three-point correlation and a third-order aperture-mass measure. The sample covers galaxies and halos above a set mass in a huge simulated volume. Three-point data add checks that pair data cannot give. The results help lensing surveys clean their signals.
arxiv-2601-18014:
Adeeba Tarannum and co-authors build a system that turns messy name and address text into clean fields. Their 2026 preprint targets a basic pain in large information systems. Free text must be split into parts like first name, street, and city before it can be used. Rule-based and statistical tools do well on clean input but fail on noisy or multilingual text. Neural models and language models, in turn, can lack steady control and repeatability.

The team's system uses large language models with those flaws in mind. Steady output matters when records feed billing, shipping, and identity checks. Better parsing cuts errors across huge record sets. The work serves any group that cleans contact data at scale.
arxiv-2601-18314:
Lina Felsner and co-authors report a student hackathon built around reproducing MRI results. Their 2026 preprint describes the design, protocol, and outcomes of the event. Students set out to replicate three influential MRI reconstruction papers. One is MoDL, an unrolled model-based network with learned denoising. The second is HUMUS-Net, a hybrid unrolled design that mixes CNN and transformer parts. The third is an untrained, physics-regularized method for dynamic MRI that uses a quantitative prior.

Reproduction is a hard test of whether a paper gives enough detail to rebuild its claims. A hackathon format turns that test into training. The outcomes show where advanced methods stand up to fresh hands. Such exercises strengthen the field's habits of care.
arxiv-2601-18714:
Judith Vilella-Cantos and four colleagues teach farm robots to know where they are in a field of vines. A vine field is a hard place to get one's place. Rows look the same, there are few firm marks, and leaves shift with the wind and the year. Tools that work in towns, with their signs and walls, fail in such sameness. Place tools for farms have lagged those for roads.

The team use a beam tool that reads range by light. They teach it codes for each place that nest like dolls, from broad to fine. A nest of codes can be both small to store and sharp to match. A cheap, firm place read could let farm robots run rows on their own. That would cut hand work in a trade short of hands.
arxiv-2601-19714:
G. Lacopo and four colleagues speed up the imaging software behind radio astronomy. Modern radio interferometers pour out enormous data volumes. Turning those measurements into sky images is a heavy computation. The coming SKA telescopes will dwarf today's instruments, so the pipelines must scale.

The team presents RICK 2.0, a new version of their radio imaging code. It uses a library for distributed Fourier transforms, the mathematical heart of the imaging step. The design aims at high performance that still ports across different supercomputers. Tests use data from precursors of the SKA telescopes. Faster, portable imaging is a precondition for the science those telescopes promise.
arxiv-2601-19814:
Marco Antonio Rosas Pulido and colleagues propose a new way to describe a city's economy. A city's firms, institutions, and spatial layout interact in intricate ways. Standard measures of economic complexity lean on what a city exports. The authors instead build a framework from three structural dimensions of economic units: abundance, diversity, and longevity.

Abundance counts how many units exist, diversity how varied they are, and longevity how long they last. Together these serve as proxies for complexity and resilience. A city strong on all three should weather shocks better. The framework gives planners a fresh lens on urban economies. It can be computed from firm-level records many cities already keep.
arxiv-2601-19914:
Maxwell Crouse and four colleagues build training data for AI agents that call tools. Synthetic data can teach smaller, cheaper models to handle multi-turn tool conversations. Many frameworks for making such data assume the tools run in a stateful environment. That environment remembers earlier calls and their effects.

Real deployments often run tools statelessly, with no memory between calls. The authors simulate complex multi-turn interactions inside such stateless execution environments. Their simulations must carry the needed context in the conversation itself. Training on data that matches the deployment setting should transfer better. The work closes a quiet mismatch between how agent data is made and how agents actually run.
arxiv-2601-20114:
J. N. Bai and four colleagues propose a way to build an exotic quantum model inside an array of Rydberg atoms. The target is the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a chain model known for skin effects, where states pile up at one edge. Their setup uses a chain of atoms with three atoms in each unit cell.

A synthetic gauge field is made by shining multi-color laser fields on the atoms. Each atom can be addressed on its own, which gives fine control over the chain. The scheme offers a clean lab test bed for non-Hermitian physics, where loss and gain are part of the model rather than a flaw.
arxiv-2601-20714:
Raul de la Rosa, Ivana Dusparic, and Nicolas Cardozo study learning agents that must cope with change. Their 2026 paper is about reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and reward. In the real world, the rules of the game can shift mid-task. Rewards may change, or new actions may open up. Most agents handle such shifts poorly.

The team presents morphin, a self-adaptive form of Q-learning. Q-learning is a classic method where an agent learns the value of each action. Morphin adjusts on the fly when the action set or rewards change. It does so without full retraining from scratch. The paper speaks to anyone who needs agents that keep working when their world will not sit still.
arxiv-2601-20914:
Nicolás Cardiel and six co-authors built a Python package to teach a core astronomy skill. Their 2026 paper presents teareduce. The package supports teaching the reduction of astronomical data. Reduction is the step that turns raw telescope output into clean, usable images. The package serves students in practical classes. Their courses process images from various instruments and telescopes.

Good teaching tools must be simple but honest. Teareduce gives students utilities that mirror real workflows. They can learn calibration and cleaning steps on actual data. The authors are astronomers and educators sharing their classroom material. Open teaching code helps other schools run the same practicals. The paper is a resource note for anyone who trains new observers.
arxiv-2601-21014:
Haixiang Sun and five co-authors make causal discovery cheaper by thinking locally. Their 2026 paper presents VISTA, a framework for learning causal structures from observational data. The task is fundamental but computationally intensive. In high dimensions, the search space grows super-exponentially. Existing methods strain under the load. VISTA answers with modular subgraph integration, as its full name spells out.

The framework splits the global problem into local subgraphs. Each subgraph is built from Markov blankets, the small sets that screen off each variable. Local structures are learned separately, then merged. A voting step integrates the pieces into one acyclic graph. Modularity keeps the cost in check as data grow. The method serves scientists who need causal maps from big, passive datasets.
arxiv-2601-21414:
Chenxu Yang and eight co-authors blend fast gut-level replies with slow careful reasoning in one language model. Human thought is often split into a quick intuitive mode and a slow deliberate one. Training a single model to switch between the two modes runs into clashes between them.

Earlier fixes mostly capped what the slow mode could output. The authors instead blend the two modes by mixing the models themselves, with the mix shifting as needed. Dynamic blending lets the system stay quick on easy items and slow down when a task demands care. That balance is key for cheap, reliable AI help.
arxiv-2601-21714:
A memory system for language model agents rebuilds past episodes in full context instead of compressing them. Long, careful problem solving needs memory that stays faithful over long spans. Most current memory tools squeeze past events into embeddings or graphs before storing them.

That squeezing cuts the context that gives each event its meaning. The authors' multi-agent design reconstructs episodes with their sequential links intact. Keeping context whole should support deeper reasoning across long tasks. The work targets agents that must stay coherent over hours of work, where a mangled memory can quietly wreck the whole chain.
arxiv-2601-21814:
Eduard Paul Enoiu, Jean Malm, and Gregory Gay argue that software teams run partly on folklore. They mean the stories, myths, rituals, jokes, and informal know-how that circulate inside development communities and shape how people actually work. Their 2026 paper sets out to define this idea properly for software engineering.

Drawing on folklore studies, the authors use a literature review and thematic analysis to characterize the concept. They gather example items. These include beliefs about where defects tend to occur. They also include the legend of the developer who is ten times better than peers. Naming this folklore matters because unwritten beliefs guide real choices about process, hiring, and quality, whether teams admit it or not.
arxiv-2601-21914:
Zhouyou Gu, Jihong Park, and Jinho Choi plan links inside vast constellations of low Earth orbit satellites. Laser links between satellites offer high-capacity, long-range connections that can make these networks resilient. Planning them well is harder than it first looks.

Existing schemes often ignore the mechanical limits of laser terminals, which must physically aim, and the uneven traffic demands around the globe. The team's 2026 preprint jointly handles link matching and traffic routing, using Lagrangian decomposition to split the big problem into solvable parts. Better link planning means more usable bandwidth from the same satellites, which affects the cost and quality of global satellite internet.
arxiv-2601-22014:
B. D. Lailey and T. A. A. Sigut check whether the standard ways of finding Be stars are biased by viewing angle. Be stars are fast-spinning stars with disks of gas around them. Whether we look at such a system nearly edge-on or nearly pole-on is its inclination, and it changes what we see.

The authors review several identification methods for bias with respect to inclination. They focus on two photometric methods that use narrow-band filters centered on the hydrogen alpha line. And one spectroscopic method that hunts for peaks in that line. Their 2026 preprint matters because biased catalogs distort everything built on them, from how common Be stars are to how their disks evolve.
arxiv-2601-22314:
Gyu Whan Chang and Giulio Peruginelli give a full account of a family of rings that sit between two classic polynomial rings. Their 2026 preprint studies domains — number systems with no zero divisors — that are integrally closed and Noetherian. The family lies between integer and rational polynomial rings in one variable.

The team sort the family by sorting the Krull domains inside it. A complete map of this kind closes a gap in ring theory. It gives algebra scholars a firm base for nearby questions. The work is pure math, with no device in view. Its value is the finished map itself.
arxiv-2601-22614:
Shyam Venkatasubramanian and a team steady transformer training with a consensus rule. Standard attention models can go unstable when the learning rate is set too high. Their 2026 preprint notes that most fixes tweak the optimizer, while the architecture itself stays untouched.

Their consensus step acts inside the model to curb that instability. Stable training at bold rates would cut tuning time and failed runs. It matters most for huge models, where one bad run costs a fortune. The work is an architectural answer to a training pain. It aims for calm by design.
arxiv-2601-22714:
Alexander Nikulin and four co-authors use vision-language models to teach latent action models what counts as a real action. Latent action models learn action codes from video, and feed the training of robot-ready systems. Their 2026 preprint notes that they fail when the scene holds distractors that move with the action.

People split true motion from noise at a glance; the team give models that task sense. Cleaner action codes should yield robots that learn faster from video. The work links language-guided vision to robot skill. It fixes a subtle, common flaw.
arxiv-2601-22914:
Fabrizio Canfora and three co-authors find exact black hole solutions with uneven, bumpy horizons. The solutions come from Einstein's equations joined with a model of superfluid pions, a kind of matter field. Their setup uses spinning pion patterns arranged as many vortices.

With that pattern, the matter equations shrink to a simpler first-order system. The gravity side becomes a known equation whose source shapes the horizon's bumps. Exact solutions are rare in gravity, and they give clean tests for theories of black holes and dense matter. Bumpy horizons stretch the usual picture of black holes as smooth spheres, showing how matter fields can deform them.
arxiv-2601-23014:
Yanwei Yue and co-authors train memory agents that manage their own memories. Unlike fixed pipelines, these agents decide how to process, store, and fetch what they learn. Training them is hard because rewards arrive sparsely, only after long chains of memory operations.

Their method, Mem-T, densifies those rewards so learning signals come more often. Denser feedback makes end-to-end training of memory policy practical. Agents with well-managed memory could handle long projects without forgetting key facts. Densifying rewards means the agent no longer waits through long memory-operation chains for a single delayed training signal. Earlier paradigms left agents wandering such chains with almost no feedback, which stalled end-to-end learning of memory policy.
arxiv-2602-02414:
Joshua Mitton and 5 co-authors detect student misconceptions directly from tutoring conversations, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A misconception is a specific wrong idea behind a student's errors, and spotting it early can stop mistakes from compounding. Teachers usually carry that burden with effort and intuition alone.

Their pipeline works in three stages. A fine-tuned language model first generates plausible misconceptions for a dialogue. Embedding similarity then retrieves the most promising candidates, and a second fine-tuned model reranks them for relevance. Tests on real dialogues from a tutoring platform compare several base models, including LLaMA, Qwen, and Claude, in zero-shot and fine-tuned modes. The full pipeline beat baselines, and fine-tuned smaller models outperformed larger closed-source ones. Ablations confirm each stage earns its place.
arxiv-2602-02514:
Pratik Lahiri and 8 co-authors optimize the whole e-commerce search page instead of just the ranking list, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Search results pages have evolved into complex two-dimensional layouts, making traditional position-biased ranking models insufficient. Existing frameworks also chase short-term clicks because long-term satisfaction, such as revenue over two weeks, suffers delayed feedback and hard credit assignment.

Their whole-page framework models the interplay among item relevance, two-dimensional layout, and visual elements. A causal approach built on quasi-experimental data produces metrics for long-term user satisfaction. Industry-scale A/B testing validated the system. Brand relevance, the primary customer experience metric, improved by nearly two percent. Revenue also rose significantly, if modestly. The design treats the page as one experience rather than a list with decorations.
arxiv-2602-02614:
Ying Wang and 2 co-authors survey the stubborn problem of proving a storage system behaves correctly, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Failures involving lost data, broken ordering promises, failed recovery, and inconsistent reads still slip past testing. The authors blame the nature of the systems themselves: executions interleave unpredictably, state evolves over very long runs, and the rules for correctness stretch across several software layers at once.

Rather than cataloguing tools by name, the survey sorts earlier work by which execution property and which failure mechanism each technique attacks. Concurrency checkers, marathon workloads, crash-recovery analysis, hardware semantics checks, and chaos-style fault injection in distributed setups all get weighed for strengths and blind spots. One chapter-length thread examines automated fuzzing and finds its founding assumptions a poor match for storage semantics. Machine learning guidance that understands state and meaning may patch that gap. Open problems close the survey.
arxiv-2602-02814:
Berk Bozkurt and 3 co-authors bound how much performance is lost when a controller acts on an estimate of the state instead of the state itself, in a 2026 paper. The classical certainty equivalence principle says optimal control of linear systems with quadratic costs can plug the best state estimate into the optimal state-feedback policy. For general nonlinear partially observed systems that shortcut is not optimal.

The authors allow any state estimate, not only the minimum mean square error one. When costs and dynamics are smooth in the appropriate sense, they derive upper bounds on the sub-optimality of the resulting certainty equivalent policies. Several examples illustrate the bounds in action. The generalization matters for practical control stacks, where the estimator is often chosen for computational reasons rather than statistical optimality. Designers can now price that choice before deploying it.
arxiv-2602-02914:
Privacy tools for faces may leak more identity than promised, according to Wenqi Guo and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Systems that protect face recognition or anonymize faces must keep some identity information to work. The authors show an adaptive attacker can learn to recover that information.

Their attack, FaceLinkGen, trains a recognition model to map protected inputs back to standard face embeddings. For recognition systems, recovered embeddings could regenerate faces matching the original person. For anonymized faces, the attack linked protected images to unprotected photos of the same person. Every evaluated method leaked identity, including two that resisted earlier attacks. The attack also worked with limited paired training data.
arxiv-2602-03114:
Digital lifelong learning after the pandemic is studied by Geeta Puri and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. What began as an emergency response during COVID-19 has become an essential pillar of education beyond formal schooling. AI and large language models have sped up that adoption, especially for adult learners balancing work and study outside traditional classrooms and schedules.

The study examines how other demographics use digital learning platforms. It focuses on learner motivations, the effectiveness of gamification, and the integration of AI. Survey data from two hundred respondents follows. Perceived relevance of digital learning rose after the pandemic, especially among young adults and women. The authors aim to give businesses, policymakers, and educators usable insights.
arxiv-2602-03414:
Geometry problems are scarce training material for AI, because good image-text pairs are expensive to annotate by hand. Zhengbo Jiao and 6 co-authors answer that shortage with Socratic-Geo, a 2026 framework where several agents build data and learn from it together. A Teacher agent writes Python scripts that draw the figures and pose the problems.

Feedback loops check each generated problem for solvability and visual validity before it enters training. A Solver agent learns by preference training, and its failures tell the Teacher what to generate next. A separate Generator learns image creation from the accumulated code triplets. Starting from just 108 seed problems, the system beats strong baselines on six benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-03514:
Modern learning systems often fit their training data exactly yet still perform well on new data, and stability is one offered account. Ronald Katende examines when that account actually holds in a 2026 paper. He models training as a trajectory through function space and measures how sensitive it is when a single training sample changes.

Katende proposes a contractive condition on how effects spread, and unrolls it into a stability certificate. A small certificate guarantees stability-based generalization, but he also proves some low-risk exact-fit regimes cannot satisfy the condition at all. In experiments, faster certificate growth goes with worse generalization across optimizers, step sizes, and changed datasets. The framework maps where stability explains success and where other causes must.
arxiv-2602-03814:
Long reasoning burns tokens, and knowing when to stop is a gamble between accuracy and cost. Xi Wang and 8 co-authors reframe that gamble as risk control in a 2026 paper called Conformal Thinking. Instead of fixing a token budget by feel, the system takes a target error rate and derives stopping rules that meet it.

An upper threshold stops reasoning when the model is confident, risking a wrong answer. A parametric lower threshold stops early on instances that look unsolvable, risking a premature exit. Distribution-free risk control tunes both from a validation set, and an efficiency loss picks the cheapest mechanism when several criteria compete. Across reasoning tasks and models, the approach saves computation while respecting the user's risk target.
arxiv-2602-04414:
O. A. Veliev constructs the spectral expansion for a one-dimensional Dirac operator with a complex, periodic matrix potential in a 2026 paper. The operator is non-self-adjoint, so its spectral theory is subtler than the textbook Hermitian case: eigenvalues can wander into the complex plane.

Veliev derives asymptotic formulas for Bloch eigenvalues and Bloch functions, uniform in the complex quasimomentum. Key spectral singularities, points where the expansion can misbehave, get close study. Spectral expansions let physicists split signals into the operator's modes, a basis for studying periodic media from crystals to optical lattices with gain and loss.
arxiv-2602-04514:
Words change meaning over time, and detecting those shifts usually relies on hard-to-interpret neural embeddings, which are numerical word representations. Bach Phan-Tat and 4 co-authors try a different route in a 2026 paper based on frame semantics, the idea that words evoke structured scenes of typical participants and roles.

Their unsupervised method uses only frame information to spot lexical semantic change. It proved effective and could even beat many embedding-based models. Detailed checks, both numerical and qualitative, showed its predictions were plausible. A further advantage is interpretation: readers can see why a word was flagged. The work offers a clearer alternative for studying language change.
arxiv-2602-04714:
Luca Stradiotti and 4 co-authors study forecasters that may refuse to predict in a 2026 paper on multi-horizon time series. Predicting many future steps at once matters in health and finance, where errors are costly. Letting a model abstain on risky cases can protect trust.

Past abstention methods assume one prediction per case, ignoring how multi-step forecasts are structured and linked. The authors formalize three natural ways a forecaster could abstain across a horizon. For each, they derive the best strategy in theory and give an algorithm that carries it out. Tests across many datasets showed their methods beat past baselines by a clear margin. The work brings principled refusal to sequential forecasting.
arxiv-2602-04914:
Perovskite solar cells are a promising next-generation technology, but their recipes mix many materials and process choices, so progress by trial and error is slow. The work is by Penglei Sun and 8 co-authors. General language models reason well yet lack the field's specialist knowledge.

The team built PVK-LLM, a model loaded with perovskite domain knowledge, and plugged it into a search procedure that learns from simulator feedback. In a real wet-lab test, the system proposed a four-part surface treatment recipe that, to the authors' knowledge, had not been reported before. Cells made with it passed 26 percent efficiency, close to world records set by long expert effort. The authors present the work as a template for other areas of materials science.
arxiv-2602-05114:
Giving every student a fresh but equally hard physics exam is a quiet logistical headache. Naiming Liu and 6 co-authors built a generative AI framework for that job in this 2026 education paper. It produces isomorphic problems: same concept and difficulty, different surface details and contexts, which support asynchronous, multi-attempt testing that resists answer sharing.

Generation uses prompt chaining and tool calls to control numeric and spatial changes while varying the story around them. Before deployment, candidate problems were screened by 17 open-source language models and compared with real student results from three midterms taken by over 200 students. About 73 percent of the deployed banks showed statistically even difficulty, and model performance patterns tracked student patterns closely. The models also flagged ambiguous items, though very small and very large models were less useful for spotting outliers.
arxiv-2602-05214:
A good representation separates the hidden factors behind data, so changing one factor changes one part of the code. Jinjin Chi and 7 co-authors pursue that disentanglement goal with flow matching in this 2026 machine learning paper. Diffusion-based predecessors pushed factors toward independence through indirect biases, yet the learned factors often failed to line up with real semantic factors.

Their framework casts disentanglement as learning flows, one per factor, inside a compact latent space. An orthogonality regularizer keeps the factors from overlapping, suppressing cross-factor interference and information leaking between them. The result is explicit semantic alignment rather than hoped-for independence. Across multiple datasets, the method improved disentanglement scores over representative baselines and also raised controllability, meaning a user can steer one factor without disturbing others, and sample fidelity. The paper adds to a broader shift from diffusion toward flow matching as the generative engine of choice.
arxiv-2602-05314:
Lei Wu wrote this 2026 algebraic geometry paper, with an appendix by Claude Sabbah, on generalized nearby cycles. The construction tracks how a family of varieties shifts as it degenerates. The classical theory, tied to Deligne and to Kashiwara and Malgrange, handles one parameter; questions involve several at once, plus logarithmic structures.

For a map from a smooth variety to a multi-dimensional affine space, Wu builds nearby-cycle modules for holonomic D-modules along logarithmic strata. Their supports are infinite unions of translated linear pieces, ruled by zeros of Bernstein-Sato ideals along monoid ideals. For each stratum the module matches the Sabbah specialization complex under a Riemann-Hilbert correspondence, extending the classical comparison theorem. As an application, the structure sheaf case gives a topological reading of those Bernstein-Sato zero loci under the exponential map, answering a question of Budur, Shi, and Zuo. The paper runs to 83 pages.
arxiv-2602-05514:
Members of Congress trade stocks while also meeting lobbyists and receiving campaign funds, which raises the question of whether some trades ride on privileged information. Benjamin Pham Roodman, Eugene Sy, and 4 co-authors build a temporal graph network to look for such information channels. Their graph joins public data on trades, lobbying ties, campaign contributions, and geographic links between lawmakers and firms.

The task is cast as classifying edges in a graph that changes over time, flagging trades that beat the S&P 500 by a clear margin over long horizons. A two-step walk-forward validation respects what information was available when, so the model cannot peek at the future. They report that the network picks up complex time-based patterns linking congressional and corporate ties to later trading performance. The study is a detection framework, not proof of wrongdoing by any individual.
arxiv-2602-06114:
A flat crystal of about a hundred trapped ions serves as a quantum simulator in work led by Bryce Bullock and 8 co-authors. The setup mimics the Dicke model, where many two-level systems couple to one shared vibration mode. Such systems can show phase changes, chaos, and entanglement far from equilibrium.

By tuning the coupling, the team saw orderly spin phases, then irregular motion matching quantum thermalization. Starting from an unstable point triggered linked growth of excitations, followed by collapse and revival patterns. Careful checks found squeezing below the standard quantum limit. The results support large ion crystals as a platform for studying light and matter out of equilibrium.
arxiv-2602-06214:
Self-driving systems split into two camps: some predict a future path as waypoints, others output steering and pedals directly. Jorge Daniel Rodríguez-Vidal and 3 co-authors bridge that gap with a vehicle motion model. Benchmarks mostly speak the waypoint language, which leaves action-based systems hard to train and compare.

Their framework rolls predicted action sequences through a differentiable vehicle model, turning them into waypoint paths. Training and scoring then happen in waypoint space, with no change to the benchmark rules. That lets action-based designs enter waypoint contests for the first time. Across several hard benchmarks, the approach improved results, reaching top performance on one leading test suite.
arxiv-2602-06314:
A handful of small asteroids have been spotted only hours before hitting Earth. Michael A Frazer and 2 co-authors ask how the coming Legacy Survey of Space and Time would have done on the real impactors of the last decade. They replay those events through the survey's solar system simulator, using real fireball records from orbital sensors.

The survey would have caught a modest share of the objects before impact, most only a few times each. Its default linking software would have formally discovered very few. A modified linker tuned for fast movers did several times better. The team predicts a small number of discoveries over the survey's life, but days earlier than today's typical warning.
arxiv-2602-06514:
Scheduling jobs across a fixed number of parallel machines to finish as early as possible is a classic optimization problem. Danny Hermelin and Dvir Shabtay attack it through short integer linear programs, programs with relatively few constraints. Recent solver improvements for such programs open a new route to faster scheduling algorithms.

Their algorithms run in pseudo-polynomial time, with costs expressed in terms of the largest processing time and the number of jobs. For moderate largest processing times, they beat previously known algorithms. The same machinery extends to related scheduling variants. The work shows how progress on a narrow solver class can pay off in a practical scheduling problem.
arxiv-2602-07014:
Qingyu Wu and seven co-authors judge visual quality for e-commerce pictures whose text is translated in place. Translation score alone misses the point: how the rendered picture looks drives whether shoppers engage. Reference-based scores like SSIM lack clear reasons, and model-as-judge scores lack fine, domain-grounded signals. Their system, Vectra, needs no reference picture and is driven by a multimodal model.

Its score splits visual quality into 14 clear dimensions. A defect-area ratio that knows where defects sit cuts annotation doubt. Its data set draws on 1.1 million real product pictures, with a 2,000-picture test set, 30,000 reasoning notes for tuning, and 3,500 expert preference labels. Its 4-billion-parameter model gives both scores and diagnostic reasons, and it lined up with human rankings better than leading commercial models on scoring.
arxiv-2602-07314:
Hom-associative algebras twist the usual associativity rule with a linear map, and their unital cases hide extra structure.  Germán García Butenegro and two co-authors study one-sided and two-sided unital hom-associative structures on general, possibly non-associative algebras.

Their key observation is that the twisting map on a one-sided unital algebra acts as multiplication by a single element. That yields a new characterization of multiplicative twisting operators and links multiplicativity to idempotents in the algebra.  Algebraists get sharper tools for classifying these structures and a clearer sense of why unital cases behave so specially.
arxiv-2602-07414:
Language models are increasingly cast as stand-ins for people in mediation and negotiation, but do they reproduce how personality shapes human conflict action?  Deuksin Kwon and seven co-authors test that question with an testing method comparing human-human and model-model dispute dialogues.

Using Big Five personality traits, the method supplies interpretable metrics for strategic action and conflict outcomes, plus a new dataset for the comparison.  The study asks whether prompting a model with a personality reproduces the personality-driven differences real people show under emotional pressure.  Social simulation teams get a direct, measurable test of a claim often assumed rather than checked.
arxiv-2602-07614:
Distributed choice systems struggle with heterogeneous data, changing environments, and coordination without central control. Rosario Napoli and four co-authors propose a Knowledge Sharing paradigm that uses knowledge graphs and graph embeddings so nodes can act on their own.

Each node builds local meaning pictures of its context and step by step aggregates vectors from neighbors through GraphSAGE, forming an ever-changing global abstraction called a Knowledge Map that supports joint choices. Experiments on shared resource orchestration across network topologies validate the design. Systems teams get an architecture for shared choices that emerge from local meaning exchange.
arxiv-2602-08014:
Supply chains span independent, competing organizations, so access control must be both decentralized and smart about insider threats. Sadegh Sohani and six co-authors propose ICBAC, a framework that pairs permissioned blockchain with federated learning to meet both demands.

Built on Hyperledger Fabric, the system uses multiple channels and three smart contracts for asset management, baseline access, and dynamic revocation. Each channel runs an AI agent that watches activity and restricts suspicious access, while federated learning lets agents improve detection together without sharing raw data. Supply-chain and security practitioners gain a design that adapts to behavior without centralizing sensitive information.
arxiv-2602-08214:
Large thought models can be attacked not by breaking them but by making them think too long, burning compute on redundant reflection. Ziwei Wang and eight co-authors offer recursive entropy to quantify resource-consumption risk in a model's reflective thought, then build RECUR, an attack that uses recursive-entropy-guided counterfactual questions to trigger over-reflection.

Under benign inference, recursive entropy falls in a pronounced pattern, but crafted counterfactuals exploit flaws in reflection to sustain wasteful thought. Extensive tests show the vulnerability across models. The paper reframes inference itself as a safety surface: efficiency attacks need no malicious content, only questions that trap a model in its own reflection loop. Defenses must watch reasoning dynamics, not just outputs.
arxiv-2602-08314:
Could a hidden particle show up when neutrinos scatter off ordinary matter? Ruofei Feng and two co-authors work through that question using a general theory that allows a dark particle to couple to neutrinos and known particles. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers every allowed interaction shape and checks it against real experiments with different neutrino sources and targets.

Current data from the COHERENT and CONUS+ detectors set limits that are weaker than those from collider and supernova records. The brighter prospect is the near detector at DUNE, which could push past older bounds and probe energy scales up to about a tera-electronvolt for dark particles lighter than roughly 50 mega-electronvolts. Readers get a map of where neutrino labs and collider searches complement each other in the hunt for dark matter.
arxiv-2602-08414:
Dementia cases worldwide doubled between 1990 and 2016, yet some studies hinted the individual risk was falling. Paula Staudt and four co-authors re-examine four decades of Framingham Heart Study data with a method that handles a key bias: people who die before diagnosis leave missing information. Their arXiv paper uses a multistate model for interval-censored illness-death data across three birth cohorts.

Among 3,828 people, 731 developed dementia, and the analysis finds no decline in risk across cohorts for either sex. Women show higher lifetime age-conditional risks, roughly 46 to 50 percent, versus about 30 to 34 percent for men, even after adjusting for education. Readers get a careful correction to an optimistic trend, plus a method worth copying in cohort studies.
arxiv-2602-08514:
A short note can still settle a precise question, and this one concerns smooth cocycles over a torus times the rotation group. Nikolaos Karaliolios studies cocycles of degree zero that cannot be deformed to constants. His arXiv note continues work from his doctoral thesis, asking when such cocycles can be simplified.

Under a full-measure arithmetic condition, each such cocycle can be conjugated to a simple model. Under the same condition, it can also be conjugated arbitrarily close to constant cocycles using a two-periodic conjugation. Readers get a sharp, narrow result: with the right arithmetic hypothesis, wild-looking cocycles turn out to be nearly trivial after all.
arxiv-2602-08614:
Fusion reactors must avoid dumping extreme heat onto plasma-facing parts, and one promising regime parks a cold, dense, highly radiative plasma volume above the X-point. Y. C. Liang and seven co-authors, with the JOREK and ASDEX Upgrade teams, simulate that X-point radiator regime in ASDEX Upgrade with the JOREK code. Their arXiv paper tracks the path from attached divertors to full detachment.

Kinetic neutrals and nitrogen impurities are modeled separately, revealing the formation and loss of a high-field-side high-density region. Once the radiator sits steady at 6.8 centimeters, seeding and fueling hold it in place, and changing the seeding rate moves it up or down as expected. Readers get a validated baseline for moving to three-dimensional simulations of radiator dynamics.
arxiv-2602-08914:
How do partners invent shorthand together, with words and gestures, while building something side by side? Kiyosu Maeda and seven co-authors study convention formation in a tower-building task. An online study with 98 people probed abstraction in language alone. A lab study with 40 pairs added gestures: one partner, seeing a virtual tower through augmented reality, guided the other to build the physical copy.

Pairs grew faster and more accurate as they built shared linguistic and gestural shortcuts, using cross-modal emphasis to flag what changed. The authors stretch chance models of shorthand growth to multi-mode settings, catching shifts in which channel partners favor. The findings guide agents that must coordinate with people in the physical world.
arxiv-2602-09214:
Vision-language models can be confidently wrong, and knowing whether doubt comes from the image, the text, or their mismatch matters for safety. Chenyu Wang and four co-authors introduce VLM-UQBench, a benchmark for modality-specific and cross-modal uncertainty, built from 600 real VizWiz samples sorted into clean, image-uncertain, text-uncertain, and cross-modal subsets. A perturbation pipeline adds eight visual, five textual, and three cross-modal distortions.

Two new metrics track how uncertainty scores react to perturbations and how they correlate with hallucinations, applied across four vision-language models and three data sets. Findings are sobering. Methods specialize by modality and depend heavily on the underlying model. Modality-specific uncertainty often accompanies hallucinations while scores give weak risk signals, and subtle instance-level ambiguity largely escapes detection. The gap between current practice and fine-grained, modality-aware uncertainty is large.
arxiv-2602-09514:
Self-run agents need long-horizon planning, yet most evaluations run short episodes in single domains without persistent economic dynamics. Xavier Hu and fifteen co-authors introduce EcoGym, a 2026 benchmark for continuous plan-and-execute decisions in interactive economies. Three worlds, vending, freelance work, and ops, share one decision process with standard plugs and budgeted actions over nearly unbounded horizons of a thousand steps or more.

Scoring follows business outcomes such as net worth, income, and daily active users, testing plan sense and toughness under limited view and chance. Trials across eleven leading language models reveal a steady tension: no model leads in all three settings, and each falters either in high-level strategy or in efficient action execution. Released as an open testbed, EcoGym aims to make long-horizon agent evaluation transparent and to probe control tradeoffs.
arxiv-2602-09714:
Alejandro Gonzalez-Garcia and four co-authors present a complete frame for fast motion planning of non-steering self-run mobile robots in highly complex but set settings. Their 2026 paper notes that usual grid-based planners struggle with scale, while many motion-wise planners impose big compute burden through search space tangle. A fixed free-space split creates a compact graph of shared box halls to beat both limits.

The split much reduces the search space without losing path detail. Online motion planning then finds a sequence of boxes and makes a near-time-optimal, motion-wise path using an exact planner. The result is a fast answer for large-scale travel, tested through wide sims and on a real robot, with build openly out as open-source software.
arxiv-2602-10114:
Coordinating several robot arms in tight spaces overwhelms centralized planners, since arms couple and collide. A 2026 paper led by Dan Evron, with three co-authors, introduces MR-STORM, a distributed sampling-based predictive control framework that runs massively parallel GPU sampling for arm control. Collision avoidance runs through plan-sharing between arms, plus a dynamic priority scheme that preserves task efficiency.

In complex simulated environments, MR-STORM beats existing baselines, and the method moves well onto real machines. Code, demos, and data are public, giving other teams a working starting point for scalable multi-arm control.
arxiv-2602-10314:
Masked diffusion models make sequences in any order with parallel decoding, but training on a huge set of masking patterns is costly and mismatched with inference-time unmasking. A 2026 paper led by Jaeyeon Kim, with four co-authors, offers Progressive UnMAsking, a simple tweak to the forward masking process that lines up training-time and inference-time masking patterns. Focusing tuning on inference-aligned masks speeds up training.

In tests, the method speeds up pretraining at the one hundred twenty-five million scale by about two and a half times, with added benefits atop common recipes like autoregressive initialization. The work offers a practical fix for masked diffusion training complexity, and the code is open-sourced for reuse.
arxiv-2602-10714:
Max Hird and two co-authors analyze the cost of learning preconditioners for sampling in a 2026 paper. Preconditioning reshapes Markov chain Monte Carlo recipes for speed, and learning the preconditioner from the chain itself often works extremely well in practice. Finite-time promises for that learned setting, however, have lagged behind.

The paper compares schemes that learn a preconditioner from target covariance or expected Hessian against schemes without preconditioning, tracking finite-time machine costs. Results cover the unadjusted Langevin recipe and the proximal sampler for regular targets, with promises on the time needed to collect about independent samples. The analysis tells builders when learned preconditioning pays for itself and when it merely adds overhead.
arxiv-2602-11114:
One workflow rarely fits every task, yet most systems search anew each time. Jialiang Wang and seven co-authors teach an open model to decompose, recompose, and decide workflows in a single pass. Decomposition learns a compact set of reusable workflow skills across domains.

Recomposition maps each new task to a sparse mix of those skills, yielding a task-specific workflow at once. A decision step then credits success or failure to each skill by its marginal effect. Across multi-domain, cross-domain, and unseen-domain tests, the one-pass generator beats refinement rivals that need many rounds, while cutting latency and cost. The work makes agentic workflows cheaper and steadier under domain shift.
arxiv-2602-11214:
Forecasting where people will walk matters for cars, cameras, and robots. Manuel Hetzel and four co-authors present DD-MDN, a chance-based forecaster that pairs scores with tuned doubt and toughness to short sights. A few-shot diffusion backbone joins a dual mixture density network.

The model learns self-tuned residence areas and ranked anchor paths, yielding diverse path ideas without preset anchors or endpoints. Tests on four path data sets show leading scores, steadiness at short sight windows, and reliable doubt. The work targets downstream planning and collision avoidance, where knowing how sure a forecast is matters as much as the forecast itself.
arxiv-2602-11514:
GUI agents are called agents at wildly other levels of autonomy. Sidong Feng and Chunyang Chen call for conceptual clarity with GUI Agent Autonomy Levels, a six-level frame that makes autonomy explicit. People now navigate web, desktop, and mobile through agents rather than clicking step by step.

The frame aims to clarify capability, responsibility, and risk, and to help benchmark progress toward trustworthy software contact. The paper is a position and frame piece, short and programmatic, arguing that without shared autonomy levels, comparisons between agents obscure more than they reveal.
arxiv-2602-11714:
Dense simultaneous localization and mapping from a single camera must track motion and build a map at once, yet tight coupling costs compute while loose coupling wastes work. Jiung Yeon and two co-authors propose GSO-SLAM, a real-time monocular system that couples visual odometry and Gaussian splatting in both directions. Joint optimization in an expectation-maximization framework refines semi-dense depth estimates and the Gaussian scene together, with no extra overhead.

A dedicated initialization step uses image data, keyframe poses, and pixel associations from odometry to approximate the final scene closely, removing the need for heuristic starts. Experiments show the system runs in real time while achieving state-of-the-art geometric and photometric fidelity in reconstruction plus strong tracking accuracy. Two-way coupling, the work suggests, beats bolting two good modules together loosely.
arxiv-2602-11814:
Maximum-a-posteriori methods work well for inverse problems when the forward process is known, especially with expressive priors and careful tuning. In blind settings, where the process itself must be recovered, they grow unstable: the problem turns non-convex and solutions may not be identifiable. Minimum mean square error estimators offer a compelling alternative that sidesteps those traps. Nathan Buskulic and one co-author compare the two approaches on synthetic two-dimensional blind deconvolution under fully controlled conditions.

Even with complete knowledge of signal and kernel distributions, MAP methods stay unstable and demand extensive parameter tuning. The linear minimum mean square error estimator, by contrast, gives a robust and reliable baseline. It also serves as an effective starting point for MAP methods, improving their results and reducing sensitivity to regularization choices. The study thus gives practitioners a steadier default and a better launchpad for fancier methods.
arxiv-2602-11914:
Shortlisting is a common and effective method for picking participants in competitive settings. To ensure fairness, a cut-off score is typically announced, allowing only players above it to enter. Hanbing Liu and four co-authors study rank-order contests with shortlists and cut-off score reveal, fully mapping stable behavior of shortlisted players for any prizes and shortlist sizes. Two goals are examined: the top solo score and total score.

For both goals the optimal contest is winner-take-all. For the top solo score, the optimal shortlist size is exactly two players. For total score, by contrast, shortlist size does not affect the outcome: any size yields the same total score. Comparing top solo scores with and without shortlists, the former is four thirds as large as the latter. Contest designers get crisp rules: shortlist to two for peak scores, any size for total scores.
arxiv-2602-12114:
Some Lagrangian systems resist standard treatment because their initial matrix is singular. That blocks the classical determinant identity. Chan-Lopez and three co-authors show the iterative Faddeev-Jackiw process is a geometrically constrained case of matrix bordering.

They introduce a reduced constraint matrix built from an orthonormal basis of the singular matrix's kernel. From it they derive an exact factorization: the extended matrix is nondegenerate exactly when the generated constraints span the kernel and the reduced matrix is nonsingular. The result ties termination of the process to the nondegeneracy of the constraint algebra, characterizing second-class systems. It also grounds a symbolic Wolfram Language engine validated on constrained mechanical systems.
arxiv-2602-12214:
The classic knapsack problem packs the most value under a weight limit, but real packing often adds an order rule. Fabio Ciccarelli led this work with two co-authors, introducing the coloured knapsack, where items carry colours and no two neighbours in the pack may share a colour. The problem is weakly NP-hard, so exact methods must be clever rather than brute force.

Two dynamic programming methods are given, with runtimes tied to capacity, item count, and colour count, plus dominance and pruning rules to speed them in practice. The linear programming relaxation is shown to need at most two fractional items, and it can be solved in linear time. Tests on a new benchmark show the methods beating top mixed-integer solvers on most cases.
arxiv-2602-12414:
Since FineWeb-Edu, most data curation for model training has relied on a single quality score from a small classifier, which hides trade-offs and blocks flexible filtering. Maximilian Idahl led this work with three co-authors, presenting propella-1, a family of small models that work in many languages, at 0.6, 1.7, and 4 billion parameters. They tag documents across 18 traits in six groups, from core content and type to safety, audience, and place relevance.

The models cover 57 languages and emit structured JSON under a fixed schema. Judged against a frontier commercial model, the 4-billion version matches it more closely than much larger general models do. The team also releases over three billion tags across major corpora, revealing sharp gaps in quality, depth of reasoning, and mix of content that single scores cannot capture, under permissive commercial-use licences.
arxiv-2602-12514:
About twenty reports, as of 2025, claim time-reversal symmetry loss in low-heat superconductors otherwise like conventional Fermi liquids. Warren E. Pickett works alone here, surveying those fragile magnetic superconductors, seen as triplet pairing, from muon data. Detected fields are barely above detection limits, giving magnetisations of at most 0.001 Bohr magnetons per atom.

Apart from fields seen below Tc, SC traits match low-heat singlet BCS superconductors, with no unusual coherence lengths or critical fields. The muon itself disturbs nearby atoms and field values, and the probe changes sample to sample plus muon, breaking time-reversal symmetry in the process. That effect deserves scrutiny. The survey traces the muon setting from normal to fluid states. There, induced currents and Yu-Shiba-Rusinov gap states couple muon moment to fluid. LaNiGa2, seen as non-unitary triplet, serves as a case study, and the paper notes a good option for it.
arxiv-2602-12914:
Quantum sensors usually need highly entangled probes and global measurements to beat standard limits, requirements that real many-body devices struggle to meet. Harshita Sharma and two co-authors show chaotic dynamics can relax both demands. Even with only partial measurement access, chaotic evolution lets initially unentangled states reach Heisenberg scaling of the quantum Fisher information over time.

In weakly chaotic regimes, spin-coherent states at the edge of regular islands in the mixed phase space prove optimal. In strongly chaotic regimes, sensitivity barely depends on the starting state. Strikingly, quantum-enhanced sensitivity survives when only about 5% of qubits are accessible. Chaos thus emerges as a robust resource for sensing under realistic constraints, rather than a nuisance to be suppressed.
arxiv-2602-13114:
Post-starburst galaxies, caught just after a starburst shut down, are laboratories for how galaxies quench. Ho-Hin Leung and eight co-authors measure spatially resolved star-formation histories, metallicity evolution, and dust for three local post-starburst galaxies from MaNGA, down to about 0.3 kiloparsecs, using a hierarchical Bayesian model. Local parameters and spatial trends are constrained together.

All three galaxies share a two-act story: an outer, weaker, slower-quenching starburst first, then a central, stronger, faster-quenching burst peaking about a billion years later. Central bursts raised stellar metallicity far more than outer ones. The pattern fits a recent gas-rich merger, with first passage triggering outer bursts and final coalescence driving the central burst. Non-axisymmetric features in burst fraction and dust maps hint at tidal effects, and rapid quenching appears driven by gas consumption plus spheroid stabilisation, not necessarily AGN feedback.
arxiv-2602-13314:
Millimeter-wave radar sees through smoke, dust, and darkness where cameras fail, but training radar perception needs large labeled data sets that are costly to collect indoors. Sim2Radar makes synthetic radar data from a single ordinary photo instead, rebuilding a material-aware 3D scene from depth, segmentation, and vision-language reasoning about materials. A physics-based ray tracer then simulates radar waves with reflection models tied to standard electromagnetic properties.

Pretraining a radar object detector on the synthetic data and fine-tuning on real radar lifted 3D detection scores by up to 3.7 points, mainly through better spatial localization. The result suggests simulated radar can supply geometric priors when real data is scarce. Emily Bejerano leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13414:
Implicit neural representations encode signals as functions, but standard MLP designs train slowly, overfit noise, and extrapolate poorly. FUTON takes a different route, modeling signals as generalized Fourier series whose coefficients come from a low-rank tensor decomposition. Fourier bases supply smoothness and periodicity, while the low-rank structure enforces a low-dimensional spectral shape, giving weighted combinations of orthonormal, separable basis functions.

Theory backs the design with a universal approximation result, and inference runs in time linear in spectral resolution and input dimension. On image and volume tasks, FUTON beat leading MLP-based methods while training two to five times faster, and it generalized better on denoising and super-resolution. Pooya Ashtari leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13814:
Finding drone position gets hard when satellite signals are degraded, blocked, or intentionally jammed. In such GNSS-denied conditions, onboard camera views can supply added guidance cues by finding stable, distinctive landmarks. This study proposes a compact convolutional segmentation framework for finding candidate visual landmarks from aerial imagery. It combines fully convolutional processing with dilation-based context finding and residual feature transfer.

Since no dedicated drone landmark data set is available, an aerial building segmentation data set is adapted as an initial test setting. Results indicate the architecture provides a workable front-end for candidate landmark finding, while further gains require extended training, drone-specific data sets, and pairing with positioning or matching tools. Sude Ertan leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14114:
Vladislav Slama and seven co-authors build a 2026 arXiv setup for stacked-ring units, known as paracyclophanes. Ring stacking steers charge split in plants and charge flow in organic chips, yet no checked theory had linked the shape of these units to their light and charge traits.

The team studied units with naphthalene diimide or pyrene parts, joined by links of varied length and stiffness. A joint TD-DFT and CC2 method gave light uptake and glow spectra that match lab tests well. A part-based account, checked in the same study, gives a step-by-step route to design stacked units with chosen light traits.
arxiv-2602-14214:
Jiahui Chen and five co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv system for content-aware video streaming. Streaming needs chunk-level importance weights to optimize viewer quality, but human annotation is costly and vision-saliency models generalize poorly. HiVid instead uses large language models as a scalable stand-in for human judgment.

Three challenges shape the design. A perception module reads frames in local windows, building a coherent view of the video step by step. A ranking module re-ranks windows globally for video-on-demand, using a language-model-guided merge sort. A prediction module forecasts future weights for live streaming, using a multimodal time-series model with content-aware attention and an adaptive horizon.
arxiv-2602-14314:
John M. Campbell, writing alone, builds a 2026 arXiv framework for q-analogues of accelerated series. Using the EKHAD-normalization method from recent work, plus the q-version of Zeilberger's algorithm, the author obtains q-WZ pairs whose sums become basic hypergeometric 3-phi-2 series with multiple free parameters. The two sums in each pair match, as required.

Unlike earlier EKHAD applications tied to specific Guillera pairs, this multiparameter approach is broad. It yields and proves new q-analogues for accelerated hypergeometric series by many authors, including Adamchik and Wagon, Apéry, Chu, Fabry, Guillera, Ramanujan, and Zeilberger. The framework thus systematizes q-analogues for series that converge fast to universal constants such as pi.
arxiv-2602-14414:
Abhinandan Dalal and three co-authors study a 2026 arXiv sensitivity problem in causal inference. Sense study tests toughness of seen-study findings, but its mix with read factors is often missed. When hidden mixers are curbed via proxies, strong links between exposure and read proxies can lift sense to left-over mixing.

The paper forms that trend in linear fits: a simple ratio of the exposure-model factor to left exposure spread gauges the lifted sense plainly. Applied to smoking and lung cancer, the setup shows rising social-class split in smoking over time lifted sense to hidden mixing in newer data. The results warn that multi-linking matters when reading proxy-based sense studies.
arxiv-2602-14514:
Aryan Das and four co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv text-led adapter for diffusion models. Form-keeping conditional making uses a base model for prompt steering. It also uses an adapter for form inputs such as sketches or depth maps.

But those adapters are wasteful, at times matching the base model in knobs, and blind to the input prompt. Training is also pricey when the spread model itself is dear. Nexus Adapters, in Prime and Slim forms, are lean text-led adapters for form-keeping making. Each Nexus Block uses cross-focus for rich mixed steering, so the adapter grasps both prompt and form. That joint grasp yields better conditional making at lower cost, fixing the waste and prompt-blindness of prior form-keeping adapters.
arxiv-2602-14614:
Priority disputes in maths turn on who said an idea first. Marius Buliga reacts to a 2026 paper on symplectic bipotentials and its conference form. He argues that most of its content was already in earlier work, some cited and some not.

Buliga points to three earlier preprints that introduced and studied the same tools. One was cited in part; the others, he says, were left out. His note lists the overlaps in detail for readers to judge. The piece serves as a public record of prior art in a narrow but active field.
arxiv-2602-14714:
Navid Noroozi studies how agents reach accord when each talks only to near peers, links shift with time, and states and inputs face hard caps, through multi-step model predictive control. He casts accord as steady rest on a shared set, seen through hulls that hold the group's spread and a strict inside rule.

Forcing each agent's next step to land in its peers' hull keeps the hull safe, he shows, but does not by itself force the strict inside trait that true accord needs. A sharp counter-case proves that point: safe and shrinking steps can still miss the mark. Control design thus learns what it must truly force, not just what looks safe.
arxiv-2602-14814:
Julien Siems and colleagues turn permutation composition, a classic test of state tracking, into code that language-style training can use. Sequence-to-sequence versions of the task clash with next-token prediction, so the team converts composition into read-eval-print-loop traces that interleave state reveals through prints and variable changes.

Linear recurrent networks that track state excel in this code setting, while transformers still fail, the authors report. Further experiments probe why tracking survives the translation to code for one architecture and not the other. State, the paper argues, must be represented, not merely mimicked. Code becomes a new lens on sequence models.
arxiv-2602-14914:
Olivier Jeunen and Shashank Gupta close a scoring debate for rank and tip systems: plus-side base tweaks beat self-scaled scores. Self-scaled inverse propensity scores, a stock tool for cutting spread in offline tests, use a times-side tweak.

New offline lore hints plus-side bases may win, yet hard proof for tests was thin. The team proves beta-star IPS, with a best plus-side base, beats self-scaled scores in mean squared miss over time. A split of the miss gap shows the old tool matches one set plus-side pick, not the best. Offline tests thus gain a proven best scorer.
arxiv-2602-15814:
Acharya and Hammoud reformulate Avey, a one-way, attention-free model, for the encoder-only paradigm. Compact pretrained two-way encoders remain the backbone of factory NLP under tight compute and memory budgets. Their strength comes from self-attention delivering high-quality two-way context with sequence-level side-by-side work, as popularised by BERT-style designs. Avey offers an attention-free alternative that naturally admits an encoder-only adaptation.

This paper adds several innovations to Avey, including decoupled static and dynamic settings, stability-oriented scaling, and neural shrinking. Results show the new design comparing favourably with four widely used Transformer-based encoders. It consistently beats them on standard token tagging and search benchmarks while scaling more efficiently to long contexts. Factory NLP teams gain a lean encoder that competes with Transformer encoders at lower cost.
arxiv-2602-15914:
Lu and Tang show that breaking detailed balance on purpose in generative diffusion can speed the reverse process with no change to the end distribution. For the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, they split the dynamics into a symmetric part and a non-reversible anti-symmetric part that spins probability currents in loops.

They then build an exponentially optimal non-reversible tweak that lifts the long-time relaxation rate while keeping the same target. The same control reshapes the broad regimes of phase shifts lately found in generative diffusion. They derive a broad rule for speciation time and show apt tweaks can speed speciation. Collapse, by contrast, rests on trace-controlled phase-space contraction set by the symmetric part, so collapse time stays fixed under anti-symmetric tweaks. Tests on Gaussian mixture models back the claims.
arxiv-2602-16014:
Dimitrijevs and colleagues run the Lights Out puzzle through Grover search on real quantum hardware, testing nine and sixteen qubit instances on public IBM and IQM machines. The puzzle, played on grids and Mobius ladders, gives a clean benchmark with known answers against which noisy devices can be judged.

IBM hardware improved between its Heron r1 and r2 generations, a visible gain across the 2023 to 2024 period, while IQM outputs sat close to uniform, signalling heavier noise. A small Grover SAT baseline helped diagnose the gap, with IQM Garnet proving the most reliable of its tested devices. The study also warns that two chips of the same revision can differ sharply, and that calibration quality often decides which device wins.
arxiv-2602-16114:
Xueqing He leads a team of six researchers who build flat-top optical solitons in media with high even-order dispersion and competing nonlinearities. Flat-top solitons balance dispersion against self-phase modulation under cubic-quintic nonlinearity. Past work covered only second-order dispersion. After the recent observation of pure-quartic solitons, the team builds families for dispersion orders four, six, eight, and ten, and studies how these solitons interact with each other.

The new solitons prove fully stable, and unlike standard solitons they carry wavy tails. Their interactions break the usual pattern: in-phase solitons push apart, while out-of-phase solitons pull together. That reversal sets them apart from familiar cases. The findings widen the set of optical solitons that dispersive nonlinear media can support, giving photonics researchers new pulse shapes whose stability and interaction rules differ from the norm.
arxiv-2602-16214:
Galactic wind can reshape local cosmic ray spectra. Yusaku Fukumoto and coauthors study that advection effect. Spectral hardening from a few hundred GV and softening from a few TV are reproduced by a velocity profile peaking near seven hundred kilometers per second. No break is added in the power-law dependence of the diffusion coefficient. A hard cosmic ray spectrum below about a TV, with an index near two, also appears at altitudes of a few kiloparsecs from the Galactic disk.

That hard spectrum favors the gamma-ray spectrum of the Fermi bubbles. With those fluxes, the authors discuss matter circulation in the Galaxy with the wind. Wind plays an essential role in maintaining metal abundance in the disk. Yet beryllium production from cosmic ray spallation runs so low that the beryllium-to-oxygen ratio in the halo should exceed that in disk gas.
arxiv-2602-16514:
Xinhai He leads four coauthors on telling neutrinos from antineutrinos in large liquid-scintillator detectors. The study covers atmospheric charged-current interactions, from the primary interaction through later clashes of final-state particles to final neutron captures.

The authors examine final-state charged leptons and hadrons, giving distinct distributions of inelasticity and captured neutron multiplicity for both kinds of events. These patterns gauge how well the two kinds can be told apart. The findings ground future atmospheric oscillation studies in such tanks, especially the determination of the neutrino mass ordering.
arxiv-2602-16714:
Renato Marcelo and co-authors present the AIdentifyAGE ontology for decision support in forensic dental age checks. Age checks matter greatly in forensic and court choices. They matter most for undocumented people and lone minors, where legal cutoffs gate protection, health care, and court process. Dental age checks are among the most trusted biological routes for teens and young adults. Yet practice suffers from varied methods, split data, and weak links between clinical, forensic, and legal systems.

The ontology gives a standard, coherent frame covering manual and AI-assisted workflows. It links observations, methods, reference data, and reported outcomes in a traceable way. It models the full medico-legal workflow, from court context and personal data through exams, dental growth methods, imaging, reference studies, and AI estimation. Built with domain experts, it aims for clarity and repeatability in a sensitive legal field.
arxiv-2602-16914:
