Kiana Farhadyar and co-authors offer a statistical view on transformers for small longitudinal cohort data. Modeling such data involves knotty time links among many variables. Transformers, successful in language and vision, allow for a key fact. The most recent time points in a person's history may not always matter most for the near future. Observations are weighted based on transformed values.

Those ideas have been underused for cohort data because large sets are typically required. The paper presents a simplified transformer that keeps the core attention mechanism while cutting parameters to gauge, suiting small sets with few time points. An autoregressive model serves as the starting point. Attention acts as a kernel-based operation with time decay. Aggregation of multiple heads, varied weighting schemes, is framed as accumulating proof on varied traits of individuals. That enables a permutation-based statistical test.
arxiv-2602-17114:
Seemron Neupane led a two-author paper presenting a low-cost, internet-connected system for remote heart monitoring in places with thin health services. Many communities lack basic facilities, and heart patients need regular checks plus fast attention when their condition turns. A remote ECG system lets community health workers support patients through telemedicine, cutting travel and its costs, though money and logistics still burden such setups.

The paper describes the design and prototype of a tele-ECG monitoring system built around three parties: the operator, the doctor, and the server that carries the data between them. Early detection and intervention are the payoff the authors stress, since heart disease caught late can prove fatal. The prototype shows how cheap connected hardware could extend cardiac oversight where clinics are scarce.
arxiv-2602-17214:
Quentin Courtade led a seven-author team probing how a material's dielectric character shapes light-dressed electrons in semiconductors. Floquet engineering tailors band structures with light, and photoemission can watch those dressed states directly. But dressing also hits free electrons outside the sample, creating Volkov states, and strong surface screening can let Volkov signals swamp Floquet ones. The paper studies that interplay in layered van der Waals materials.

Combining a Fresnel-based model with an electron-scattering account of Volkov amplitudes, the team extracts lower bounds for the real dielectric functions from polarization-dependent sideband strengths. Stronger pump fluence yields high-order sidebands with clear nonlinear signatures. In their geometry, the semiconductors' near-transparency below the band gap lets the pump bounce inside the sample, producing delayed Volkov replicas through evanescent-field dressing.
arxiv-2602-17314:
Valdemar Švábenský led a four-author survey of open datasets in learning analytics, educational data mining, and artificial intelligence in education. Open data supports checking, teamwork, and trust, and it brings authors notice, standing, and cites. Yet how often data actually joins papers, and what habits surround them, stayed unclear, above all at flagship conference venues.

The team hand-checked well over a thousand papers from three flagship meetings over five years, finding and sorting well over a hundred sets across over two hundred papers. Most of those sets had escaped all prior surveys. The study offers the most complete gathering and analysis to date. It gives fine sorting, gap analysis, usable tips, and an eight-item PRACTICE checklist. It also gives a noted list of sets and papers to spur wider open data use.
arxiv-2602-17414:
David Yallup, writing alone, presents Nested Sampling with Slice-within-Gibbs, a method for Bayesian evidence work in large models whose likelihood splits, such as layered Bayesian models. The method samples from the constraint-bound prior using a Slice-within-Gibbs kernel: an outer update of high-level knobs then inner block updates over local values.

A budget split caches per-block shares so each local update checks fit in constant time rather than redoing the global constraint at growing cost. That cuts per-swap cost from quadratic to linear in group count, and overall cost from cubic to square under standard rules. The split extends easily beyond separate data, shown on Markov-shaped latent values. Tests on hard benchmarks show scaling to thousands of axes with exact evidence figures even on curved shapes where gradient-based samplers struggle.
arxiv-2602-17514:
Dion Li, writing alone, proposes a kinetic route to helicity-constrained decay. In two-dimensional, three-velocity particle-in-cell runs of freely decaying subion turbulence, spots show nonzero electric-magnetic field alignment. In the early electron-scale phase, those spots match drops in a fixed-gauge structure-integrated magnetic-helicity diagnostic. That pattern matches a fall in the Saffman helicity-variance plateau value.

Li puts forward a history-dependent, source-compensated helicity density meeting an exact local balance identity. It opens the way to Saffman-type correlation integrals with mid-scale plateaus roughly steady under standard flux-decorrelation assumptions. In the runs, such plateaus stay nearly unchanged across the kinetic span. Under rough self-similarity, that plateau fits the decay rule of constant field-length product. For net-helical starts, mixed-sign patches form fast as global fractional helicity falls. Decay then fits the cancellation-dominated rule best.
arxiv-2602-17614:
Obaidullah Zaland and team address a privacy hole in federated split learning. Clients share intermediate representations, known as smashed data, with a server. U-shaped split learning spares weak client devices and keeps raw data and labels local. Yet those shared intermediates can still leak private facts.

The authors first show an adversary rebuilding client data from smashed data. They then propose KD-UFSL, which pairs microaggregation with differential privacy to blunt the attack. Tests on four benchmarks raised rebuild error a lot and cut structural similarity between original and rebuilt images by up to two fifths in some cases. Privacy gains hold while the global model's utility stays intact, a balance big-data deployments need.
arxiv-2602-17714:
Robert Kimberk analyzes a long memory circular convolution model. It is built from a circulant matrix times a random normal vector. The model yields an evolving long memory time series with a power law spectral density.

Its spread, a beta location scale family, links to the unit centered spherical distribution and to spherical stats. Study of the fixed circulant matrix gives estimates of several traits. These are the discrete Fourier spectral trend, the inner dimension, the density shape parameter, the matrix condition number, and a main component analysis. R code examples serve as the hands-on element of the work. Readers can copy the code into an R editor and explore the model.
arxiv-2602-18114:
Yiding Feng and two co-authors tackle online sharing of scarce resources when demand shifts without warning. Their 2026 paper sets a hard limit: the method may look at only one past example per time step. Each arriving request needs set amounts of several resources and brings a reward drawn from an unknown pattern tied to its type.

The team builds a rule that splits the task into three parts: guessing reward patterns, setting target service rates with a simplified plan, and accepting or turning down requests as they arrive. When past examples show both type and reward, the rule's shortfall grows only with the square root of time. When examples show type alone, full adaptivity can still reach a shortfall that grows only as a power of log time under one mild condition. The work shows strong results are possible with very little past data.
arxiv-2602-18414:
Jan David Fischbach and eight co-authors give light-scattering calculations a compact frequency language. Their 2026 paper treats the transition matrix, a full account of how an object scatters light linearly, widely used for multi-scatter problems. Checking that matrix at many discrete frequencies costs heavily in compute and memory and hides the physics behind spectral features.

The team instead represents the matrix by pole expansion, capturing fine frequency detail within a chosen band through resonant parts. A matrix-valued variant of the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson algorithm builds the expansion cheaply from few direct evaluations. Examples range from easy scatterers to quasi-dual bound states in a continuum. Open-source tools let the wider community perform the same pole expansion.
arxiv-2602-18614:
Massoud Dehghan and two co-authors test patch size in medical transformers. Their 2026 paper notes Vision Transformers are now state-of-the-art in vision tasks and serve as backbones in large vision models. While architectural improvements draw research, patch size, a crucial initial choice, remains underexplored, particularly in medical domains with two- and three-dimensional imaging.

Using twelve medical datasets, seven two-dimensional and five three-dimensional, the team fine-tunes Vision Transformers on one GPU across patch sizes one, two, four, seven, fourteen, and twenty-eight. Smaller patch sizes of one, two, and four achieve the best results across nearly every set. Balanced accuracy improves up to twelve point seven eight percent for two-dimensional data and twenty-three point seven eight percent for three-dimensional data, at higher cost. An ensemble fusing predictions from sizes one, two, and four boosts performance, especially for two-dimensional data.
arxiv-2602-18814:
Tilted and tilting multi-rotor drones can manoeuvre in ways ordinary quadrotors cannot, but modelling them accurately is slow, fiddly, and error-prone. Nicola Cigarini, with two co-authors, presents RotorSuite in 2026, a MATLAB and Simulink toolbox for modelling and simulating a wide class of multi-rotor platforms through both analytical and physics-based approaches.

The toolbox aims to make the modelling step reliable enough for analysis, control design. Validation of emerging contact-aware aerial platforms, which have moved from passive flying sensors toward versatile robotic systems. With comprehensive documentation and example use cases, RotorSuite is pitched as a tool for teaching, research, and industrial development alike, lowering the barrier to working with modern tilted rotor designs.
arxiv-2602-19114:
Photonic quantum computing promises speed, but deep learning integration lags. Hongdong Zhu, with eight co-authors, bridges the gap in 2026 with the Kaiwu-PyTorch-Plugin. It brings the Coherent Ising Machine into PyTorch. Classical inefficiencies in energy-based models are the target.

Three integrations drive the framework. Boltzmann sampling accelerates. Training data improve through active sampling. Hybrid architectures emerge, including quantum Boltzmann machines with variational autoencoders and quantum diffusion. Tests on single-cell and web-text datasets reach state-of-the-art performance. A comprehensive quantum-classical paradigm thus gains concrete support. Energy-based modelling and data selection both benefit.
arxiv-2602-19214:
Blazars are active galaxies whose light flickers across many timescales, and some light curves hint at repeating cycles that could reveal binary black holes or the physics of their jets. M. A. Hashad and two colleagues re-examine five blazars with previously claimed year-long cycles, using Fermi gamma-ray data through early 2025, plus one newer candidate source.

They apply period-finding tools and strip out slow trends first. That step usually strengthens the cycle signal. Only one source, PG 1553+113, shows a clearly lasting cycle. The others fade over spans of a few thousand days. Forecasts for the next four years use both a classic statistical method and a Transformer model. They point to weaker cycles ahead, except in the new candidate, where the signal is expected to grow.
arxiv-2602-19314:
Scans taken at just 2 percent of normal radiation dose are noisy, and lining them up with normal-dose scans is itself hard. Guoliang Gong and Man Yu revisit the image purification strategy, which builds an intermediate image distribution with aligned anatomy to help denoising models preserve structure. The original version, they note, leaves the image background untreated and has no dedicated mechanism for cleaning lung tissue.

Their improved version, IPv2, adds three modules that remove background, add noise, and then remove noise. Together they give the model denoising ability in both background and lung regions while training data is built, and they support a fairer evaluation protocol at test time. On a real-world patient lung CT set, IPv2 improved background suppression and lung restoration across several mainstream denoising models.
arxiv-2602-19514:
Pulak Mehta studies a new security risk: autonomous AI agents that hire human workers via marketplaces through REST APIs and Model Context Protocol integrations. The attack surface resembles CAPTCHA-solving services, except with reach into the physical world, since hired humans can act in the real world. The paper measures the threat on RENTAHUMAN.AI, a marketplace for agents to post tasks and handle escrow payments.

Of 303 bounties analyzed, 99 came through programmatic channels such as API keys or MCP. Six abuse classes appear, including credential fraud, identity impersonation, referral fraud, automated reconnaissance, social media manipulation, and authentication circumvention, purchasable for a median of 25 dollars per worker. Seven screening rules flag 52 bounties with a single false positive, showing basic defenses can help.
arxiv-2602-20114:
Models can be made to forget. Machine unlearning removes what training examples contribute when they are incorrect, biased, or leaking private information. It is now seen as critical for safe and fair AI. A 2026 arXiv paper by Kairan Zhao and two co-authors turns to vision transformers, the architecture unlearning research has neglected.

Vision transformers now rival CNNs, yet vision forgetting benchmarks cover language models, diffusion models, and CNNs, not these models. This work builds the first benchmark for them. It tests unlearning methods across model families including ViT, Swin-T, and DINOv2, and across different sizes. Datasets vary in scale and difficulty. Methods represent basically different approaches. Both single-shot and ongoing unlearning setups are used. The paper also focuses on algorithms that use extra structure.
arxiv-2602-20214:
AI agents now act for people, but no system keeps a checkable, trusted record of their deeds. New rules like the EU AI Act now demand automatic logs for high-risk AI. The gap bites hardest on personal hardware, where no provider holds the log. A 2026 arXiv paper by Jing Zhang, working alone, argues for a Right to History: a full, checkable record of agent deeds on one's own machines.

Zhang builds on Floridi's work on rights over personal information. He stretches that idea from facts about a person to deeds done for them. The principle is set out as five system rules with proof sketches. It is built into PunkGo, a Rust kernel. That kernel joins Merkle-tree audit logs, capability-based permissions, energy-use limits, and a human approval step. Readers gain a rights claim for agent accountability and a kernel design that enforces it.
arxiv-2602-20814:
Materials whose electrons interact strongly are hard to model well without paying the high cost of hybrid-functional calculations. Dmitry Korotin, Anna Anisimova, and Vladimir Anisimov offer a cheaper path in this 2026 arXiv paper. They build a single shared set of localized Wannier functions for both standard and hybrid calculations, then fit on-site and between-site Hubbard parameters by shrinking the mismatch between the two descriptions.

The fitted parameters reproduce hybrid results for electronic structure at a fraction of the cost, which also makes structural relaxation and later many-body work practical. The authors test the method on three oxides with distinct characters: magnesium oxide, nickel oxide, and vanadium oxide. In each case the mapped parameters match hybrid band gaps, densities of states, and magnetic moments, and improve on standard methods while staying cheap to run.
arxiv-2602-21314:
Matrix completion can estimate causal effects in panel data even when missingness follows treatment selection, provided treated observations are few relative to controls. Eli Ben-Michael and Avi Feller discuss that proposal in this 2026 arXiv paper, commenting on a 2025 paper by Choi and Yuan. They applaud the original work and examine it from two complementary angles.

First, the proposal exemplifies a split-apply-combine strategy behind many modern panel estimators, including difference-in-differences and synthetic control. Second, the authors confront the statistical last-mile problem, the gap between theory and practice, with suggestions to partially close it. Challenges of policy evaluation with panel data are considered, with an application to right-to-carry laws and violent crime.
arxiv-2602-21514:
Liang Li and four co-authors explore I/O optimizations for graph-based, disk-resident approximate nearest neighbor search. On SSD-backed indexes, I/O dominates, accounting for 70 to 90 percent of query latency. Their I/O-first framework organizes techniques along three dimensions: memory layout, disk layout, and search algorithm.

A page-level complexity model explains how page locality and path length jointly determine page reads, and the model is validated empirically. Using consistent implementations across four public datasets, the team quantifies single-factor effects and cross-dimensional synergies. Memory-resident navigation and dynamic width give the strongest standalone gains. Page shuffle and page search are weak alone but complementary together. A principled composition, OctopusANN, cuts I/O sharply, beating Starling by about 4 to 38 percent in throughput and DiskANN by about 88 to 150 percent at matched recall.
arxiv-2602-21614:
Shan Shan and three co-authors design multiple access schemes to improve max-min fairness for pinching-antenna multigroup multicast links. Antenna spots and resource shares are jointly optimized. Three schemes are studied for group sends.

Treating interference as noise yields a closed-form power share plus a sequential element-wise method for antenna spots. Non-orthogonal access adds a recursive power design with bisection search. Time-split access splits into pinching switching, with spots optimized separately before convex time-power shares, and pinching multiplexing, where spots join time-power resources in a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker solution. Tests show the pinching-antenna design beats fixed-antenna systems. Time-split switching leads via noise-free transmission, noise-treating access trails as a simple lower bound, and non-orthogonal access beats time-split multiplexing, sometimes even topping switching at high power with uneven group mixes.
arxiv-2602-21714:
Whether fully flexible elastic tethered surfaces crumple or stay flat has been debated for decades. Some theories predict crumpling without bending rigidity, while most simulations find flat surfaces. Recent work on perforated ideal membranes suggested that removing surface area might offer a route to crumpling. A. D. Chen and three co-authors ran extensive simulations of two fully flexible surface models in which self-avoidance can be tuned smoothly toward the ideal limit.

In the thermodynamic limit, the surfaces stay flat with a size exponent of one for any finite degree of self-avoidance, with or without perforations. The result settles the debate in favor of flatness for self-avoiding tethered surfaces.
arxiv-2602-21814:
Large language models always fail the car wash problem, a viral thinking benchmark needing hidden constraint guesses. Heejin Jo presents a variable split study, 20 trials per setup across 6 setups, 120 trials total, testing which prompt design layers in a live system enable correct answers. Using Claude Sonnet with fixed settings, she finds the STAR method alone raises scores from 0 percent to 85 percent, a strong result.

Adding user profile context via vector store lookup adds a further 10 points, while RAG context adds 5 more, reaching 100 percent correct in the full-stack setup. The results suggest ordered thinking scaffolds, notably forced goal notes before answers, matter far more than context adds for hidden constraint tasks.
arxiv-2602-22014:
Modern language models are usually trained on ever-larger piles of text, with size prized over variety. Louis Estève and three co-authors ask whether picking diverse training data can shrink the pile without losing quality, using a French ModernBERT model as the test case. They compare several diversity-driven sampling methods to find which selection rule works best.

Diversity-driven sampling beats random sampling of the same size on some tasks by a clear margin, the authors report. Strikingly, a model trained for a few hundred hours on a modest diverse set matches one trained far longer on a dataset many times larger. The study suggests that careful data choice, not just bulk, can make pretraining cheaper and greener.
arxiv-2602-22214:
Similarity search over high-dimensional data powers modern retrieval, but one-size-fits-all search wastes effort on queries of very different popularity. Teodor-Ioan Calin proposes adaptive prefiltering: split the query space into frequency tiers following Zipfian patterns, and give each tier a search policy matched to its history and local density. Budgets flow where queries actually go.

On a large image benchmark with CLIP embeddings, frequency-aware budgeting matches static search recall with about a fifth fewer distance computations, while keeping latency under a millisecond on GPU indices. Lightweight frequency tracking adds little overhead, and a coherence-based fallback covers unseen queries gracefully. Retrieval systems gain a cheap, principled way to spend compute where it pays.
arxiv-2602-22414:
Lattice cryptography rests on hard problems like shortest and closest vector problems, but new problem variants can refresh that foundation. Julia VanLandingham defines two new problems, SIAP and CAP, for solving those tasks inside Simultaneous Approximation lattices. She gives dimension- and gap-preserving deterministic polynomial-time and space reductions from the classic problems to their SA-lattice counterparts.

The reductions show SA-lattice instances are just as hard as general instances, making the new problems credible candidates for cryptographic use. The author also shows the reductions are optimal regarding integer inflation. Cryptographers gain two fresh hard problems with hardness tightly tied to the classics.
arxiv-2602-22614:
Murchana Khusroo and one co-author chase solitary plasma waves through geomagnetic storms. Solitons are localized, nonlinear waves that hold their shape and speed over time and distance, common in near-Earth space, yet their storm-time behaviour is little studied. The team compares magnetosonic soliton signatures across storms from Solar Cycles 24 and 25.

Using high-resolution magnetic field data from the Cluster II mission, they built a multi-diagnostic framework from several leading analytical techniques to detect and characterize these waves reliably. Solitary structures in both storms clustered in early storm intervals, before the main phase. That timing hints the waves could serve as early warning signs of stronger geomagnetic activity to come.
arxiv-2602-23114:
Xudong Yan and four co-authors gather knowledge for combo zero-shot learning with WARM-CAT. The task spots novel trait-object combos from seen ones, but current methods dip under spread shift. Their approach gathers full knowledge in text and visual modes from raw data to update models.

A flexible update weight controls adjustment, letting the model adapt to spread shift during testing. A ranking queue stores images for models. Since the model tends to prefer combos already in the queue, we warm the queue by seeding it with training images for seen combos. Unseen models are made using the map learned between seen and unseen text models. Text and visual models are lined up by joint learning. We introduce a test set, C-Fashion, and clean the noisy MIT-States set. Wide tests show top performance on four test sets in closed and open settings.
arxiv-2602-23414:
Vrutant Mehta and four co-authors simulate helium-ignited binary white dwarf mergers in 3D to probe Type Ia supernova origins. These supernovae serve as cosmic distance indicators and matter for galactic nucleosynthesis, yet their progenitors and explosion mechanisms remain ambiguous. Gaia hypervelocity white dwarfs support helium-ignited double-degenerate explosions.

Two binary systems near helium ignition evolve under two codes, AREPO and FLASH, with fixed initial conditions. The first model yields a double detonation of the primary plus hypervelocity ejection of the surviving secondary, matching the D6 scenario. In the second, the secondary also detonates in its core, fully disrupting both stars. Despite different solvers, networks, and meshes, the codes broadly agree, though yields differ with the networks used. Results strongly support both the D6 and quadruple detonation channels for at least some Type Ia supernovae. The authors also explore observational signatures including X-rays with XRISM's RESOLVE.
arxiv-2602-23714:
Anjitha Ashokan and one co-author study how edge deletion changes the eccentricity energy of coalesced graphs. The eccentricity matrix of a graph keeps the largest entries in each row or column from the distance matrix, replacing the rest with zeros. Eccentricity energy is the sum of absolute values of the eigenvalues of that matrix.

The paper investigates edge deletion for graphs formed by n-coalescence of l copies of the complete graph K2n, where n is at least 3 and l is at least 2. The authors prove eccentricity energy increases whenever an edge is removed. That result identifies a class of graphs whose eccentricity energy exhibits monotonic growth under edge deletion.
arxiv-2602-23814:
Chongyang Xu and six co-authors present a framework for two-handed robot manipulation that builds directly on a pretrained three-dimensional geometric model. The 2026 paper argues that older methods lean on flat images with weak depth sense, or on point clouds that are hard to obtain reliably in real rooms.

The policy fuses geometry-aware codes, flat semantic features, and body sense into one state picture. A diffusion model then predicts a chunk of future actions together with a future three-dimensional code that decodes into a dense point map. Predicting how the scene will change, alongside the actions, gives strong spatial foresight from color images alone. Tests in simulation and on real robots beat flat-image and point-cloud baselines on success, coordination, and spatial prediction.
arxiv-2602-23914:
Peter Schürger and two co-authors review exact factorization as a framework for quantum many-body problems, going beyond its best-known use for electron-nuclear systems. The 2026 review traces the method from its origins in the nineteen seventies, when it mainly served multi-component systems. In the electron-nuclear case, it offered an exact version of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation for nonadiabatic dynamics.

The review also covers two less familiar branches. One branch is exact factorization for many-electron systems, already used in the nineteen eighties. The other branch is a recent extension to molecules inside optical cavities, which adds photons to the electron-nuclear picture. By gathering those formulations together, the paper shows how one exact splitting idea adapts across electronic, nuclear, and photonic degrees of freedom, and where each variant has drawn attention.
arxiv-2602-24014:
Na Min An and five co-authors introduce DeBiasLens, an interpretable, model-agnostic framework for reducing social bias in vision-language models. The 2026 paper argues that current debiasing mostly attacks surface bias signals after the fact, leaving the model's internal dynamics unexplored and its reasoning opaque.

DeBiasLens trains sparse autoencoders on multimodal encoders, using face images or captions without social attribute labels, to find neurons highly responsive to specific demographics, including underrepresented groups. Selectively deactivating the neurons most tied to bias for each group reduces biased behavior without degrading semantic knowledge. The work lays groundwork for auditing tools that prioritize social fairness in real-world AI systems, by making bias localizable inside the model rather than merely measurable in its outputs. In short, the fix works inside the model, not just on its outputs.
arxiv-2603-01714:
Jinluan Yang, Yuxin Liu, Zhengyu Chen, and colleagues pick better training data for agents that use tools. Their 2026 work faults the usual filter, which keeps only winning runs and tasks with middling pass rates. A winning run may still waste steps or never show recovery from an error, so outcome alone misleads.

Their frame, TopoCurate, merges many trial runs of one task into a single map of shared states. On that map, good runs stand out by recovery skill, lean steps, and varied strategy. For practice tasks, the frame favors tasks rich in error branches and mixed plans. Tests on two agent benchmarks show steady gains for both fine-tuning and reward-based training. The map makes interaction structure, not just wins, drive what agents learn from.
arxiv-2603-01914:
Shixiang Song, He Li, Zitong Wang, and colleagues let each token in a language model choose how much compute it needs. Their 2026 work builds on recurrent models that loop a fixed number of times per token. Fixed loops waste effort on easy tokens and starve hard ones of extra passes.

Their model, AdaPonderLM, learns token-wise early exit during pre-training with no hand-set pruning ratios. Gates that grow stricter by iteration decide when each token stops looping, under a monotonic halting mask. Cached key and value states for halted tokens are reused, which keeps training and testing consistent. Across several backbone sizes, inference compute drops by about a tenth at equal quality. Gate analysis shows hard tokens, with high loss, indeed earn more passes than easy ones.
arxiv-2603-02214:
Jungwon Seo, Ferhat Ozgur Catak, Chunming Rong, and Jaeyeon Jang map a new way for models to team up in this 2026 paper. In federated inference, private models owned by different parties answer queries together. They share neither their training data nor their inner weights. No shared framework yet explains how such teamwork should work.

The authors name two must-haves: privacy at query time and real gains from teamwork. They formalize the setup as shielded joint computation. Then they trace the trade-offs when privacy, uneven data, and limited oversight collide. A working example shows friction in privacy, teamwork, and fair rewards. Their claim is that query-time teamwork behaves in ways training-time teamwork does not predict.
arxiv-2603-02314:
Stefan Arseneau, J Hermes, Maria Camisassa, and colleagues weigh the outer layers of white dwarfs in this 2026 paper. A white dwarf's hydrogen skin forms its whole visible surface. Yet theorists model its mass poorly, and observers have few direct checks. That gap clouds white dwarf masses and cooling ages.

The team fits a mixture model to gravity shifts in light from almost five hundred white dwarfs. Radius data come from the Gaia space mission's spectra. The joint fit traces how mass grows with radius across the sample. Results match leading evolution models closely. Models with thick, mass-dependent hydrogen skins beat a fixed-skin model. Careful progenitor modeling thus matters, and gravity shifts offer a promising probe of these thin skins.
arxiv-2603-02514:
Tram Thi Minh Tran, Adrian Wong, Callum Parker, and colleagues examine non-human voices in crisis planning in this 2026 paper. Resilience planning usually centers human participants and interests. Species and ecosystems affected by crises rarely get a seat at the table. A workshop with HCI researchers probed how technology might represent them.

Scenario discussion mixed with two design probes: a voice agent and an immersive embodied prototype. Participants debated choices like voice, embodiment, and realism rather than usability. Giving non-humans a voice proved far from a neutral translation act. It raised tensions over legitimacy, authority, and authenticity in the process. Crisis planning, the authors argue, is a critical site for studying AI-mediated representation of the more-than-human world.
arxiv-2603-02614:
Amr Hamada, Kiran Jain, Hanna Strecker, and colleagues infer the Sun's far-side magnetic field in this 2026 paper. Space weather forecasting needs a full view of solar magnetism. The far hemisphere has no direct, continuous magnetic measurements. Helioseismic maps do reveal far-side active regions, but without polarity signs.

The crux is guessing the signs of opposing parts of each seismic signature realistically. Their method assigns polarities stably to large structures from resolved substructures. A bimodal variance profile locates the polarity boundary inside each region. Hale's polarity rule then sets the east-west ordering for the solar cycle. The output is far-side magnetograms ready to merge with near-side data. Full-Sun boundary conditions should improve coronal and solar wind models and forecasts.
arxiv-2603-02714:
Reese Pathak and Nikita Zhivotovskiy bound how large a random Gaussian process can grow over a convex set. Their 2026 paper revisits Gaussian width, a measure that controls many error bounds in statistics and learning. Standard proofs lean on generic chaining, a powerful but indirect construction.

The authors give two decompositions based directly on the set's geometry. One uses projections of Gaussian vectors onto scaled copies of the set, the other uses fixed points of a penalized local width. Linking these to the Wills functional ties the width to the set's intrinsic volumes, its built-in size measures. In the end, a single peak term among those volumes controls the width, and the worst case recovers the classic Dudley bound.
arxiv-2603-03014:
Heather Johnston, O. Panić, S. Reffert, and colleagues test whether pebble accretion explains why giant planets favor middleweight stars. Surveys show the giant planet rate rises then falls with star mass, peaking near twice the Sun's mass. Their 2026 population synthesis runs a pebble-driven core growth model across many synthetic systems.

Matching three combined radial velocity surveys required assumptions grounded in observations: faster accretion but shorter-lived disks around heavier stars. Under those rules, the synthetic population closely matched the real occurrence pattern and planet properties. The model also predicts runaway gas growth starts farther out and earlier around heavier stars. The match supports pebble accretion as the engine behind the observed trend.
arxiv-2603-03414:
Patrick J Mineault, Thomas L Griffiths, and Sean Escola argue that artificial intelligence has a blind spot shaped like the human mind itself. Modern systems are oddly uneven: brilliant at some tasks, helpless at nearby ones. Their 2026 paper blames a missing training signal they call cognitive dark matter, brain functions that shape behavior but are hard to infer from behavior alone.

The missing domains include metacognition, mental flexibility, episodic memory, lifelong learning, abductive reasoning, social and common-sense reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The authors show that benchmarks and large neuroscience datasets both over-measure what systems already do well. Their research program proposes three new data types: latent variables from cognitive models, process traces like eye movements and think-aloud records, and paired neural and behavioral data. Training on process, not just outcomes, could smooth the jagged profile.
arxiv-2603-03614:
Jian Zhang, Wafa Johal, and Jarrod Knibbe track how the felt size of an object drifts as sight and touch disagree. Tangible interfaces can decouple the senses, showing one size while the hand feels another. That opens design tricks but raises a question. Perception also leans on prior beliefs, updated in a continuing cycle that is poorly understood. Their 2026 study follows eighty participants judging size over time in visuo-haptic tasks.

Three contributions emerge. The experiments reveal how size perception drifts during prolonged mismatched feedback. They measure the separate effects of visual priming, being shown a size first, and dead-reckoning, the body's own position sense. And they present a model of visuo-haptic perception as a cyclical, self-adjusting system. The findings bear directly on illusory perception in virtual reality and on how vision and touch cooperate and diverge.
arxiv-2604-00114: Junkai Dong and three colleagues ask when a commensurate Wigner crystal dopes itself and turns metallic. Such charge crystals are usually pinned into insulators, even by weak pinning. Their rule weighs the charge gap of the locked-in crystal against a packing bias whose sign picks electron or hole doping. Self-consistent work for rhombohedral multilayer graphene reveals a broad metallic phase beside the insulating one. The theory also accounts for an island of reversed Hall conductance lately seen near a thought-to-be Wigner crystal phase there.
arxiv-2604-00214: Tsai, Brahmbhatt, and Avraamidou present Parametric Region Search, a primal heuristic for mixed-integer bilevel optimization that hunts high-quality feasible solutions quickly. The method draws on multi-parametric optimization, exploring step by step regions set by the lower-level problem's critical regions. Tests show it often finds strong primal solutions against known derivative-free metaheuristics such as DOMINO-COBYLA and DOMINO-ISRES. It also pairs with other methods such as DOMINO-COBYLA to improve overall discovery.
arxiv-2604-00314: Bardia Azizian and Bajic propose a lightweight, plug-and-play prefilter that spots image regions most relevant to a text prompt before compression. Traditional human-centric codecs waste bits on task-irrelevant detail, and existing machine-coding methods assume fixed tasks and cannot adapt to open-ended prompt-driven models. The module keeps important detail while smoothing less relevant areas, and works with conventional and learned encoders. It cuts bitrate by 25 to 50 percent on VQA benchmarks without losing task accuracy.
arxiv-2604-01014: Liu and team propose AutoMIA, an agentic tool turning member guessing attacks into self-search and plan growth. Member guessing audits training data leakage, but current methods rely on fixed, hand-built rules that move poorly across large models. Given scenario specs, AutoMIA searches the attack space by building working logits-level plans and tuning them through evaluation feedback. By splitting plan reasoning from running, it crosses the attack space in a model-free way. Tests show it matches or beats top rivals while dropping manual feature design.
arxiv-2604-01814: Balogun and Jonah study 28 GHz millimeter-wave spread in offices, vital for beyond-5G systems but thinly evidenced indoors. Using TMYTEK-based tests of path loss, material blocking and coverage gains, they find path loss follows free-space theory with an exponent of 2.07. Material effects vary sharply: desk panels block far more than display boards, against thickness-based guesses. Reflector tuning yields a solid mean gain, improving coverage. The study offers new measured benchmarks and design guidance for steady indoor millimeter-wave rollout.
arxiv-2604-02014: Ren studies wild superattracting maps where the usual tools break down at a prime degree. For the clean family he proves a full digit sum law. For higher fibers he builds a coefficient level theory with a digit weight bound, a leading monomial result, and a recursion for pure powers. These yield a branch word and a radius formula for the inverse Böttcher coordinate. Tail changes beyond the first graded term preserve those leading facts, recovering earlier degree results as special cases.
arxiv-2604-02414: Xue and Yang construct BF type Lagrangians for non abelian Dijkgraaf Witten theories by gauging an abelian theory. When gauging permutes operators of the original theory, the result uses cohomologies with local coefficients. The authors analyze structure and gauge changes with homotopy theory, construct the operator spectrum, and verify the Lagrangians by matching elementary linking invariants.
arxiv-2604-03014: Du and four colleagues introduce GTC for multi-modal recommendation, filtering content by each user's tastes. Dominant methods split shared preference signals from modality-specific noise, but wrongly assume item content matters equally for all users and ignore joint modality effects. GTC uses an interaction-guided diffusion to keep only personalized features. It also optimizes a tractable lower bound of total correlation across modalities, capturing full joint dependencies. On standard benchmarks, GTC beats prior best methods by up to 28 percent on NDCG@5.
arxiv-2604-03214: Ghose sketches Nelson's stochastic mechanics as a random-process reconstruction of nonrelativistic quantum theory, with diffusion set by the reduced Planck constant. The Born rule falls out of the diffusion itself, not as an added postulate, and collapse needs no extra axiom, while nonlocality softens beside Bohmian guidance. Linking quantumness to diffusion scale also suggests a continuum from classical to quantum behavior.
arxiv-2604-03314: Suharitdamrong and colleagues adapt foundation models to multimodal tasks with CoLA, a low-rank method that adds a cross-modal path beside the usual within-modality path. Dual-stream models like DINO plus BERT can then learn shared and modality-specific signals without interference. CoLA beats LoRA by around 3 percent on vision-language benchmarks and 2 percent on audio-visual ones, while staying parameter-efficient.
arxiv-2604-03514: Guévremont and colleagues pinpoint why some catalytic porous monoliths underperform. Uneven flow and partial use of the catalytic surface cap yield even at low Damköhler numbers. They use Pd-coated silicone blocks for p-nitrophenol cleanup with pore-scale flow models. They tune a reaction model and check it across samples and flow rates. Random blocks need up to ten times the pumping power of TPMS structures at matched pore share for the same molar output.
arxiv-2604-03814: Felix Stillger and colleagues built InCaRPose, a transformer that estimates relative camera poses inside cars, where fisheye distortion and tight spaces defeat standard calibration. Frozen backbone features plus a transformer decoder recover metric-scale translation in one step, within the plausible range of cabin mounts. Trained only on synthetic data, it generalized to real cabins and stayed competitive on the 7-Scenes set. A small backbone still kept precision high enough for real-time driver monitoring.
arxiv-2604-04014: Sanhanat Deesamutara and colleagues built a numerical optimization method to pull X-ray reverberation responses from active galaxy light curves. The approach needs no prior shape for the accretion disc and corona, only that light curves mix direct and singly-convolved signals across bands. Recasting the equations in matrix form, the team minimized the gap between observed and rebuilt curves with a gradient method. Tests on synthetic curves showed sturdy recovery, including at signal-to-noise ratios of at least 100.
arxiv-2604-04314: Zhou and Dana introduce HeartbeatCam, a wearable system that captures context at moments of heightened stress. A consumer smartwatch stress signal triggers an open-source augmented-reality glasses camera, recording a short image-audio clip for later review and annotation. People often grasp a stress trigger only after the fact, and therapy clients struggle to recall session-to-session details. The system pairs body signals with contextual capture so clients and clinicians can jointly interpret what set off each stress moment.
arxiv-2604-04514: Bhardwaj presents SuperLocalMemory V3.3, The Living Brain, a local-first agent memory system copying the cognitive memory taxonomy. AI coding agents hold vast parametric knowledge yet cannot recall an hour-old conversation. Building on V3.2's information-geometric foundations, V3.3 adds five contributions. They span a Fisher-Rao distance metric, Ebbinghaus adaptive forgetting, seven-channel cognitive retrieval, long-term implicit memory via soft prompts, and a zero-friction pipeline. On LoCoMo it scores 70.4 percent in zero-LLM Mode A, with large gains on multi-hop and adversarial items.
arxiv-2604-04714: Xu and eight colleagues offer a Transformer-based model identifying trustworthy stellar sources on Chinese historical plates to complete their astrometric mapping. China has collected nighttime plates since 1900, now scanned, with sources taken by software and matched with star maps and the Gaia catalog. Poor early storage and later deterioration impeded source matching. The model takes cutouts of detected sources and uses multi-scale fusion to find trusted stellar sources. Trained on plates with good calibration, the classifier finished registration for 1353 of 1883 plates.
arxiv-2604-04914: Zangooei and four colleagues study how to reason about deep reinforcement learning agents used in systems and networking, from video streaming to wireless control and congestion control. Current checks focus on single fixed input states, giving narrow coverage and demanding heavy manual work to pick relevant cases. The authors instead formulate symbolic properties, rules that must hold across ranges of inputs, with monotonicity and robustness as examples. They show how existing tools can analyze those broader properties, opening safer deployment for agents that face varied real states.
arxiv-2604-05014: The StarVLA Community presents StarVLA, an open codebase for vision-language-action research, aiming to unify generalist embodied agents. Building such agents requires perception, language understanding, and action, yet methods remain split across incompatible designs, codebases, and evaluation rules, blocking fair comparison and repeat work. StarVLA offers a modular backbone-action-head design using both vision-language bases and world-model bases, with typical action decoding styles. By joining those pieces under one roof, the code aims to make vision-language-action methods easier to compare, reproduce, and extend.
arxiv-2604-05214: Brady and six colleagues take on two-generated minimal Taylor algebras built on a domain of just four elements, a tightly bounded classification problem in universal algebra. They prove that no such algebra is simple, meaning it always carries nontrivial congruence structure. They then list every one of these algebras up to isomorphism and term equivalence, closing the four-element case in full.
arxiv-2604-05414: Choy explains why dropping a step called orthogonalization from training, and saving it for inference, improves rotation estimates in deep learning. His study of SVD gradients for 3-by-3 matrices finds a rank-3 backward pass whose distortion peaks when predictions sit far from true rotations. He also shows Gram-Schmidt gradients skew unevenly across parameters, backing direct 9D regression plus SVD only at inference.
arxiv-2604-05614: Wulff and four colleagues ground hierarchical robot vision-language-action models by aligning their words with their deeds. A contrastive model scores how well sub-task descriptions match visual observations and action paths, enabling preference learning that sharpens grounding. On the LanguageTable benchmark the method rivals fully supervised fine-tuning while cutting annotation costs.
arxiv-2604-05814: The CMS Collaboration reports the first coherent upsilon(1S) photoproduction measurement off heavy nuclei in ultraperipheral lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV. Probing gluon structure near momentum fraction 10 to the power -3, they find suppression to about one quarter of a no-nuclear-effects baseline. The gluon suppression factor, just over one half, slightly exceeds phi-meson values despite a much higher scale.
arxiv-2604-06314: Parente, Narayanan, and Torrey present the first evolving grain size distribution in a semi-analytic galaxy model. Their model covers production, shattering, coagulation, accretion, and destruction, matching key data. The grain mix evolves from large grains at high redshift to a flatter shape at low redshift. Massive systems transition earlier, at a metallicity set by depletion. Extinction curves steepen in ultraviolet-optical slope and gain a pronounced 2175 angstrom bump toward lower redshift, matching Milky Way properties. Stars supply large grains, while shattering and gas accretion drive small-grain growth.
arxiv-2604-06514: Sato and Yasuhara resolve the structure of link concordance complements. Donald and Owens gave two link concordance groups with a marked part, each splitting off the knot concordance group while leaving complements generated without end. While never openly posed as a problem, their structure arises from their work itself. Sato and Yasuhara prove both are a direct sum of endless integer copies and endless two-element cyclic copies. They define prime elements and a unique prime decomposition theorem, yielding a standard normal form for the group structure.
arxiv-2604-06914: Bou Chaaya and Bennis study vehicle-to-infrastructure systems where stations gather wireless and visual data. Each unit tunes its resources locally while all units work together for network performance. The authors recast as multi-agent learning with rotation patterns of positions. A self-taught setup aligns mixed signals to extract vehicle spots, and an equivariant network with message passing lets agents decide while sending signals past partial blind spots. Tests with ray-tracing and graphics data show over twofold hit-rate gains and over 50 percent better results over rivals.
arxiv-2604-07014: Pineda builds his theory from cause and one-ness of event sight. Distinct watchers need finite time to talk, forcing a maximal transfer-information speed between any frames. Still frames are defined by fixing shape traits of spatial distance without appeal to it, magnets, or physics laws. For these frames, the cause rule fixes the causal group to the forward mixed Lorentz group times stretches. The math used is quite basic.
arxiv-2604-07214: Fang and three colleagues speed up the prep of Gibbs states, the thermal states used as inputs in quantum computing. Their trick uses the detectability lemma in place of simulating Lindblad evolution, cutting out that overhead. For local Lindbladians with M terms, the cost drops by a factor near M. The same lemma, paired with a singular-value trick, also speeds ground-state projection and sharpens the gap dependence for commuting local cases.
arxiv-2604-07314: Paçal and six colleagues show that the light-emitting direction of single defects in hexagonal boron nitride is not fixed. Using energy-resolved spectroscopy at room temperature, they watch the emission dipole rotate by up to 40 degrees across the vibronic spectrum, driven by coupling to lattice vibrations. Cooling to 6 kelvin largely suppresses the rotation, since few acoustic phonons remain. First-principles calculations confirm the effect, marking a basic limit on polarization fidelity in solid-state quantum networks.
arxiv-2604-07414: Vázquez and seven colleagues design control changes with hard proof for self-run systems that stray outside their planned domain. Their method widens current chance-based system models to cover surprise cases, checking and adapting behavior at the same time. The system thus keeps hard proof in unforeseen settings rather than merely reacting. Early tests show higher reliability through adaptation, with proof kept even outside the planned domain.
arxiv-2604-07714: Cao and four colleagues study momentum-space linkage entropy at quantum phase shifts. Looking at Su-Schrieffer-Heeger, quantum XY chain, and Haldane models, the shape shift rule gives exact tie p equals 1/2 in the linkage spectrum, yielding entropy of ln 2 in momentum space. In one size, key momenta are lone points; in two sizes, smooth sheets. Subgrid splits behave not so: entropy becomes time-linked and hits a minimum at key times. Momentum-space linkage entropy in the right base gives a test of changing quantum phase shifts.
arxiv-2604-07814: Mahmood, Yu, and Anwer build AgriChain, a dataset for diagnosing plant disease from leaf photos. It holds about 11,000 expert-curated images across crops and diseases, each with a disease label, a confidence grade, and an expert-verified chain of reasoning. Draft explanations from GPT-4o were checked by an agricultural engineer against standard visual descriptors. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-3B on the set yields AgriChain-VL3B, which scores 73.1 percent top-1 accuracy on a 1,000-image test and beats strong baselines.
arxiv-2604-08114: Zhou and six colleagues present StoryEcho, a generative storytelling system for picky eating in children. Picky eating can limit dietary variety and tense family feeding routines. Existing food tools focus on mealtime help or standalone learning tools, offering limited support for connecting low-pressure story time with children's real food exploration. StoryEcho centers on a narrative mirroring loop: tailored stories model sensory play through a steady counterpart, and children's later food encounters feed back into story feedback and future stories. A 14-day field study with 26 families evaluates it.
arxiv-2604-08314: Wang and three colleagues analyze the parallel peculiar velocity correlation function using Cosmicflows-4 survey data. Cosmicflows-4 extends peculiar speed measures much deeper, cutting viewer impact on cosmic variance. They examine cosmic variance spread with varied correlation tools. Large peculiar speed errors plus skewed data across northern and southern halves yield large stat errors in the correlation function. To address this, they try varied weighing schemes and build a more accurate peculiar speed tool.
arxiv-2604-08514: Joy and three colleagues study how disability symbols work with new tech for people who share their disability status. In twenty three remote design sessions with interviews, sketching, and storyboards, people imagined symbols on wearables, phones, and portable tools. Symbols worked best with user control over who sees them and optional paths to explain them. That control supports agency while cutting misreading, and the findings point toward systems shaped by symbol, carrier, and context.
arxiv-2604-08714: Tomio and three colleagues study immiscible to miscible quenching instabilities in flat binary Bose-Einstein condensates of rubidium isotopes 85 and 87 in a round box. Sudden drops in interspecies scattering length trigger instabilities driven by large vortices and sound waves. Sound prevails over long times. Kinetic energy spectra meet classic Kolmogorov chaotic scaling at onset, then show a bottleneck effect before small scale loss. Swirl and sound production stay stable in the miscible regime.
arxiv-2604-08814: M. Adriamirado and 42 colleagues propose GAPE, a genetic method for building deep learning tools for the PROSPECT reactor neutrino test at Oak Ridge. GAPE creates energy and place gauges and sorters for inverse beta decay signals from common backgrounds, and adapts to other particle physics machine learning problems. Tested against standard PROSPECT pathways on the same information, its sorter offers nearly 2.8 times better signal to background ratio, with period set training cutting time linked biases.
arxiv-2604-08914: Kerur and five colleagues present Nemo-Nemo, a working crash fault proof agreement system for wide area networks that bridges crash fault and hostile fault proof design. Command spread through a cause linked DAG lets all copies propose commands with self taming traffic. Multi leader design removes the single leader choke point, and splitting spread from agreement logic rides out stalled commits. Missed deadline bids are by rule delayed, never dropped, and DAG commits in just two network hops match older crash fault latency with far higher throughput.
arxiv-2605-00014:
Kelath Murali Manoj, Nagamani Sukumar, Taufia Hussain, Mahendra Kavdia, and Abhijith Anandakrishnan present the second part of a murburn-based account of how neurons produce electrical signals. The standard view rests on ions crossing the membrane. The murburn framework instead reads neuronal activity as redox-mediated electronic dynamics. This paper compares that reading with established models, sets out the lab evidence, and draws predictions from it.

The authors argue the model's strength is prediction without parameter fitting. Outputs such as conduction velocity, waveform shape, and threshold behavior are linked to redox kinetics, transport rates, and conditions like oxygen supply and solvent traits. They extend the picture to cardiac tissue, photoreceptors, and man-made redox materials. They also note that joining quantum-level electron transfer to large-scale signals like EEG remains future work.
arxiv-2605-00414:
Sai Niranjan Ramachandran and Suvrit Sra unify two model families that look nothing alike: decision trees, discrete and hierarchical, and diffusion models, continuous and dynamic. They establish a precise mathematical correspondence between hierarchical trees and diffusion processes in suitable limiting regimes. Underneath both, they find one shared optimization principle, which they call Global Trajectory Score Matching.

An idealized form of gradient boosting turns out to be asymptotically optimal for that principle, which ties a workhorse of tabular learning to the theory. Two practical offshoots follow. One generates tabular data with higher fidelity at half the computing cost of rivals. The other, a distillation method, transfers a tree's hierarchical decision logic into a neural network, landing within a whisker of the teacher's performance on many benchmarks. The paper's value is mainly conceptual: two literatures turn out to share a skeleton.
arxiv-2605-00714:
Christian Kranhold and 5 co-authors design mirrors for future gravitational-wave detectors that keep their reflectivity while shedding the coating noise that limits sensitivity. In detectors such as ET-Pathfinder, thermal noise in the thick dielectric coatings of test-mass mirrors dominates the band where signals live. Metasurface mirrors could thin the coating, but fabrication errors and rough line edges cap their reflectance in practice.

The hybrid design stacks a fabrication-tolerant one-layer metasurface on a spacer and a much reduced Bragg mirror. Full-wave simulations evaluate the optics, and a Monte Carlo analysis with realistic fabrication scatter, including edge smoothing from roughness, estimates yield. The bare metasurface reflects superbly when perfect, and about 99.9 percent at realistic yield. A Bragg support of only seven layer pairs covers the remaining transmission. The hybrid's thermal noise lands an order of magnitude below the project's coating budget.
arxiv-2605-01114:
Daniela Rodrigues and Laura A. Hatfield give a formal approach to variable selection in difference-in-differences studies, a common method for gauging policy effects. The method rests mainly on a same-trends assumption for control-group outcomes, often relaxed by assuming trends move together only within groups sharing measured values. Choosing which variables to include there is often ad hoc.

Using graphical criteria, the authors show parallel trends is rarely justified without conditioning, and unconditional and conditional versions can conflict. Even a time-invariant covariate with a stable effect can be a useful grouping variable. They extend the framework to multiple periods, treatment-confounder feedback, and estimation, arguing many difficulties stem from misalignment between the estimator's adjustment set and the set the method requires.
arxiv-2605-01314:
Shubhankar Paul and nine co-authors examine how tiny regions of metal and insulator form and grow inside vanadium dioxide as it switches between the two states. The team uses the material as a test case for systems where electron behavior and crystal structure change together.

They probe films with two kinds of grain size, made by two growth methods, using both large-scale tests and infrared imaging that maps the regions directly. Their reversal curve data show how supercooled metal patches interact with the solid around them, which shapes the lag between heating and cooling runs. The study links film growth, region interaction, and the birth of new regions into one measured picture.
arxiv-2605-01514:
Srivaths Ramasubramanian and seven co-authors built MANOJAVAM, a chip design that runs principal component analysis end to end on an FPGA. The method, a workhorse for shrinking data in fields from imaging to genomics, spends most of its cost on matrix multiplication and the singular value step.

Earlier chips cover only one of those stages, lean on high-level synthesis that limits tuning, or use fixed-point math that caps size. MANOJAVAM unifies both stages. A grid of systolic arrays streams matrix blocks for the multiply. A parallel Jacobi unit with pipelined rotation hardware handles the singular values, fed by a two-tier cache that adapts to each stage's access pattern. Built on two Xilinx boards, the large build cuts singular value time by over twentyfold against a high-end graphics card. It also slashes total energy, making the design fit both data centers and edge boxes.
arxiv-2605-01914:
Lu Gao, Zhe Han, and Yunshen Chen use deep learning to forecast how road pavement wears out over time. Wear depends on materials, weather, design, and factors that are hard to observe. Better forecasts help road agencies plan repairs and spread limited funds. The team draws on Texas data gathered over eighteen years, covering work history and road condition.

Their data holds twenty-one measures, such as cracking, rutting, raveling, and roughness, from more than one hundred thousand road sections. They test neural networks, including convolutional and long short-term memory models. Early results are promising, and in their case study the convolutional model beat standard machine learning methods at predicting condition values.
arxiv-2605-02014:
Sammy Sharief and colleagues introduce Mira, a score for checking how accurate a proposed conditional distribution is. Conditional models predict an outcome given inputs, and judging them normally needs hard evidence calculations. Mira uses only joint samples from the true process and the idea that two distributions match if they give the same mass to every region.

From that idea, the authors derive a closed form for the Mira statistic and its average score. When a candidate matches the truth, they can also compute reference values and uncertainty. Mira thus allows Bayesian model comparison by direct validation of the posterior, bypassing evidence. Tests on toy cases and inference tasks show the score works as intended.
arxiv-2605-02114:
Jakob Nogler and Virginia Vassilevska Williams relate two extensions of the replacement paths problem in graphs. The basic problem asks, for each edge on a route from a source to a target, the best detour when that edge fails. One extension frees the target and asks from one source to all vertices. The other keeps the target but allows two edge failures at once.

No reduction between those two extensions was known, and the two-failure version looked plausibly harder. In directed unweighted graphs a proven gap exists, while undirected cases share many algorithms. The paper's title states its main claim for undirected graphs: the dual-fault problem reduces to the single-source problem, linking their difficulty more tightly than expected.
arxiv-2605-02414:
Kentaro Kawato and Shosei Sakaguchi study how large a trial should be when the winner will be rolled out to everyone else. In a test-and-roll design, a decision maker tests on some units, then gives the rest the treatment that did better. A bigger trial improves the final choice, but it also leaves more trial units stuck with the weaker option for a time.

The pair argue that a standard worst-case regret rule can shrink trials too far. They propose a rule that weighs the worst-case gain from adding one more matched pair against its cost. For both simple yes-no outcomes and measured outcomes, the analysis points to a clear benchmark: the trial should cover about a third of the group. No prior belief about effects is needed.
arxiv-2605-02814:
Axi Niu, Jinyang Zhang, and Senyan Qing present IConFace, a face restoration method that uses other photos of the same person to keep identity details. Heavy damage can erase the very traits that make a face that person. A generative model may return a sharp, plausible face that is subtly someone else, since the target alone no longer decides the answer.

Up to three same-identity references can guide the repair. A hybrid backbone keeps damaged and reference images as dense visual tokens, preserving local evidence, while an identity path adds compact guidance and a structure path reinforces the target's layout. A human-audited benchmark checks whether lasting local identity traits survive. With references, the method led on compatibility; without them, it led on learned quality scores.
arxiv-2605-03014:
Stephen E. Henrich, Yann Mambrini, and Keith A. Olive assess whether current detectors can catch a class of dark matter candidates that decoupled from the early universe while still moving near light speed. Such ultrarelativistic freeze-out is generic for heavy portal interactions with strong coupling and low reheating temperatures. The candidates are cold today, but their production story differs from the standard freeze-out picture, and so do their detection prospects.

Using a portal model with a heavy mediator as the test case, the authors find leading underground experiments have already excluded much of the candidate space. Viable room remains above the neutrino fog across a wide mass range. A next-generation detector due to start taking data soon should reach deep into the lighter mass band. For heavy portals, these candidates are often easier to detect than freeze-in rivals.
arxiv-2605-03314:
Jiaqi Wei, Xuehang Guo, Pengfei Yu, Xiang Zhang, Wanli Ouyang, Siqi Sun, Qingyun Wang, and Chenyu You address a timing problem in streamed reasoning. When should a model speak while it is still thinking? In a single token stream, early output commits the model in public. Yet waiting delays the first useful content.

Their Side-by-Side method mixes partial disclosures with continued private reasoning. It releases only content the reasoning so far supports. Training pairs answer prefixes with their supporting reasoning steps. Reinforcement learning then restores full reasoning strength. On math and science benchmarks, across two model scales, the trade-off between accuracy and waiting time improved.
arxiv-2605-03414:
Brielen Madureira, Mariana Madruga de Brito, and Andreas Niekler compare three ready-made entity recognition tools for finding place names in German news about extreme climate events. Location extraction feeds climate impact research, but tool choice can quietly steer which countries a study concludes were covered.

Flair, spaCy, and Stanza produced notably different toponym pools on the same articles. Those contrasts flowed into three country-assignment methods and yielded distinct calls on each document's geographic focus. The study warns that off-the-shelf tool selection is itself a research decision with downstream effects on media prominence findings.
arxiv-2605-04014:
Muhammad Naeem Anwar and Timothy J. Burns use recent CMS measurements of the exotic X states at the Large Hadron Collider to predict a missing partner particle. The X(6600), X(6900), and X(7100) appear to be tetraquarks made of two charm quarks and two charm antiquarks. The measured quantum numbers of the X(6600) match the authors' earlier prediction and imply a lighter scalar partner, the X(6400), decaying to pairs of J/psi mesons.

Indications of such a state may already sit in CMS fits, which include a peak near that mass. Anwar and Burns give predictions for the masses and decay properties of the scalar and other partner states. The predictions are framed as experimental tests. They can discriminate between quark and diquark models of these first exclusively heavy tetraquarks.
arxiv-2605-04414:
Luke Levine and five co-authors study uniform mixing in continuous-time quantum walks, where a walker spread over a graph should reach an equal probability at every vertex at some moment. A classic result says complete graphs almost never achieve this, apart from the smallest few.

By allowing the graph's edges to carry phases, a freedom called signing, the authors show some signed complete graph does mix uniformly. Their proof uses a stopping rule that reduces the global question to a local one. As a bonus, they find an orientation of a Hamming graph that mixes faster than any previously known, and families of directed rings with average uniform mixing.
arxiv-2605-04614:
Ben Lowe, Fernando C. Marques, and André Neves count minimal Lagrangian surfaces, special area-minimising surfaces inside products of hyperbolic surfaces, organised by their genus and area. Counting such surfaces with a precise growth rate is a way to probe the geometry of the ambient space.

For genus above one, they count these surfaces by area. The number with area at most a given bound grows like a specific power of that bound. The leading constant is explicit. It is built from a function introduced by Mirzakhani. Similar results hold for products of nonpositively curved surfaces and for a higher-genus surface times a circle. They also prove the Lagrangian area spectrum is rigid.
arxiv-2605-05214:
ZhengXiao He and six co-authors adapt the Mamba sequence architecture for classifying medical time series such as heart and brain signals. These signals mix long-range timing patterns with structured links between channels, which convolutional and recurrent models handle poorly and transformers handle at quadratic cost. Their MedMamba design follows three principles drawn from how body signals behave.

A lightweight channel-mixing module handles cross-channel structure, multi-scale convolutional tokenisation splits timing patterns by scale, and bidirectional Mamba blocks gather global context at linear cost. Across six benchmark datasets covering brain signals, heart signals, and human activity, MedMamba consistently outperformed leading methods, the authors report. The design shows how signal-specific principles can guide architecture choice.
arxiv-2605-05614:
Powerful lasers blasting solid targets create tangled electromagnetic fields that can drain energy and distort implosions. J. Peebles and four co-authors measured those filamentary fields with proton radiography at the OMEGA EP laser facility. Earlier shots of spherical implosions had shown odd field structures spread through the corona, the hot cloud around the target.

In simpler flat-target experiments, the team varied material, target size, pulse shape, and intensity. Field growth turned out to be dominated by laser energy and the target's atomic number. The data support a secondary instability, growing from the expansion-driven Weibel instability, as the main driver.
arxiv-2605-06014:
Ran Ben-Basat and four co-authors prove that a fast heuristic used in quantization is nearly as good as true random rotation. Randomized Hadamard transforms replace costly random rotations in tasks such as model compression and nearest neighbor search. One such transform can fail on worst case inputs, leaving coordinate values far from the desired Gaussian shape.

The authors show that composing two transforms brings every coordinate's distribution close to Gaussian, within a bound that shrinks as dimension grows. Plugged into modern compression schemes, two transforms match the rotation based performance. Three transforms also tame correlations across coordinates, which vector quantization needs. A quick moment check on each input lets systems adapt the number of transforms at runtime.
arxiv-2605-06314:
Ye Su, Jian Li, and Yong Liu ask when l2-boosting overfits benignly in high dimensions. Benign overfitting, where a model fits noise yet still predicts well, is understood in l2 geometry, but greedy ensembles carry an l1 style implicit bias that breaks standard spectral tools. The coupling between coordinate selection thresholds is nonlinear, so the authors isolate that algorithmic bias through exact risk asymptotics for continuous time boosting over many features.

Under a pure noise model they prove benign overfitting fails at the linear rate here. Greedy selection concentrates noise into sparse active sets, and excess variance decays only logarithmically. Spiked designs show the same slow rate before risk can vanish. Studying the boosting flow's subdifferential dynamics yields a tuning free early stopping rule that recovers optimal prediction rates for bounded signals.
arxiv-2605-06514:
Reiley Dorrian, Mizuki Ohno, Elena Williams, Adrian Llanos, and Joseph Falson analyze superconductivity in thin films of a lanthanum-bismuth compound under parallel magnetic fields. Such tests are often used to infer the nature of the superconducting state. Several pair-breaking effects can suppress superconductivity at once, yet studies often miss some of them.

Using a multi-mechanism framework, the team studies how the response changes with film thickness and resolves field-enhanced superconductivity in the thin limit. That lets them estimate the role of spin exchange scattering alongside paramagnetic and orbital effects. Their reading also reshapes how critical temperature, the Pauli limit, and scattering times in two-dimensional superconductors should be read.
arxiv-2605-06714:
Yiwen Xu, Tariq M. Khan, Yang Song, and Erik Meijering survey edge deep learning, where neural networks run on devices near the data instead of distant servers. Running models at the edge enables real-time decisions shaped by local conditions. Their review centers on computer vision, with particular attention to medical diagnostics, where fast on-site analysis can change care.

The authors explain foundational principles, sort edge hardware into a new categorization by performance and usage scenario, and cover deployment techniques such as lightweight design and model compression. Practical applications show the impact of edge models in real settings. The survey closes with future directions and adoption obstacles, serving as a reference for researchers and practitioners.
arxiv-2605-06814:
Debolina Halder Lina and Arlei Silva introduce model-to-data distillation, which moves what a complex graph neural network learned into the graph itself. Desirable traits like accuracy, fairness, and robustness usually stay locked inside the sophisticated model that learned them, limiting transfer to simpler models. Their method instead jointly learns augmented node features and graph structure that encode the teacher's behavior.

The enriched graph becomes a lasting transfer medium: simple networks trained on it normally recover much of the teacher's behavior. Experiments cover fairness-aware networks, attention networks, and graph transformers as teachers, with student models keeping comparable predictive performance while inheriting teacher traits. The paradigm trades model complexity for data complexity.
arxiv-2605-07214:
Yuping Yan and four co-authors let a team of language-model agents design solution methods for hard optimization problems. Earlier model-based heuristic design used rigid single workflows that converged too early and explored poorly. HMACE instead splits each generation among four specialized agents that propose, generate, evaluate, and reflect.

Behavior-aware retrieval, light filtering, and a fitness-based archive keep the search diverse and avoid wasted evaluations. Across traveling salesman, packing, and scheduling problems, the framework achieved a strong quality-to-cost balance against single-agent and multi-agent rivals. On two tasks it posted the lowest average gaps while spending far fewer tokens than baselines.
arxiv-2605-07414:
Chen and five colleagues expose a safety gap in image agents that plan and run chains of tools to build or edit pictures. Each step alone can look harmless, yet the combined chain can produce an unsafe result, which leaves prompt only jailbreak defenses short. Their target is tool calling text to image agents, where a planner splits a request into tool steps.

The team presents OrchJail, a fuzzing framework guided by orchestration, meaning it learns from successful jailbreak tool traces and their links to prompt wording. It steers the search toward prompts that tend to set off unsafe multi step tool behaviour, instead of surface level word changes. Across representative tool calling image agents, OrchJail raises attack success rates, improves image fidelity, and lowers query costs. It also stays robust against common jailbreak defenses. The work frames tool orchestration as a critical attack surface that earlier work missed.
arxiv-2605-07514:
Bo-Kai Ruan and three co-authors diagnose world action models by asking whether their imagined futures actually fit the actions they claim to follow. Such models plan by predicting future observations and actions together, but a future can look plausible while being dynamically wrong. The authors name that alignment action-state consistency and study it across model types.

Consistency separates successful from failed rollouts across many tasks and tracks learned value estimates closely. One boundary case misleads: static failed futures can look deceptively consistent. A test-time strategy ranking rollouts by agreement among predicted futures improved success on two robot benchmarks, with no extra training or reward modeling.
arxiv-2605-07714:
Prajwal Pisal and two co-authors screen alloy nanocatalysts for converting carbon dioxide with hydrogen, using adsorption energy distributions as the guiding descriptor. These profiles capture the many distinct binding sites on a nanoparticle's facets, but earlier screens could not resolve activity, product selectivity, and stability facet by facet at the same time.

They extend the framework to single crystal facets, combining facet profiles with facet abundances and a plain-language analysis of product choice among one-carbon products. Machine-learned force fields computed adsorption energies for about one point four million setups across thousands of surfaces and hundreds of metals and alloys. The analysis found composition-facet combinations whose adsorption patterns point to methanol, methane, formic acid, or carbon monoxide, ready for lab testing.
arxiv-2605-07914:
Aristotelis Ballas and Christos Diou argue that two popular routes to better generalization each fix only half the geometry.
