Sharpness-aware methods seek flat minima; gradient-alignment methods make gradients agree across data distributions. For learning across multiple distributions, the authors derive an excess-risk decomposition with two leading terms, one governed by alignment and one by curvature.

The average Hessian enters one term inverted and the other directly, and a counterexample shows neither term bounds the other, so optimizing only one cannot guarantee low risk. Their SAGE method therefore probes curvature with the polar factor of each layer's gradient and injects descent noise scaled by cross-distribution disagreement. On domain-generalization and multi-task benchmarks it set a new state of the art on DomainBed and improved base solvers.
arxiv-2605-08114:
Paolo D'Alberto studies how to shrink the key-value cache of a language model. The goal is to save memory without wrecking its answers. Three schemes are compared under the same bit budget. One is a plain scalar baseline. One treats keys and values in unlike ways. One applies the full transform pipeline to both.

D'Alberto starts from the geometry of vectors on a sphere. He traces how a projection step on keys inflates inner-product variance. The softmax then amplifies that growth. In tests, the mixed scheme wins at the most common budget on every measure. Treating keys like values is worse at all budgets. A crossover in key error at other budgets adds nuance.
arxiv-2605-08214:
Mohammed Aman Bhuiyan and colleagues build speech tools for Bangla, a language where recognition and speaker diarization still lag. Long recordings, varied acoustics, and wide speaker differences make both tasks hard, and off-the-shelf models are tuned for other languages.

For recognition, the team fine-tunes a regional Whisper model on about fifteen thousand curated Bangla segments, with heavy augmentation including noise, reverb, echo, clipping, and pitch and time changes. For diarization, they fine-tune the pyannote segmentation model and swap it into the community pipeline. The paired systems target practical long-form Bangla transcription that also says who spoke when.
arxiv-2605-08314:
Wenhao Wu, Zishan Shao, Kangning Cui, Jinhee Kim, and coauthors make low-rank transformers serve faster in practice. Cutting a model down with singular value decomposition shrinks its size on paper. In production, the factorized weights fragment execution. The overhead also differs between the prompt phase and token-by-token decoding.

FlashSVD maps several public compression families into one factorized format. It serves them with phase-specific kernels. It adds dense key-value decoding and packed MLP execution. It also replays per-layer CUDA graphs. In serving tests, decoding ran up to about two and a half times faster. Average gains were solid across families. Compression pays only when the runtime is rebuilt around it.
arxiv-2605-08414:
Pedro Julián-Salgado, Pavel Castro-Villarreal, Leonardo Dagdug, and Denis Boyer study a diffusing particle that keeps teleporting back, now on a ring instead of an open line. Resetting models appear across natural science, and the key design question is the rate that minimizes the mean time to find a target. Bounded domains with several possible reset sites were largely open.

The authors place an absorbing target on a circular track and let the particle reset to multiple sites drawn from an arbitrary distribution. Using the ring's propagator, they compute the Laplace transform of the survival probability and the mean first-passage time. The results support a mirror transition picture of how optimal resetting changes on closed tracks.
arxiv-2605-08614:
Devin Yasith De Silva and eleven coauthors benchmark language models on turning factory sensor rules into maintenance advice. Engineers write symbolic rules that fire on sensor conditions, but choosing the right fix takes years of asset specific practice. Their DiagnosticIQ test holds thousands of expert checked questions built from real rule and action pairs across many asset types.

Five variants probe failure modes from harder distractors to flipped conditions. Practitioners average well under half correct, confirming deep specialist demand. Top models cluster tightly, yet all crack under harder distractors, and many repeat the original answer even when conditions invert. Industrial AI learns the bottleneck is calibration under change, not raw detection skill.
arxiv-2605-08714: Gopikrishnan Chirappurathu Remesan studies a class of time based equations with spread terms of two space orders and a cubic term. The edge values are fixed at zero. With a Galerkin scheme and tight bounds, he proves weak answers to the class exist and are the sole ones for smooth starts. A finer pass then proves the same for rough starts. Both space orders are dealt with at once. The result gives a firmer base for models where strong smoothing and fast growth clash.
arxiv-2605-08814:
Wei Cao, Hao Xu, and Xiaolei Diao recognize Chinese characters the system has never seen in training, a constant need given the huge character set. Retrieval methods that match a whole character picture against its structural description in one vector often miss fine component differences, while detailed patch matching is noisy and slow over all candidates. Their network learns global and local views of both picture and description together.

A filtering mask mutes structural symbols with no visual form, and a two stage search recalls candidates globally, then reranks only the top few locally before fusing scores. Results stay competitive across splits, shine with little training data, and cut large scale search cost sharply.
arxiv-2605-09114:
Rob Landers and Kaben Kramer build a formal framework for consistency in distributed systems, where machines pass messages and each observer sees only part of a growing record of causes. Their 2026 paper models each observer with two linked tools. A closure filter fixes which past events it must have seen. An ordering rule sorts forks that run side by side.

Inside the framework, the authors derive a clear order. It tells when one setup can honestly read another setup's data. They show that a lost consistency level never returns during migration. They also show that spotting a reversed order needs the very record that could have stopped it. Known models appear as points in this space, and new unnamed setups are predicted too.
arxiv-2605-09214:
Zhao and three colleagues give the first fast rates for forward KL regularised offline contextual bandits, where prior analyses were inapplicable or slow. Reverse KL regularisation already enjoys epsilon inverse type fast rates, unlike standard epsilon inverse squared sample complexity, while forward KL lagged. Their streamlined analysis delivers tilde O epsilon inverse upper bounds for tabular and general function approximation settings, under single policy concentrability.

A convex analytical pipeline covers both settings through a fresh use of the pessimism principle, fully sidestepping older proof routines built on the mean value theorem. The team also provides rate optimal lower bounds, showing the upper bounds tight in statistical rates. Lower bounds also show forward KL sample complexity recovers the unregularised slow rate when regularisation is low, similarly to reverse KL. The work closes a gap between forward and reverse KL theory, and its convex route may prove useful beyond bandits.
arxiv-2605-09314:
Sun and four colleagues trace how persuasive context makes language models abandon facts they know, a safety flaw whose inner workings were poorly understood. A handful of mid-layer attention heads almost entirely decides the model's answer, placing answer options at distinct vertices of a low-dimensional polyhedron.

Persuasion does not blur belief or merely lower confidence; it triggers a discrete latent jump from the correct vertex to the persuasion target vertex. The decision heads do not weigh evidence; they copy the option token their attention lands on, so persuasion works by redirecting attention. The team isolates a rank-one evidence-routing feature: editing it steers the model's choice, and removing it blocks persuasion. Shallower attention heads build that feature from persuasive keywords in the input, with every step checked by intervention, in open-source models and realistic poisoning cases like Generative Engine Optimisation.
arxiv-2605-09414:
Mahrous and a colleague examine whether emojis carry sentiment signals that travel across languages, platforms, and asset communities in online financial communication, where their stability is unclear. From big Twitter and StockTwits collections in four languages, they measure cross-community divergence. They test sentiment models trained on emoji-only, text-only, and text-plus-emoji inputs.

Emoji frequencies vary by community, most of all by language, but their semantics and sentiment polarity stay largely stable. Cross-asset transfer shows minimal degradation while cross-language transfer stays the hardest, and adding emojis consistently shrinks transfer gaps against text-only models. Financial communication thus shows a partially shared emoji code, and emojis offer compact sentiment cues that work across languages and improve model generalisation across markets and platforms.
arxiv-2605-09514:
Bozkurt and five colleagues tackled causal inference when a hidden confounder distorts observational data. Proxy causal learning sidesteps the hidden factor with bridge equations built from treatment- and outcome-related proxies. Earlier doubly robust proxy methods leaned on fixed kernels or simple models, while flexible neural methods usually used only one bridge.

The new framework learns both bridges with neural networks, including a neural mean-embedding estimator for the treatment bridge, plus a doubly robust correction from a final regression stage. It handles continuous and structured treatments and returns full response curves, not just binary effects. The authors prove consistency and show wins over baselines and single-bridge neural methods on synthetic and image-valued benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-09814:
Liu and three colleagues found a sharp separation in streaming space complexity for Maximum Cut when the algorithm must output an approximate cut, not just its value. For dense graphs, O(n/ε²) space suffices and Ω(n) space is necessary. For graphs with Θ(n/ε²) edges, the picture changes markedly: the problem needs Ω(n log(ε²n)/ε²) space for any ε growing faster than 1/√n, and that bound is tight across the full ε range.

The authors also gave an Ω(n log n/ε²) space lower bound against deterministic algorithms for outputting a (1−ε) approximation to the maximum cut value. Similar techniques yielded an analogous separation for Densest Subgraph. For every constant-arity constraint problem over a constant-size alphabet, plus the Similarity problem, dense-stream space improves by shaving a logarithmic factor.
arxiv-2605-10014:
Monteiro and three colleagues built Elemental Alchemist, a generative tool for meaning-based control of particle systems across levels of detail. Editing particle visual effects matters for digital stories, but results artists can steer remain hard to reach. Users must find the settings that match their own goals. That task needs a clear grasp of the system and how settings map to high-level intents, such as making a fire look angry.

The system has two parts. A scene-based brush palette makes tools based on scene context. A generative panel shows key low-level settings and turns them into mid-level meaning traits and high-level idea-level controls. A test with 10 novice and 5 expert VFX artists showed the system helped users reach their intents.
arxiv-2605-10614:
Riya Tapwal and two colleagues stop secret leakage in multi-agent pipelines. Such systems introduce a risk: secrets accessed by one agent can spread through shared context and reappear later, even without adversarial intent. They call this propagation amplification, where leakage risk grows across agent boundaries as content reaches later generators. Their 2026 paper proposes Prism.

Prism is a defence treating credential leakage as a growing risk during generation. At each step, it combines 16 signals spanning lexical, structural, information, and contextual features into a risk score. That enables per-token action in zones. Credential reproduction is often preceded by a shift in dynamics, marked by entropy collapse and rising logit concentration. Across a 2,000-task benchmark covering 13 attack types and three pressures, Prism achieves an F1 of 0.832, precision 1.000, and recall 0.712. It shows zero leakage and a utility score of 0.893 on the same benchmark.
arxiv-2605-10714:
Fred Philippy and co-authors gather prior research and data sets on Luxembourgish to argue that low-resource language tech needs more than cross-lingual transfer. Cross-lingual transfer, using high-resource guidance through many-tongue models, has become central to spreading language tech to low-resource languages, often achieving strong scores with little tagged target-language data.

Across findings, the authors observe a deep link between transfer and language-only efforts. Transfer can greatly improve target-language scores, but its success depends deeply on high-quality, task-aligned target-language data. Such resources in low-resource settings are often too limited alone to drive strong scores, yet reach their full potential only within a cross-lingual framework. Transfer and language-only development should therefore be treated as paired parts of a lasting low-resource pipeline, and the paper offers practical guidelines for joining and weighting them.
arxiv-2605-10814:
Anuk Dayaprema and Alex Waldron prove a sharp convergence theorem for Yang-Mills flow on a family of noncompact spaces called ALE gravitational instantons. Yang-Mills flow smooths a connection on a bundle downhill along its energy, much as heat flow smooths temperature, and it sits at the heart of modern geometry.

Their result extends a parabolic gap theorem the pair had proved over the four-sphere, now covering spaces that stretch to infinity while staying locally hyperKähler. In plain terms, low-energy starting connections must settle into instantons, the energy-minimizing self-dual or anti-self-dual shapes. Geometers gain a noncompact gap theorem with the sharp edge the compact case already enjoyed.
arxiv-2605-10914:
Alin Morariu, Chris Jewell, and Jess Bridgen introduce gemlib.mcmc, a library for Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampling that makes hard Bayesian inference composable. State-transition models drive epidemic and ecology work, but inference over large latent states with tangled likelihoods stays hard.

The library lets developers chain special kernels with Python's right-shift operator. Each new kernel needs only two methods, while chaining and hardware speedups run on their own. Demos on partly observed epidemic models show long inference routines collapsing into short, reusable code. Modelers get the flexibility of hand-built samplers without the usual implementation burden.
arxiv-2605-11014:
Yadang Alexis Rouzoumka and five colleagues make diffusion-based out-of-distribution detection fairly comparable across backbones. Conclusions about such detectors shift with backbone choice, corruption settings, and test-time budget, muddying which method truly wins.

Their shared backbone-equated protocol aligns standard corruption levels and logical test-time cost across diffusion backbones. Within it, Canonical Feature Snapshots detectors probe a frozen backbone with only a few native internal activations at low-noise levels. On a controlled CIFAR-scale test, the strongest one-forward variant leads, and even a tiny decoder-only variant stays competitive. The signal, it turns out, concentrates in sparse internal states rather than full denoising runs. OOD researchers get fair comparisons and a lean detector family.
arxiv-2605-11214:
Noah Trupin and Yexiang Xue frame constraint enforcement in generative sampling as a correction scheduling problem. Hard constraints are usually imposed by projection, once at the end or after every update. But this changes the distribution of states that future updates depend on. So delayed projection can yield samples that are feasible yet inconsistent with planned sampling dynamics.

Taking one-step constraint defect as a local sign of geometric mismatch, the team offers adaptive scheduling. This state-based policy gives budget to steps that most strongly perturb the trajectory. End and stepwise forms arise as limiting cases. Across rollouts on set manifolds and a learned projected diffusion sampler, the adaptive route wins back seventy-one point two percent of full stepwise benefit with 75 percent fewer fixes. Model builders get constraint timing as a first-class design variable.
arxiv-2605-11414: Udayangani and two colleagues propose Generative Diffusion Prior Distillation for classifying partial time series, where inputs are cut short by latency and cost. Full-sequence teachers can overwhelm short-context students, since their full-context features are too strong a target. Their framework treats student features as degraded views of full-context features, learns a diffusion prior over teacher features, and samples target representations that best explain the missing long-range information. Tests across earliness settings, datasets and architectures show it closes the full-to-partial gap.
arxiv-2605-11614: Huang and Hooker show standard fairness testing for pricing is invalid. Pricing systems set auto insurance, credit and lending rates, and regulators demand proof of no bias. The audit fits pricing on protected traits and valid factors, then tests with least squares errors. But pricing algorithms are fixed. Residuals reflect fit error, not sampling noise, making old errors invalid. Among rates from 34 Illinois car insurers, every one fails group parity. Minority areas pay 34 to 158 dollars more yearly than matched white zip codes.
arxiv-2605-11814: Yihao Wang and twelve colleagues build a 2026 benchmark for memory in personalized healthcare agents, a high-stakes setting where past benchmarks only covered everyday chat. MedMemoryBench synthesizes long, clinically grounded patient journeys through a human-agent pipeline, yielding about 2,000 sessions and 16,000 turns validated by experts. Its streaming protocol tests memory while cases are still being built, and mainstream architectures showed severe bottlenecks, above all in medical reasoning and noise resilience.
arxiv-2605-11914: Madona Mekhael and four colleagues tune nonlinear metasurfaces after they are made by turning one against another. They use the Pancharatnam-Berry phase for nonlinear C3v-symmetric plasmonic surfaces inside a multipass cell. They shifted second-harmonic peaks smoothly across a 900 to 970 nanometer pump range. A full tuning cycle took 120 degrees of turn, showing these geometric-phase surfaces form a tunable nonlinear platform.
arxiv-2605-13014: Lin, Wang and You study Connes spectral distances between quantum states under unitary transformations, working with spectral triples built from matrix algebras on finite-dimensional spaces. They prove some finite spectral triples have Lipschitz seminorms equal to operator norms. They also construct triples where Connes distances equal quantum trace distances exactly. These concrete examples clarify links among Connes distance, trace distance and other quantum distance measures, and illuminate the geometry of finite spectral triples.
arxiv-2605-13114: Fang, Zhang, Shang and Ma ask whether AI data centres, which vent continuous low-grade waste heat, can double as carbon removal engines. They model a heat-pump-upgraded direct air capture system integrated with data centres and assess it region by region across the United States. Waste heat substantially improves net removal and lowers capture cost; in carbon-intensive regions integration flips capture from net-positive to net-negative emissions. Under a 2030 scenario with more GPU-heavy centres and cleaner grids, several states remove more than they emit.
arxiv-2605-13514: Erik Solhaug and twenty-two colleagues report COOLJ1153+0755, a rare duo of quasars each lensed by one massive galaxy cluster. Found in DECaLS imaging and confirmed with Magellan telescopes, the system shows two quasars each split into four images by one cluster. One is a classic Type I quasar at redshift 1.524, the other a dust-obscured Type II quasar at redshift 1.939. A lens model gives a cluster mass near 3.3 times ten to the fourteenth solar masses, lifting the known sample from seven to eight systems.
arxiv-2605-13614: The CMS Collaboration performs the first dedicated hunt for pair production of new scalars from the Inert Doublet Model, using proton-proton collisions. The model predicts four extra scalar bosons, and the lightest, H, is stable and a viable dark matter candidate. The target final state has exactly two opposite-charge same-flavour leptons with missing transverse momentum and little hadronic activity. No significant excess appears, and exclusion limits at 95 percent confidence cover H masses up to 108 GeV for a mass split of 78 GeV.
arxiv-2605-13914: Kolhatkar and Sahoo prove a trade-off in a type of changed gravity, where a background-inert coupling in coincident f(Q) gravity swaps against the clustering strength. The swap stems from a deeper trade-off between the first amplitude and the growth factor today. They set out a check that works out the first amplitude for each posterior draw, so it matches the clustering strength the sampler favors. Two data lines test the idea across standard and hybrid models.
arxiv-2605-14014: Kimura and eight co-authors offer Dywave, a live token scheme for mixed Internet-of-Things sensor signals. Such signals shift over time and span many scales, which trips up fixed token rules. Dywave splits signals with wavelet layers, marks time edges that match real physical events, and squeezes dull stretches while keeping time order intact. Tests on five real-world sensor sets gauge how well the scheme works.
arxiv-2605-14414: Hamai and Wakabayashi present a non-variational method for maximally localised Wannier functions. Their method unifies gauge smoothing and the position operator problem into one fixed system. Discrete adiabatic transport across degeneracies emerges as part of solving for vectors. In this gauge, Bloch overlaps show linear phase dependence, letting Wannier centres be found by fixed-point steps. The approach finds the origin of mesh-dependent spread scaling in graphene, an effect of non-commuting operators forcing defects along a seam.
arxiv-2605-14714: Kim, Dong and Xie propose planner-initiated siting for AI data centres, whose energy demand is outrunning grid interconnection and transmission expansion. Current processes react only after projects join a multi-year queue. Their framework screens sites with reliability gates, assesses market impact under firm, pause and shift flexibility envelopes, and ranks sites by entropy-weighted multi-criteria scoring. On a synthetic two-thousand-bus Texas system, flexibility is claimed to widen the siting frontier by up to about one fifth.
arxiv-2605-14814: Zhang and Lei develop a global Hamiltonian model for spin-orbit coupling networks in ellipsoid-ellipsoid binary asteroid systems. Single-resonance methods fail where multiple modes coexist and interact. Elliptic series of the coupling model allow numerical building of full networks. In a typical synchronous region, the authors map dynamical edges of different modes. The region covers synchronous spin-orbit, spin-spin, and spin-orbit-spin resonances, plus doubly synchronous ones. A secondary resonance from strong coupling between the primary and secondary asteroids is found.
arxiv-2605-15314: Antesh Upadhyay, Arda Fazla, and Abolfazl Hashemi study nonconvex stochastic optimization when gradient noise grows with distance from the starting point, the Blum-Gladyshev model. They prove that normalized gradient descent with momentum converges with a single gradient sample per step, and that a variance-reduced variant reaches the best possible rate under mean-square smoothness. The guarantees cover both standard smoothness and a generalized form where curvature scales with gradient size.
arxiv-2605-15714: Sunil Kothari and ten colleagues press for early checks in annotation pipelines over late validation. Data quality caps model gains, yet work fixates on methods, not timing. Software lore shows late defects cost 4 to 100 times more. The team sorts triggers into pre-annotation, post-annotation, and post-review. An error-propagation model pins down when timing shifts rates versus only costs. A survey of 47 papers finds only 4 percent report validation timing. The team urges reporting QA timing and running timing experiments.
arxiv-2605-16014: Xiao and six colleagues review a decade of work on how lasers influence atomic nuclei. Topics include laser-driven excitation, assisted radioactive decay, and precise control of nuclear isomers for optical clocks. The survey covers theory, such as time-dependent Schrödinger treatments of alpha and proton emission. Experiments highlighted include excitations of thorium-229, krypton-83, and scandium-45.
arxiv-2605-16314: Puddu presents a phase-based view of special relativity, building its motion rules from phase sync of local wave states. If travel follows sheets of constant phase and matter carries a built-in rest-frame swing, he derives time dilation, energy, and momentum from fixed phase buildup along paths. Proper time becomes the phase count of an internal clock, and the Minkowski gap emerges as the square form that fits phase rules across observers. Mass relates to rest-frame rate, joining motion rules with wave motion without new laws.
arxiv-2605-16514: Migacev and three others apply AICON, a reactive robot framework, to the Tower of London test for Parkinson's and stroke planning. Without advance planning or human cognition knowledge, AICON reproduces difficulty ordering across 24 problems better than structural parameters, generalizing to held-out problems. AICON outperforms a planning baseline for reduced-capacity groups, better capturing healthy controls. AICON's paper predicted this dissociation: its failure modes resemble Parkinson's patients struggling with goal hierarchies, not move counts. The finding suggests that as planning capacity falls, human behavior shifts toward AICON's reactive mode.
arxiv-2605-16614: Dutta and Tushar introduce Magic Secret Sharing, a quantum scheme in which the secret is computing power itself rather than a classical message. A shared entangled state and one local phase gate spread the resource so no single party gains any non-Clifford advantage alone. The full group can rebuild it and run a logical T gate. A test on a 156-qubit IBM machine confirms the security bound and high fidelity for the authorized party.
arxiv-2605-16714: Huang and colleagues present GRID, an end-to-end framework for building security knowledge graphs from long cyber threat-intelligence reports. It creates traceable article-graph alignments, then turns document-to-graph learning into a scripted task bank of multi-select questions with triple-level matching targets, giving steadier rewards than judging full graphs with a language model. On 249 articles, the task-bank model reaches 84.62% precision, 64.91% recall, and 68.53% F1, with lower token use and deployment cost than rivals.
arxiv-2605-16814: Guberman, Coughlin and Joglekar find how much speed-space detail kinetic runs need for linear and nonlinear Landau damping in the 1D Vlasov-Poisson system. Using a unified cascade-balance logic, they derive scalings for key Fourier and Hermite mode numbers under collisional diffusion. The scalings depend on bounce frequency, wave number times Debye length, and e-e collision rate. Checks against 800 Vlasov-Fokker-Planck runs show strong match with the forecast bounce-frequency and collision-rate links.
arxiv-2605-16914: Constantin and colleagues compare beam deposits of conserved amounts in two initial models for collisions: string SMASH and saturation McDipper. SMASH works at low energies as a hybrid initial condition, while McDipper, based on the color-glass condensate, works in perturbative QCD. Both yield longitudinally resolved initial states for 3D simulations. The goal: interface their ranges and study initial-state dynamics at middle energy. Tracking energy, charge, and baryon number from 62.4 GeV to 5.02 TeV, they find agreement at lower energies but changed energy and baryon deposits at higher energies.
arxiv-2605-17314: Deng tests whether wrong drafts from a smaller, domain-trained model can unlock skill in a stronger learner that standard on-policy training misses. Injecting mismatched wrong drafts into a Mathstral-7B learner's training beats matched-wrong and no-draft variants on reserved MATH-500 and out-of-distribution AIME tests. The recipe, trained on one graphics card with no extra tuning stages, reaches about 72 percent on MATH-500, the best published mark for that model.
arxiv-2605-17614: Jingsen Feng and Xu Chu formulate a tensorial Taylor-Aris theory for rods in tube flow. Classical theory treats mixing as scalar, while tube flow adds varying shear. Solving the orientation problem closes a transport equation whose reduction shows how each diffusion-tensor part enters the one-dimensional limit. Streamwise alignment cuts radial diffusivity and amplifies cell response, raising the Taylor coefficient by about 23 percent at aspect ratio 1000 and about 30 percent if slender. Simulations validate the coefficients, and the operator yields a spectral model of finite-time relaxation.
arxiv-2605-17914: Tianchi Li and colleagues give language models feedback on their own reasoning for loop invariants. For a failed check, the model sets out its reasoning in plain steps, which become first-order logic claims a checker can test alone. A faulty implication locates the precise reasoning error, steering the next fix. LORIS solves 445 of 460 main-benchmark C programs at a 93.1% rate.
arxiv-2605-18014: Endalamaw Ewnu Kassa and four colleagues present a spectrometer built from a single germanium PN photodiode. The system exploits chromatic dispersion, where uptake depth gives carrier delays coding spectra as RF amplitude and phase signs. The team extracts DC voltage, RF amplitude, and RF phase across 15 modulation rates, forming a 31-feature vector. Five models solve reconstruction, with wave-group splitting and cross-validation to prevent leakage. Single-line reconstruction using Gaussian regression achieves 0.178 nm accuracy, with cross-validation error of 0.342 nm.
arxiv-2605-18314: Jiazhen Lei's 2026 paper presents Janus, a hybrid active-passive radio built for agile ambient Internet of Things networking. Batteryless networking needs a nimble physical layer, but testbeds suffer split radio paths, high idle power, and clumsy controls. Janus unifies passive and active transmission in one front end, with parameters abstracting physical-layer behaviour into concise controls. A system control plane handles mode switches while an energy plane manages harvesting across sources. A compact prototype matches dedicated radios on 3GPP, Wi-Fi AMP, and Bluetooth landscapes with less configuration overhead.
arxiv-2605-18414: Rohith Uppala shows in a 2026 paper that prompt instructions alone cannot secure tool access for language-model agents. When unauthorized tools stay visible in context, models pick them in 48 to 68 percent of adversarial scenarios. Role-escalation attacks reach 96 percent unauthorized invocation. Per-tool allowlists cut violations to as low as 4.0 percent but never to zero. His fix is a proxy-enforced attribute-based access control layer for MCP that filters tool registries at discovery time, giving 0 percent unauthorized invocation by design.
arxiv-2605-18714: Songsong Yu and three co-authors present, in a 2026 study, generative post-training for unified multimodal models. Current training splits understanding and generation: sparse text versus dense pixels. That split skews spaces and blocks mutual support. Their tests find high-level semantic tasks, above all segmentation, work best as proxies. Unlike low-level tasks that distract with texture detail, segmentation adds shape semantics lifting perception and layout fidelity. Their Semantic Generative Tuning uses it as a proxy to align both skills and lift scores across benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-18814: Junwei Deng and six colleagues audit trajectory-based data attribution, which credits training samples by unrolling training. The methods serve data selection, valuation, and diagnosis, yet no full error analysis had checked their faithfulness. The authors sort total error into config, algorithm, and system levels, and name optimizer mismatch as the dominant config error. They pair each error source with remedies and practical guidance for downstream use.
arxiv-2605-18914: Mahboob Ul Haq models decoherence in superconducting charge qubits with a drift model built on memory multi-fractional Brownian motion. A time-varying Hurst exponent and memory kernel capture shifting noise and long-range correlations that standard models miss. The quantum extension uses a time-dependent Caldeira-Leggett environment. Four results follow: relaxation and noise act independently on energy decay, varying exponents fit observed spectra better than fixed ones, and adaptive kernels preserve correlations with no added damping. Simulations predict coherence times matching theory when charge noise dominates.
arxiv-2605-19214: Nikhil Cherian Kurian and eight colleagues propose a fairness fix for medical imaging AI at the set decision point. Group scores can hide harm: some groups get too many positive calls, others too few. Their worst group penalty targets the worst gaps in true and false positive rates at once, across age, sex, and race. On two imaging sets, it cuts equal odds and equal chance gaps while barely denting accuracy. It keeps diagnostic power while making care fairer at the point of use.
arxiv-2605-20014: Silvan Peter, Patricia Hu and Gerhard Widmer present a precise, simple way to align recorded audio with a written score without transcribing the audio first. Features that track onsets and spectra in sequence are lined up against score positions by a dynamic-programming method adapted from symbolic alignment. The method beats widely used audio-to-audio approaches on solo piano recordings. It stays flexible across timbres and runs at worst linearly in the score and audio lengths.
arxiv-2605-20114: Mattia Fogagnolo, Giorgio Gatti and Alessandra Pluda define scalar curvature lower bounds for 3D Riemannian manifolds whose metrics are only continuous. It rests on growth of the Hawking mass under inverse mean curvature flow. They also prove stability for metrics with nonnegative curvature in this flow sense. So they extend such bounds to merely continuous metrics.
arxiv-2605-20314: Liu and three co-workers study why repeating a smaller dataset can train faster than using a larger one. The small-versus-large gap appears across tasks, designs and optimizers and defies prior theory. They argue sampling biases spur layer-wise growth, an effect stronger on small datasets. Repeating small data is thus not just a fallback when data are scarce but a useful bias for tuning, above all in reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2605-20414: Someki and nine co-workers handle long audio with PlanRAG-Audio, a planning-based retrieval framework. Long recordings swamp audio language models with speech, speaker, emotion and sound cues spread over time. Instead of feeding whole recordings, the system plans which modalities and time spans a query needs and pulls only matching text and audio. Tests show better reasoning accuracy and steadier results as duration grows, with inference cost decoupled from raw audio length.
arxiv-2605-20614: Mohammad Mardini and ten colleagues analyze four extremely metal-poor stars found in Gaia data, seeking the most primitive stars known. Their lead star is strongly enhanced in rapid neutron-capture elements, with europium high relative to iron. High-resolution GHOST spectra from Gemini-South underpin the chemical and motion analysis. Best-fit models point to massive first-generation supernova progenitors of about 20 to 30 solar masses, and one star links kinematically to the Atari structure.
arxiv-2605-21214: Marcel Hussing and colleagues formalize behavior-consistent reinforcement learning, seeking policies that perform well and stay similar across training runs. Their key observation is that maximum-entropy reinforcement learning can anchor runs to a common uniform prior and control divergence. For Boltzmann policies, setting temperature in proportion to Q-function disagreement bounds pairwise KL divergence between policies. They then propose QED, a state-dependent temperature schedule using double-critic disagreement as a single-run proxy.
arxiv-2605-21514: Samuel Koovely and Alexandre Bovet propose conditional entropy of heat diffusion as an entropic measure for continuous-time temporal networks. Common entropy measures based on modeling diffusion on graphs, such as entropy rate and spectral entropy, do not extend easily to temporal networks. This is due to changing rates and one-way flows. Instead, they propose this entropy of heat diffusion for continuous-time temporal networks. They show it is monotone in time, yielding an info-based analog of the second law of thermodynamics for uneven diffusion.
arxiv-2605-21814: Wrick Sengupta and co-authors develop a theory for the sharp ridges on outer flux surfaces of stellarators. Mapping vacuum quasisymmetry to the eikonal equation of optics, they derive ridge rules, reading ridges as field-line caustics where field lines focus. They prove a coil-design theorem: ridges and thread-like coils must lie on the zero-determinant manifold of the magnetic gradient tensor. The constraint unifies plasma ridges and external coils, explains the gradient lengthscale as a coil parameter, and is backed by numerical evidence.
arxiv-2605-22214: Michael Rennick and co-authors present a free energy lattice Boltzmann model for fluid systems with any number of distinct components. The method keeps absent components from nucleating on their own. A novel surface tension scheme conserves momentum globally to machine precision, with a mobility-free flux correction that keeps absent components absent. Benchmarks span liquid lenses, Janus droplets, four-phase separation, and six-component layered Poiseuille flow, matching theory throughout. Patterned liquid surfaces and tiny-channel emulsion droplet generation show its practical reach.
arxiv-2605-22514: Vu studies single smooth answers of n polys in n unknowns over a field of char zero. The focus is stacked systems, where each poly is a stack of base polys. Using this shape cuts the system to the base unknowns, lifting symbol speed. A chance method finds all single smooth answers with poly cost. One use is polys in the subring made by free base polys. Next is fixed polys under finite mirror groups, whose rings are poly. Examples: symmetric, B-type, I-type, and special groups.
arxiv-2605-22714: Temkit asks whether the polarity of earlier turns in a long chat biases a language model's later judgments, an effect he calls AMEL. Across 84,088 calls to 12 models, identical items shift toward the prevailing polarity of their history, most strongly when the model is unsure at baseline. The bias does not grow with history length, and negative histories induce about one and a half times the bias of positive ones. The remedy is a fresh context per item, with balanced history as a fallback when batching cannot be avoided.
arxiv-2605-22814: Goli and others argue that curiosity driven exploration in 3D worlds fails without spatial persistence and episodic memory, since agents loop and earn rewards for revisiting forgotten states. Their agent keeps a 3D reconstruction as a persistent world model, while its policy runs as a sequence model over RGB views to carry trajectory history. Trained by curiosity alone on HM3D, the agent beats active mapping baselines, generalizing zero shot to Gibson and AI made worlds. The same policy adapts to apple picking and image goal navigation tasks.
arxiv-2605-22914: Ferrara and five coauthors explain the color diversity of super-early galaxies seen by JWST beyond redshift ten. In their Attenuation-Free Model, radiation-driven outflows push dust to large radii, cutting how much light it blocks. Applied to 32 confirmed galaxies, the model places them in massive halos with modest star formation rates. It proposes an evolution from a dust-hidden red phase to a UV-bright blue phase as outflows clear galactic centers.
arxiv-2605-23114: Li and Kacprzak improve surrogate models for weak lensing mass maps with flow matching. Weak lensing maps encode structure evolution and enable map inference, but standard methods rely on costly N-body simulations, while GAN surrogates over-smooth maps and miss details. Their residual flow matching network conditions on matter density and clustering amplitude, learning a probability flow from label-specific noise to convergence maps. Against the GAN benchmark, fidelity improves from below 10 percent and below 20 percent to below 1 percent and below 5 percent for basic and higher-order statistics.
arxiv-2605-23214: Xia and five coauthors study reach for Rydberg atom quantum unit arrays. Rydberg units offer quantum-limited sense and broadband tuning. They embed the unit front end in a reach model, giving a third-order base model keeping linear gain and leading cubic curves. A Bussgang split turns curved response into linear gain plus range-tied noise. They derive post-mixing SINR and tractable reach math. Results show Rydberg units beat old units in sparse setups, but noise erodes the edge as density grows.
arxiv-2605-23314: Dou, Yu, and Hou explore how the infall path of falling systems shapes cluster-driven quenching. Group-linked systems follow a distinct quenching track vs lone systems. At early infall stages, group systems exhibit a higher quiet fraction, matching pre-work in group-scale halos. However, after joining the cluster zone, the rise in their quiet fraction is delayed to smaller d_R vs lone systems. This suggests a shield pattern, in which group-scale halos buffer member systems against rapid cluster-driven quenching.
arxiv-2605-23414: Wang and three colleagues name a quiet failure mode of multi-agent language-model systems: plans can execute perfectly yet fail because agents misjudge what they know when judging feasibility. They call it epistemic miscalibration in planning, hidden while plans stay self-consistent and shifting as new information arrives. Their workflow, EPC-AW, picks plans whose evaluations hold steady across agents and refines calibration from past mismatches instead of checking feasibility head-on. Tests lift system success by an average of 9.75 percent.
arxiv-2605-23814: Zhang and Sinigaglia present ROSSINI, a new sky-mapping tool that takes spectra across a wide field without costly integral field units, using a slitless approach. The tool takes detector images of the same field, turning the telescope or the spread direction between shots, then joins them with tomography into a full 3D data cube. Tests build toy data cubes, mimic the tool and its detector images, and win back the input cube. ROSSINI rebuilds test cubes with percent accuracy in a few hundred rounds at tiny cost.
arxiv-2605-23914: Pagonas and four colleagues present VineLM, a manager for agent workflows that picks the language model for each step as the work unfolds. It does not fix one plan in advance. Instead, it maps runs as a branching tree of model choices, using checkpointing and profiling to judge accuracy, cost, and delay without testing every path. On database-query and maths-reasoning workflows, it beat fixed plans, gaining up to 18 percent accuracy at the same budget. Offline profiling cost fell by 98 percent or more.
arxiv-2605-24214: Tadmor asks whether the symmetries behind hyperbolic conservation laws can be derived rather than assumed. Entropy functions, tied to symmetry, are usually imposed on such systems, and Friedrichs questioned whether the symmetries themselves could be deduced. Tadmor introduces a variational frame that answers him: an entropy function emerges as an extreme case. From it, Dafermos's rule follows, deduced rather than imposed.
arxiv-2605-24314: Huang, Ma, and Zhao determine permutation groups for certain cyclic codes over finite fields, groups that matter for weight distributions and decoding. Using two distinct matrix pictures, they link very long codes with special generator polynomials to codes of prime length. They mainly settle the groups for codes with lengths built from distinct primes and special generator polynomials. For length pq, they give the groups for cyclotomic-polynomial generators and others, apparently the first work on generators dividing the pq-length polynomial but not the prime-length ones.
arxiv-2605-24714: Marco Zanni and others optimize status-update age in integrated sensing and communication systems. A base station talks to an environment and a monitor, choosing among sensing, communication, or joint operation. The goal is minimizing a discounted infinite-horizon cost combining monitor age with sensing and communication costs. For a single source, a Markov decision process yields an optimal policy with an ordered threshold form. For multiple sources, a restless bandit formulation yields Whittle index policies comparable in indexable regimes and effective beyond them.
arxiv-2605-24914: Ali Noshad leads MVR-cache, a semantic cache for language models cutting cost and wait time. It spots when a new prompt matches one already answered. Current caches lean on crude similarity scores, capping hit rates. MVR-cache splits prompts with a learned segmentation model, then compares pieces with fine-grained multi-vector retrieval. Its training goal comes from theory tying the objective to cache hits under strict correctness rules. Reinforcement learning handles the non-differentiable optimization, and hit rates rise by up to about a third.
arxiv-2605-25214: Vasily Lubashevskiy and Ihor Lubashevsky develop a cloud-function formalism for supraliminal processing, the conscious handling of sensory information in large brain networks. It joins neural field theory with the shape of perceived objects and their place in the surroundings as seen first-hand. Its main equation resembles a Schrödinger-type equation with a nonlinear non-Hermitian Hamiltonian plus Lotka-Volterra-like terms. Applied to changes of mind, it explains revisions during action as fast preconscious processing meeting slower conscious comparison.
arxiv-2605-25414: Hyung-Suk Yoon and Seung-Woo Seo tackle distribution shift in robot imitation learning, where agents fail on states never seen in expert demos. Their framework runs in phases: offline learning first broadens coverage with extra demos, using a discriminator to train the policy. Online, the system detects shift as it occurs and adapts through self-taught imitation on fresh experience. The scheme thus pairs robust offline preparation with adaptive online correction. Tests in MuJoCo simulations show better robustness and adaptation than baselines.
arxiv-2605-25514: Yanglong Song and eight colleagues move generative search from item-only to query-item modeling at Quark. Existing methods flatten queries and items into one sequence without marking boundaries, mixing intents into one noisy target. Their QGS encodes interactions as query-item pairs with a query-conditioned objective, turning a noisy marginal into a clean conditional. A linear HSTU encoder replaces attention with causal recurrence, cutting per-layer cost from quadratic to linear with no ranking loss. Online tests show CTR up 0.62 percent and duration up 3.55 percent over baseline.
arxiv-2605-25614: Long and Nam examine when norm and distance functions are strongly quasiconvex in finite-dimensional normed spaces. The Euclidean norm is already known to have the property on bounded convex sets, but no complete picture exists for general norms. They give exact criteria for a norm to have the property on a convex set. They also open the study of strong quasiconvexity for distance functions, offering new geometric insight and extending several existing results.
arxiv-2605-25914: Liu and Pikhurko prove Turán densities for hypergraphs contain genuine intervals. A Turán density caps how dense a family can be while dodging banned patterns. For uniformity three or more, the density set holds a real interval reaching one. That settles a question posed in 2007 by Frankl and co-authors. It also shows the density set has Hausdorff dimension one, the largest possible. That settles a 2016 question of Grosu, who had not known if it was even nonzero.
arxiv-2605-26014: Liang and ten colleagues teach video-language models to reason inside their own hidden states rather than in words. Current systems externalise reasoning through written chains of thought, keyframe picks or external tools, which adds latency and forces visual evidence into text. Their STORM framework trains models to follow bounded continuous latent trajectories instead. One stage aligns latent tokens with thought-video representations from generated videos. A second stage uses answer-only supervision to internalise the process. At run time, no videos are regenerated and no frames are reinserted.
arxiv-2605-26314: Nils Bonfils and Christoph Becker's 2026 paper asks how much of ICT's rising carbon impact comes from surveillance capitalism's gear. They frame the model as harvest of user data for forecasts and profit, powered by tracking, number-crunching, use, AI training, and storage. They compare X, once Twitter, with Mastodon, a nonprofit alternative, gauging network traffic from tracking work. Corporate overhead, excess resource use from company habits, emerges as a proxy. X's overhead sets a lower bound on carbon output from for-profit work that adds nothing to users.
arxiv-2605-26614: Li and three colleagues develop a spectral route to Sidorenko-type inequalities, which bound how often a small bipartite pattern appears inside a larger graph. They prove the conjecture equals a stronger spectral version involving the graph's largest eigenvalue, and use it to pin down sharp supersaturation counts for complete bipartite graphs and even cycles. Both constants are best possible, attained by random graphs and split graphs respectively.
arxiv-2605-26714: Altinoklu and Musavian give pinching antenna systems, bendable radiating points strung along a waveguide, a new control: tuning phase mismatch in guided waves to set each point's radiated weight on its own. The result is a beamforming design that tunes weights freely while still matching old equal-power setups. In multiuser downlink tests, the tunable design beats standard arrays and prior pinching designs, with the biggest wins where interference rules.
arxiv-2605-27014: In a 2026 paper, Rashid presents ReasonOps, a single operational paradigm for trustworthy verified reasoning with language models. Current systems hide logical inconsistencies, invent false steps, and offer weak reliability guarantees, while methods stay split across proof, assurance, and neuro-symbolic camps. ReasonOps treats it as a watched, checkable process, joining reading, autoformalization, theorem proving, runtime checks, and adaptive fixes. A braking-system case shows the workflow in action.
arxiv-2605-27214: Caballero and Villamizar study how the cycle structure of a permutation carries over to its symmetric tensor power. They answer an earlier Problem 8.1 by giving formulas for the fixed points of the tensor power. They also handle the case where the original permutation holds at most one cycle longer than a single point, giving formulas for the number of cycles of each length there. The results turn a structural question about tensor powers into explicit counts that can be computed from the original cycle decomposition.
arxiv-2605-27314: Vito Mengers and Oliver Brock show reactive robot control can handle tasks with several competing goals. They extend a graph of estimators with adaptive nullspace projections, so lower-priority motions yield wherever gradients meet instead of following a fixed ranking. The method solves 200 simulated navigation and pushing problems and 49 of 50 real pushing trials.
arxiv-2605-27414: Yair Segev and colleagues show pneumatic spread of solid particles for stratospheric aerosol injection. A water-repelling coat lifts the submicron share from 10 percent untreated to between 50 and 85 percent treated, with 300 nanometer grains beating 500 nanometer ones. Roughness data from atomic force microscopy predicts which types disperse best, and a feasible aircraft fleet could sustain a climate-relevant layer.
arxiv-2605-28014: Zhao and colleagues improve self-distillation for reasoning models by teaching insights instead of whole solutions. Their ROSD method contrasts each flawed rollout with a correct one, locates the first error, and trains only from that point onward. The approach beat standard self-distillation and reinforcement baselines while keeping reasoning diverse and training stable.
arxiv-2605-28614: Erick Ross and Hui Xue study equidistribution of CM points and RM curves along fixed geodesics and around fixed points in the complex upper half-plane. Duke showed in 1988 that CM points of fundamental discriminant spread evenly as the discriminant goes to negative infinity, with a similar result for RM curves. Ross and Xue prove the same even spread along every fixed rational geodesic and around every fixed CM point. The proofs tackle the aggregate Linnik problem for arbitrary binary quadratic forms.
arxiv-2605-28714: Michael Galarnyk and ten colleagues build IPO-Mine, a toolkit and dataset for section-structured analysis of long, multimodal IPO filings. The open-source toolkit downloads and parses filings into standardized section-structured text with extracted images, handling documents that often exceed 500,000 tokens. The resulting dataset covers over 109,000 filings and amendments from 1994 to 2026 with more than 76,000 images. Tests show leading multimodal models often disagree with expert human judgments on chart quality and misleadingness, exposing alignment gaps in long regulatory documents.
arxiv-2605-29114: Teymoorianfard and colleagues probe reasoning-enabled vision-language-action models for self-driving cars under realistic input corruptions. Using NVIDIA's Alpamayo models in closed tests, attacks succeed on up to 89 percent of reasoning targets and 72 percent of path targets, raising crash rates. The study is the first broad black-box test of such models under text corruptions, with a reasoning test framework covering meaning, structure, and safety. The authors also release a benchmark for attacks and defenses on reasoning, and they urge stronger testing and defenses for driving safety.
arxiv-2605-29214: Xiaohan Liu and colleagues build a sensitive mid-infrared upconversion detector boosted by a cavity pump. A single-mode pump at 1064 nm is enhanced 36-fold inside a low-loss cavity, enabling conversion up to 22 percent at 55 watts inside. The noise floor falls below one femtowatt per root hertz, at least ten times better than before. Single-frequency pumping supports high-fidelity spectral mapping, attractive for precise mid-infrared spectroscopy where photons are scarce. The system combines high sensitivity, fast response, and room-temperature operation.
arxiv-2605-29614: N. G. Koudafokê and three colleagues model a thermo-managed MEMS coupling an HP memristor with resonators. Using the linear drift device model, they analyze motion with Lyapunov rates, split diagrams, and phase portraits. Results show shifts between quasi-regular and chaotic swings, plus twin regimes. Device settings, on-state and off-state drag, oxide thickness, and ionic flow, strongly shape sizes, ringing rates, and shifts. State-shifting drag tunes coupling and shares energy between resonators. Next to JJ systems, the HP device design needs no cooling.
arxiv-2605-29714: Aditi Khandelwal and four colleagues probe how expert routing shifts when an English-centred mixture-of-experts model keeps training on many tongues. Early and middle layers spread routing across tongues, while tongue-specific routing shows up mainly in the last layers. Shared word pieces across tongues help steer which experts fire, the team finds. From that pattern they tune only tongue-specific and shared experts in the last layers, a lean fix that rivals full tuning there while touching under two percent of weights.
arxiv-2605-29914: Bo Peng and Diana Valencia model carbon gas escape from young rocky building blocks, which may explain Earth's low carbon versus primitive meteorites. Their model tracks heat and gas release in porous chondritic bodies, using redox states of ordinary, enstatite, and carbonaceous groups. When gas pressure tops confinement, global cracks vent the excess straight to space. Carbon loss runs stronger in oxidized carbonaceous bodies than in non-carbonaceous ones; middle-size bodies lose most, the largest and smallest keep more. The findings favor drier bodies as Earth's carbon carriers.
arxiv-2605-30114: Thomas Ransford extends a coefficient formula for de Branges-Rovnyak norms. The formula expresses a norm through Taylor coefficients of a function and a related one. It was known for functions holomorphic near the closed disk, but can fail for others in the space. Ransford extends it to square-integrable functions with finite right side, if the related one is square-integrable or rational. Under weaker integrability, it still holds given an extra weighted finiteness condition. He gives a limit form valid for all non-extreme points and functions there.
arxiv-2605-30214: Fabian Mewes, Anne Lauscher and Vagrant Gautam contribute GRUFF, a dataset for pronoun fidelity in German: reusing specified pronouns despite distractors. English work misses German's grammatical gender and agreement. GRUFF covers four gender agreement systems and four sets. Models show agreement for masculine and feminine entities without context, but not for the neopronouns xier and en. Robustness to distractors is weak, though encoder models do better in German than in English. Occupational stereotypes correlate poorly across cases and models, except related ones.
arxiv-2605-30314: Grant Hamblin and six co-authors introduce SpecBench, testing spec-level reasoning for agents: writing complete, unambiguous, consistent and correct specs. Current benchmarks such as SWE-Bench focus on implementation, testing code generation given fixed requirements. SpecBench tasks come from the Request for Comments process of open-source projects: each agent gets a proposal, the codebase, and past RFC discussions, and must spot omissions, ambiguities, inconsistencies, or wrong assumptions. Predictions are judged against maintainer notes; tasks span Kubernetes, React, Rust, TVM and vLLM, and the best agent, GPT-5.4, hits 44 percent.
arxiv-2605-30414: Ansh R. Gupta and 35 co-authors fit JWST spectra of 39 AGN at high redshift from CEERS and RUBIES. Little red dots are hard to model, but mass guesses for these AGN shift only modestly with or without AGN parts. These AGN at low redshift match the local black hole to mass relation, while those at high redshift show raised ratios. This shift over about 500 million years comes from mass changes, not from a shifting black hole mass spread.
arxiv-2605-30514: Suryash Yagnik and five co-authors present 5WBENCH, a balanced 5,000-sample benchmark with 1,000 examples per 5W category (Who, What, When, Where, Why). They present MAAT (Multi-phase Adapter-Aware Targeted Unlearning), a framework operating on LoRA adapter weights. MAAT is the first method to achieve high forgetting and high retention on Why-type causal knowledge.

arxiv-2606-04114:
J Eduardo Vera-Valdés tests in 2026 whether the pace of global warming has genuinely accelerated, a question that recent studies answered in opposite ways using data ending just a year apart. Dating the change matters for how fast societies should expect further warming.

He shows that structural-break tests cannot reliably date a smoothly accelerating trend, so he tests curvature directly with two new trend forms whose baseline is exactly steady warming. Across five major temperature records from 1970 to 2025, both forms found significant acceleration once natural wiggles were controlled. Expanding-window analysis dated detectability to windows ending in 2023 or 2024 for three datasets, and not yet for two others. The gentlest specification projects the least extra warming by 2050.
arxiv-2606-04314:
Bin Duan, Meiru Che, and Guowei Yang propose BayesWarp in 2026, a testing framework that hunts for neural network failures by mutating the parts of an input the model actually relies on. Global mutation and coverage-guided fuzzing both waste effort, either wandering off-distribution or missing diverse faults.

BayesWarp first finds decision-critical regions with interpretability tools, then mutates there, steering the search with Bayesian optimization that tracks its own uncertainty. The goal is many different failures that stay close to real data in distribution and meaning. On handwritten digits, small photos, and a large image benchmark across six models, it improved failure discovery, diversity, case quality, and critical-neuron coverage under a fixed budget. Fine-tuning on its failures then improved the models.
arxiv-2606-05114:
Ronnie de Souza Santos and colleagues report how software engineering students used large language models to write research papers in this 2026 arXiv experience report. The setting was an empirical methods assignment in a third-year software architecture course. Students wrote a short research paper using either a rapid review or a gray literature review method. They had to disclose how they used language models along the way.

The researchers analyzed 146 student disclosure statements with a cross-analysis process that combined language-model-assisted categorization with manual verification and refinement. Students reported weaving the tools into brainstorming, methodological clarification, organizing findings, and refining their writing. They also voiced concerns about inaccuracies and the need to verify generated content. The report draws lessons for teaching, arguing that reflective, disclosed use of these tools should be built into empirical software engineering education rather than treated as a side channel.
arxiv-2606-05214:
Roberto Ricci and Giuseppe Dattoli develop an analytic umbral approach to Bessel moments in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bessel moments are integrals of products of Bessel functions. Umbral calculus evaluates them formally by turning Bessel products into Gaussian integrals over operators. The manipulations give correct answers in favorable ranges but can produce series that diverge at relevant values.

The cubic moment is the example: the expansion yields an Appell series whose convergence domain excludes the equilateral case even though the integral is finite. Replacing the expansion with an analytic umbral transmutation, built on Mellin-Barnes integrals with Ramanujan's Master Theorem selecting the spectral ground state, removes the obstruction. It reduces the cubic moment to a one-dimensional Barnes integral, equivalently a Meijer G-function, recovering the known value. The same mechanism handles cubic products and the fourth moment, while the fifth moment emerges as the first higher-rank case.
arxiv-2606-05414:
Avinash Baidya and colleagues tackle early failure alerting for dialogs and agent runs in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task is to decide, while a conversation or trajectory is unfolding, whether it is likely to fail, yet supervision exists as a final success or failure label for the trajectory. Across five benchmarks spanning customer support, task-oriented dialog, persuasion, tool use, and planning, relevant failure evidence occupies 5 to 11 percent of turns. It appears after 59 to 84 percent of a trajectory.

Their two-stage system learns turn-level evidence with an attention-based predictor that estimates failure risk from histories. It pairs that with a stopping policy that lets users pick an accuracy-versus-earliness operating point at inference time. The predictor improved quality by up to 10 percent over naive prefix supervision. The full system improved by 42 percent over state-of-the-art trigger policies, at lower training cost per operating point.
arxiv-2606-05914:
Cochard and Simon publish a full year of real job records from a French national computing center in a 2026 arXiv paper. Scheduling research needs genuine workloads, but public traces are often short, old, or missing memory data. The IN2P3 Computing Center in Villeurbanne serves CNRS researchers nationwide. Its 2024 dataset logs every submitted job with execution details.

Forty-four million jobs came from about a thousand users. The cluster peaked at three hundred twelve machines running forty-six thousand concurrent threads. Memory usage, often absent from older traces, is included throughout. A full year lets seasonal, monthly, and weekly user rhythms show up in simulation. Researchers can test scheduling algorithms against behavior no synthetic trace invents. The authors analyze the trace's shape alongside releasing it. Recent, memory-rich, year-long data is the dataset's selling point.
arxiv-2606-06114:
Dianxing Shi and colleagues ask where an overseer should tap a self-improving agent to keep it safe in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents evolve by training on their own generated signals, gaining skill but risking capability decay and safety drift. Human feedback works for static models; its role mid-run was unmapped. ANCHOR simulates human supervision with a language-model framework, delivering feedback at chosen phases of the loop.

Two open-source systems of this kind were tested across coding, mathematical reasoning, and safety. Even limited oversight cut safety degradation sharply. Core performance on the growth objectives stayed stable. Watching the output-checking phase proved the most effective intervention point. Raising oversight beyond that bought diminishing returns. The guidance: place sparse oversight at the checking phase, not everywhere. Self-evolution with a well-placed anchor stays controllable. Designers of autonomous improvement loops gain an evidence-based oversight budget.
arxiv-2606-06214:
Huifan Gao and co-authors tackle the readability of code written by language models in this 2026 arXiv paper on software engineering. Generated code can run correctly yet be painful for humans to read, and readability is a subjective quality that resists direct training. Their tool is representation engineering, which steers a model by nudging its internal activations along chosen directions. Past work steered one trait at a time, but readability has several faces at once.

The team defines a joint principal component problem that extracts one steering direction per readability metric while respecting shared constraints. Their multitask method, MRepE, applies those directions together to control three readability metrics in coordination. Theory clarifies the trade off with correctness, and experiments show the steering vectors consistently improved answers to readability related queries. The drop in code correctness stayed limited when the steering strengths were chosen with care.
arxiv-2606-06314:
Anshima Singh and David Silvester help neural PDE solvers aim their effort in this 2026 arXiv paper. Physics informed neural networks learn solutions of partial differential equations by training at scattered collocation points. For problems that evolve in time, with sharp features moving through many dimensions, spreading points uniformly wastes most of them on calm regions. The solver struggles exactly where the action is.

Their framework, DAS PINNs, treats space and time as one unified domain, with no step by step marching. A normalizing flow network, called KRnet, learns where the equation's residual is large and generates fresh points concentrated there. Hard regions are found and tracked across space and time automatically. Five benchmark problems confirm the behavior, from moving features in two spatial dimensions to localized structures in up to eight. The adaptive edge grows as dimension rises, where uniform sampling fails fastest.
arxiv-2606-06414:
Shahin Atashbar Tehrani, Elham Astaraki, and Fatemeh Arbabifar teach machine learning models the inner structure of the proton in this 2026 arXiv paper. The proton structure function, called F2, measures how the proton's constituents share its momentum at different probing scales. Physicists usually compute it by solving the DGLAP evolution equations. This study instead learns it directly from high precision BCDMS scattering data, treating the physics as a regression problem.

Four algorithms compete: support vector regression, gradient boosting, Gaussian process regression, and a multilayer perceptron network. With cross validation and tuned settings, the perceptron and the Gaussian process led on accuracy. The perceptron was most sensitive to steep nonlinear rises at low momentum fraction. Support vector regression, while less sharp, was the most stable across data folds against noise. Training and validation scores converged closely, suggesting the models learned real physics, not noise.
arxiv-2606-06514:
Nishit Singh recasts fairness as a symmetry in this 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning ethics. A classifier, he argues, is fair if flipping a sensitive attribute, say gender or race, leaves its output unchanged, with merit features held fixed. Bias is then symmetry breaking, and fairness work becomes symmetry restoration. He implements that restoration as a penalty in the training loss. The penalty punishes any output change under the flip.

The framework was tested on four synthetic datasets with varying noise, correlation, and built in bias. It cut fairness violations by upwards of ninety percent, at an accuracy cost of around five percent. No causal graph is required, and the method is computationally light, since it trains no adversary network. It applies to any sensitive attribute expressible as a bit flip. Singh notes this suits settings whose local discrimination never appears in mainstream benchmarks built around a few standard datasets.
arxiv-2606-06614:
Lechen Zhang, Jiarui Liu, and Tal August put real people back into the evaluation of AI personalization in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most tests of whether models adapt to users run on synthetic data, which can flatter the systems. The team collected five hundred fifty real human conversations and thousands of human judgments. They covered personalization's three stages: extracting user attributes from chats, matching them to new prompts, and folding them into a response.

Every stage disappointed. Models extracted noisy attributes from real conversations. They disagreed with people about which attributes were relevant. Their personalized responses won human ratings no better than generic ones, though model judges scored them much higher. Two lightweight training interventions closed part of the gap in the first two stages. But learned reward models correlated only modestly with human ratings. Judging personalization as humans do remains hard to automate.
arxiv-2606-06914:
Websites nudge visitors into giving up personal data through deceptive design tricks. Zewei Shi and co-authors defend users against a new twist in this 2026 arXiv paper. Attackers can groom AI systems themselves. They seed scarce corners of the web with fake but benign looking examples. Models learn from those samples and start treating deception as normal.

Their DPAgent framework stations four specialized agents in the middle. One purifies the latent space against grooming. One generates tasks, one detects deceptive patterns, and one repairs interfaces. The system caught about ninety one percent of groomed samples. Its detection score set a new best mark. It explored most pattern types while visiting a tenth of the pages rivals needed. It also repaired seventy seven percent of flagged interfaces. A sweep of four hundred eighty five live sites found deceptive patterns almost everywhere.
arxiv-2606-07014:
Electricity prices in one European zone echo what happens across its borders. Chomon and Ziel build that echo into a forecasting model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Europe's day ahead auction links dozens of bidding zones. Transmission lines carry both power and price pressure between neighbors.

Their Networked Spatio-Temporal Model maps the zones onto a metric graph. A neighborhood measure defines how strongly zones inform each other. The model blends each zone's own price history with cross hour and seasonal patterns. Fuel prices, emission prices, and forecast fundamentals join as predictors. The study spans thirty nine bidding zones in a streaming setup. The networked model consistently beat purely local rivals. The authors frame the gain as information propagation. What happens in one market is, measurably, news for its neighbors.
arxiv-2606-07114:
Wireless networks must share power and spectrum while users interfere with each other constantly. Chee Wei Tan and Chen fuse optimization with deep learning to manage that tangle in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework, DIFFRACT, rests on standard interference functions, the math behind classic power control. They develop a duality theory showing these functions are differentiable monotone operators.

That theory lets iterative management algorithms be unrolled into neural network layers. The resulting architecture learns end to end by gradient descent, directly at the network edge. Satellite to ground links and open radio access networks are the motivating settings. Both face fast changing channels and strict quality demands. DIFFRACT maximizes network utility while respecting stochastic service constraints. Experiments confirmed the framework behaves as theory predicts and scales to realistic loads. The Perron-Frobenius viewpoint ties the learning machinery back to classical spectral theory. Resource control becomes trainable without abandoning mathematical guarantees.
arxiv-2606-07314:
An Pham, Nguyen, and Usman benchmark language models on debugging quantum software in this 2026 arXiv paper introducing QBugLM. Quantum program bugs are nasty because they often produce silently wrong answers rather than crashes. Their framework automates the evaluation pipeline across several agents: injecting known bugs from a taxonomy into programs written in OpenQASM 3.0, asking models to find and fix them, then validating repairs by simulation.

In their case study, two models, Claude 4.6 Sonnet and Qwen3 Coder Next, were tested under different prompting strategies and bug categories. Feedback mattered enormously: one retry with feedback lifted first-try success from below 25 percent to above 80 percent in their runs. Surprisingly, simpler structured prompts sometimes beat chain-of-thought prompting, which asks the model to reason step by step. The authors present the framework as reusable infrastructure for tracking quantum debugging ability as models improve.
arxiv-2606-07514:
Song and co-authors generalize a single-photo 3D reconstruction method to every kind of camera in this 2026 arXiv paper on UniSHARP. View synthesis renders new viewpoints from one image, powering virtual reality and robot navigation. The base method, SHARP, assumed ordinary pinhole cameras, but real devices shoot wide-angle, fisheye, and panoramic images with distortion. UniSHARP aligns all these images inside an omnidirectional latent space, arranging its 3D Gaussian primitives along rays with radial distances instead of a flat grid.

Semantic features from the image and features from a camera encoder are decoded jointly into the Gaussian cloud. That cloud is the set of three-dimensional blobs from which views are rendered. The authors built a benchmark spanning camera types and scenes, split by field of view. Across that benchmark UniSHARP outperformed other methods by a margin. The project page shows reconstructions from perspective, fisheye, and panoramic inputs.
arxiv-2606-07714:
Ghanadian, Nejadgholi, and Al Osman look inside models that detect suicide ideation in text, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models are usually judged by overall accuracy alone. In mental-health work that is not enough, because clinicians need to know whether a model responds to real risk factors or to accidental patterns in the data.

The team compared models trained on original posts with models trained on topic-augmented data, where posts were enriched with topic information. Using visual and geometric analysis of the models' internal representations, they measured how clearly psychological risk topics were encoded. Augmentation made underrepresented risk factors stand out much more distinctly inside the model. The examples named include immigration stress, family problems, and financial crisis. The authors argue that augmentation therefore improves not just scores but also how structured and auditable the model's reasoning is.
arxiv-2606-07814:
Mukherjee and co-authors speed up a bottleneck in quantum optimisation in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, QAOA, solves hard combinatorial problems by tuning two sets of angles, gamma and beta. Finding good angles classically means searching a high-dimensional landscape, and sampling noise corrupts every measurement.

The team noticed that feature matrices built from QAOA samples have strong low-rank structure: a few patterns carry most of the information. Their algorithm, HGLE, encodes low-energy samples into a weighted Ising feature matrix, then compresses it by leverage-score sampling, keeping the rows that matter most while provably preserving the main geometry. The compressed problem drives a classical trust-region loop that estimates the angles at a fraction of the original cost. Formal guarantees cover rank preservation and energy approximation error. A further result shows the compressed problem keeps the same minimiser as the full one.
arxiv-2606-08114:
S. Afonso, J. M. Gomez Llorente, and J. Plata test how well a standard quantum protection technique survives realistic noise, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Continuous dynamical decoupling defends a qubit against decoherence by bathing it in a continuous control field. Most theory addresses longitudinal noise, the fluctuations that cause pure dephasing. Real devices also suffer transverse noise, and the two can be anisotropic, stronger in one channel than another.

The authors evaluate the method's efficiency analytically for generic qubit setups with both noise types. Their approach, a sequence of unitary rewrites, recasts the noise as effective stochastic terms. Their spectral properties depend on the control settings, including the noisy Landau-Zener transitions as the control field ramps up.
