That description lets them design mitigations by reshaping the effective noise. The conclusion is encouraging: continuous decoupling holds up well against generic noise, transverse cases included.
arxiv-2606-08714:
Ali Kafili Gavgani and colleagues report a failure first, then a fix, for learning to control an unstable aircraft, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multirotors are limited by under-actuation: they cannot independently command every direction of motion. Tilt-rotor configurations overcome this with thrust-vectoring rotors, gaining full actuation at the price of a highly unstable plant. The authors first evaluate a direct approach, training perceptrons, recurrent networks, and transformers to map states directly to control signals. That strategy fails to stabilize the system.

The main contribution is a hybrid: a neural network working alongside a conventional controller, each covering the other's weaknesses. The conventional controller supplies the stabilizing backbone that pure learning could not discover. The network compensates for the nonlinearities and model errors that fixed controllers handle poorly. The work is an honest case study in the limits of end-to-end learning for control.
arxiv-2606-08914:
Lee and colleagues watch beginners create charts with conversational AI, and catalog how the process goes wrong, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tools like ChatGPT let people make and read charts by typing plain requests, a practice the authors call vibe visualizing. That ease draws in novices with low visualization literacy, who may not spot errors in what the AI returns. The team ran a study with twenty novices, recording their ChatGPT conversations, interviews, and questionnaire answers.

From the records they built a codebook covering the AI's faithfulness, its chart errors, its responses when challenged, and user prompting habits. Four themes emerged: output quality, recurring ChatGPT errors, user misuse, and what shapes trust. Replaying the opening prompts on Gemini and Claude exposed different failure modes in each. Yet every model produced some fatal issues that could mislead a decision. The authors close with design recommendations for safer AI visualization tools.
arxiv-2606-09214:
Linh defeats the last purely algebraic test for whether an equation system has solutions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Hasse principle expects a rational point whenever local points exist everywhere. When it fails, the Brauer-Manin obstruction is the usual explanation; does its algebraic part always suffice? For homogeneous spaces, the question was open in this sharp form.

Over any number field with a root of unity of odd prime order, Linh builds a homogeneous space of the special linear group, with finite 2-nilpotent stabilizers. Its algebraic Brauer group is constant and unramified, so that obstruction is blind, yet local points exist in every completion and no rational point exists. The failure comes from the transcendental part: a first for homogeneous spaces of connected linear groups. Adapting Borovoi and Kunyavskii's idea, it closes a door: algebraic methods alone cannot decide the Hasse principle here.
arxiv-2606-09314:
Huang and colleagues generate dexterous robot grasps from a learned prior instead of hand-tuned contact physics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Dexterous grasping means choosing a full multi-finger hand configuration that holds an object stably. Learning-based methods usually lean on carefully tuned contact losses or costly contact-based refinement at test time. KPGrasp instead describes each grasp as 3D hand keypoints in plain Euclidean coordinates, in the object's own frame. A Transformer flow-matching model learns the distribution, trained on the standard loss alone.

On the Dexonomy benchmark it reached a grasp success rate of 76.3 percent, beating the strongest comparable baseline by 47.4 percent, while cutting penetration depth to 2.4 millimeters. It also led the DexGrasp Anything benchmark with no fine-tuning. Batched inference takes only 0.032 seconds per grasp. Trials on 20 diverse real objects confirmed the pipeline deploys on physical hardware.
arxiv-2606-09614:
Martin Dindoš, Linhan Li, and Jill Pipher settle when a heat-type equation with rough coefficients can be solved from its edge fluxes in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task is the Neumann problem for a parabolic operator on a Lipschitz cylinder, a tube with a jagged rim. The coefficients are mere bounded, rough maps, tamed only by a Carleson condition, a budget on how wildly they can swing.

For each power p in the data's L-p class, the team proves the problem is solvable. The catch is scale: the Carleson budget and the rim's jagged slope must both start small enough. The grip on the solution comes as a bound on its edge-poking gradient peaks. Twin tasks were closed sooner: the Dirichlet task by others, the regularity task by this same team in both small and large budget worlds.
arxiv-2606-09714:
Philipp Eller merges several sky neutrino datasets into one joint fit for the first time in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos are ghostly particles made in Earth's air by cosmic rays. As they fly, they morph between three flavours, a process called oscillation. Big detectors on three continents have each tracked this morphing for years, but joint fits were thought to need insider access.

Eller shows one shared physics model can describe all of them at once. The fit spans Super-Kamiokande, IceCube-DeepCore, and KM3NeT/ORCA, plus reactor data from Daya Bay. It covers more than eight hundred thousand events in fifteen hundred bins, tuned by ninety-one parameters. No sharp clashes showed between the sets. The joint fit gave tight values for the mixing traits of neutrinos. It also leaned toward the normal mass order, where the third mass state is the heaviest, over the flipped order.
arxiv-2606-10114:
Liu and Huang design control hardware that could scale superconducting quantum computers to thousands of qubits, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum engineering. Their architecture works at four kelvin and splits the job. Optical fibers distribute shared pulse templates, while local cryogenic CMOS circuits handle transmission control, amplitude programming, envelope shaping, and microwave upconversion in the fridge itself.

Moving high-speed waveform synthesis and memory access out of each cryogenic channel cuts per-channel power dissipation compared with fully cryo-CMOS controllers. Unlike purely photonic approaches, the design keeps local programmability for pulse selection, timing updates, and phase control, and stays compatible with real-time feedback for quantum error correction. First-order models of power, memory scaling, and fidelity limits, cross-checked with a three-level transmon simulation, suggest the approach is feasible for scalable control.
arxiv-2606-10214:
Singhal proves a conjecture about the structure from algebra attached to random directed networks, in a 2026 arXiv paper on chance and number theory. The sandpile group of a graph is a finite abelian group encoding its chip-firing dynamics. Its p-Sylow subgroup, the part built from a prime p, has a conjectured limiting distribution for random directed bipartite graphs. The conjecture came from Bhargava, DePascale, and Koenig. Standard proof tactics count surjections onto each possible group, but here those moments often diverge to infinity.

He resolves the divergence by restricting attention to a highly likely subset of graphs where the surjective moments are well behaved. He discards a rare odd set whose share of the distribution vanishes even though its share of the moments explodes. Computing the moments on the good set then pins down the limiting distribution, settling the conjecture.
arxiv-2606-10414:
Ohashi studies special algebraic curves in this 2026 arXiv paper in pure mathematics, over fields where arithmetic wraps around a prime number of steps. The objects are hyperelliptic curves, given by an equation where one variable squared equals a polynomial in the other. A curve is superspecial when its Jacobian, an associated geometric object, splits into supersingular elliptic curves. Ohashi writes such curves in Rosenhain form, a standard shape whose parameters locate the branch points.

The main theorem concerns a superspecial curve in this form. Each parameter, each difference from one, and each pairwise difference must be a perfect square in the field with p squared elements. That condition prunes the search space sharply. Building an enumeration algorithm on it, Ohashi counted the isomorphism classes for genera four and five in each characteristic up to forty-one. For genus six the count reaches thirty-one, settling previously open cases.
arxiv-2606-10614:
Beomjun Kim and colleagues teach robot hands from human videos in this 2026 arXiv paper on robotics. Dexterous manipulation is where robot data hurt most: teleoperating one small task can take days. Their Dexterous Point Policy skips robot demonstrations entirely. The bridge is a shared representation: three-dimensional keypoints of objects and hands, pulled from human videos. A transformer policy trains on those keypoints for both seeing and acting, since wrists and fingertips move alike across bodies.

On real-robot tasks spanning pick-and-place and tool use, the policy attains 75.0 percent success in the reported trials. A leading vision-language-action baseline reaches only 1.0 percent. The method also generalises strongly to scenes it never saw in training, including multi-object setups and entirely new object categories. Choosing the right abstraction, keypoints rather than pixels or raw joints, is what closes the embodiment gap.
arxiv-2606-10714:
Berk and Ulcigrai study when sped-up copies of a flow ignore each other in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two flows are disjoint when their joint behavior is as unstructured as possible. Rescaling time by a rational factor gives a new flow, and earlier work settled disjointness of rescalings only in genus one. The authors treat smooth area-preserving flows on surfaces of genus at least two.

For almost every such flow with the standard saddle count, any two rational rescalings with different absolute values are disjoint. The proof uses Birkhoff-sum tail estimates and a new geometric ingredient: rigidity times of bounded type, produced by degenerating a translation surface toward a flat torus with bounded-type rotation number.
arxiv-2606-10914:
Levkin and colleagues excite spin motion with light in a nearly compensated ferrimagnet in this 2026 arXiv paper. A ferrimagnet has two opposing magnetic sublattices; near the compensation point their pulls nearly cancel. Femtosecond pulses, acting through the inverse Faraday effect, set the Néel vector precessing in two modes that rotate in opposite senses.

Near compensation the two mode frequencies draw together and grow sharply field-sensitive. At one critical field they coincide, both modes flip their handedness, and the two-frequency motion collapses into a single linear oscillation set by the pump pulse. A second pulse can then steer the spin trajectory, a control knob for magnonic devices.
arxiv-2606-11314:
Perel and six co-authors present TRON in a 2026 arXiv paper, a rendering framework for real-world 3D scenes. It combines 3D Gaussian ray tracing with neural rendering to render scenes realistically under novel lighting, dynamic object motion, object insertion, and material editing. Purely physical approaches struggle with relighting because reconstructed geometry, materials, and light transport are imperfect. Pure neural renderers lack an explicit scene model, limiting fine-grained editing.

TRON bridges the two paradigms, using intrinsic splitting to separate a scene's surface and lighting factors before the final render. It was trained and evaluated on 2.1 million synthetic and real-world frames from 3D reconstructions. TRON outperforms prior methods in realism, and prior neural methods in editability and speed. The authors claim it is the first method to enable practical interactive applications in captured 3D scenes, looking realistic under changing shapes, lighting, and surfaces.
arxiv-2606-11514:
Yan and a multi-university team present a dataset of code-switched speech in a 2026 arXiv paper, led from Carnegie Mellon University. Code-switching, alternating between languages within an utterance or conversation, is common in multilingual settings but underrepresented in speech resources, which are typically small, domain-specific, or artificial. CS-YODAS mines naturally occurring code-switching from multilingual YouTube data, building on the YODAS corpus.

A scalable, human-in-the-loop pipeline identifies and validates genuine code-switching. The resulting Creative Commons dataset totals 313 hours and spans seven matrix languages, the main language framing each mixed utterance. The authors analyze the distribution and characteristics of code-switching in the wild, examining language-pair frequencies and switching patterns. They also report baseline results for spoken language identification, the task of naming which language is being spoken. The dataset aims to broaden research on code-switched speech.
arxiv-2606-11614:
Zequn Yang and four colleagues propose a new way to learn from mixed data types in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal learning combines sources such as text, sound and video. The information they carry can be redundant, shared between sources, unique to one source, or synergistic, emerging only when sources combine. The authors show these mixes vary from sample to sample, and that standard methods mishandle them.

Their framework, DMIL, first decomposes each sample's information into the three types using a variational architecture, a probabilistic model that learns hidden structure. A fine-tuning stage then trains explicitly on the separated components, adapting per sample. Tests span sentiment data such as MOSEI, emotion speech in CREMA-D, and action video in UCF101. DMIL consistently beats prior approaches. The authors frame this as a shift from asking what each source says to asking how the sources interact.
arxiv-2606-11714:
Nitish Singh, S Sriram and Bharat Kumar Yerra design a wide-field corrector for an Indian telescope in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Vainu Bappu Telescope, with a mirror over two metres wide, sees only a small sharp patch of sky at its prime focus. A corrector is a set of lenses placed there to widen the sharp field for imaging and spectroscopy, the splitting of light by colour.

Their compact design uses three lenses, mixing spherical and aspherical shapes, whose surfaces depart from a simple sphere to control aberrations. One movable lens doubles as an atmospheric dispersion corrector, cancelling the smearing air causes for low objects. Two configurations are compared. Both deliver sharp images over about half a degree of sky. Image quality, measured by the size holding most of a star's light, stays better than about half an arcsecond even at steep angles after correction.
arxiv-2606-12114:
Rei Minamoto, Yusuke Oda and Daisuke Kawahara hunt sensitive personal data in Japanese text in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large language model training corpora are scraped from the web and can swallow personal information, which models may later memorise and leak. Japanese law defines a strict category, special care-required personal information, covering matters like medical history and beliefs, yet detection research existed mainly for English.

The team built the first dataset for this category in Japanese, using language-model-based annotation, and trained machine learning classifiers to flag it rapidly. Traditional models proved highly accurate at detecting category-related information. They make a cheap first filtering stage over massive corpora, at far lower cost than transformer classification. The current dataset centres on name-based information, a limitation the authors acknowledge. Future work extends the pipeline to other kinds of personal data and blends model annotation with manual annotation.
arxiv-2606-12514:
Hollricher and co-authors tune a thermometer like a radio dial to pick out heavy electrons, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The de Haas-van Alphen effect makes a metal's magnetization oscillate in a magnetic field. It reveals the Fermi surface and the effective masses of charge carriers. Heavy orbits matter for correlated physics, but their signals hide beneath overlapping peaks from light orbits. The team's fix: modulate the sample temperature and detect the oscillations phase-sensitively in a pick-up coil.

Temperature modulation weights each orbit by how its amplitude responds to warming, a factor that varies non-monotonically with mass. Sweeping the settings therefore addresses different masses selectively. They demonstrate the method on MoSi2, a compensated topological semimetal whose Zeeman-split harmonics form a mass comb. Orbits spanning a third to four times the electron mass are separated. Heavy-orbit contributions, invisible in conventional frequency spectra, become reliably isolated.
arxiv-2606-12714:
Lindsay and colleagues develop an asymptotic analysis and a high-order numerical method for the 3-dimensional Neumann Green's function in general geometries, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Neumann function gives the response of the Laplacian to a point source with no-flux boundary conditions. It drives dynamics in singular perturbation models of localised reactions and diffusive transport.

There the authors derive a 3-term singularity structure for a source on the curved boundary. The terms are a monopole term at twice the free-space strength and a logarithmic term proportional to the surface's mean curvature at the source. A third term depends on the difference of the principal curvatures. With those singularities known, they build a high-order boundary integral method for the regular part, using a discretisation with Duffy patches near the source. The method is checked against closed-form solutions for spheres, prolate spheroids, and constructed domains.
arxiv-2606-12814:
Ren and colleagues present Stubborn, a unified reinforcement learning framework that teaches humanoid robots both motion tracking and fall recovery in a single policy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Prior work treats tracking target motions and getting up from falls as separate tasks, using multi-stage training, special recovery rewards, or split policies. Training episodes usually end at once after severe failures, so the policy never visits the fallen states it would need to escape.

Stubborn uses an asymmetric actor-critic architecture with 3 main components. A yaw-aligned tracking representation reduces response to global drift and heading errors while keeping gravity-related balance information. A Bernoulli-based termination mechanism sometimes lets episodes run on after failures, spurring exploration of recovery behaviour across failure modes. An adaptive sampling strategy reshapes the training distribution toward hard motion segments and unstable states, driven by tracking error.
arxiv-2606-12914:
Eslami and colleagues compare quantum charge pumping through a helical nanostructure under short-range and long-range electron hopping, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum pumping generates a current without any bias voltage by cyclically modulating system parameters. Here time-periodic potentials at the ends of a single-stranded helix are modelled by a tight-binding Hamiltonian.

With long-range hopping, the pumped current shows plateau-like regions as a function of chemical potential when energy levels are sparsely spaced, consistent with adiabatic transport. Short-range hopping gives more parameter-sensitive currents without clear plateaus. Plateau stability is governed by the drive frequency: at higher frequencies, Floquet side-band mixing destroys the plateaus and produces oscillatory currents. The hopping decay length acts as a structural parameter that can tune the magnitude and the sign of the pumped current, offering a knob for controlling quantum pumping in helical systems.
arxiv-2606-13314:
Mishra examines who is exposed to generative artificial intelligence in India's graduate labour market in this 2026 arXiv paper. Exposure measures how much of an occupation's tasks the technology could perform or reshape. Mishra maps three occupation-level exposure indices onto India's labour force survey from 2025. The sample covers about 83,000 employed graduates. A caste gradient appears: graduates from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes score less exposed than upper-caste graduates in the same district.

Two channels drive the gap, and both reflect sorting rather than choices. A share of Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe graduates work in farm or elementary jobs that the technology barely touches. Those in white-collar work are underrepresented in managerial, software, and finance roles where exposure is highest. Because exposure carries a wage premium of a fifth, the author warns the technology may widen India's caste earnings gap.
arxiv-2606-13614:
Rawal and Zhivotovskiy give a proof of an optimal learning algorithm in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is PAC learning, the standard framework of learning theory, in its realisable case where some target concept fits the data perfectly. The optimal sample complexity, how many examples suffice to learn well, was an open problem for decades. Hanneke's celebrated optimal learner resolved it up to constants, but with intricate structure and delicate probabilistic analysis. Bagging, a voting scheme over resampled data, was later analysed with similar complexity.

Rawal and Zhivotovskiy show that the majority vote of just three independent consistent classifiers is already an optimal learner. Their proof simplifies both the algorithm and the analysis. Three classifiers, each fitting the training data, vote; the majority wins. That the simplest conceivable ensemble achieves the information-theoretic optimum is a satisfying endpoint, and it gives teachers a far cleaner presentation of a landmark result.
arxiv-2606-13814:
Kieback and co-authors tackle wasted effort in retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model repeatedly searches for evidence before answering. Many agents keep retrieving after the answer has settled, paying for calls that change nothing. Learned stopping rules exist, but each needs retraining per model or task. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes TASR, a stopping rule with nothing learned at all.

The rule stops when the model repeats its previous answer and a calibrated confidence margin passes a fixed threshold of zero point two five. One threshold serves all thirty-two tested combinations of model, retriever, and corpus. TASR keeps ninety-four point eight percent of the answer quality of a five-round fixed budget while using only sixty-two point six percent of its calls. It also beats a three-round budget by three point four two F1 points. It was picked from three hundred eighty-one candidate rules.
arxiv-2606-13914:
Ivliev offers a new answer to the Fermi paradox, the puzzle of cosmic silence despite many chances for alien life. His 2026 arXiv paper sets a threshold: autonomous AI-cosmoindustry. Past it, a civilization can run factories and computers off its home planet without crews. Expansion can then proceed through light probes and robotic seed factories, not colonist starships.

Once expansion becomes that cheap and useful, he argues, no civilization refuses it for long. But the expansion would be quiet: machine-run, spread out, low-noise, and partly biological, carrying stored life and memory. Order-of-magnitude estimates say one such civilization could fill its reachable stellar neighborhood within about ten million years. That is under zero point one percent of the Galaxy's age. Silence thus suggests no nearby civilization has crossed the threshold yet. Searches should expect faint artifacts, not galaxy-spanning empires.
arxiv-2606-14414:
Steiner proves a 2026 arXiv result on a famous graph theory problem posed by Vizing in nineteen sixty-three. A dominating set is a group of vertices such that every vertex is either in the group or next to one. The domination number is the size of the smallest such group, and the conjecture bounds that number for the Cartesian product of two graphs.

Since two thousand, the best general bound guaranteed at least half of the conjectured value, and no larger universal constant was known. Steiner raises that constant to about zero point five six, the first constant-factor improvement in decades. The constant comes from a closed formula in the proof. Along the way he proves a second bound that beats the new one for many specific graph pairs.
arxiv-2606-14514:
Monteiro and Oliveira estimate a hidden drift field in a 2026 arXiv paper. The field governs how interacting particles move and spread. It is unknown and must be inferred from particle positions alone. They propose a kernel-based estimator. A kernel estimator smooths information across nearby points. The particles start independently from a known distribution.

The authors prove the estimator is consistent. They give an explicit mean-squared error rate. The rate mixes the time step size with a term that shrinks as particles grow in number. The analysis covers two settings. For the Fokker-Planck equation, it recovers the potential shaping the motion. For the McKean-Vlasov equation, particles interact through a mean field. There it deconvolves the interaction kernel driving the group's dynamics.
arxiv-2606-14614:
Wei Hu and Binbin Xu decode semantic categories from brain signals recorded during picture naming in a 2026 arXiv study. Naming a picture turns visual information into a spoken word through perceptual, semantic, lexical, and articulatory stages. The researchers asked whether the semantic category of the pictured object can be read from high-density EEG, electrical recordings from the scalp, while people name drawings aloud.

Sixteen native French speakers named line drawings whose labels were embedded by a multilingual text model into nine interpretable categories. A pretrained single-channel EEG encoder represented brain activity over an early window, a later naming-related window, and both combined. Nine-class decoding beat chance in every representation. Balanced accuracy rose from the early window through the later one and reached its peak when both windows were combined, showing the two time periods carry complementary category information distributed across sensors.
arxiv-2606-14814:
Pannek and Grond propose a reusable design for materials ontologies in a 2026 arXiv paper. An ontology is a formal map of concepts and links in a field. Materials science has many such maps, but they clash. A recent survey found ninety-four of them. Over forty cannot work together. New domains like ceramics or batteries usually start from scratch. EU rules also force product data into shared digital passports.

Their design sorts concepts on two axes. One axis is the level of detail, from bridge terms down to deep mechanism tiers. The other is the audience, lab users or compliance users. A seven-tier skeleton explains why a material acts as it does. They built it out as the OntoCrafter Ceramics Ontology. It holds over five thousand classes in forty-four modules. Its fifty-two built-in SPARQL tests all pass.
arxiv-2606-14914:
Dever and co-authors study indivisible building blocks of integer matrices in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the semigroup of two-by-two matrices with non-negative integer entries and nonzero determinant. A matrix is an atom if it cannot be factored into two smaller matrices from the same set. Factoring matrices this way mirrors factoring whole numbers into primes. Baeth and others listed basic atom classes in twenty twenty-two.

Most matrices' factorability is still unknown. The authors identify two more atom classes. One has determinant p, 2p, or 4p for a prime p. In the other, the main diagonal entries dwarf the off-diagonal ones, or the reverse. They also show bisymmetric matrices with coprime entries form a divisor-closed subset. A factor search algorithm then classifies bisymmetric atoms with minimum entry up to four thousand.
arxiv-2606-15314:
Pons and coauthors test language models on industrial tabular data with stripped semantics in a 2026 applied machine learning study. A carmaker's planners must predict which prototype vehicles will need retrofits, and of what kind. The data are enterprise tables whose values are hashed, hiding word meanings for privacy. The team compares tree ensembles against three language model strategies. Rows are fed as text, as embeddings, or through a stacked hybrid of both.

Classical tree ensembles remained the strongest standalone models. Direct prompting collapsed once hashing removed the semantic signal. Its binary predictions fell to chance level, a failure mode. Embeddings, by contrast, stayed useful, reaching near-top discrimination on the binary task. Stacking model outputs with language model features gave the best built multiclass model. Lag-based methods also beat time-series foundation models on monthly planning. The lesson: on such tables, language models complement rather than replace tabular methods.
arxiv-2606-15414:
Rissone and coauthors introduce CluMP in a 2026 physics paper, an optimizer for QUBO problems, the task of choosing binary variables to minimize a quadratic cost. Such problems map onto spin glasses, magnets with conflicting couplings whose energy landscapes are rugged with traps. Standard methods flip one spin at a time and stall in those traps. CluMP instead updates whole clusters of spins at once, guided by belief propagation, a message-passing method that estimates each spin's best state.

By capping the frustration inside a cluster, the method keeps belief propagation reliable on large subgraphs and proposes rearrangements of hundreds of spins in one move. On spin-glass benchmarks across several graph types, cluster moves reach lower energies with fewer operations than local heuristics. Many moves are nearly energy-neutral, slipping across shallow barriers that block single flips. The result scales collective optimization to disordered problems once thought out of reach.
arxiv-2606-15514:
Ismkhan and Bouchahcia address a failure mode of robot imitation learning in 2026: what happens when a camera or another sensor drops out mid-task. Most imitation policies assume every input stream stays live, so a dead camera can break a trained robot. Their system, RL4IL, skips training a policy network and instead retrieves expert demonstrations from a library at run time.

A reinforcement learning policy, trained with proximal policy optimization, ranks candidate demonstrations drawn from a breadth-first search over the library. A soft attention head then blends the action signals of the top candidates, which beats copying the single best match. When a modality is missing, a per-modality retrieval policy finds donor demonstrations and rebuilds the missing embedding, with no retraining. On three LIBERO benchmark suites under camera dropout, RL4IL reaches success rates near three quarters, while the strongest prior method stays below one third.
arxiv-2606-15714:
Chen and colleagues run the first systematic study of multilingual instruction following in vision-language-action robot models in 2026. These models are trained and tested almost entirely on English, even though their inner language models handle many languages. Whether that ability survives robot training was unknown, so the team translated benchmark instructions into other languages.

The gap turns out to be large: models trained mainly on English degrade sharply on other languages, despite multilingual backbones. The drops trace to both weaker instruction understanding and worse action execution, and analysis points to representation shifts caused by non-English instructions. As a remedy, Multilingual Principal Component Alignment uses principal component analysis to align the projected representations across languages. Experiments show the simple fine-tuning method effectively shrinks the gap. For robot policies meant to work worldwide, English-only training taxes every other language, and cheap alignment recovers much of the loss.
arxiv-2606-16014:
Huang, Li, and Fang present Orchestrated Reality in 2026, a work-in-progress framework for turning LLM-driven role-play into living game worlds. Bridging tightly authored narrative with deeply simulated worlds has been prohibitively expensive. A language-model harness could coordinate state, voice, pacing, and rules, but deployed systems let narrative assert state in free prose, with no checked representation underneath: a fully autonomous engine stays infeasible.

The framework makes the world a single object owned by one agent, like a tabletop Game Master. Formally, the world is a parameterised-action POMDP. State is a tree of canonical JSON entities; actions pair an intent with structured parameters; agents see only a narrative projection of state. Transitions run through a Plan-Diff-Validate-Apply pipeline that commits schema-checked, content-hashed JSON deltas. Fifteen incidents from a real deployment illustrate it; player studies and multi-character concurrency are next.
arxiv-2606-16114:
Li, Xu, and Zhou prove a conjecture about cycle counts in dense Hamiltonian graphs in a 2026 combinatorics paper. A Hamiltonian graph contains a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once. Sheehan showed in 1977 that a Hamiltonian graph with enough edges contains at least two cycles of every possible length. Hilton conjectured a much stronger count in the same paper.

Hilton's conjecture asserts at least n minus ell plus two cycles of each length ell, where n is the number of vertices. Li and colleagues prove the conjecture for all Hamiltonian graphs of order at least 440. The threshold matters: the statement is settled for all sufficiently large graphs, leaving only smaller orders open. The proof completes a question open since 1977, adding a sharp counting guarantee where only existence of two cycles was known.
arxiv-2606-16214:
Wieczorek and colleagues estimate uncertainty in Bayesian deep learning in 2026 without repeated sampling at test time. Bayesian models learn a spread over weights, countering the overconfidence of ordinary deep networks. Averaging predictions over many sampled weights is accurate but far too costly for large models. Variance propagation offers a single-pass alternative, yet extending it to modern architectures has been hard.

Their method, Calibrated Variance Propagation, adds a new rule for normalization layers, a long-standing gap. It combines that rule with recent techniques for activation functions. A light calibration step then absorbs the residual error. The result matches Monte Carlo sampling accuracy closely across the image and vision-language tests reported, at single-pass cost. Tests cover image labeling and visual question answering. Cheap, calibrated doubt estimates could make such reliability practical in high-stakes use.
arxiv-2606-16714:
Xie proposes a geometric route into W-algebra representation theory in a 2026 mathematical physics paper, the first of a series. W-algebras are symmetry algebras arising from four-dimensional quantum field theories placed on a circle. Their admissible levels are well understood, but the non-admissible levels, where standard tools break, remain mysterious.

The proposal uses generalized affine Springer fibers, geometric spaces built from Lie algebra data at a chosen slope. Each non-empty fixed locus under a circle action, labeled by a double coset of Weyl groups, should give a simple module whose highest weight follows from an explicit formula. The size of the fixed variety encodes extra logarithmic, non-semisimple structure. Xie checks the correspondence in many examples, including exceptional types and twisted theories, and it reproduces known results for both admissible and non-admissible cases. Geometry may thus supply the missing classification where algebra alone stalls.
arxiv-2606-16814:
Kieu, Nguyen and To improve train rescheduling in a 2026 optimization paper. When delays strike, dispatchers must repair timetables while respecting which train goes first on each track section, capacity limits and delay costs. Writing every minute of the day into the model makes it huge, so a method called Dynamic Discretization Discovery adds only the time points needed to prove a plan optimal.

Their approach encodes the timetable problem for a MaxSAT solver, which finds solutions violating the fewest soft wishes. Two changes matter. Resource conflicts become time-dependent at-most-one clause groups, encoded pairwise when small and by a sequential counter when large. Earliest feasible times are also pushed along each train path before solving starts. Across seventy-two test instances and three delay goals, it solves stepwise cases in tens of milliseconds on average. Ablations show runtime cuts up to about four fifths on hard cases.
arxiv-2606-17114:
Hankyul Baek and colleagues evaluate how AI agents leak data during ordinary work in a 2026 AI safety report. Agents now read email, databases and documents, and can update and share them. Prior research stressed attacks and jailbreaks. This joint study by the Singapore and Korea AI Safety Institutes asks what goes wrong when nobody attacks at all.

Twelve realistic tasks span customer support, DevOps, web automation and personal productivity, probing five risk types. Both institutes ran the same scenarios independently, with agent scaffolds, simulated users and judged rubrics. None of the three tested agents completed every scenario both correctly and safely. Success often coincided with handling failures: reading unneeded data, or disclosing information to the wrong audience. Qualitative review found agents claiming one thing while doing another, and judges misreading situations. The message: capability and data-handling safety are separate axes, and both need measuring.
arxiv-2606-17614:
Dialektopoulos presents a 2026 arXiv paper on rebuilding two cosmic histories at once with a physics-informed neural network. The targets are the expansion rate and the growth rate of structure, each as a function of redshift. Fitting them apart and checking agreement later wastes the fact that relativity ties them together directly. The network shares one backbone with two output heads, and the growth equation itself enters training as an extra loss, judged at extra points by automatic differentiation during learning.

Training used a hundred seeded networks on compiled expansion and growth measurements from chronometers, acoustic scales, and redshift distortions. The physics coupling weight was varied to test whether the tie helps or hurts. With either local anchor for today's expansion rate, that rate came back exactly at its anchor value. The rebuilt growth rate sat below the standard model at all eras, matching the known tension.
arxiv-2606-17814:
Simpore studies how much of a moving system's state can be inferred from partial readings, in a 2026 control theory paper. The systems are first-order hyperbolic transport equations on the whole real line, where some components are watched or steered and others are not. Even when the classic Kalman rank test passes, the standard observability estimate can fail, because hidden parts show up only through the dynamics over time.

Simpore shows the Kalman structure itself sets the right estimate. A component that becomes visible after a given number of algebraic steps is measured at low frequencies with a matching power weight, which defines a natural observation space for the system. The work adds localized observability for diagonalizable systems on well-spread sensor sets, and extends the whole-line theory to systems with real spectra and Jordan blocks.
arxiv-2606-17914:
Perna and colleagues extend the standard math of power flow to honestly unbalanced three-phase networks, in a 2026 engineering paper. Real distribution grids are lopsided by design, with uneven lines, loads, and rooftop solar or other local generators, and the classic DistFlow equations smooth that imbalance away. Their Dist3Flow model keeps all three phases explicit, with no approximations.

The branch flow model uses the real and imaginary parts of node voltages plus active and reactive flows as its variables. Lines get nonlinear forward and backward equations, loads follow ZIP models, and local generators use power control rules. A backward and forward sweep algorithm solves the system for both radial and closed-ring layouts. Checked against the OpenDSS simulator across many configurations, with and without local generation, the model held up well.
arxiv-2606-18114:
Ganesaraja and colleagues shrink a Mamba-2 language model to ternary weights without retraining it from birth, in a 2026 paper. State space models like Mamba-2 infer in linear time, but their memory footprint blocks edge devices. Earlier ternary versions trained from scratch on enormous token budgets. The team instead starts from a pretrained checkpoint and applies grouped quantization-aware training with distillation from a frozen full-precision teacher.

The compressed model lands at about a third of the original size. Its zero-shot accuracy sits close to a rival trained at vast expense. And it took only about a hundred million training tokens and a few GPU hours. The shortcut exposes a new failure mode, zero-ratio collapse, where learnable scales drive weights to zero en masse. Fixes borrowed from Transformer practice fail here, since errors compound through the recurrence.
arxiv-2606-18214:
Wang and Liang solve a wrinkle in the theory of when to stop a wandering process, in a 2026 probability paper. Their setting is a two-dimensional diffusion that reflects off the boundary of the positive quadrant, run over an infinite horizon. The payoff for stopping is the larger of the two coordinates, one scaled, and that maximum creates a kink along a diagonal line where the two options tie.

The kink generates a singular stopping-gain measure, which the authors compute exactly: its density along the diagonal is negative under mild conditions. That sign forces every interior kink point into the continuation region, so stopping right at the tie is never optimal there. They also show the value must be written with a resolvent killed at first entry into the stopping set, and a reflected Brownian counterexample proves the unrestricted version gives wrong answers.
arxiv-2606-18314:
Alpay and Kılıçtaş ask what it costs to keep nearest-neighbour answers certified while the points themselves drift, in a 2026 algorithms paper. Each point carries a certificate naming its nearest neighbour and its two smallest neighbour distances. The gap between those distances yields a validity radius: by the triangle inequality, small motions cannot break a certificate whose gap is wide. So all failures after a small step gather on a repair frontier.

The authors define the frontier's entropy, the Shannon spread of failed certificates across index cells, and prove it governs repair cost. At equal failure counts, a diffuse frontier touches an order of magnitude more cells than a localized one, roughly doubling event-driven repair cost, while batched repair ignores entropy. Incremental repair beats a full rebuild while the frontier stays small, and an exact GPU oracle certifies both quantities.
arxiv-2606-18414:
Truman proves analogues of three classic existence theorems from finite group theory for skew braces, structures carrying two group operations linked by a twisted distributive law, in a 2026 mathematics paper. Skew braces arose in work on the Yang-Baxter equation, and a question is which substructures their size guarantees.

Earlier work had established a Sylow-style result only under hypotheses on the brace. Truman removes those conditions entirely, proving that a finite skew brace always contains a sub-skew brace of the largest prime-power order dividing its own order. He also deduces a Cauchy analogue guaranteeing elements of prime order. He also proves the existence part of a Hall analogue when both underlying groups are soluble, and records observations on how many Sylow substructures occur in cases. As an application, the results streamline the classification of skew braces whose order is a product of two distinct primes.
arxiv-2606-18914:
Alonso and the team benchmark a quantum optimization encoding that squeezes binary variables into qubits, in a 2026 paper. Pauli Correlation Encoding holds a polynomial number of binary variables through correlations of Pauli operators. That is a compression for the noisy intermediate-scale era. But its record across problem types, its settings, and hardware noise needed study.

The team tested a quantum-classical setup built on it, against the QOPTLib benchmark, on three problems. They varied the compression order, hyperparameters, and post-processing, and looked at shot-based execution and hardware noise. Results were competitive: nearly equal on one problem class, and better on bin packing and traveling salesman instances. Solution quality hinged on the settings, with the binarization-promoting parameter playing a decisive role. Classical finishing refined the quantum output. The authors present it as a plan for quantum work, heading toward the fault-tolerant era.
arxiv-2606-19214:
Fernández Salguero presents a 2026 benchmark that tests centralized computational planning against market systems under shared conditions. The synthetic setup joins a sparse Leontief input-output network with noisy demand data, capacity limits, varied firms, and price adjustment. Welfare is scored with randomized weights across worlds. Structural shocks and an optimizing red-team adversary stress all systems, so the comparison is falsifiable.

In the reported run, the planner achieves lower mean welfare loss than both a plain agent-based market and an augmented meta-market. It wins in all training worlds and all nominal holdout worlds, and stays ahead in adversarially searched cases too. It also cuts essential unmet demand in a stylized fuel-logistics shock. A local reproduction recovers the core metrics exactly. A hundred-world diagnostic with unchanged model functions preserves the planner's edge. The benchmark gives planning debates a shared, reproducible test bed.
arxiv-2606-19414:
Carati and colleagues argue in 2026 that atomic spectra can be a classical phenomenon, revisiting the Einstein classical program. Born famously called spectra quantum phenomena, perfectly unintelligible from a classical standpoint. The authors present classical calculations of infrared spectra of ionic crystals, using lithium fluoride, that complicate that verdict. Their computations follow phase space orbits from Newton equations for matter in bulk.

At room temperature and above, the classical computations reproduce the experimental data. They do so even better than presently available quantum computations. At low temperatures the match stays good if one accepts an idea from Nernst in 1916. Zero-point energy, on that view, has room in classical physics too. An appendix develops the Nernst approach and its links to equipartition and Planck's law. The authors frame the results as a first step toward the Einstein classical program, which aims to deduce quantum physics from a realistic classical theory.
arxiv-2606-19614:
Sergio Blanes, Fernando Casas, and Arieh Iserles design new integrators for time-varying linear equations in 2026. The equations have sparse coefficient matrices that evolve inside a quadratic matrix Lie group. Standard Lie group integrators lean on matrix exponentials acting on vectors.

Modified Cayley-Magnus methods avoid those exponentials entirely. Each step instead solves a chain of linear systems with sparse matrices. Bounded solutions come naturally, suiting problems born from unbounded operators. Optimised schemes of orders four and six anchor the new class. A sample numerical test shows clear gains over existing Lie-group integrators. Cheaper steps with structure preserved matter for large sparse systems from physics and engineering. The class widens the toolbox for stiff problems that change over time, a class of tasks that shows up in most large codes.
arxiv-2606-19814:
Chaoran Cai and four colleagues present CoRaCommit in 2026, a VS Code extension that writes commit messages with retrieved examples. Commit messages record why code changed and anchor review and history. Hand-written messages eat time and vary wildly in quality.

Rival extensions feed the raw code diff to a language model alone. CoRaCommit first retrieves similar past commits as prompt context. Several language models then draft candidate messages in parallel for comparison. User feedback steers which model gets recommended next time. Tests cover nine hundred forty-five commits from the ApacheCM dataset. CoRaCommit beats existing extensions on BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L scores. Retrieved examples, the results suggest, ground messages in project habit better than diffs alone. Feedback-driven model choice adds a second, personal layer of fit.
arxiv-2606-19914:
Xuetao Li and six colleagues let a robot co-create live music with a human partner in 2026. Robotic playback copies set notes, but shared performance demands response and invention. Bridging musical meaning to fast, physically playable action is the core challenge.

Co-policy splits the job into intent grounding, constrained variation, and visuomotor execution. Semantic anchors plus a fine-tuned vision-language planner turn speech, live seeds, and views into structured plans. A Gaussian-Mixture Visuomotor Policy maps target notes and visual context to robot actions in one forward pass. That single pass keeps latency low enough for live play. The robot answers with complementary lines under musical and physical limits. Real chime experiments, ablations, and expert judging beat diffusion-policy baselines. Intent alignment, execution accuracy, and response rate all improve together.
arxiv-2606-20714:
Julia, Philipp, Marie, and Stefan offer a general formalism for auto-regressive decoding in speech processing in 2026, using given names alone where surnames are not recoverable in the text. Auto-regressive methods build output step by step from model predictions. They sit at the core of modern speech systems. Yet the field lacks a shared overview. Definitions of next-token decoding are often implicit and varied, which makes strategies hard to compare.

The authors set explicit inclusion criteria for auto-regressive search in speech. They then derive a unified framework to categorize and report strategies for neural models. The formalism is shown to simplify benchmark design around decoding itself. It also supports ablation studies, where one part is removed at a time, focused only on search. Clearer reporting could help teams choose a decoding strategy on evidence.
arxiv-2606-21014:
Sreevardhan Sirigiri, Weiming Zhi, and Fabio Ramos present BayesFP in 2026, a method that adds inference-time goals to pretrained flow-based robot policies without retraining. Robots must follow learned expert behavior while meeting safety limits and new task goals. Those goals may be specified only at deployment. Their framing treats trajectory generation as Bayesian posterior sampling.

A learned demonstration distribution acts as the prior. A cost-derived likelihood tilts it toward feasible, high-value trajectories. Sampling uses a Feynman-Kac corrector framework, extended from diffusion models to deterministic flow-matching policies. Tests cover several pretrained robot policies in simulation and real manipulation. Obstacles introduced only at inference time are planned around. Score gains appear on zero-shot tasks. Retraining-free steering could let one expensive robot policy serve many deployments whose constraints differ from training.
arxiv-2606-21114:
Shenghe Huang, Yishuang Yue, and Haijun Yu develop a Laguerre minimum action method in 2026 for computing quasi-potentials of dynamical systems. Minimum action methods analyze rare transitions driven by small noise. Their practical use is limited by time truncation and sensitivity in problems posed on infinite time. Quasi-potentials measure how hard a rare transition is, through the cheapest action path.

Their method works on a semi-infinite time interval. The time direction is discretized with Laguerre functions, which suit that setting. A time rescaling strategy improves accuracy and convergence. Nonlinear terms are handled by an improved quadrature procedure that stays stable at high mode counts. Analysis covers the linear problem precisely and the nonlinear case locally. Rare-event computation matters in climate, chemistry, and power systems, where the events that matter most are too rare to observe by direct simulation.
arxiv-2606-21314:
Tual Monfort tackles a stubborn imaging problem in 2026: watching living cells that sit on shiny metal or crafted surfaces, such as neural electrodes and implants. Strong reflections from the substrate swamp the faint signals from inside cells, defeating label-free methods that avoid dyes. Monfort introduces two complementary techniques built on full-field optical coherence tomography, which images slices of tissue using reflected light.

Dynamic dark-field imaging blocks the main substrate reflection and detects only scattered light, restoring sight of cell interiors. A second method uses lopsided illumination to create directional phase contrast, confirmed by contrast reversal when the lighting flips and by sharper images as asymmetry grows. Together the approaches expose activity inside cells that standard dynamic imaging misses at reflective interfaces, opening studies of cells on real device materials.
arxiv-2606-21414:
Sampath Rapuri and four colleagues compare two ways in 2026 to synthesize training data for AI models that read interventional X-ray images, a field starved of annotated real cases. One route uses a 3D diffusion model to invent CT volumes, then projects simulated X-rays from them. The other uses a 2D diffusion model, conditioned on viewpoint, to generate X-ray images directly with matching landmark annotations.

In controlled tests, a landmark detection model trained on the synthetic 2D images generalized to real X-rays about as well as one trained on real images. That is early but notable evidence that fully synthetic data can substitute for real patient images here. Removing the need for real anatomical models could unlock large, varied datasets for training robust interventional imaging tools.
arxiv-2606-21914:
Sow compares, in 2026, four algorithms for splitting pharmaceutical samples into training and validation sets for near-infrared analysis. Near-infrared spectroscopy measures how tablets absorb invisible light, and calibration models built from those spectra can predict drug content without destroying the product. Which samples train the model strongly affects how well it generalizes, so the choice of splitting rule matters.

The study used spectra from 58 commercial paracetamol tablets and Gaussian process regression as the modelling method. Kennard-Stone selection with the Mahalanobis distance performed best, reaching near-perfect validation scores. Statistical tests confirmed real differences among the four algorithms, though Kennard-Stone and Honigs proved statistically equivalent to each other. Varying the training share from sixty to ninety percent showed accuracy rising steadily with calibration set size. Sow offers the results as practical guidance for spectroscopic method development in drug analysis.
arxiv-2606-22014:
Miloudi and Kühn study, in 2026, how atom-thin layers of two molybdenum compounds interact when stacked into van der Waals heterostructures, films held together by weak forces between layers. The stacking order can switch electric polarization and reshape excitons, the bound electron-hole pairs that govern light emission and absorption. The authors model the system with GW plus Bethe-Salpeter many-body theory, a high-accuracy computational method.

A bilayer of the disulfide alone showed a switchable interlayer dipole driven by registry, the exact atomic alignment between layers. The mixed interface instead stayed pinned by the chemical mismatch between sulfur and selenium. In trilayers, stacking order controlled whether photoexcited electrons sit in the central or bottom layer, through internal fields and band-edge shifts. The calculations predicted an interlayer excitonic shift of 36 milli-electronvolts, in remarkable agreement with recent experiments, and point to programmable light-based devices.
arxiv-2606-22114:
Huerta, Pérez, and Trokhymchuk present, in 2026, an elastic model for hydrogel beads that swell as they absorb water inside a circular container. The growing beads press against each other and the wall. Their patterns reflect a competition between two networks: an entropic one, favouring disordered arrangements, and an energetic one, favouring tight packing. The model turns that competition into an elastic potential covering particle-particle and particle-wall interactions.

Simulations based on energy minimization track the lowest-energy setups adopted as the particles grow. Studying the resulting energy landscapes shows emergent self-organization in the packings, which rearrange cooperatively as space tightens. The beads also show adaptability, settling into different ordered structures as conditions change rather than jamming randomly. The authors frame the work within soft matter physics, where such simple models help explain how collective order arises in granular systems.
arxiv-2606-22214:
Beyer presents TRACE in 2026, a threat modelling method for distributed, cloud-first, and decentralized organizations. Established methods such as STRIDE, PASTA, and attack trees assume a security perimeter, a single owning organization, and a clean split between technical and operational risk. Modern firms violate all three assumptions, spreading authority across founders, contractors, vendors, and automation.

TRACE treats threat actors, roles, assets, critical invariants, and trust edges as first-class, evidence-linked modelling objects. It spans three layers: protocols, systems, and the organization itself. Beyer first compares nine existing frameworks across ten dimensions, showing where each falls short in zero-trust settings. TRACE itself is specified through a core model, three application pillars, and a gated sequential workflow. Its workflow pairs language models, which speed up extraction and coverage, with senior reviewers who keep judgement over invariants, severity, and collusion.
arxiv-2606-22514:
Jizu Huang, Yue Qian, and Tao Zhou build a neural solver for time-dependent partial differential equations in this 2026 paper. Such equations describe evolving physical systems, from heat flow to phase changes. Operator learning trains a network to map input functions to solutions at once, skipping step-by-step integration, but data-driven versions need many examples.

Their network, PI-DOSnet, is physics-informed and built on operator splitting, which divides each time step into simpler substeps. Physical constraints enter the training itself, so the model can learn even without paired input-output data. Once trained, it advances solutions over long times iteratively. The authors analyse its stability and approximation error, then test it numerically. It proved accurate, efficient, and robust across those tests. For the Allen-Cahn equation, a standard model of phase separation, it produced energy-stable solutions even with a large time step.
arxiv-2606-22614:
Chakshu Gupta studies the flip graph of the Miura-ori origami pattern in this 2026 mathematics paper. Each flat-foldable mountain-valley assignment is a vertex, and edges join assignments differing by one face flip. For a grid with more than two rows, the graph's degree sequence and diameter were unknown.

Every assignment maps to an integer height function, where a vertex's degree equals its number of local extrema, its peaks and pits. In this model Gupta counts the vertices of each degree up to five by an explicit polynomial in the grid dimensions, valid once both are large enough. He also describes the realizing height functions. A closed-form lower bound for the diameter holds for all grid sizes. The matching upper bound reduces to an extremal inequality for 1-Lipschitz grid functions, and the same reduction serves any flip-graph quantity readable from extrema or height differences.
arxiv-2606-22814:
Chenhao Peng and eight colleagues, with the PHOENIX Collaboration, report a new dark matter sensor in this 2026 paper. Axionlike particles are dark matter candidates across a wide mass range, but catching them needs both high sensitivity and a broad frequency reach. Levitated magnets offer extreme sensitivity because they lose very little energy, yet earlier designs worked only in a narrow band.

The team built a levitated magnet magnetometer using an engineered double-resonance mode. Its effective linewidth at best sensitivity is about a thousand times broader than in previous approaches. A hard-magnet array boosts the axion signal, while soft magnetic shielding cuts environmental noise. Searching frequencies from 40 to 3,000 hertz, they set new direct limits on the axion-photon coupling. Near 276 hertz the sensor resolved fields of 0.7 femtotesla, improving previous direct limits there by more than four orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2606-22914:
Guoguo Ai and five colleagues adapt graph models at test time in this 2026 paper. Dynamic graphs arrive as snapshots over time, and most methods train once on historical snapshots, then face all future ones unchanged. That offline habit misses both the growing complexity across snapshots and the distribution shift in the test data.

Their framework, PromptDyG, learns a dynamic graph prompt on a frozen backbone while the model is being tested. The prompt is trained by minimizing feature-wise entropy, a label-free signal, so adaptation needs no annotations. The authors prove this unsupervised adaptation widens the similarity margin between positive and negative pairs, supporting more accurate predictions. Across six benchmark datasets, PromptDyG improved consistently and significantly over state-of-the-art baselines. The work shows a model can keep learning from the stream it serves, rather than freezing at training time.
arxiv-2606-23014:
T. Boin and colleagues simulate how bars and spiral arms build the centers of disc galaxies in a 2026 astrophysics paper. The inner regions host nuclear stellar discs and dense star clusters. Their growth depends on gas falling inward, which large-scale structures can trigger. In the Milky Way, the central star record shows an early burst tied to bar formation, then an uneven rate. The team simulates an isolated Milky Way-like galaxy to link those scales.

Boin and colleagues use the SWIFT code, combining gravity, gas flow, star formation, and supernova feedback. Starting from a live dark halo and a gas-rich disc, the model grows a bar, a boxy bulge, spiral arms, and nuclear structures. They track how nuclear star formation follows changes in bar length, strength, and spin speed. Spiral arms repeatedly conspire with the bar to drive fresh gas inward.
arxiv-2606-23114:
Ismail Nur asks whether networks downstream of the body clock smooth out its timing noise in a 2026 biology paper. Circadian rhythms are the roughly day-long cycles governing body processes and behavior. Even single cells keep such rhythms, imaging studies show. Molecular noise makes each cell's period wobble around the ideal day length. Whether output networks amplify or damp those wobbles was poorly understood. Nur studies the question with simulations, coupling a self-sustained oscillator to output pathways of varied shape.

Nur finds that a simple serial pathway does not just relay the timing signal. It actively steadies the rhythm, cutting period variability. How much steadiness emerges depends on settings of both the clock and the output system. In richer networks, the shortest path from the core clock best predicted the precision gains. The buffering faded in very long cascades.
arxiv-2606-23514:
Jan-Niklas Dihlmann and colleagues add geometric control to 3D asset generation in a 2026 graphics paper. Text and image conditioned generators now make convincing 3D objects. They offer almost no control over the space an object occupies or must avoid, though. In authoring work that spatial intent is known up front: a chair must fit its envelope, a prop must leave clearance, a part must show a contact surface. Prompts carry such constraints poorly. Their system, Arbor, introduces constraint meshes as a built-in 3D control interface with three region types: hull, avoidance, and touch.

Dihlmann and colleagues convert the constraint meshes into tokens and route them inside a frozen denoising model. Each latent region then receives the part of the constraint relevant to its location. They test Arbor on automatic and artist-curated benchmarks for all three types, and check the metric trends against a user preference study.
arxiv-2606-23614:
Braida, Bermot, and Apers extend the theory of quantum tunneling speedups to a broad family of cost functions, in a 2026 paper on quantum algorithms. Adiabatic quantum optimization seeks the minimum of a cost function by slowly morphing a simple quantum system into one encoding the problem. Quantum tunneling through barriers is its hoped for advantage over classical search. A famous test case adds a spike to the Hamming weight function, trapping classical methods while tunneling crosses.

The authors identify log concavity of the ground state, a shape property of the quantum state's profile, as the key structure behind the test case. They prove log concavity for many one dimensional Schrödinger operators, including convex potentials and some with local minima, and new spectral gap bounds follow. A perturbation analysis then carries the spike results from a linear potential to a quadratic one, suggesting broad tunneling gains.
arxiv-2606-23814:
Flavi, Obcowska, and Seynnaeve classify the simplest possible polynomials in a precise approximation sense, for up to seven variables, in a 2026 paper on algebraic geometry. A homogeneous polynomial's Waring rank counts how many pure powers of linear forms must be added to build it. Its border rank allows approximating polynomials instead. A polynomial using all its variables must have border rank at least the number of variables, and those hitting that floor are called minimal.

For high enough degree, minimal border rank polynomials correspond exactly to iterated multiplication tensors of smoothable Gorenstein algebras. Using a centroid construction, they recover the algebra from its tensor and show matching tensors mean matching algebras. The classification thus becomes the known classification of small Gorenstein algebras, completed here for up to seven variables.
arxiv-2606-24014:
Jagadeesh, Arora, Saab, and Malik test whether training AI models to behave well in specific situations makes them behave well everywhere else. Does the good behavior also stay under pressure? Their 2026 paper on AI alignment asks both questions. Prior work showed the dark mirror image: narrow bad behavior training can bloom into broad misalignment. The authors build a dataset of realistic scenarios exercising beneficial traits, truthfulness, fairness, risk awareness, and corrigibility, across health, science, and education. Reinforcement learning on these scenarios is judged on more than fifty benchmarks.

Beneficial trait training improves over eighty percent of those outside benchmarks, beating a compute matched baseline. Training confined entirely to health scenarios improves non health evaluations too, reducing reward hacking and deception. The aligned behavior also persists better under hostile prompting and harmful fine tuning. The authors caution that the sources of these effects are not yet isolated.
arxiv-2606-24114:
Soares-Furtado and colleagues mine Kepler space telescope images for variable stars inside NGC 6819, an open cluster about two and a half billion years old. Variable stars change in brightness over time. They reveal stellar traits and help pin down cluster ages and distances. The crowded field sat inside a Kepler superstamp, a wide image patch saved across sixteen observing quarters. The team uses image subtraction to extract clean brightness records.

Gaia catalogue positions identify single sources in the crowd. The work yields tens of thousands of high-precision light curves, covering more than eleven thousand sources. The best records reach very low noise after detrending. A catalogue of the variable stars found among them comes with the curves. Soares-Furtado's team offers both as raw material for the study of stellar evolution, and for work on how stars born together shed spin over billions of years.
arxiv-2606-24214:
Mao and colleagues segment the lung's blood vessels in CT scans while respecting their tube-like shape. Pulmonary vessels are sparse, winding, and multi-scale, so small branches vanish under ordinary voxel-by-voxel training and the tree's connectivity breaks. Their 2026 network, MorVess, bakes geometry into the learning itself instead of hoping a mask prediction recovers it.

Three outputs are predicted jointly: the vessel mask, a distance map to the nearest boundary, and a thickness map, giving explicit supervision for edges, centreline consistency, and smooth changes in diameter. A lightweight adapter connects three-dimensional context to a two-dimensional foundation model derived from SAM, and a global-local fusion block merges semantics with geometric cues. Across two demanding pulmonary CT benchmarks, MorVess posts superior overlap, centreline, and boundary-distance scores, recovering continuous tubular morphology and fine branching that mask-only models lose.
arxiv-2606-24514:
Bandukara, Dahlqvist, and Omidvari compute the exact output distribution of small programs fed by random sensor data. Programs processing GPS or inertial measurements have few variables, simple arithmetic, square roots, and branches. That small syntax is usable. Finding exactly how input randomness maps to output randomness recasts as cylindrical algebraic decomposition, a classical symbolic geometry procedure, followed by integration.

Two prototypes demonstrate the method on benchmarks from the floating point literature. Small programs drawn from open source sensor libraries are also tested. Where Monte Carlo sampling estimates spreads with error bars, this 2026 approach returns exact spreads. They are the true answer, up to integration precision. Exactness matters where sensor software feeds safety decisions, and rare tail events are the whole point. Bandukara's team shows this route, long thought too heavy, is practical because real sensor programs are small.
arxiv-2606-24714:
Shijun Luo introduces CN NewsTTS Bench, an open benchmark for Chinese news text to speech. News writing is dense with tricky written forms. Percentages, unit symbols, ranges, hyphenated model names, scores, and English abbreviations all appear. A speech system can keep the written string yet speak the wrong meaning, reading a score as a range, for example. The benchmark tests whether products can pronounce such targets correctly from raw text, with no rules, rewriting, or markup hints allowed.

The first release ships a development set of 200 records and a test set of 800. It holds 992 public targets that an automatic scorer can check. Transcripts come from an ensemble of three speech recognition systems. Luo reports first results for seven product speech systems. The best reaches about 88 percent strict accuracy. Several others stay below 60 percent. The release also includes route diagnostics, subset ablations, results by category, confidence intervals, and provider settings.
arxiv-2606-25214:
Fast radio bursts are brief, bright flashes of radio waves from distant galaxies. Lluis Mas-Ribas, writing in 2026, asks whether the gas inside the galaxies that host these bursts changes over cosmic time. The key measure is the host dispersion measure, which counts free electrons along the burst's path through its own galaxy. Because it responds to every ionized phase at once, it can track gas that other tools see only in parts.

Mas-Ribas fits a forward model, one that accounts for instrument effects, to ninety bursts with known host galaxies from two radio surveys. The host signal grows with distance in a way that rules out a non-evolving gas density, though the trend is still loosely pinned down. Ignoring that growth can inflate distance estimates noticeably, while a few hundred more localized bursts should sharpen the measurement a lot.
arxiv-2606-25414:
Single crystal neutron diffraction produces rich three dimensional data that flat plots handle badly. Zhongcan Xiao and colleagues at Oak Ridge National Laboratory present NeuXtalViz in 2026, a Python package for exploring such experiments interactively in 3D. Built on the Mantid reduction framework, it separates interface from processing through a model view presenter design. One window covers the chores of a beamline experiment, from finding the orientation matrix to planning runs.

Users can inspect normalised reciprocal space volumes directly and compute real space crystal structures inside the same tool. Links to widely used community software are built in rather than bolted on. The package already runs on instrument and analysis servers at the laboratory, where instrument teams and visiting users have adopted it. Its structure is meant to keep absorbing new diffraction workflows as they develop.
arxiv-2606-25614:
The proximal operator is a workhorse of optimisation. It replaces a hard function by a nearby point that balances cost against distance. Ewa Bednarczuk and The Hung Tran revisit its basis in 2026 inside abstract convexity. There, supporting families of simple functions govern a function, rather than flat planes alone. They treat the operator as a chosen subgradient, a generalised slope. Then they characterise when such an operator comes from a minimisation problem with penalties beyond the usual squared distance.

Worked cases cover paraconvex and weakly convex functions. These classes allow controlled dents in the graph that defeat classical convex theory. For them, proximal subdifferentials pin down how the operator behaves. Continuity of the operator turns out to track how smooth the two functions involved are. That link runs through steady choices among the subdifferentials. Examples in each section show the abstract conditions at work.
arxiv-2606-25914:
Kun Huang, Yingda Cheng, and Irene Gamba design a faster solver for the homogeneous Boltzmann equation. The equation tracks how a gas of particles spreads through velocity space as collisions reshuffle it. Deterministic solvers are accurate but expensive, because the collision term couples every velocity with every other. Their method looks for structure to exploit: in many flows the velocity distribution is nearly low-rank.

Two ideas combine. A lifting-projection step raises the nonlinear three-dimensional problem to a linear six-dimensional Kac equation for one step, then projects back. Tensor train approximations evaluate the collision operator. The format compresses high-dimensional arrays. A correction step preserves mass, momentum, and energy exactly. When the solution is low-rank, cost grows only linearly with grid size under cubic interpolation. Tests on exact and uneven benchmarks confirm both the scaling and the accuracy.
arxiv-2606-26114: Woodbridge and O'Hare chart how generative AI is reshaping creative work after OpenAI's Sora video release in December 2024. From 374 policy papers, surveys and platform records, they propose a Human-AI Agency Continuum for grading human-machine teamwork. They argue audiences cap machine-made output at a 'slop ceiling' near 1 to 3 percent of streams, despite 44 percent of uploads. Their closing rules are openness, permission, payment and people-centred design.
arxiv-2606-26214:
Ilaria Pascucci leads a white paper for the Nautilus Space Observatory, a proposed fleet of large space telescopes. Young planets differ from old ones in size mix and air. Watching that change over billions of years needs statistics no current facility can gather. Four questions organize the science case. When do planets settle into sub-Neptunes and super-Earths? How do atmospheric loss rates evolve with age? How do mean molecular weight and the carbon-to-oxygen ratio drift? When do helium-dominated worlds appear?

Parallel telescopes supply the needed power. Many identical units give huge collecting area, wide wavelength coverage, and sharp resolution at once. Statistical samples across ages become feasible for the first time. The answers would isolate the physical processes that sculpt planets and their atmospheres. The paper frames the mission for NASA's Cosmic Origins and Exoplanet Exploration programs, tying the design to the Astro 2030 Decadal Survey.
arxiv-2606-26414:
Laurent Beaudou, Florent Foucaud, Lucas Lorieau, and Prafullkumar Tale study the Directed Geodetic Set problem on directed graphs, networks of one-way links. The problem asks for a small set of vertices such that each remaining vertex sits on some shortest one-way path linking two chosen ones. The authors use parameterized complexity, which measures cost growth by one structural feature of the input rather than its whole size.

The problem is already known to be hard when measured by solution size, even on graphs with no directed cycles. The authors prove a kernel, a shrunken equivalent instance, whose size depends on the vertex cover number, which counts how few vertices touch every link. They also show that dependence cannot improve much under a standard assumption. A second kernel uses solution size, maximum degree, and directed diameter, extending earlier work on undirected graphs.
arxiv-2606-26614:
Kuangshi Ai, Patrick Phuoc Do, and Chaoli Wang present HiLSVA, a system that keeps humans in charge of AI-assisted scientific visualisation. Language model agents can drive visualisation tools by chat. Earlier systems prized autonomy, leaving users little control or insight. HiLSVA instead plans first, then acts under explicit human oversight. Each step's provenance, its full history, is recorded.

Users can hand work back and forth between themselves and the agent. They give instructions in words or manipulate the visualisation directly. Execution runs in a sandbox, keeping workflows safe and reproducible. The system also learns at test time from user feedback. Case studies and a controlled study with twelve participants tested several autonomy levels. Mixed-initiative working improved task completion, user control, and transparency across expertise levels. A trade-off appeared between execution speed and human oversight.
arxiv-2606-27114:
Zhang and colleagues tackle uplift modelling, which estimates how a treatment changes one person's outcome. Two hurdles dominate: borrowing strength across treated and untreated groups, and hidden confounders that bias records.
