Such speeches were rolled into sets of that great speaker's works. They were not his, for all that. A bishop of Antioch makes the same point on a gospel. Serapion, who held that see about the year 200, treats the Gospel of Peter with care. The article lists such books and asks who truly made them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinowitz-elij:
Elijah David Rabinowitz was a Russian rabbi of the Kovno land. Joseph Jacobs and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pikeln in 1845. His father was rabbi of three towns in turn. The boy learned Talmud and rabbinics at his father's side. By fifteen he knew a great deal of both.

In 1873 Poneviezh called Rabinowitz to its rabbinate. He served that town for a full twenty years. He was then named rabbi of Mir in his place. The entry traces a life spent in two pulpits. It shows the slow rise of a Talmud boy to fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romano-leone-ju:
Leone Romano was an Italian scholar born at Rome in 1292. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Rome after 1350. His full name is Judah b. Moses Romano.

The article calls him a gifted thinker and fine Latinist. He knew scholastic philosophy well. With Benjamin b. Judah he centered Roman Jewish learning. His cousin Immanuel became his devoted pupil despite being older. Romano translated major medieval philosophy into Hebrew. By 1328 he had finished the Liber de Causis. He rendered Aquinas, Averroes, and Albertus Magnus as well. He compiled a Hebrew Italian glossary of philosophy terms. King Robert of Naples studied under him at court. The entry shows Latin learning opened to Hebrew readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rouen-hebrew-an:
Rouen is the ancient capital of Normandy, set on the right bank of the Seine. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews likely settled there as early as the Roman period.

The first record tells of a harsh persecution early in the eleventh century. King Robert the Pious sought to force baptism on all Jews on his lands. Many were killed or took their own lives rather than convert. Jacob ben Jekuthiel won the pope's help to stop the attacks. In 1066 many Rouen Jews followed William the Conqueror to England.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salaman-charles:
Charles Malcolm Salaman was an English journalist and dramatist born in London on September 6, 1855. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a son of the composer Charles Kensington Salaman.

Salaman wrote verses for many of his father's best known songs. He also supplied words for music by Macfarren and by Osborne. His own plays include the farcical comedy Deceivers Ever, staged in 1883. Dimity's Dilemma played the Gaiety, and A Modern Eve the Haymarket. He edited Pinero's published plays and wrote Woman, Through a Man's Eye-glass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jose: Samuel ben Jose ben Bun, or Abun, was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In his time, it is said, the Jerusalem Talmud was arranged and completed by his father, Jose. A few of Samuel's own sayings survive in that Talmud, in Rosh ha-Shanah, Berakot, Sotah, and Kiddushin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sason-jacob-ben:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Jacob ben Israel Sason, a Palestinian Talmudist. He flourished at Safed at the end of the seventeenth century. Sason studied under Isaac Alfandari. Safed was still a famed center of Jewish learning. His career was cut short by an early death.

Sason wrote Bene Ya'aḳob, printed at Constantinople in 1714. The book comments on part of Isaac ben Abba Mari's Sefer ha-'Iṭṭur. It also holds fourteen responsa and new readings. Those treat Maimonides' code and Jacob ben Asher's four Ṭurim. Death stopped the work before it was done. Sason was only thirty-one years old. The entry draws on Azulai, Conforte, and the standard catalogs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreiber-simon:
Bernhard Friedberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Simon Schreiber, an Austrian rabbi. He was born at Presburg, in Hungary, in 1821. He died at Cracow on March 25, 1883. Simon was a son of Moses Schreiber, the famed Moses Sofer. In 1842 he became rabbi of Mattersdorf.

In 1857 Schreiber declined a call from the congregation of Papa. In 1860 he accepted Cracow's invitation instead. He became the top leader of Galicia's Orthodox Jews. His word carried weight in worldly matters as well as religion. His shrewdness won him a seat in the Austrian Parliament in 1879. In 1880 he founded the Hebrew weekly Maḥaziḳe ha-Dat. It is still published at Lemberg in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semites-origina:
Semites, first called Shemites, names the peoples listed in Genesis as descendants of Shem. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the term. Genesis names Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram among those descendants. The entry tests that old list against history and language.

Elam, for one, was old and warlike, yet its language was not Semitic. The authors suggest it entered the list through Semitic settlers there. They also weigh rival views on the hard name Arphaxad. Readers get an early scholarly attempt to match a biblical family tree with real peoples of the ancient Near East.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shulamite-r-v-s:
Shulamite is the name given to the heroine of the Song of Songs. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on her. The name appears only once in the whole poem. That single mention comes near the Song's end.

Some modern critics read her as a shepherd's bride. Solomon's desire for her drives their reading of the poem. She resists his bid to place her in his harem. Her name likely means a native of Shulem. Eusebius matched Shulem with the town of Shunem. The Greek version supports that link, the entry argues. Some critics then identify her with Abishag of Shunem. Abishag had served David and figured at his court. The entry weighs a one-word name against a full love story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-samu:
Simeon ben Samuel was a philosopher and cabalist of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was of French or German birth, they report. His book Adam Sikli is also called Hadrat Kodesh.

Written in 1400, the work treats the Ten Commandments at length. It covers God's thirteen attributes and the thirteen articles of faith. A commentary called Gillayon accompanies the main text. A cabalistic meditation in prayer form follows it. Its title's letter values carry mystic meaning, he explained. Later scholars printed extracts of the work abroad. Hottinger used it in a grammar of four languages. Wolf added a Latin translation to the extracts. The entry preserves a late medieval blend of faith and mysticism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-snail-13814:
Snail is the English rendering for the Hebrew word shabbelul. Emil G Hirsch and I M Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word occurs only once, in Psalm fifty-eight. The Targum and Talmud agree with that rendering. The Septuagint and Vulgate give wax instead.

The psalm speaks of the snail melting away as it goes. That image may come from its trail of slime. It may also come from its retreat into cracks and crevices. Many mollusks live in Syria and Palestine, the entry notes. The shabbelul was used as a cure for boils. Other Talmudic notes deal with the snail's egg and shell.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soncino-13914:
Soncino was an Italian family of Hebrew printers of great fame. M Seligsohn and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The family took its name from the town of Soncino. It traced its line back to a Moses of Speyer. Israel Nathan ben Samuel first set up the family press.

He opened his Hebrew press at Soncino in 1483. His first work, the tractate Berakot, appeared in 1484. The press moved often, to Naples, Brescia, Fano, and Pesaro. Branches later worked at Constantinople and at Salonica in Turkey. Soncino prints were prized for fine type and correctness. The first Hebrew Bible was printed by that house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinhardt-jose:
Joseph Steinhardt was a German rabbi born about 1720 and active in Alsace and Bavaria. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He served as chief rabbi of Upper Alsace early in his career. In 1763 he was called as rabbi to Fürth. He stayed there until his death in 1776.

Steinhardt ranked among the foremost Talmudists of his time. Scholars sent him questions from Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, and Switzerland. He held very conservative views on religious practice. His chief book, Zikron Yosef, printed at Fürth in 1773, collects his responsa and rulings. Later works add notes on the Pentateuch and on a Talmud tractate. The entry preserves the record of a widely consulted rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sun-rising-and-:
Knowing sunrise and sunset fixes the hours of Jewish observance. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Sabbath and festival times depend on those moments. Strict reading makes each day run sunrise to sunset. Ibn Ezra supports that view in his commentary.

Hebrew has rich words for dawn and dusk. One term names the rising of the morning before sunrise. Poets call dawn the brows of the morning. The morning star bears two Hebrew names in sources. Twilight, between the suns, troubled the rabbis most. They could not tell if it belonged to day or night. So they guarded it against trespass on either side. The entry explains the clock that governs sacred time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmud-commenta:
Commentaries on the Talmud explain its dense text for later readers. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Richtmann wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Such works form only a small part of legal literature. Responsa and code commentaries bulk far larger. Early scholars felt no need to write them.

When the Talmud closed, its tradition still lived in memory. The first gaonate period wrote no commentaries either. Paltoi Gaon first glossed passages inside his responsa. His son Zemah paraphrased hard texts he quoted. Zemah also built a lexicon to aid Talmud study. Saadia Gaon is said to have commented on the Talmud. The last great geonim added much more in this field. Sherira mostly explained difficult terms for readers. The entry traces commentary from glosses to a genre.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ten-14314:
Ten, as a number in the Bible and rabbinic writing, is surveyed here. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Counting began with fingers and toes, they note. The Hebrews used the decimal system, and ten stayed a base unit.

Ten shapes the measures of Noah's ark and the Tabernacle. It gives the count of the commandments and of Egypt's plagues. Passover and the Day of Atonement fall on the tenth day. Abraham gave a tenth, and tithes followed that pattern. The article also tracks ten in the Talmud and Midrash. There it marks completion and perfection again and again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-triesch-14514:
Triesch, a city in Moravia, owed its Jewish congregation to exiles from Iglau. Gotthard Deutsch and M. L. Stern wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Those exiles likely arrived shortly after 1426. They traded in Iglau by day and slept outside its limits. Wool was their chief ware, sold to Iglau cloth-makers.

Freedom of residence in 1848 shrank the congregation. Czech national feeling later hurt Jewish trade standing. Jews still led in cloth, furniture, and match making. Its rabbis included the cabalist Mordecai Bet ha-Levi. His manuscripts burned in the great fire of 1824. Eleazar Löw served twice around 1800 to 1820. About 300 Jews lived among 5,000 residents in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-usque-14614:
Usque was a family named for Huesca in Spain, famed for the Ferrara Bible. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its members fled the Inquisition through Portugal to Italy. Abraham Usque, born Duarte Pinel at Lisbon, heads the entry. He reached Ferrara sometime after 1543.

At Ferrara he built a large printing house. Its imprint was a globe with a verse from Isaiah. Between 1551 and 1557 it issued some twenty-eight Hebrew books. Judaeo-Spanish rituals and Portuguese works appeared there too. His chief work was the Ferrara Bible of 1553. It revised an older Spanish rendering of the Hebrew. One issue honored the Duke, another Dona Gracia Nasi. New editions ran at Salonica and Amsterdam for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vital-14714:
Vital was an Italian family of scholars and mystics. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its best known member is Hayyim Vital. Hayyim was born at Safed in 1543. He died at Damascus on May 6, 1620. His father was Joseph Vital.

Legends fill Hayyim's life story. A dream of the prophet Elijah turned him toward Kabbalah. He studied alchemy for over two years. Then he became the chief disciple of Isaac Luria. Hayyim wrote down Luria's teachings for later readers. That record made him central to Jewish mysticism. The entry tells his visions alongside the plain facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-15014: Worms, as a family name, is traced by Joseph Jacobs for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The kin came from Frankfort-on-the-Main and from England. Their line runs back to Aaron Worms of Frankfort in the mid 1700s. A great-great-grandson won a baron rank in Austria in 1871. A later kin, Baron Henry de Worms, rose to the British peerage as Lord Pirbright. The short entry gives the line and points to a family tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yod-15114: Yod is the tenth sign of the Hebrew letter set. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broyde wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name seems tied to the word yad, meaning hand. The old Phoenician sign looks a bit like a hand. The sound is that of the English letter y. With the vowel i it melts into a long i sound. As a count sign it holds the worth of ten. The name of God is at times shown by this sign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeebi-israel-15:
Israel Zeebi (1651-1731) was a top Talmud man of Hebron in Palestine. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lazarus Grunhut wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Benjamin Zeebi of that town. On his mother's side he came from Abraham Azulai.

His sire died when the boy was four years of age. His mother raised him and saw to his school work. At age eighteen he wed a girl of a good house. For near thirty years he led the Jews of Hebron. He is said to have backed Nehemiah Hayyun in his day. He wrote to five great sages of his age on the law. His full name was Abraham Israel in his late years. His son brought out two books of his work in 1758.
jonson-bartholomew-fair-1614:
Ben Jonson wrote Bartholomew Fair for the London stage in 1614, setting the whole comedy at Smithfield's famous cloth fair. Jonson loved to mock pretension, and the fair gives him a whole city of targets. The play opens with a famous induction that teases the audience itself.

At the fair, a stiff Puritan named Zeal-of-the-Land Busy denounces the fun while enjoying it. Pickpockets, puppet shows, ballad singers, and a foolish justice fill the scene. A puppet play within the play settles several quarrels at once. Jonson's sprawling comedy shows Jacobean London at its loudest, full of appetite, folly, and noise.
journal-of-discourses-vol-14:
Federal pressure on plural marriage opens in Volume Fourteen, from 1872. Court cases loom as Washington turns its guns on Utah's ways. The Saints brace for a long legal war over their faith.

Young defends religious liberty with all his famous force and scorn. Sermons frame the fight as a test of America's own first freedoms. Speakers urge calm, unity, and strict obedience to church counsel. The kingdom's long stand for its way of life begins here. Readers hear a prophet turn lawyer, patriot, and war chief at once in these talks. The legal fight he foresaw would run for two long decades.
joyce-dubliners-1914:
James Joyce published Dubliners in 1914, his fifteen stories of Dublin paralysis, ending with The Dead in snow. The book that reinvented the short story had waited nine years, fought printers and censors, and seen an edition burned. Joyce called his method a style of scrupulous meanness, aimed at a chapter of his city's moral history.

The Sisters, Araby, and Eveline trace childhood, youth, and public life in a city of missed chances and drink. A Little Cloud, Counterparts, and The Boarding House weigh clerks, drunks, and matchmakers in Dublin's lower middle class. Gabriel Conroy, in The Dead, learns at a Christmas party that his wife loved a dead boy more than him. Snow, general all over Ireland, closes a story many rank the greatest in the English language. Joyce's epiphanies, moments that reveal a soul, changed fiction's craft for good.
lamarck-zoological-philosophy-1914:
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published his theory of how animal life changes in French in 1809. Hugh Elliot translated that work into English in 1914 as Zoological Philosophy. Lamarck argued that living things pass on changes gained through use, need, and habit.

His best-known example involves giraffes stretching toward higher leaves over many generations. He also set out a broad account of how species descend and change over time. Charles Darwin later offered a different mechanism, but Lamarck came first. Readers get the first full theory of evolution, stated before Darwin was born.
lawrence-prussian-officer-1914:
Lawrence's first story collection appeared in 1914, led by the title novella of a Prussian cavalry officer and his orderly. Their relation of discipline, resentment, and buried feeling hardens until it breaks in violence in a lonely forest.

The volume also holds 'Odour of Chrysanthemums', his great story of a miner's wife waiting for a husband who comes home dead, and 'The Christening'. Many pieces draw on the mining country of his youth in Nottinghamshire. Lawrence writes working lives from inside, without pity or polish. These stories announced a major talent and still stand among his finest work in short fiction.
mach-sensations-williams-1914:
Mach's Analysis of Sensations, in the 1914 English translation by Williams and Waterlow, asks what the world is made of at bottom. His answer is plain sense data: colors, sounds, pressures, heat, and cold. Mind and matter, he argues, are two ways of grouping the same basic stuff.

A table, a body, and a thought all count as bundles of such elements in different patterns. That view, later called neutral monism, refuses to split the world into two rival kinds of thing. Thinkers in physics and in the study of mind both drew on the book for years.
maier-arcana-arcanissima-1614:
Michael Maier read the myths of Egypt and Greece as coded alchemy in Arcana arcanissima, published in 1614. Maier, a physician at the court of Rudolf II and a voice for the Rosicrucians, decodes hieroglyphs and the fables of the golden age. Every god and hero hides, in his reading, a step in the making of the stone.

The Latin text piles symbol on symbol with a scholar's glee, daring the reader to follow. Maier's grand claim, that ancient fable is veiled chemistry, shaped how his age read both myth and matter. The work stands as his mytho-alchemical masterwork, central to the strange learning of the Rosicrucian years.
mckechnie-magna-carta-commentary-1914:
William Sharp McKechnie published Magna Carta: A Commentary on the Great Charter of King John in 1914, in its second edition. McKechnie, a Glasgow professor of law, took the charter of 1215 clause by clause. His aim was to show what each clause meant to the barons who forced it on King John.

McKechnie separated the charter's real medieval sense from the grand meanings later ages read into it. Famous clauses on judgment by peers and no sale of justice get careful, sober treatment. He printed the Latin text and tracked each clause's later fate. The book became the standard scholarly commentary on Magna Carta, the reference against which popular claims about the charter are still checked.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-14: Fourteenth in line, volume fourteen bears etext number 3564. The title in its head note carries the year 1815. Bourrienne wrote the memoirs, and Widger produced this Gutenberg file. Beyond those head facts, the sample gives a reader only terms of use and fund appeals. The narrative that should follow is absent from the sample held here. For that reason this entry describes the file, not the volume's contents.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-14:
The Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, closes with volume fourteen, Chrysostom's homilies on the Gospel of John and on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Philip Schaff's set ended here in 1886. Eighty-eight homilies cover John's gospel, preached at Antioch in his early years.

Chrysostom treats John as the most spiritual gospel, aimed against heretics who shrank Christ. The thirty-four Hebrews homilies, preached later at Constantinople, take up the high priesthood of Christ and the call to endure. His voice darkens as exile nears. The volume ends both the Chrysostom block and the whole first series. Schaff's second series, on the Greek and Latin fathers after Nicaea, stands separately.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-14:
The second series of the Nicene Fathers closes with volume fourteen: the canons and decrees of the seven ecumenical councils. Schaff and Wace's 1890 series ends on the documents that defined orthodox faith for east and west alike. From Nicaea in 325 to the second council of Nicaea in 787, the councils span four and a half centuries.

Each council's creeds, definitions, and canons stand here in English, with the letters and debates that explain them. The reader watches the church fix the Trinity at Nicaea, Christ's two natures at Chalcedon, and the fate of icons at the last. Few volumes pack so much consequence into official prose. It is the legal spine of ancient Christianity.
norwegian-constitution-1814:
Norway's constitution was signed at Eidsvoll on 17 May 1814. Norwegians seized the moment when Denmark, beaten in the Napoleonic wars, had to hand Norway to Sweden. An assembly of 112 men wrote the charter in a few spring weeks, claiming their country's freedom on the model of America and France.

The text makes Norway a free, independent, and indivisible kingdom with a limited hereditary monarchy. Power is split among the king, the Storting as legislature, and independent courts, and a wide share of men gained the vote for the age. Sweden forced Norway into a union that year, but let the constitution stand almost untouched. Norwegians celebrate the 17th of May as their national day. The charter is among the world's oldest written constitutions still in force.
openalex-w2011868814:
Samira Miyamoto, Imperio Lombardi, Katherine Berg and colleagues created a Brazilian version of the Berg balance scale. Their paper appeared in 2004. The scale tests functional balance in older people. Clinicians needed a sound Portuguese version for Brazil. The team tested whether its scores were reliable.

Two bilingual translators rendered the scale into Brazilian Portuguese. A panel settled differences, and back translation checked the work. Older patients and therapists tried the draft version. Items that many found unclear were rewritten and retested. Six questions changed during that process. Later tests on older patients showed very high agreement. Scores matched closely within and between testers. The version was judged ready for clinical use.
openalex-w2016899314:
Julie Perez and Cyrille Goarant worked on faster identification of Leptospira bacteria in New Caledonia. Their paper appeared in BMC Microbiology in 2010. Leptospirosis is a disease spread through water and animal urine. The standard lab test has known weaknesses. Knowing the infecting strain helps track outbreaks.

The team tested whether PCR product sequences could name the strain. Two standard test products showed useful sequence differences. They checked the method against a fuller typing method. Samples from local patients and animals matched well. They found one group with no known reference strain. They also found a group only in introduced Rusa deer. That deer is likely its animal reservoir in the area.
openalex-w2207949614:
Jacqueline Kerr, Jennifer Emond, Hannah Badland, and colleagues published this study in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2015. The IPEN study asked how neighborhood features, as residents perceive them, relate to walking and cycling for transport. Rates of both habits are low and vary widely between countries, which makes choosing design fixes hard.

Self-reported data came from nearly fourteen thousand adults in seventeen cities across twelve countries. Participants rated their neighborhoods on a standard walkability scale and reported recent travel habits. Walking for transport was linked to perceived housing density, mixed land use with good access, connected streets, looks, and safety. The team modeled the strength and shape of each link, city by city.
openalex-w2299123914:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this performance study in the European Physical Journal C in 2016. Muons are among the cleanest signals at the Large Hadron Collider, central to Higgs and new-physics searches. The paper documents how well ATLAS finds and measures them in its first thirteen-TeV proton collision data.

Decays of J/psi and Z particles into muon pairs served as the yardsticks. Reconstruction efficiency came out near ninety-nine percent across most of the detector's range. Isolation efficiency ran between ninety-three and one hundred percent, depending on settings. Momentum was measured to within about two percent in the detector's heart, and simulations matched the real data closely throughout.
openalex-w2972679514:
Benjamin Evans, Panayiota Kotsakiozi, André Costa-da-Silva, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2019. It follows up on releases of genetically modified Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in Jacobina, Brazil. The modified males carried a dominant lethal gene meant to crash local mosquito numbers and curb dengue, Zika, and related fevers.

Jacobina is ringed by dry scrubland where this mosquito cannot breed, making it a natural test island. The team sampled mosquitoes there with egg traps after the releases. Their genetic checks show that genes from the released strain passed into the wild population. That finding matters for any program that releases engineered insects into nature, since the released genes did not simply vanish.
openalex-w3029408214:
José Carcione, Juan Santos, Claudio Bagaini, and Jing Ba published this study in Frontiers in Public Health in 2020. It simulates a COVID-19 epidemic with a deterministic SEIR model. Such a model sorts people into susceptible, exposed, infected, and recovered groups and tracks how they move between them.

The authors stress their example, modeled on Italy's Lombardy region, is not a rigorous case study, since key inputs were uncertain. They first varied the model's settings to see how each shaped the curve. They then fitted the model to deaths reported up to early May 2020. In that run the epidemic peaked after about five weeks, and the spread rate fell below the break-even point as isolation measures bit.
openalex-w7204212614:
Armando Isamu de Almeida Yamada and Gleisson Amaral Mendes published a Portuguese-language case study in Brazil in 2026 on generative artificial intelligence in software development. The exploratory study had two stages. First, eleven teachers and software professionals answered a questionnaire about their perceptions of the tools. Second, three software engineering students each built the same application twice, once without and once with generative AI help.

Perceptions were mostly favorable, citing productivity, fewer errors, support for learning new technologies, and the need to keep skills current. In the experiment, average build time fell from about seventy-five minutes to thirty-eight, with every planned function still delivered. The authors conclude that generative AI optimizes development work as a support, without replacing the developer's technical knowledge.
openalex-w7204276814:
Lucas Xavier Brito led a Portuguese-language essay, in Brazil in 2026, on key-overcoming physical education inside Brazil's full-time schools. Extending the school day changes what physical education can be. Grounded in a review, the essay joins the key-overcoming perspective, built on body culture and systematized knowledge, to research on integral schooling and full-time schooling.

The authors identify four ways the subject can be emptied out: turned into recreation, narrowed to selective sport, broken by curricular discontinuity, or settled into a secondary place. Against these, they discuss teacher training, curricular organization, diversified body culture content, and school running. A longer day is a possibility, not a guarantee, they conclude; it depends on teaching intention and problems.
openalex-w7204459014: Paloma Francisca de Souza Aguiar and eleven co-authors in Brazil released a Portuguese-language review in 2026 on the association between metabolic syndrome and the risk of major cardiovascular events in adults. Metabolic syndrome groups together problems such as abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, abnormal blood sugar, and disturbed blood lipids. Each of these strains the heart and vessels. The review asks how strongly carrying that cluster raises an adult's risk of major cardiovascular events, a question that guides screening and prevention in everyday practice.
openalex-w7212116614:
Alan Maycon Carlos Araujo leads a team that reads the blood work of dogs sick with leishmaniasis in Iguatu, Ceara. The disease is spread by sand flies and is caused by a tiny parasite. Dogs are a key host in towns, and the disease is a risk to people as well. The team pulled twenty blood tests of sick dogs from a town clinic. The files ran from 2021 to 2025.

Low red cell counts led the list of faults. Most of that anemia was of the plain, steady kind. Counts of platelets and of some white cells fell, while other white cells rose. In most sick dogs, the blood showed weak signs of fresh repair. The pattern helps vets judge how far the disease has gone. It also flags the dogs that need close watch and swift care.
openalex-w7213766514:
Igor José Dias e Silva and co-workers analyse adverse reaction reports for four antibiotics in older Brazilians. Their 2026 study covers notifications from 2021 to 2025. Ageing, multiple medicines, and other illnesses can raise the risk of drug reactions in this group.

Over twenty-seven hundred drug-linked notifications were identified. Ceftriaxone accounted for more than half, used by ciprofloxacin, a combined sulfa drug, and amoxicillin. The Southeast region gathered over half of all reports. The team examined severity, outcomes, age group, and the body system affected, counting unique reports carefully to avoid duplication. Such monitoring, they imply, is essential for safer antibiotic use in older patients.
openalex-w7214023214:
Karolina Dessimoni Victória leads a team analysing newborn deaths in Manaus from 2015 to 2024. Their 2026 ecological study uses aggregated data from the Amazonas health surveillance infant mortality panel. Rates per thousand live births and yearly trends were calculated with a standard regression method.

Over the decade, more than three thousand neonatal deaths were recorded among hundreds of thousands of births. Early deaths, in the first week, formed three quarters and rose slightly each year. Total and late neonatal mortality stayed stationary. Perinatal conditions caused most deaths, with congenital malformations second. Both cause groups were flat over time, a stability the authors treat as no ground for comfort.
openalex-w7214128814:
Edinardo Aguiar do Nascimento and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva analyse inclusive schooling policy and reading for autistic students in Brazil. Their 2026 study is library-based, grounded in schooling norms and studies from 2008 to 2026. Four axes organize the analysis, from the legal right itself to classroom conditions.

Brazilian rules advanced, securing enrolment in regular classes, accessibility, specialist support, and individual planning, they find. Barriers persist in teacher training and in joining regular and specialist teaching. Assessment often fits the student's profile poorly. Legal guidance still translates weakly into meaningful literacy practice. Inclusion cannot be measured by school access alone, they conclude. Participation, permanence, and real learning complete the right.
openalex-w7214170914:
Pablo Henrique dos Santos Silva and Josiane da Costa Vieira Rezende analyse integrated management systems in Brazilian public universities. Their 2026 library and documentary study reads three named systems through information science. Current digital government and data protection laws, plus official tech manuals, complete the sources.

The systems integrate information flows and support digital governance, they find. Challenges include a weak tech base, cultural resistance, and users' low information skill. Fit with the general data protection law is a further strain, above all in federal institutions. Success depends mostly on users' information training, they conclude, and on changing the official processes around the systems rather than keeping old routines in digital form.
openalex-w7214181014:
Liliane da Silva dos Santos studies pedagogical documentation as continuing teacher training in early childhood education. Her single-author 2026 qualitative case study works in a public unit of Florianópolis's municipal network. Four teachers, in two shared-teaching pairs across nursery and preschool, took part.

Open questionnaire answers, teaching records, planning, and institutional documents formed the corpus, read by content analysis. Documentation is recognized as a tool to make learning visible, reflect on practice, and organize planning, she finds. Its systematic training use depends on institutional time, collective analysis spaces, and pedagogical mediation. Documentation becomes a structuring axis of training, Santos concludes, only when used intentionally, reflectively, and together.
openalex-w7214709214:
Kelven Everton de Oliveira Sampaio led a 2026 integrative review on toe walking in children with autism spectrum disorder. Autistic children often show motor differences in balance, coordination, and gait, and walking on the toes is a common one. Reviewing studies from 2015 to mid-2026 across three databases, the team kept eleven and examined the brain and body bases of the gait pattern and what physiotherapy can do.

Gait changes in autism proved multifactorial, involving neurological, sensory, muscle and bone, behavioral, and psychomotor factors together. Toe walking was linked to sensory differences, balance, postural control, and movement patterns. Interventions such as auditory feedback, serial casts, orthoses, dance therapy, and motor learning strategies showed positive results, though mostly in small studies. Assessment and treatment, the authors conclude, should fit each child and aim at function, autonomy, and participation.
openalex-w7214921814: Felipe Colombelli Pacca led a 2026 article on the challenge of judging medical competence in Brazil. A new national exam of medical training promises an external, standardized, periodic reference to compare medical courses. National course guidelines describe what graduates should be able to do. The authors discuss how judging can capture abilities not directly visible, using a competence model and programmatic assessment, where many small judgments build one larger picture. The sample for this entry ends early in the abstract, so the full argument and conclusions are not given here.
opuscula-quaedam-chemica-georgii-riplei-: Opuscula quaedam chemica, dated 1614 in the catalog, is a Latin gathering of short alchemical writings. Its title names George Ripley's marrow of chemical philosophy, and ten canons on the philosopher's stone by an unknown author. A mirror of alchemy by the Franciscan monk Elias follows. So does a paraphrase of Augurelli's Chrysopoeia, a poem on making gold. The hosted sample shows only repeated copyright pages and the garbled start of that title page. This note reports the contents as listed, and nothing more.
outline-of-occult-science-steiner-1914:
Rudolf Steiner set out his full cosmic system in An Outline of Occult Science. The English edition appeared in 1914, from his German work. Steiner called his path anthroposophy, a science of the spirit.

He describes hidden worlds that trained sight can perceive. Earth, he says, passed through ages from Saturn to Atlantis and beyond. Souls return in new lives across those ages. The book is dense and wholly sure of itself. Followers treat it as a core text. Others read it as a bold map of a world seen only by its author.
pankhurst-my-own-story-1914:
Emmeline Pankhurst published My Own Story in 1914, her autobiography of the militant suffragette campaign. Pankhurst led the Women's Social and Political Union in Britain, whose members chained themselves to railings, broke windows, and endured prison hunger strikes. She wrote the book to win support, including in America.

Pankhurst told of her Manchester childhood, her marriage, and the slow turn from peaceful pleading to open militancy. Prison scenes, forcible feeding, and the death of Emily Davison at the Derby mark the campaign's hardest years. She judged each act by one test: did it win attention for the vote? The memoir remains the leader's own account of the suffragette fight.
petrie-amulets-1914:
W. M. Flinders Petrie, the great digger of Egypt, wrote this study of amulets in 1914. He based it on the vast finds from his own digs along the Nile. Few men of his time had held so many small finds in their own hands. His eye for types was famed among the men of his field.

The book sorts amulets by type and shows each with clear plates. Petrie tells what each form meant and how its use changed through Egypt's long past. His scheme gave the study of amulets a firm base in real finds from the ground.
philippine-folk-tales-pg12814: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Mabel Cook Cole's Philippine Folk Tales, the title page and contents, with no tale text visible. The title page dates the compilation to 1916 and credits Cole as compiler and annotator. The contents sort the tales by people: a large Tinguian group with Aponibolinayen and the Sun. An Igorot group follows, with creation and flood stories and Lumawig on Earth, and a third group from the wild tribes of Mindanao.
planck-theory-heat-radiation-masius-1914:
Max Planck's lectures on the theory of heat radiation became, in Morton Masius's 1914 translation, The Theory of Heat Radiation. The German lectures grew from Planck's work on how hot bodies give off light and heat. To fit the facts, he had proposed in 1900 that energy comes in small packets. His constant, written as h, measured those packets.

The book works through the laws of radiation step by step, with care and rigor. It shows where the older physics failed and why the quantum step was forced. Historians treat the text as a founding document of quantum theory. Physics changed course inside its pages. The treatment stays a model of clarity.
plaw-113-100-2014: Some United Nations envoys are barred from entry by Public Law 113-100 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The bar hits any representative to the United Nations found to have engaged in spying against the United States. The act widens an older rule in a foreign relations law. Terrorist activity now stands next to spying as a ground. The person must also pose a threat to United States national security interests, as the amended text goes on to state.
plaw-113-101-2014:
Federal spending data opens wider under Public Law 113-101, the Digital Accountability and Transparency Act of 2014. People call it the DATA Act for short. The 113th Congress passed it to expand the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006. Section 2 lists its purposes. Direct agency spending must be disclosed to the public.

Contract, loan, and grant spending must link to the programs behind it. That link lets taxpayers and policy makers track federal spending with more ease. The act also sets data standards for the whole government. Spending data must be steady, sound, and searchable on USASpending.gov.
plaw-113-102-2014: Three more years for a planned museum come from Public Law 113-102 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. It amends the National Law Enforcement Museum Act, Public Law 106-492. Section 4 of that act had set a termination span of 13 years. The act strikes 13 years and inserts 16 years. A second section sets the start date. The change takes effect as if the act had passed on November 8, 2013.
plaw-113-103-2014: Penthouse living rules in the District of Columbia are clarified by Public Law 113-103 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. It amends the 1910 act that regulates the height of buildings there. The old text spoke of penthouses over elevator shafts and barred home use above the top story. The act strikes the shaft limit so the rule covers penthouses in general. Home use is allowed in a penthouse of one story, 20 feet or less above the roof.
plaw-113-104-2014: Public Law 113-104, the Kilah Davenport Child Protection Act of 2013, was approved by the 113th Congress in 2014. Section 2 orders a report from the Attorney General within 180 days, and again 3 years later. The report covers penalties for child abuse laws in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and each territory. It must note if a place adds harsher penalties when a child suffers grave bodily harm. Lasting loss of a mental function counts as well. Section 3 widens a penalty rule for some domestic assaults.
plaw-113-105-2014:
Public Law 113-105, the American Fighter Aces Congressional Gold Medal Act, was passed by the 113th Congress in 2014. It awards one Congressional Gold Medal to the American Fighter Aces as a group. The honor marks their heroic service in defense of the nation's freedom across the history of aviation warfare. Section 2 defines the group and gives the record behind it.

An ace is a fighter pilot who destroyed 5 or more confirmed enemy planes in air combat during a war. More than 60,000 United States fighter pilots have flown since World War I. Fewer than 1,500 of them became aces.
plaw-113-106-2014:
The Doolittle Tokyo Raiders receive a Congressional Gold Medal under Public Law 113-106 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. They were World War II members of the 17th Bombardment Group. The medal honors their heroism, valor, and skill in the bombings of Tokyo. Section 1 sets out the facts of the raid.

On April 18, 1942, 80 air crewmen led by Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle volunteered for a mission called extremely hazardous. They did not know the target in advance. After a Japanese picket ship spotted the carrier Hornet, the planes took off 670 miles from Japan's coast.
plaw-113-107-2014: Two small Arizona parcels may be conveyed under Public Law 113-107 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The land sits inside the Coconino National Forest and runs to about 2.67 acres. Private buildings stand on the parcels. Owners built them in reliance on a survey from May 1960 that later proved wrong. The Secretary may pass all federal rights by quitclaim deed. The buyer must speak for most owners of private land next to the parcels, by power of attorney.
plaw-113-108-2014:
World War II members of the Civil Air Patrol receive a Congressional Gold Medal under Public Law 113-108 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Section 1 gives the findings. The unpaid volunteers of the patrol gave fine service in aid, combat, and national work in a time of great need. They flew their own planes on key tasks for the military.

Their tasks included attacks on enemy submarines off the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. The patrol began on December 1, 1941. Its war work set the stage for its later role as a nonprofit public service group. Congress chartered it as the Auxiliary of the Air Force.
plaw-113-109-2014: One dealer duty drops out of the Clean Air Act under Public Law 113-109 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Section 207(h) of that act had required dealer certification of new light-duty motor vehicles. Dealer certification means a seller's formal proof tied to a new car or light truck. The act strikes paragraph 1 of that part in full. Paragraphs 2 and 3 are then renumbered as paragraphs 1 and 2. The enrolled text does nothing else.
plaw-113-110-2014: Eatonville, Washington, gains a named post office under Public Law 113-110 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The Postal Service runs the site at 103 Center Street West in that town. From passage on, its legal name is the National Park Ranger Margaret Anderson Post Office. Laws, maps, and records that point to the site point to it by that name.
plaw-113-111-2014: A De Pere mail site gains a new name under Public Law 113-111, approved by the 113th Congress in 2014. The Postal Service site at 123 South 9th Street in De Pere, Wisconsin, must be known as the Corporal Justin D. Ross Post Office Building. References to the site in federal laws, maps, rules, records, and other papers count as references to that name.
plaw-113-112-2014: Public Law 113-112, passed in 2014 by the 113th Congress, names one post office building in New York. The Postal Service site at 14 Main Street in Brockport must be known as the Staff Sergeant Nicholas J. Reid Post Office Building. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-113-113-2014: Cottleville, Missouri, gains a named post office under Public Law 113-113 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Head out on Highway N to number 5323 and you reach the site in question. Congress directs that it be called the Lance Corporal Phillip Vinnedge Post Office. Older papers that name the site count, in law, as naming it by the new title.
plaw-113-114-2014:
Shimon Peres receives the Congressional Gold Medal under Public Law 113-114 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Section 1 gives the facts of his life. Peres was born in Poland in 1923. His family moved to Tel Aviv in 1934, and kin who stayed in Poland were murdered in the Holocaust. Before Israel won independence, he earned the trust of leaders such as David Ben-Gurion.

Congress calls Peres the last living member of Israel's founding generation. He served in top posts for over 70 years. The list includes head of the navy, Minister of Defense, Foreign Minister, Prime Minister, and President. The findings credit him with work that served United States interests.
plaw-113-115-2014: Burleson, Texas, gains a named post office building under Public Law 113-115 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The building stands at 232 Southwest Johnson Avenue. Its new legal name is the Sergeant William Moody Post Office Building. In maps, rules, and files of the United States, a mention of the site is read as a mention of that name.
plaw-113-116-2014:
Public Law 113-116, the Monuments Men Recognition Act of 2014, grants the Congressional Gold Medal to the Monuments Men as a group. The 113th Congress passed it for their heroic role in World War II. They preserved, protected, and returned monuments, art, and objects of cultural worth during and after the war. Section 2 gives the group's history.

On June 23, 1943, President Franklin D. Roosevelt formed a commission for the salvage of art and historic monuments in war areas. It set up the Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives Section under the Allied Armies. Its members were museum directors, curators, art historians, artists, architects, and teachers.
plaw-113-117-2014: Public Law 113-117, the North Texas Invasive Species Barrier Act of 2014, frees some water transfers from a wildlife law. The 113th Congress passed it on the Lacey Act Amendments of 1981. Section 2 amends an earlier act, Public Law 112-237. After the words zebra mussels, it adds other fish, wildlife, and plants found in Lake Texoma. The ban covers species barred by section 3 of the Lacey Act or by title 18. The head note names the North Texas Municipal Water District and the Greater Texoma Utility Authority.
plaw-113-118-2014: Fixing two gold medal laws is the work of Public Law 113-118, the Gold Medal Technical Corrections Act of 2014. The 113th Congress passed it in June 2014. Section 2 amends Public Law 108-368, the act for Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., and Coretta Scott King. It rewrites who may present the medal, naming the Speaker of the House and the President pro tempore of the Senate. It strikes the word posthumously. A new part sends the medal to the Smithsonian Institution for display after the award.
plaw-113-119-2014: Public Law 113-119, the Sandia Pueblo Settlement Technical Amendment Act, tweaks a land trust law in 2014. The 113th Congress amended the T'uf Shur Bien Preservation Trust Area Act. One change swaps the word conveyance for the phrase title to be conveyed. A new part covers a failed land swap. If the swap is not done 30 days after this part takes effect, a transfer must follow. On request, National Forest land marked on an October 2013 map passes to the Interior Secretary, to be held in trust.
plaw-113-120-2014:
The 65th Infantry Regiment, the Borinqueneers, receives a Congressional Gold Medal under Public Law 113-120 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The regiment is known as the Borinqueneers. Section 1 traces its start. In 1898 the United States gained Puerto Rico by the Treaty of Paris, which ended the Spanish-American War. By the next year Congress had approved a unit of volunteer soldiers there.

In May 1917 the unit was sent to the Panama Canal Zone. Army policy at the time held most segregated units to noncombat roles. In June 1920 the unit took the name 65th Infantry Regiment. It served as the Army's last segregated unit made up mainly of Hispanic soldiers.
plaw-113-121-2014:
Public Law 113-121, the Water Resources Reform and Development Act of 2014, aims to improve the rivers and harbors of the United States. The 113th Congress passed it in June 2014. It also covers the saving and growth of water and related resources. Title I is called Program Reforms and Streamlining. Its sections run from 1001 onward.

Early sections join and speed up project studies. They merge studies, hasten reports, and cut duplicate reviews. Later sections speed up permits and changes to projects by non-federal partners. One section speeds up hydropower at Corps of Engineers sites. Open books on project accounts also appear in the list.
plaw-113-122-2014: Public Law 113-122, the Collinsville Renewable Energy Production Act, revives two hydroelectric licenses in Connecticut. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. The licenses are Federal Energy Regulatory Commission projects 10822 and 10823. The town in the act is Canton, Connecticut. Even though a license has ended, the Commission may act at the town's request. It may bring the license back and give two more years to start building. The sample ends as a transfer step begins.
plaw-113-123-2014: Public Law 113-123, the World War II Memorial Prayer Act of 2013, was approved by the 113th Congress in 2014. It directs the Interior Secretary to place a plaque or inscription at the World War II Memorial in the District of Columbia. The words are those President Franklin D. Roosevelt prayed with the nation on D-Day, June 6, 1944. The Secretary must design, obtain, and install the piece. No federal funds may pay for it. Private gifts may be taken and spent for that end.
plaw-113-124-2014: Algal blooms and low-oxygen water are the subject of Public Law 113-124 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Its long short title ends with the words Amendments Act of 2014. Hypoxia means water with too little oxygen for sea life. Section 3 rewrites part of the 1998 act on the joint task force for these blooms. The edits change how members are named, from a list of named posts to a representative from each. List items are then renumbered in the sample.
plaw-113-125-2014: Public Law 113-125, the Reliable Home Heating Act, deals with emergency shortages of home heating fuel. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. Home heating fuel means heating oil, natural gas, and propane. Section 2 covers state emergency orders. When a governor declares an emergency over a fuel shortage, the first span runs 30 days. If the governor finds the shortage has not ended, up to two more 30-day spans may follow. The federal motor carrier office must honor those added spans for relief trucks.
plaw-113-126-2014:
Public Law 113-126, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2014, was approved by the 113th Congress on July 7, 2014. It backs funds for spy work and related work across the United States Government. The head note also names the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. A further charge is the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I grants the funds and sets a classified schedule. It also allows shifts in staff caps and covers the community management account. Title II funds the CIA retirement system. It adds special retirement credit for service on detail to another agency, under two retirement plans.
plaw-113-127-2014: Federal land in El Dorado County, California, goes into trust for a tribe under Public Law 113-127 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The land is about 40.852 acres in El Dorado County, run by the Bureau of Land Management. A map dated June 7, 2012, marks it as the conveyance boundary. The trust serves the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians. Valid rights, easements, and rights-of-way stay in place. Class II and class III gaming on the land is barred at all times.
plaw-113-128-2014:
Public Law 113-128, the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, was passed by the 113th Congress in 2014. It amends the Workforce Investment Act of 1998. The aim is a stronger workforce development system for the United States. The tools are fresh ideas, better alignment, and better job, training, and school programs. Growth for workers and for the nation is the end in view.

Title I covers workforce development work. Its first parts deal with system alignment. States must keep workforce boards and file unified or combined state plans. Local areas and local boards get their own rules. A later part covers how boards are funded, and one covers measures of success.
plaw-113-129-2014: Property terms in a Utah water law are clarified by Public Law 113-129 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The law is the Provo River Project Transfer Act, Public Law 108-382. One edit ties the Pleasant Grove property term to the date a parcel is conveyed. A second edit rewrites the Provo Reservoir Canal term. The canal is now a water conveyance facility, with its bridges, fixtures, and rights-of-way held with it. The text adds a forebay and fixes the canal's reach near the Jordan Narrows.
plaw-113-130-2014: A joint clinic to be built in Marina, California, is named by Public Law 113-130 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The joint outpatient clinic of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Defense will stand in Marina. The site is the crossing of the proposed Ninth Street and the proposed First Avenue. The clinic must be known as the Major General William H. Gourley VA-DOD Outpatient Clinic. Federal laws, records, and other papers must use that name for it.
plaw-113-131-2014: Public Law 113-131, the Black Hills Cemetery Act, moves small burial grounds out of federal hands in South Dakota. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. The Agriculture Secretary must convey, at no charge, all federal rights in named cemeteries. The grounds sit on National Forest System land in the Black Hills National Forest. Local groups that now tend the grounds receive them. Each grant adds up to two acres next to the cemetery. The extra land covers unmarked graves and room to grow.
plaw-113-132-2014:
A national memorial for Distinguished Flying Cross holders is named by Public Law 113-132 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The site is the March Field Air Museum in Riverside, California. Section 2 gives the medal counts behind the honor. In World War II, 126,318 members of the Armed Forces won the cross. About 21,000 won it in the Korean conflict, and 21,647 in the Vietnam War.

Since Vietnam, more than 203 members have won the medal in times of conflict. The findings add a caution on the counts. The National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis burned in 1973. Many more holders of the cross may thus lack records.
plaw-113-133-2014: Public Law 113-133, the Hill Creek Cultural Preservation and Energy Development Act, clarifies a Utah boundary law from 1948. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. The old act defined the outer boundary of the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation. A 1955 act had already amended it once. The new section 5 states its aim in its first line. The State of Utah may give up land to the United States, for the good of the Ute Indian Tribe. The sample ends in the middle of that grant.
plaw-113-134-2014: Public Law 113-134, the Pascua Yaqui Tribe Trust Land Act, was passed by the 113th Congress in 2014. It deals with federal inholdings in Arizona. The terms name the Pascua Yaqui Tribe of Arizona, a tribe the federal government recognizes. A map dated January 15, 2013, shows the land in scope. Parcel A is about 10 acres of federal land on that map. All federal rights in Parcel A are declared held in trust for the tribe. Valid rights held by others stay in place.
plaw-113-135-2014: Public Law 113-135, the Three Kids Mine Remediation and Reclamation Act, covers a polluted mine site in Nevada. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014 to convey federal land in Clark County. The land transfer serves the cleanup and reclamation of the Three Kids Mine Project Site. Federal land means about 948 acres in the site. The Bureau of Reclamation and the Bureau of Land Management hold that ground. The act also names the redevelopment agency of the City of Henderson.
plaw-113-136-2014: Public Law 113-136, the Idaho Wilderness Water Resources Protection Act, keeps old water works running in two Idaho wilderness areas. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. The areas are the Frank Church-River of No Return Wilderness and the Selway-Bitterroot Wilderness. The Agriculture Secretary must issue a special use permit to owners of a water storage, transport, or diversion site. The site must sit on National Forest System land. Its use, upkeep, and rebuilding may go on if set tests are met.
plaw-113-137-2014: Fish stocking in a Washington park group is kept alive by Public Law 113-137 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Its short title names the North Cascades National Park Service Complex. The group joins North Cascades National Park with the Ross Lake and Lake Chelan recreation areas. The Interior Secretary must allow stocking in certain lakes of the group. A plan from June 2008 guides the work. Its full name is the Mountain Lakes Fishery Management Plan and Environmental Impact Statement.
plaw-113-138-2014:
The Vet Center in Prescott, Arizona, is named by Public Law 113-138 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. It becomes the Dr. Cameron McKinley Department of Veterans Affairs Veterans Center. Section 1 gives his life in brief. Cameron K. McKinley was born on December 9, 1930, in Shreveport, Louisiana. He served in the Marine Corps Reserve there from 1947 to 1949.

At Wiesbaden Air Force Hospital he gave therapy to troops and their families during and after the Vietnam War. From 1981 to 1995 he was Chief of Psychology at the Prescott VA Hospital. There he set up a rap group for Vietnam veterans with post-traumatic stress. That group formed a local chapter of Vietnam Veterans of America.
plaw-113-139-2014: Jersey City, New Jersey, gains a named post office building under Public Law 113-139 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The site at 369 Martin Luther King Jr. Drive in Jersey City must be known as the Judge Shirley A. Tolentino Post Office Building. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-113-140-2014: A Tallmadge mail site is renamed by Public Law 113-140, approved by the 113th Congress in 2014. The Postal Service site at 162 Northeast Avenue in Tallmadge, Ohio, must be known as the Lance Corporal Daniel Nathan Deyarmin, Jr., Post Office Building. The act is framed as a redesignation, since the site had a name before. References to the site in federal laws, maps, rules, records, and other papers count as references to the new name.
plaw-113-141-2014: Public Law 113-141, the Lake Hill Administrative Site Affordable Housing Act, conveys a Forest Service site in Colorado. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. The Lake Hill Administrative Site is about 40 acres of National Forest System land in Summit County. A map from June 2012 shows the parcel. When the county makes a fit offer and accepts a set condition, a transfer follows. The Agriculture Secretary uses a 2005 facility act to convey the site to the county.
plaw-113-142-2014: Public Law 113-142, the Huna Tlingit Traditional Gull Egg Use Act, allows a small egg harvest in Alaska. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. Members of the Hoonah Indian Association may gather eggs of glaucous-winged gulls in Glacier Bay National Park. The Interior Secretary sets the terms of the harvest. It may run no more than twice in a calendar year. It may use up to 5 spots in the park. A harvest plan part starts as the sample ends.
plaw-113-143-2014: Public Law 113-143, the Veterinary Medicine Mobility Act of 2014, frees vets who travel with controlled drugs. The 113th Congress amended the Controlled Substances Act. A vet who is registered need not hold a second registration to carry and hand out such drugs. The work must be the usual course of veterinary practice at a site away from the vet's main place. The site must be in a state where the vet holds a license. The sample ends as one more limit on the site begins.
plaw-113-144-2014: Public Law 113-144, the Unlocking Consumer Choice and Wireless Competition Act, restores a rule on unlocking phones. The 113th Congress passed it in 2014. It wipes out a 2012 rule of the Librarian of Congress on mobile wireless devices. The older text, as it stood on July 27, 2010, takes its place at once. The act then orders fresh rulemaking by the Librarian. The Register of Copyrights makes a proposal first, after talks with a Commerce Department official named in the text.
plaw-113-145-2014: Israel's Iron Dome gets fresh funds from Public Law 113-145, a joint resolution of the 113th Congress from 2014. Its title calls it the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Resolution, 2014. One sum is granted for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2014. The sum is $225,000,000 in added Procurement, Defense-Wide funds. The Defense Secretary must pass the money to the Government of Israel. It buys the Iron Dome defense system, which counters short-range rocket threats. The funds last until September 30, 2015.
plaw-113-146-2014:
Public Law 113-146, the Veterans Access, Choice, and Accountability Act of 2014, seeks to widen care for veterans. The 113th Congress passed it to improve access to medical services from the Department of Veterans Affairs. Title I turns to care from providers outside the department. Its short title in the contents list speaks of access, choice, and accountability.

Section 101 widens the use of deals with outside groups for hospital care and medical services. Two sections deepen joint work. One pairs the department with the Indian Health Service, and one with Native Hawaiian health care systems. A pilot program of stronger contract care is renewed and changed.
plaw-113-147-2014: Tyrone, New York, gains a named post office building under Public Law 113-147 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Drivers find the site at 815 County Road 23. Congress orders that it be known as the Specialist Christopher Scott Post Office Building. A cite to the site in any federal paper is, by the act's terms, a cite to the new name.
plaw-113-148-2014: Public Law 113-148, passed in 2014 by the 113th Congress, names one post office in California. The Postal Service site at 6937 Village Parkway in Dublin must be known as the James 'Jim' Kohnen Post Office. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-113-149-2014: A Lexington Avenue site in New York City is named by Public Law 113-149 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The site at 450 Lexington Avenue in New York, New York, must be known as the Vincent R. Sombrotto Post Office. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-113-150-2014:
Public Law 113-150 carries the name Sean and David Goldman International Child Abduction Prevention and Return Act of 2014. The 113th Congress passed it to press for full respect of the 1980 Hague Convention on child abduction. Partner countries owe each other duties under that pact. The act also sets steps for the prompt return of children taken to other countries.

Title I covers actions of the Department of State. It calls for a yearly report, standards and aid, and deals worked out with other states. Title II covers actions by the Secretary of State in answer to abductions. The contents list breaks off as those actions begin.
plaw-113-151-2014: Alden, New York, gains a named memorial post office under Public Law 113-151 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The site sits at 13127 Broadway Street in the town. It takes the name Sergeant Brett E. Gornewicz Memorial Post Office. When a law, map, or record speaks of the site, the act reads it as speaking of that name.
plaw-113-152-2014: Public Law 113-152, the Improving Trauma Care Act of 2014, widens one word in the Public Health Service Act. The word is trauma. Under title XII, trauma now means harm from a push of force. It also means harm from an outside agent of another kind. Heat, electric shock, chemicals, and radiation are the agents named. The same new sense is set in two places. One place serves the trauma systems grant programs. The other serves the joint program for trauma research.
plaw-113-153-2014: Public Law 113-153, passed in 2014 by the 113th Congress, names one post office building in New York. The Postal Service site at 198 Baker Street in Corning must be known as the Specialist Ryan P. Jayne Post Office Building. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-113-154-2014: Cemetery desecration joins a religious freedom law under Public Law 113-154 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. It amends the International Religious Freedom Act of 1998. The desecration of cemeteries now counts among the breaches of the right to religious freedom. Findings call cemeteries sacred sites of deep worth to many faith and ethnic groups. Congress finds that graves are defaced or wrecked due to their faith ties, worldwide. Such attacks strike at free worship, worst of all when states back or allow them.
plaw-113-155-2014: Nebo, North Carolina, gains a named Forest Service building under Public Law 113-155 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The Grandfather Ranger District site at 109 Lawing Drive in Nebo must be known as the Jason Crisp Forest Service Building. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-113-156-2014: Public Law 113-156, the Money Remittances Improvement Act of 2014, lets the Treasury lean on state bank exams. The 113th Congress amended title 31 of the United States Code. The Secretary may rely on exams by a state oversight body for a class of financial firms. The class must be one that has to meet the reporting rules on money deals. Or the state body must test that class for such compliance. The power sits in a new item of section 5318.
plaw-113-157-2014: Autism parts of the Public Health Service Act are renewed by Public Law 113-157 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Its short title is the Autism Collaboration, Accountability, Research, Education, and Support Act of 2014. People call it the Autism CARES Act of 2014 for short. Section 2 sets up a national push on autism spectrum disorder. The Health and Human Services Secretary must name a serving official to oversee it. That official works with the Defense and Education heads.
plaw-113-158-2014: Philadelphia's 30th Street Station is renamed by Public Law 113-158 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The station at 2955 Market Street is known to most as 30th Street Station. It must now be known as the William H. Gray III 30th Street Station. Any mention of that station in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-113-159-2014:
Public Law 113-159, the Highway and Transportation Funding Act of 2014, extends road and transit programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund. The 113th Congress passed it in August 2014. Title I is called Surface Transportation Program Extension. Subtitle A extends the federal-aid highway programs and covers office costs.

Subtitle B extends highway safety programs. It names the traffic safety office and the motor carrier safety office. A sport fish restoration act is named there as well. Subtitle C covers public transportation. Its first sections deal with set-share grants for rural areas and how grant funds are split.
plaw-113-160-2014: One thousand more Afghan special immigrant visas are added by Public Law 113-160 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Section 1 amends the Afghan Allies Protection Act of 2009. For a brief span in 2014, 1,000 more principal aliens may gain special immigrant status. The span ends on December 31, 2014. A person's qualifying work must end on or before that date. The person must also apply to the Chief of Mission by that date. The power to grant the status ends the same day.
plaw-113-161-2014:
Public Law 113-161, the Near East and South Central Asia Religious Freedom Act of 2014, creates a special envoy post. The 113th Congress passed it to guard the faith rights of religious minorities in two regions. The President may name a Special Envoy inside the Department of State. The envoy holds the rank of ambassador and serves at the President's pleasure. The post calls for a person of known standing in human rights and religious freedom.

Section 3 lists the envoy's duties. The first is to promote the faith rights of minorities in the two regions. The sample's duty list also covers watching and fighting bias and incitement aimed at such groups. It covers care for the money and safety needs of those groups as well.
plaw-113-162-2014:
Public Law 113-162, the Assessing Progress in Haiti Act of 2014, measures how Haiti has recovered since a huge quake. The 113th Congress passed it to track recovery and growth work there. Section 2 gives the scale of the disaster. On January 12, 2010, a quake struck near Port-au-Prince, the capital of Haiti. About 220,000 people died, among them 103 United States citizens.

The findings count 300,000 hurt, 115,000 homes wrecked, and 1,500,000 people displaced. A joint needs review put harm and losses at $7,804,000,000. The findings also note deep poverty before the quake. They note hunger for more than 6,700,000 people and a cholera outbreak from October 2010.
plaw-113-163-2014: The short title Victims of Child Abuse Act Reauthorization Act of 2013 belongs to Public Law 113-163 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. It renews subtitle A of the Victims of Child Abuse Act of 1990. Section 2 aims to improve how child abuse cases are probed and brought to court. One edit strikes the years 2004 and 2005 from section 214B. The years 2014 through 2018 take their place, in two spots. A new section 214C then adds grant accountability rules, as the sample shows.
plaw-113-164-2014:
Public Law 113-164 is a joint resolution of the 113th Congress, called the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2015. It funds the government for fiscal year 2015 on a stopgap basis. Section 101 grants such sums as may be needed. Funding follows the rates set in the spending acts for fiscal year 2014, on the same terms. Work covered is work done in fiscal year 2014 under those acts.

The first act named in the list covers farm, rural, and food and drug work for 2014. Money comes from the Treasury and from agency receipts and funds. Like other laws of its kind, it keeps projects and work going rather than setting new policy. The sample ends part-way through the list of prior acts.
plaw-113-165-2014: A stamp for wild species in many lands is renewed by Public Law 113-165 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Its short title is the Multinational Species Conservation Funds Semipostal Stamp Reauthorization Act of 2013. A semipostal is a stamp sold above face value for a cause. Section 2 amends the 2010 act behind the stamp. It strikes the words 2 years and inserts 6 years. That swap stretches how long the stamp may be sold.
plaw-113-166-2014: Federal law on muscular dystrophy research is amended by Public Law 113-166 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Its short title names Paul D. Wellstone and adds the words Community Assistance, Research and Education Amendments of 2014. Section 2 edits a Public Health Service Act part on the National Institutes of Health. One edit fixes a misspelling, Muscoskeletal, to Musculoskeletal. A second edit adds Becker, congenital, and limb-girdle forms after Duchenne in a list of types. Study of heart and lung function is added as well.
plaw-113-167-2014: How a land sales law treats condominiums is clarified by Public Law 113-167 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The law in scope is the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act. Section 1 adds an exemption for homes in condominium form. The sale or lease of a condominium unit is exempt, if it is not already exempt under another part. The act then defines the term. A unit's owner must hold sole ownership of the unit, plus a shared share of the common parts. The unit must be an improved lot.
plaw-113-168-2014: Public Law 113-168, the Tribal General Welfare Exclusion Act of 2014, sets a tax rule for tribal welfare aid. The 113th Congress amended the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. A new section 139E states the core rule in one line. Gross income does not include the value of any Indian general welfare benefit. Such a benefit is a payment or service for a tribal member, or a spouse or dependent. It must flow from a tribal government program run under set guidelines.
plaw-113-169-2014: A water settlement in Nevada is ratified by Public Law 113-169 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Its short title is the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe - Fish Springs Ranch Settlement Act. Section 3 ratifies the deal, as the contents list shows. The base deal is dated May 30, 2007. A 2013 supplement, dated November 20, 2013, updates it. Later sections cover waivers and releases of claims. They also cover how claims are met, who gains from the deal, and court reach.
plaw-113-170-2014: Public Law 113-170, the All Circuit Review Extension Act, stretches a court review span for whistleblowers. The 113th Congress amended title 5 of the United States Code in 2014. The review in scope covers rulings of the Merit Systems Protection Board on whistleblower cases. Section 7703 had set the span at 2 years. The act strikes 2-year and inserts 5-year, in two places. One place covers the worker's own review path. The other covers review by the Director.
plaw-113-171-2014: Small text fixes to an older memorial law are made by Public Law 113-171 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The law is section 313 of the Consolidated Natural Resources Act of 2008, Public Law 110-229. That law covers the Bainbridge Island memorial. In three places, the words Japanese American Memorial gain one word. They now read Japanese American Exclusion Memorial. Two of the fixes touch headings, and one touches the body text.
plaw-113-172-2014: The Defense Production Act of 1950 is renewed by Public Law 113-172 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. Section 1 amends section 717 of that act. The end year moves from 2014 to 2019. Section 2 improves the Defense Production Act Committee. Its job shifts from advise the President to coordinate and plan for the work. The text names the powers in scope as the priorities and allocations authorities. The chair is the head of the agency the President charges with lead coordination.
plaw-113-173-2014: Public Law 113-173, the Examination and Supervisory Privilege Parity Act of 2014, guards secrets shared with bank regulators. The 113th Congress amended the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010. Some non-bank firms covered by that act share exam facts with federal and state regulators. The act adds state bodies that license, oversee, or test sellers of consumer financial products. Sharing with them does not waive, wreck, or affect any privilege or secrecy in the facts shared.
plaw-113-174-2014: Two education advisory panels gain one more year under Public Law 113-174 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2014. The first is the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity. The second is the Advisory Committee on Student Financial Assistance. Both sit in the Higher Education Act of 1965. In section 114 and in section 491, the year 2014 is struck. The year 2015 takes its place in each spot.
plaw-113-175-2014:
Public Law 113-175, the Department of Veterans Affairs Expiring Authorities Act of 2014, extends VA rules set to lapse. The 113th Congress amended title 38 of the United States Code. Title I covers health care powers. Section 101 extends the duty to give nursing home care to some veterans with service-linked disabilities.

Later sections extend pilot programs. One gives counseling in retreat settings to women veterans newly out of service. One helps with child care for some veterans in care. One extends grants to veterans service groups, as the contents list begins to show. The act is a yearly renewal vehicle, not new policy.
plaw-113-176-2014: Public Law 113-176 is a joint resolution of the 113th Congress, approved in September 2014. It approves the site of a memorial in Washington.
