They drew on a cross-national survey of adults aged fifty and older, covering more than one hundred thousand people in twenty countries. Five risks were tested against memory scores: living alone, inactivity, obesity, depression, and heart and metabolic conditions.

All five risks were tied to worse memory on average, but the strength of several links changed by region, and a few even flipped direction. Living alone, obesity, and inactivity behaved least consistently across northern, western, eastern, and southern Europe. Results also shifted with education and age in parts of the analysis. The authors warn that dementia prevention plans imported wholesale from one region may misfire in another. Local context, they argue, should shape which risks a program targets first.
pmc-13244514:
Zhenyuan Yu, Shuwei Zhang, and Ze Lu reviewed the two-way traffic between iron and mouth bacteria in gum disease. Their narrative review appeared in the Journal of Oral Microbiology in 2026. Periodontitis is driven by oral pathogens, yet it also tracks with body-wide disease. Iron sits at the crossroads: too much free iron feeds radical damage and a form of cell death called ferroptosis.

In periodontitis, blood iron and its carrier transferrin fall while storage and control proteins rise, a signature of iron locked away by inflammation. That misdistribution shelters pathogens, fans inflammation, kills ligament cells by ferroptosis, and eats into jaw bone. The same iron disorder ties gum disease to anemia and other systemic conditions. Chelating or rebalancing iron looks promising as therapy, the authors say, but solid clinical trials are still missing. The review frames gums as an iron story, not only a plaque story.
pmc-13246514:
Lee and Leite published this publisher correction in Behavior Research Methods in 2026. It corrects their earlier article on propensity score analysis, a statistical method for comparing groups in observational studies, when some data are missing in ways that depend on the missing values themselves. Their paper had introduced a method called dual-forest proximity imputation for filling in such gaps.

A publisher correction is a formal notice that something in the published record was wrong and has now been fixed, so that readers and future citations rest on the corrected version. The notice itself presents no new data or analysis. Readers who use the dual-forest method should check the corrected article to see exactly what changed.
pmc-13247314:
Zhang, Zhao, and Liu re-examined how a protein switches on, in this 2026 Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal study. Proteins are often pictured flipping between two fixed shapes, but the authors suspected the innate immune adaptor STING works more subtly. Using long molecular-dynamics simulations and network inference, they watched how binding a small signaling molecule reshaped the protein's whole range of motion.

The ligand did not simply snap STING from closed to open. It reweighted the energy landscape, suppressing stretched-out shapes and favoring activation-ready intermediates, while communication routes inside the protein condensed from scattered paths into shorter, focused channels that transmit signals more efficiently. The authors propose allosteric activation as landscape reweighting, a model that may explain regulation in many flexible proteins.
pmc-13248314: Dwivedi and colleagues published this correction notice in 2026 in the Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology. It fixes their earlier paper on gene activity and chemical marks on DNA in cows with subclinical mastitis, a hidden udder infection. Two values in Table 1 were printed wrong for the gene OXCT1, one for its measured activity change and one for a methylation change at its promoter. The notice records the correct figures and leaves the study's findings and conclusions unchanged.
pmc-13250214:
Kola and co-authors set out a plan for reviewing survival when patients with lung scarring need a breathing machine. Their 2026 BMJ Open protocol covers interstitial lung diseases, a group of disorders marked by lung inflammation or scarring. Patients in sudden breathing failure often enter intensive care, yet evidence on whether invasive ventilation helps them is thin.

The review will search four databases for trials and observational studies in adults receiving invasive ventilation. Main outcomes are deaths in hospital and at one year, with time off the ventilator and length of stay also tracked. Planned subgroup checks include disease subtype, lung pressure problems, and timing of ventilation. Study quality will be graded with standard tools before results are combined where the data allow.
pmc-13251614:
Nijina Li and Hao Zhang trace a molecular driver of atrial fibrillation in this 2026 study. The common irregular heartbeat disorder scars the heart's upper chambers and disrupts their energy factories, and a chemical tag placed on RNA may help drive that damage.

In rats with the disorder, both the tagging enzyme, called TRMT10C, and the tags themselves ran high, alongside excess splitting of the energy factories and more scarring. Silencing the enzyme cut splitting proteins and scar tissue and slowed the disease. It works by stabilising the message for a receptor protein, the team shows. The pathway offers fresh targets for treatment research.
pmc-13253714:
Kulachatr Panyawechamontri and co-authors report a 2026 plant study aimed at making more protein in tobacco plants. Nicotiana benthamiana is a common host for fast, short-term protein making. The team shrank a standard gene carrier, pBI121, by cutting parts it did not need, then tuned the fluid used to deliver genes into leaves.

The smaller carrier raised gene message levels about twofold for two test proteins, GUS and ASM. Protein levels rose 1.76-fold and 1.75-fold. A tuned buffer, plus a helper that blocks gene silencing, gave the highest output, offering a practical boost for plant-based protein work.
pmc-13254114:
Sarah Polk and a large team test phone-based memory checks for early Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 study. They followed 202 people aged 52 to 85, of whom 152 were cognitively unimpaired and 50 had mild cognitive impairment. Participants did remote memory tasks on their own, testing object and scene detail and memory for links.

Within 30 weeks, the impaired group declined more on a familiarity-based task. Those who also had amyloid, a brain protein tied to Alzheimer's, declined more in object memory precision too. Change on the phone task matched multi-year change on in-person tests, supporting frequent remote testing.
pmc-13254314:
Katarzyna Osowska, Julian Szymański, and Witold Libionka share a brain recording data set in a 2026 paper. During deep brain stimulation surgery, thin electrodes record neuron signals as they pass through deep brain areas. Open data sets of these recordings are scarce, the authors note.

Their set holds 6,646 processed recordings from 132 patients with conditions such as Parkinson's disease, dystonia, Huntington's disease, and epilepsy. Signals were filtered and cleaned with an automated pipeline, and an expert labeled examples from three deep brain structures. The data aim to support structure classification and better targeting methods.
pmc-13254514:
Ettore Greco and colleagues make an all-wood resin for 3D printing in a 2026 study. Most printing resins come from petroleum. Their resin blends a lignin-derived monomer with acrylated guaiacol, then adds treated pinewood flour up to a stated loading level.

The mix flowed well for room-temperature printing and cured under light. Printed parts showed strong bonding between the matrix and wood flour. Adding the flour raised the glass transition temperature from 38 to 62 degrees Celsius and lifted stiffness and strength. The authors say biomass resins can narrow the gap with fossil-based ones.
pmc-13254714:
Alina Pant and colleagues review ambulance services in low- and middle-income countries in a 2026 paper. Ambulance systems in these settings range from basic setups to partly integrated national networks. The team searched four databases in March 2025 and included seventeen studies published between 2009 and 2023.

Analysis surfaced five recurring barriers: weak oversight, thin financing, workforce shortages, poor communication, and limited sites. Underneath them sits a deeper problem the authors stress: the system is split into separate pieces. Local volunteers and other responders routinely fill the gaps left by formal services, yet policy frameworks barely acknowledge them. That disconnect, more than raw scarcity alone, explains much of the weak performance. The authors recommend bridging formal and informal systems, making the volunteer tier professional rather than ignoring it. Better staffing and teamwork, they conclude, would lift outcomes even before large new spending arrives.
pmc-13255214:
Jiaona Liu and co-authors build lab models of heat stroke kidney injury in a 2026 study. Exertional heat stroke, a life-threatening overheating during exercise, often damages the kidneys, yet standard models are scarce. The team exercised mice under heat stress, testing water loss and humidity levels, and also heated human kidney cells in dishes.

Water deprivation clearly worsened kidney damage, raising waste levels in the blood. A setting of 39.5 degrees with 65 percent humidity gave severe but survivable injury. In cells, a set mix of muscle protein and vitamin C best mimicked the injury. The models now support mechanism and drug studies.
pmc-13256314:
Vahidreza Tehranirad and colleagues report a 2026 MRI study of mesenteric panniculitis, an inflamed, scarring condition of the fatty tissue that suspends the intestines. It is usually treated as a rare incidental finding. The team reviewed standardized 3-Tesla MRI examinations from 312 people, most with chronic inflammatory bowel conditions, plus sixty controls without bowel inflammation.

Using a rule requiring at least three of five characteristic signs, they found the pattern in nearly nine of ten patients with bowel inflammation, versus one of sixty controls. Crohn's disease cases formed the largest subgroup, followed by sigmoid diverticulitis and ulcerative colitis. The changes clustered in the left upper abdomen. The authors argue these mesenteric changes are a common imaging companion of chronic intestinal inflammation rather than a curiosity.
pmc-13258114:
Beom-Su Kim and colleagues measure spinal rotation in three dimensions against breathing capacity in scoliosis in a 2026 study. Two hundred fifty patients who had full-spine scans and breathing tests within a year were analyzed. Rotation was measured vertebra by vertebra with a standard method, and a new asymmetry index compared the main curve with its compensating curve.

All rotation measures tracked worse lung function, and the asymmetry index tracked it most strongly. Air volume percentages fell steadily as the gap between curve rotations grew. Adjusted models kept the index informative even after accounting for the usual two-dimensional curve angle and chest shape. Subgroup checks by cause supported the pattern. Spine surgeons gain a richer severity signal: rotational mismatch between curves may flag breathing risk that flat images underestimate.
pmc-13259614:
Shirley Salcedo Arteaga and colleagues measured chromosome damage in Colombian mothers and newborns living near pesticide-sprayed fields. Córdoba's farm communities face heavy exposure, and what crosses the placenta is poorly charted. Their 2026 case-control study pairs eighty-six mothers with their babies, exposed and unexposed.

A specialized assay counted micronuclei, tiny fragments that betray genomic instability, in blood from both generations. Exposed mothers and newborns both showed significantly more damage markers. Newborns in the sprayed area carried a five-fold higher prevalence of elevated counts. The authors read this as evidence of genotoxic agents reaching the womb, and call for protective policies.
pmc-13260214:
Zeyu Liao, Yahui Fu, and Ran Li trace a fat-handling enzyme that first protects, then abandons, the diabetic heart. Diabetic cardiomyopathy drowns heart cells in lipids, and the enzyme ACOT1 moves oddly across its stages. Their 2026 mouse study flips the enzyme up and down at each stage.

Early on, extra ACOT1 improved pumping and calmed oxidative stress, but its later disappearance worsened remodeling. The enzyme tags a fat-making switch, SREBP1c, with a lactylation mark under high lactate. That mark drives the switch into the nucleus and opens the fatty acid gate CD36. Fat floods in, poisoning the heart, a chain the authors propose blocking.
pmc-13260714:
Funso Akinola Alaye, Omar Gelo, and Human-Friedrich Unterrainer proposed in 2026 a new process model of addiction centered on attention. Existing theories explain reward learning, cue reactions, and emotion control well, they argue, but miss the moment attention flips toward addictive behavior. Their Strategic Distraction Motive model names the trigger: an experience judged impossible to engage, voice, or resolve.

When a person appraises a live problem as insoluble, attention shifts to the bounded, familiar world of addiction talk and behavior. That shift protects short-term coherence and social footing while postponing the threat. The model makes three testable predictions about timing, content, and how such pivots reshape replies to other people. The authors present addiction here as context-sensitive attention management under strain, and they bound the claim to that process level.
pmc-13261614:
Zhaocheng Liu and colleagues unveiled in 2026 an ultrasensitive test for cancer mutations in blood-borne tumor DNA. Such fragments can guide therapy and flag relapse, but they swim in a sea of normal DNA. Their dual hairpin-competition CRISPR system stacks two filtering layers: one while copying the DNA, one while the Cas14a enzyme checks it.

The double filter multiplied the system's power to tell mutant from normal DNA by nearly sixtyfold. It reliably found four therapy-relevant mutations at shares as low as two thousandths of one percent of total DNA. Grouped testing kept similar sensitivity. On 22 patient plasma samples, its calls for one key lung cancer mutation matched the reference droplet method every time. The test runs on standard laboratory machines, cutting both cost and turnaround against sequencing.
pmc-13262114:
Eric Chen and co-authors report Salmonella escaping the gut to infect blood, skin, and bowel at once. The bacterium usually causes brief food poisoning, but vulnerable hosts can suffer invasive disease. Their 2026 case follows a seventy-five-year-old man with diabetes, circulation trouble, and liver cirrhosis.

Days of diarrhea gave way to a red, swollen leg with a calf ulcer. Blood, wound, and stool tests all grew the same Salmonella, fully drug-sensitive. Scans showed inflammation without any abscess pocket, a rarity for this pattern. Seven days of intravenous ceftriaxone cleared everything, with no heart infection and no relapse at three months.
pmc-13264014:
Silje-Marie Jensen and colleagues report a 2026 study of how blood fats and inflammation markers change during the day after a meal. Thirty-four healthy young adults fasted, ate a standard breakfast, and then gave blood samples many times over twenty-four hours. Laboratory methods measured lipoprotein particles, which carry fats in the blood, along with several inflammation signals.

Very low density lipoproteins rose sharply a few hours after eating, fell back, and rose again later. High density lipoproteins moved in the opposite pattern. One inflammation marker, interleukin-6, climbed strongly about ten hours after breakfast while others changed little. The results show why the exact time since a meal can alter test results in both research and clinic visits.
pmc-13264114:
Fauzia Yasir, Majida Kazmi and Saad Ahmed Qazi build a large benchmark for Urdu character recognition in a 2026 data article. Urdu is spoken by hundreds of millions of people, yet public training data for reading its script remain scarce. Wide variation across printed fonts makes recognition hard, and the lack of a shared test set blocks fair comparison between systems.

Their collection renders forty-eight character classes, covering letters and numerals, across more than two hundred fonts. Systematic changes in shape, brightness, blur and noise expand the base images into hundreds of thousands of labeled examples. Fixed training, validation and test splits are provided. Developers gain a common yardstick for building recognizers that handle real Urdu print more reliably.
pmc-13264314:
Hongyan Wu and colleagues report rupture of a cesarean scar pouch caused by infection outside pregnancy in a 2026 case report. Scar diverticula, small pouches in the old surgical cut, are a known late complication as cesarean rates rise. Rupture during pregnancy is documented, yet rupture driven by womb infection in a non-pregnant woman is exceptionally rare and easy to misdiagnose among causes of pelvic pain and abnormal bleeding patterns.

A thirty-nine-year-old woman with two prior cesareans had lower abdominal pain plus bleeding between periods and after intercourse. Camera surgery confirmed a ruptured pouch holding pus, which was repaired. Culture grew E. coli. Risk clues, imaging and management steps are outlined for earlier recognition.
pmc-13264614:
Sally A Fahim and a large team published a 2026 lab study on Anchusa azurea, a plant long used in folk care for joint pain and skin wounds. They tested its extract alongside cisplatin, a strong cancer drug with harsh side effects, on cancer cells grown in dishes. The aim was to see if the plant boosts the drug.

The extract slowed bone and oral cancer cells while sparing normal skin cells, and the pair worked better together than either alone. Treated cells showed lower levels of two inflammation signals and higher levels of proteins that drive cell death. Chemical profiling found 50 plant compounds, led by rosmarinic acid. The authors call for animal tests next.
pmc-13264814: Arun Kumar Dubey and colleagues published a correction notice in 2026 for their paper comparing deep learning models that outline lungs in chest X-rays for infection screening. The correction fixes the author list order, which had placed the last author first in error. The proper order starts with Dubey and ends with Md Nasre Alam. It also fixes one author's affiliation, which carried a stray letter before the college name in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The notice states the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13264914:
Katja Radon and colleagues survey how worldviews relate to zoonotic disease knowledge and habits in four Latin American countries, in 2026. The survey covered Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, and Guatemala. It focused on Indigenous peoples and local communities living near rich wildlife. Beliefs about nature may shape contact with animals and risk.

Interviewers visited households and questioned 2,903 people aged ten and older. Analysis grouped respondents into three outlook classes. The largest group, just over half, held a relational outlook with strong spiritual ties to animals. Other groups held more dualistic outlooks. The study then compared knowledge, concern, and practices such as hunting across these groups.
pmc-13265014:
Kadriye Demir and Erkan Çelik published a 2026 eye study comparing the two eyes of patients who developed macular swelling after cataract surgery in one eye only. The swelling, a common cause of poor sight recovery, may reflect a thickened choroid, the blood layer under the retina. Using the healthy fellow eye as control cancels out surgery effects shared by both.

They studied 25 patients, with swelling appearing on average 6.2 weeks after surgery. The central retina was far thicker in affected eyes, as expected. The choroid beneath was slightly thicker too, but the gap did not reach statistical significance, which the authors link partly to the small sample. They suggest choroid thickening after surgery mostly mirrors general post-surgery inflammation rather than a disease-specific mechanism.
pmc-13265714:
Hai-Yang Hu and colleagues review osteoarthritis within the web of age-related diseases, published in 2026. Joint degeneration often coexists with osteoporosis, obesity, diabetes, and high blood pressure in older patients. How these conditions push each other remained underexplored. Organ cross-talk is the organising idea.

Shared pathways include mechanical stress, metabolic disturbance, and inflammation. Each comorbidity can worsen joint disease, while joint disease worsens overall health in return. Common medicines for older patients also shape the picture. The authors call for integrated treatment and research into shared molecular pathways, supporting drug reuse and risk-guided care.
pmc-13266214:
Ye Jin Yoo and colleagues compare two non-surgical treatments for early kidney cancer, published in 2026. Focused radiation, called SABR, was set against heat ablation in stage one disease. Many patients are older or unfit for surgery. Adjusted comparisons balanced the groups for fair testing.

Cancer outcomes were comparable after adjustment. Kidney function decline over time was similar, despite the radiation group starting lower. Radiation stayed effective despite older age and less favourable tumours. Only one serious non-kidney side effect occurred, bleeding after marker placement. The authors support radiation as a viable alternative to ablation.
pmc-13266414:
Zeyu Wang wrote a 2026 review on pairs of Chinese herbs and how they may help metabolic disease. Such pairs are the core unit of classic Chinese herbal practice, where herbs take roles like monarch and minister. The review links this old idea to gut microbes, the tiny living things in the bowel.

Wang sums up recent work on obesity, type 2 diabetes, and fatty liver disease. Herbal pairs seem to reshape gut microbe groups and the chemicals those microbes make. They may also repair the gut wall and calm signals sent along the gut-to-organ axis. The review closes with open problems and steps needed before wider clinical use.
pmc-13266614:
Dominika Jakubczyk and the team publish a unified protocol for growing human small airway cells at an air-liquid interface, in 2026. Primary cells model the breathing barrier more closely than endless lab lines or animal lines. Air contact on one side mimics the real airway setting. A single workflow from thaw to barrier forming was missing.

Steps cover thawing after freezing through to a sealed barrier layer. Electric resistance readings track strength without harming the culture. The guide targets teams with limited airway culture practice. Each stage gives practical, clear steps for steady barrier models.
pmc-13266814:
In Sub Kim and co-authors ask in 2026 whether chest CT scans reveal a hidden structural risk for collapsed lung in young adults with a sunken chest shape. Some people suffer a spontaneous pneumothorax without visible blebs, so the team measured lobe size, shape, and tissue density in patients, chest-shape patients, and healthy controls aged 20 to 30.

Lobes from pneumothorax patients showed higher surface area relative to volume, less compact shape, and wider density spread. A machine learning model sorted patients from controls accurately, then flagged many chest-shape patients as carrying a similar pattern. The work suggests risk can be read from scan geometry and density, though follow-up studies must confirm who actually collapses a lung.
pmc-13269314:
Akira Saito and Takamasa Mizuno published a journal article in 2026 on electrical stimulation and stretching at the ankle. The stimulation makes calf muscles contract through pads placed either over a nerve or over the muscle itself. They tested whether it changes how much stretch a person can tolerate.

After stimulation and five minutes of stretching, the gain in ankle bend was small and alike across groups, about two to three degrees. Muscle-tendon stiffness fell by similar amounts in all groups. Stretch tolerance rose clearly only after stimulation, by 9.0 percent over the nerve and 6.9 percent over the muscle. Rest alone gave a 1.5 percent rise. Pad position did not matter much.
pmc-13269514:
Florian Heilmann, Leif E Langsdorf, and Torsten Schubert published a journal article in 2026 on interference control in teen athletes. This control is the ability to ignore distracting cues while responding. Boys aged 15 to 18 did nine versions of a reaction task, varying the pictures shown and whether they answered with finger, hand, or foot.

The 91 boys included 28 handball players, 34 soccer players, and 29 non-players. Mismatched cues slowed everyone, and sport pictures plus harder movements slowed responses further. Sport pictures, though, shrank the distraction effect itself. No steady advantage appeared for either athlete group over non-players. The authors say task demands shaped scores more than group membership did.
pmc-13269814:
Jae Hyeon Park and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on blood safety testing before transfusion across Korea, using ten years of insurance claims. Checks include blood type matching, antibody screening, and crossmatching donor blood. Claims from 2011 to 2020 were sorted by hospital type.

The analysis covered nearly 43 million claims from over 20 million patients. Large hospitals matched national standards closely, while primary hospitals and clinics scored zero on a key typing ratio. Automated typing grew in most settings but barely in primary hospitals. For a first transfusion, 71.5 percent of primary hospital patients and 68.3 percent of clinic patients got blood after crossmatching alone, without antibody screening. The authors urge training and reform.
pmc-13269914:
Dorian de la Fuente and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on how people vary and adapt their emotion control in daily life. A sample of 161 people aged 14 to 78 completed six online thinking tasks. For 14 days they also reported their emotional experiences and control strategies as life unfolded.

Thinking performance fell with age across all three domains tested. Older age, however, went with less variation in emotion control strategies, both within and between strategies. Flexibility, meaning matching strategy to situation, stayed stable with age. Thinking scores did not explain daily control variation. Flexibility showed curved links with unpleasant mood: both low and high sensitivity to context went with worse mood.
pmc-13270414:
Zachary Vinton and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 60-year-old man with progressive fatigue, upper belly pain, and iron deficiency. His gut camera exam showed normal-looking lining in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. Random tissue samples were taken anyway, and they changed the picture.

The biopsies revealed duodenal-type follicular lymphoma, an uncommon slow-growing cancer, with no sign of the same cancer elsewhere in the body. Body scans showed no focal uptake in the duodenum, only doubtful faint uptake in nearby nodes. He was treated with a single antibody drug, rituximab. Follow-up scans showed a complete metabolic response, and repeat biopsies found no remaining lymphoma.
pmc-13270714:
Asmaa Namoos led a 2026 retrospective study, one looking back at health records, on fall-related injuries in older cancer survivors. Cancer treatment can cause nerve damage, weakness, bone loss, and tiredness, all of which may raise the risk of a harmful fall.

Using records from a Virginia health system, the team studied 19,370 survivors aged 65 and older from 2013 to 2023. Seven percent had a new documented fall injury, and eight percent had any such injury in the period. Black survivors showed a higher documented risk than White survivors, at 4.915 percent versus 4.048 percent, a gap the authors treat as a racial disparity needing attention.
pmc-13271814:
Austin J. Mendoza and Julie S. Haas wrote a 2026 neuroscience journal article on electrical coupling in thalamocortical networks, the circuits that relay sensory information from the thalamus to the cortex of the brain. Inhibitory cells in a relay-station nucleus are extensively linked by electrical synapses, direct cell-to-cell connections usually credited with synchronising rhythms.

The authors built a computer network of relay and inhibitory cells in a ring, feeding sensory-like inputs in sequence. Each added electrical link changed spike rates and timing in both cell types. Coupling unexpectedly raised cortical response rates and duration while reducing how closely cortical spikes correlated with the input sequence. They argue these embedded links powerfully shape sensory relay in realistic networks.
pmc-13271914:
Aleksandra Krawczyk and colleagues set out in 2026 a trial protocol testing midwife-led teaching sessions against pregnancy-related anxiety. This anxiety centers on the pregnancy itself, birth, and early parenthood, and it often goes unnoticed in routine care. Poland's high caesarean rate makes fear of birth a pressing concern there.

The planned trial will enroll 74 women with low-risk pregnancies and raised anxiety scores, split evenly between groups. One group gets four to six private sessions with a trained midwife covering birth knowledge, pain control, and coping skills. Anxiety change late in pregnancy is the main outcome, with birth mode also recorded.
pmc-13272414:
Xingtao Jin and coauthors map in 2026 research on immunotherapy for chronic hepatitis B, a virus infecting hundreds of millions and driving liver scarring and cancer. Reviving the immune response is among the most promising routes to a functional cure. Bibliometric mapping shows where that effort concentrates and where it may head.

The team analyzed 3,029 articles published between 2005 and 2025 from two databases, charting countries, institutions, journals, and keywords. China and the United States led in volume and influence, while a French national institute ranked as the most prolific single institution. Keyword trends point to the field's emerging hotspots for the next research cycle.
pmc-13272514:
Emilia Jalil leads a 2026 study of young trans women and travestis in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and their HIV status. The work uses baseline data from a peer-led support study run in 2022. People aged 18 to 24 joined if they were not on HIV prevention drugs or not in HIV care.

Of 164 people enrolled, 13 percent were living with HIV, and 68 percent of those did not know it before the study. Among those tested for timing, a third had a recent infection. Younger age, less schooling, and risk from crack or cocaine use were linked to a new diagnosis.
pmc-13272614:
Jandiara Pozzetti leads a 2026 study of landfill leachate, the dark liquid that drains from buried waste, after several treatment steps. Chemical tests alone cannot show whether treated liquid still harms water life. The team used acute and chronic toxicity tests on algae, small water animals, and brine shrimp.

Liquid treated by biological steps was less toxic than raw leachate. Yet a later step using clumping, settling, and powdered carbon removed stubborn compounds while toxicity rose for most test species. The authors link that rise to leftover metals and chlorides from treatment chemicals. Brine shrimp differed, showing falling toxicity after each stage, perhaps due to salt tolerance.
pmc-13272814:
Yuya Komai leads a 2026 study of AvatarLLM, a system that lets a digital avatar speak in the style of a real person it models. Avatars are useful when a person operates them remotely, but they also need to act alone. For avatars that look like a real individual, speech should reflect that person's personality.

The system combines a large language model with speech synthesis to produce personality-consistent utterances. In tests, its utterances were judged as more likely to reproduce the modeled person than the actual person's own utterances were. How an utterance was perceived also shaped how the voice itself was perceived. The work probes what makes generated speech feel like a specific individual.
pmc-13272914:
Alireza Mohammadi leads a 2026 study of children's access to urban park green space in Ardabil, Iran. Access supports children's physical, mental, and social growth, but varies sharply in fast-growing cities. The team used a modified floating catchment method, which weighs park appeal, distance, and catchment size, across 6,417 census blocks.

Central and southwestern neighborhoods had dense parks and good access, while northern and northeastern areas lacked green space. In 2,615 blocks, 42 percent of children had no access to any urban park. Child-dense areas also showed park shortages under the tuned method. The authors call for new parks and better planning in deprived, child-heavy districts.
pmc-13273214:
Kunquan Lai and co-authors built a framework for sorting reading errors in chest CT scans in a 2026 study. Lesions next to the pleura, the lining around the lungs, are easy to misread. The team wanted to classify why readings fail rather than just count failures.

They studied twenty patients at a county hospital, chosen because their cases were hard, and confirmed each final diagnosis by tissue or lab proof in most cases. Eighteen cases showed major or moderate disagreement with the first reading. Two radiologists sorted the errors into three types: misread features, missed findings, and failures to combine information. Misleading features caused two thirds of errors. Agreement between raters was substantial. The authors ask for larger multi-center testing before clinical use.
pmc-13273514:
Yehua Yang and colleagues studied soil microbes that cycle nitrogen in yellow soil in a 2026 paper. These microbes drive how nitrogen moves through farm soil, and fertilizer practice shapes their response. The team compared soil with a long history of nitrogen fertilizer against soil without one.

Adding nitrogen for a short term changed microbe diversity, gene abundance, and species mix clearly in the long fertilized soil, with the highest dose driving the biggest shift. Soil that had never been fertilized long term responded much more weakly to the same additions. Chemical differences in the soil explained much of the community pattern. The authors conclude that fertilizer history decides how strongly microbes react, a point that should guide nitrogen management in yellow soil regions.
pmc-13273714:
Ryan Nishi and co-authors rated YouTube videos about scaphoid fractures as patient education in a 2026 analysis. The scaphoid is the wrist bone broken most often, usually in young active people. Patients search online for guidance, where quality and openness vary greatly.

They examined the fifty most viewed English language videos with standard transparency criteria, a readability style scale, and a score built for this fracture. Physicians made half the videos. Median scores were low for transparency and modest for how understandable the content was, and the fracture specific score reached only half its maximum. Physician videos scored higher on transparency yet lower on clarity than other sources. The authors call for clearer authorship, evidence citations, and patient centered delivery.
pmc-13274214:
Assala Abu Mukh and colleagues wrote a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on adding a second ligament repair to knee ACL surgery. Rebuilding the anterior cruciate ligament with a hamstring graft is standard, but some knees still twist loosely and re-tear. The extra procedure rebuilds the anterolateral ligament on the knee's outer side.

Searching five databases in early 2025, the team screened 4,373 reports and kept twelve studies with 1,274 patients. Follow-up averaged about thirty-one months in both groups. Knees with the added repair showed far less rotational looseness on the pivot shift test, with odds about one fifth of the standard group. The review supports the combined operation for objective stability.
pmc-13276514:
Harrison Zhang Dai and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a rare benign tumor of the eye surface in a toddler. Conjunctival stromal tumors were first described in 2012 and have been reported fewer than sixty times. They are rarer still in children, and this patient is the youngest yet.

The eighteen-month-old girl had a slowly growing mass on the tear duct opening of her right upper eyelid. The lump was not attached to the eyeball, and her vision was normal. Surgeons removed it completely. Under the microscope it showed the tumor's signature mix of bland spindle cells, odd inclusions, and giant cells with flower-like nuclei. Staining matched the diagnosis. The authors note it is only the third case in a child and urge doctors to consider it at any age, while distinguishing it from a similar growth linked to body-wide syndromes.
pmc-13276814:
Jiawei He leads a 2026 first-in-human test of a new scan tracer for prostate cancer. The tracer targets a receptor called NTSR1, while the standard tracer targets PSMA, a protein common on prostate cancer cells. Twenty-three men at Xiangya Hospital had both scans before surgery to remove the prostate.

In men who had no hormone treatment yet, the standard tracer found more cancer and missed less. After short hormone treatment, the pattern flipped and the new tracer found more lesions. Tissue tests matched that shift, as one target fell and the other rose. The authors suggest using each tracer at the stage where it works best.
pmc-13277214:
Dipak Khadka leads a 2026 field study of medicinal plants used by Guoshan Yao communities in the Nanling Mountain foothills of Guangdong, China. Their plant knowledge is fading as society changes and younger people learn less of it. Interviews with 86 household members aged twenty to ninety recorded the plants and how the knowledge passes on.

The team documented 224 medicinal plants, most often used for injuries and bone or joint problems. About three in five people still relied on plants for basic care, though many reported a decline. Knowledge was strongest when it came from parents or from several sources at once. Sharing learning beyond the family could help keep this heritage alive, the authors say.
pmc-13277414:
Jisook Lee heads the author group for part seven of the 2025 Korean resuscitation guidelines, published in 2026. Children's cardiac arrest usually follows breathing failure or injury rather than a primary heart event. Prevention therefore anchors the paediatric basic life support section.

Hospitals are urged to run early warning scores that flag deteriorating children for rapid response. For infant chest compressions, all rescuers should use the two-thumb encircling technique for proper depth and rate. Lay rescuers may attach a defibrillator for children aged one year or older after initial CPR cycles. Choking infants receive alternating back blows and chest thrusts before moving to CPR if they become unresponsive.
pmc-13277714:
Alannah Miranda and colleagues pilot a process-focused scoring system for daily-life skills tests in a 2026 study. Standard skills tests record whether people complete tasks like managing money or medicines. The new system, NEUPSA, also scores the thinking processes behind each performance.

Eighty-eight people from a cannabis and bipolar disorder study took a standard skills test. Raters scored memory, attention, impulse control, processing speed, and planning during the tasks. Several NEUPSA domain scores matched scores on standard computer tests of thinking. Healthy people generally outscored the clinical groups, and scores separated cannabis and bipolar groups as well. The authors call for more work and wider testing of the tool.
pmc-13278414:
Ozgenur Cetinbag-Kuzu leads a 2026 study testing a Turkish version of a music reward questionnaire. The extended Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire measures how much pleasure people take from music, across several dimensions. Few validated tools exist for Turkish speakers. A total of 266 adults aged eighteen to sixty-five completed the translated survey online, including musicians and non-musicians.

The Turkish version held twenty-four items in six factors and showed excellent internal consistency. Scores were stable when a subgroup retook the test three weeks later. Musicians scored higher than non-musicians, as expected. The authors judge the tool valid and reliable for studying individual differences in musical pleasure among Turkish-speaking adults, including work on music perception.
pmc-13278614:
James K Karichu leads a 2026 study that builds a framework for judging the value of patient self-monitoring technologies, devices that let patients track chronic disease at home. Payers and assessment bodies often miss what makes such tools valuable. The team combined an AI-assisted literature review with interviews of ten payer and clinician respondents in the United States, United Kingdom, and Germany.

The framework links three parts: value drivers, evaluation criteria, and evidence generation. Respondents weighted decision making at sixty percent clinical value, twenty percent economic, and ten percent each for humanistic and societal value. Treatment benefit, diagnostic accuracy, and health care use were the key drivers. Shared criteria could streamline evidence demands and widen patient access, the authors argue.
pmc-13278814:
Mason F Carstens leads a 2026 study that designs and validates a device for measuring knee stiffness in animal models of arthrofibrosis, a condition where joints stiffen after injury or surgery. Reliable stiffness measures are essential for testing treatments before human use. The new device combines a torque sensor, motor, and position encoder in one aligned unit, with custom brackets for mice, rats, and rabbits.

Joint stiffness was induced in all three species, then measured outside the body after defined recovery periods. The new device matched a previously validated device on measurement variability in every species. Torque-angle curves were reproducible across the species-specific ranges. A standardized, cross-species platform should make studies easier to compare, the authors argue.
pmc-13278914:
Bin Peng and Yanxia Zhang combine three bedside measures to identify a hard-to-spot heart failure type, in a 2026 study. Heart failure with preserved pumping strength hides among other forms because no single test settles it. Lung ultrasound lines, a blood hormone marker, and heart chamber size each reflect a different facet.

Two hundred twenty patients admitted with acute heart failure at one hospital were assessed. Each marker alone separated the preserved type only weakly to moderately. Together the three reached clearly better discrimination, and a fuller model improved further. Decision analysis suggested the combined approach beats treating everyone or no one the same. The authors frame it as bedside characterisation, not a standalone diagnosis.
pmc-13279214:
P R Brustio and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of relative age effects in rugby union and rugby league. The effect describes how children born early in a selection year are overrepresented because they are older and bigger than peers born later. Searching six databases, the team pooled 26 studies and compared the share of players born in the first versus the last quarter of the year.

Among male players, 34.8 percent were born in the first quarter against 16.9 percent in the last, roughly doubling the odds. The bias was smaller in female players and strongest in youth categories, fading but not disappearing at senior level. Higher competition levels showed descriptively larger effects, particularly for youth males. Wide differences between studies urge caution about the exact size, yet the direction is consistent. The authors' synthesis gives selectors a quantitative basis for correcting birth-date bias in talent pathways.
pmc-13279314:
Aman Kumar Singh and colleagues published a 2026 paper presenting CA2PNet, a deep learning network that segments biomedical images, outlining structures such as lesions or organs pixel by pixel. Accurate outlines underpin diagnosis, surgery planning, and tumor measurement, yet anatomy varies widely between patients and target regions are often small. The design builds on two earlier networks and adds four components: a spatial attention module, global max pooling, enhanced pyramid pooling for features at several scales, and progressively widening convolutions.

On the Kvasir-SEG endoscopy dataset the network scored a mean overlap of 85.15 percent, and on the BUSI breast ultrasound dataset 82.78 percent, beating the state-of-the-art models they compared against. Tests supported the gains. The authors credit finer local detail kept alongside whole-image context, which helps the model hold boundaries across scales. They position the architecture as a general tool for computer-aided diagnosis pipelines.
pmc-13280314:
Michelle Ji Yeon Yoo gives a 2026 review of how to tune meat nutrition for infants and older adults. Early growth and aging both raise protein needs, through fast tissue build in babies and stiff protein use and weak digestion in old age. Red meat gives complete proteins with all essential amino acids, plus iron, zinc and B vitamins. Bioactive compounds like creatine and taurine add worth. Soft texture matters most for these groups.

Meat types and cuts split in amino acid profiles, so cut choice shapes diet quality. Moderate heat, high pressure, dry ageing and fruit enzymes can unfold and cut proteins. Right conditions free amino acids and short peptides that the small gut absorbs with ease. Too harsh conditions can harm the gains. The review maps process settings to digestibility aims for the young and the old.
pmc-13280914:
Md Mahiuddin Sarker and colleagues published a 2026 photochemistry study measuring how efficiently light triggers electron transfer inside halogen-bonded complexes, partnerships of a bromine molecule and a halide ion. These complexes absorb light through a charge-transfer band that can drive metal-free reactions, yet efficiency numbers were scarce. The team formed complexes from four bromine compounds and three halide donors, irradiated them at three ultraviolet wavelengths, and measured trihalide yields.

Quantum yields, the fraction of absorbed photons producing the reaction, ranged from about 0.2 to 0.8. Wavelength checks showed the reaction starts from the charge-transfer absorption rather than from exciting either partner alone. Stronger acceptors and stronger donors gave the higher yields, and those pairings absorb at lower energies, closer to visible light. The authors frame the results as design rules for greener photochemistry that might one day run on near-visible light.
pmc-13281414:
Dolors Casellas-Vidal and colleagues measured muscle stiffness in healthy children for a 2026 study. A sound-based scan can gauge how stiff a muscle is without needles or pain. Such scans lack standard values for children. The team scanned five arm and leg muscles in forty-four children aged three to fourteen. Each muscle was read at rest and while stretched to its full passive range. The team also logged food habits, activity, fitness, and sleep.

Repeat scans matched closely, which marks the method as steady. Children who ate closer to a Mediterranean diet, rich in plants and olive oil, showed stiffer muscles when stretched. That link held in all five muscles. Sleep length tied to stiffness in mixed ways by muscle and state. Daily activity showed no steady pattern. The authors offer the values as a base for judging sick or injured children.
pmc-13282114:
Mengyang Jacky Li and co-authors describe a 2026 microscopy method for filming brain activity in three dimensions at high speed. Their tool uses a special light beam, called a Bessel beam, stretched along its axis. That shape turns slow three-dimensional scans into fast flat frame scans under a fluorescence microscope, which makes glowing cells visible. The setup is compact and low cost, and its focus can be tuned without moving its centre.

The team used the microscope to map blood flow in the brains of normal mice and mice after stroke. They paired it with light-based stimulation to chart links between nerve cells in living tissue. They also tracked immune cells in the brain after single-cell laser damage, watching varied responses over time and space. The authors say the speed, depth, and flexibility open new ways to study how brain cells, blood vessels, and immune cells interact.
pmc-13282414:
Juntao Sun and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of the global and Chinese burden of maternal sepsis and infections from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts to 2036. These infections around pregnancy threaten mothers, fetuses, and newborns. The team used Global Burden of Disease data, trend statistics, and forecasting models to compare China with world patterns across incidence, deaths, and disability.

China moved against the global direction. Its age-standardised incidence fell while the world's rose. Death and disability rates in China dropped by more than three quarters, far outpacing global falls of about half. Prevalence also shrank in China while growing worldwide. Within China, new cases concentrated in younger mothers, while death and disability weighed heaviest on older ones. Models project the divergence to persist through 2036, with China's burden still falling. The authors urge targeted action for the high-risk regions and groups the data expose.
pmc-13283214:
Childhood maltreatment echoes through thinking skills toward suicide risk in bipolar disorder, Natalia E Fares-Otero's 2026 network study traces. Early abuse and neglect raise risk and worsen outcomes in this illness. The paths from early harm to suicidal acts were still poorly mapped.

A total of 249 adults with bipolar disorder in a stable phase took part. Surveys covered abuse and neglect types, thinking tests, impulsivity traits, and suicidal acts. Network models linked early harm to weaker executive skills and slower thinking. Emotional abuse showed the strongest link to suicidal thoughts in the network. Links to attempts were weaker but present. Care that targets these paths may aid prevention.
pmc-13284014:
COVID-19 booster shots link to lower flu death risk in a 2026 Brazil study by Daniele Melo Sardinha and colleagues. Hospital data covered lab-confirmed flu cases nationwide during 2024. The team asked which traits predict death and whether vaccines changed odds.

A total of 15,995 hospitalized flu cases entered the analysis set. Overall, about one in eight patients died during hospital care. Flu A dominated cases and carried higher death risk than flu B. Weighted models tied booster shots to modestly lower death odds. Flu shots and the antiviral oseltamivir also linked to protection. Breathing distress marked higher risk.
pmc-13284314:
Clear glue in foldable screens needs a model that joins timed stretch with slow flow, propose Zhaoxu Zhou and colleagues in 2026. These glues bond display layers and bend again and again in use. Heat and time change how they deform, so stress forecasts need both traits at once.

Stress release tests at three heat levels set the model constants for the glue. One part of the model handles timed stretch and recovery of the layer. A named flow formula handles the slow yield part of its response. Fits matched the measured release curves well across the full heat range. Computer runs on a simple foldable stack backed the lab results closely.
pmc-13284414:
Katherine W. Eisenberg and Kavita K. Patel offer a policy commentary, published in 2026, on how to govern AI systems that act on their own in clinical care. Such systems now book visits, start orders, and shape insurance choices, while rules for safety and oversight lag behind. Primary care shows the strain, since full guideline care would take more hours than a day holds.

The authors urge three steps. Health systems should sort AI actions by the harm an error could cause. Buying and payment rules should require basic testing standards. Shared oversight tools also need stable funding across systems. Without such steps, they argue, well-funded centers will manage risk better and current gaps in care will widen.
pmc-13285014:
Ann Katrin Reuter and co-authors compare flipped and lecture teaching in a 2026 dental education study. In flipped classes, students learn core content alone before class, then use class time for active work. First-year dental students were split between flipped and standard lecture groups across one school year, with 138 students included.

Flipped students rated most parts of teaching higher, notably prep, flexibility, group learning, contact with teachers, and drive to take part. Study interest and learning tactics did not change clearly in either group in the survey results reported here. The authors suggest flipped formats can lift the felt quality of teaching, even when habits stay much the same.
pmc-13285414:
Picking the best curve to chart chicken growth is the aim of a 2026 systematic review by Kholofelo Mogalanyane Thankge and co-authors. Growth curves guide feed plans, slaughter timing, and breed picks, all of which drive profit. The team searched four databases with set terms and screened work under PRISMA rules, keeping forty-nine papers from 1995 to 2024.

The logistic curve saw the most use, with the Gompertz curve a close second in the papers gathered here. On fit quality, Gompertz and Weibull curves led, both scoring near-perfect match marks. The authors back those two for farm use, saying sound curves help cut feed cost and time slaughter age well.
pmc-13285814:
M Myllynen and colleagues review real-world use of broad genomic profiling for solid tumors in Finland in a 2026 retrospective study. The testing era covered runs from 2017 to 2020, when such profiling first spread into routine European care. Their aim was to show who got tested, what the tests found, and whether the results changed treatment.

Records covered 297 patients, most with spread disease and heavy past treatment, led by prostate, breast, and pancreatic cancers. About two in three patients carried at least one change that could guide drug choice. Even so, test results drove the treatment decision for only about one in four patients. Survival varied by how usable the findings were, giving later Finnish trials a real-world yardstick for what profiling can deliver.
pmc-13285914:
Yuanyuan Sun and colleagues weigh artemisinin compounds for autoimmune thyroiditis in a 2026 narrative review. Care for the inflamed thyroid still rests on hormone replacement and watchful support, with little that slows the immune attack itself. Compounds drawn from Artemisia plants have calmed immune activity in lab models, and the review asks how far that promise reaches for the thyroid.

Work in animals found that one derivative eased thyroid inflammation, lowered thyroid antibodies, and softened signals that draw immune cells into the gland. Studies outside the thyroid hint at wider effects on cell growth paths, danger sensors, and stress defenses in cells. The authors stress that nearly all proof stays preclinical and comes from purified compounds, not plant products. Careful thyroid-focused trials must come first, with safety and dose work, before any clinic use.
pmc-13286014:
Kushin Mukherjee and colleagues ask whether a large language model can learn which colors people link with which ideas. Published in 2026, the study builds on a curious fact: people reliably match even abstract words to particular colors. The team wondered whether patterns in text and images alone could teach a system those links.

GPT-4 rated associations between 71 colors and a range of concepts, concrete and abstract. Its ratings matched human ratings closely and beat earlier image-based methods. Color palettes built from the model's ratings helped people read charts about as well as palettes built from human data, sometimes better. The authors suggest that web-scale data quietly carries the structure behind these associations.
pmc-13286114:
Rachel E Colbran and colleagues hunt signs that rectal prolapse will return after repair in a 2026 cohort study. Fixing a slipped rectum with surgery helps most patients, yet about one in ten sees the problem come back. The team checked whether scans and pressure tests done before surgery could flag the patients most at risk.

The study held 155 patients, nearly all women, treated with robotic surgery at one center between 2017 and 2025. Return of prolapse struck 16 patients over a median watch of about three and a half years. Diabetes stood as the lone clinical trait tied to return in simple comparisons. Scan signs also mattered. A pocket hernia, a bowel pouch dropping into the pelvis, and thinner hip muscle each showed up more in the return group. That pattern hints muscle loss and sugar control deserve care before surgery.
pmc-13286214:
Raouf Hammami and colleagues check how steady one-leg hop gap scores stay in young soccer players in a 2026 reliability study. Coaches read the gap between legs as a flag for lopsided power, yet growth spurts can scramble both legs and scores. Boys aged 8 to 16 hopped for distance on each leg in two rounds, split into groups before and after their growth peak.

Sixty-four players took part, and repeat scores agreed well in both age bands. Measurement wobble stayed small in each group when set against the spread of scores. The younger group, though, needed a bigger real shift before a coach could trust that change had truly happened. Older players cleared that bar with room to spare, so the authors back the test for tracking teens while urging care with readings from the youngest players.
pmc-13286614:
Hamza Talbi and many colleagues describe an eight-year-old girl whose widespread tuberculosis was found only after three abdominal operations. The 2026 case report comes with a warning: the disease imitates ordinary surgical problems. The girl had an autoimmune joint condition treated with drugs that suppress immunity, a known risk for severe tuberculosis.

She first seemed to have an appendix abscess, then a blocked bowel with more abscesses. After her third operation she developed severe breathing failure. Chest imaging showed the tiny, seed-like spots of miliary tuberculosis across both lungs, plus inflammation near the bowel. A tuberculosis blood test was positive. Intensive care and standard tuberculosis drugs brought full recovery. The authors urge imaging the chest early in such puzzles.
pmc-13286814:
Lara Farber and colleagues revisit who benefits most from lung valve treatment in severe emphysema in a 2026 retrospective study. One-way valves deflate the worst lung lobe, yet patients who can barely walk were long excluded from trials as too risky. Records of 54 Berlin patients were split at a six-minute walking distance of 140 meters, comparing lung function, quality of life, and walk-test details after treatment.

Both groups gained lung function and quality of life to a similar degree. The frailest walkers, though, added far more distance than the stronger group, a mean gain past one hundred meters against roughly a dozen. Their heart rates also settled further from baseline to follow-up, hinting at a cardiovascular dividend, while oxygen levels changed alike. The authors argue the lowest walkers should not be turned away.
pmc-13287214:
Amalia A Sofianidi and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a drug that links an antibody aimed at TROP2, a protein common on cancer cells, to a cell-killing payload. The drug, sacituzumab tirumotecan, already shows promise in breast and lung tumours, and the review asks what role it might play in cancers of the female reproductive organs.

Large late-stage trials are under way for cervical, ovarian, and womb cancers. Early safety reports describe mainly blood-related side effects, mouth soreness, and hair loss, judged manageable so far. The authors note that survival and response results are still awaited, and marker testing may later help select patients most likely to benefit.
pmc-13287314:
Tamara Backhouse and colleagues describe, in a 2026 paper, how a mixed group built staff training for care homes together. The training aimed to improve personal care help for residents living with dementia. Five care home staff, two relatives, two researchers, and a relative who also does research met weekly at a university. A resident and another relative advised the work from outside the main group.

The group met ten times over eleven weeks and wrote short reflections after each session. Members followed different paths, since staff, relatives, and researchers gained different things from the work. Many reported new skills, confidence, and stronger relationships. Some costs appeared too, since researchers found the pace intense and staff had to catch up on missed work. The paper offers practical lessons for teams planning similar shared projects.
pmc-13288214:
Kaixin Zhang and co-authors made the first saddle-shaped carbon sheet speckled with oxygen and boron in 2026, built around a bowl-shaped core in only two steps. Earlier sheets of this family lay flat, and curved versions were thought too unstable to isolate.

Crystal snapshots confirmed the saddle shape. Bulky side arms steadied the structure and let one version stack into neat double layers that flattened the bowl, an unusual change driven by packing rather than inner strain. The bent shape also exposes boron sites, sharply raising their pull on partner molecules. Two methanol guests were caught bound at once, a first for this family.
pmc-13288414:
Yohannes Minyilu and co-authors built an image diagnosis benchmark in 2026 for neglected tropical skin diseases in Ethiopia, where labelled photos are scarce. A new set of 1,495 skin photos in three classes was gathered at Arba Minch University, with heavy imbalance between classes.

Their best route first borrows features from a ready-trained network, then trains a small custom network on those features, with image augmentation mixed in. The DenseNet121 route reached accuracy the authors report as 96.6%, with a close rival close behind. A funnel scheme sorted methods step by step. The authors ask for more data and fairer class balance in the next round.
pmc-13288714:
Walid Al-Qerem leads a 2026 cross-sectional online study of Jordanian adults living with chronic illness, asking how reading health information well relates to daily quality of life. A total of 901 complete Arabic surveys combined two quality-of-life tools, a medication adherence scale, and a twelve-item health literacy scale.

Better health literacy and steadier medication taking both went with higher scores on the long-term conditions questionnaire and on the EQ-5D index, while taking more medicines pulled scores down. Machine-learning models, led by gradient boosting, predicted outcomes only modestly better than plain regressions. The two quality tools overlapped yet emphasized different ground, one leaning social and self-management, the other leaning clinical burden.
pmc-13288814:
Heba Tarek Emara and co-authors test a teaching session on AI views in Egypt in 2026. Mansoura University hosted the study. Surveys hit 220 students before the session. They hit 189 students after it. The year was 2024 to 2025.

Just 15.9 percent had prior AI teaching. Most of that came from social media. Outside courses fed the rest. After the session, good knowledge passed half the group. Good attitudes passed half as well. Good practice ratings more than doubled. Poor ratings shrank on both fronts. Familiarity and enthusiasm grew after teaching. Confidence in using the tools lagged, though.
pmc-13288914:
Chun Qi, Luca Dell'Amico, and Giulio Goti report a light-driven route to sugar-linked cage molecules in a 2026 synthesis paper. The targets join sugars to bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane, a tiny cage that mimics a benzene ring in drug design. Older routes needed fragile activated sugars prepared in advance. Their method starts from shelf-stable sugars and creates the reactive partner in place under light.

The in-place partner is a glycosyl iodide formed during the reaction. It adds across a strained propellane molecule through an atom transfer radical process. That single step locks the sugar onto the cage carbon. The route worked for both protected sugar types, the reactive armed kind and the calmer disarmed kind. Avoiding isolation of delicate intermediates makes the sequence simpler to run. The authors present it as a general way to build saturated sugar analogues for drug discovery.
pmc-13289014:
Alessandro Ruggieri and colleagues use AI to link epilepsy and depression in 2026. Their study mines health records across Europe. Seven nations fed data to the work. Models were trained in each nation alone. The team sought risks in both ways.

About 2.2 million people had epilepsy. About 9.7 million had depression. Female sex flagged depression risk in epilepsy. Low income flagged it too. Some brain drugs also flagged it. In depression, male sex flagged epilepsy risk. Poverty flagged it as well. Shared signs point to a heavy load of illness. The work may aid risk checks in clinics.
pmc-13289114:
Khashayar Saybani and colleagues comment on new US diabetes tech guidance in 2026. The guidance comes from the American Diabetes Association. It treats devices as core care, not extras. It urges wider and earlier use. Choice should fit each patient's life.

Glucose sensors are urged from diagnosis on. Finger checks still matter for safety. Pump systems that dose on their own are favored. They suit type 1 and some type 2 cases. Strict entry bars are discouraged. Shared data and staff training are stressed. Training should aid access, not block it. The piece weighs gains and hurdles in real clinics.
pmc-13289214:
Masanori Nagaoka and colleagues test vibration for balance loss after brainstem stroke in 2026. The syndrome is lateral medullary syndrome. Some patients keep leaning to one side. That lean delays return to daily life. A damaged signal path to the cerebellum may cause it.

One case led, then seven more patients joined. Balance was tested three ways. Vibration on the hurt-side leg helped all patients. At least one test improved for each. Vibration on the good side helped just three. No test got worse with vibration. Three patients then did mixed training. Long-term gains could not be proven in that small set.
pmc-13289314:
Benny Harold Rashuamán-Conche headed a 2026 cohort study on frailty and death in systemic lupus erythematosus in Peru. Frailty means low reserve and higher risk from stress, and it already predicts damage growth in lupus. Whether it predicts death in Latin American patients was less clear, so the Almenara cohort was used to test that link.

The single-center group covered 2012 to 2025 and held 495 patients, of whom 92.1 percent were women and 19.4 percent met the frail cutoff at baseline. Mean age at diagnosis was 35.0 years in this group. Frailty was scored with the SLICC Frailty Index and tracked against vital status from health records. Survival curves split by frail status and adjusted models then weighed frailty against other risks.
pmc-13290014:
Mahdi Kadkhodazadeh and colleagues study fluid collected from dental pulp stem cells as a bone signal, in 2026. The fluid, called conditioned medium, carries the cells' secreted factors without the cells themselves. Periodontal ligament stem cells were bathed in three strengths of the medium. The team tracked growth, movement, and bone-forming activity over fourteen days. Tests ran in plain growth medium and in bone-promoting medium.

The lowest strength, ten percent, worked best across most measures. It raised growth factor release, cell growth, and bone markers more than stronger mixes did. Movement peaked early for both the lowest and middle strengths. Adding the fluid to bone medium gave the strongest bone induction of all. The pattern fits hormesis, where a small dose helps and larger doses add inhibitory factors. The authors say dose tuning is essential before clinical use of such secretome products.
pmc-13290914:
The gut's chemical messengers sit at the center of bowel inflammation, Yuhong Liang and colleagues review in 2026. In inflammatory bowel disease, gut microbes shift and their metabolic products shift with them; the review maps how three metabolite families talk to the immune system and the gut barrier.

Short-chain fatty acids feed colon cells and calm immunity through surface receptors and gene-switch effects. Bile acids, reshaped by microbes, signal through nuclear and surface receptors to balance barrier and immune tone. Tryptophan breakdown products, including indoles, engage the aryl hydrocarbon receptor to steer inflammation. Patients typically run low on the first two families. Liang and colleagues argue these pathways offer concrete targets for future diagnosis and metabolite-based therapy.
pmc-13291014:
Serena Dattola leads a 2026 study on brain scans in mild cognitive impairment. The team asked if electrode count changes what scans reveal. Seventeen patients wore a dense cap for resting recordings. The same recordings were thinned for comparison.

Three layouts held 173, 64, and 18 channels. Networks were rebuilt across 84 brain areas. Graph scores were set against a standard cognition test. Links to cognition looked clearer with more channels. The trend sat mostly in alpha and beta bands. No link survived strict checks for many tests. The dense layout still sorted cognition levels best. Setup cost can thus be weighed with open eyes.
pmc-13291614:
Past wealth gaps come with deep, often hidden error bars. Mattia Fochesato and Samuel Bowles tackle that problem in a 2026 methods study. Old homes, graves, and records hint at past inequality. Each hint carries bias from how it survived.

Their method joins several statistical tools in one suite. Bias and uncertainty are traced at every estimation stage. Final results come out as probability ranges, not single points. Code is shared for other teams to use. Modern inequality debates gain a firmer past baseline. Policy choices can weigh ancient lessons with honest doubt. Point values alone should no longer drive big claims.
pmc-13292114:
Sabine Mogwitz and colleagues study work-family conflict in healthcare fathers during COVID-19, in a 2026 paper. The German VOICE study surveyed health workers online at four points between April 2020 and May 2022. Fathers numbered 2,844 across the waves, compared with age-matched mothers and childless male colleagues. A smaller group of 188 fathers answered at two or more waves for longitudinal checks. Conflict scores captured how job and home demands collided.

Fathers reported conflict near mothers' levels in most waves and above them in one. Conflict crept upward from the first wave to the last. Heavier workload, exhaustion, and moral worries raised conflict, while trust in the institution protected against it. Younger age, living with a partner, children at home, virus contact, and full-time work also raised scores. More fathers than childless colleagues worked full-time hours. They urge flexible, father-aware policies for future crises.
pmc-13292314:
Nao Suzuki and co-authors report chiral light-handling polymers whose effects depend on careful mixing, in a 2026 study. The polymers join fluorene and thienopyrroledione units, each repeat carrying one handed center. They were built by direct arylation coupling to keep defects low. Dissolved alone, the chains showed only faint optical handedness. Adding 1-butanol to the chloroform solution clumped the chains into stable aggregates.

Those aggregates answered polarized light strongly, both in absorption and in glowing emission. How the poor solvent was added mattered as much as the recipe itself. Slow dropwise addition with controlled stirring gave the most repeatable spectra. Dissymmetry factors near two hundredths ranked among the best for single-chirality polymers. The team says the mixing protocol, not just the molecule, secures reproducibility. Such materials could serve polarized-light devices and sensors. Their recipe-first lesson applies across aggregate-based optics.
pmc-13292514:
Halla Halldorsdottir, with co-authors, tests a 2026 pair of blood proteins as fortune-tellers for critical COVID-19: heparin-binding protein from activated white cells and endothelin-1, a vessel-tightening signal. Outcomes tracked were death by sixty days and the need for a ventilator.

Standard inflammation markers such as CRP and interleukin-6 ran high in both groups but did not separate survivors either. The authors conclude these admission levels, however dramatic, do not forecast the course.
pmc-13292914:
Yusuke Tominaga and co-authors present two cases from 2026 involving men whose heart surgery in childhood later caused fertility problems. Both men had Fontan circulation, a repair for single-ventricle heart defects that leaves venous pressure chronically high. That pressure can swell veins in the scrotum, a condition called varicocele, and damage sperm production.

Both chose microsurgical repair of the varicocele, with blood thinners managed carefully around the operation. Semen quality improved in each case, and sperm returned in the first man. The authors suggest repair deserves consideration in selected patients, while warning that recurrence risk may be higher.
pmc-13293714:
Berkay Ayhan, Edip Rencüzoğulları, and Mehmet Emre Yıldırım describe, in a 2026 case report, a young man with two separate benign blood vessel tumors in his skull bones. Such skull tumors are rare, and having two at once with spread to the brain lining is rarer still.
