Both were fully removed in surgery, and the left one showed signs of invading the dura, the brain's tough outer cover. The case adds a rare pattern to the record.
pmc-13294114:
Alexander T. Hong, Jacob Lifton, and Hossein Ameri describe widefield dye imaging in retinitis pigmentosa for a 2026 study. Patients scanned between 2017 and 2024 at an academic center were compared with age-matched controls lacking inherited retinal disease. The team timed dye flow from choroid flush and catalogued central and peripheral vessel features.

Groups held 30 eyes from 15 patients and 28 eyes from 14 controls. Central transit times matched, but laminar flow and peripheral vein filling ran much slower in patients. Peripheral vessel dropout appeared in 93% of patient eyes, with pigment-linked blocking in 87%. Distinct widefield patterns may aid reading of these complex scans.
pmc-13294214:
Dongjie Ma and coauthors report staged keyhole surgery for a rare double lung defect in a 2026 case. A 28-year-old woman had coughed and spat blood for a year, with masses in both lower lungs. Three-dimensional CT showed intralobar sequestration on both sides, joined by a channel across the back of the chest and fed by several aorta branches, plus Aspergillus infection confirmed by lavage testing.

Drug therapy failed, so surgeons removed the worse left lower lobe first through one small port. After rehab, the right lower lobe and connecting tract were handled six months later. Tissue checks confirmed the defect and fungal threads. At one year, lung expansion and exercise capacity stayed well preserved.
pmc-13294414:
Osama Alrusayni and colleagues report two Saudi girls with mid-aortic syndrome in a 2026 case report. The rare narrowing hits the middle aorta rather than the usual chest spot and can drive dangerous blood pressure in children. Both patients were 10 years old and presented with body-wide hypertension that resisted standard control.

Heart ultrasound showed a normal arch but odd diastolic flow in the descending aorta, a clue that clinched the diagnosis. The authors warn clinicians not to dismiss odd pressure readings in quiet children, since missed narrowing can turn catastrophic. Early echo checks and referral shape safer management.
pmc-13294514:
Basile Njei, Ulrick Sidney Kanmounye, and Javad Sarvestan lay out a 2026 protocol for an explainable AI companion in primary biliary cholangitis care. Current care leans on static lab markers and splits symptom tracking from risk scoring, while portal hypertension danger lacks good noninvasive flags. Their multiphase plan enrolls at least 600 adults across academic liver centers.

Lab trends over time, stiffness scans, and frequent patient reports will feed boosted models with plain-language explanations, yielding an activity index and complication forecasts. Delivery runs inside the health record through a standard app framework. Testing covers record simulations with clinician crossover, then a live pilot on usability and mental load.
pmc-13295114:
Simone H Crouch and colleagues review cash transfer programmes and teenage well-being in poorer countries in a 2026 article. Money given to households can ease tight budgets and shape diet, schooling, and health behaviour during adolescence. Most earlier proof covered babies and young children, leaving teenagers understudied.

Trials and near-experimental studies from 2012 to 2025 were gathered, with 19 meeting the entry rules from 164 finds. Nearly all ran in sub-Saharan Africa and mixed conditional, unconditional, and combined payment designs. Benefits appeared most often for schooling, money security, sexual health, and mental well-being, while direct evidence on teenage nutrition stayed sparse.
pmc-13295414:
Emma M. Pyneandee and colleagues argue that the molecules usually blamed for infertility also help make babies, in a 2026 review on reactive oxygen species. These chemical by-products of oxygen metabolism damage sperm and eggs in excess, which is why antioxidants are marketed to couples trying to conceive. The authors gather the other side of the story, sorting the helpful roles of these species into three groups.

Gentle oxidation welds sperm DNA packaging shut during maturation, builds the sperm's energy sheath, and wakes up enzyme precursors needed for ovulation, implantation, and labor. It also silences brake proteins so signaling cascades can run. Controlled destruction helps too, clearing infections and pruning cells through programmed death. Finally, these species manage the iron and copper sitting at the heart of key enzymes. Sweeping them away carelessly, the authors warn, can tip patients into reductive stress.
pmc-13295914:
Hélène Levassort and colleagues follow, in 2026, whether waste toxins that build up in kidney disease track with worsening mood. Depression is common in this group, and such toxins may fuel brain inflammation, but the link had not been tested over time.

Within a large French cohort, 2,165 adults not on dialysis were followed for about four years with repeated mood scores and blood toxin measures. One toxin, phenylacetylglutamine, was tied to mood scores creeping upward over time, while two others linked to higher average scores. The authors ask whether lowering toxins could ease symptoms.
pmc-13296014:
Li Li and colleagues compare, in 2026, early versus later tube feeding for adults with sepsis in one Chinese intensive care unit. Guidelines urge early feeding, but the team check records from 2015 to 2024, matching patients so the two groups look alike.

Among 2,205 patients, those fed within two days faced higher death risk at both one and two months than those fed later in the first week. Stomach retention was also more common with early feeding, and risk ran highest in younger men and the sickest patients. The authors suggest feeding timing should be tailored, not automatic.
pmc-13296314:
Audrey K. Chigome and colleagues test a set of antibiotic quality indicators in South African primary care during a 2026 feasibility study. The indicators build on the World Health Organization AWaRe system, which groups antibiotics by how carefully they should be used. Surveys at four clinics in Gauteng were paired with interviews of clinic staff.

Every surveyed patient with a respiratory infection had received an antibiotic. Most indicators scored well on whether they could be applied and measured in these clinics. Staff, however, knew nothing of the AWaRe system and had no stewardship programme or local prescribing guidance. Shortages, patient expectations, and fear of complications shaped prescribing. The authors argue the indicators can work locally if stewardship support follows.
pmc-13296414:
Shuxin Wang and colleagues improve a nature-inspired search algorithm to place wireless sensors more evenly, in a 2026 simulation study. Sensor networks often leave blind spots when nodes cluster badly. Their improved Northern Goshawk method adds a chaotic starting layout, shifting search weights, and a mixed mutation step to escape poor solutions.

On standard test problems the improved method approached the best known values more reliably than the original algorithm. Applied to sensor placement, it reached higher coverage in both flat and three-dimensional test areas. Node layouts also came out more uniform, with fewer uncovered gaps. Network designers get a tested option for planning deployments in difficult terrain, at least in simulation.
pmc-13296614:
Bruna Suzarte Campelo and colleagues ask whether kangaroo care changes a stress-related gene's chemical markings in premature babies, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Kangaroo care means prolonged skin-to-skin contact, and it may shape how stress genes are regulated. Blood samples from seventy-five preterm infants were taken at birth and at two discharge points.

The gene studied makes the serotonin transporter, a protein tied to mood and stress responses. Marking levels at thirteen sites stayed broadly stable over the hospital stay in both care groups. One site differed slightly at final discharge, but the gap vanished after statistical correction for multiple testing. The authors call for larger studies with longer follow-up before drawing conclusions.
pmc-13296814:
Zain Mohammed Al Muqbel and colleagues report, in 2026, a severe snakebite case in a six-year-old boy bitten in rural Pakistan. Venom wrecked his blood clotting, thinned his blood cells and swelled his leg so badly that surgeons feared pressure damage inside the limb.

Antivenom and transfusions failed to settle the clotting failure, and cutting the limb open was judged too risky while bleeding stayed uncontrolled. After transfer to Bahrain, five plasma exchange sessions steadied his blood, melted the swelling and saved limb function. The authors highlight plasma exchange when standard care stalls.
pmc-13297414:
Federico Mucci and colleagues map the active trial landscape for depression that resists standard treatment, in a 2026 survey of trial registries. Care for such patients is shifting fast, with device, drug, and mixed programmes all in play. The team searched three registries and kept 237 unique trials in adults after cleaning and merging duplicates.

Device-based brain stimulation formed the largest share, near half of all trials. Drug strategies with new mechanisms came second, at just over a third. Biologic agents and digital-hybrid programmes formed small slices. Most trials were mid-phase with modest sizes, though nearly two thirds used standard clinician rating scales. The authors call for shared outcome measures, longer follow-up, and sorting patients by biological markers.
pmc-13297714:
Xibei Yu and Chunyan Song propose a hybrid scheme for sending wireless data on chaotic signals, in a 2026 paper. Chaos-based keying hides data in noise-like waves, and index modulation squeezes extra bits into the choice of wave itself. Their system sends several data streams beside one reference signal, each stream tagged by its own code.

A twisted copy of the chaotic wave, made by a Hilbert transform, completes the hybrid index trick. The authors derive error-rate formulas for plain noisy channels and for fading radio paths with echoes. Rate and spectrum use are worked out as well. Simulations matched the formulas and beat the base system, supporting the design for crowded wireless links.
pmc-13297814:
Energy drinks may wear down tooth enamel, while the evidence on sports drinks and cavities stays murky, conclude Bella Weijia Luo and co-authors in a 2026 systematic review. Searching three databases, they gathered studies linking these beverages to erosion, decay, and saliva changes.

Ten studies covering 5,805 people aged 6 to 89 met the criteria, though 70% carried high or serious risk of bias. Heavier energy drink use consistently tracked with more dental erosion. Sports drink findings conflicted between studies, and caries results were inconclusive for both drink types. Given the thin, low-quality evidence base, the authors press for better-designed research before firm guidance can be given.
pmc-13297914:
Yi Liu and colleagues describe SIRI-YOLO in a 2026 paper on spotting foreign objects on coal mine conveyor belts underground. Low light, heavy background noise, and objects at very different sizes make such detection hard. Their model revises the YOLOv11n detector with an illumination network, a stronger feature module, an improved feature pyramid, and a new loss function.

Tests used images containing large coal chunks and anchor rods, plus a public low-light dataset for a further check. The reported system reached high precision and recall while staying small and fast, beating mainstream YOLO versions in the comparisons shown. The authors present it as a practical aid for mine safety monitoring.
pmc-13298714:
Aykut Turhan and colleagues test an immune score as a prognostic tool in locally advanced stomach cancer, in a 2026 retrospective study. Patients received a four-drug chemotherapy regimen before surgery. The score combines albumin, an enzyme marker, and a blood cell ratio to reflect inflammation and nutrition.

Among 128 patients at one centre, high-risk scores predicted clearly shorter survival and shorter time before progression. The link held after adjustment for age, stage, and whether surgery happened. Discrimination was moderate rather than strong. The authors suggest the score can add risk information beside standard factors, pending external validation in larger prospective groups.
pmc-13299414:
Rio Wakasugi and a large team show how a green tea compound protects the blood vessel lining barrier, in a 2026 cell study. Endothelial cells gate what passes between blood and tissue, and the inflammatory mediator thrombin loosens that barrier by driving a phosphorylation cascade. The tea catechin EGCG was tested against this process.

Treatment reduced inhibitory phosphorylation on the phosphatase that relaxes cell contraction, and it quieted the opposing kinase signal. Together those effects lowered contraction-related phosphorylation, blocked stress fibre formation, and preserved the adhesion junctions between cells. The authors map a molecular route by which a dietary compound maintains barrier integrity.
pmc-13299514:
Anwar Alhashem and a team test an Arabic version of a fall prevention education programme for older women in Riyadh, in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. Falls rank among the biggest threats facing older adults as life expectancy grows. The programme, adapted from an established injury prevention toolkit, was compared against a non-equivalent control group before and after delivery.

The intervention group improved sharply in knowledge, practical skills, and intention to act preventively, with large effect sizes for knowledge and skills. Adjusted analyses confirmed those gains. The authors recommend placing such programmes in community clubs and social services, and activating family support for prevention habits at home.
pmc-13299814:
The oldest known patient with a rare gene flaw of brain growth is a woman of 64, and her mind ill health breaks the mold. Dominika Szczęśniak and her team tell her tale in a 2026 case study. Her flaw sits in the NBEA gene, tied to a state most told of in kids with slow growth and fits.

As an adult she fell, again and again, into dark spells of mind. Thoughts that foes meant her harm and that her health was in peril filled those spells, with deep dread at their side. Her last tag was a mixed state in which mind strain shows in the body. Mild slow wit was guessed too, from her school, work, and social path. Youth fits could not be proved, and she barred brain scans. The team say the case widens what this gene flaw can look like in late life.
pmc-13300414:
Sugar-burning enzymes may moonlight as guardians of the genome, Vivienne X. Y. Chua and colleagues propose in a 2026 yeast study. Working with baker's yeast as a stand-in for human cells, they found that the glycolytic enzymes TPI and GAPDH physically interact with Rad9, a checkpoint protein that answers DNA damage.

The authors suggest these enzymes can override the checkpoint, letting damaged cells keep dividing. The link offers a fresh angle on why fermentation-heavy cancer cells resist radiation.
pmc-13300914:

Artificial intelligence and fast sequencing now let teams model benefit and harm from many data layers at once. The authors propose a combined genetic, epigenetic, and computational framework, while listing the practical gaps that still block routine use.
pmc-13301114:

Impedance drifted down gently, near four ohms per month, a change the authors describe as expected settling rather than deterioration. Starting values at implant sat comfortably in range. The authors call the first year reassuring for this high risk population while asking for larger series with longer horizons before declaring the devices fully proven here.
pmc-13301414:

Every conduction interval shortened afterward, heart rate climbed from about sixty to eighty-nine beats per minute, and the atropine challenge barely moved it, confirming the vagal brake had been cut. The authors present the protocol as feasible, safe, and effective.
pmc-13303214:
Deaths naming both diabetes and fatty liver climbed steeply in America, Hongzhou Liu and colleagues chart in a 2026 study of national death certificates from 1999 to 2023. Because clinical fatty liver disease cannot be read directly from certificates, the team built a proxy from liver codes plus recorded metabolic conditions. Trend models and forecasts through 2040 shaped the work.

Deaths listing both conditions rose about tenfold, and proxy liver deaths climbed at a similar pace, though both stayed small in absolute terms. The authors frame the pattern as a watch signal from surveillance data, not proof of biological change.
pmc-13304514:
Wojciech Rzeski and Weronika Rzeska review young barley products as functional foods in a 2026 narrative synthesis. Shoots cut early carry a chemical mix quite unlike ripe grain, sold as dried grass powder or juice products.

Key compounds include two signature flavones, plant acids, green pigments, protective enzymes, vitamins, and minerals. Lab and animal work points to effects on oxidation balance, inflammation signals, and metabolic controls, plus cancer cell slowing in dishes. pmc-13304814:
Xiaochen Gu highlights a 2026 featured study on drug delivery into pancreatic cancer, a tumor wrapped in dense tissue that chokes blood flow. Thick matrix, squeezed vessels, and high fluid pressure together keep medicines from reaching cancer cells.

Treating leakage, tissue mechanics, and fluid pressure as one moving system may guide smarter carriers for stiff, poorly fed tumors.
pmc-13306214:
Francesca Crespí-Payeras compared food and activity habits between melanoma patients and controls in a 2026 study from Barcelona. A total of 130 patients from Hospital Clínic joined with 166 controls of similar age and sex balance.

Answers gathered from January 2016 to February 2020 covered body mass index, diet quality, cooking style and movement habits. Body mass showed no clear link to melanoma in the reported results. Limiting sugary foods linked to lower risk, while dairy restriction, processed meat and unhealthy cooking each linked to higher risk, pointing to habit patterns worth testing further.
pmc-13307414:
Zhaoyue Men and co-authors review in 2026 the two way contest over itaconate, a small molecule the body makes during infection and swelling. The body forms it from a step in the energy cycle, and it builds up in large amounts when germs attack.

Itaconate can slow germs directly by tagging key enzymes they need to grow, and it can steer immune cells to clear germs as well. Some germs fight back by breaking it down or by rewiring their own chemistry to endure it. Timing matters too, as early and late phases call for unlike defence plans. Related drugs might one day aid care for hard to treat infections.
pmc-13307614:
George Triantafyllou and co-authors pool in 2026 what MRI scans show about the anterolateral ligament, a small knee band that helps steady rotation and backs up the cruciate ligament. Their search gathered 26 studies with 2706 knees in total, and they merged rates with random effects models.

Scans showed the ligament in 92.96 percent of knees overall in the pooled results, yet the full path showed in only about half the cases. The shin bone part showed most often, and the meniscus part showed least often. Country and knee bend both shaped how often the band was seen. Shared scan rules are needed before results can be compared with full trust.
pmc-13308314:

Hidden infections made up nearly two-fifths of all active hepatitis B cases and appeared even in children. Many hidden cases lacked both standard antibodies, which makes them easy to miss. The authors link hidden infection to past medical procedures and urge molecular screening where risk is high.
pmc-13310214:

The flow crosses a thin moving needle set at a slant inside a porous material, carrying living microbes along with three particle types. Equations were solved with a standard numerical solver, then a neural network checked the accuracy and stability of those results. Raising several settings, including fluid thickness traits and microbe transport numbers, slowed the flow, while a steeper slant sped it. Heat rose with chemical reaction and activation energy settings. Microbe density also shifted with the settings. The author reports the trends as design guidance.
pmc-13310614:
Ellene Yan and co-authors compare disability paths after surgery in older patients with and without likely cognitive impairment in a 2026 study. Knowing who recovers slowly helps teams flag risk early and plan discharge support. Thinking problems before surgery may mark that slower path.

Across several centers, 307 older non-cardiac surgery patients answered cognition and disability surveys before surgery and at 30, 90, and 180 days after. A short dementia screen split the group, with 17 percent screening positive for probable impairment before surgery in the cohort. Disability was scored on a world health scale with a patient-acceptable cutoff. The authors track how the two groups diverged and which adverse outcomes clustered where.
pmc-13310714:
Katelyn Sellick led a 2026 mouse study on how pancreas alpha cells sense amino acids, the building blocks of protein. Mice lacking the carrier only in alpha cells were given a drug that raised amino acids in the blood. Their alpha cells grew less and released less glucagon than normal mice, in both sexes. Other nutrient signals stayed intact. The work marks the carrier as a key link between food signals and glucagon control.
pmc-13310914:
Zhenxu Bai and colleagues build a microbial mix to protect rice with less chemical spray in a 2026 study. Rice faces fungal diseases and insect pests, and heavy chemical use harms soil and water. Lab tests found an equal three way blend best, with strong blocks on two fungi. A biochar seed coat cut sheath blight sharply and helped seeds sprout under infection. Field plots with 30 to 40 percent less chemical matched or beat full dose care on major diseases and pests. Wider farm tests should follow.
pmc-13311014:
Xue-Yu Wang and colleagues test zedoary turmeric oil against tumor spread to the brain in mice in a 2026 study. The oil from a traditional herb aids blood flow and pain, yet its power against brain metastasis was unknown. A protein called S100A14 that drives spread was the target.

The oil reshaped star shaped support cells, curbed tumor move and invasion, and cut signals that draw suppressor immune cells. Five oil parts bound the target protein directly and steadied it against heat and cutting enzymes.
pmc-13311114:
Yuwen Zhang presents a brain signal framework for tracking mental load in Korean sound learning in a 2026 study. Learners often err on Korean phonemes, and brain wave signals that track load shift fast and vary by person. Older methods model that load poorly, so an attention based design was built.

Three parts work in sequence: a shape guarded encoder compresses raw brain signals, a routing part focuses on key time slices, and a predictor reports load with doubt bounds. A spread step carries doubt through the whole chain to steady the output. Tests showed accurate load tracking during sound tasks, with clearer logic than past tools.
pmc-13311214:
Chun-Lin Ying and co-authors examine the 2026 hospital series on primary lymphoma of the gut and the gut problems it can cause. Bleeding, blockage, and tearing of the bowel are the main risks studied.

Charts for 148 patients treated at one Chinese hospital from 2019 to 2025 were reviewed. Gut problems occurred in 58.1 percent of patients, most often bleeding from stomach ulcers or blockage in the small bowel. Four factors stood out on their own: high blood pressure, a tumor starting in the bowel, deep growth into the bowel wall, and anemia. Spotting these traits early could help teams act before a crisis.
pmc-13311614:
Nora Elise Verberne and colleagues present their 2026 Swedish register study on mental illness around pregnancy in women with a history of premenstrual disorder. Hormone sensitivity may raise risk at other hormone-shifting life stages.

The study covered over one million women and about 1.8 million pregnancies recorded from 2003 to 2020. A premenstrual disorder before pregnancy was flagged from diagnoses or drug records. First mental illness episodes from pregnancy start to twelve months after birth were grouped into eight kinds, from depression to psychosis. Adjusted models estimate how much the earlier disorder raises the odds of each kind.
pmc-13311914:
Adam Yousfi and co-authors report a 2026 randomized trial on whether a virtual simulator speeds learning of the 3D exoscope, a camera system replacing the surgical microscope. No such simulator existed before this work.

Forty medical students with no surgical past were split between 45 minutes of simulator training and no training. All then did a needle-threading task on a physical model under a real exoscope, three times. The trained group moved between targets faster, with a median total of 4 minutes 26 seconds against 5 minutes 17 seconds in this trial. Both groups improved with practice. Brief virtual practice gave a real head start.
pmc-13312114:

The protocol first uses Golden Gate Assembly with standard connectors to build single-gene units from promoter, coding, and terminator parts. Those units then go into yeast cells together, where the yeast's own recombination system stitches them into a multigene plasmid. The authors walk through how connectors are built and show the full workflow on the beta-carotene pathway. They report simpler handling, less need for special skill, and much faster results than conventional routes.
pmc-13312514:
Natalia Gorbokon and a large team report a 2026 tissue microarray study measuring how often cancers lose part of chromosome 9p21. Complete loss clustered in mesothelioma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and bladder urothelial carcinoma, while single-copy loss led in squamous cell carcinoma, leiomyosarcoma, and esophageal adenocarcinoma. Staining confirmed MTAP and p16 protein vanished when both copies were gone and faded with one. The authors supply prevalence figures to guide targeted therapy trials.
pmc-13312814:
Claudia Piemontese and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, the pain drug grapiprant in dogs with osteoarthritis, pairing clinical scores with blood metabolite profiling. Grapiprant blocks the EP4 prostaglandin receptor and promises a safer profile than standard anti-inflammatory drugs, but its real-world effect on canine joint pain and body chemistry had not been tracked together.

Owner surveys showed pain and disability scores improved during treatment and partly slipped back afterward, and walkway gait measures improved by day 60. Plasma chemistry separated clearly before and after treatment. The shifts read as lower inflammation and better energy metabolism, a first step toward blood markers of drug response.
pmc-13314514:
Xuying Zhao and co-workers study a blood index and heart disease risk in fatty liver patients in a paper put out in 2026. The triglyceride-glucose index marks insulin resistance and has tied to heart disease and death in people with metabolic fatty liver, but whether diabetes changes that tie was unproven.

The team studied 812 patients with this liver state who came to their hospital between January 2021 and January 2025. Patients were split by whether they had coronary heart disease, and blood measures were compared across groups. Models then weighed how the index and kindred measures tied to heart risk, and whether diabetes modified the link, as the design states. The answer can refine risk sorting for a large and growing patient group.
pmc-13314814:
Karl Eugen Mengel and colleagues present, in a 2026 German registry study, the German data on late-onset Tay-Sachs disease in adults. The lysosomal storage disorder, caused by a missing enzyme that lets material accumulate in neurons, begins after infancy in this form and unfolds slowly. From a gangliosidosis registry, the authors reviewed sixteen adult patients for how the disease declared itself and which symptoms followed.

Onset wears masks: developmental disorder in preschoolers, cerebellar signs in children, or leg muscle weakness like motor neuron disease in adults. The start means cases are often missed. Mental illness proved common, affecting 62.5 percent of the cohort, with psychoses in ten of sixteen patients spanning severe depression, bipolar disorder, and schizoaffective pictures. Treatment leaned on atypical antipsychotics, calming drugs, and mood stabilizers. The authors urge clinicians to keep this rare disease on the list when mental and nerve signs arrive together.
pmc-13315114:
Jingshu Liu and a large team grade China fight against a mountain form of visceral leishmaniasis through a One Health lens, in a study printed in 2026. The sandfly-borne disease was once well controlled but surged again in the early 2000s, with risk of wider spread.

The team scored seven endemic provinces on 2022 data with a set weighted tool. The average total came to 47.77 out of 100, with a spread from 38.59 to 61.72 across provinces, as stated in the report. Disease control scored highest among the big blocks, while inner support lagged, and the natural setting was the weakest subpart, by the scores given. Social conditions scored near the top. The grades show where a joined human, animal, and environment plan must shore up to hold the disease down.
pmc-13315614:
Hossam-Eddine Ejjebli and co-authors report in 2026 a case where a large lung clot was the first sign of a hidden blood disease. A 67-year-old woman with no clear clot risk factors came in with sudden breathlessness, and scans showed wide clots in both lungs with strain on the right side of the heart.

No leg clot was found. The unprovoked clot, heart strain, and subtle blood count oddities led to testing for a marrow growth disorder. Tests pointed to polycythemia vera carrying a JAK2 change, masked because iron shortage had kept hemoglobin and hematocrit from looking high. The case warns that normal-looking counts can hide the disease.
pmc-13316214:
G. Suay and a multicenter team report in 2026 real-world results for first-line osimertinib in advanced lung cancer carrying EGFR mutations, treated across eastern Spain. The drug is standard care, yet new upfront combinations are reshaping practice, and how to handle disease that grows in only a few spots remained unclear.

The retrospective cohort measured response rate, real-world progression-free and overall survival, and access to later therapy. Planned checks compared exon 19 deletion with the Leu858Arg change and baseline brain spread. Local ablative therapy for limited progression was a special focus for prolonging drug benefit.
pmc-13316614:
Mehran Mohammadi and Nikzad Ghanbari surveyed, in a 2026 study, how online exclusion and parents' phone habits shape heavy smartphone use among Iranian young adults. They separate being shunned online into direct, indirect, and ignored forms, and ask whether feeling that parents ignore them for phones carries the effect.

A total of 428 adults, mean age 28.03 years in the sample, filled validated questionnaires. Indirect online exclusion linked directly with heavier phone misuse, while direct exclusion worked through stronger feelings of parental phone snubbing. Being ignored online showed no clear link. The results suggest family phone habits belong in programs that aim to cut compulsive use, not just screen rules for the young person alone.
pmc-13317314:
Yuduo Guo and co-authors identify, in a 2026 study, an immune brake called PD-1H, or VISTA, that helps glioma brain tumors silence the body's defenses. The brake sits mostly on myeloid cells, the tumor's dominant immune population, rather than on the T cells most research targets.

Human tumor checks linked high brake levels with suppressive cell crowds, few killer T cells, more checkpoint molecules, and worse patient outcomes. In dishes, the brake pushed myeloid cells toward suppression and curbed killer T cell growth; in mice, it sped tumor growth. Blocking it with an antibody is now the therapeutic test the work sets up. The findings widen checkpoint therapy beyond its usual targets.
pmc-13318514:
Ruben Blokzijl and Catarina Rydin present a 2026 phylogenomic study of Ephedra, an ancient gymnosperm genus whose family tree has long resisted agreement. They gathered a large set of nuclear low-copy genes using a bait set designed for the group.

Before building trees, the authors checked for copied genes, shuffling within genes, and mixed sequences that could mislead the analysis. Those problems turned out to have limited effect, though cleaning them sharpened the results. A solid tree split the genus into American, Mediterranean, and Asian groups, with the first two as closest relatives. Many branches still showed clashing gene trees, which the authors link to incomplete lineage sorting and possibly past hybrid mixing.
pmc-13318614:
Yaqin Wei and colleagues present a 2026 retrospective study of older Chinese patients. All had type 2 diabetes. The team tested a combined index of triglycerides, glucose, and body mass. They asked whether it tracks with diabetic eye disease. Data came from a diabetes complications warning dataset.

Among 1,076 patients, eye disease prevalence was 47.68 percent in the group analysed. After adjustment, upper index quarters faced higher odds of retinopathy. The lowest quarter served as the reference group. Odds roughly doubled in the top group. Curve analysis suggested the link was not a straight line. The authors propose the cheap index as an aid for sorting patients. It is built from routine measures already collected.
pmc-13318714:
Fuyuan Zhang and co-authors review, in 2026, the two-way conversation between immune cells and stromal cells after a heart attack. Heart failure after myocardial infarction grows from harmful remodelling and fibrosis. Repair is not simple scar formation, they argue. It is a shifting dialogue between cell types over time.

Immune cells covered include neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes. Stromal partners include fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and pericytes. Signals pass through cytokines, chemokines, and fibrotic pathways. The review maps when and where each exchange happens. It explains how healthy repair tips into lasting fibrosis and heart failure. New treatments targeting the immune-matrix axis are summarised as possible ways to prevent that slide.
pmc-13320414:
Juan Rodriguez and co-authors build a blood gene tag score for breast cancer risk in a 2026 study inside a Swedish screening plan. A blood test that flags risk years before a tumor shows could sharpen who gets close screening. Chemical tags on DNA in blood stay steady over time and may catch early body shifts that precede tumors.

Blood from 377 women who later grew breast cancer and 378 matched peers was scanned across a wide tag chip. A first city set gave 87 tag sites tied to later risk, and 22 of them held up in a second city set and formed the score. The score tracked risk across tumor types, stood apart from known risk factors, and held steady up to five years before diagnosis. It matched a gene risk score and lifted short term sorting.
pmc-13321014:
Viswakalyan Kotapalli and colleagues share a 2026 high-throughput protocol for mapping where proteins sit on the genome. Proteins that shape chromatin, including transcription factors and histone marks, guide gene use, cell identity, and disease. Older mapping assays work but are slow and hands-on. The CUT and RUN method cuts DNA only near a chosen target.

The protocol runs the method in a 96 well plate format for many samples at once. Steps cover targeted DNA enrichment, library building, sequencing, and data analysis, with pointers to the founding papers by Skene and Henikoff and by Meers and others. The goal is sharp, genome wide maps of gene control proteins with far less labour.
pmc-13322814:
Zhong Wang and colleagues compare two follow-up treatments for HER2-positive breast cancer in a 2026 real-world study from Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University. Their group covers 184 people who still had invasive disease after drug treatment given before surgery, in records from 2019 to 2022.

One group received T-DM1 and the other received trastuzumab plus pertuzumab, with disease-free survival as the main measure. Disease progressed in fewer T-DM1 patients, and some higher-risk groups seemed to gain more, though the overall gap was not firm in statistical terms. Low platelet counts at a severe grade were more common with T-DM1, and no deaths were linked to treatment in either group.
pmc-13322914:
Xiaohua Li and colleagues report twin toddlers who both developed the same leukaemia, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. The monozygotic brothers were admitted close in age with fever and abnormal blood findings, and marrow tests gave both a diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

Both boys carried the same ETV6::RUNX1 fusion gene and received chemotherapy under the CCLG-ALL-2018 protocol for two years. Each reached complete remission and stayed in remission for more than two years after treatment ended. The authors read the matched case as support for an origin before birth and a two-hit account of childhood leukaemia, and they review earlier twin reports.
pmc-13323014:
Kamontá Heidelburg, Meagan Scott and Tai A Collins argue for remaking social-emotional learning for Black youth, in a 2026 article aimed at school psychologists. Standard programmes, they say, often carry white, middle-class values. Those values can miss the needs of Black students and other minoritised youth.

Five parts anchor their plan. They are Afrocentrism, anti-oppressive frameworks, a strength-based stance, student empowerment and healing, and proven practice. Research support is given for each part. Advice covers system-level change, school work, community links and policy. The goal is better grades, behaviour and well-being, with school psychologists acting as advocates for fair treatment in daily work.
pmc-13323314:
Zijun Yan and co-authors test virtual reality training to shift attention bias in obsessive-compulsive disorder, in a 2026 feasibility study. Fifteen patients with contamination-focused symptoms, all on medication, split between VR training twice weekly for four weeks and routine outpatient care.

Five patients in each group finished the four-week follow-up. Virtual scenes provoked moderate obsessive symptoms and anxiety, as intended, and every VR patient rated the challenge level as right, with better subjective focus reported. Such bias training aims to loosen the pull of feared cues that standard computer tasks present weakly. The authors judge the approach feasible and call for larger controlled trials of its therapeutic value.
pmc-13323614:
Sascha Milin, Felix A. Ebel, and Ingo Schäfer review the use of performance-enhancing substances in everyday life and at work, a quiet counterpart to doping in sport. Their 2026 narrative review gathers studies on use contexts, motives, substance groups, prevalence, benefits, and risks, linking use to heavier workloads, time pressure, and limited chances to recover. Unlike sport, where anti-doping rules form a formal system of bans, tests, and sanctions, no comparable control regime governs daily life.

Use typically aims at short-term demands: tiredness, heavy mental load, stress, emotional strain, and physical complaints while working, including working while ill. Stimulants, mood and sleep regulators, painkillers, and dietary supplements are the main groups, and all but the supplements are often prescription-only. The review frames the pattern as a health and workplace issue, not a cheating scandal, and calls for clearer rules and support rather than moral judgment alone.
pmc-13323814:
Matthew M Burg traces a century of treating psychological factors in heart disease, in a 2026 review article. Stress and emotion in cardiac risk run from surgeon John Hunter, who died after an argument, through the type A behaviour work of Rosenman and Friedman.

Depression took centre stage from the mid-1980s, with pooled studies tying even mild symptoms to new and repeat cardiac events, and trauma stress joined the list later. Group cognitive programmes, stress skills training and related care cut events or silent ischaemia in several trials the author recounts. The review asks where the field stands now and how psychological care should be built into cardiac practice next.
pmc-13324214:
Jop W Schneijdenberg and co-authors split right ventricle contraction into directions in tetralogy of Fallot, in a 2026 3D ultrasound study. Fifty patients with this repaired congenital heart disease and fifty healthy controls gave dynamic 3D meshes of the right ventricle from commercial software.

A custom tool separated contraction into lengthwise, radial and front-to-back components and worked out each share of ejection fraction. The front-to-back share fell in patients against controls and drove most of the functional decline, while the lengthwise share rose in partial compensation. The authors argue that direction-level measures can sharpen decisions for adults living with repaired Fallot anatomy, where right ventricle failure looms large.
pmc-13324314:
Alice Bernard and co-authors set out the ELIEO trial protocol in 2026, testing early against late use of lung bypass support in severe ARDS. Veno-venous ECMO is normally a rescue step when ventilators fail, yet hints suggest earlier use may help some patients more.

The prospective randomised multicentre trial will enrol 508 adults with severe ARDS. One group starts ECMO within 24 hours of reaching a specialist centre, while the other follows standard ARDS Network care with ECMO held as rescue. Death from any cause at ninety days is the main outcome, with organ scores, function, bleeding and intensive care measures tracked secondarily under a staged statistical design.
pmc-13325314:
Piyarat Suntarattiwong and team tested a multi-germ PCR panel for children thought to have meningitis or encephalitis at a big hospital in Thailand. Their 2026 paper looks at the FilmArray brain panel, which detects multiple germs in spinal fluid at once. Rapid, at-once finding matters in central nervous system infection, where early pathogen identification shapes treatment and prognosis.

The panel's specificity was high, but its sensitivity was low, because some germs common in the tropics are not included in the test. The authors caution that clinicians using the panel should weigh clinical signs and the local epidemiology of central nervous system disease in warm settings, rather than treating a negative result as exclusion. The paper thus serves as a practical guide to the panel's strengths and blind spots in warm-climate child care.
pmc-13326314:
Snieguole Kaseliene and colleagues survey mothers on breastfeeding support in Lithuanian maternity hospitals in a 2026 study. Skilled support helps mothers start and keep breastfeeding, but local evidence on how mothers rate that help was scarce.

A total of 572 women who had delivered healthy full-term babies answered an online survey in June 2022. About 65.7 percent gave birth in Baby-Friendly hospitals, and 76.2 percent were still breastfeeding when surveyed. Overall support scored a median of 65.0 out of 110 points, a middling verdict. Care in the first hours after birth earned the highest marks, at a mean of 3.76 out of 5 in the ratings.
pmc-13328114:
Gabriel Hoffmann and team showed that a brain vessel measure is skewed by starting blood volume. Their 2026 study set blood oxygen MRI vessel response, usually read during high carbon dioxide breathing, against direct brain blood flow response from arterial spin labelling. Data from fifty people at 3 Tesla held both response measures plus relative blood volume and oxygen uptake, plus dynamic simulations.

Grey and white matter differed sharply in blood oxygen response, while blood flow response was much the same across tissues. Between-person and within-person checks showed the grey-white gap in blood oxygen response mostly mirrors blood volume gaps, not artery travel time or starting blood flow. Simulations also pointed to a slow fall in oxygen use during high carbon dioxide breathing. The team holds that blood oxygen response leans hard on blood volume, a link that matters for vessel disease or tumor studies where blood volume shifts.
pmc-13329814:
Minghe Yao and colleagues test a traditional Chinese formula against diet-driven metabolic harm in mice in a 2026 study. Danlou tablet is used for heart disease care and adjusts fat handling, so the team asked whether it also counters obesity and insulin resistance. Mice ate a high-fat diet for 22 weeks, with treatment given during that span.

Treated mice gained less weight and fat, handled glucose better, and showed less liver fat, swelling, and oxidative stress in the reported checks. Gut microbe balance moved back toward normal, with shifts in key groups. Blood and liver data linked gains to restored fat burning in the liver and calmer immune pathways. The authors frame the effect as acting through the gut and liver link.
pmc-13330114:
Wenfeng Zheng and co-authors study how comparing oneself to others can cut both ways for student creativity in a 2026 report. Comparison may spark helpful envy that drives useful ideas, or harmful envy that drives ideas meant to hurt. The team tested a dual-path model with a three-wave survey of college students.

Stronger comparison habit predicted both kinds of envy in the reported results. Helpful envy carried the link to general creativity, while harmful envy carried the link to harmful creativity. A classroom climate focused on mastery weakened the harmful path, but did not change the helpful path. Schools can thus curb harmful ideas while keeping drive for good ones, the authors argue.
pmc-13330614:
Hiroki Satou, Akihito Tampo, and Motoi Okada report balloon control of bleeding during a long ambulance ride in a 2026 case. A 41-year-old man was run over by heavy machinery and suffered severe liver injury with bleeding shock. Local resources were limited and the trip to a major centre was long.

A doctor-staffed ambulance crew placed an aortic balloon catheter en route as his state worsened, with breathing tube support as well. Partial blocking came first, then full blocking as arrest neared. At hospital he received large transfusions, damage-control surgery with liver packing, and vessel blocking by catheter. No balloon harms arose. He left intensive care on day seven.
pmc-13333314:
Punsita Tangkum and colleagues describe an exceptionally rare ear infection in a 2026 case report: cryptococcal disease of both ears and mastoids in a woman whose immune weakness had a hidden cause. The fungus Cryptococcus usually attacks the lungs or brain of people with weakened immunity, and ear involvement is almost unheard of.

The 34-year-old Thai woman developed progressive hearing loss in both ears, with ear fullness and painless discharge starting on the left. Three years earlier she had swollen neck glands with granulomatous inflammation that no test could explain, treated empirically for two years as a suspected mycobacterial infection. Workup of the ear disease identified the fungus and also uncovered adult-onset immunodeficiency from autoantibodies against interferon-gamma, a defect that had left her open to such infections. The authors present the pairing as a warning that unexplained opportunistic infections should trigger a search for this acquired immune flaw.
pmc-13333714:
Jing Shen and co-authors surveyed perioperative comfort care in children's anesthesia across China in a 2026 national study. Comfort therapy covers the steps that calm children and ease pain around surgery, and the team mapped how widely hospitals use it.

The online survey ran from March to May 2025 and drew 150 valid responses, mostly from top-grade tertiary hospitals. Preoperative visits happened everywhere, and most hospitals gave education, fasting guidance, and anesthesia plan explanations. Still, many centers relied on non-routine premedication for anxiety, and practice varied in areas such as parental presence. The authors gathered both closed and open answers to pinpoint barriers. The findings supply a baseline for standardizing gentler anesthesia care for children.
pmc-13334814:
Da Cai and co-authors tested pesticide residues in everyday vegetables from Shandong, China, in a 2026 food safety study spanning four years. Shandong leads China in vegetable output, so what lingers on its produce matters widely.

Between 2018 and 2021 the team tested 1,067 samples of 23 daily-eaten vegetables for 33 common pesticides. Residues turned up in 34.7 percent of samples, and 10.2 percent carried several pesticides at once. Procymidone, carbendazim, and thiamethoxam were detected most often, but six banned products, including carbofuran and phorate, also showed up. Carbofuran, omethoate, and avermectins most often breached legal limits. Chronic risk was modeled for different age groups by both fixed and chance-based methods, giving officials a residue baseline and a risk ranking.
pmc-13335814:
Wei Zhang and colleagues study 2026 the drug canagliflozin easing kidney filter lining injury via melibiose in a gut-dependent manner. The drug reduces albumin in urine in patients with diabetes kidney disease beyond its glucose effect, but mechanisms remain unclear. The authors analyzed 85 patients treated with the drug and 85 controls over 26 weeks to explore whether gut microbes and their products contribute to kidney protection. The drug reshaped gut microbes, notably boosting a gut bacterium and increasing plasma melibiose levels.

In mice, the drug eased kidney filter lining injury and albumin in urine. Similar effects were replicated by fecal microbe transfer, the bacterium, or sugar giving. In detail, this sugar bound to and activated GLO1, reduced a harmful byproduct, and blocked the AGE-RAGE pathway, preserving kidney filter lining health. Furthermore, oral sugar supplement reduced albumin in urine in patients with early-stage kidney disease.
pmc-13336414:
Tao Zhao and co-authors tamed a flexible porous framework to separate xenon from krypton in a 2026 materials study. The two noble gases are near-twins physically, and flexible metal-organic frameworks that might distinguish them tend to need high pressure to open their gates.

Their strategy adjusted pore size and polarity together, weaving 20 percent chlorine into the ZIF-7 framework. The polarized pores recognize xenon preferentially while holding capacity. The optimized material reached a selectivity of 30.8 for xenon over krypton in a 20/80 mixture by standard estimation, and simulations traced the preference to strong xenon-chlorine contacts. Flow-through breakthrough tests delivered krypton purer than 99.9 percent in the reported runs, showing the tuned flexibility works at low concentrations too.
pmc-13336814:
Ji-Yeon Lee and colleagues built a blood based metabolic profiling method in 2026 to track colorectal cancer progression. Systemic metabolic shifts could yield prognostic tools, but serum analysis needs robust platforms and frameworks that survive variation between patient groups. The team used fluorine NMR to measure serum amino acids in 152 colorectal cancer patients.

A ratio based normalisation step reduced cohort variability, and network analysis then revealed pathway changes as cancer advanced. The framework points toward serum markers that could aid prognosis and treatment choice without invasive sampling. Larger validation cohorts will decide whether the signals hold up in routine clinical use.
pmc-13337114:
Jie Pan and colleagues find a stabilizer that shields melanoma from immune attack in a 2026 study. Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer, and many patients never respond to checkpoint therapy because tumors raise extra brakes. WDR12 was high in nonresponders, and blocking it genetically drew in more killer CD8 T cells with stronger function.

WDR12 works with a chaperone part, CCT7, to stabilize another checkpoint, CD276, on tumor cells. A screened drug, SU14813, binds WDR12 specifically and destabilizes CD276, freeing T cells. In animals, WDR12 targeting plus PD-1 blockade beat either approach alone. Cutting one stabilizer could collapse a backup brake system that frustrates immunotherapy.
pmc-13337514:
Cong Xia and a large team engineer a donor pig whose organs carry seven genetic edits for transplant research in a 2026 study. Pig organs could ease the human organ shortage, but immune rejection and silenced added genes have blocked progress. Earlier multi-gene pigs suffered unstable expression from inserted promoters.

Using CRISPR, the team knocked out three sugar antigen genes that trigger hyperacute rejection. Four human protective genes were placed into the Rosa26 safe-harbor site, driven by the pig's own promoters for stable, tissue-appropriate expression. The three target sugars vanished from cells and tissues, while protective proteins appeared steadily in vessel linings and major organs such as heart, liver, and kidneys in the reported checks.
pmc-13337614:
Srinivas Samavedam argued in a 2026 editorial that machine learning can beat classic ICU scores at death risk prediction. Death risk estimates shape talks with kin and choices to step care up or down. They also guide use of scarce ICU beds. APACHE II and SOFA scores date from an old era and miss complex links in severe illness. The editorial looks at a study of 5,553 ICU stays in India.

Three models, logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost, forecast ICU deaths from routine health records and beat the old scores in checks on the same data. Samavedam urges keeping the clinical sense in the old scores while adding machine learning flex. The piece gives doctors a fair view of promise, limits, and safe uptake.
pmc-13337714:
Cristina Madaudo and a large team review heart muscle inflammation in myocarditis for 2026. Causes vary, and immune responses shape outcomes from full recovery to a weakened, enlarged heart. Both the fast innate response and the later adaptive response play parts.

In viral cases, danger signals switch on pathways that raise inflammatory messengers and recruit cells such as neutrophils and killer cells. Imbalance between helper cell groups can keep inflammation going and drive scarring. Look-alike self proteins and inherited risk can sustain the attack. Beyond standard heart failure care, the review weighs targeted immune therapies and newer markers that may guide closer, patient-specific treatment.
pmc-13337814:
Liu Long and colleagues test links between hard exercise and movement skills in schoolchildren in a 2026 study. The question was whether body weight carries part of that link. Children aged 8 to 12 in South Punjab, Pakistan, formed the study group.

A total of 1,360 children from 85 schools were tested with a standard Canadian skills protocol. Most children, 79.9 percent in the reported share, had normal weight, while smaller shares were overweight or obese. Normal-weight children logged more weekly steps and stronger skill scores. The team then checked whether body mass index explained part of the link between exercise and skills, with age and sex accounted for.
pmc-13339014:
Elia Pascucci and colleagues test zinc oxide nanoparticles with ultrasound in worms in a 2026 safety study. Iron-doped particles may serve in medicine, and a lipid-coated version aims to be gentler. Ultrasound can activate such particles, so combined effects need checking.

Caenorhabditis elegans worms were exposed to plain particles, coated particles, ultrasound alone, and combinations. Survival, particle spread, egg laying, body bends, and reactive species were tracked. Full results compare whether coating softens harm and whether sound adds risk. Using a simple animal first helps flag dangers before any move toward medical use in people.
pmc-13339114:
Hugo Morales-Briceño and colleagues map extra movement disorders in genetic brain conditions in a 2026 data review. Dystonia, chorea, and jerky extra movements appear in many single-gene disorders with slow development or epilepsy. The full gene and symptom range was not yet charted.

A search of past reports gathered 210 single-gene conditions as reported. Group analysis split them into two large sets, one centered on development disorders and one on epilepsy syndromes. Dystonia was the most common movement type in both sets. Subgroups differed by brain scans, body features, and movement mix. The map gives doctors a data-led route when a child's movements hint at a genetic cause.
pmc-13339414:
Manon C. Wilpshaar and colleagues check whether cancer registries hold data fit for policy use in a 2026 study. Registries built for clinical care are now asked to serve drug approval and value judgments. Three European cancer registries with different aims were audited.

A reference list of essential data items was built from literature and expert input. All three registries lacked parts of comorbidity, added therapy, patient-reported, cost, and safety data as reported. Inclusion rules differed sharply by original purpose. The authors urge disease-specific core datasets so registry owners can benchmark and close gaps before policy reliance grows.
pmc-13339514:
Marion Simonetta-Moreau and colleagues tracked botulinum toxin use in 2026 for hyperkinetic movement disorders in France from 2015 to 2023. Dystonia, tremor, and myoclonus are disabling and often treated with botulinum toxin type A, yet real world patterns were poorly documented. The team used the national hospital discharge database to classify patients by diagnosis code.

Annual counts of injections and treated patients, adherence, and reinjection intervals were analysed across four groups. National trends reveal where access, dosing, and follow up vary. Health planners can use the picture to balance supply, training, and patient access for movement disorder care.
pmc-13339614:
Pauline Howell and a large team test testicular safety of a pretomanid tuberculosis regimen in a 2026 trial. Rodent studies had flagged sperm harm at high doses, though primate and hormone data looked clean. Men with drug-resistant lung tuberculosis in South Africa and Georgia took part.

Twenty-six men received the four-drug BPaMZ course for 26 weeks, then were watched to week 78 as reported. Average total sperm count rose from 48.8 to 68.8 million per sample by week 26 in the reported means. Most men gained count and concentration. Hormone checks accompanied counts, together supporting preserved fertility function on this regimen.
pmc-13339914: Lynn Farrell and colleagues issued a 2026 correction. It amends wording on fulfilment scores in a study of burnout among Irish cancer care staff. Only one methods sentence was wrong. Higher scores now simply mean higher fulfilment. The authors state this plainly. Results do not change. Interpretation does not change either.
pmc-13341614:
Getting liver surgery patients walking early is harder than protocols assume, in a 2026 review by Yan Zhang and colleagues. The team mined their unit's recovery-pathway quality archive for 320 elective hepatobiliary surgery patients treated from January 2022 to December 2024.

The pathway prescribed out-of-bed activity by the first postoperative day and at least 30 meters of walking by day two, alongside eight standardized care components. Records captured who actually complied and what barriers nurses documented, plus length of stay and first flatus timing. Mapping real-world compliance and its obstacles is a first step toward making enhanced recovery promises hold at the bedside.
pmc-13342214:
Miaomiao Huang and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of naringenin, a plant flavonoid, as a possible treatment for depression. Because current drugs often bring side effects, the team gathered animal studies to judge whether the compound eases depressive-like behavior and how it might act.

Searching five databases through November 2025, the authors pooled 13 studies covering 212 rats. Treated animals did better on swim, suspension, and open field tests and drank more sweetened water, while markers of inflammation and oxidative stress fell and key brain chemicals recovered. All proof so far comes from animals, so the authors call for careful human trials before any clinical use.
pmc-13342814:
Keiichi Takei reports a 2026 pilot study using eye tracking to watch gaze and performance during squat-based video game exercise. Eight healthy young adults played a squat exergame under three setups: plain play, play while doing mental subtraction, and one-leg squats meant to raise balance and muscle demand.

Added demands slowed play and shifted where eyes landed on screen regions such as commands, the avatar, and the score. Squat scores fell hard in the one-leg setup, and counting tasks pushed more gaze outside the set regions. Takei suggests gaze measures can reveal how task demands split attention during active gaming, though larger and more varied groups must confirm the patterns.
pmc-13343014:
Loren Kock and colleagues track quitting methods in England in a 2026 repeat survey study covering 2016 to 2023. Disposable vapes surged after mid-2021, and the team asked whether that rise changed how smokers used vapes, prescription help, or other aids when trying to quit.

Surveys covered 8,323 adults who smoked and had made a quit attempt within the past year. Vape use in quit attempts had been falling, then reversed sharply, climbing from 27.7 percent in June 2021 to 40.6 percent by December 2023. Use of other non-prescription methods fell in mirror image, while prescription and specialist support kept declining steadily. Disposable vapes, the authors conclude, reshaped quit attempt habits.
pmc-13343514:
Björn N. Koch and co-authors recount failed attempts in 2026 to oxidize xenon hexafluoride into a xenon(VIII) species. Ruthenium hexafluoride, one of the few agents strong enough to oxidize a related bromine compound, was mixed with XeF6 in dry hydrogen fluoride under varied conditions, hunting for a [XeF7]+ salt.

Instead of the hoped-for cation, reactions released fluorine gas and gave either a known xenon(V) salt or a brand-new compound, [Xe2F11][RuF6], characterized by crystal diffraction and vibration spectra. Calculations suggest a [XeF7]+ solid could in principle hold together, but under these conditions any such cation falls apart too fast to catch, closing one route to xenon(VIII).
pmc-13344414:
Burcu Eser and co-authors studied in 2026 why some people with stable schizophrenia struggle to read minds from face cues. Trouble judging thoughts and feelings from the eyes is well known in this illness. It was not clear whether low drive, flat affect, or muddled thought drove the trouble. pmc-13397514:

pmc-13398714:

pmc-13400114:

pmc-13400214:

pmc-13400514:

pmc-13400614:

pmc-13401314:

pmc-13401414:

pmc-13401714:

pmc-13403814:

pmc-13407014:

pmc-13412014:

pmc-13412714:

pmc-13417714:

pmc-13419014:
