The minor procedures room ran higher than the operating room by a mean gap of 2.32 colony units in the reported comparison, and higher than the day suite by 1.25 in the same measure. Field-style sterility outside main theaters is common in minor work, so the size of the gap matters for consent and wound care advice. Cleaner air follows stricter protocol in a dose-like way here.
pmc-13420614:
Esteban Ciliberti and colleagues review antibody-drug conjugates in gynecological cancers, drugs that ride a targeting antibody straight into tumor cells before releasing a toxic payload. More than 210 such drugs sit in clinical testing in the count the authors cite, and fifteen gained approval across cancers in the past decade. Gynecological tumors were slower to benefit than breast or lung cancers.

The review draws on database searches, major cancer conference reports, and trial registries to map where each drug stands. Cancer-specific surface anchors make the tailored strikes possible, and biomarker testing decides who should receive them. Strong phase three results could reset standard care for several of these cancers. The authors balance that promise against toxicity and cost challenges that clinics already feel.
pmc-13420714:
Tina Dutta and Abhinav Kumar apply topic modeling to map where India's Ayush healthcare system, covering traditional and alternative medicine, is placing its focus. Mountains of unstructured policy text hide the system's true priorities from plain reading. A statistical method that clusters documents by word patterns lets themes surface without hand coding.

The study aims to name current focus areas, trace how priorities shifted over time, and expose themes that institutional talk leaves out. Policy research in Indian healthcare had not used this method before, by the authors' account. Such maps can show whether stated strategy matches where attention and money actually flow. Ministries gain a mirror for their own discourse, useful when drafting the next plan cycle.
pmc-13421114:
Chengxin Li and colleagues test whether a sugar-handling score predicts kidney stone history in United States adults, using the national nutrition survey from 2011 to 2020. The score estimates how well the body disposes of glucose, standing in for insulin resistance without a clamp test. The analysis enrolled 31,566 participants with the needed measures.

Weighted regression models, followed by matched comparisons that balance the groups, judged the link between the score and past stones. Standard insulin resistance markers had shown patchy power for this outcome, leaving room for a better gauge. Kidney stones are common, painful, and increasingly tied to metabolic health, so a sharper risk marker has clinic value. The national sample gives the result weight across age and background groups.
pmc-13421214:
Boldrini and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether fertility treatments raise breast cancer risk. Assisted reproductive technologies use hormone drugs to stimulate egg release, and these hormones also act on breast tissue. The review drew on large cohort and case-control studies, pooled analyses, and guidelines.

Overall, the evidence did not show a real, consistent rise in breast cancer after these treatments. Comparisons against untreated infertile women were more reassuring than comparisons against the general public. Some studies found modest risk rises in subgroups, such as women with no prior pregnancy, many stimulation cycles, or inherited risk, but results clashed and numbers were small. Progesterone support looked safe across studies. Hormone stimulants raised estrogen briefly, yet large studies found no lasting rise in breast cancer rates.
pmc-13421614:
Hritika Pai and co-workers tracked thinking, sleep, and distress in 2026 among 118 head and neck cancer patients in India during cancer therapy, while they joined the MORE rehab program. The guided program mixed body workouts, thinking drills, and mind-and-mood tactics three times weekly for eight weeks.

By week twelve, felt thinking trouble, sleep, and mental distress had all clearly got better, regardless of patient background. The paper backs set mixed rehab as supportive care during grueling cancer treatment, while calling for large random trials to confirm the gains in wider trials.
pmc-13421914:
Zhen Cai leads a twenty-one-author team reporting two-year results, in a 2026 paper, for teclistamab in Chinese patients with multiple myeloma that had returned despite three classes of therapy. Teclistamab is a bispecific antibody that drags T cells onto myeloma cells, and this China cohort of the MajesTEC-1 study now has twenty-seven months of follow-up.

Twenty-six participants received the drug under the skin weekly, with some stepping down to fortnightly dosing after sustained responses. About seventy-seven percent responded, all deeply, and three quarters of responders reached complete response or better. Median progression-free survival was about twenty-five months. Quality of life improved across several measures, and serious new infections became rarer over time. The authors support continued use in this heavily pretreated group.
pmc-13422314:
József Tímár and colleagues review the comeback of farnesyltransferase inhibitors in cancer in a 2026 paper. Early trials failed because the drugs were given without markers to pick responders, stalling the field. Two approvals revived interest, lonafarnib for childhood progeria and tipifarnib for HRAS-mutant head and neck cancer.

New lab work shows these inhibitors can boost KRAS blockers and other targeted drugs, giving the class a second chance in combination therapy. The review insists future trials must use predictive markers, or they risk repeating the first generation's costly mistake.
pmc-13422814:
Xiaoxiao Hu leads a large team reporting, in a 2026 study, a previously unnoticed population of killer immune cells standing guard where fat meets breast tumour. Fat around a tumour is immunologically active territory, yet how fat cells direct the innate-like gamma-delta T cells living there was unknown.

Single-cell sequencing and spatial mapping of paired patient samples revealed NKG2A-carrying gamma-delta T cells clustered at the fat-tumour boundary, armed for cytotoxic attack and in close conversation with dendritic cells. Nearby fat cells, their fat-burning pathway switched up, secreted the lipid signal LTB4, which the experiments show programmes these T cells' activation. The authors describe a local surveillance network with implications for immunotherapy in fat-rich cancers.
pmc-13425414:
Liu and colleagues built a 2026 prediction model for thirty-day death risk in critically ill cancer patients, adding two iron-related blood measures, ferritin and total iron-binding capacity. They trained the model on 1,137 intensive care patients from one large United States database and checked it on a second database. Their method uses a neural network pre-trained to learn from small tables of data.

About twenty-six percent of the training patients died within thirty days. High ferritin and low iron-binding capacity each predicted death on their own, while plain serum iron did not. The model beat eight rival machine learning methods, with strong accuracy at home and solid accuracy abroad. Blood cell counts, a waste product called lactate, and ferritin drove its predictions most. The authors offer it as an explainable risk tool for intensive care teams.
pmc-13425614:
Deng and colleagues pool the evidence on machine learning forecasts for intracerebral hemorrhage, bleeding inside the brain, a stroke type with high death and disability. Doctors need warning of three dangers: the bleed expanding, poor recovery, and death. Their 2026 systematic review and meta analysis gather eighty three studies covering 136,840 patients. Each model is scored on discrimination, the ability to rank a poor outcome above a good one.

Models that fused clinical data with radiomics, number sets mined from brain scans, performed best on all three tasks. Top scores came for death prediction, with slightly lower ones for bleed growth. The fine print matters: most scores came from internal validation, tests on data kin to the training set, and outside validation stayed rare. Plain logistic regression matched fancier algorithms more often than hype suggests. Strong tools exist, the authors conclude, but hospitals should demand outside proof before trusting them.
pmc-13425814:
Ming Jun Kuck, Nicola J. Paine, and Eef Hogervorst modeled stress and quality of life during the menopausal transition in a 2026 path analysis. An anonymous online survey gathered 269 valid responses from women aged 40 to 60 classed as premenopausal, perimenopausal, or postmenopausal under STRAW+10 criteria. Measures covered negative life events, perceived stress, social support, resilience, self-efficacy, and menopause-specific quality of life.

Path modeling treated negative events as the starting point and tested whether perceived stress carries their effect toward psychosocial well-being. Results help clinicians see which supports might buffer women when life events and hormonal change collide. Women in the group spanned the years just before, in the midst of, and just past the change of life, which makes the mix broad.
pmc-13426914:
Konadu and colleagues reported in 2026 on bacterial vaginosis, an imbalance of vaginal bacteria, in early pregnancy in the middle belt of Ghana. The condition is common among women of African descent and has been linked to early birth and other poor outcomes. The team followed pregnant women in the Kintampo area from before 20 weeks of pregnancy through delivery, testing vaginal swabs with a standard scoring method.

Konadu enrolled 1,180 women, and about three in ten tested positive for the condition in early pregnancy. Early birth, low birth weight, and fetal loss were all slightly more common in positive women, but none of the gaps was strong enough to rule out chance. Being younger and unmarried raised the odds of infection. The authors urge targeted screening of higher-risk women and finer lab methods to sort subtypes.
pmc-13427314:
Martina Cacciapuoti and coauthors measured two microRNAs in Gitelman syndrome in a 2026 study using the rare salt-wasting tubulopathy as a natural model. People with Gitelman syndrome are protected from angiotensin II driven cardiovascular remodeling, so their biology mimics lifelong blockade of that hormone pathway. Sixteen patients from the Padua nephrology cohort were compared with twenty-one matched healthy volunteers for plasma miR-155 and miR-103, both implicated in angiotensin signaling and hypertension.

Expression of both microRNAs was higher in patients in the study's framing, complicating simple stories about their role in vessel remodeling. Clarifying these signals could refine understanding of how angiotensin reshapes the cardiovascular system. The Padua group has long kept a roll of such rare cases, which lets a test like this draw on years of stored blood and case notes.
pmc-13427414:
Julia Bicker and colleagues coupled disease and wastewater models for a large city in a 2026 study calibrated to Munich's first COVID-19 wave. Clinical reporting misses infections and arrives late, while wastewater surveillance captures viral RNA from symptomatic and symptom-free people alike, yet sewer numbers are hard to translate into prevalence. Their combined model was built to scale to big urban populations.

Simulations quantified how sampling protocols, rainfall, viral decay, normalization choices, and intervention timing bend the relationship between wastewater readings and true disease levels. Proper normalization emerged as decisive, giving public health teams rules for reading sewer data during future outbreaks.
pmc-13427714:
Ono and colleagues reported in 2026 on early-stage mouth cancer, oral squamous cell carcinoma, in patients aged 15 to 39 years. Cancers in this young group may behave in distinct ways from those in older people. The team compared 48 young patients with 69 patients aged 65 or older, all treated with surgery for stage I or II disease, and tested tumor tissue with stains and gene probes.

Ono found that young patients' tumors sat on the tongue far more often, in nearly all cases, and spread along the surface more often. Their tumors also showed more budding, small clusters of cancer cells at the edge, and more abnormal p53 stain patterns. Even so, young patients survived better overall. Invasion deeper than 5 millimetres was the strongest warning sign in the young group.
pmc-13429114:
Mansour Tobaiqy and Sulafa Tarek Alqutub review, in a 2026 paper, the side effects of incretin-based drugs, the class behind popular diabetes and weight-loss treatments. These drugs mimic gut hormones and deliver weight loss, blood sugar control, and heart and kidney benefits. The authors searched major databases for studies from 2005 to early 2026 and gathered 60 studies and safety reports. Evidence ranged from trials to real-world surveillance by regulators.

Gut complaints dominated: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation were the commonest harms and the main reason patients quit. Kidney problems appeared rarely, usually alongside fluid loss from gut illness. Gallbladder issues were uncommon and tied to fast weight loss and prior risk. Pancreatitis stayed rare in trials, and human data showed no rise in thyroid cancer. Newer signals, from eye changes to hair loss, rest on weaker evidence the authors flag as such.
pmc-13430414:
Arifin and Handayani systematically reviewed in 2026 what makes patients accept Internet of Things technology in health care, from wearable monitors to connected home devices. Following standard review guidelines, they searched eight databases for studies from 2016 to 2024 and kept sixty-two that directly measured patient perspectives.

Perceived usefulness was the strongest driver of acceptance, appearing in eighty-nine percent of studies. Ease of use followed at seventy-six percent, and trust and security at sixty-eight percent, with cost-effectiveness in about half. The main barriers were data security worries, privacy concerns, low digital literacy, and resistance to change, each appearing in a third to two fifths of studies. Most included studies rated good to excellent in quality. The authors offer design and policy strategies to raise acceptance and cut abandonment.
pmc-13430814:
Moataz Derbala and colleagues test the FIB-4 score for spotting advanced liver scarring in Qatari residents with metabolic fatty liver disease. Scarring stage drives long-term outlook, and FIB-4 is urged as a first non-invasive screen, yet its accuracy may shift across populations.

Adults with the disease seen at Hamad Medical Corporation in Qatar from 2023 to 2024 were reviewed, with FIB-4 computed from routine blood tests. Liver biopsy served as the main truth standard, with FibroScan as a second comparison. Clinics in Qatar get a local verdict on whether a cheap blood-based score can be trusted to flag advanced scarring.
pmc-13430914:
R Dattani and colleagues report a preventive primary-care model for cardiorenal metabolic disease in Harrow, North West London. The condition bundles obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, and chronic kidney disease, and early action can slow kidney decline and heart risk.

The Harrow hub built a personalised, multi-disciplinary pathway to find high-risk patients, tune their care, and offer lifestyle and psychosocial support. A logic model co-designed by the team guided delivery and evaluation, with two record-identified cohorts invited, including adults aged 20 to 80 with raised body mass and pre-diabetes. The paper reports first-year clinical outcomes for a joined-up prevention model.
pmc-13431014:
Shi and colleagues published a 2026 study reading the chloroplast genome of a rare plant. Amorphophallus josefbogneri is a tuber plant native to southwest Thailand. Chloroplasts are the green cell parts that run photosynthesis, the plant's food-making system. Reading their genome helps sort how species in this genus relate.

The full genome runs about 173,000 DNA letters in a four-part ring shape. The team catalogued 128 genes, including 83 that code for proteins. Family-tree analysis grouped the plant with five close cousins in the genus. Relatives include species grown for food starch and showy garden flowers. The genome gives marker makers a base for spotting this species by DNA. The data also aid conservation checks on wild stands of the plant.
pmc-13431914:
Anagha P Vincent and co-authors set out a design frame in 2026 for layered vanadium oxide battery parts that gain guest ions before use, a trick called pre-intercalation. Zinc batteries draw fans as a safer, cheaper pick than lithium cells, with water-based fluids that cannot burn. Guest ions slipped between the oxide layers act as pillars that hold the stack apart.

The frame joins two effects: wider gaps and shifts in local charge pull. Guest size, charge strength, water state, and electron traits set how fast zinc ions move and how well the stack holds through rounds of use. Water held in the layers wins a new role as an active charge softener that trims the pull on moving ions. The rules span single, double, and triple charge guests and reach past zinc to other multi-charge storage plans.
pmc-13434014:
Yuki Y Yamauchi and colleagues ask why mammal brains differ in neuron mix despite sharing a layered cortex. Excitatory neuron subtypes sit in distinct layers across mammals, yet the balance between subtypes varies markedly by species for largely unknown reasons.

Comparative tissue study across eight mammal species found a deep-layer expansion seen only in rats, in the touch cortex. That rat feature traced to a longer early phase of deep-layer neuron production before switching to upper layers, confirmed by birth-dating and single-cell gene reads. Timing of deep-layer production was governed by a genetic program for progenitor ageing, including canonical Wnt signalling, showing that developmental timing, not just size, sculpts cortex diversity.
pmc-13434114:
Changwoo Pyo and co-authors printed radio switches in 2026 from a fluid-grown layered stuff for next-wave 6G fronts, and found that its flaws help rather than hurt. Such fronts must run past a hundred billion cycles with lean loss, high block, and no idle draw, a bar that chips and spring switches strain to clear.

The stuff's ragged edges cage copper threads in set paths, which yields fast flips at low energy and thousands of clean rounds. Loss read near zero and block ran high at test pitch. A speed mark from the pair beat all past two-layer switches. A flipped wiring plan tamed self-flips and lifted power room. Full delay and phase kits prove the kit fits real fronts.
pmc-13434714:
He and colleagues studied PGAM5, a mitochondrial protein linked to several cancers, as a driver of acute myeloid leukemia. Its role in this disease had been unclear. Database analysis showed PGAM5 strongly overexpressed in leukemia patients versus healthy controls. High levels were tied to a poor outlook for those patients.

Silencing PGAM5 in leukemia cell models halted the cell cycle and slowed growth. It also sparked programmed cell death in the treated cells. The team traced the effect to sugar fuel use. PGAM5 supports glycolytic flux through the transcription factor HIF-1 alpha and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway in these cells. After silencing, glucose use, ATP output, and lactate output all fell in the leukemia dishes. Restarting the pathway with a PI3K activator partly brought growth back. That backs PGAM5's role and marks it as a possible drug target for leukemia.
pmc-13435414:
Tingting Qiao's team studied PET scan measures in 2026 to predict hidden lymph node spread in untreated ALK-positive lung cancer. They reviewed 157 patients scanned before treatment, measuring tumor size and four metabolic scores from FDG PET/CT, then checked which scores lined up with node spread found at pathology. Spread was present in nearly half the group, and spread cases showed larger tumors with higher scores on every measure.

Tumor size and peak uptake stood out as independent predictors, and combined scores separated cases with spread that scans had missed. Oncologists get a pre-treatment aid for planning surgery and therapy, not a replacement for pathology. The single-marker limits mean the scores should support, not settle, node decisions.
pmc-13435914:
Batista and colleagues published a 2026 trial report on unequal decline in diabetic heart disease. In diabetic cardiomyopathy, high blood sugar slowly weakens the heart muscle. The ARISE-HF trial tested a drug called AT-001 in 625 patients. This report compares how Black, Hispanic, and white patients fared over 15 months.

On placebo, Black and Hispanic patients lost exercise capacity far faster than white patients. Quality-of-life scores also fell hardest among Black patients in the trial. The drug showed a trend toward slowing decline in Black and Hispanic patients. That trend did not reach firm statistical ground in this analysis, though. The authors call the gaps a reason for closer, fairer follow-up care. Exercise testing supplied the main outcome measure across the trial arms.
pmc-13436314:
Huamei Lin's team studied white matter PET signal in 2026 as a marker across the Alzheimer continuum, using 672 participants from a U.S. initiative and two Chinese cohorts. White matter florbetapir uptake is often dismissed as noise, yet its biology was unclear. The team tracked normal-appearing white matter retention over time, linked it to blood and spinal fluid markers, cognition, and lecanemab treatment effects.

Retention rose in preclinical stages and leveled in symptomatic stages. It predicted cognitive decline on its own, tracked tau markers, and fell after lecanemab. With cortical PET, it lifted amyloid detection accuracy to ninety-two percent. Alzheimer teams get a dynamic white matter marker for early detection, prognosis, and treatment monitoring, pending wider replication.
pmc-13436414:
Chunlin Feng questions the fold change math in a study of CMY-219, an enzyme that resists a paired antibiotic, in 2026. The study had reported a twenty seven fold rise for avibactam and a four thousand fold rise for cloxacillin. Feng divides the printed values to check both claims.

Avibactam values of 9,900 and 400 nanomolar give a factor near twenty five, not twenty seven. Cloxacillin values of 22,000 and 3.7 give a factor near 5,946, far above four thousand. Exact ratios matter for computer docking work, Feng notes. The letter asks the authors to show their method.
pmc-13437614:
Yana Wang and colleagues interviewed nurses about change fatigue, the weariness building when health reforms arrive one after another without pause. Surveys can count the problem but miss how it feels. Their 2026 study held deep, semi-structured talks with seventeen clinical nurses from December 2025 to February 2026. A classic seven-step reading method distilled the talks into four themes.

Nurses described bodily and mental strain: poor sleep, low mood, and running on empty. Many triggers fed it, from shifting rules and new computer systems to training piled atop full wards. The harm spread beyond the nurse, touching care quality, family life, and the wish to leave the job. Coping took many shapes, from leaning on colleagues to quietly lowering effort. The authors advise managers to track fatigue as reforms roll out, to stage changes with breathing room, and to fund real support rather than praise alone.
pmc-13437714:
Faareha Mazhar and colleagues measured how nickel and zinc ions grip fragments of tau, a protein that steadies nerve cell scaffolding and clumps in Alzheimer's disease. Metals may help drive that clumping, and tau's histidine and cysteine sites are likely handholds. Their 2026 study built five short tau pieces, some with one grip site, one a mutant, and one with both, then tracked binding with acidity measures and light spectroscopy.

Nickel took different holds by piece, favoring the cysteine sulfur in the combined fragment. Zinc's grip on that same two-site fragment grew much stronger than on single-site pieces, since the peptide could wrap the ion with two anchors. Such details matter: the form a metal takes at body acidity shapes whether it stays harmless or seeds aggregation. They stop at chemistry: no cells or animals were tested, so the step from binding to brain harm remains to be shown.
pmc-13438114:
Jinseob Lee and colleagues taught a deep learning system to read faint single-molecule glow signals human-designed rules cannot sort. Fluorescence imaging tracks single proteins by light, yet distinct events often produce near-identical brightness traces. Their 2026 study fed the network short three-dimensional image sequences, tiny blocks of space-time, and let it hunt for hidden patterns without built-in physics rules or hand-made features.

The system learned to tell true binding from stray, nonspecific sticking with accuracy up to ninety-seven percent, and kept that skill across data from different days. It also followed DNA being built in real time, sensing tiny changes in distance between a glowing tag and the growing strand's end, a feat beyond standard analysis. They pitch the approach as a way to widen single-molecule imaging, including minimal labels or unlabeled targets.
pmc-13438314:
Cheng-Wei Lu and colleagues tested birch sap rich in polysaccharides against acute seizures in rats. The sap fraction had already been measured as mostly small sugar chains. Rats received it by mouth for seven days before kainic acid, a chemical that reliably triggers seizures. Their 2026 study tracked behavior, brain waves, and blood flow during attacks, then read brain tissue for damage, inflammation, barrier leaks, and glutamate handling.

The higher sap dose calmed seizures clearly, cutting convulsion scores and spiking on brain wave traces. Blood flow dips during attacks were softened, and neurons in cortex and hippocampus survived better. A master inflammatory pathway was dialed down, and the cytokine spill fell with it. Glutamate balance righted, as clearance machinery rose and release machinery fell. The authors present the sap fraction as a natural candidate, while noting rat work is a long road from a human epilepsy drug.
pmc-13438714:
Lulu Jin and colleagues built a hybrid nanoparticle that hunts and dismantles endotoxin, the bacterial poison tipping infections into organ failure. Endotoxin, a fat-and-sugar molecule from the coats of Gram-negative bacteria, fires the immune system at vanishingly small doses. Their 2026 design borrows a plant protein that recognizes the poison with rare precision.

Tiny vesicles from the plant carry that protein, called LORE, on their surface, where it grabs endotoxin out of the mix. Fused cerium-based nanozymes then do the demolition, snipping the poison's phosphate groups and sugar bonds in its toxic core. Tests showed the paired action calming inflammation both locally and across the body. The authors frame the chimera as a biocompatible detox route with real translational promise. More broadly, they pitch the pattern, a specific catcher welded to a chemical wrecker, as a template for clearing other stubborn toxins.
pmc-13439014:
Çiçek and colleagues test whether technology addiction predicts visual problems in young teenagers, in a 2026 multicentre case-control study in primary care. The study included 585 students in grades 5 through 8 at three randomly selected public middle schools. Forty-seven students with diagnosed visual impairment or corrective lenses formed the case group; the other 538 students without visual problems served as controls. Interviews gathered screen habits and scores on a technology addiction scale.

Students with visual problems scored significantly higher on total technology addiction and on every subdimension: social media, instant messaging, online gaming, and website browsing. Longer daily screen time and irregular sleep traveled with higher addiction levels. Girls scored higher on messaging and website use, boys higher on gaming. Statistical modeling found gaming duration and total addiction score significantly predicted visual problems. Çiçek recommends school health services treat heavy gaming as a flag for eye checks.
pmc-13439314:
Voss Neal and colleagues follow language recovery after a stroke in the brain's left half, asking whether shrinkage of the untouched right half matters, in a 2026 study. Many survivors keep declining slowly, which may reflect a minority facing fresh degenerative disease. The team studied 72 adults with MRI scans taken soon after stroke and again six or twelve months later. Naming skill was tracked with the Boston Naming Test, a standard picture-naming check.

Bigger strokes tracked with faster shrinkage on the injured side, but not with shrinkage on the right side. Faster right-side shrinkage instead tracked with poorer naming recovery over the year. Shrinkage on the injured side showed no clear tie to recovery. The authors suggest that right-side volume loss signals a separate disease process underway, one that could flag patients who need closer monitoring and support.
pmc-13439714:
Schacherer reflected in 2026, on receiving the Genetics Society of America Medal, on a career spent asking why no two living things are quite alike. The award honors mid-career geneticists, and Schacherer was cited for work on population genomics in yeast, the genetic layout of complex traits. The evolution of yeast mitochondrial genomes, plus leadership of the 1000 Yeast Genomes Project and training of young scientists.

Writing in the first person, Schacherer traces the question from childhood curiosity about variation in plants, animals, and people to study at the Louis Pasteur University in France. Admiration for the founders of genetics, who built the field's frame from natural diversity without knowing DNA existed, runs through the account. The yeast genome project is presented as a reference frame for studying diversity and domestication, the shaping of wild species by human use, across a whole species.
pmc-13440014:
Gabriela Pacheco Carniel's team linked discrimination to eating behaviors in 2026 among 1,502 Brazilian undergraduates in Porto Alegre. Discrimination may shape eating through stress pathways, yet intersectional patterns were little studied. Food approach and avoidance scores from a validated questionnaire were modeled against self-reported discrimination by weight, race, gender, and sexual orientation, alone and in sixteen combined strata.

Weight plus sexual orientation, weight plus gender, and weight plus race showed the highest food approach scores, while sexual orientation plus gender raised avoidance and weight-linked strata lowered it. Weight discrimination sat at the center of both patterns. Campus health teams get an intersectional map for eating support that must address stigma, not only nutrition.
pmc-13441714:
Hongzhi He and colleagues compare treatment strategies for early oesophageal cancer that pathology flags as high risk, pooling studies in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Endoscopic resection can remove superficial cancers, yet tissue checks sometimes reveal traits tied to lymph node spread or return. What to do next, surgery, combined approaches, or other therapy, lacked randomised proof. Searches across four databases to December 2025 found thirty-four studies for the network.

Resection followed by oesophagectomy, full removal of the gullet, gave the most favourable estimates against surgery alone. Gains were clearest for disease-specific and recurrence-free survival, with overall survival pointing the same way short of significance. No other strategy separated clearly from surgery alone. Checks for inconsistency were mostly clean. The authors read the combined route as promising for surgical candidates, while noting that selected retrospective patients limit the claim.
pmc-13441814:
Xiaoling Wu and colleagues trace a molecular route by which acupuncture may ease polycystic ovary syndrome, linking needle treatment to tiny RNA parcels in a 2026 study. The flagged enzyme ran high in the syndrome model, and forcing it higher triggered ferroptosis and slowed granulosa cell growth, an effect a ferroptosis blocker reversed. Four weeks of acupuncture improved ovary structure and egg maturation in rats while normalising the enzyme and death markers. Treated animals' follicle fluid vesicles carried extra miR-873-5p, a small RNA that parcels delivered into granulosa cells to dial the enzyme down. Blocking that RNA erased the benefit.
pmc-13441914:
Gustavo Donoso and colleagues survey future animal professionals across Latin America about pig welfare, reporting in 2026. Universities in the region are expanding welfare teaching, yet student views were little documented. An online survey reached 216 veterinary and animal science students in Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, and Honduras. Clustering sorted respondents by how much they valued welfare, how much they valued welfare education, and how confident they felt raising pig welfare issues.

Three groups emerged from the answers. Every group agreed that animal welfare matters, which set a shared floor. Groups diverged on the worth of swine welfare teaching and on confidence to speak and act on pig issues. Where students got their information predicted group membership in risk analysis. The authors offer universities a map of where teaching lands well and where confidence still lags, plus directions for sharpening curricula.
pmc-13443214:
George S Liu and colleagues present a 2026 hearing study that scores brainstem responses to single sounds, a feat long blocked because each trial's signal hides in noise. Their method combines single-trial amplitude with similarity to a template, defining detection thresholds from the spread of individual scores rather than from averaged waves.

Combined scores gave lower detection thresholds than amplitude alone and let the team rank above-threshold hearing across subjects. Strikingly, some subjects with normal average thresholds still showed above-threshold deficits, a gap the usual test misses. Clinics gain a finer hearing check, though larger patient trials must confirm the method before routine use.
pmc-13443314:
Yong Song and colleagues compare how yoga and Wuqinxi spread as health habits in a 2026 study. Yoga roams the world, while Wuqinxi, a Chinese five-animal routine, stays more regional at grass roots. Talks with studio heads and teachers shaped a survey that drew 389 valid replies, split 210 for yoga and 179 for Wuqinxi.

A five-part talk frame, who says what through which path to whom, guided the models. Content range showed the strongest tie to spread success, with a weight of 0.6464 in their model. Teacher skill came next, then venue quality, then modern paths. Buying acts carried part of each path's force. Gains from teachers, content, and paths ran stronger for Wuqinxi. The authors offer the frame for health habit campaigns.
pmc-13445514:
Abdus Sattar and colleagues ask why fat stem cells from one donor build bone well while cells from another lag, in a 2026 lab study. Such cells are easy to harvest and prized for bone repair, yet donor-to-donor swings block standard use. The team paired bone-building tests with measures of cell metabolism and donor traits.

Cells came from twenty-six donors and grew under bone-forming conditions for two weeks. Bone cues switched on across donors, with a late metabolic stamp: lower fuel uptake per cell and stronger charge across the power plant membrane. Early metabolic reads failed to predict later mineral build-up, while late activity linked in reverse to calcium laid down. Donor age, weight, and blood sugar showed no link to bone outcomes.
pmc-13445814:
Yikuan Yang and Mingli Song present a 2026 interview-based study of nine upper-school students with special school needs in reduced-size classrooms in Norway, taking on deficit views of separate settings. Through in-depth talks and theme-based analysis, the team caught how learners felt fitting in, teacher bonds, and well-being.

pmc-13451314:

pmc-13481614:

pmc-13482814:
Tang and colleagues measure how much city greenery cools the air in 2026 by pairing weather stations across three Chinese megacity regions, Beijing, Shanghai, and the Pearl River Delta cluster. pmc-13483414:

pmc-13483914:

pmc-13484914:

pmc-13485214:

pmc-13486514:

pmc-13486914:

pmc-13487914:

pmc-13488014:

pmc-13488214:

pmc-13490414:

pmc-13490514:

Microscopy and spectroscopy confirmed the molded coating formed correctly on the crystal surface. pmc-13490614:

pmc-13491614:

pmc-13491914:

pmc-13493814:

pmc-13493914:

Plumbing geometry, the authors conclude, is not decoration; it shapes the statistics forecasters rely on.
pmc-13494114:

pmc-13495114:

pmc-13495214:

pmc-13495314:

pmc-13495414:

pmc-13495514:

pmc-13496514:

pmc-13500614:

pmc-13500714:

pmc-13501714:

pmc-13501814:

pmc-13503814:

pmc-13504214:

pmc-13504814:

pmc-13505114:

pmc-13505514:

pmc-13505614:

pmc-13506114:

pmc-13507114:

pmc-13507214:

pmc-13508414:

pmc-13508514:

pmc-13509014:

pmc-13510914:

pmc-13512814:
Kaixiang Lin and colleagues report an insect study, published in 2026. It covers how the fall armyworm moth picks one gene segment version. The gene makes a chloride channel. Several insecticides target that channel. Its exon 3 comes in three forms. The forms are mutually exclusive. The rules for choosing between them were unknown.

The team worked in a moth cell system. They used shortened test genes. They measured the three variants across life stages. They deleted or swapped gene regions to locate control elements. One candidate control region sits inside an intron. Another sits inside the exon itself. Both affect inclusion of the 3B form. This offers entry points for future pest-control ideas based on splicing.
pmc-13516514:
Piyanut Xuto and colleagues tracked belly fat measures in Thai women through pregnancy and after birth, split by pre-pregnancy body mass index. The split used the Asian cut-off of 23, below the standard 25, because risk rises earlier in Asian bodies.

Two separate groups totalled 192 women: 110 followed from week 12 of pregnancy and 82 followed from delivery to week 24. Women above the cut-off started with clearly higher waist-to-height ratios and arm sizes than those below it. After birth, the below-cut-off group returned under the 0.50 waist-to-height line by week 8, while the higher group stayed above it at week 24. Xuto offers the 2017–18 data as a baseline for Thailand's later adoption of the lower cut-off in pregnancy care.
pmc-13516714:
Narayanaswamy Venketasubramanian and four colleagues pool trial evidence on NeuroAiD, a natural product sold as MLC601 or MLC901, for stroke recovery in a 2026 meta-analysis. Drugs that aid rehabilitation after ischaemic stroke are scarce. The team gathered randomised trials comparing the product with placebo or standard care. Six papers covering seven trials fed the analysis, with about fifteen hundred patients scored for daily function and over seventeen hundred for movement.

Recovery favoured the product at one month and stayed ahead at six and twelve months, with gains lasting up to two years. Movement scores improved too, most strongly in the first two months. Patients with moderately severe strokes gained the most. Reports described the product as safe and well tolerated alongside standard care. The authors support starting it early with rehabilitation, while noting two trials carried unclear bias risk.
pmc-13518314:
Wilbur Hudson leads a nine-author push to spot drug-resistant staph in twenty minutes in a 2026 study. Standard resistance testing takes two to three days, leaving doctors guessing at the first antibiotic. Infrared spectroscopy reads a bacterium's chemical fingerprint, and earlier work separated resistant from sensitive Staph aureus after an hour or two of drug exposure. This team asked whether twenty minutes suffices.

Seven strains bathed in weak ampicillin while spectra were taken at set marks. Models built on a few laser-picked bands classified strains with about ninety-one percent accuracy at twenty minutes, holding under the harshest test, leaving one strain out entirely. The telling bands mapped to wall-building chemistry, and microscopes confirmed walls thickening and breaking in sensitive strains only. Hudson's team calls it proof of concept for near-bedside resistance answers.
pmc-13518914:
Erik Koppert, Roya Zarmehr Zamin, Suyeon Lee, and Kyu-Ho Yi run a 2026 pilot study on whether an injectable hyaluronic acid complex can shrink enlarged facial pores. Pores widen as skin loses collagen, elastin, and its own hyaluronic acid with age. The product, Hybrid Cooperative Complex, blends high and low weight forms of the acid to remodel skin rather than fill it.

Ten healthy adults received two sessions under a standard point protocol, with photos and rating scales tracked to day 180. Pore refinement peaked around day 120 for most participants, then partly faded, though skin stayed better than baseline. Koppert and colleagues suggest pore change could time maintenance visits, pending larger controlled trials.
pmc-13520314:
Ruo-fei Jia and colleagues describe in 2026 a rescue method for a side branch of a heart artery that closes suddenly after a stent is placed in the main vessel. When normal rewiring fails, their method borrows a technique from blocked-artery work and passes under the stent layer.

Among 9,832 procedures from 2019 to 2023, only 15 patients needed the rescue approach. Flow was restored in every case, and a flow measure called QFR averaged 0.91 after treatment, above the set safety cut-off. No perforation or trapped device occurred. Because cases were few and highly selected, the report suits experienced centres facing the same emergency.
pmc-13521014:
Ayano Sugiyama-Finnis and colleagues compare in 2026 how engineered chimeric antigen receptors switch on different immune cell types grown from blood stem cells. Receptor therapy succeeded first in T cells, while designs tuned for other lineages may behave unevenly across cell families.

Stem-derived T cells, natural killer cells and myeloid cells activated across several receptor designs, whereas B cells responded only to certain designs. Gene programmes showed lineage as the dominant influence, with design tuning growth, inflammation and cytokine signals inside each lineage. Single-cell tracking linked design choices to downstream programmes. Small group sizes make the work exploratory, yet useful for tailoring future cell therapies.
pmc-13523214:
Deborah Ekusai Sebatta leads a team studying ownership of genomic data in Uganda in a 2026 qualitative study. The team interviewed forty-nine people, including researchers, ethics members, lawyers, community advisers, and regulators. Four discussion groups were held with study participants and caretakers. A lens focused on colonial power was used to surface power gaps in cross-border research.

Six concerns emerged: weak regulation, limited access to shared data, unclear ownership, missing benefit-sharing rules, disputed rights over ideas, and deep power gaps. Many participants believed northern partners owned the data, a belief that eroded community trust. Ugandan researchers disagreed among themselves about ownership versus simply keeping the data, and called for co-ownership. The authors conclude that current rules mirror colonial patterns and hurt local researchers and participants.
pmc-13523314:
Esra Zehra Biçer Özdemir and Melih Gaffar Gözükara examine at-fault crash involvement among motorcycle couriers in Ankara, Türkiye, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Three hundred seventy-two working couriers recruited through networks completed an electronic questionnaire covering employment model, working conditions, crash history, mental health, risky riding, and musculoskeletal symptoms. The outcome was a self-reported at-fault crash in the previous year.

Nearly four in five couriers reported at least one such crash, a strikingly high share. Company-employed and self-employed couriers had higher odds than freelancers. Repeated non-collision falls showed the strongest association, while bad weather and owning the motorcycle also raised odds. Heavy traffic exposure and risky riding scores did not remain significant. The authors argue that working conditions and employment structures deserve attention alongside rider behavior.
pmc-13524914:
Zhu and co-authors explored in 2026 how acetylation of proteins other than histones shapes cancer behavior, working across many tumor types and focusing on colon adenocarcinoma. Acetylation is a chemical tag that changes how proteins act, and its non-histone targets are less understood than the histone marks on DNA packaging. The team combined genomic, protein, and single-cell data to build a scoring system.

From the multi-omics analysis they derived a fifteen-gene score, called AIScore, that separated patients into groups with different survival outlooks. Tumors with high scores showed a more immunosuppressive neighborhood, where cancer cells interacted closely with SPP1-positive macrophages, a type of immune cell that can shield tumors. The score tracked prognosis across the pan-cancer data and in colon cancer specifically. The authors propose AIScore as a tool for predicting outcomes and for spotting patients whose tumors resist immune attack.
pmc-13526314:
Arpit and colleagues report a 2026 study from Indore, India, testing a rapid strip test for cryptococcal meningitis, a fungal brain infection that can kill when diagnosis is slow. Sixty spinal fluid samples from suspected cases were checked three ways: ink microscopy, fungal culture, and a lateral flow assay, a strip test that reads antigen, also run on blood serum.

Microscopy never gave a false positive, but it missed many true cases, catching only about six in ten. The strip test performed strongly on both fluid and serum, with good sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values, and it matched culture closely while giving answers at the bedside in minutes. Culture takes days that meningitis patients may not have. A cheap strip that works on serum as well could speed treatment in clinics with thin lab support.
pmc-13527914:
Farida Rendrayani and three colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of training needs among pharmacists in Indonesian primary health centers. The topic was medication therapy management, a structured service that helps patients use long-term medicines well. Six focus groups brought together 32 pharmacists. They were drawn from all 32 provinces of the country.

Participants asked for standardized training built around real daily practice. They wanted content on the chronic diseases they see most often. Distance, cost, patchy internet access, and competing duties stood out as obstacles. Backing from institutions and follow-up after training were seen as supports. The authors suggest weaving such training into continuing professional development. That way the skills would survive in routine care.
pmc-13529714:
Mostafa Y. Nassar and seven colleagues build a sponge-like composite to pull a toxic chemical from water in a 2026 study. The target is 4-nitrophenol, a stubborn industrial pollutant. The sponge joins a charged polymer with activated carbon made from Ficus leaves. Lab tools checked the material's structure and surface. Batch tests then tuned the cleanup settings.

Best results came at neutral pH with a dose of 1.5 grams per liter. Two hours of contact removed about ninety-five percent of the pollutant. Uptake followed patterns for single-layer chemical binding. Capacity reached about sixty-five milligrams per gram of sponge. The material kept over ninety percent removal in real wastewater with rival ions present. The authors call it a cheap, green option. Early column tests and safety screens backed its promise.
pmc-13530214:
Yang Jiao leads a 2026 upgrade of a vision model that spots surface damage on wind turbine blades. Shifting light, cluttered backgrounds, and flaws of many sizes defeat ordinary detectors in real wind farms. Four design changes target those weaknesses inside a popular detection framework.

A new backbone blends local detail with wide scene context, while an attention block in the middle layer sharpens focus on damaged spots. A lighter feature pyramid and a revised scoring loss lift detection of hard cases. On seven flaw types the upgraded model beat its base version and the nearest rival, with the highest recall.
pmc-13530814:
Bram and the PLUTO Study Group present in 2026, as conference poster 16, a prospective check on leg alignment after transphyseal knee ligament reconstruction. The teenagers studied were within two years of finishing growth. This technique threads the graft through the growth plate, which carries a small risk of bending the leg.

The multicenter cohort included 99 patients, evenly split by sex. Alignment films were taken about a year after surgery, and changes were judged against the uninjured leg to cancel out natural growth. Median changes were small on every measure, and no patient developed a leg length difference of a centimeter or more. Still, about a third of patients shifted at least one mechanical axis zone, and roughly one in seven shifted a key angle by five degrees or more. No growth complication required intervention during the year.
pmc-13531814:
Mahdi Aghaalikhani and co-authors present a 2026 case of aggressive bone cancer arising beside a metal rod implanted decades earlier. A 49-year-old man developed thigh pain and swelling near hardware placed in 1990 after an open thigh fracture. Intermittent symptoms began in 2013 and were first treated as chronic bone infection.

Imaging showed a destructive lesion hugging the old fixation site, and open biopsy confirmed high-grade osteosarcoma while cultures stayed negative. Strong chemotherapy plus hip disarticulation cleared the disease, with nine years free of spread. Late pain around old hardware deserves cancer on the checklist.
pmc-13531914:
Omar Alhumaidan leads a 2026 simulation of iron fortification in Saudi flour, testing whether current rules help those short on iron without overloading others. Computer modeling followed world guidance to estimate usual intake by sex, then applied every legal fortification level to see adequacy and excess shift across the population.

Baseline intake averaged about 13 milligrams daily for men and 12 for women. Inadequate intake fell sharply at every level, nearly vanishing at the top level. Exceeding the safe ceiling stayed negligible except slightly at that top level. A middle level near 30 parts per million balanced benefit and safety best.
pmc-13532914:
Alice Zhu and colleagues review in 2026 tools that predict survival for people with gastrointestinal stromal tumours, the most common tumours of their type in the gut. Many scores and calculators exist, yet their quality and accuracy had not been judged as a group. The review found 47 studies, with 38 building tools and 9 testing them.

One calculator from a major cancer centre was tested most often. Its pooled score for telling apart who stayed free of return was solid in outside groups. Readers see which tools have real outside proof and where reporting still falls short for clinical use.
pmc-13534214:
Pirollo and colleagues put essential oils under the microscope, literally, to see how plant extracts kill a costly fish parasite. Sparicotyle chrysophrii is a flatworm that clamps onto the gills of gilthead sea bream, a Mediterranean aquaculture staple, and chemical treatments face resistance and residue concerns. Their 2026 in vitro study bathed adult parasites in five oils across a range of strengths, then examined the damage with scanning electron microscopy and tissue sectioning.

Cinnamon, oregano, and thyme oils, plus a commercial blend, killed every parasite within an hour at the top concentration tested. Microscopy showed why: the worm's outer skin, the tegument that protects it and feeds it, eroded, wrinkled deeply, and tore. Its attachment clamps let go, with damage worsening by dose and time even below lethal levels. Inside, tissues degenerated into vacuolated, disorganised remnants, suggesting membrane disruption and osmotic collapse.
pmc-13534414:
Arkadiusz Rychlik presents in 2026 RimNet, a sound-based deep learning tool for finding defects in aluminium wheel rims. Workshop checks today rely mostly on eyes and touch, so hidden flaws can be missed. The method strikes each rim once, turns the sound into time-frequency images, and lets a network judge condition.

Training used 930 labelled examples spanning shape faults, material defects, and sound rims. File-level accuracy reached high levels, and no wheel was misjudged under the test protocol. Wrong calls carried wider uncertainty, and a companion app gives live results with confidence scores for each rim.
pmc-13534614:
Georgios Kirtsanis and colleagues classify in 2026 bacterial simulants of biological warfare agents using heat-breakdown gas analysis plus deep learning. Fast, accurate identification protects public health, yet bacterial chemistry is highly complex. Eight species at three strengths were analysed, producing four forms of data from each run.

Two-dimensional chromatograms paired with advanced deep networks gave the best accuracy and F1 scores across tasks. Models trained on some classes were also tested on unseen classes to check generalisation. Detection limits were mapped for every setup, and the dataset was released publicly for reuse.
pmc-13534714:
Eduardo Morello and colleagues develop in 2026 a combined psychological risk score and test its link to sports injuries in football players. Stress, anxiety, perfectionism, coping, and sleep can all shape injury risk beyond body measures alone. A total of 281 players aged 16 to 32 completed standard questionnaires at season start.

Emotional symptoms and sleep were tracked monthly, and club medical staff logged time-loss injuries all season. Higher combined scores linked to higher injury rates across follow-up. Patterns differed by sex, with stress control standing out in males and depressive symptoms in females.
pmc-13535514:
Je Hyun Chin and colleagues studied how calcium deposits and surgery choice affect return of ductal carcinoma in situ. Published in 2026, the study looked back at 365 patients with DCIS treated at a Seoul clinic between 1997 and 2020. DCIS, an early breast lesion that has not spread, raises worries of both too little and too much treatment, so risk sorting matters.

Tumors that did not respond to hormones and those with extra HER2 ran older, more calcium-rich, and higher grade. For return in the same breast, full breast removal and wider clear margins each cut risk on their own, a result matched checks backed up. For return in the other breast, calcium deposits linked to better results on their own, most of all in hormone-driven disease. The authors argue that calcium deposits mean different things by outcome and tumor type, urging care tuned to each tumor's biology.
pmc-13536614:
Douglas A. Nelson and colleagues test in 2026 how short amyloid-beta exposure disrupts insulin signalling in human blood-brain barrier cells. Brain insulin resistance and vessel problems appear early in late-onset Alzheimer disease, and the barrier is a key insulin entry point. Two cell models were exposed to amyloid forms for one hour, then given insulin.

In the main cell line, one amyloid form blunted insulin-driven Akt activation and flipped a second signal from calming to mild stimulation. The other form lowered resting Akt only. Findings point to early barrier-level targets for deeper study of Alzheimer mechanisms.
pmc-13536714:
Yue Wang and colleagues ask joint replacement patients what they want from recovery exercise in a 2026 survey at a Chinese hospital. A total of 295 people who had a first hip or knee replacement compared paired exercise options that varied in pain level, staff presence, intensity, frequency, and session length. Choices were made from the second day after surgery, once recovery exercise had begun.

Pain during exercise mattered most by a wide margin, with mild or moderate pain strongly preferred over severe pain. Having a health professional present ranked next, followed by exercise intensity. How often sessions ran and how long they lasted mattered much less. Patterns were broadly similar across age and sex groups. The authors advise programs that control pain well, include professional guidance, and keep intensity moderate to support lasting participation.
pmc-13536814:
Shota Kaburaki and colleagues pilot a timing question for a targeted drug in a rare vessel inflammation disease in a 2026 single-center study. Thirty patients newly diagnosed with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis started steroid treatment. The pilot compared patients who began mepolizumab, a drug that lowers steroid need, within thirty days against those who had not begun it by that point. Steroid exposure over the next year was the main measure.

Only six patients started the drug early, against twenty-one in the comparison group at the thirty-day mark. Later oral steroid totals ran much lower in the early group, as did daily doses at one year. Disease activity scores reached zero in both groups by three months. The authors stress the small, nonrandom design and call the findings early clues only.
pmc-13538214:
Angela Ammirabile and colleagues test whether scan texture analysis improves survival prediction for bowel cancer spread to the liver in a 2026 study. Surgery plus drug therapy can cure some patients, yet standard scores predict survival poorly. Records for 306 patients who had liver surgery between 2010 and 2020 supplied pre-surgery scans. Computer features from tumors and a thin rim around them were added to clinical models.

Clinical factors alone predicted survival modestly. Added scan features helped slightly in the full group and helped more when scans fell within thirty days of surgery. The best model combined clinical, tumor, and rim features, beating established scores by a wide margin. Five-year survival in the group was near forty-one percent. The authors stress short scan-to-surgery gaps for best accuracy.
pmc-13538414:
Shambhavi Shetye and colleagues examine anemia patterns in young children with inherited energy metabolism errors in a 2026 forward-looking study. These disorders impair energy production across organs, and iron shortage may worsen features. Red cell measures in children up to three years old were compared with age-matched controls, including a ratio index used to hint at anemia cause. Blood count networks were also mapped for pattern differences.

Anemia appeared often in both groups with no clear gap between them. The ratio index ran high in most children in both groups, again without a clear gap. Network maps still showed distinct clustering in the disorder group, and white cell shares ran slightly higher without reaching firm significance. The authors call the network findings exploratory only.
pmc-13538514:
Riku Hirano, Tomohiro Kizuka, and Seiji Ono study confidence and speed judgment in side vision in a 2026 experiment. Objects look slower away from center gaze, possibly because fuzzy input leans on expectations favoring slow motion. Observers compared a moving test patch against a steady reference at two side positions across a speed range, rating confidence after each choice. Pupil size was recorded as a possible bodily sign of confidence.

Average confidence ran lower at the farther side position, matching blurrier input there. Modeling linked lower confidence to slower felt motion and wider uncertainty. Stronger confidence also came with larger brief pupil swelling. The authors argue that felt certainty actively shapes speed perception rather than merely reporting it, tying sense data and self-knowledge together.
pmc-13538614:
Şenay Çaylan and colleagues rank what helps staff adapt at work in a 2026 study. A learnability score bundles mental flexibility, a habit of asking questions, openness, and reflective learning as drivers of adapting. Expert views fed a fuzzy scoring system that weighs many factors at once and ranks plans. Rankings were then stress-tested across varied scenes for stability.

Asking questions and mental flexibility came out as the strongest parts of the score. The authors read the pattern as proof that sharp thinking and an open mind power learning at work. Rankings held steady across the test scenes, backing the method's soundness. Plain guidance follows for bosses who must design change plans on firm ground rather than guesswork.
pmc-13538714:
Wei Gao and colleagues build a multimodal learning system for early fault warning in warp knitting machines in a 2026 study. Vision checks spot defects only once fabric damage shows, too late for prevention. The framework fuses sensor streams and fabric images into one shared code space, learns process patterns by rebuilding hidden states, and fabricates extra examples of rare faults to fix class imbalance.

On ten thousand hours of real factory data, the system beat rival baselines across metrics with a high combined score and detection in about a tenth of a second. Faults were flagged before visible defects emerged. The authors offer the design as a practical route to smart maintenance in high-speed textile production.
pmc-13539714:
Rui Zhang and colleagues build a scan-based risk score to forecast immune drug outcomes in advanced lung squamous cancer in a 2026 look-back study. Forecasting who stays free of spread on immune drugs remains hard in this subtype. Baseline combined scans from 129 patients yielded image features. Those passing repeat checks were cut down through staged models into a risk score, checked against a deep learning rival.

The score split patients into risk groups, with the high-risk group facing over fourfold hazard of spread. Accuracy held fairly steady from one to three years, hinting the score captures starting risk rather than shifting calls over time. The score held up on its own in full models. The deep network performed worse. The authors offer the tool as scan-based support for treatment choices, pending larger testing.
pmc-13539914:
Xiao Lin leads a 2026 multi-omics study hunting for genes that push artery plaques toward their dangerous late stage by ageing the immune cells inside them. Plaques rich in aged macrophages, the scavenger cells of the blood vessel wall, tend to progress.

Working from public gene datasets, the team narrowed age-related changes to six hub genes, all concentrated in macrophages in single-cell data. One gene, TNFSF13, stood out in cell-talk analyses and sat mainly in the plaque core among fat-filled macrophages. Tests on human coronary artery tissue confirmed higher levels there. The authors name TNFSF13 a driver of macrophage ageing in plaque growth, pending direct experiments.
pmc-13540814:
Sinem Yalnızoğlu Çaka, Sümeyra Topal, and Gülbu Tanrıverdi listen, in a 2026 qualitative study, to mothers describing life for their young children after the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes in Türkiye. Children aged three to six are especially exposed to disaster harm because of their stage of development.

Interviews with twenty-one mothers who stayed in the affected region produced three themes. Daily life broke down around sleep, eating, clinginess, withdrawal, and play that replayed the trauma. Illness and hygiene needs met blocked access to medicines and routine vaccines. Faith, family networks, community help, and traditional practices carried families through. The authors call for child-centred, culturally aware disaster care.
pmc-13543614:
In 2026, Chengdong Ma and colleagues published a study unravelling a three-step gene cascade that times flowering in Prunus mume, the ornamental and fruit tree known as mei. Flowering control in woody perennials differs from annual plants and matters for breeding. The team characterised a transcription factor, PmbHLH130, whose levels answer day length and which concentrates in leaves, then mapped what switches it on and what it switches on in turn.

Inserted into a model plant, extra copies of the gene brought flowering forward, proving its promoter role. The factor sits downstream of the plant's internal clock proteins and of another regulator, PmIDD5, and it directly activates PmCOL5, a known flowering gene. The chain from clock to cascade to bloom gene, the authors conclude, gives breeders named handles for adjusting when this prized tree flowers.
pmc-13545114:
Alexander Nasr and colleagues published a 2026 study defining drug-level targets during anti-TNF induction therapy in children with Crohn's disease, aiming at deep remission, where symptoms quiet and the bowel lining heals. Seventy young patients starting infliximab or adalimumab at four centres gave blood and stool samples across a year. Drug trough levels, total exposure, and clearance were estimated with population models, then matched against who reached deep remission.

Just under half the children, 48.6 percent, reached it, with no advantage for either drug. Clear infliximab trough thresholds marked the goal at successive visits, and higher overall exposure helped for both medicines, while fast infliximab clearance predicted failure. Older age, low albumin, higher weight index, and inflammation markers forecast that fast clearance at baseline. The authors supply concrete numbers clinicians can dose toward, rather than waiting to see who responds.
pmc-13546514:
Anqi Liu and co-authors engineered in 2026 tiny packages called extracellular vesicles to regrow blood vessels inside damaged tooth pulp. Restoring a blood supply is the hard part of regenerating pulp, the living tissue at a tooth's center. Their vesicles carried a vessel-promoting protein, EphrinB2, and wore a DNA tag that homes to the cells lining blood vessels.

In cell tests, the targeted vesicles boosted vessel cell growth, movement, and tube formation more than untargeted ones, working through a known signaling route. Packed into a soft gel and placed in root canals, they released slowly and, after transplant in mice, supported well-vascularized pulp-like tissue. The work lays groundwork for treatments that rebuild living teeth rather than simply filling them.
pmc-13546714:
Muhammad Gunawan and a large team compared in 2026 two freezing mixtures for preserving Bali bull semen, the standard egg-yolk-based extender and a newer one built from tiny fat bubbles called nano-liposomes. Semen from nine bulls was frozen in each mixture and thawed for checks on movement, survival, membrane health, and DNA damage, with a computer system tracking swimming patterns.

Both mixtures preserved quality well, with no clear differences on the main measures, and swimming patterns stayed in the desired range. The liposome mixture gave more even results from sample to sample. The authors favor it as an alternative because its recipe is clearer, more consistent, and avoids the biosecurity worries of egg yolk.
pmc-13547414:
Muhammad Haris Saleem, Arslan Ahmed Amin, and Turki Alsuwian designed in 2026 a fault-tolerant controller for wireless vehicle charging. Such a system can stumble when its power converter fails or the charging coils misalign. Their design adds spare switches and a neural network trained with physics equations inside it, which watches converter signals and directs a controller that spots and isolates faults in real time.

In tests, the system kept current tracking accurate, held its fault signal inside safe bounds even when parameters drifted, and settled in about a fifth of a second after disturbances. Steady-state error fell to a small fraction of rival methods. The authors present the scheme as insurance for reliable contactless charging on future electric vehicles.
pmc-13548614:
Qinyue Su and colleagues build and test a prediction chart for serious kidney outcomes in sepsis patients whose kidneys have already failed, in a 2026 multicenter study. The outcome bundle, called major adverse kidney events within thirty days, captures death, dialysis need, and lasting kidney damage. Records from eight Shanghai hospitals formed the building set, while patients from an earlier period at another hospital served for outside checking.

Seven routine indicators survived the selection process, including how long the kidney injury lasted, its stage, combined antibiotic use, nutritional risk, peak heart rate, early fluid balance, and coma score. The chart discriminated well in the building set and acceptably in the outside set, with charts of predicted versus actual risk lining up sensibly. The authors offer it as an early warning tool to flag patients for closer kidney protection.
pmc-13548714:
Dongping Mo and colleagues test whether an unusual white blood cell type can reveal breast cancer that has reached the armpit lymph nodes, in a 2026 study. The cell type is read together with routine blood markers. Node status steers treatment, yet confirmation still relies on invasive biopsy. Analyzing blood from 184 patients, the team measured low-density neutrophils, cells linked to tumor support, and screened a basket of inflammation and tumor markers.

The unusual neutrophils ran higher in patients whose cancer had spread to nodes. Statistical selection kept seven candidate markers, and five, including the neutrophils, two tumor markers, and two inflammation ratios, independently predicted node spread. A scoring chart built on them performed respectably and held up in an outside patient group. The authors suggest the blood panel could help flag node involvement before surgery.
pmc-13551714:
Rebecca H. Correia, leading twelve colleagues, published a 2026 mixed-methods study of episodic virtual primary care in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, Canada. Such services offer quick online visits without an ongoing clinician relationship. The team surveyed adult users about access, medical complexity, and experience, then analyzed free-text answers alongside the numbers, comparing people with and without a regular clinician.

Most users felt virtual care met their needs, yet survey scores looked rosier than written comments. People lacking a regular clinician, and those with more complex needs, rated experiences less favorably and more often sought help for chronic problems or prescription renewals. Some disliked the technology and preferred in-person care, so the authors call virtual care a partial gap filler.
pmc-13551814:
Yeshen Zhang, leading eleven colleagues, published a 2026 national cohort study of a combined inflammation and insulin resistance index and death risk in cardiovascular-kidney-liver-metabolic syndrome. The index marries a C-reactive protein and triglyceride-glucose measure with body shape measures. Data came from 14,203 affected adults in a United States survey spanning 1999 to 2018, followed for a median of over eleven years.

The highest quarter of the combined indices carried the lowest survival and raised risks of cardiovascular and overall death in adjusted models reported by the authors. Competing risk analysis, which accounts for other causes of death, confirmed the cardiovascular link. Curve shapes varied between linear and nonlinear across indices, and subgroup checks supported the pattern.
pmc-13551914:
Gadisa Fikadu, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 study of burn care in Harar, eastern Ethiopia. The team reviewed records at a hospital emergency center. All 182 admitted burn patients from June 2021 to June 2024 were included. A set checklist pulled the facts from each chart. The team described injury types and outcomes, then modeled what tied to poor results.

About one fifth of patients had poor outcomes. Burns over thirty percent of the body carried the highest odds of a poor result by far. Care given before hospital arrival also raised the odds. So did having other medical conditions. The team reads early care as a sign of severe injury and referral paths. They urge community burn prevention and sound first aid.
pmc-13554114:
Abdullateef Salisu leads a large team gathering views on mobile nutrition vans serving hard-to-reach parts of Gombe State, Nigeria, in a 2026 study. Poor nutrition still harms many mothers and small children in the north. Thirty mothers joined five group talks after using the service at least three times. Fifteen health workers, chiefs, faith leaders, and programme staff gave separate interviews.

Users and staff agreed the vans eased access by cutting long trips. They credited the service with fewer hospital visits and better health for mothers and children. Fewer birth problems tied to anaemia and better child growth were named. Visits came only every three months, bad roads blocked some trips, and language gaps hurt talks. Staff asked for more visits and better planning.
pmc-13554214:
Nivea Roy leads a seven-author team releasing a public scan set for throat cancer staging in a 2026 study. Research on this cancer lacked shared data, making model results hard to compare. Their set gathers 1,029 CT scans from six collections, all trimmed to the voice box at even spacing. Six deep learning models were then tested on two staging tasks.

A custom three-dimensional model won the early-versus-late staging task, with accuracy near eighty-five percent. The hardest task, spotting the most advanced tumours, tripped every model on pure sensitivity. One larger model recalled such cases best after tuning. Heat maps showed models looking near the cartilage, as doctors would, though overlap stayed modest. Shared data and code aim to make future results comparable.
pmc-13554314:
Mungmee and Punyarat test a simple imaging ratio in this 2026 surgical study of intradural spinal tumors, growths inside the spinal cord's protective sac. They reviewed forty-six adults treated between 2018 and 2024 with hemilaminectomy. That is a bone-sparing operation that opens only one side of the vertebra. For each patient they measured the tumor's occupancy ratio. That is its cross-section against the spinal canal on MRI scans.

The approach worked well overall: surgeons removed tumors completely in 44 of 46 patients, and 80.4 percent improved neurologically by a median follow-up of 27 months, while only two patients worsened. But the fuller the canal, the worse the recovery. In adjusted analysis the occupancy ratio was the sole independent predictor of failing to improve, each unit increase raising the odds of non-improvement by a factor of 1.31 in the model. The authors offer it as an easy preoperative counseling tool needing external validation.
pmc-13555714:
Ian G Bemis leads a seven-author team testing pet cats near California dairy farms hit by bird flu in a 2026 study. The H5N1 virus spread through dairy herds there during 2024 to 2026. Cats are newly recognised hosts, with a high death rate once infected. Twelve cats living within two kilometres of farms gave blood samples.

Three of those cats carried neutralising antibodies, proof of past infection. Living close to dairy farms tied significantly to testing positive. Contaminated raw milk and raw-meat diets are known infection sources for cats. Because cats carry receptors for both bird and human flu, mixed infections could breed new strains. The authors flag cat monitoring as part of outbreak control near farms.
pmc-13555914:
Meiyan Jiang leads a ten-author team adding a helpful fungus to the roots of a medicinal angelica plant in a 2026 study. The plant serves as both medicine and food, and its root-zone bacteria shape its quality. The fungus, a strain of Aspergillus niger, had already raised yields while cutting fertilizer in pots and fields. This study asked how it reshapes the bacteria around the roots.

Treated plants absorbed nutrients better and built up growth hormones in their roots. Helpful Proteobacteria grew more abundant in the root zone. Tests with 832 isolated strains showed the fungus boosted these bacteria through microbe interplay and by changing root secretions. Certain phenolic acids from roots proved to be the key signals. The authors pitch the fungus as a sustainable production strategy.
pmc-13556214:
Jie Li and five colleagues mapped in 2026 how an archaeal cell builds its RNA polymerase, the multi-part machine that reads genes. The archaeal enzyme resembles the main polymerase of complex cells, yet nobody had traced its assembly inside a living cell. Working with the methane-producing archaeon Methanococcus maripaludis, the team combined column separation, native purification, antibody tests, mass spectrometry, and test-tube disassembly.

Assembly turned out to be modular and ordered, passing through five main subcomplexes, with one stable three-part piece marking a directional route. Cells keep the parts in careful balance: forcing extra copies of two small subunits jammed assembly, cut the finished enzyme, and slowed growth. A heat-shock chaperone protein travelled with the subcomplexes and may assist. The framework fills a long gap and mirrors assembly logic seen in more complex cells.
pmc-13558314:
Yunjie Shi and colleagues measured how much extra colon length surgeons can gain while preserving the left colic artery in low rectal cancer operations, publishing the cadaver study in 2026. A tension-free join after removing the rectum is vital, since tight joins leak far more often, yet the length each mobilisation step buys had not been quantified. The team performed standard artery-preserving resections on 18 fresh cadavers and measured gains step by step.

Freeing the splenic flexure added about 6 centimetres, while high ligation of the inferior mesenteric vein added about 14 centimetres, the largest gain with the artery kept. Sacrificing the artery added more, but at the cost of blood supply, and malrotation cut the vein step's gain. Surgeons can use these numbers to plan joins and margins before operating.
pmc-13558614:
Shahgol Rahbari and four colleagues fed broiler chickens in 2026 omega-3 fats to test whether the supplement protects heart and liver under crowded housing. High stocking density stresses fast-growing birds and raises deaths. Their trial placed 420 day-old chicks in a two-by-two design. Standard or dense housing was crossed with a plain diet or one enriched in omega-3. At forty days the team measured organ weights, blood enzymes, tissue structure, deaths, and liver gene activity.

Crowded birds on the enriched diet showed lower heart weight ratios than the other groups, and supplementation cut deaths under both densities. Liver enzyme levels in blood fell with omega-3, lung artery walls stayed thinner in the crowded supplemented group, and heart muscle cells were smallest there. Two fat and sugar handling genes in the liver shifted with diet and density. The authors back omega-3 as a practical shield for intensive production.
pmc-13558714:
Rocky Lai and nine colleagues test tuberculosis vaccine plans in diverse mice. A new tuberculosis vaccine to replace BCG stalls for lack of a mouse model matching human diversity. Their 2026 study uses Collaborative Cross and Diversity Outbred mice, which mirror outbred diversity. It compares two strategies to boost BCG defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

One strategy, BCG::ESX-1Mmar, expresses the esx-1 region of Mycobacterium marinum.
