The other, BCG/ChAd:TB, boosts BCG immunity with a chimp adenovirus vector carrying antigens Ag85A, TB10.4, and RpfB by nose. Both plans protected mouse strains poorly protected by BCG alone. Yet bacterial control did not track with survival, a caution for mouse readouts.
pmc-13560214:
V Donadio and an international expert panel present a shared protocol for detecting phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in skin biopsies, a promising test for Parkinson's disease and related disorders. Their 2026 consensus paper grows out of a November 2024 meeting in Bologna, where top labs weighed methods that vary widely. A Delphi survey settled the disputed points afterward.

Unanimous agreement covered the biopsy technique, the fixative, cryostat sectioning, the staining method, and the use of high-power fluorescence microscopy with marker co-localization. Delphi rounds fixed the open points: sample numbers, section thickness, punch size, best sites when symptoms are one-sided, and how to count the protein load. The panel settled on phosphorylated alpha-synuclein as the optimal marker of misfolded protein in skin. The authors intend the protocol to widen use and carry the test toward everyday practice.
pmc-13563814:
Bruno Sserunkuuma and eight colleagues count how often blood pressure crashes after spinal anaesthesia for caesarean birth at a Ugandan referral hospital, and what predicts the crash. The drop can endanger mother and baby within minutes. Their 2026 cross-sectional study at Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital enrolled every second eligible mother across August to October 2022, reaching 394 women. Records supplied personal, obstetric, and anaesthetic details, and regression sorted the independent drivers.

The crash was the norm, not the exception: 67.5 percent of mothers met the definition. Four factors raised the odds independently: a block reaching above the T6 level, a spinal drug dose over ten milligrams, an emergency rather than planned operation, and skipping a preventive blood-pressure drug. Seven women suffered a dangerously high block. The authors recommend a preventive vasopressor for every caesarean under spinal anaesthesia at their hospital, plus sharper attention to dose and block height.
pmc-13563914:
Naomi Zucker leads a 2026 interview study of staff who treat opioid use disorder with buprenorphine by telehealth in southeast Pennsylvania. Twenty-five prescribers, clinic staff, counselors, program heads, and pharmacists told how remote care compares with in-person visits and which patients it suits.

Most held largely positive views of telehealth for its power to widen access to care. They differed, though, on how such care compares in quality and on how stable a patient should be first. Despite those disputes, most agreed that remote care beats no care at all. The talks give policy makers a grounded view of staff concerns behind telehealth rules.
pmc-13569214:
Shin and colleagues studied in 2026 whether microscope findings from ear swabs match how bad a dog's ear infection looks. Canine otitis externa, meaning inflammation of the outer ear canal, is a common reason for vet visits. The team reviewed 318 dogs seen at a specialist skin service.

Severity scores rose in step with the total microscope score across the cases. Higher counts of round bacteria and rod bacteria each went with worse clinical scores. Scores for Malassezia, a yeast that also infects ears, showed no such link to severity. Dogs whose slides contained neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, had clearly worse severity scores. The authors say swab findings add real information beyond the eye exam, mainly for bacteria and neutrophils.
pmc-13569314:
Caitlin Raymond examines, in a 2026 descriptive cohort study using a large shared health record network, blood clot rates after extracorporeal photopheresis. That is a light-based blood treatment used for graft-versus-host disease and a skin lymphoma. About three thousand patients with no recent clot history were followed for new clots within five and thirty days of the procedure.

Thirty-day vein clot risk was about six percent, with events accumulating gradually rather than clustering right after treatment. Risk ran much higher in graft-versus-host patients than in lymphoma patients, and artery clots were uncommon. The pattern suggests the underlying illnesses, not the procedure itself, drive most risk, though a small procedure effect cannot be ruled out without a comparison group.
pmc-13569414:
Arnas Kunevičius's team reviewed drug and gut-microbe treatments in animal models of autism, in a 2026 systematic review. No drug yet eases autism's core symptoms, and animal studies of new candidates have been hard to compare because methods, measures, and reporting vary widely. The team synthesised 52 studies from 2010 to 2025 that reported behavioural outcomes after drug or gut-microbe treatments.

The drugs spanned oxytocin-related drugs, agents rebalancing brain excitation and inhibition, metabolic drugs, cannabinoids, purine-based treatments, and probiotics, prebiotics, and faecal transplants. Across models, many approaches softened autism-like behaviours through neurotransmission, inflammation, metabolism, or the gut-brain axis. The authors argue for a systemic view of autism biology and standardised preclinical research to bridge the gap to human trials.
pmc-13569814:
Lei Huang and Huachi Li analyze, in a 2026 study combining single-cell and large cohort data, how steroid production inside bladder tumors may drive cancer progression. Gene data came from a small set of tumor and normal samples plus a cancer atlas cohort of about four hundred tumors.

Tumor cells with high steroid pathway activity formed more connections with neighbors, showed stronger stem-like traits, and sat in a quieter immune environment. A risk model built from differing genes predicted patient outlook well. Genes marking high steroid activity also tracked with poorer survival. The work nominates steroid metabolism as both a warning sign and a possible treatment angle in bladder cancer.
pmc-13571714:
Rondón-Carvajal and colleagues published a 2026 case report about one critically ill lung transplant patient. The patient was twenty-two years old and worsened badly in intensive care after the new lungs failed early. Doctors needed lung tissue to learn why, yet standard forceps biopsy often gives tiny crushed samples.

At the bedside, Rondón-Carvajal used cryobiopsy, a method that freezes and pulls out larger, better kept tissue pieces. A thin cryoprobe passed through the airways while a small balloon guarded against bleeding. The sample showed high grade acute cellular rejection, meaning the immune system was attacking the graft strongly. Treatment was stepped up with immune calming therapy, and the patient then improved, though one case cannot prove the method beats forceps biopsy.
pmc-13574714:
Yiqi Zhao, Kyle Hunt, and Jun Zhuang compared Arctic security strategies across ten countries with data, not just narrative. Climate change and geopolitical rivalry have made the Arctic a strategic arena, yet scholarship on national strategies has stayed fragmented and qualitative. Their 2026 study mined 107 policy documents from the eight Arctic states plus observer states China and India, using a human-led, AI-assisted text workflow.

All ten countries agreed broadly on climate and environmental concerns, but diverged sharply on territory and resources: the United States and Russia stressed sovereignty, while Finland advocated demilitarisation. Large states loomed large in others' documents; smaller Arctic states drew less attention. The authors offer the comparison as a foundation for Arctic security governance and policy debate.
pmc-13574914:
Mathias Ausserwinkler leads a 2026 population study on how people with rheumatoid arthritis rate their own health. The data come from the Paracelsus 10,000 study, a large health survey. Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term disease where the immune system attacks the joints.

Among 9,399 people, 293 had doctor-diagnosed arthritis of this type. Poor or very poor health was reported by 55 percent of that group, against 31 percent of others, and the link held after other factors were taken into account. Older age, metabolic syndrome, and smoking tied to worse ratings. Higher activity levels, more schooling, and closer fit to a Mediterranean diet tied to better ratings, pointing to habits care teams can support.
pmc-13576014:
Marlaine Figueroa Gray, Matthew P Banegas, and Nora B Henrikson explore how serious illness puts people's legacy goals at risk in a 2026 interview study. Legacy goals cover how a person hopes to be remembered and what they want to leave behind. Such goals can steer treatment choices, yet care teams rarely ask about them.

The team held hour-long phone interviews with Kaiser Permanente Washington members who had received palliative care in the prior year. Five themes emerged: people actively planned for legacy, illness itself threatened those plans, money and insurance strain loomed large, and patients believed care would improve if teams knew their goals. Participants also wanted a way to share legacy goals with their teams. The authors urge palliative care to ask about legacy directly.
pmc-13576114:
Marina Fassarella and Hauke Smidt ask why gut microbiome science so rarely reaches the clinic, in a 2026 perspective review. Two decades of work have tied gut microbes to many diseases. Yet proven treatments built on that science remain few, despite wide public interest.

The pair review the field's real wins, from stool transplants to diet-based care, then grade the field against standards from translational medicine. Missing pieces include clear staging from lab to population, two-way flow between clinic and laboratory, and design centred on patient needs. Extra hurdles come from the microbiome itself: huge complexity, wide person-to-person variation, and uneven methods. Their proposed framework stresses training researchers in translation and tighter coordination across teams. The authors frame the puzzle as solvable with discipline borrowed from other fields.
pmc-13576614:
Marina Teixeira de Vries Mársico and colleagues analyzed twenty commercial wet cat foods sold in Brazil, covering beef, chicken, and fish flavors. They measured moisture, protein, acidity, fat and protein oxidation, biogenic amines, and trace elements. Moisture ranged widely, and protein content varied from roughly a third to nearly nine tenths of dry matter.

Signs of oxidation appeared in some samples, and histamine, putrescine, and cadaverine pointed to microbial activity or lower-quality raw materials. Mercury turned up in some products, though levels stayed within international reference values. Because cats detoxify poorly through the liver, the authors call for tighter quality checks and routine surveillance of wet pet food.
pmc-13579014:
Thamra Al Ghafri and colleagues make the case for stronger public health expertise in Oman, where clinical careers have clear training ladders but public health roles often do not. Public health work spans six linked skills, from epidemiology and surveillance to health policy, promotion, environmental health, and systems leadership. Recent crises, from COVID-19 and mpox to rising chronic disease and climate risks, have exposed the gap.

The essay draws on models such as the United Kingdom's Faculty of Public Health and regional field epidemiology programs in Saudi Arabia and Egypt. It names familiar barriers, including budgets tilted toward curative care and promotion rules that ignore policy and surveillance work. Accredited specialization, fair pay, and career ladders are presented as the practical route forward.
pmc-13579214:
Weiß and a large team build in 2026 tiny rotors from DNA origami, folded DNA scaffolds, steered by magnets. Magnetic control is attractive for nanorobotics because it works through tissue and ignores chemical signals.

The team attached magnetic nanocubes with strong, directional magnetization to long DNA origami bundles at chosen sites, then filmed and steered hundreds of individual rotors. Under steady fields the rotors clamped into alignment; under rotating fields they turned in step. Varying how many cubes each rotor carried and how far apart they sat changed the twisting force. It reached the range of tens of piconewton nanometers at field strengths below ten millitesla in their microscope measurements of single rotors. Computer simulations of the assemblies reproduced the measured forces and showed the cubes acting collectively rather than independently.
pmc-13580414:
Larissa Lopes Fonseca and colleagues test light based germ killing as a partner to drug care for radiation damaged jaw bone, in a 2026 rat study. Twenty six male rats took a single strong radiation dose to the left jaw, then lost the first molar ten days later. Groups split into no care, drugs alone, light therapy alone, both together, and a non radiated control, though some animals were lost along the way.

Scans, X-rays, and tissue checks told a steady story. Radiated rats left untreated fared worst, with bone form badly broken down. Every care plan improved repair over neglect. The combined plan won across the board, keeping bone layout soundest and new bone growth best organized. The authors back the pairing as a promising shield against the dreaded late injury called osteoradionecrosis.
pmc-13582714:
John Ian Wilzon Dizon and a large team of co-authors ask how student drive builds teamwork skills in health training, in a 2026 study from two Hong Kong universities. Undergraduates from three fields took month long joint modules on fractures or on new respiratory infections. Surveys measured two kinds of drive, for knowledge and for accomplishment, plus faith in the team and four shared practice skills.

Both drives predicted all four skill areas directly. Team faith also predicted every skill area. The split came in the pathway: drive for accomplishment built skills partly through team faith across all four areas. Drive for knowledge mostly worked alone, reaching team mediation in just one area, grasp of roles. Course designers should feed both drives, the authors say, and shape team tasks to honor the difference.
pmc-13585414:
Eva Desbrousses and colleagues report a striking lab curiosity in a young patient with severe aplastic anemia in this 2026 case paper. Aplastic anemia is a bone marrow failure that leaves the blood short of all cell types. Their patient, a 19-year-old woman, was treated with immune-damping drugs plus eltrombopag, a drug that pushes marrow to make more cells.

Blood samples sent to the lab kept arriving with brown serum after spinning, a rare sight that raised fears of blood breakdown inside the vessels. Tests ruled that danger out, with only a mild rise in one pigment measure. Once the drug was stopped, the brown color faded away. The authors explain that eltrombopag itself absorbs visible light, and they flag the effect so labs do not chase a false alarm.
pmc-13587114:
Marta Pirronello and a large team track B cells over four years in people with multiple sclerosis treated with cladribine. Cladribine is a pill taken in two short yearly courses that reshapes the immune system for lasting calm. Their 2026 study followed 36 patients with the relapsing form of the disease, sorting B cells into fine subtypes with high-detail flow methods, and compared samples from untreated patients and healthy donors.

Memory B cells fell hard and stayed low. One subtype, called marginal zone-like, fell deepest of all and was slow to return, while fresh, calmer B cells rebuilt the ranks. Those same cells proved to be the strongest makers of inflammatory signals and of IgM antibodies, and they carried markers for showing fatty antigens to other immune cells. The team frames them as both the drug's prime target and a marker of response.
pmc-13587314:
Fatemeh Kholusi and colleagues check pet birds and their sellers in Isfahan, Iran, for a diarrhea-causing parasite. The parasite, Cryptosporidium, passes between animals and people and can drag on dangerously in those with weak immune systems. Their 2026 study collected 223 samples from pet shops across the city. Most came from ornamental birds, and thirty from the people selling them. Staining and gene tests then named the parasite types.

About one bird in twenty carried the parasite, and a higher share of sellers, roughly one in eight, did too. Nearly all finds were the type C. parvum, which readily infects people. In two shops, birds and sellers were infected at the same time, hinting at direct passing between them. The authors recommend regular testing in pet shops as a guard for both trades.
pmc-13587514:
Pooneh Jebalbarezi and colleagues feed broiler chickens a natural germ-killing peptide to see if it can stand in for antibiotics. Farm antibiotics are falling from favor as resistance spreads, and peptides like CAP18, first found in rabbit white cells, kill bacteria by tearing their membranes. Their 2026 trial raised 480 day-old chicks on four diets: plain feed, feed with an antibiotic, or feed with CAP18 at two doses.

Growth, eating, and feed efficiency under CAP18 matched the plain and antibiotic groups. Gut health improved, with a friendlier balance of gut bacteria and, at the higher dose, a taller, shallower gut lining suited to soaking up food. Meat from peptide-fed birds resisted spoilage markers better and held more water after cooking than meat from the antibiotic group. Blood antibody levels also rose at the higher dose. The authors name the lower dose as enough for most gains.
pmc-13591214:
Aleena Amir Malik leads a large team pooling trials on two heart troubles that often strike together: atrial fibrillation, a chaotic heart rhythm, and heart failure with a weakened pump. The question was whether burning tiny spots inside the heart to fix rhythm, called catheter ablation, beats drug care. Their search gathered 13 studies with more than 130,000 patients whose pump strength was reduced or mildly reduced.

Ablation was linked to far fewer deaths overall and from heart causes, the pooled results show. Pump strength rose and a strain marker in blood fell. Hospital stays for heart causes, though, did not clearly drop. Malik and the team rate the proof as fair to strong, and call for more work on the mildly reduced group.
pmc-13592314:
Jialing Song leads a 2026 team building a noble metal free catalyst that turns nitric oxide, a pollutant gas, into ammonia with electricity. Their design wraps paired iron compounds, a carbide and a nitride, inside graphitic carbon shells. Each partner takes a distinct job at the two faced interface. The carbon skin eases gas flow past the water film that normally chokes the surface.

At a mild voltage the catalyst produced ammonia at a top tier rate with over 94 percent of charge going to the target. Carbide sites grip and wake the gas, while nitride sites rich in missing nitrogen atoms split water to supply reactive hydrogen. Song and the team offer the split labor design as a rule for cleaning exhaust while making a valued chemical.
pmc-13595014:
Setia and colleagues describe in 2026 an unusual rescue operation for acute mesenteric ischemia, a sudden cutoff of blood flow to the bowel that kills up to half its victims. They moved the bowel's main artery to a new connection when standard fixes were exhausted.

The patient, a 55-year-old woman, arrived with a blocked superior mesenteric artery and ischemic bowel on imaging. A retrograde stenting attempt through an open approach failed, and she was ineligible for the conventional operations. Surgeons therefore transposed the artery, sewing it end-to-side onto a healthy stretch of the lower aorta, a technique previously reported mainly for two rare compression syndromes. Her symptoms resolved completely, and scans at six weeks and at ten months showed the transposed artery open and working. The article details the operative steps for others facing the same dead end.
pmc-13595514:
Bushra Bibi and colleagues studied shame and low mood in TB patients in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. From June to December 2023, 349 patients from Peshawar and Haripur took a TB shame scale and a mood screen, with full mood scores for 159 who screened in. TB shame can put people off tests and pills at patient, crowd, and clinic levels.

Self-shame hit 64.8 percent and crowd-shame 49.9 percent, while low mood hit 45.6 percent of all patients. As either shame rose, low mood grew worse. The authors urge shame-cutting and mind care to be built into TB care, not tacked on as an extra, if patients are to stay in care and get well.
pmc-13595614:
Hani Atef and co-authors present Deep Aerenchyma, an AI pipeline that measures the air channels inside rice roots automatically, replacing slow hand tracing of root slices. These lacunae move oxygen through flooded roots. They shape both methane emissions from paddies and the plant's water flow. That makes them a breeding target. Yet they have been hard to phenotype at scale, as the 2026 report notes.

A vision transformer model learned from 1,760 annotated images gathered across countries, growth stages, and farming systems. It segmented root tissues and air spaces with high overlap against human markings, and its air-to-cortex ratios on a held-out set matched manual measurement almost exactly. Expert reviewers rated the machine's output at least as consistent as human annotation. Released as open software with an online demonstrator, the pipeline revealed reproducible differences across varieties, water regimes, and environments in six test cases.
pmc-13595714:
Danni Chi and co-authors interviewed sixteen male psychiatric nurses at a specialist hospital in China. The men described how they came to see themselves as professionals. Their field is female-dominated. It also carries a double stigma: men in nursing, and nursing in psychiatry. Their qualitative study drew out three themes from the men's career stories.

Entry was often pragmatic, followed by early shock before commitment settled in, a phase the authors call stumbling into commitment. Growth came through relationships with patients and teams, shifting the men from task completion toward judgment about prevention and de-escalation. Physical strength, expected of them in crises, became a source of pride when fused with restraint and relational care. Managers are advised to support early adaptation, safety, and mentorship, since identity formed slowly and unevenly and fatigue ran alongside the commitment.
pmc-13597514:
Qi Dai leads a thirteen-author team building an intelligent system that grades medical students' hands-on clinical skills without a human examiner in the room. Assessment of practical skills has long depended on manual observation. That approach is slow and variable. Their 2026 study uses contrastive learning to standardize the judgment. The technique teaches a model by comparing performances.

Validation showed the system could separate proficiency levels within specific surgical procedures. Under its best settings, scoring of one procedure reached about ninety-four percent accuracy, rising to about ninety-six percent when answers within one point counted as correct. The authors emphasize the package of a unified standard, a visible process, and objective scoring, with immediate feedback to trainees. They present the system as a way to make clinical training more rigorous and efficient at the same time.
pmc-13598114:
Rene Marquez-Franco and co-authors compared the wiring of three brain targets used for deep brain stimulation in treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder, using the personal brain scans of twenty-two patients treated in Cologne. Stimulation outcomes vary between centers partly because each target plugs into the brain's obsessive circuitry differently, and the team reconstructed each patient's fiber pathways.

The accumbens and capsule target showed the strongest structural links to fronto-limbic regions. Those regions include the orbitofrontal cortex, cingulate, and insula. The links match the affect, salience, default mode, and reward networks central to OCD. This was the target these patients actually received. The bundle and subthalamic targets carried their own distinct profiles. The authors argue that patient-specific connectomics could eventually guide target choice, matching the stimulation site to the network a given patient's symptoms run on rather than to habit.
pmc-13599114:
Nadeem Ashraf and colleagues asked whether hepatitis B drug therapy predicts outcomes after liver-cancer surgery. Liver cancer tied to this virus burdens health worldwide, and drugs may cut new cancers and returns after surgery. Their study followed 410 liver-cancer patients after liver surgery at one Wuhan hospital, tracking survival, tumour traits, and liver healing by drug use.

After strict screening, 93 patients showed smaller tumours, less tumour death, and better raw results, yet drug therapy no longer mattered once other factors were allowed for. Tumour death alone predicted worse survival, while heavy tiny-vessel spread, poor grading, and advanced stage drove outlook. Ashraf and colleagues conclude drug gains likely work through tumour biology.
pmc-13612614:
Samuli Helle and colleagues examined whether two overlapping crises shifted birth sex ratios in Finland between 2000 and 2024. Wars, disasters, and economic shocks have been linked to fewer male births, through sex-specific fetal loss or prenatal adjustment, and pandemic effects reported elsewhere have been mixed. The study used monthly census data covering the entire population: 1,355,037 live births and 4,096 stillbirths.

Bayesian time-series models found no evidence that COVID-19 changed the proportion of males among live births or stillbirths. An increased male share among live births appeared four months after Russia's attack on Ukraine, but the authors label that finding exploratory rather than confirmatory. Finland's sex ratios, read as a population-health indicator, thus showed marked resilience to double trouble.
pmc-13615014:
Seyed Mohammad Mahdi Moshirian Farahi and Jude Mary Cénat reviewed brain-scan evidence linking racism to brain change. Racial discrimination acts as a chronic stressor raising mental-illness risk, yet scan studies in racialised people were few and scattered. Their 2026 narrative review synthesised 19 neuroimaging studies across the lifespan in Black and other racialised people.

Discrimination tracked with stronger alarm-network links, weaker prefrontal links, frayed white matter, and thinning in cingulate cortex and hippocampus. These shifts tie to heightened vigilance, emotion dysregulation, and higher mental and physical health risk. The authors fault small, snapshot, low-diversity designs and call for longitudinal, multimodal, more diverse research.
pmc-13615314:
Kexin Liang, Simeon C. Calvert, and J. W. C. van Lint review in 2026 how much time drivers need to take back control from a partly self-driving car, and how much time the car should give them. In conditional automation the car drives itself until it reaches its limits, then hands over. Give too little time and the takeover is rushed and unsafe; give too much and the driver drifts out of attention.

Following standard review methods, the authors selected 100 articles and drew lessons from both earlier reviews and hands-on studies. They walk the full takeover sequence, from the alert to steady control, and sort what stretches or shrinks the time drivers need. Car makers can use the synthesis to set time budgets that fit real human limits across drivers and road scenes, not a single ideal number.
pmc-13615414:
Priya Sumithran and Louise A Baur published this 2026 commentary untangling the crowd of frameworks for defining obesity. It is written for practising clinicians. Body mass index still anchors monitoring, but recent treatment advances have spawned competing systems. Clinicians are left unsure which applies when. The authors compare three: from the Lancet Commission on Clinical Obesity, the European Association for the Study of Obesity, and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology's 2025 algorithm.

Despite separate origins, the systems agree. All hold that BMI alone is insufficient. All advise confirming excess fat with a body measurement, to catch abdominal fat below the BMI cut-off. All urge assessment of its impact and tailored, holistic care focused on complications rather than weight alone. Left unresolved are the best meanings of the condition, fair access to treatment, and treatment targets. The authors present the systems as partners, not rivals.
pmc-13616414:
Hongjie Hu leads a team testing a compound extract of the herb Abrus cantoniensis against liver damage from aflatoxin B1, a potent poison made by moulds on stored food. The herb appears in traditional liver-protecting formulas, yet proof for this toxin was missing. Computer network analysis and docking pointed to a major growth-and-survival pathway, PI3K-AKT, as the extract's likely route, and lab plus animal work then tested the call.

In poisoned mice the extract eased damage in both liver and gut. It adjusted two immune signalling routes. It also reshaped gut microbes toward groups that make more butyrate. Butyrate is a fatty acid that feeds the gut wall. In cell tests it switched the predicted pathway on. Food-poison defence that runs through both liver signals and gut microbes matches how the body actually meets this toxin.
pmc-13617114:
Yanan Zhao and four colleagues link round-the-clock activity habits with eyesight in middle school students in Tianjin, China. They recruited one thousand two hundred twelve students from five districts using stratified cluster sampling. Each student wore an accelerometer for seven straight days, so sitting, light activity, vigorous activity, and sleep were measured rather than guessed, and eye exams recorded uncorrected visual acuity.

Nearly three quarters of the students were nearsighted, with rates rising by grade and running higher in girls. Students sat for over nine hours a day on average, while vigorous activity and sleep both fell short of guidelines. Statistical selection linked more vigorous activity and longer sleep with better acuity, and more sitting and light activity with worse acuity. The authors say daily schedules, not single habits, should guide myopia prevention in schools.
pmc-13617214:
Shiqi Wang and thirteen colleagues develop a label-free imaging method that reads tumor metabolism to diagnose and grade glioma, the most aggressive common brain tumor. Standard diagnosis relies on tissue pathology, which shows cell shape but not the living metabolic landscape. Their system uses two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging, which times how long molecules glow after laser pulses, mapped through phasor analysis.

The method revealed distinct hotspots rich in reduced flavin adenine dinucleotide, a metabolic molecule, and those niches lined up closely with deposits of collagen IV in the tumor surroundings. Imaging across four glioma subtypes separated tissue regions by metabolic pattern. Tracking tumors over time in a mouse model then showed the signatures could distinguish levels of malignancy. The authors propose the hotspots as an optical biomarker that could one day guide surgery in real time.
pmc-13619014:
Stephen P. Becker led a 2026 study testing short sleep questionnaires for early adolescents with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, known as ADHD. Sleep problems are common in this age group and in ADHD, yet few brief tools have been thoroughly checked for both child and parent reports. The team gave PROMIS Pediatric Sleep Disturbance and Sleep-Related Impairment short forms to 341 children aged ten to twelve, about half with ADHD, along with measures of ADHD, anxiety, and depression symptoms.

Both forms showed strong internal consistency and reasonable links to related measures, with partial support for telling sleep problems apart from other symptoms. Children with ADHD scored higher on both disturbance and daytime impairment than peers, and most gaps held after excluding children taking stimulants. Daytime impairment linked especially strongly and uniquely to depression.
pmc-13619714:
Derek K Afflu and five colleagues report emergency heart-lung machine support for a Jehovah's Witness in cardiogenic shock, the state where the heart cannot pump enough blood. Members of that faith refuse transfusions, which makes extracorporeal membrane oxygenation risky because the circuits usually cost blood. Their patient, a sixty-one-year-old man with kidney failure and a replaced aortic valve, arrived with worsening breathlessness and heart failure signs.

The team used the machine as part of resuscitation while following a bloodless protocol built on careful tube placement and tight circuit management. He was weaned off support and discharged without receiving any blood products. The authors set out the tactics they used to limit blood loss and support the body's own blood production. Their point is that temporary mechanical support can fit bloodless care even in an emergency, adding to a small but growing set of such cases.
pmc-13621514:
Lotte Habermann-Horstmeier and Lukas M Horstmeier ask where muscle symptoms sit inside the symptom web of ME/CFS, the chronic illness also called myalgic encephalomyelitis. Muscle problems rank among its most disabling features, yet their relation to the rest of the illness is unclear. The pair analyzed registry data from 736 people with physician-diagnosed ME/CFS, testing them against fourteen symptom domains.

Breathing problems, flu-like symptoms, and temperature-regulation trouble each independently predicted muscle problems, with cardiovascular symptoms joining in a trimmed model. Deeper digging found muscle trouble strongly entangled with those same body-system symptoms, and factor analysis fit them onto one hidden factor of physiological dysregulation. Separate looks by sex hinted women's muscle problems tied to more domains than men's, though the formal interaction test stayed inconclusive. Menopause-age groupings shifted the patterns again. The authors treat the subgroup findings as exploratory signposts for follow-up.
pmc-13621614:
Agnese Comelli led a team investigating a drug-resistant Klebsiella outbreak in a newborn intensive care unit in Bangui, Central African Republic. The bacterium produced enzymes that defeat many standard antibiotics, and bloodstream infections in newborns can kill quickly. Working in a health-ministry hospital supported by Médecins Sans Frontières, the team compared forty-four infected newborns with one hundred fifty-three controls from late 2023 into early 2024.

Cases died at three and a half times the control rate, and over half fell ill within three days. Maternal risk factors for newborn infection stood out as the strongest predictor. The unit ran above full occupancy when the outbreak began, and early infection-control practice scored poorly. A package of practical measures within a month halted spread, and the outbreak ended in about two months. The authors stress microbiology access and infection control as lifesaving infrastructure in low-income settings.
pmc-13624414:
Purnendu Kumar Sharma and colleagues present a lab platform that keeps real human skin alive and working for up to four weeks. Skin from twenty donors supplied 199 samples, and gene activity was tracked over time. The tissue kept its layered structure and its mix of skin, support, and immune programs after a short early settling phase.

With the platform steady, the team drove lasting swelling with two immune signals for three weeks and found that a Janus kinase blocker drug calmed most of that response. Skin from older donors reacted to a senescence-targeting treatment by week three. Ultraviolet light caused stress damage that sunscreen eased, showing the system suits drug and product testing alike.
pmc-13624514:
Grass and colleagues re-analysed in 2026 a Swedish trial of diabetes testing in pregnancy to test how growth charts change its message. Large for gestational age means a newborn weighing above the top tenth for its stage. The trial, CDC4G, covered 47,080 pregnancies at eight delivery units in 2018.

With the Swedish chart, the share of large babies fell clearly after the criteria switch. With the international chart, that fall was not seen in the main group. Severe largeness, above the top three percent, changed only under some charts and some subgroups. In the subgroup whose diagnosis changed under the new criteria, two charts showed fewer large babies and one did not. The authors warn that a trial's verdict can hinge on which chart defines the outcome.
pmc-13624814:
Takayuki Yoshida and colleagues tested an ultrasound-guided obturator canal approach for hip-region nerve blocks in cadavers. Standard injections below the pectineus muscle spread unevenly into the obturator canal, risking patchy blockade. Their cadaver study placed needle tips directly in the canal under ultrasound in six leg specimens from four donors, injecting 5 millilitres of blue dye.

Dye reached the pelvic cavity via the canal in all six specimens, matching the predicted spread. The authors judge 5 millilitres enough to fill the canal, supporting a more reliable block. Yoshida and colleagues present the approach as anatomically feasible, pending clinical trials.
pmc-13627214:
Jean-François Dufour and Annalisa Berzigotti, publishing in 2026, review the non-drug treatment of fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction, known as MASLD. The disease grows from excess calories, poor-quality food rich in processed items, sugar, and red meat, plus sitting and broken sleep. Lifestyle change attacks those roots at once, which is why its benefits spill past the liver into heart and metabolic health generally.

Weight loss stays the cornerstone, and even modest loss helps, with or without obesity at the start. Exercise adds its own protection, lowering the odds of liver fat, scarring, and liver cancer in step with dose, partly apart from the scale. The hard part is keeping change alive for years, so the authors call for team support and markers that personalize advice.
pmc-13627714:
Manuel Kuhn leads a team checking whether a computer reading doctors' notes can recover the dimensions of mental illness. Diagnoses sort patients into boxes, while the Research Domain Criteria framework scores two brain systems instead: positive valence, tied to reward, and negative valence, tied to threat. The team extracted those scores with language software from the notes of 358 psychiatric patients at McLean Hospital and set them against standard mood questionnaires.

Deeper depression and stronger loss of pleasure each tracked with lower positive and higher negative scores, just as theory predicts. Anxiety tracked only the negative system, again matching the framework. The match between machine-read notes and trusted scales, the authors argue, validates note mining as a window on symptom dimensions that charts already contain but diagnoses hide.
pmc-13629114:
Ismael Fernández-Fernández and four colleagues measured how able Spain's vascular access nurses feel at using research proof in daily practice. Their 2026 study surveyed 51 of these nurses across the land. It then followed up with deep interviews.

The nurses rated themselves highly on knowledge and on grasp of their local setting. Knowledge rose together with trust in their own skill. Scores dipped for workplace factors. Weak systems and little formal training hold back lasting change. Those interviewed told of learning by doing. They also bent their plans to each setting. The authors urge structured training in this field. They also urge formal backing for the specialist role. Drive alone should not be wasted.
pmc-13630214:
Leyan Zhang and five colleagues studied how to fix lighting in corridor-style teaching buildings in central China. Classrooms lit from one side often sit dim, above all on the north face. Lighting also eats campus energy. The team took one such building at Hunan University of Technology as their case. They blended on-site measures with daylight simulation.

Four mixed patterns joined daylight and electric light at varied densities. A targeted layout joined them in testing. The tests scored brightness, evenness, and hours at target light levels. Every pattern improved daylight use a lot across the scores. Reliance on electric light during teaching hours fell. The authors offer the framework as guidance for like buildings. Corridor-style schools under similar climates can use it.
pmc-13630414:
Ramesh Singh and Ketul C Popat published this 2026 study engineering a surface for titanium orthopaedic implants, combining titania nanotubes with a two-layer peptide coating to promote bone growth and resist infection. Bare titanium integrates slowly and can harbour bacteria. The team grew nanotube arrays on the metal, anchored a dipeptide, Fmoc-FF, onto them. They then deposited a second layer of the self-assembling FF peptide that clings through stacking and hydrogen bonds to the anchored base.

The coating stayed in place for 28 days in buffer, more stable than peptide on titanium or nanotubes alone. The nanotubes plus peptide cues created a matrix-like setting where stem cells adhered, grew and differentiated toward bone. The self-assembling peptide layer reduced bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation compared with unmodified titanium. The authors present the dual-mode functionalisation as a strategy for implants that integrate faster and infect less.
pmc-13630814:
Marius Tacke and six colleagues paired two AI agents to write models of how materials deform. The models must respect the laws of physics. Building such models normally takes years of specialist work. Single language models can draft them quickly. Yet they sometimes produce equations that break basic physical laws.

In their system a Creator agent drafts a neural network model for a material. An Inspector agent audits it against nine physical constraints. It sends violations back for repair. The pair was tested on brain tissue, rubber, and pig skin with two model backbones. Adding the inspector raised the share of fully lawful models. The survivors matched or beat expert-built models. They held up even on loading patterns never seen in training. The authors pitch the split as a general trust upgrade.
pmc-13631514:
Dan Zhao led a 2027 paper introducing pIR, a small, scalable plasmid platform for non-viral DNA delivery that drops antibiotic resistance genes. Standard plasmid backbones rely on such genes for selection, raising regulatory and biosafety worries, while commercial antibiotic-free systems cost much and limit tinkering. The new platform uses an R6K gamma origin plus a Cre enzyme system in a bacterial host. The resistance gene is cut out when arabinose is added, leaving a vector that keeps replicating.

The team confirmed the strain by PCR, genome sequencing, and protein blotting, then showed the platform working in cell culture and in mice. A reporter plasmid performed in transfected cells and in mouse muscle after electroporation. A tumor-antigen version was tested in tumor-bearing mice, and a GLP-1 version raised blood hormone levels. The platform offers an open alternative to licensed systems, with animal proof across three uses.
pmc-13631814:
Alexandre Soares Ferreira Junior and six colleagues reviewed what is known about gut leakiness in patients who receive donor stem cell transplants. A transplant from another person can cure blood diseases, yet treatment also harms the gut lining. A leakier gut may let microbes and their products cross into the body. The authors searched the literature through December 2025 for every study that measured this leakiness in transplant patients.

Twenty-one studies covering more than eleven hundred patients used twenty-two different measurement methods. Tests using swallowed probe substances usually showed real changes over the transplant course. Blood-marker tests gave mixed and often unclear results. Conditioning treatment, diet, gut microbes, and immune response all predicted leakier guts. Links to later outcomes conflicted between studies, so the authors advise using several methods together in future work.
pmc-13633414:
Danijela Jovanovic and four colleagues describe a patient whose blood disorder was the first sign of hidden cancer. The disorder destroys red blood cells as they squeeze through tiny vessels, leaving fragments in the blood alongside a shortage of platelets. It usually points to two better-known conditions, yet widespread cancer can produce the same picture. Their patient was a previously healthy fifty-seven-year-old woman.

Standard treatment for the look-alike conditions failed to help her, and her lab pattern carried warning signs the team now highlights. The search uncovered metastatic signet-ring cell cancer of the digestive tract. A bone marrow examination gave early evidence of spread, shortening diagnosis. The authors lay out a practical way to separate cancer-driven cases from the look-alikes. Their core advice is to hunt for hidden cancer early when the pattern and poor treatment response line up.
pmc-13635214:
Haobo Zhang and four colleagues published this 2026 dataset of brain recordings made while people listened to Mandarin speech. Understanding how the brain handles a tonal language needs direct, detailed recordings, yet open data of this kind barely exist. Four patients who were awake during brain surgery listened to continuous spoken sentences. Electrode grids with up to two hundred fifty-six contacts lay on the brain surface and captured fast local activity, synchronized with the audio.

The release packages the recordings in standard formats that other labs can open directly. It includes processed signal layers, word and syllable alignments, tone and stress markings, speech sound measures, and maps of where each electrode sat on each person's brain. Mandarin makes a strong test case because pitch changes word meaning. The authors intend the resource to support fine-grained study of tone, syllable structure, and higher language patterns during natural listening.
pmc-13636114:
Byron Hyde wrote this 2026 commentary on a paradox in medicine: doctors are ethically obliged to disclose scientific uncertainty honestly, yet doing so often makes patients trust them less. Evidence-based medicine promised communication grounded in what studies show. Meanwhile the replication crisis exposed how shaky that evidence can be; in cancer research, Hyde notes, only about 40 percent of studies could be replicated in the checks he cites.

Patients, he argues, can read candour about doubt as incompetence rather than integrity. His remedies work on two levels. Systemically, he calls for school reform to raise public science literacy, so uncertainty is understood as normal science. In the clinic today, he suggests hedging language and realistic expectations about what treatment can achieve. None of it works, he warns, without compassionate doctor-patient relationships underneath. Preserving that human bond matters even more as commercial pressures and artificial intelligence reshape medicine, he concludes.
pmc-13639014:
Sneha Mantri and thirty colleagues report the proceedings of a 2026 think tank on preventing Parkinson's disease before it starts. Specialists from neurology, farming, public health, policy, and patient groups met in Gainesville, Florida, in November 2025 for the first meeting of its kind.

The group named eight priorities, summed up as the eight C's, ranging from counting cases accurately to building coalitions and securing lasting funding. Their position statement urges action for people at risk, the clinicians who advise them, and policymakers. The document frames prevention as a shared public task rather than a clinic-only concern.
pmc-13641014:
Arkaprabha Giri and eleven colleagues present a materials study on upgrading a commercial resin used to capture carbon dioxide straight from air. The resin's amine groups do the capturing, but it holds too few of them and degrades in oxygen over time.

The team grew extra amine-rich chains directly on the resin by polymerizing a small ring compound called azetidine in place. The treated resin captured over forty percent more carbon dioxide than the original under dry air conditions and held up through 150 capture-release cycles under simulated exhaust gas. The authors present the one-step upgrade as scalable for direct air capture plants.
pmc-13642114:
Ruiqi Liu and colleagues report a photonics design study, published in 2026. It solves a size-versus-tolerance trade-off in vertical couplers. These couplers link lasers to silicon chips. Smaller couplers are usually ruined by tiny alignment errors. The team combined repeated computer optimisation with a physics-guided layout. Control points are concentrated where the light waves nearly match in phase.

Their coupler transfers just over ninety-eight percent of the light. Its footprint is only twenty micrometres long. It kept over eighty percent efficiency under misalignments. Waveguide width errors far larger than usual were also tolerated. The authors call this the highest tolerance per unit length yet reported for this coupler type.
pmc-13645214:
Brandon Dulisse and four colleagues present a study of cryptocurrency mixers, services that pool and redistribute coins to hide transaction trails, in real money laundering cases. Technical and legal debates had said little about how mixers work inside actual criminal schemes.

Examining thirty-two court cases, the team found activity concentrated in few hands: five mixers linked to over six billion dollars in illicit funds. Non-custodial mixers moved most total volume, while centralized ones moved most crime-linked funds. Actor roles fell into overseers, personal users, and enablers. Takedowns prompted quick substitution, so the authors urge proactive, internationally coordinated responses.
pmc-13645614:
Olfa Smaoui and six colleagues report a fatal case of widespread Aspergillus flavus infection in a fifty-four-year-old man with no known immune weakness. The fungus attacked his spine, causing an infection of the vertebrae and nearby discs. He arrived with five months of worsening back pain and weakness in both legs. Scans showed abscesses around the spine, and early tissue tests wrongly pointed to tuberculosis.

Fungal cultures and special stains later identified the true cause, and drug tests showed which antifungal medicine still worked against it. Further checks suggested the infection had also reached his lungs and a sinus cavity. His immune tests came back normal, with no clear reason for his vulnerability. Even with targeted antifungal therapy, his condition kept worsening. The authors warn that this fungus can mimic tuberculosis and urge early fungal testing in similar spine cases.
pmc-13647214:
Husni Farah and seven colleagues review how chemicals made by gut microbes steer the production of blood cells in the bone marrow. The marrow's stem cells answer to a stream of microbe products: short-chain fatty acids from fiber, tryptophan derivatives, bile acids, and a compound called TMAO. Each product works through distinct switches, from gene-tag editing to a receptor that senses aromatic chemicals to inflammation control centers. The review maps these routes one by one.

When the signaling goes wrong, the consequences reach anemia, blood and solid cancers, graft-versus-host disease after transplant, and heart disease. The authors gather the mechanistic evidence for each link. They close with treatment ideas that target the microbe-to-marrow conversation itself, such as adjusting diet, microbes, or the products between them. The review frames blood formation as partly a gut-driven process, which widens where doctors might intervene.
pmc-13648314:
Roman Stengelin argues in a 2026 essay that culture hides in plain sight throughout child development research, even in studies that never mention it. Developmental science claims a universal picture of childhood. Its evidence leans heavily on convenience samples from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies, a cluster the author calls the minority world. Those samples are rarely described as cultural, so their particular ways of growing up pass as typical.

The article first sketches the shared cultural makeup of those overrepresented communities, including variation within them. It then shows how that makeup shapes the questions asked, the methods chosen, the findings produced, and the theories built. A study run anywhere, the author insists, is a cultural endeavor. Researchers get a challenge to mark their samples, contextualize their claims, and stop generalizing one kind of childhood to all children.
pmc-13649514:
Lingyun Xu and Jing Wu built a triage tool that uses just three values from a routine blood count to flag patients with high monocyte levels who need fast blood specialist review. A high count is most often harmless, yet it can be an early sign of two serious blood diseases. Their tool was trained on a large United States care database.

The tool sorted risk well in training and in two outside checks, one a small Chinese cohort where all patients had marrow tests and one a huge intensive care dataset. High monocyte load paired with low platelet counts marked the risky pattern. At one test cut-off, the tool caught nearly all true cases. The authors stress it guides order of review, not diagnosis.
pmc-13649714:
Mingzhu Jin and six colleagues hunted for a drug target in the aging blood vessel lining of skin. Tissue aging reshapes vessel, immune, and support cells together, yet clear vessel states that drugs could hit were unknown. The team built a machine age clock from three public skin datasets, then checked its calls in 15 fresh skin samples.

Aged skin held a cluster of vessel support cells marked by a gene called MYO1B, with vessel cells sliding toward that state. A switch gene, ETS1, bound the marker's control zone and rose with age. A known diabetes drug bound that switch, calmed the slide, and in aged rats restored skin thickness while cutting age marks. The authors name the pair a hittable niche.
pmc-13650014:
Juan Wang and five colleagues review trial evidence on stopping antibiotics early in cancer patients who develop fever while their infection-fighting white cells are very low. Standard care keeps broad antibiotics running until cell counts recover, yet longer courses raise the risks of resistance, side effects, and gut infections. The review therefore asks whether stable patients can stop sooner.

Fifteen randomized trials with 1,692 participants were pooled. Stopping early cut antibiotic use by roughly three and a half days on average, with a larger saving in children than in adults. Deaths from any cause did not differ between the early-stop and continue groups, and new bloodstream infections, treatment failures, and returning fevers were also similar. The authors conclude that early stopping looks safe for stable patients without fever, while noting that bigger adult trials would firm up the finding.
pmc-13650614:
Dongzhe Li and two colleagues review how microbes and metabolism in bile may connect gallstones to gallbladder cancer. Most gallbladder cancers arise in organs scarred by stones and chronic inflammation, yet only a small minority of people with stones develop cancer. Local conditions in bile, on stone surfaces, and in the wall itself are therefore under suspicion.

The review sorts evidence by the material studied and the disease stage, from stone formation through chronic injury and precancerous change to established cancer. Salmonella is the most studied microbial candidate, though estimates swing with local carrier rates and detection methods. A metabolic product called TMAO reliably alters cholesterol handling and stone formation, while its cancer link rests on thinner cross-sectional and mouse data. The authors argue that paired samples of bile, stone, wall, and tumor from the same patients would finally separate cause from coincidence.
pmc-13651514:
Shantanu Mishra and seven colleagues edit single molecules atom by atom with the tip of a scanning probe microscope. Skeletal editing rewrites a molecule's core framework late in a synthesis, and the team had already shown that voltage pulses could delete oxygen from a seven-membered ring or shrink the ring itself.

Swapping the ring's oxygen for sulfur changed the outcome decisively: pulses on the sulfur version mainly cut the sulfur out, with little of the rearrangement seen before. The result shows that picking the heteroatom during molecular design steers which edit the tip performs. The authors argue that pairing tip-induced chemistry with deliberate heteroatom choice gives a powerful strategy for building elusive ring systems one molecule at a time. They imagine uses in drug discovery and materials design.
pmc-13659214:
Paola Emilia Ferrara led a 2026 systematic review of magnetotherapy for pelvic floor dysfunction, including stress urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse. Pelvic floor disorders erode quality of life and sexual function, and muscle training remains first-line care, yet adherence can falter and alternatives are sought. The team searched PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov under PRISMA guidance, registering the protocol prospectively, and kept six randomized controlled trials from 2009 to 2025 in adult women.

Magnetotherapy modalities varied, and controls received placebo, sham treatment, or conventional muscle training. Despite heterogeneous protocols and outcome measures, magnetotherapy appeared to reduce symptoms and improve quality of life across the trials. The authors present it as a promising non-invasive option that may improve adherence. Clinicians get a cautious endorsement: the signal favors magnetotherapy as an adjunct or alternative, but small, varied trials mean larger standardized studies should confirm the benefit.
pmc-2563014:
Meyer, Paarmann, D'Souza, and co-authors present the metagenomics RAST server, a public tool for analysing community DNA. Metagenomes are random samples of genomes from microbes living together in soil, water, or the gut. By 2008 the hard part had shifted from producing sequences to making sense of them.

Cheap, high-throughput sequencing flooded labs with data they could not annotate alone. The server automatically sorts sequences by evolutionary origin and by function. A shared public service let small teams study whole microbial communities without building their own computing pipelines.  Results return as tables and pictures that bench scientists can read directly.
pmc-3816614:
Scher, Sczesnak, Longman, and co-authors link growth of the gut germ Prevotella copri to higher risk of arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is a common systemic immune disease caused by a mix of genetic and outside factors. Animal models suggest gut bacteria help support the systemic immune response needed for joints to swell.

The team profiled gut microbes in patients and found Prevotella copri expanded in those at risk. That correlation points to the gut as a cause in joint disease. It supports trials of diet or microbe-targeted treatment to prevent arthritis.  The finding shifted attention from joints alone to the gut-joint axis overall.
pmc-4373114:
Nyaga, Arbyn, and Aerts presented Metaprop in 2014, a Stata command for meta-analysis of proportions. Meta-analysis has become an essential way to combine evidence from many similar studies. Proportions, such as the share of patients with a trait, need methods suited to binomial data.

Metaprop produces summary statistics and displays for this common task inside Stata, a package many health researchers already use. Accessible software matters, since a sound method helps no one if few can run it. Pooled proportions inform screening, diagnosis, and disease burden estimates. The command made a specialized analysis a routine option for clinical and population studies.
pmc-4877414:
Greenland, Senn, Rothman, and their co-authors wrote a guide in 2016 to misreadings of statistics. Misinterpretation and abuse of tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power have been criticized for decades, yet remain rampant. No simple reading of these concepts is at once intuitive, correct, and foolproof.

The guide works through the most common wrong readings and shows what each measure actually says. A P value, for instance, is not the probability that a claim is true. Clearer understanding would cut false claims across medicine and science. The paper is widely assigned to researchers who report trial and study results.
pmc-4934014:
Haeussler, Schönig, Eckert, and their co-authors evaluated scoring algorithms for CRISPR guide RNAs in 2016. The success of CRISPR/Cas9 editing depends on choosing the right guide RNA sequence. Various websites help with that choice, each using its own prediction algorithms.

It was unclear how far those predictions agreed with actual editing results. The team tested on-target and off-target scoring methods against measured activity. They then integrated the best findings into CRISPOR, a guide selection tool. Better scoring means fewer wasted edits and fewer unwanted cuts elsewhere in the genome. The evaluation gave CRISPR users an evidence base for picking guides.
pmc-5889714:
Miten Jain, Sergey Koren, Karen Miga, and many colleagues reported a human genome sequenced with nanopore reads in 2018. They used a pocket-sized device that pulls long DNA strands through tiny pores. The reads were far longer than those from older machines.

Long reads let the team assemble stretches that short reads cannot span, including some hard repeat regions. The work also showed direct detection of chemical marks on DNA. Gaps and errors remained, but the proof of principle was strong. The study marked a step toward cheap, portable genome sequencing outside big centers.
pmc-7263814:
Derek Chu and a large international team published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2020 on three simple barriers against the virus that causes COVID-19. The virus spreads mainly from person to person through close contact. The team gathered studies from health care settings and from everyday settings such as homes and public places.

They weighed the evidence on keeping physical distance, wearing face masks, and protecting the eyes. Their pooled results supported each measure, with larger distances and well fitted masks linked to lower transmission. At a time when no vaccine or cure existed, the review gave governments and hospitals a firm evidence base for rules that many people found burdensome but that slowed the spread.
pmc-7779014:
Jaina Mistry and co-authors described in 2021 the state of Pfam, a database that classifies proteins into families and domains. Sorting a protein into the right family is often the quickest way to guess its job. Since the database was last formally described, its thirty-third release alone added several hundred new families and improved many existing entries.

The article explains how families are built, how entries are refined, and how users can reach the data more easily. It also covers the website and tools that serve the classifications to the research community. Pfam's groupings are woven into countless other databases, so this update documents a piece of shared infrastructure that much of bioinformatics depends on.
pmc-9825514:
The UniProt Consortium reported in 2022 the enhancements behind the 2023 edition of UniProt, the universal protein knowledgebase. UniProt aims to give users a complete, high quality, freely accessible set of protein sequences, each annotated with what is known about its function. It is consulted by researchers in nearly every branch of the life sciences.

The article describes improvements to the data processing pipeline that imports and annotates sequences, and to the website through which users reach them. It also covers how the resource keeps pace with the flood of new sequences while holding its quality bar. These behind the scenes upgrades decide how quickly a newly discovered protein becomes usable knowledge.
podcast-dannyjones-4zE7TaV-m14:
Andrew Bustamante spent years as a CIA officer and now runs a business teaching tradecraft to civilians. On Danny Jones's podcast, he makes a case most guests on this show would reject. He argues that government secrets are often a good thing. Some secrecy, he says, protects people who would otherwise die.

Bustamante explains how classification decisions look from inside an agency, where the cost of a leak can be a source's life. Jones challenges him with the show's usual suspicion of hidden power. The friction makes the episode useful: a defender of secrecy arguing with a host whose brand is exposure. Listeners hear the strongest version of the state's case, from a man who lived it, and can weigh it against the whistleblowers heard elsewhere in this series.
podcast-dannyjones-Yw6hLi90B14:
Dr. David Cook joins Danny Jones to argue that fixing your eyes can raise how smart you feel and act. The episode title puts the claim plainly: better vision, better mind. Cook works on how the eyes feed the brain.

Cook explains how strain, poor tracking, and weak eye teamwork can drag down reading and focus. He lays out steps he says can train the eyes and free up the mind. Jones asks which parts rest on strong tests and which rest on his clinic work. Listeners who struggle with screens and print will find a new way to think about both.
poincare-science-method-maitland-1914:
Science and Method, in Maitland's 1914 translation, gathers Poincare's essays on how scientists actually think. He turns from finished proofs to the messy work that comes before them. Chance, invention, and habit all get close attention.

Poincare tells how new math often arrives whole in the mind after rest, as if worked out below awareness. He also weighs chance in physics and the early claims of relativity with care. Few books show the creative side of science so honestly, or with such light touch. He treats his own sudden insights as data, not as private magic. Readers meet a great mind watching itself at work.
pope-rape-of-lock-1714:
Alexander Pope wrote The Rape of the Lock after a real quarrel between two families. A young lord had snipped a lock of hair from a lady, and both houses fell out. Pope hoped a comic poem might laugh them back together. A short version appeared in 1712, and the fuller five-canto poem in 1714.

Pope treats Belinda's stolen lock as an epic war, complete with guardian sylphs and a card game played like a battle. The poem even descends into the gloomy Cave of Spleen. The satire mocks fashionable London while admiring Belinda's glittering world. Every couplet is polished to a shine. The poem is widely called the finest mock-epic in English.
procopius-wars-persian-dewing-1914:
Procopius of Caesarea served on the staff of Belisarius, the great general of the emperor Justinian, and wrote the history of his wars. H. B. Dewing translated the work for the Loeb series, and the first volume, from 1914, covers the Persian War in books one and two. Procopius writes as a witness with a classic historian's training.

Rome and Persia clash over the Caucasus passes, Armenia, and the desert frontier towns. Sieges, embassies, plagues of locusts, and the sack of Antioch fill the tale. Procopius praises and blames with a cool, sly hand. His books are the chief source for the wars of Justinian's age. The Greek style hides sharp judgments under smooth praise.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
London's comic weekly Punch began its number of January 14, 1920, with Charivaria, its column of short jokes on the week's news. Volume 158 was then running, and Britain was settling into the first full year of peace after the Great War.

Early jokes report that the Premier had grown fond of a white terrier puppy brought from Colwyn Bay, and doubt that Lloyd George taught it to chase its own tail. Other items mock a man who summoned his neighbour for calling him an O.B.E., praise the Scots kilt as healthy dress for boys, and welcome a road surface that does not harm fish.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-146:
Charivaria fronts Punch, volume 146, for January 14, 1914, with short jokes on the Chancellor abroad, Balkan arms, and a society wedding. The new year found Europe arming and the column in its usual dry temper.

The Chancellor, in North Africa, is said to be studying camels to learn the nature of the last straw. Turkey's purchase of the dreadnought Rio de Janeiro for over two million pounds is judged safe, since no one risks so costly a ship in war. A coal king's daughter married Lord Redesdale's son on a snowy day, and Lloyd George's suffragette guards stay in place.

Punch, volume 146, for January 21, 1914, prints a cartoon on earthquakes and golf before its Charivaria column. Two players find the links poor; the reply is that even earthquakes have their use, since one would make better golf.

The column then reports Major-General Leonard Wood's finding that the American army is practically unarmed. He calls for over a million pounds of guns. The peace party, the column jokes, accepts an army so long as it stays unarmed. Orange women win at Drury Lane, and Zabern is to be renamed Säbeln after a victory in Alsace.

Punch opens volume 146 on January 7, 1914, with a cartoon calling the monarch of the glen a new land-seer. A poem follows, Amende Déshonorable, in which a man keeps a hard New Year watch with his own conscience.

Heavily the night drags; he calls himself slack, weak, and foolish by choice, swears that next year he will be energetic, virtuous, and kind, then glances at the clock. It is ten past midnight, the year is already old, and he bravely resolves to begin next year instead. Readers get the resolutions season in one honest confession.
raleigh-history-of-the-world-1614:
Walter Raleigh wrote The Historie of the World in the Tower of London, where he sat as a prisoner of King James. The huge work of 1614 begins with the Creation and runs through the rise and fall of empires to Rome. Raleigh, once the queen's favorite and a sea captain, now had only books, time, and a fallen name.

He weighs kings and nations on the scales of fortune and God's judgment, in rolling, stately prose. The history stops far short of his own age, yet his age read its own fears in it. It was the Jacobean age's great universal history, and its author's fate hangs over every page. Few books join learning and doom so tightly.
reuchlin-de-verbo-mirifico-1514:
Johannes Reuchlin, the German humanist, wrote De Verbo Mirifico, On the Wonder-Working Word, in 1494, and this Tübingen printing dates to 1514. The dialogue is the founding work of Christian Kabbalah, and it is in Latin. Reuchlin, the best Christian Hebraist of his age, stages a talk among a Jew, a pagan philosopher, and a Christian on the power hidden in names.

The speakers hunt for the one name that works wonders. They pass from the names of God in Hebrew to the name of Jesus, read as a five-letter key. Reuchlin paid for his defense of Jewish books with years of trial by the church courts. The dialogue shows the Renaissance mind at its boldest.
robert-louis-stevenson-pg3814:
E. Blantyre Simpson wrote this life of Robert Louis Stevenson as number two of the Spirit of the Age series, for John W. Luce of Boston and London in 1906. The book's two heads, printed at the front, are Stevenson's Apprenticeship and Across the Seas. A series note promises a set of little books in uniform dress.

Four pictures are listed. Stevenson appears as advocate in 1875 for the frontispiece, and as an Edinburgh student in another plate. The Teller of Tales shows him in his prime as a story writer. A portrait painted by Count Nerli in Samoa in 1892, reproduced by Mrs. Turnbull's leave, closes the life in his last home.
roman-britain-in-1914:
Professor F. Haverfield reported on Roman Britain in 1914 for the British Academy, in its Supplemental Papers, number three. Humphrey Milford published the paper at London in 1915 for the Academy. A plate of pottery stamps and stamped ware from Holt, described in detail, opens the record.

His contents give a retrospect of finds made in 1914, place by place. Raedykes near Stonehaven, the Wall of Pius, and Traprain Law lead the Scottish sites. Chesterholm, Corbridge, Ambleside's fort at Borrans, Ribchester, and Richborough follow. A second list runs from Wroxeter and Lincoln to London, country houses and farms, Lowbury, Beachy Head, and Parc-y-Meirch in North Wales.
royce-war-insurance-1914:
War and Insurance, published in 1914, collects Royce's essays on the two subjects of its title, written as Europe went to war. The pairing is deliberate: war is loyalty organized for destruction, insurance is loyalty organized for protection, and Royce studies both as social inventions.

He argues that insurance, mutual loyalty made concrete in actuarial form, shows how the economic machinery of trust might one day replace the machinery of battle. The essays are practical, humane, and characteristically hopeful. They show Royce applying his philosophy of loyalty to the most urgent question of his final years.
russell-knowledge-external-world-1914:
Bertrand Russell gave Our Knowledge of the External World as his Lowell Lectures in 1914. The book argues that the physical world can be built logically from sense-data. What we directly sense are colors, sounds, and touches. Tables and stars, Russell claims, are constructions out of such data and their relations.

This method, he hoped, would replace loose inference with exact construction. He applies it to space, time, matter, and other minds. The lectures made his analytic method famous with students. They shaped the philosophy of logical atomism that followed. The book is still a clear entry into Russell's early thought.
sanger-family-limitation-1914:
Margaret H. Sanger issued Family Limitation in a revised sixth edition dated 1917. In a brief opening note she says working readers already grasp why such guidance matters, so she offers no long defense. Her aim is practical help drawn from French and Dutch doctors she rates highly, put into plain English that any reader can follow.

Sanger also explains what she leaves out. She skips several devices she has not seen used well enough to endorse with confidence. The methods she does describe, she argues, can keep a woman from conceiving when she does not want a child. She closes the note in blunt terms, warning that careless habits by either partner can defeat any method she gives.
savigny-vom-beruf-1814:
Savigny's pamphlet On the Vocation of Our Age for Legislation and Legal Science appeared in German in 1814. It answered a call by the jurist Thibaut for Germany to adopt one civil code at once, on the French model. Savigny, then a young Berlin professor, said no, and his no changed legal history.

He argues that law grows from a people's spirit and history, like language, and cannot be manufactured by a drafting committee. Germany, he claims, lacks the shared legal science a good code would need, so a code now would freeze error into law. The pamphlet launched the historical school and delayed German codification for most of the century. It is often called the most consequential legal pamphlet ever written. Its argument still echoes whenever reformers ask whether law should be made or grown.
selected-speeches-on-british-foreign-pol:
Edgar R. Jones, a Member of Parliament, edited this set of speeches on British foreign policy from 1738 to 1914. The World's Classics first issued the volume in 1914. Speakers range from the elder Pitt, Earl of Chatham, through Sheridan, Canning, Peel, and Palmerston.

Each speech ties to a crisis: Spain in 1738, the partition of Poland, peace talks with France, and the Polish question in 1848. House and chamber dates head each entry. Students of politics can trace how British leaders argued war, peace, and honor across nearly two hundred years of debate in both houses at Westminster.
shaftesbury-second-characters-1914:
Anthony Ashley Cooper, third Earl of Shaftesbury, left these writings on art at his death in 1713, and they stayed in draft for two centuries. Benjamin Rand edited them as Second Characters in 1914, a sequel in spirit to Shaftesbury's famed Characteristics. The subtitle, The Language of Forms, names his theme: how shapes speak.

Treatises and notes take up painting, sculpture, gardens, buildings, and the rules of taste. Shaftesbury held that beauty and moral sense spring from one root, and that good art shows order the mind can feel. His remarks helped set the terms for British writing on art through the 1700s and still reward slow reading.
shiva-samhita-vasu-1914:
The Shiva Samhita is an old Sanskrit text on Hatha Yoga. Rai Bahadur Srisa Chandra Vasu gave it English dress in 1914. The print holds the Sanskrit text with the new dress at hand. Shiva speaks the teach as a talk to his wife Parvati.

Breath rules, seats, seals, and deep thought fill the five parts. The text maps the fine nerves and winds of the hid body. It tells how the yogi may wake the coiled force at the spine's base. The book is a chief text for the study of yoga and Tantra.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5014:
James Monroe gives eight yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from December 12, 1817, to December 7, 1824. Three stars part each address from the next. The first claims a rare cause for cheer. At no time has the country stood in so glad a state. The earth's fruits have filled it with plenty. A wide and gainful trade has swelled its income. The public credit stands at a rare height.

Works of defense move on under a well-laid plan. The free government grows stronger each day, Monroe adds. It rests on the people's gain and love. Local jealousies give way to wider views of policy. He then reports a deal on the Lakes. His predecessor began that deal with Britain. It cuts the naval force both lands keep there. Set terms now bind each side on the matter. Neither party may keep more force than the pact allows.
stein-tender-buttons-1914:
Tender Buttons, published in 1914, is Stein's most famous experiment: prose poems on objects, food, and rooms. She takes the plainest things, a carafe, a plate, roast beef, a chair, and describes them until language itself becomes the subject.

Her most quoted line calls a carafe a blind glass. Nothing is described the way a dictionary would describe it; instead, words are set side by side for their sound, weight, and surprise. Critics in 1914 mocked the book as nonsense. It is now read as verbal cubism, a landmark of modernist writing that changed what prose could do.
steiner-christianity-mystical-fact-1914:
Rudolf Steiner, the Austrian thinker who founded Anthroposophy, wrote Christianity as Mystical Fact in his Theosophical years. This English edition appeared in 1914. The book reads the Gospels as mystery wisdom, the fruit of ancient initiation rites.

Steiner argues that the writers of the Gospels spoke in the language of the mysteries, veiling deep truths in story. John's Gospel, in his reading, records an initiation: the raising of Lazarus as a waking from temple sleep.
